title: It Gets Worse review – Leo Reich is a rare star and the future of TV comedy | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The hot comic has made Fresh Meat for generation Z with this London sitcom. Produced by A24 and guest starring Andrew Scott, it is profound and properly funny – even if you’re easily triggered by houseshare horrors
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: The hot comic has made Fresh Meat for generation Z with this London sitcom. Produced by A24 and guest starring Andrew Scott, it is profound and properly funny – even if you’re easily triggered by houseshare horrors
Content: Domestic bliss … Olive Gray as Sam, Emily Fairn as Abi and Leo Reich as Ethan in It Gets Worse.Photograph: Ana Blumenkron/A24 FilmsView image in fullscreenDomestic bliss … Olive Gray as Sam, Emily Fairn as Abi and Leo Reich as Ethan in It Gets Worse.Photograph: Ana Blumenkron/A24 FilmsTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewIt Gets Worse review – Leo Reich is a rare star and the future of TV comedyThe hot comic has made Fresh Meat for generation Z with this London sitcom. Produced by A24 and guest starring Andrew Scott, it is profound and properly funny – even if you’re easily triggered by houseshare horrorsHannah J DaviesThu 22 Oct 2026 17.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 17.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn his 2023 standup special Literally Who Cares?!, Leo Reich bemoaned the fact that his life wasn’t more like aTV comedy. “All the sitcoms I watched as a teenager really made me imagine that being in my early 20s would involve a lot more navigating the dating scene in the big city,” he groaned. “And a lot less Googling the words ‘death toll’.” Reich was playing a caricature of a self-absorbed zoomer, who had taken up smoking during the pandemic because “some part of me decided it might be worth cutting 20 years off my life”. Behind this performance there was, of course, a rather big dollop of truth: life for gen Z has – for the most part – been less sitcom, more doom-filled rolling news bulletin.Reich – now 28 – is a rare comic to land an HBO special, and now an A24/Channel 4 series, putting him in the ideal position to redress the balance with his very own sitcom. Like HBO’s I Love LA (spiritually gen Z, if written by a millennial, Rachel Sennott), it juxtaposes grossness with aspiration. And like Girls before it, it is helmed by a perfectly un-self-aware protagonist, Ethan (Reich), whom – we are told at the outset – has had “one of the easiest lives in recorded human history”. There are hints of Fresh Meat, too, and traces of Reich’s comedy hero Simon Amstell in its dry neuroticism and Jewish-themed LOLs. Sometimes, it verges on the satirical – as when Andrew Scott cameos as a hookup who offers Ethan free therapy as foreplay. (Ethan tempers his complaints by saying that at least he hasn’t “lived through Aids” – Scott’s character, Brian, snaps back: “How old do you think I am?!”)As well as Ethan, we follow his uni pals Sam (Olive Gray) and Abi (Emily Fairn), who have been living with him in a London houseshare. They’re all moving out and need their deposits back, except Ethan has somehow made a ginormous hole in the wall with a drill, and doesn’t seem fussed about fixing it. As someone who has lived in more houseshares than I can remember, this feels particularly triggering. Reich might have been trying to shock the audience with lines like “my last therapist rimmed me”, but seeing someone play fast and loose with their household’s finances is more likely to solicit an emotional response from Generation Rent. Despite being chronically unemployed, Ethan will be fine, his friends say, because he has his parents’ house to go back to. Except that he doesn’t want to go home, so decides to inflict himself on an ex (as moving home, he reckons, would mean “[paying] rent in bad vibes and homophobia”).Meanwhile, Sam – artsy and queer like Ethan – ends up in an anarchist warehouse with a shared Mubi account, while Abi – northern, conformist, seemingly hiding all kinds of stress behind her rictus grin – moves in with her normie boyfriend Tom (Sean Delaney), and the cracks between the friends begin to deepen. “You want to pretend like you’re an adult!” Sam snaps at Abi. “Better than pretending I’m a child,” says Abi. Sick burn.It Gets Worse is, in many ways, a classic sitcom about surviving your 20s, complete with intensely awkward sex scenes (“Pull out!” “I’m not even in!”) And yet there’s a lot more going on here. Zadie Smith – at first inexplicably; later somewhat explicably – is our narrator. As well as Scott, Lena Dunham makes an appearance as the horrifying girlboss CEO of the data-mining startup where Abi works, and “fellow badass white woman with zero fucks left to give”. Amelia Dimoldenberg pops up as a university frequaintance who sparks Abi’s jealousy. Every episode is named after the characters it features, except when they aren’t (see: a chapter set at a funeral with the Auden-parodying title “Stop all the Cocks”). There’s an episode about a rather sexless sex party, which ends up feeling like a plot device for more beef between the characters, while references to “incel” culture, Andrew Tate and ChatGPT seem more like period-appropriate window-dressing than anything deeper.But, gladly, It Gets Worse is truly funny, propelled along by Reich’s zinger-filled, often profound script. The cast are solid, too, not least Vicki Pepperdine as Ethan’s highly-strung mum, plotting a move from the London suburbs to the Kent countryside because “almost everyone we know has been stabbed”. At the end of the second episode, Tom inadvertently calls Ethan a flop, to which he says: “We’re too young to be failures – in 10 years, then we’ll have failed.” In 10 years, Reich will probably be running British television – and, you imagine, breathing a sigh of relief to have his 20s far behind him.It Gets Worse is on Channel 4.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionTV comedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform snowflake Zia Yusuf demands safe space from ITV’s racism hunters | John Crace | The Guardian
description: How can it be right that undercover reporters failed to ask permission to expose party’s racist and misogynist views?
Author: John Crace
Headline: How can it be right that undercover reporters failed to ask permission to expose party’s racist and misogynist views?
Content: Zia Yusuf has also been posing as something he isn’t: the shadow home secretary.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAView image in fullscreenZia Yusuf has also been posing as something he isn’t: the shadow home secretary.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAReform UKReform snowflake Zia Yusuf demands safe space from ITV’s racism huntersJohn CraceHow can it be right that undercover reporters failed to ask permission to expose party’s racist and misogynist views?Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.56 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 14.03 EDTShareThe world has gone mad. What has happened to the country when you can’t even have a bit of racist and sexist banter with your mates at work? Time was when up to 20 million viewers would settle down to watch Till Death Us Do Part, for 30 minutes of laughter with Alf Garnett moaning about black people while calling his wife “a silly old moo”. That was a Britain that was worth living in. These days the thought police are everywhere. The wokerati from London, Oxford and Cambridge who are out to ruin everyone’s lives. What’s wrong with letting sleeping racists lie?Well, Zia Yusuf has had enough and he’s not going to take it any more. After the ITV exposéwhich revealed racist remarksby members of the party, he has posted a six-and-a-half-minute video on social media promising extreme retribution against the undercover journalists who posed as Reform-friendly.You have to love the irony. Because for the past six months, Zia has been posing as something he isn’t: the shadow home secretary. Now he may be equally as half-witted as Chris Philp, but the last time I checked, they weren’t the same person. Maybe Zia has a crush on the Philpster. Longs for the gym bod and absence of brain. Zia isn’t even an MP. When the Gorton and Denton Reform association prefer the dislikable Matt Goodwin, you know how loathed you are.Hoping to add some gravitas by sitting in front of a union jack in a wood-panelled room, Zia prepares to address the nation. And it turns out that he’s not the slightest bit bothered that some Reform members are racists and misogynists – it was probably as much of a surprise to him as it was to the rest of us. What really seems to bother him is thatITVdidn’t ask permission to film colleagues being racist. Which is a bit like being annoyed that Pete Hegseth wanted to broadcast a live execution because it was being streamed on pay per view.Zia has clearly never heard of undercover public interest journalism. And he’s crushingly disappointed by the deception. He had imagined that ITV would have taken the trouble to personally write to him, asking permission to film people being racist. And he would have happily let them do so. Because then everyone would have known exactly what was going on. I mean, think of the possible consequences of not doing it this way. It might turn out that there were dozens of other undercover journalists in Reform. All just hoping to catch each other out. No one at Reform HQ might be who they say they are.There was no knowing where any of this could end. It was quite possible even that Robert Jenrick was a plant. That his defection from the Tory party had been a plot dreamed up by Kemi Badenoch. A long game to place one of the least trusted and least talented Conservative politicians at the heart of Reform.And it had worked brilliantly. Nigel Farage had taken the bait and had appointed Honest Bob as his so-called “shadow chancellor”, making Reform look more and more like a care home for unsuccessful Tories. Job done with Nige tanking in the polls. Some day in the future, Kemi would reward Jenrick with a peerage. The Conservative establishment looking after one another as usual. How things ought to be.First, though, Zia was promising retribution. He wasn’t just alleging that crimes had been committed by ITV. He was stating it as a fact. Which might get a little awkward for him. The most detailed crime was that ITV had directly affected the outcome of a council election in which Reform had lost one ward by 24 votes. The facts were this, apparently. ITV had paid their journalists to put a curse on the 200 leaflets they had been asked to distribute by Reform so that the people reading them voted for Labour and the Conservatives.Sometimes you wonder if a man can actually be this dim. At which point you have to consider if the whole video is a double bluff and that Zia is also a Tory stooge who has managed to embed himself at the heart of Reform. That his desire to deport women and children is just a front. Because first, the journalists weren’t being paid by ITV to canvass for Reform. They were being paid to be undercover journalists.And second, the idea that 200 leaflets could swing 24 voters is clearly absurd. Of the 200 leaflets it is likely that all 200 of them would have been put straight in the recycling. A leaflet changes the mind of about one person in 10,000. Leafleting is something parties do for their own benefit. To make them feel like they are doing something useful.Having got all this off his chest, Zia wanted to express his hurt. His disappointment. The psychological damage that had been done to Reform activists and workers in HQ. Men and women who had been entitled to believe they had been in a safe space, where racist outbursts would be well received and applauded. Only now they had been forced to consider the possibility that some people might find them offensive. How could that possibly be right?The violation had been so severe that Zia had been forced to issue a Reform Victim Support card for those most badly affected by the ITV investigation. Much like the yellow card that people with cancer get given. Find yourself on a crowded train full of foreigners and you just brandish the card and all black and brown people are obliged to leave the carriage and give you a seat. And if the police come across a dishevelled-looking man wearing a teal tie and babbling about how foreigners have ruined the country, they can call the hotline number on the back of the card and a Reform outreach worker will come and pick them up and take them to a refuge.Who would have guessed that the snowflake slayer in chief would turn out to be the biggest snowflake of all? Hiding in plain sight. “We will never give up,” Zia concluded. On day one of a Reform government, perhaps Nige would create safe spaces where people could be as abusive to foreigners and women as they liked. This was a Britain of which we could all be proud.Explore more on these topicsReform UKITVInvestigative journalismFar rightTelevisioncommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s all God’s creation’: farmers continue a ‘Jewishly inspired’ agrarian tradition | Judaism | The Guardian
description: In the US, a growing number of Jewish people are seeking purpose and community through farming
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In the US, a growing number of Jewish people are seeking purpose and community through farming
Content: Wendy Rhein at her farm in Tryon, North Carolina, on 4 October 2026. Rhein and her family incorporate their Jewish faith into their farming practices.Photograph: Mike BellemeView image in fullscreenWendy Rhein at her farm in Tryon, North Carolina, on 4 October 2026. Rhein and her family incorporate their Jewish faith into their farming practices.Photograph: Mike BellemeJudaism‘It’s all God’s creation’: farmers continue a ‘Jewishly inspired’ agrarian traditionIn the US, a growing number of Jewish people are seeking purpose and community through farmingAndrea CooperThu 22 Oct 2026 15.18 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 15.51 EDTShareWendy Rhein is trying to round up the sheep hanging out among the hazelnut and walnut trees of her Chutzpah Hollow farm in Tryon,North Carolina.“Hi, Brea. Come on down. I hear you,” Rhein calls to the bleating queen of the flock. If the Barbados black belly ewe moves, the rest will follow.Brea, a bottle-fed lamb named Hadassah and their flock mates bound down the hill when Rhein rustles a box of kosher tea biscuits. The small treat reveals something different about this farm. Rhein is remarkable for several reasons: she’s a female farmer in a male-dominated industry and a single mother who had no farming experience when she launched her farm at age 52. She’s also Jewish.View image in fullscreenWendy Rhein examines an injured sheep at her farm in Tryon, North Carolina.Rhein, who also works as vice-president of a faith-based advocacy organization, is part of a renewed interest among Jews in farming as an expression of their religion, culture or values. Shani Mink, co-founder of the Jewish Farmer Network, often hears “Jewish farmer – isn’t that an oxymoron?” Mink’s organization serves about 1,800 farmers, most of them first-generation agriculturalists, and offers conferences, classes and farm-to-table Shabbat dinners.There is no solid estimate of the number of Jewish farmers in the country; the US Department of Agriculture’s census of the farming workforce doesn’t collect data on religion. But as Mink points out: “Jews have been farmers from time immemorial. The Jewish tradition is an agrarian tradition” – evidenced by how many holidays, such as the autumn harvest celebration Sukkoth, are tied to the agricultural calendar.The Jewish AgriculturalSociety, chartered in 1900, helped people facing persecution in eastern Europe relocate to US farmland, where they could gain skills and independence. By 1933, more than100,000 Jewsearned some or all of their living from farming, according to Gary Moore, professor emeritus at North Carolina State University. But as the US population shifted away from agricultural work, many Jewish people moved into cities and suburbs. Some are returning to rural environments and family roots to farm, inspired by principles of their faith and building better food systems.View image in fullscreenWendy Rhein and her son Samuel vaccinate sheep at their farm.View image in fullscreenWendy Rhein on her farm.Rhein grew up in Detroit, the daughter of a man who was raised on a dairy farm he couldn’t wait to leave. In contrast, she loved the idea of raising livestock and being closer to her food sources; she challenged herself to prepare every ingredient she and her two sons consumed, down to the ketchup, while living in a high-rise with a kitchen “the size of a postage stamp” in Washington DC. When the pandemic hit, she started to search for land and research a new venture selling starter flocks of sheep.Her brother, who lives about 45 minutes away in Asheville, showed her properties for sale over FaceTime. “I did not step foot on to this land or into this house until the day of our closing,” she said. Now she owns a 10-acre property.Despite rising Jewish interest in land stewardship, Mink noted that most Jewish growers are “the only Jewish person in their farming community or the only farming person in their Jewish community”. In Rhein’s case, the nearest synagogue is almost an hour away. For her, that means “how I practice being a Jew on a day-to-day basis is how I farm and how I am attached to and care for this land”.Rhein donates 10% of everything she raises to a local food bank, a reflection ofpe’ah, a Talmudic concept that describes giving part of the harvest to the needy. She prays over every duck, chicken and sheep she slaughters so her family may eat.“It’s all God’s creation,” she said. “It is a gift that we get to be part of it. We are stewards. We are not owners.”View image in fullscreenA pig at the Rhein family farm.But she also differs in her interpretation of some principles. The concept ofbal tashchitfocuses on limiting waste, so she keeps a pig to eat food scraps – a controversial decision for some Jews who don’t eat pork due to kosher dietary practices, many of whom disagree with her choice online.“I am very clear this is not a quote-unquote ‘Jewish farm’,” Rhein said, “but I do consider us to be a Jewishly inspired place.”Blending traditions and futuresA number of Jewish farming organizations focus on both community building and skills building. TheSacred Slaughter Institutetrains students to become ashochets, ritual slaughterers of kosher meat; the butchering process calls for prayer, a highly sharpened knife and a single clean cut to lessentza’ar ba’alei chayim, or animal suffering.Elsewhere, at the 20-acre non-profitAdamah Farmin Falls Village, Connecticut, Jewish people in their 20s and 30s come for three-month farming fellowships. Located at the Isabella Freedman Jewish Retreat Center, Adamah sells vegetables and herbs through membership in its community-supported agriculture (CSA) model.View image in fullscreenThe Rhein family’s home and farm.View image in fullscreenSamuel Rhein, 16, helps his mother vaccinate sheep at the family farm.Adamah Farm co-founder Shamu Sadeh said the work “is a process of reinvigoratingJudaismand the Jewish community with an ecological perspective, and of reinvigorating the ecological environmental community with people who feel spiritually connected”. Graduates work in food rescue programs, food policy, environmental groups and Jewish social services, among other fields; a small percentage are farmers.Rabbis Shoshana and Philip Ohriner run the 16-acreMa’alot Farmsin Los Gatos, California, with grants from community organizations and foundations. The farm nurtures hundreds of varieties of produce, from olives and broccolini to marionberries, a type of blackberry. Almost everything is given away to people facing food insecurity, including kids in afterschool programs and seniors with nutritional needs.View image in fullscreenWendy Rhein picks chestnuts at her farm.Ma’alot’s marketing doesn’t refer to Judaism. Still, “you cannot step on to Ma’alot Farms without feeling our Judaism permeate everything”, Philip Ohriner said, “from the way in which we care for our staff and provide a living wage for them and benefits, to the ways in which we seek to share our abundance to feed the hungry, to seek to bring equity and justice more fully into our world.”AtEkar Farm, located at an eldercare community in Aurora, Colorado, executive director Jason Plotkin offers intergenerational gardening programs and donates about 20,000lb of organic produce annually to groups including Hope Communities, which serves refugees, and Spirit of the Sun, an Indigenous-led organization. The farm grows epazote, Thai hot chilies and bitter melon among its crops based on requests from recipients. Plotkin grew up Jewish but wasn’t religious. “I actually have learned more about my Jewish identity working for Ekar,” he said, “than what I brought into it.”Non-profit farms exemplify the idea oftzedakah,or charity, a requirement in Jewish tradition. Small-scale for-profit farms strive to be community partners in their own ways.Zalman (Robbie) Friedman operates a subscription and delivery service for local kosher meat fromRobariah Farmsin South Deerfield, Massachusetts. A certifiedshochet,he tends to about 1,000 birds, including meat chickens, egg layers and turkeys. About a quarter of his customers aren’t Jewish but appreciate Robariah’s regenerative farming practices. His birds have plenty of room to move and dine on fresh pasture every day thanks to mobile coops. “We raise a slower-growing variety that’s very active on the grass,” he said.The laws ofkashrut, or keeping kosher, outline how to slaughter an animal but are less specific about its care, Friedman said. “Why can’t it be done in a way that also honors the life of the animal, which is also a very important Jewish value and Jewish practice?”View image in fullscreenWendy Rhein sits on her porch with her dog after a day of farmwork.Jewish guidance can show up even in crop selection. Ian Yosef Hertzmark grows ancient grains such as emmer, einkorn, spelt and Persian wheats, among other crops, on the 32-acreMigrash Farmin Baltimore county, Maryland. He plants ancient grains in the fall to beyoshon,or “old”, taking root before Passover (the Torah forbids eatingchadash, or “new” grain). Hertzmark finds fulfillment in having “a relationship with land in an observant and seasonal context”.Rhein agrees. She feels “more self-aware, more confident, more alive and whole as a human being here, doing this, than I ever felt living in Manhattan … This way of life – attaching yourself to land and animals and seasonality – is a constant sense of joy.”Explore more on these topicsJudaismFarmingFarm animalsNorth CarolinaReligionShare

title: Coogan, Burnham and the fight to revive Middleton: could it be grist to the mill for struggling British towns? | Greater Manchester | The Guardian
description: Turnaround initiated by the now prime minister and led by the actor could provide blueprint for other neglected areas
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Turnaround initiated by the now prime minister and led by the actor could provide blueprint for other neglected areas
Content: A mural of former footballer Paul Scholes and actor Steve Coogan, top, looms over the town, as does its historic cotton mill, right. There are ambitions to revitalise the site in the same manner as Weir Mill in Stockport, left. Composite: Jon Super/Alamy/Guardian DesignTurnaround initiated by the now prime minister and led by the actor could provide blueprint for other neglected areasSave high street by taxing online sales at higher rate, Burnham urgedWhat makes a good town? Here are five key ingredientsByJosh HallidayNorth of England editorThu 22 Oct 2026 07.22 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 07.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former England footballer Paul Scholes and the actor Steve Coogan stare out from beside a fish and chip shop in Middleton, nearManchester. Looming over a mural of the pair – and the whole town – is an enormous former cotton mill that powered its economy a century ago.The deafening looms and spindles of Warwick Mill fell silent decades ago, replaced in recent years by TikTok “urban explorers” who share videos of themselves crawling through its abandoned shell.Yet the old building may have life inside it yet: last month Rochdale council wrestled Warwick Mill out of the hands of its absentee owner, a millionaire Chinese businessman, under whom it had been derelict for years.View image in fullscreenThe dilapidated Warwick Mill in Middleton town centre.Photograph: Jon SuperNow the Grade II-listed site is at the centre of plans Andy Burnham believes could turn Middleton, where he wasonce a trainee journalist, into a blueprint for the future of Britain’s struggling towns.“It used to be good,” said Dorothy Kersh, in the town square with her husband, Ernie, both of them 83. “In the 70s we had a cinema, we had banks. It’s lost character and we’ve hardly got any shops. We haven’t even got a bank now – I never thought NatWest would leave Middleton. It’s just going downhill.”Middleton, a town of about 50,000 people a few miles from both Manchester and Rochdale, is in the type of existential crisis suffered by most British towns.A decade or so ago, locals could find virtually everything they needed in its neat square of grocers, butchers and banks. But a giant Tesco has hoovered up the cash since it opened in 2013, compounding the rise of online and out-of-town shopping.In addition to the loss of all its banks, the town saw the remains of its last post office closed by Modella Capital, the newprivate equity owner of WH Smith, days before Burnham became prime minister.Now the shopping precinct offers little more than bookmakers, vape shops, pawnbrokers and fast-food outlets.View image in fullscreenThe mayor of Greater Manchester, Bev Craig, announced plans to rejuvenate Middleton’s town centre earlier this year.Photograph: Jon SuperIts geographical identity feels muddled. Middleton was historically in Lancashire but has a Manchester postcode and dialling code, although residents pay their council tax to Rochdale. The region’s lauded tram network does not stop here.“It’s really a dying town,” said Tim King, outside a large post office branch that closed down years ago. “We’ve only got one cash machine and that’s at Tesco, and there’s never any money in it. We’ve lost out on the trams. We haven’t got anything down here, to be honest.”But six miles from the birthplace of the modern co-operative movement in 1844, a community fightback is under way.Months before he departed for Downing Street, Burnham launched a mayoral development corporation for Middleton, giving local leaders power to set lower business rates, acquire underused land and property, and build 1,500 new homes.View image in fullscreenRose Marley, the chief executive of Co-operatives UK, is helping to lead efforts to turnaround the town.Photograph: Jon SuperThe body is led by Coogan, the Bafta-winning creator of Alan Partridge, and Rose Marley, the chief executive of Co-operatives UK. Crucially, residents and business owners will have a seat at the table: a survey of 2,000 Middletonians is shaping the agenda of this new mayoral body – with Warwick Mill and other empty buildings identified by locals as an immediate priority.Wearing a hard hat and hi-vis vest during a tour of Warwick Mill last month, Coogan said the Middleton of his childhood was a “thriving” town but that “over the last 35 years there has been a kind of a bank ride” by firms registered in the British Virgin Islands, China and the US: “All that money has been extracted but very little has been put back into the infrastructure.”Coogan said the project was about more than attempting to revitalise his home town. It was a chance to reverse the political and economic malaise that has seen former Labour voters shift to rightwing populist parties such as Reform UK in post-industrial areas across Britain.“There’s a problem in this country which is post-industrial neglect,” he told the Guardian. “The idea, the Blairite approach: it’s called multinationalism, there is nothing we can do, throw your hands up, you’ve just got to see what happens, we can’t help these people.“Leaving that vacuum will mean that the extremists, populist extremists, will fill that gap. That’s the problem with top-down, well-meaning, but disempowering, philanthropic, centralised socialism.People don’t want to receive charity, they want to be empowered.”View image in fullscreenSteve Coogan at the launch of Middleton Co-operating in 2024.Photograph: Gary Roberts/AlamyCoogan is part of a group called Middleton Co-operating, which aims to “rewire the whole of the economy locally” by taking infrastructure and everyday essentials into public control.Its plans include using renewable energy, such as solar panels and small wind turbines, to help power a secondary school and a hospice. A trial involving heat pumps and solar panels on a terrace of Edwardian homes is also being put together.Banks could soon return too, with plans for a banking hub where Lloyds, NatWest and others could open on different days of the week, alongside financial advisers.The group, which was backed by Burnham when he was mayor and in June won £4.5m funding from the national lottery’s solidarity fund, wants to expand into food production, early years support, mental health provision and adult social care.“These are all things that have the biggest impact on people’s day-to-day lives and they’re generally all owned by big business and private equity – they cost too much and are a cause of a lot of stress in the community,” said Mark Fraser, a founder of Middleton Co-operating.View image in fullscreenLeft to right: Marley; the leader of Rochdale council, Neil Emmott; the Courteeners frontman, Liam Fray; Andy Burnham, the then mayor of Greater Manchester, and Coogan marking the launch of Middleton’s mayoral development corporation in 2025.Photograph: Middleton MDCEarlier this year, an arts venue run by Middleton Co-operating was forced out of the town’s sprawling shopping centre – which was owned by two London-based real estate companies and incorporated in the British Virgin Islands – as it could not afford the £43,000-a-year rent and service charge demanded by the landlord. In its place a pawnbroker moved in on a 10-year lease.“It was a bit of a sickener,” said Fraser. “It was a lesson, in that they were saying they loved what we were doing for the community, but when it came to it, what counts is the bottom line.”View image in fullscreenVape and mobile phone shops are among the current retail offerings in Middleton town centre.Photograph: Jon SuperEven with Coogan’s star power and the prime minister’s backing, the scale of the challenge is huge.Warwick Mill is an utter wreck and could cost tens of millions of pounds to bring back to life. To Fraser, it is a symbol of a town where people feel “neglected and forgotten”, and most had lost hope in its future.“The cost of rescuing and converting something of that size is colossal,” said Tim Heatley, the co-founder of the property firm Capital & Centric, which specialises in turning unloved old buildings – such as former mills and even multistorey car parks – into sought-after homes.It was a 7pm telephone call from Burnham that turned Heatley on to Warwick Mill in January this year.The then mayor told Heatley he had seen Capital & Centric’s renovation of the dilapidated Weir Mill in Stockport and asked him to take a look at the Middleton site.View image in fullscreenThe Grade II-listed Weir Mill in Stockport, pictured during refurbishment works in 2023.Photograph: pictotaker/AlamyAs it happened, Heatley had already been in contact with Kam Lei Fong, the Macau-based developer who owned Warwick Mill. But with Burnham onboard, the project accelerated.“For me, the opportunity is much bigger than doing a nice conversion of an old mill,” he said. “Warwick is absolutely colossal and has loomed over Middleton for more than a century. If we can fill it with life again, it has the potential to become an anchor for the town … and give confidence for investment to follow around it.“The challenge now is turning all that momentum into an actual place, getting Warwick fixed up, full of people and properly part of Middleton again. Ideally before Andy’s next career move leaves us needing to find somebody else to cut the ribbon.”Explore more on these topicsTown and countryGreater ManchesterSteve CooganAndy BurnhamRegenerationCommunitiesLocal politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Heartbreak, hope and human imperfection: Leonard Cohen’s greatest songs – ranked! | Leonard Cohen | The Guardian
description: A decade after his final album, and his death, we rate the best of the Canadian singer-songwriter who brought a deep, spiritual wisdom to love and grief
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: A decade after his final album, and his death, we rate the best of the Canadian singer-songwriter who brought a deep, spiritual wisdom to love and grief
Content: Cohen … the self-confessed ‘lazy bastard in a suit’.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCohen … the self-confessed ‘lazy bastard in a suit’.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesRankedLeonard CohenHeartbreak, hope and human imperfection: Leonard Cohen’s greatest songs – ranked!A decade after his final album, and his death, we rate the best of the Canadian singer-songwriter who brought a deep, spiritual wisdom to love and griefAlexis PetridisThu 22 Oct 2026 10.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 18.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. First We Take Manhattan (1988)The synth-heavy production on 1988’s I’m Your Man has always been divisive – even Leonard Cohen’s longtime collaborator Anjani Thomas subsequently expressed misgivings – but on its opening track, it really works. The Pet Shop Boys-ish arrangement chafes against Cohen’s growling vocal, amplifying First We Take Manhattan’s shiver-inducing sense of brooding menace.19. Going Home (2011)Seven years – and a personal financial crisis – after 2004’s half-hearted Dear Heather, Cohen returned to the studio with his powers freshly marshalled. As if to underline the point, Old Ideas opened with the sharply witty Going Home, on which Cohen’s muse addresses the listener directly, disparaging the artist himself as “a lazy bastard in a suit”.18. Memories (1977)Cohen famously called his 1977 LP Death of a Ladies’ Man “a catastrophe”, which perhaps reflected more on its drug- and booze-soaked recording with dangerously erratic producer Phil Spector than the finished album. It’s an outlier in Cohen’s catalogue, but one with much to commend it. Certainly, he maintained an understandable fondness for the rock’n’roll-influenced Memories, often performing it live.17. Almost Like the Blues (2014)View image in fullscreenBlack humour … Cohen in Paris, 2012.Photograph: Joel Saget/AFP/Getty ImagesCohen’s renaissance continued apace on Popular Problems. Released the day before his 80th birthday, it sounded suspiciously like a masterpiece. Almost Like the Blues found him reflecting sorrowfully on man’s inhumanity to man – not merely torture, killing and war, but “all my bad reviews” – and staring down his own mortality, replete with a jab at Richard Dawkins.16. A Thousand Kisses Deep (2001)Shruggingly titled, largely recorded in collaborator Sharon Robinson’s garage and packaged in a sleeve featuring a selfie, Ten New Songs was an understated return to recording after Cohen’s five years of Buddhist study. But beneath its unassuming veneer lurked beautiful songs: the chanson-like A Thousand Kisses Deep is an exquisite reflection on regret and time’s passing.15. Death of a Ladies’ Man (1977)Nowhere else on this album does the cocktail of Cohen’s songwriting and Spector’s more-is-more approach to production gel so perfectly: the title track is a fantastic song. Moreover, the weight of Spector’s arrangement, the way it causes the tempo to drag, seems to complement rather than suffocate its mood.14. You Want It Darker (2016)Other artists have made albums that looked imminent death in the face – Warren Zevon’s The Wind, Queen’s Innuendo – but You Want It Darker, released less than three weeks before the end of Cohen’s life, may be the most poised and affecting. “I’m ready, my Lord,” he sang on its title track, a complex, thorny examination of faith.13. Chelsea Hotel #2 (1974)View image in fullscreenIn Frankfurt, 1976.Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/AlamyIn which a brief tryst with Janis Joplin – “We fell into each other’s arms through a process of elimination,” he later recalled – turns into a kind of eulogy, not just for the late singer, but for the era in which they met. It’s haunted by the sense of optimism extinguished.12. Everybody Knows (1988)Rock stars of a certain vintage were wont to write despairing state-of-the-world addresses in the late 80s – Lou Reed’s New York is full of them – but Everybody Knows is a cut above, its relentlessly bleak worldview leavened by black humour: “Everybody’s got this broken feeling, like their father or their dog just died.”11. Avalanche (1971)Against stiff competition, Songs of Love and Hate may be Cohen’s darkest album. Avalanche is its claustrophobic heart, a relentless, shimmering guitar figure, a confusing but compelling tumble of imagery, with his voice at its most poisonous. Nick Cave called it one of “the essential pillars that hold up the structure of my artistic world”.10. Dance Me to the End of Love (1984)Inspired by the story of theLagerkapellen– concentration camp orchestras whose music accompanied forced labour and executions – there’s something eerie about Dance Me to the End of Love’s klezmer-inspired melody and lyrical pleas for lifelong fealty. The latter are filled with intimations of darkness; it’s never entirely clear that love will overcome them.9. The Future (1992)“I’ve seen the future, baby, and it’s murder”: Cohen’s apocalyptic response to the sociopolitical upheavals of the early 90s – most obviously the Los Angeles riots – depicted a world in which “attitudes are all extremist and they’re all defensive”. Thirty-four years on, it sounds grimly prophetic, its upbeat soft-rock backing only serving to amplify the unease.8. Tower of Song (1988)View image in fullscreenDeep reflection … Cohen in 1987.Photograph: Christian Rose/Roger Viollet/Getty ImagesCohen found writing a trying experience – lurid stories abound of him beating his head against the floor while working on Hallelujah. He poured it all into the thrillingly vivid, mordantly funny Tower of Song, which has often struck a chord with other artists, covered by everyone from Phoebe Bridgers to Tom Jones to the Jesus and Mary Chain.7. Anthem (1992)Anthem is home to perhaps Cohen’s most-quoted lyric: “There is a crack in everything, that’s how the light gets in.” But in truth, it’s just one among a plethora of memorable lines in the song’s gospel-infused paean to hope and human imperfection, a song he later suggested represented “everything my whole work and life had gathered around”.6. I’m Your Man (1988)Even by the standards of Cohen’s synth era, the backing of I’m Your Man is low-rent and cheesy, but it fits perfectly with a song about abasement. Its emotional tone shifts from lustful to desperate to hopeless: “A man never got a woman back, not by begging on his knees,” he notes in a moment of clarity, then carries on regardless.5. Hallelujah (1984)‘More than a song’: the enduring power of Leonard Cohen’s HallelujahRead moreHallelujah’s progress from an album Cohen’s US record label refused to release to his most famous song – via, of all things, a cover by John Cale that appeared on the soundtrack of Shrek – is fascinating. Cohen later proposed a moratorium on its use in films, but, in truth, it has survived ubiquity with its power to move intact.4. So Long, Marianne (1968)Cohen’s original intention was to try his luck as a Nashville songwriter. If you squint, you can just about make out the shape of a county song in So Long, Marianne’s beautiful admission of guilt, although it’s hard to imagine the Music Row treatment could improve on its wonderfully ramshackle string accompaniment.3. Bird on the Wire (1969)View image in fullscreenGloomy self-reflection … Cohen in 1967.Photograph: Jack Robinson/Getty ImagesAnother Cohen classic with country music in its bones – Kris Kristofferson said he wanted the opening lines on his gravestone – Bird on the Wire was coaxed out of a depressed Cohen by his then girlfriend, Marianne Ihlen. It sounds utterly, authentically defeated, like one long sigh, destined to soundtrack moments of gloomy self-reflection for the rest of time.2. Suzanne (1968)There are infinitely worse ways to start your debut album than with a song so good, it immediately becomes a standard, covered by Nina Simone, Neil Diamond, Roberta Flack and Aretha Franklin. Some recompense, perhaps, for the titular lady’s refusal to let Cohen touch her perfect body with anything other than his mind.1. Famous Blue Raincoat (1971)Reducing Leonard Cohen’s oeuvre to 20 songs is a thankless task: the compiler is abundantly aware that umpteen deserving songs have been neglected. Similarly, there’s no head-and-shoulders “best” song, merely personal favouritism. Still, you listen to Famous Blue Raincoat’s disconsolate depiction of a love triangle – in the form of a letter to the other male party – and boggle at the idea Cohen was dissatisfied with such an impossibly beautiful song, which so perfectly conjures up an atmosphere of shadowy small-hours reflection, and which comes complete with one of his loveliest melodies (subsequently pinched on – crikey – Leo Sayer’s When I Need You).Explore more on these topicsLeonard CohenRankedPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to face the end of the world – according to Plato and the Stoics | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Fearing future catastrophe is nothing new – ancient Greek and Roman philosophers all visualized the apocalypse
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Fearing future catastrophe is nothing new – ancient Greek and Roman philosophers all visualized the apocalypse
Content: Plato posits that the world will exist for eternity, but that human development will be continually hindered due to periodic terrestrial catastrophes.Illustration: Photograph: Getty Images/Frame: Ibrahim RayintakathView image in fullscreenPlato posits that the world will exist for eternity, but that human development will be continually hindered due to periodic terrestrial catastrophes.Illustration: Photograph: Getty Images/Frame: Ibrahim RayintakathMemento mori: a series about deathWell actuallyHow to face the end of the world – according to Plato and the StoicsFearing future catastrophe is nothing new – ancient Greek and Roman philosophers all visualized the apocalypseChristopher StarThu 22 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 13.37 EDTShareDo your feelings of existential dread extend beyond your own personal mortality? Do they include fears about the survival of our culture and institutions, our species, nonhuman life and the Earth itself? Do you feel like there’s nothing that can help to wrap your head around the biggest problem we face: the end of the world as we know it?Apocalyptic expectations are on the rise. According to a 2022Pew Research Center survey, 39% of Americans believe that we are living in the end times.Yet the feeling that the world is coming to an end is nothing new. Anticipating and preparing for the end of the world is an ancient practice. In fact, many of the ways in which we envision future catastrophes can be traced back to the ancient Mediterranean world.Greek and Roman authors set up their accounts of the end of the world as the product of reason rather than divine revelation – the product of the rational study of the laws of nature that govern the universe. They saw the end of the world as an inevitability and typically saw the aftermath, if there was one, as a repeat of the cycle of human development. The main piece of wisdom they seek to provide is how to face catastrophe without fear.‘We live in grief-phobic societies’: experts on how to get more comfortable with deathRead moreThis is particularly true of the Epicureans and Stoics. Their goal is to meet all events up to and including the end of the world with equanimity. The Roman poet Horace offers a summation of this ideal in his Odes: the “righteous and resolute man” will remain “undaunted even if the sky should fall and the ruins strike his head”.These ancient texts do not explicitly offer solutions or means of avoidance, and as Horace makes clear, they can envision the end of the world as the ultimate test of masculine endurance. Yet they also provide an understanding of the long perspective of human history, and how humanity relates to cosmological and geological history. Unlike our doomsday prepperism, their form of preparation did not require any building projects or financial expenditures; rather, they encouraged preparation that was psychological, epistemological and ecological. This required one to study nature in order to understand its workings and the place of humanity within it.My new book,How to Face the End of the World, offers several passages from ancient Greek and Roman authors about the end of the world in the original Greek and Latin, along with my translation and introduction. The collection begins with a passage from the archaic Greek poet Hesiod’s Works and Days. The other texts are by ancient philosophers: Plato, Lucretius and Seneca. Each developed different scenarios for how the world could end, but all posited that the end would come from the forces of nature, rather than the wrath of the gods.Ancient Greek and Roman accounts of world destruction, as well as Jewish and Christian apocalypses, tap into what is likely an underlying psychological truth about these types of stories. They are a means to understand the future, and to realize the hidden natural and divine forces at work in the cosmos. Their power to reveal ultimate truths and to prepare us to face the future may explain why stories about the end of the world are found across cultures and why they have persisted from the ancient world to today.HesiodHesiod (ca 700BC) is the classical world’s intellectual forefather for envisioning the end of humanity. One of Hesiod’s most famous stories is the myth of the metallic races. It traces the succession of humanity from the ideal time of the primordial “golden race” to the present “iron race”.Hesiod predicts that at some point in the future, Zeus will destroy the current iron race. He enigmatically makes no mention of what will happen after this destruction. His silence served as an impetus for later authors to imagine different scenarios, ranging from a continuation of the cycle and a return to the Golden Age, to the end of humanity and the world itself.Also contained in Hesiod’s account is the suggestion that humans can avoid Zeus’s wrath by honoring the gods and living a just and simple life. The prophecy of doom is not a fixed certainty, but rather a warning of what could happen.PlatoPlato (420sBC–347BC) is perhaps most famous today for the portrayal of his hero, Socrates, and for the political philosophy of the Republic. Less well known is that he invented thestory of Atlantis,which serves as part of his theory of cyclical global catastrophes.double quotation markThe world does not end, but advanced societies doIn his dialogues Timaeus and the Laws, Plato posits that the world will exist for eternity, but that human development will be continually hindered due to periodic terrestrial catastrophes. In short, the world does not end, but advanced societies do.With his stories, Plato appears to be testing the imagination of his audience. In the Laws, it seems clear that he is engaging in a thought experiment about how human society might rebuild after a global catastrophe. Unlike the violent post-apocalyptic narratives of today, Plato imagines that the survivors would live in peace and work together.Epicurus and LucretiusEpicurus (341BC–270BC) believed that the goal of life is pleasure and freedom from disturbance. For Epicurus and his followers, there was a strong connection between ethics and physics. In other words, understanding the nature of the universe was linked to living a good life.Epicurus theorized that the cosmos consisted of atoms and void, as opposed to the other elements of earth, air, fire and water; that the gods existed, but did not care for humans. As a result, death was nothing to us – simply the dissolution of atoms back into the void. There was no punishment or reward to expect in the afterlife.Very little of Epicurus’s work survives from the reported 300 volumes he composed, but a brief account of how worlds end is preserved in one of his letters: “A world is an encasement of a heaven, which contains stars and an earth and all phenomena and is separated from the infinite; it ends with a boundary that is either thin or thick and when this boundary breaks apart everything within it will be ruined.”Epicurus’s most famous disciple was the Roman poet Titus Lucretius Carus (ca 98BC–ca 55BC). One key way in which Lucretius departs from and develops Epicurus’s teachings can be seen in his accounts of the end of the world. Lucretius offers two scenarios: slow, gradual decay, or one sudden day of destruction.StoicsWhen we come to Stoic cosmology, we seem to leave the realm of plausibility and have to abandon our deep-seated notions of time’s arrow moving in one direction. But if you prefer to think of time as moving in great cycles of creation and destruction, or ever had the feeling of deja vu, the Stoics are for you.Founded by Zeno of Citium (ca 334BC–ca 262BC) in Athens during the late fourth century BC, the Stoics argued that “creative fire” was the primal building block of the cosmos. Eventually this fire would consume everything and then the cosmos would be reborn, events known as theekpyrosis(conflagration) andapokatastasis(restoration).Only brief fragments and reports, some of them hostile, remain of the early Stoics on this theory. Some Stoics even rejected the idea of cyclical conflagrations. There are no detailed accounts of how the conflagration would unfold or how humans should prepare for it in the fragments that survive of the early Stoics. Most likely, it was believed to lie in the distant future.The Stoic perspective on the end of the world changed during the Roman period. For example, as part of his daily practice of ethical philosophy, the emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote a brief reminder to himself in his Meditations that the end will come very quickly.The most detailed Stoic accounts of the end of the world survive in the works of Seneca the Younger (ca 4BC–AD65). Among Greek and Roman authors, Seneca had the greatest interest in the end of the world. He wrote about it throughout his career, exploring different apocalyptic scenarios in several of his philosophical works, as well as one of his plays, the Thyestes.double quotation markUnderstanding nature’s cycles could help one to live a better life by understanding that death is a part of natureAlthough Seneca’s descriptions of destruction go into great detail, he is not solely focused on the catastrophe itself. Rather, exploring the end of the world serves a deeper philosophical and therapeutic purpose. Like the Epicureans, the Stoics closely connected the study of ethics and physics. Understanding nature’s cycles could help one to live a better life by understanding that death is a part of nature, both for the individual and for our world.In his Natural Questions,Seneca also considers how people would react when experiencing a global catastrophe. Seneca states that the destruction is close at hand, so perhaps his interest in human reactions to catastrophe was part of his own psychological preparation for the event.What is the wisdom provided by these Greek and Roman authors? How might their visions of the end of the world help us today, if at all? On one level, we can see the origins of several narratives and ideas that are still very much alive today: the myth of decline from the Golden Age, Plato’s story of Atlantis, the Epicurean theory of total planetary destruction, as well as the Stoic theory of eternal return. Overall, however, it may simply seem depressing to read account after account of the end of the world.Nevertheless, there may be value in envisioning the various forms that future global catastrophes could take. In 2020, a group of scholarspublished a piecearguing that morbid curiosity and exposure to apocalyptic and similarly frightening narratives can provide psychological tools and resilience when real catastrophes hit.One of the members of the team, the literary scholar Mathias Clasen, wrote that mental time travel, the ability to imagine possible futures, has been important for human development. Apocalyptic narratives serve a key purpose in that they allow humans to imagine and plan for the “worst-case scenario”.Other scholars, such as philosopher Hans Jonas,have urged usto accept that the odds are high that catastrophe awaits us in the future. We should not only envision the future as catastrophe but wager that the future will be bad rather than good. Yet this is not simply a prediction of doom and despair. As the contemporary philosopher and cultural critic Slavoj Žižek noted in Too Late to Awaken: What Lies Ahead When There Is No Future?, perhaps envisioning the future catastrophe as inevitable is paradoxically the way to avoid it.Ancient philosophers might be best known for writing lengthy tomes. They did not compose works summarizing their theories of the end of the world but rather included them within larger philosophical arguments on nature, ethics and politics. But there also was the tradition of distilling ideas into a short work, or enchiridion, that one could keep close to hand – the literal meaning of the word. We can perhaps let the ancient Greek and Roman apocalypses discussed here and collected in my book serve as a low-stakes method of doomsday prepping.Excerpted fromHow to Face the End of the World: An Ancient Guide for Apocalyptic Times(2026), published by Princeton University Press and reprinted here by permissionChristopher Star is professor of classics and director of the Axinn Center for the Humanities at Middlebury College. His books includeApocalypse and Golden Age: The End of the World in Greek and Roman ThoughtExplore more on these topicsWell actuallyMemento mori: a series about deathPhilosophyPlatoClassics and ancient historyPhilosophy booksShare

title: Every Briton should stockpile water and food supplies, government advises | UK news | The Guardian
description: Be Ready campaign aims to prepare UK for impact of climate crisis, technological dependency and threats by hostile state
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Be Ready campaign aims to prepare UK for impact of climate crisis, technological dependency and threats by hostile state
Content: Wes Streeting with Gen Sir Roly Walker at the opening on Thursday of a Rheinmetall factory in Telford, West Midlands.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWes Streeting with Gen Sir Roly Walker at the opening on Thursday of a Rheinmetall factory in Telford, West Midlands.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianUK newsEvery Briton should stockpile water and food supplies, government advisesBe Ready campaign aims to prepare UK for impact of climate crisis, technological dependency and threats by hostile stateDan SabbaghandJasper JollyThu 22 Oct 2026 14.10 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 09.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery Briton is being urged to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in new government guidance designed to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency.TheBe Ready campaignis aimed at persuading people to stock up with supplies to last 72 hours, amid growing official concern about the impact of the climate crisis, technological dependency and hostile state threats.Dan Jarvis, the security minister, said that “those who can follow this advice should follow this advice”. It amounted to “simple steps to be ready for everyday emergencies” as part of a wider, community-oriented effort “to improve our resilience as a nation”, he said.Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, added that Britain also needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure.“Terms like ‘hybrid warfare’ and ‘grey zone threats’ do not accurately capture or convey to the general public what I prefer to describe as ‘state-sponsored terrorism’,” he said.“So in the face of those threats, which are not hypothetical but real, and not somewhere else but increasingly here, we have to step up and take seriously our national resilience as well as our national defence.Royal Navy lacks resources to counter Russian threat in high north, MPs warnRead more“It’s really important that we ask households and businesses, are they prepared? Are they ready? Do they know how they would respond in the event of everyday challenges that might manifest themselves?”People are advised to keep a ready supply of blankets and cash at home plus a first aid kit, a torch with batteries and a wind-up FM radio. Three litres of water per person per day should be stored for drinking – and more is needed for cooking and washing, the guidance adds.The government hadindicated in Augustthat UK citizens would be told to stock up on tinned food but the Be Ready campaign from the Cabinet Office is more specific. It will be followed up with an advertising campaign on social media and radio.Stocking up for three days is considered to be a realistic and practical proposal for households and would bring the UK in line with France, the Republic of Ireland and the Netherlands in advising people how to prepare for serious disruption.Ministers timed the launch of the campaign to come before the winter storm season after a series of intense storms that have battered the UK in recent years. Tens of thousands of homes were left without power in the Midlands, the south-west and Wales afterStorm Goretti hit in January, with winds reaching nearly 100mph.There is also concern about the potential impact of the “super El-Nino”, a global phenomenon that could lead to 2027 being the hottest year ever recorded and uncertain weather patterns, affecting global food supplies and energy systems.The guidance emerged as 32 UK government websites were taken offline in a precautionary measure in response to the discovery of asecurity vulnerability in the PHP programming languageused by millions of websites around the world.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBritain’s National Cyber Security Centre sent out 50,000 alerts to affected organisations, in a reminder of the high degree of dependency that modern societies have on the internet and other critical technologies.Spain and Portugal were suddenly left without power for several hours in April 2025, in a cascading failure triggered by voltage instability in the network. About 55 million people were affected in the incident, the worst blackout in Europe in recent memory.People also need to consider how to respond to hybrid warfare attacks by Russia or other hostile states, including cyber-attacks that could knock out payment systems used by businesses or cause supply chains to collapse, Streeting said.The minister was speaking at a new tank gun barrel factory in Telford in theWest Midlands. The factory, owned by the German manufacturer Rheinmetall, is part of efforts to accelerate rearmament in the face of Russian military threats, but Streeting also emphasised that the public should be prepared for hybrid warfare, or sabotage actions that stop short of outright war.Russian spy ships have been tracked by the Royal Navy monitoring undersea pipelines and cables that connect the UK to the continent of Europe and elsewhere, raising concerns they could one day be attacked, though this would represent a major escalation by Moscow.European states have become increasingly vocal about thethreat of sabotage efforts by enemies, particularly Russia, which can cause disruption or even directly threaten safety. These efforts have included anexplosives-laden dronefound next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport in August, and a series of explosions and fires at defence facilities.Britain has only rarely embarked on public information campaigns, with governments of both parties reluctant to be accused of scaremongering. A 1980 campaign advising people on how to survive a nuclear war,Protect and Survive, advised people how to build a bomb shelter at home and retain enough food for 14 days.Explore more on these topicsUK newsInfrastructureWes StreetingClimate crisisDefence policyTelfordManufacturing sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Revealed: billionaire Reform donor was in business with foundation linked to Iranian regime | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Sasan Ghandehari’s partnership with religious foundation raises questions about past dealings with republic criticised by Nigel Farage
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Exclusive: Sasan Ghandehari’s partnership with religious foundation raises questions about past dealings with republic criticised by Nigel Farage
Content: Nigel Farage (left) with Sasan Ghandehari, who says he runs a $10bn fund called HP Trust.Photograph: Jeff Gilbert/AlamyView image in fullscreenNigel Farage (left) with Sasan Ghandehari, who says he runs a $10bn fund called HP Trust.Photograph: Jeff Gilbert/AlamyReform UKRevealed: billionaire Reform donor was in business with foundation linked to Iranian regimeExclusive: Sasan Ghandehari’s partnership with religious foundation raises questions about past dealings with republic criticised by Nigel FarageRowena MasonWhitehall editorThu 22 Oct 2026 12.39 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 13.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage’s newest billionaire donor was in business with a powerful Iranian religious foundation under the authority of the country’s supreme leader, raising questions about his past dealings with the hardline republic.Hossein Ghandehari, also called Sasan, was little known in the UK until he pledged to give millions to Reform UK this summer anddonated £50,000 to Farageto cover the cost of two passes for the Davos World Economic Forum.He has said he is moving his tax residency from Switzerland to the UK in order to make “regular payments” of more than “one or two million” to the party.The 61-year-old Iranian-born British businessman, who says he runs a $10bn (£7bn) fund called HP Trust, has declined to give details about how his family made its money beyond saying the fund owns assets in Europe and North America.Now, a French arbitration decision unearthed by the Guardiansheds some light on Ghandehari’s past dealings with Iranian state-linked entities between 2013 and 2016.It also reveals Ghandehari’s further Iranian business links toanother Reform UK donor, John Richard Simpson, an administration professional and church warden from Potters Bar, north of London. Simpson’s design firm, Interior Architecture Landscape, counts the Ghandehari family as a client and gave £200,000 to Reform UK last year.Farage has been highly critical of Iran over the past year, and in March accused it of being abigger dangerto the UK than Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin.The French judgment reveals that Ghandehari was the major investor behind a deal to supply and build a fibre-optic cable to carry telecoms traffic across Iran in a joint venture with a state-linked Iranian partner.The businessman’s HP Trust was the ultimate owner of Ori Group, which took a 49% stake in the venture, called Omran Razavi International Co, in 2015.The other 51% of the venture was owned by Astan Quds Razavi (AQR), a multibillion pound religious foundation in Iran’s second city of Mashhad.AQR’s leader at the time was ayatollah Abbas Vaez Tabasi, who was appointed custodian of the foundation by the first supreme leader, Ruhollah Khomeini, and served from the 1979 revolution until his death in 2016. Vaez Tabasi had been an ally of some reformers but remained close to the next supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, and,according to the BBC, was reported by state media in 2009 to have said of opposition protest movements that those behind “sedition” in the country were “enemies of god” who deserved to be executed under sharia law.The joint venture ended in about 2016, with the Ghandehari-backed entities being pushed out of the deal as a hardliner was appointed to replace Vaez Tabasi.View image in fullscreenLawyers for Sasan Ghandehari said his involvement was intended to promote political change through greater access to information.Photograph: Jeff Gilbert/AlamyThe US imposed sanctions on AQR in 2021, saying it controlled “large swaths of the Iranian economy, including assets expropriated from political dissidents and religious minorities, to the benefit of supreme leader Ali Khamenei and senior Iranian government officials”. It describes it as abonyad, one of the “opaque, quasi-official organisations generally controlled by current and former government officials and clerics that report directly to the supreme leader”.Ghandehari’s lawyers said it would be misleading to characterise him as “working with Iran” without the context that, after 2016, he was targeted by Iran’s supreme national security council with the false allegation that he was working with hostile western powers. They also said his involvement was intended to promote political change through greater access to information, which he believed was why the US and French authorities authorised the project.Tom Keatinge, the director of the Centre for Finance and Security at Rusi, the foreign affairs thinktank, said dealing with Iran “has always been a risky business as a financial institution because of this blurring between kind of state and the private sector. The private sector is not free to operate. It’s just very hard to operate in that country without touching a live rail.”He said there was clearly a range of positions among ayatollahs but it would be “pretty difficult to operate in an industry like telecoms” without the acceptance of the core leadership.The judgment also revealed that, until 2016, Ghandehari’s HP Trust was the owner of Orico General Trading LLC, which was contracted to supply telecoms equipment from France’s Alcatel-Lucent and transport it from Dubai to Iran. After 2016, this company was transferred to Simpson, the administration professional, who was responsible for winding down Orico’s operations and taking hundreds of staff out of the region.Simpson told the Guardian he acquired the company after Iranian extremists took over AQR, when the project’s assets were seized and those involved faced political persecution on national security grounds, including accusations of working for hostile western governments. He said his plan was to wind down the business, adding that he carried out detailed checks before acquiring Orico.Ghandehari’s lawyers said AQR was independent and respected, and therefore the only viable choice for a joint venture in Iran. They said Ghandehari had never met Vaez Tabasi and that he did not regard him as an advocate for freedom or human rights but had believed him to be the only force in the Iranian hierarchy capable of holding back the hardliners in order for the project to go ahead.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe original contract for the deal was awarded to the Omran consortium in 2012 by the Iranian state-owned Telecommunication Infrastructure Company of Iran.According to Iranian corporate filings, Omran Razavi International Co also owned stakes in two majority state-owned banks, Bank Mellat and Bank Tejerat, in 2013. Both were subject to sanctions over involvement in Iran’s nuclear programme at that point.Ghandehari’s lawyers said Omran Razavi disposed of the small stakes in the banks before HP Trust’s Ori Group signed its agreement for a 49% stake in the venturein December 2014. They added that the deal was fully approved by authorities in France and the US.In 2016, AQR took over the whole of the joint venture. Around the same time, the project’s chair, Mohammed Reza Noory, ended up in Iran’s infamous Evin prison, serving an 18-year sentence.Ghandehari and Noory are both named on leaked judicial papers published by the hacktivist group Edaalat Ali as having being under investigation in Iran after the deal collapsed. Ghandehari’s lawyers say he first became aware of the “bogus allegations” during French court proceedings and that the intelligence services had not given him any further details. Ghandehari’s representatives said fabricating financial and social cases against its targets to discredit them was part of the Iranian regime’s playbook and had been widely documented and recognised by western governments, human rights organisations and independent journalists.Ghandehari’s lawyers said he had not been to Iran for 30 years and his wealth had no connection to the country, since his ancestral property and assets were confiscated in 2016.Farage has been highly critical of Iran’s government this year, supporting Donald Trump’s war against it, and attending a protest outside the Iranian embassy with pro-democracy activists in the spring. Last week he warned about Iranian agents entering the UK via small boats across the Channel.Ina joint interviewwith Farage and Ghandehari in July, the Telegraph described Ghandehari’s business deal in Iran without mentioning its connections to Iranian regime-linked companies. It described it as a project to bring access to high-speed internet to Iran that would help drive reform, but that it later went wrong and resulted in Ghandehari’s assets being confiscated.It is still not clear how Ghandehari and his family have built up their extraordinary wealth. His fortune is said to have gone from an estimated $2bn, when his late mother bought a property on London’s “billionaire’s row” in 2008, to a reported $10bn now.In a recentcourt case over a Picasso painting, Ghandehari was asked to provide proof that he could afford £1.5m in legal costs. His lawyers pointed only to a brochure from his Davos trip with Farage, with a description that he controls a trust with a “collective investment value in excess of $10bn”.View image in fullscreenThe Picasso painting at the centre of the court case was Femme dans un rocking-chair.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesAt one point, he offered a letter from a “partner in a leading accountancy firm” confirming he was the principal beneficiary of HP Trust, and drawing an annual income from it. However, this was later withdrawn, as Ghandehari decided he did not want its contents to enter the public domain.Explore more on these topicsReform UKIranParty fundingMiddle East and north AfricaNigel FaragenewsShareReuse this content

title: Minister insists she backs migration policy after joking she couldn’t lie about supporting it | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Miatta Fahnbulleh says reference to ‘awkward’ interview was meant to be lighthearted and self-deprecating
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Miatta Fahnbulleh says reference to ‘awkward’ interview was meant to be lighthearted and self-deprecating
Content: The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, repeatedly refused to say she was in favour of the ILR rule changes during a Sky interview.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, repeatedly refused to say she was in favour of the ILR rule changes during a Sky interview.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesImmigration and asylumMinister insists she backs migration policy after joking she couldn’t lie about supporting itMiatta Fahnbulleh says reference to ‘awkward’ interview was meant to be lighthearted and self-deprecatingRowena MasonWhitehall editorThu 22 Oct 2026 14.04 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 14.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe energy secretary has been forced to clarify that she backs Shabana Mahmood’s migration policy, after earlier joking that she had not been able to “lie” about supporting a key element of the changes.Miatta Fahnbulleh made the original remarks to a journalists’ event in Westminster, referring to an “awkward” Sky News interview in which she repeatedly refused to say she was in favour of plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to get permanent residency.She told the event: “I made three promises to myself when I came into politics. The first was never lie, which has created some awkward moments, including being interviewed by Sophy Ridge yesterday.”The implication that she could not bring herself to lie about supporting the changes appears to have gone down badly among colleagues in government, although No 10 refused to be drawn on whether they requested her to issue a clarification.Fahnbulleh posted a statement on social media on Thursday evening saying: “Today I made what was meant to be a lighthearted, self-deprecating remark. I didn’t get it right and it hasn’t come off as I intended.“I fully support our home secretary and the government’s position on migration reform. As I said earlier this week, it’s absolutely right that people should have to make a contribution to this country in order to earn citizenship.”The clarification represents a twist in the cabinet split over the issue of the migration changes, with Fahnbulleh and Angela Rayner among those not keen on elements of the original plan.Mahmood, the home secretary, is consulting on plans to increase the period before foreign workers can claim indefinite leave to remain (ILR) from five to 15 years, backdated to apply to anyone arriving from 2021 onwards.View image in fullscreenThe home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, arrives in Downing Street to attend the weekly Cabinet meeting on Tuesday.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/ShutterstockShe has previously hinted that her plan to make it harder to claim permanent residencecould be watered downby exempting care workers from the new rule.However, there were reports on Tuesday that she was holding firm against making changes. A senior ally told the Times that she had the prime minister’s support, saying: “Andy has been on Shabana’s side throughout this row over ILR. He is holding the line.”This week it was reported thatFahnbulleh appeared to criticise the planson her Peckham constituency website in a post about a community discussion that was later removed. She was quoted as saying: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.”And earlier this year, Rayner, the housing secretary,publicly criticised the plans, while dozens of Labour MPs oppose the changes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHome Office lifts deportation order for man, 62, who has lived in UK for 50 yearsRead moreOne of the leading opponents, Mike Tapp, a former immigration minister who clashed with Mahmood over the policy, said thehome secretary should “read the room”in relation to the strength of feeling about the changes.“It’s important we do the right thing. If people have come to the country and genuinely worked in the sector, they shouldn’t be punished and should have the right to apply for settlement after five years as they expected,” he said.MPs campaigning for changes to Mahmood’s policies believe they have a chance of convincing Andy Burnham to exempt care workers, given reforming adult social care is an issue close to his heart. However, theHome Officehas said that would lead to an exodus of foreign workers from the sector when they are no longer bound by the terms of their visa.No 10 stressed on Wednesday that Mahmood was “carefully considering” more than 200,000 responses to a consultation before finalising the planned changes.Asked whether tweaks to the home secretary’s revamp – including no longer applying the policy retrospectively – could be ruled out, Burnham’s press secretary said: “We set out proposals for consultation. We’ve consulted on what the transition arrangement should look like for people already in the UK who have not received settled status.“The home secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to ensure we get this right and have the right arrangements in place.”Earlier this week, aHome Officespokesperson said: “This government has announced reforms that mean settlement must be earned and not automatic. We are currently considering responses to our consultation on elements of these reforms.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumMiatta FahnbullehShabana MahmoodLabourHome OfficenewsShareReuse this content

title: US judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in $10bn lawsuit against BBC | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Judge threatens to dismiss Trump’s BBC lawsuit unless he cooperates with discovery process and sits for deposition
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: Judge threatens to dismiss Trump’s BBC lawsuit unless he cooperates with discovery process and sits for deposition
Content: Donald Trump walks to board Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on 21 October 2026.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump walks to board Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on 21 October 2026.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpUS judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in $10bn lawsuit against BBCJudge threatens to dismiss Trump’s BBC lawsuit unless he cooperates with discovery process and sits for depositionJeremy Barrin MiamiThu 22 Oct 2026 13.18 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has been ordered by a US judge to cooperate with the discovery process mandated for his lawsuit against the BBC and to sit for a deposition by 11 December – or else he could be subject to sanctions, including the possible dismissal of the $10bn lawsuit.The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by theBBCthat spliced together two comments made nearly an hour apart by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot.
