The BBC has acknowledged that this specific edit was misleading, but Trump has gone on to claim, falsely, that the BBC did not just edit his speech but used AI to insert words into his speech.While the broadcast was not readily available to view in Florida, Trump’s team has argued that he was personally damaged by the broadcast under Florida’s Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act.During a lengthy hearing dealing with a variety of discovery issues, federal magistrate judge Enjoliqué Lett on Thursday also rejected a request by Trump’s legal team to prevent the seven-hour-long deposition from being videotaped, though it will only be accessible to attorneys in the case.Lett agreed with contentions from the BBC’s lawyers that Trump’s team had not been sufficiently forthcoming in handing over internal documents relevant to the case ahead of an 18 December deadline for discovery.“We still have a completely lopsided [situation] here on discovery. They have produced absolutely nothing of any substance,” attorney Charles Tobin, on behalf of the BBC, argued in a Miami courtroom.The documents that Trump’s team have turned over have primarily been either pulled from the internet or provided by the BBC itself.“It strains credulity that a thorough search has been done in order to determine that all of these requests have been responded to,” Lett told Alejandro Brito, Trump’s Florida-based attorney. “The court is not satisfied that anyone is doing a thorough job.”The judge gave the plaintiffs 30 days to produce the relevant documents. While she acknowledged that the discovery process can be “burdensome” on both parties, she said that “failure to do so could result in sanctions, including possible dismissal of the suit for failure to prosecute the case and engage in meaningful discovery process”.Of the Trump team’s obligation to adequately participate in the discovery process, the judge said: “This is the last opportunity to do so.”After discussing the discovery process, the judge turned tothe BBC’s request to compel the president’s team to agree for a deposition,after a previously scheduled date – 16 October – was cancelled for what Trump’s counsel said were “other matters of national importance”. While the BBC noted that Trump was actually campaigning in Georgia on that day, leading Tobin to conclude that the plaintiff’s team had transmitted “fake news”, Brito said the president was “involved in a host of things” on a daily basis that the BBC’s legal team “has no idea” about.While Lett said she was obligated to adhere to the discovery schedule mandated in the case, that timeline could be extended by district court judge Jeffrey T Kuntz. Tobin, representing the BBC, said his side was willing to push back the timeline for Trump’s deposition if Kuntz adjusted the discovery schedule.Lett once again threatened sanctions – including dismissal – if Trump’s team did not comply with her deposition order.“The lesson for the day is that no plaintiff is above the law, and no plaintiff is above the orders of the court,” Tobin said.In a filing on Wednesday, Trump’s team said he would be willing to sit for a deposition during the second or third week of January.During the hearing, Lett also allowed the BBC’s subpoena to Mar-a-Lago, Trump’s Florida club, to go ahead, despite protests from Trump’s attorney that the business was separate from the president.Brito, Trump’s attorney, contended that the president does not run the club. “The president’s occupation is the president of the United States,” he said. “It has nothing to do with Mar-a-Lago as far as his occupation.”Tobin, representing the BBC, vehemently disagreed. “To say that Mar-a-Lago is not tied to this president or his reputation ignores the fact that he hosts [Ukrainian president] Volodymyr Zelenskyy, he hosts the president of Ireland, [Russian president] Vladimir Putin – he uses Mar-a-Lago as a location to publicize his reputation as a symbol of his personal power, so it is inextricably intertwined. His business successes are a measure of his reputation.”In issuing the ruling, the judge agreed that the club “falls within the scope of discoverability”.“I think it is intertwined with his profession and therefore any harm that may be alleged under his professional trade and occupation would be reflected with how he conducts business with Mar-a-Lago, at least for discovery purposes,” she added.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpBBCLaw (US)US politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Child health in England at risk from sharp rise in NHS waiting times, report says | Children's health | The Guardian
description: CQC research finds long delays are making conditions harder to treat and highlights regional disparities in care
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: CQC research finds long delays are making conditions harder to treat and highlights regional disparities in care
Content: Although some adult waiting times have improved children are having to endure longer waits to be treated, in part due to rapidly rising demand and falling staff numbers.Photograph: SolStock/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAlthough some adult waiting times have improved children are having to endure longer waits to be treated, in part due to rapidly rising demand and falling staff numbers.Photograph: SolStock/Getty ImagesChildren's healthChild health in England at risk from sharp rise in NHS waiting times, report saysCQC research finds long delays are making  conditions harder to treat and highlights regional disparities in careAndrew GregoryHealth editorThu 22 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThousands of children inEnglandare experiencing some of the sharpest rises in waiting times for healthcare in the history of the NHS, a report has revealed.While some adult waiting times have improved, children and young people are being “hit hardest” amid soaring demand and falling numbers of staff, according to the annual state of care report by the Care Quality Commission.In community health services alone, 80,000 children and young people have been waiting more than a year for an appointment – almost 11 times the number of adults, the report said. Experts said that was “wholly unacceptable”. Children’s health conditions were getting worse and becoming harder to treat as a result, they added.NHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry findsRead moreMore broadly across health and social care services in England there were signs of improvement, including more GP appointments, increased use of digital solutions and shorter waits for elective care. The report also highlighted examples of local innovation, including neighbourhood models and integrated care teams.But improvements were struggling to keep pace with rapidly rising demand for health and social care. In many areas, including mental health services, patients’ needs are also becoming more complex.Persistent inequalities across the entire health and care system mean people’s experience of care is fractured and heavily dependent on where they live and who they are, according to the report.Poorest children in England 40% more likely to be hospitalised for lung infectionsRead moreAcross all areas of the country and every part of the health and social care system, there was “unwarranted variation” in access to services, quality of care and outcomes, the CQC said.Some adults with cancer were waiting far too long to begin treatment after being diagnosed, while there remained “sustained pressure” in urgent and emergency care.But the report highlighted how children in particular were bearing the brunt of long waiting times. And, despite growing demand, health visitor and school nurse numbers were “continuing to decline”, the CQC said.It also raised concerns about regional variations in rates of children being admitted to hospital for diabetes and asthma, and sounded the alarm over particularly high rates of rotten teeth among children in some areas.UK children will be one of unhealthiest generations in decades, doctors sayRead moreDr Ronny Cheung, of the Royal College of Paediatrics and ChildHealth, said community health services existed to support some of the country’s most vulnerable children outside hospital, including those with complex conditions, developmental disorders and safeguarding needs.“Yet these children face some of the longest waits in theNHS, while waiting times for adult community services have improved. It is wholly unacceptable that more than one in four children still wait over a year for treatment, and without urgent action, too many more will be left to suffer unnecessarily.“As a paediatrician, I am sick of seeing children wait so long for support that they miss crucial opportunities to improve their health and development.”Behind the figures were children struggling at school, families pushed to breaking point and conditions becoming more complex while they wait, Cheung added.The CQC chair, Julia Neuberger, said that while some health and social care services were “working well”, improvements were not keeping pace with demand. “To repair a fracturing system, there must be a collective response,” she added.The Department of Health and Social Care said the report showed “the scale of the challenge this government inherited” when it was elected in 2024. “While the CQC recognises signs of progress on waiting lists, cancer care and general practice, patients and families rightly expect faster improvements – which is why the secretary of state has committed to go further to end corridor care, transform support for mothers and children, and deliver a new national care service,” a spokesperson added.Explore more on these topicsChildren's healthCare Quality Commission (CQC)Health policyEnglandChildrenNHSHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russell Brand raped woman even though she screamed in pain, court hears | UK news | The Guardian
description: Parents, colleagues and others encouraged her to go to police but she feared she would not be believed
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Parents, colleagues and others encouraged her to go to police but she feared she would not be believed
Content: Russell Brand (right) arriving at Southwark crown court, London, on Thursday.Photograph: James Manning/PAView image in fullscreenRussell Brand (right) arriving at Southwark crown court, London, on Thursday.Photograph: James Manning/PAUK newsRussell Brand raped woman even though she screamed in pain, court hearsParents, colleagues and others encouraged her to go to police but she feared she would not be believedEmine SinmazThu 22 Oct 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 13.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA woman told her mother that Russell Brand had raped her and “didn’t stop even when she screamed out in pain”, a court has heard.The woman also told a colleague she was “bleeding everywhere” and that Brand had shouted at her, saying, “Look what you’ve done to my fucking sheets”, Southwark crown court heard on Thursday.The woman told her parents, friends, boyfriend and a sexual health nurse about the alleged attack and several encouraged her to go to the police but she feared she would not be believed, the court was told.Brand faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. The 51-year-old denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.The court heard on Thursday from 24 witnesses connected to the woman, who alleges Brand anally raped her at his London townhouse after picking her out from a crowd at one of his standup performances at the Hammersmith Apollo in early 2009. She alleges they had consensual vaginal sex before the comedian “flipped” her over and raped her.Giving evidence over video link, a friend who had accompanied the woman to the gig said the comedian had signed off the show by saying: “If you see me out in the foyer and you think ‘I really fancy him and would like to have sex with him, but I can’t because it is Russell Brand’, you probably can … my age range is from 16 to death.”The woman’s parents said their daughter had confided in them shortly after the alleged attack and feared she had contracted HIV. In a witness statement read by the junior prosecution counsel, Suki Dhadda, the woman’s mother said: “She said he forced anal sex on her and didn’t stop even when she screamed out in pain and asked him to stop.”Her father said his daughter told him: “They were having sex, she asked him to stop, she kept saying she had been assaulted. I turned to her in the car and asked her if she asked him to stop, and she said ‘yes’ several times. It was then I said to her: ‘You have been raped, that’s rape.’”The woman’s colleague told the court the alleged victim was “ashen, greyish, and looked ill” when describing shortly after the alleged attack how Brand had “really fucking hurt” her.The colleague told the court: “She described that he got aggressive and pushed her down on the bed and she couldn’t breathe and she was trying to say stop because it was hurting her. I said: ‘Did you stay stop?’ and she said: ‘Yes, multiple times.’”Recalling the woman’s account, the colleague added: “She was bleeding everywhere, from her anus, and he shouted at her, Mr Brand, he said: ‘Look what you’ve done to my fucking sheets’ or something like that, and she was very embarrassed.”The witness said she told the woman she had been raped and encouraged her to go to the police but the woman replied: “They won’t believe me. I went to his house.”A friend of the woman also told the court that she had encouraged her to go to the police, but the alleged victim “felt it wasn’t worth it”.“She didn’t think she would be believed,” the witness said. A couple of days after the alleged attack the woman told her Brand had treated her “like an animal”. “She was in a lot of pain and asked him to stop anally raping her and he wouldn’t,” her friend said.Another friend recalled how the woman had told her that Brand called her “dirty” after the alleged rape and how “he had gone from being charming to violent and cold-hearted”.The friend added the woman’s “face was as white as a sheet” when she bumped into Brand at the Edinburgh festival in the summer after the alleged attack.In her witness statement read to the court, the friend said she was at the festival when Brand was “pinging off” the woman’s phone with messages and calls.“She was concerned that he had tracked her down because he was still pursuing her in the lead-up to that. He was becoming increasingly frustrated that she wasn’t responding to him. I could see he really want to see her and have sex with her from the using crude sexual language in the messages,” the friend said.In 2024, the woman confided in another friend about the festival encounter and said she had replied to one of Brand’s messages saying: “I wouldn’t treat a dog the way you treated me.”Another friend spoke of the toll the alleged rape had had on the woman, saying she had been a “bright, confident and bubbly girl” but the encounter with Brand had “changed her”. “It’s like she lost respect for herself after that day. She blamed herself for what happened,” the friend said in a witness statement.The woman’s former boyfriend told the court that she had not wanted to have anal sex but had “surrendered”. In cross-examination by Brand’s barrister Ian Winter KC the man was asked about a witness statement he had given in June 2025 in which he said the woman had “come round” to having anal sex.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Unsafe water, burning eyes and kerosene slicks: residents demand answers on River Taff leak | Environment | The Guardian
description: People near south Wales river were told to keep windows and doors shut after thousands of litres of kerosene from a GE Aerospace site got into the water
Author: Eben Muse
Headline: People near south Wales river were told to keep windows and doors shut after thousands of litres of kerosene from a GE Aerospace site got into the water
Content: Health officials have told people to keep away from affected parts of the River Taff.Photograph: Jeremy Inglis/AlamyView image in fullscreenHealth officials have told people to keep away from affected parts of the River Taff.Photograph: Jeremy Inglis/AlamyEnvironmentUnsafe water, burning eyes and kerosene slicks: residents demand answers on River Taff leakPeople near south Wales river were told to keep windows and doors shut after thousands of litres of kerosene from a GE Aerospace site got into the waterEben MuseThu 22 Oct 2026 13.58 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 14.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOily slicks of kerosene still appeared to be leaking into the River Taff this week, several days after a breachof thousands of litres was spotted by members of the public.The breach into the Welsh river was identified last Friday, after people reported strong chemical odours emanating from it. Natural ResourcesWales(NRW) officers arrived on site soon afterwards to identify the source of the pollution and were assisted by the south Wales fire and rescue service, which placed absorbent mats and booms to contain as much kerosene as possible.Residents along the Taff were advised to keep windows and doors closed last week, after it emerged that thousands of litres of kerosene from a GE Aerospace site in Nantgarw, Rhondda Cynon Taf had entered the river. Four kilometres (2.5 miles) of waterway were affected, according to NRW.View image in fullscreenNRW was unable to confirm what quantity of kerosene entered the river.Photograph: Natural Resources WalesGE Aerospace is a US multinational company that designs and builds military and commercial aircraft systems and engines. Its site in south Wales is among the world’s largest maintenance, repair and overhaul facilities for commercial aircraft engines, employing more than 1,350 people. In 2017 GE Aerospace was the recipient of £5m in funding from the Welsh government, intended to support innovation and sustainability in the aerospace sector.Despite early estimates of a volume of about 25,000 litres of kerosene spilled, NRW was unable to confirm what quantity entered the river, and could not comment on possible enforcement action while its investigation was under way and it gathered information.Public Health Wales advised that the community should avoid all contact with contaminated areas along the busy stretch of river, which runs parallel to many popular trails on both banks, including the Taff trail. People near the river had been complaining of sinus problems and headaches.“Kerosene vapours may be mildly irritating to the respiratory system. Our current assessment is that people who can smell kerosene may experience temporary irritation, particularly if they are exposed for prolonged periods,” said the health body.Sarah Llywelyn, who lives in a riverside home in Glan Y Llyn downstream from the GE Aerospace facility, was among those who reported the leak to NRW.“The smell was absolutely unbelievable. My eyes burned as soon as I opened our door into the garden. I knew it must have been huge because of the smell, and it’s a fast-flowing river – it was essentially unsafe from the point of contamination to Cardiff Bay. We moved here because of the river. What I want more than anything is for lessons to be learned. This should never happen again.”A visit by the Guardian to the site found oily slicks still leaking into the Taff five days after the incident began. NRW believes that the pollution has now been stopped from entering the river.An NRW spokesperson said: “Fuel that entered the drainage system before the leak was stopped by the operator could remain within parts of that network and whilst containment measures help reduce and capture pollution, they are not always able to separate all fuel from flowing water. Our work to investigate this incident and assess environmental impacts is ongoing.”Prof Steve Ormerod, from Cardiff University’s Water Research Institute, confirmed that the photos of the leaks appeared to show the kerosene still entering the waterway through the bunding (a secondary storage system, usually to catch overflows). “The Taff has been recovering from its grossly polluted past,” he said. “So this incident is a potential setback to clean water species such as salmon, dippers and kingfishers that have been recolonising the river.“Kerosene is a mixture of paraffins, naphthenes and benzene-like chemicals that risk direct toxicity to aquatic organisms, reductions in oxygen transfer across the water surface, and suffocation through impaired gill function in fishes or insects. Effects on feather waterproofing are also likely in the birds that have no choice but to enter the water to feed. Overnight rain was insufficient to raise river levels and flush the Taff, so kerosene will still be lurking in backwaters and eddies along the river.”Gerwyn and Jordan Lewis from Ynysgau farm, directly opposite the site of the main spill into the river, said they were advised by NRW that the river was unsafe for animals to drink from due to kerosene pollution, meaning that areas of the farm with access to the river could not be safely grazed.“We simply cannot take the chance of our animals becoming seriously ill or dying. Our winter feed stocks could now be depleted at an alarming rate, leaving us facing the possibility of having to purchase substantial additional feed at considerable expense.“We also operate a tourism business comprising campsite pitches and glamping accommodation, a sauna and cold plunge facilities, all beside the affected river.”A GE Aerospace spokesperson said: “The safety of our employees, neighbours and environment remains our top priority. We are continuing to work closely with Natural Resources Wales to address a fuel spill that occurred during repair work at our site on Friday 16 October. The source was identified and isolated on Friday, and containment and clean up are ongoing, with specialist teams working both on and off site.”Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentWalesRiversAerospace industryPollutionOil spillsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Raye wins 2026 Mercury prize for This Music May Contain Hope | Mercury prize | The Guardian
description: Singer who has had record-breaking Brit awards success adds to haul thanks to massively ambitious big-band album
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Singer who has had record-breaking Brit awards success adds to haul thanks to massively ambitious big-band album
Content: Raye accepts the 2026 Mercury prize.Photograph: JM Enternational/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRaye accepts the 2026 Mercury prize.Photograph: JM Enternational/Getty ImagesMercury prizeRaye wins 2026 Mercury prize for This Music May Contain HopeSinger who has had record-breaking Brit awards success adds to haul thanks to massively ambitious big-band albumBen Beaumont-ThomasMusic editorThu 22 Oct 2026 17.24 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRaye is the winner of the 2026Mercury prize, for her second studio album, This Music May Contain Hope.Her win – for a hugely ambitious 73-minute record that spanned big band jazz, power balladry, funk and more – caps an ongoing renaissance for a British singer who at one point was in the doldrums, lashing out publicly at her record label for not letting her release a studio album.Since that low in 2021, she split from that former label and found huge success with two albums: My 21st Century Blues, which won her six Brit awards – still the record for a single Brits ceremony – and This Music May Contain Hope, which topped the UK charts and contains the global hit Where Is My Husband!View image in fullscreenRaye and fellow Mercury competitor Olivia Dean, whose album The Art of Loving has spent 55 weeks in the UK Top 10Photograph: JMEnternational/Getty ImagesThe judging panel said: “Raye displays real imagination and scope in showing what an album can be, going beyond any one style or genre to realise her vision. The judges agreed that Raye’s superb album will serve as a huge inspiration for years to come.”The award, handed out yearly to the best British or Irish album as voted for by a panel of music industry figures, comes with a £25,000 prize.While This Music May Contain Hope didn’t have universally positive reviews – “there are flaws, but in fairness it pays off more often than it fails”, was the opinion of the Guardian’s pop critic Alexis Petridis – the judges hailed its “scale, structure, ambition and sheer charm”.Raye: This Music May Contain Hope review – a wildly ambitious epic of unbridled self-expressionRead moreWhere Is My Husband! proved to be a powerhouse lead single, reaching No 1 in the UK, No 6 in the US and delighting audiences globally with Raye’s witty rat-a-tat-tat delivery as she expressed her frustration at her romantic failures including “lonely acrobatics, unzipping my dress at 2am”.It adds to a strange and heartening career for the 28-year-old singer, born Rachel Keen in west London, who started out by shuttling between genres and netting hits as a guest vocalist on pop-dance singles before finally being able to let her stylistic diversity shine on her album projects.As lighthearted as songs like Where Is My Husband! are, she has also written about more serious subjects, such as a sexual assault she faced from a music producer.View image in fullscreenRaye with her award, and her live band at the Mercury prize ceremony.Photograph: JM Enternational/Getty ImagesAccepting the award at the ceremony in Newcastle, Raye said: “I cannot tell you how grateful I am to be holding this. I’m shaking, I’m jet-lagged, I’m tired, I’m grateful!”She alluded to her difficult years with her former label, saying: “Albums are so important, and not to be bitter – because I feel like I’m mostly at peace with my past – but to come from a place where it’s all about singles and chasing the next thing, I just feel so grateful to be recognised.”View image in fullscreenKing David-Ike Elechi and Stan Woodward of Knats onstage during the 2026 Mercury prize ceremony.Photograph: JM Enternational/Getty ImagesShe also talked about the central topic on the album: “Hope is a very cheesy word, especially for us British people, we don’t do that deep stuff like that, but hope is something we all need … so I hope that message comes across to anyone who needs it.”Elsewhere on the shortlist, Paul McCartney missed out in the first year he was nominated for the prize, for his reflective albumThe Boys of Dungeon Lane. In a video message, he said he was “chuffed” and “surprised” to be nominated on a shortlist alongside “such a group of really amazing artists”.Suede, who opened the ceremony by performing their stridently pro-European anthem Dancing With the Europeans, weren’t able to add a second Mercury win to their trophy cabinet, after winning for their self-titled debut in 1993, the second year the award ran.Nor could Dave, who won for his own debut album, Psychodrama, in 2019; he and McCartney were the only artists not to perform at the ceremony.Pulp – the winners in 1996 – performed for the second year in a row: last year for their nominated album More, and this year representing the all-star compilation album Help, created to raise funds for the charity War Child.Florence + the Machine now have the ignominious honour of being the Mercury’s joint highest nominee without winning, tying with Radiohead on five unconverted nominations.View image in fullscreenPulp, who won the award in 1996, performed at the ceremony as representatives of the all-star charity album HelpPhotograph: JMEnternational/Getty ImagesRaye also beat stiff competition from Olivia Dean, whose album The Art of Loving has been one of the most successful albums by anyone in the singer’s generation, spending every one of its 55 weeks since release in the UK Top 10.‘Geordie optimism is this rigorous spirit of hard graft’: Newcastle jazz band Knats break out of the north-south divideRead moreAfter losing its sponsor in 2024 and taking place in a rather low-key ceremony, the Mercury prize has repositioned itself, moving away from London to Newcastle in 2025 and scaling up in size to the city’s Utilita Arena.In its inaugural year in its new home, the Mercury was awarded to local boy Sam Fender – though Newcastle jazz band Knats, who wowed the arena crowd with virtuosic bass soloing and spoken word poetry, weren’t able to secure back-to-back Tyneside wins this year.There has been some consternation, though, that its focus is becoming more commercial than in the past – and not distinct enough from the Brit awards.View image in fullscreenFlorence Welch of Florence + The Machine, performing at the Mercury ceremony. This year marked the fifth time the group had been nominated for the award without having won it.Photograph: JMEnternational/Getty ImagesIn 2025, seven of the 12 nominated albums reached the UK Top 3, while this year six of the nominations reached No 1, and another two were Top 3 hits. All but two of the albums (Suede’s Antidepressants and the Help charity compilation) were released by or in partnership with the three major labels: Universal, Warner and Sony.Previously the UK’s independent music scene has been better represented, including in winners such as Arctic Monkeys, Dizzee Rascal, Sampha and Ezra Collective.This year’s judging panel featured musicians, broadcasters, journalists and consultants: Afrodeutsche, Danielle Perry, Jamie Cullum, Lea Stonhill, MistaJam, Phil Alexander, Sian Eleri, Sophie Williams and Will Hodgkinson, with Jeff Smith as chair.Explore more on these topicsMercury prizePop and rockAwards and prizesRayenewsShareReuse this content

title: James Bond finalists to screen-test for role this week – reports | James Bond | The Guardian
description: Actors in the mix to play 007 in Denis Villeneuve’s installment include Callum Turner and Jack Lowden
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: Actors in the mix to play 007 in Denis Villeneuve’s installment include Callum Turner and Jack Lowden
Content: Callum Turner and Jack Lowden are said to be in the running for the Bond role.Composite: Gisela Schober/Getty Images,Matt Baron/BEI/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCallum Turner and Jack Lowden are said to be in the running for the Bond role.Composite: Gisela Schober/Getty Images,Matt Baron/BEI/REX/ShutterstockJames BondJames Bond finalists to screen-test for role this week – reportsActors in the mix to play 007 in Denis Villeneuve’s installment include Callum Turner and Jack LowdenAdrian HortonThu 22 Oct 2026 17.16 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 21.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe search for the nextJames Bondmay finally be nearing its end: according to reports, a very select group of actors will screen-test to become the next British agent 007 this weekend.According to theHollywood ReporterandVariety, citing several sources, a group of actors reportedly including Callum Turner and Slow Horses’ Jack Lowden, will appear in front of cameras as the secret agent this weekend in London.The tests supposedly include three elements: stunts, camera presence and dialogue. Reports vary that between three and five actors are finalists for the role, which was vacated by Daniel Craig after 2021’s No Time to Die. Despite speculation to the contrary, Sinners’ Jack O’Connell and Wuthering Heights star Jacob Elordi are not testing, according to the Hollywood Reporter.The Bond effect? How MI6 fascinates spy watchers around the worldRead moreDune film-makerDenis Villeneuveis set to direct the next installment of the Bond franchise for Amazon MGM studios, which bought the series rights as part of an $8.45bn (£6.9bn) deal in 2022. The Peaky Blinders writer Steven Knight will pen the script.The company, which paid more than $1bn last year to wrest “creative control” from the Broccoli family, has neither confirmed nor denied the reports, and referred the Hollywood Reporter to its earlier statement: “The search for the nextJames Bondis under way. While we don’t plan to comment on specific details during the casting process, we’re excited to share more news with 007 fans as soon as the time is right.”In April of this year, Amazon film executivesurgedfans to exercise patience in waiting for the casting announcement, citing an abundance of caution in making the closely watched decision. “I know you’re all wondering when we’re going to announce who’s playing James Bond,” said Courtenay Valenti, the company’s head of film. “Don’t get too excited. Please know that we’re taking the time to do this with care and deep respect. It is the dream of a lifetime for all of us to bring audiences this next chapter, and it’s a responsibility we don’t take lightly.”Villeneuve, a “diehard Bond fan”, has said the opportunity to add to the beloved franchise is what drew him away from the Dune franchise that has consumed the better part of a decade of his life.“I said, ‘Maybe it’s a good idea to go back to this project, not out of nostalgia, not because I miss it, but the opposite – I’m tired of it,’” hetold Empireof Dune: Messiah, which will premiere this December. “I want to make sure that I will be severe with the material. That I will not be complacent,” he said. “I thought, ‘When it’s done, I need a very powerful rocket to pull me away from Arrakis.’ When I was asked to do the next Bond, I said: ‘OK, this is what I need.’”It’s been more than 20 years since the last full screen test for Bond; future Superman Henry Cavill was reported to be a finalist, but the role eventually went to Craig, who first appeared in 2006’s Casino Royale.Speculation over the new Bond has intensified in the months since Villeneuve was revealed as director in 2025. The film is still reportedly positioned for a 2028 release.Explore more on these topicsJames BondDenis VilleneuveAction and adventure filmsThrillersnewsShareReuse this content

title: What makes a good town? Here are five key ingredients | Regeneration | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham pledged a new lease of life for Britain’s high streets. We look at how he can achieve it
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: Andy Burnham pledged a new lease of life for Britain’s high streets. We look at how he can achieve it
Content: Jaywick Sands in Essex, Barnsley in South Yorkshire, and Harpenden in Hertfordshire.Composite: Martin Godwin/John Morrison/Richard Saker/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenJaywick Sands in Essex, Barnsley in South Yorkshire, and Harpenden in Hertfordshire.Composite: Martin Godwin/John Morrison/Richard Saker/Guardian DesignTown and countryRegenerationWhat makes a good town? Here are five key ingredientsAndy Burnham pledged a new lease of life for Britain’s high streets. We look at how he can achieve itSave high street with higher online sales taxes, PM urgedMiddleton’s revival could be blueprint for other townsRichard PartingtonandMichael GoodierThu 22 Oct 2026 08.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the road to Downing Street,Andy Burnhampromised a new dawn for Britain’s towns and high streets.For too long places outside the big cities had been “forgotten or written off”, he argued after the Makerfield byelection. To help towns like those in his constituency, he said his government would make sure that the places Westminster had neglected would now get fairness.Four times more people live in Britain’s towns than in cities. Since the turn of the millennium, big cities andmore prosperous towns have grown significantly fasterthan weaker local economies. In Manchester, the population rose byalmost a third, amid arenaissance in Cottonopolisthat its former mayor capitalised on before entering No 10.In sharp contrast, towns have been growing more slowly than cities on average, and are ageing faster as well. Some are in population decline, including Barrow-in-Furness in Cumbria (6%), Peterlee in County Durham (11%) and Rishton in Lancashire (13%).To turn things around, experts say the prime minister will need to nurture the ingredients of local economic success. Here we chart five of the critical components.Job opportunities and the drivers of deprivationA map showing proportion of neighbourhoods in each local authority that are among the 10% most deprived in EnglandRoughly every five years official estimates of local deprivation in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are made using a range of statistics for an index of multiple deprivation.Each metric is critical for a town’s success: income, employment, education, health, crime, housing and the living environment.Jaywick Sands, near Clacton-on-Sea in Essex, has led the rankings in England since 2010. The least deprived neighbourhood is in the town of Harpenden, near St Albans in Hertfordshire.View image in fullscreenBrooklands estate in the seaside town of Jaywick Sands, Essex. The area is the most deprived in England, according to the UK government.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianMost parts of the country have pockets of deprivation. But there are also clear patterns: towns, particularly in the north of England, the Midlands and incoastal areas, typically have the highest share of the most deprived neighbourhoods.When it comes to the vitality of a town, income and employment levels are critical for supporting high streets. Boston in Lincolnshire has the lowest level of resident earnings in Great Britain, with people earnings about half as much as those in St Albans. Employment levels are lowest in Gravesham in Kent, followed by Blaenau Gwent in south Wales and Hyndburn in Lancashire.Local financial clout and the power to use itA line graph on local government spending powerAfter more than a decade of austerity, local authorities across the UK lack the financial firepower to meet rising demand for critical public services and to support economic activity.The low point was reached in about 2019, when local spending power in England had been cut by about a quarter from 2010 levels. Analysis by the Institute for Government shows the most deprived local authorities ended up with significantly deeper cuts than affluent ones.Funding levels have started to recover but will take until at least 2028-29 to return to 2010 levels after inflation is taken into account.Transport connections and public servicesA bar graph showing reductions in local bus journeys in England by regionTransport and other physical infrastructure – including housing, superfast broadband, water and power – are central to the prosperity of a place. High standards of healthcare and education provision are also vital. Without these ingredients, households will struggle to reach their local high street or travel to work. Businesses will also lack access to a skilled, healthy workforce.During the 2010s more than one in four bus services werecut in England. Rural communities and towns suffered most. Subsidies have been cut, and – as with trains – fares have risen. Burnham has made public control over buses and cheaper fares a priority. Official figures showWarrington, the prime minister’s home town, had the biggest fall in miles travelled by bus since 2010 of any English local authority.Regions outside London and the south-east have also had significantlylower levels of investment.High street vacancy ratesHigh street rent and vacancy rates in England and WalesRetail accounts for 5% of the UK economy and less than a 10th of employment. But its visible position on the high street gives it outsize influence on public perception about local economic performance.Over the past two decades the internet has transformed the high street.Online spendinghas rocketed from less than 3% of total retail sales in Great Britain in 2006 to more than 25%. As a consequence, many mainstream shops have either closed or been replaced by vape shops, bookmakers and barbers. Official data showshigh street retail employmenthas fallen most in the East Midlands.View image in fullscreenGlass Works Square, Barnsley, South Yorkshire. Retailers have suffered from weaker levels of consumer demand amid the cost of living crisis.Photograph: John Morrison/AlamyRetailers have suffered from weaker levels of consumer demand amid the cost of living crisis – compounding the challenge in places where households are feeling the pinch most. Closures have been most pronounced in the north of England, the Midlands and deprived coastal towns.Analysis by the Centre for Cities shows places where retailers pay higher rents (which it said could reflect resilient consumer demand) typically have the lowest vacancy rates. At one end of the scale is London, with high rents and 7% of shops with shutters drawn. At the other is Newport, where despite low costs, 19% of all units lie empty.The arts, culture and community cohesionLocal government spending on culture per person by year 2010-25 at 2025 pricesSocial capital – the strength of communities, relationships and trust – is a key ingredient of economic success, not just a nice to have. However, Britain has suffered ahollowing out of the associations, clubs, organisations and infrastructurethat were once the beating hearts of communities.Local council spending on culture, sport and other related areas such as tourism and libraries has nosedived since 2010. Towns and rural areas have faced bigger cuts than big cities. Figures show councils spent a net £92.84 per person on culture in 2010-11 after adjusting for inflation. That has halved – last year a net £46.43 a head went on culture and sport.Looking at total rather than net spending reveals the areas that have cut the most. Hart district council spent £82.36 a head in 2010-11 – that has since been cut to £8.75. Havant’s spending went from £40.04 a head in 2010-11 to £5.66 in 2025-26.While the vast majority of councils have cut arts spending, others have increased it. Mole Valley spent £109.02 last year on culture and related services, up from £58.16 in 2010-11.Explore more on these topicsRegenerationTown and countryCommunitiesLocal governmentPublic sector cutsUK cost of living crisisUK unemployment and employment statisticsNorth-south dividefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Race to rearm: Telford gun hall brings tank barrel production back to the UK | Manufacturing sector | The Guardian
description: Defence secretary says Britain must manufacture at scale as Germany’s Rheinmetall opens Midlands factory
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Defence secretary says Britain must manufacture at scale as Germany’s Rheinmetall opens Midlands factory
Content: Wes Streeting, defence secretary, inspects the equipment used by Rheinmetall to produce large-calibre weapons.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWes Streeting, defence secretary, inspects the equipment used by Rheinmetall to produce large-calibre weapons.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianManufacturing sectorRace to rearm: Telford gun hall brings tank barrel production back to the UKDefence secretary says Britain must manufacture at scale as Germany’s Rheinmetall opens Midlands factoryJasper JollyThu 22 Oct 2026 12.59 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 13.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor the last 20 years, Britain was unable to put a barrel on its tanks without buying from abroad. Relying on foreign allies seemed like a reasonable choice during years of relative security (for wealthy countries at least) after the end of the cold war.ButRussia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022has changed the calculation – and prompted ascramble to rearmamong European countries, including the UK.Evidence of that scramble was on display on Thursday in Shropshire, where the UK defence secretary,Wes Streeting, opened a factory hastily constructed by Germany’s Rheinmetall to make barrels for artillery and British tanks.Such was the urgency that Rheinmetall’s chief executive, Armin Papperger, said the company had started investment “off the back of a handshake” before Christmas last year with Gen Sir Roly Walker, who leads theBritish armyas chief of the general staff, without waiting for a formal contract.Eight months later, production of the first barrels at the factory inTelfordhas started. Papperger said he was in talks to produce more ammunition in the UK as well, with a decision due in the next six to eight months.Streeting said: “It is not enough to simply out-innovate those who would wish us harm – though we must. We must also out-produce them too. Because advantage increasingly belongs to those who can manufacture at scale and field the capability fastest.”View image in fullscreenFrom left: Armin Papperger, chief executive of Rheinmetall, Wes Streeting and Gen Sir Roly Walker.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThe factory takes a 3.2 tonne, 8-metre cylinder of specialised steel alloy and drills a hole through it to make the barrel shape. The surfaces are then honed to remove imperfections, before another turning tool adds spiral rifling to add to artillery accuracy. A specialised machine – one of only two in the world – increases the pressure inside the barrel to about 15,000 times the air at sea level to harden it for the explosive power needed to propel shells as far as 30km (18 miles).The Ukraine war will go down in history as the moment when militaries woke up to thebrutal new reality of drone warfare. But for all the focus on uncrewed weapons, Walker said they cannot rival more traditional armaments for sheer firepower.“InUkraine, we know that both sides fire tens of thousands of rounds of artillery ammunition every day, and that generates a weight of fire and levels of lethality across the battlefield that drones alone cannot replicate,” said Walker, in a speech at the factory opening.He said it had been “sad” when the UK was unable to continue centuries of artillery manufacture that had lasted through the Napoleonic wars, two world wars and the cold war. Much of that work was carried out at the Royal Arsenal in Woolwich, which opened in the 17th century (and whose workers set up a football club that moved to north London in 1913). Yet production ceased in 1967, with the work scattered first around the country and then in some cases moving abroad.The new Telford gun hall will bring that capability back to the UK, albeit starting with production for guns for German-made, self-propelled, remote-control howitzers that take Nato-standard 155mm ammunition. However, in the future it will also be able to make slightly smaller tank barrels that use 120mm rounds. These include the Challenger 3 tank, which is now going through final testing, and a British version of the remote-control howitzer planned for after May 2028.View image in fullscreenGen Sir Roly Walker, chief of the defence staff, peers down a 155mm artillery barrel during a tour of the new gun hall in Telford.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThe factory will be able to make 245 barrels a year, plus 50 breeches – the part at the base of the barrel – although Papperger said annual capacity could theoretically be expanded to as much as 1,000 within four or five years, but only if the orders came in. Exports may also be on the agenda.Papperger added that Nato allies could manage with smaller output than Russia and its client states because of their higher quality. A Russian barrel will be able to fire about 500 times before breaking, while the products from Telford should survive as many as 4,000 shots, he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRoyal Navy lacks resources to counter Russian threat in high north, MPs warnRead moreThe Telford investment followed anagreement in 2024between Keir Starmer, then prime minister, and his German counterpart, Olaf Scholz. It was part of a wide-ranging pact for the two largest military spenders in Europe to work together more closely.Rheinmetall employs about 685 people in Telford, although only 35 will work in the gun hall, rising to 100 when it is at full capacity – hardly enough to kickstart the“reindustrialisation” of Britaindesired by Andy Burnham. The bulk of the workers in Telford make the Challenger and Boxer armoured vehicles in a joint venture with Britain’s key arms maker, BAE Systems.Rheinmetall has been among the biggest beneficiaries of the massive increase in European spending on defence and in supplying arms to Ukraine. US intelligence services in 2024 reportedlyfoiled a Russian plot to assassinate Pappergerin apparent retaliation against the company’s production of weapons for Kyiv.The German company’s market value has risen from about €4.2bn (£3.5bn) in the days before Russia’s invasion to €47bn on Wednesday, though it has dropped back from a peak of nearly double that last year. Rheinmetall and other European defence companies, including BAE Systems and the British jet engine maker Rolls-Royce, have benefited particularly from European governments eager to reduce reliance on the US arms industry at a time when the White House has shown itself willing to divert supplies to its own militaries ahead of allies.Papperger said more governments were saying they wanted control over their weapons production. That could help to mollify Donald Trump, the US president, who has shown himself willing to undermine previously firm alliances.“To be a strong partner, you need strong armies,” said Papperger. “But on the other side, you need a strong industry. And this is what we do at the moment. We build up the industry.”Explore more on these topicsManufacturing sectorDefence policyBritish armyWeapons technologyTelfordMilitaryWes StreetingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: With albums under threat, Raye’s Mercury win is a triumph for grand statements | Mercury prize | The Guardian
description: Her winning album has its longueurs, but there’s something heartening about its risk-taking – and the Mercury prize needs big bold records like this to stay relevant
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Her winning album has its longueurs, but there’s something heartening about its risk-taking – and the Mercury prize needs big bold records like this to stay relevant
Content: Raye with the 2026 Mercury prize.Photograph: JMEnternational/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRaye with the 2026 Mercury prize.Photograph: JMEnternational/Getty ImagesMercury prizeWith albums under threat, Raye’s Mercury win is a triumph for grand statementsAlexis PetridisHer winning album has its longueurs, but there’s something heartening about its risk-taking – and the Mercury prize needs big bold records like this to stay relevantThu 22 Oct 2026 19.18 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 19.31 EDTShareIt was generally agreed that last year’sMercury prizeceremony was a vast improvement on its predecessor. In fairness, the bar was set pretty low: hosted without an audience – or indeed a corporate sponsor – in what looked like a broom cupboard at Abbey Road, the 2024 Mercury prize seemed to suggest the whole jig was up.Instead, the event was relocated to Newcastle’s Utilita Arena, the general public rather than record label grandees provided the audience, and something approaching a sense of genuine excitement attended the event.And yet somehow, said excitement didn’t sustain. The announcement of this year’s nominees seemed to be greeted with something approaching a shrug: a smattering of headlines noting that Paul McCartney had been nominated for the first time, aged 84, and that was about it.Raye wins 2026 Mercury prize for This Music May Contain HopeRead moreYou wonder what the problem is. Not the albums nominated, all of which had plenty to commend them, from the punk-y “Geordie noir” jazz of Knats’ A Great Day in Newcastle, to the appealingly off-message take on pop proffered by former Little Mix star Jade on her solo debut, That’s Showbiz Baby!Perhaps the Mercury shot themselves in the foot by giving the 2025 award to local boy Sam Fender’s People Watching, an album that’s exceptionally good, but was already hugely successful, clearly not in need of any kind of profile or sales boost (Fender gave his prize money away to the Music Venue Trust).That People Watching actually won the Mercury is easy to forget, a minor consideration lost amid its platinum sales figures and string of hit singles, one of which went on to spend nearlysix monthsat No 1.Perhaps people are just losing interest in albums in an age defined by streaming, a means of distribution that privileges single tracks and playlists? More than half of the 40 biggest-selling albums of 2026 thus far are either greatest hits collections or longstanding back catalogue classics; that chart contains only seven albums that actually came out this year, which hardly suggests a widespread hunger for new releases in the format.One of those, though, was Raye’s This Music May Contain Hope,the winner of this year’s Mercury. It was an album that spawned a single huge hit single – the retro soul of Where Is My Husband! – but that nevertheless made spawning a huge hit single seem beside the point: 73 minutes and 17 tracks long, divided into four sections, it’s an album that flies in the face of the suggestion that no one really listens to albums from soup to nuts any more.Its saga of romantic despair, which stylistically leaps from soul to swing to house music to 50s easy listening schmaltz, is clearly intended to be consumedin toto.Not everything the singer-songwriter tries over its lengthy course works. Fabulous songs – The WhatsApp Shakespeare, Beware.. The South London Lover Boy, the Hans Zimmer-assisted Click Clack Symphony – coexist with moments where it slips into self-indulgence: Fields offers a lengthy dialogue between the singer and her grandad, and the closing track, Fin, lasts six minutes, four of which consist ofRayereading out the album’s production credits.Still, the highlights are hugely impressive, and there’s something to be said for the degree of risk-taking involved, given the risk-averse tenor of the times.Raye: This Music May Contain Hope review – a wildly ambitious epic of unbridled self-expressionRead moreMoreover, choosing it as the Mercury winner sends out a defensive signal. This is what an award that has occasionally seemed surplus to requirements now exists in order to celebrate: the grand statement, the right for artists to indulge themselves at length in a climate that favours short and sharp releases.But after two years in a row of awarding No 1 hit albums, in future will the judging panel see fit to award grand statements from underground artists too, or only to A-listers?Explore more on these topicsMercury prizeRayePop and rockAwards and prizescommentShareReuse this content

title: Ali G: Who Iz I? review – Sacha Baron Cohen’s high-stakes satire punches up and down with spectacular bad taste | Movies | The Guardian
description: Baron Cohen’s live-ammo prankster is back, 20 years on, but has to battle with his own irrelevance in search of big laughs and the approval of a new generation
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Baron Cohen’s live-ammo prankster is back, 20 years on, but has to battle with his own irrelevance in search of big laughs and the approval of a new generation
Content: ‘Blunders with the semi-intentional force of an XL bully into the issue of whether jokes are still allowed’ … Sacha Baron Cohen in Ali G: Who Iz I?Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Blunders with the semi-intentional force of an XL bully into the issue of whether jokes are still allowed’ … Sacha Baron Cohen in Ali G: Who Iz I?Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyMoviesReviewAli G: Who Iz I? review – Sacha Baron Cohen’s high-stakes satire punches up and down with spectacular bad tasteBaron Cohen’s live-ammo prankster is back, 20 years on, but has to battle with his own irrelevance in search of big laughs and the approval of a new generationExclusive: Republican leader embarrassed by film says he plays to sue Sacha Baron Cohen: ‘A liar and a pervert’Peter BradshawThu 22 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you liked Sacha Baron Cohen’s Ali G the first time around, you’ll like this less; if you disliked it, you’ll dislike this more; if you suspected it was racist, you’ll be more emboldened to say so – especially as Baron Cohen has dreamed up a whole new character apparently to pre-empt and mock precisely that objection. Broad and crass as it often is – in fact always is – this Ali G sequel is sometimes funny: the athletic vigour of our hero’s pranking and punking is like the umpteenth Jackass film at which you might find yourself laughing, and Baron Cohen blunders with the semi-intentional force of an XL bully into the issue of whether jokes are still allowed.Republican leader embarrassed by Ali G film says he plans to sue Sacha Baron Cohen: ‘A liar and a pervert’Read moreUnlike the first film,Ali G in Da Housefrom 2002, this is not a full written-through narrative. It is basically another live-ammo series of hoaxes with some spectacular bad taste perpetrated upon the deserving and less deserving; it satirises the shamelessness of anti-woke free speech martyrs, punching up and down with grossout cringe, and the targets include some big names who shouldn’t be revealed here. There are two other subordinate characters: Erran Morad, a sinister Mossad/IDF officer turned US security consultant (who appeared inBaron Cohen’s Who Is America? TV series), and a new figure: Dr Nira Cain-N’Degrocello, a grotesquely supercilious white liberal who is the self-appointed scourge of cultural appropriation. The dupes are built into a big silly climax fabricated with body doubles and (presumably) covert reshooting.The insurmountable problem is that the film keeps having to tell you who is and isn’t “in on it”: at the beginning, over the closing credits at the end and even briefly in the middle of the action. Well, Ali G was from so very long ago, and even the high-water mark of Baron Cohen’s Borat popularity was quite long ago, and the online media scene now so fragmented that … yes … people have forgotten, a whole new generation doesn’t know. People really don’t recognise him.The high concept is that Ali is now washed up, short of money and unpopular, and old-school media figure that he is, he disapproves of a plan by his heavily pregnant partner Julie (Morgana Robinson) to launch an OnlyFans account. But on trying to sell his fax machine in a Staines high street pawn shop, an old fax chunters out of it with an offer from HBO for a new show. Overexcited, Ali and Julie head off to the US to sucker some people in the traditional style; the smallscreen setup blown up to high-def cinematic proportions. His fictional woke tormentor decides to take him down and, by employing the Israeli hardman, tries to convince credulous and aggressive Republicans that Ali is a Mexican terrorist whose baby must be prevented at all costs from being born on US soil. The movie does make a few people look silly, yes, although Baron Cohen doesn’t land a huge punch on a big name the way he did in the Borat sequel.So who iz Ali G and what iz the point of trundling him out again? The first film implied he was once a Robert Smith-type goth, but that is now forgotten about. Interestingly, one person who this film doesn’t allude to is Tim Westwood, the BBC Radio 1 hip-hop DJ and son of the Bishop of Peterborough whose speech mannerisms were held to be one influence on Baron Cohen’s great creation, and proof positive that white people did indeed patronisingly ape a street way of speaking.Westwood’s subsequent all-too-unfunny history, perhaps, doesn’t mesh with trying to revive Ali G now as comedy IP. The movie outings of Ricky Gervais’s David Brent and Steve Coogan’s Alan Partridge worked better because they could more plausibly represent the melancholy of getting older and irrelevant. Ali G feels older in the wrong way, and the On-the-Buses humour with Julie is tired. The best bits will be available on TikTok and Instagram reels soon enough.Ali G: Who Iz I? is out on 22 October in Australia and 23 October in the UK and USExplore more on these topicsFilmAli G: Who Iz ISacha Baron CohenComedy filmsComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Flo & Joan: With Feeling review – sisters turn an old rock setlist into hilariously neurotic songs | Comedy | The Guardian
description: Richly wrought lyrical wit and sumptuous harmonies enhance the duo’s clever new show – along with plenty of backchat
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Richly wrought lyrical wit and sumptuous harmonies enhance the duo’s clever new show – along with plenty of backchat
Content: ‘Bring back shame’ … Nicola and Rosie Dempsey AKA Flo & Joan.View image in fullscreen‘Bring back shame’ … Nicola and Rosie Dempsey AKA Flo & Joan.ComedyReviewFlo & Joan: With Feeling review – sisters turn an old rock setlist into hilariously neurotic songsShepherd’s Bush Empire, LondonRichly wrought lyrical wit and sumptuous harmonies enhance the duo’s clever new show – along with plenty of backchatBrian LoganThu 22 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe last time Flo & Joan played Shepherd’s Bush Empire, they found a setlist on stage left by beloved indie-rock band the Feeling on the previous night. It made the sisters contemplate their own relationship to the music industry. AreFlo & Joana proper band or doomed for ever to remain “musical comedy”? The problem with which, they deadpan here, is that “no one takes it seriously”. Cue this new show, its structure inspired by that chance discovery. Tonight, the duo play a suite of new songs that, title by title, matches the setlist of the band who preceded them four years ago.And so goes the first half of With Feeling, which by turns delivers on and subverts that challenge – and proves handsomely entertaining either way. In the sisters’ hands, Fill My Little World becomes a neurotic number about the surfeit of stuff (cheap food, fast fashion, AI slop). Never Be Lonely returns to a favoured topic, Flo & Joan’s toxic co-dependency – with an added sight gag involving Joan (AKA Rosie Dempsey)’s questionable trumpet skills. Further numbers address the risks of poor punctuation and the need, in a society giddy on unfiltered self-expression, to “bring back shame”.Ilford Boy review – Barbra Streisand teaches teen to smile about the way we areRead moreElsewhere, those secondhand titles inspire bits of business or bad puns rather than whole new songs. That’s just as much fun: Flo & Joan are more expansive on stage than they used to be, amusing one another very infectiously as they navigate – via a wide array of musical styles, sibling backchat and surprise interventions – to the end of their setlist stunt.Then comes act two, in which they unleash their rock band fantasies (leathers, bandanas, drumkit) on some well-loved numbers from their back catalogue: the one about social gaffes and the eternal cringe they engender (The Rest of My Life); the nonsense spoof folk song Lady In the Woods. As ever with Flo & Joan, you get richly wrought lyrical wit, sumptuous harmonies and musical surprises – this time with a droll top layer of bathetic rock posturing. A proper band, they may never be – for which, when improper is this much fun, we should all be grateful.On tour until 12 DecemberExplore more on these topicsComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Super Graphic Spectacular review – Chappell Roan dazzles at her gloriously gay mini-festival | Chappell Roan | The Guardian
description: With performances by Christina Aguilera, Lola Young and Tinashe, the pop star brings a colorful vision to life in support of LGBTQ+ charities
Author: Emma Madden
Headline: With performances by Christina Aguilera, Lola Young and Tinashe, the pop star brings a colorful vision to life in support of LGBTQ+ charities
Content: Chappell Roan and Christina Aguilera performing at the Super Graphic Spectacular in Los Angeles.Photograph: Izzy NuzzoView image in fullscreenChappell Roan and Christina Aguilera performing at the Super Graphic Spectacular in Los Angeles.Photograph: Izzy NuzzoChappell RoanReviewSuper Graphic Spectacular review – Chappell Roan dazzles at her gloriously gay mini-festivalShrine Auditorium, Los AngelesWith performances by Christina Aguilera, Lola Young and Tinashe, the pop star brings a colorful vision to life in support of LGBTQ+ charitiesEmma MaddenThu 22 Oct 2026 14.52 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 16.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAtChappell Roan’s Super Graphic Spectacular, the sincerely camp pop star imagines a world where the most vulnerable among us aren’t wielded as scapegoats, and where life can be good, so long as we are good to one another.That better world takes the form of a two-night extravaganza at Los Angeles’s Shrine Auditorium, part kiki ball, part fabulous revue, celebrating the first anniversary of theMidwest Princess Project, the non-profit Roan founded in 2025 to support transgender youth and LGBTQ+ communities.‘We’re at a crisis point’: Chappell Roan, Shirley Manson and Eli on playing Olivia Rodrigo’s women-led festivalRead moreNamed after her breakout album, The Rise and Fall of a Midwest Princess, the non-profit has raised more than $800,000 and supported more than 60 organizations in its first year. Its work extends the promise at the heart of Roan’s music: that queer people, particularly those who grew up feeling estranged from their surroundings, can find somewhere to belong. For an artist whose rise has been inseparable from the extravagant performance of identity, the event offers a way to translate that feeling of collective recognition into practical support.The Shrine Auditorium, with a capacity of about 6,300, is at least 10 times smaller than the crowds Roan usually plays to. The bill, however, is hardly modest. Pop starsLola YoungandTinasheshare the stage with drag acts and burlesque performers whose influence on Roan’s gleefully excessive presentation is unmistakable. Hosting the festivities isCaleb Hearon, everyone’s favorite algorithm-touted gay guy. “Why’s a man here? It feels like Chappell doing Make-A-Wish,” he jokes at the beginning of the night.View image in fullscreenLola Young performs at Super Graphic Spectacular.Photograph: DusanaOn the first of the two nights, straight men are in the minority. They dangle from the arms of their fabulous girlfriends, who wear sequins and cowboy hats, like accessories themselves, dressed in black bandanas and Spider-Man tees. Both groups queue for the same bathroom. “Restrooms are non-binary tonight,” a security attendant announces. Roan has not skimped on a single detail.She has transformed the Shrine into a rococo burlesque ballroom, its gilded scrollwork set against great, swooping red velvet curtains.Blaine Petrovia, the night’s opening act, slides down a tall pole at the center of the stage, executing extravagant, sensual flourishes in a slutty circus routine.There is hardly a pause between the night’s five acts as Hearon ushers performers on and offstage, vamping about straight men (why are they all fake photographers?) and straight women (ditto, but witches?).Lola Young, the first of the night’s two guest singers, takes the stage in what might be called normal-people drag, looking a little out of place. She performs just three songs, closing with her hit Messy. An extraordinary vocalist still early in her career, Young has yet to master stage presence or crowd management, though her awkwardness remains charming, much as it did whenPinkPantheressused to sheepishly carry a bag on stage.The house band remains the same throughout, presumably to lend the night some cohesion, but Roan’s two guest singers struggle to distinguish themselves from it. The coherence of Roan’s universe is also its limitation: the show is so thoroughly organized around her sensibility that its glammed-up, exaggerated arrangements don’t quite work for everyone. Tinashe, the night’s second guest singer, is a case in point.Tinashe’s latest album, for my money one of the best of the year, is supremely chic. Here, the band distorts its sleekness into chintz. It’s a testament to Tinashe’s deftness as a performer that she rises to the occasion, delivering Roan-filtered versions of her songs with ease, but the crowd doesn’t quite respond in kind. When she singsNobody Wanna Dance Anymore, the audience largely proves her right. Devastatingly, that is one of the only two (two!) songs Tinashe is allotted.View image in fullscreenRoan performing at Super Graphic Spectacular.Photograph: Izzy NuzzoThe space made for Roan proves worthwhile when the headliner launches into an extraordinary hour-and-a-half set. It confirms her status as one of the greatest performers in pop, and possibly in any genre, working today. She emerges relatively understated, by her standards, in a gray gown, with a long red fishtail woven into her hair.Roan’s world is one of ballroom, drag, glam rock, girlhood splendor and sex. She hiccups her way through Midwest Princess hits – Femininomenon, Casual and Super Graphic Ultra Modern Girl – without a hair out of place.By now, Roan’s production is so perfected that the cracks that peek through tonight feel graciously illuminating. Several songs into her set, she begins to look noticeably nervous, taking swigs from her lilac Stanley cup, forgetting lyrics and smiling diffidently. “I have a surprise,” she announces, telling the crowd that she is about to bring out a guest who has “paved the way”. Cyndi Lauper? I think. Madonna, if we’re being incredibly ambitious.Cyndi Lauper on fun, fashion and freedom of expression: ‘We have braces on our brains’Read moreThenChristina Aguileraappears in black lingerie, and Roan, who has spent the evening functioning with the precision of the well-oiled Femininomenon she is, suddenly becomes a giggling fan. Aguilera sings Beautiful, accompanied by piano, while Roan watches from the bench in disbelief.There is something especially moving about hearing a song you have taken for granted, through sheer ubiquity, suddenly acquire a new resonance. As Aguilera sings Beautiful to a predominantly queer audience, the familiar becomes elemental again. “Words won’t bring you down.”Roan appears charmingly nervous as the two duet her indie-folk balladCoffee, forgetting her words again and regaining her composure only after Aguilera leaves the stage. Then she becomes the slick, precise performer again, leading the crowd into the YMCA’s sexier, uncloseted cousin, Hot to Go!She closes with the song that traces her escape from her conservative Missouri upbringing into a world of her own making. InLos Angeles, surrounded by fabulous gays, Pink Pony Club needs little explanation. Pink confetti bursts overhead, and the fantasy she once sang about is no longer somewhere else. It is here.Explore more on these topicsChappell RoanPop and rockLos AngelesLola YoungLGBTQ+ rightsElectronic musicChristina Aguileralive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: We will make the net-zero transition work for Britain – approving the Jackdaw gasfield is part of the plan | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Protecting jobs and strengthening energy security in the short term does not mean wavering on Labour’s deep commitment to a cleaner, greener future, says UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Author: Andy Burnham
Headline: Protecting jobs and strengthening energy security in the short term does not mean wavering on Labour’s deep commitment to a cleaner, greener future, says UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Content: From left, Douglas Alexander, Miatta Fahnbulleh and John Healey at the St Fergus gas terminal following the announcement on the Jackdaw gasfield, Peterhead, 21 October 2026.Photograph: Paul Reid/PAView image in fullscreenFrom left, Douglas Alexander, Miatta Fahnbulleh and John Healey at the St Fergus gas terminal following the announcement on the Jackdaw gasfield, Peterhead, 21 October 2026.Photograph: Paul Reid/PAOpinionGasWe will make the net-zero transition work for Britain – approving the Jackdaw gasfield is part of the planAndy BurnhamProtecting jobs and strengthening energy security in the short term does not mean wavering on Labour’s deep commitment to a cleaner, greener futureAndy Burnham vows UK will hit net zero target despite Jackdaw gasfield approvalThu 22 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 14.01 EDTShareOn Wednesday, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, gave the go-ahead for gas production to begin at theJackdaw gasfieldin the North Sea. This has been the subject of fierce debate for many years, with strong views on both sides. I want to explain what the decision means and how it fits with Britain’s climate commitments.At a time of acute global instability, it makes sense to responsibly use our resources here at home. Gas from this field will begin heating our homes and powering our businesses this winter. In the longer term, it will significantly strengthen our energy security byincreasing domestic gas production by about 6%and support the UK’s energy supply for more than a decade. Wednesday’s decision will also protect hundreds of jobs in Scotland and add almost £3bn to the UK economy over the lifetime of the project.There has been much speculation about what this announcement means for Britain’s commitment to addressing the climate crisis. I want to be clear that our determination is unwavering. The simple truth is that even as we pursue our ambitious target ofnet zero by 2050, we will need oil and gas for years to come as a bridge to that clean-energy future. And imported gas has a higher carbon footprint than gas produced at home. The transition to net zero is a process, not a moment. I want Britain to make that transition on our terms: reducing our dependence on foreign fossil fuels, supporting good jobs and growing our economy so we can help people with the cost of living.I know this news will be warmlywelcomed in Aberdeenand by oil and gas workers across Scotland. Their jobs support families, businesses and entire communities. Yet, like many others, their industry has suffered from deindustrialisation, with too little thought given by politicians to the places left behind. I will not be so careless with people’s lives. Our oil and gas workers have powered our nation for decades, and they will continue to play a key role for decades to come. Last week, I promised the Scottish people that we wouldreindustrialise their nation. I believe the transition to clean energy represents the best chance we will ever get of making that happen. I am determined to ensure that the next generation of energy jobs is created across Scotland and all nations of the UK.That is why, alongside the decision on Jackdaw, we are establishing anenergy wealth fund– something that, frankly, should have happened more than 40 years ago. It will begin with an initial £2bn and allow us to convert future North Sea oil and gas tax revenues into clean-energy programmes across the country. This investment in renewable energy will enable us to substantially delink gas and electricity prices by the end of this parliament and bring down bills in the long term.This government is taking a pragmatic approach that supports our oil and gas industry today, while driving the growth of the clean-energy industries of tomorrow. We are also making a sustained effort to bring energy costs down over the next decade and in line withthose of our European neighbours. I know, however, that people need breathing space right now. I will do everything I can to ease the pressure on household budgets in the short term. One of my first acts as prime minister was toremove VATfrom electricity bills, and households have seen that reduction in their bills this month. I have now asked the chancellor and the energy secretary to look at removing standing charges from gas bills at the earliest opportunity.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policyRead moreI will ensure the government continues to take action to reduce both gas bills and electricity bills as part of our fundamental changes to the energy system.The manifesto on which Labour was elected committed us to issuing no new oil or gas licences to explore new fields in the North Sea and to reaching net zero by 2050. I stand by both promises. Britain has just emerged from its hottest summer on record, during which we had nurses collapsing on hospital wards, bus driversworking in intolerable conditionsand families losing everything to wildfires. More extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead. The climate crisis is no distant threat. It is here, on our doorstep, affecting people’s lives and livelihoods. I am personally committed to confronting it, and I will not abandon the responsibility we have to future generations.There are two ways we can transition to clean energy. One way, the traditional Whitehall way, is to make people carry the burden of change while others take the rewards. The other is to make the transition work for people by creating good jobs, backing British industry, keeping bills as low as possible, strengthening our energy security and giving communities a greater say over their future. This government chooses the second path.I want Britain to believe in itself again. We can have secure energy, strong industries and a cleaner future. And we can make net zero mean jobs, opportunity and prosperity. That is how we bring back hope.Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United KingdomDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
