title: Donald Trump has sold out Ukraine. He makes appeaser Chamberlain look like a man of iron principle | Simon Tisdall | The Guardian
description: Europe’s leaders can no longer trust a word that comes out of Washington. No more slaps on the wrist – we need concrete steps to punish Trump, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Author: Simon Tisdall
Headline: Europe’s leaders can no longer trust a word that comes out of Washington. No more slaps on the wrist – we need concrete steps to punish Trump, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Content: Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Alaska in August 2025.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersView image in fullscreenVladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Alaska in August 2025.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersOpinionDonald TrumpDonald Trump has sold out Ukraine. He makes appeaser Chamberlain look like a man of iron principleSimon TisdallEurope’s leaders can no longer trust a word that comes out of Washington. No more slaps on the wrist – we need concrete steps to punish TrumpThu 22 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.12 EDTShareHistorical comparisons are always inexact. No one conflict precisely mirrors another. Yet Donald Trump’s shameless appeasement of Vladimir Putin carries more than a noxious whiff of Neville Chamberlain’s failed attempt in Munich in 1938 to head off war with Nazi Germany. To be fair to the former UK prime minister – and history largely hasn’t been – his peacemaking efforts had the enthusiastic backing of most people in Britain and France who, like him, were desperate to avoid a repeat of the horrors of the first world war. Trump enjoys no equivalentpublic support for his treachery. Nor does he face the prospect of a US war with Russia. His betrayal of Ukraine is cynically self-interested, globally dangerous and utterly contemptible.US-Russian talks on agreeing the shoddy terms of a precedent-setting American sell-out of Ukraine are at an advanced stage, after meetings in St Petersburg this week. Trump has zigzagged over the war ever since returning to office. Now, panicked byrecord-low poll ratings, he seems determined to scapegoat Ukraine and force its de facto capitulation.Recent steps– his shocking decision to fund Putin’s war machine by buying Russian diesel, his waiving of tougher sanctions, his mysterious, lethal interruptions in US satellite and intelligence sharing with Kyiv, and his renewed attempt to oust Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy – mark Trump out as the skulking Judas, the craven Brutus of the modern age. He makes Chamberlain look like a man of iron principle. All that’s lacking is an umbrella.Why does Trump act this way? Partly, it’s personal. Hedoesn’t like Zelenskyyand it’s obvious why. Ukraine’s leader is everything he is not: courageous, principled, morally unimpeachable, hard-working and politically savvy. Partly, it’s money and power. Trump has set his shrivelled, grasping heart on normalising relations with Putin’s repressive rogue regime, opening the way for lucrative deals on energy, raw materials, and control of the Arctic and outer space. He likes the idea of a world dominated by three all-powerful blocs and authoritarian leaders: himself, Putin and China’s Xi Jinping. And partly it’s the unexplained, sinister hold Putin appears to exercise over this former society playboy, New York real-estate developer andserial bankrupt.Whatever Trump’s motivations, the short-term consequences of his betrayal are potentially fatal for Ukraine’s bid to repel the Russian invaders and survive as a sovereign democratic state. Formuch of this year, Ukraine has been winning, or at least holding its own, in the contested lands of the Donbas and along the Black Sea littoral. More than that, by using homemade missiles and drones, it has taken the fight to Russia’s industrial heartlands and oil refineries, significantly undermining Putin’s ability to fund his war. Zelenskyy has also been winning the battle for international opinion, particularly in Europe, which itself is underescalating Russian hybrid attack. Amid Trump’s egregious backsliding, European nations have taken the lead in supporting Kyiv militarily, financially and diplomatically.It’s hard not to wonder whether there’s a connection between Trump’s sudden, divisive, decisive lurch towards unabashed support for Putin and the fact thatRussia, suffering unsustainable battlefield casualties, severe economic damage and deepening international isolation, is at increased risk of regime-toppling humiliation. Whatever the truth, Trump’s Putin bailout – his duplicitous Russia rescue act – could turn the tide.Trump’s perfidy is the shame of the world, and it is the world – and not only Ukraine – that will pay the price over the longer term. This calculated attempt to force Kyiv’s submission imperils everyone. Ukraine, if it is allowed to fall, will haunt Europe and the wider geopolitical biosphere for decades, as was the case with Czechoslovakia after 1938. Trump’s Molotov-Ribbentrop-style pact with a warmongering dictator,an indicted war criminal, a smirking, bigoted mass murderer, may fatally compromise the western alliance and spell the end of Nato as an effective defence against eastern totalitarianism. Who among the democratic governments of western Europe, in the Elysée, in the German and Polish chancelleries, in Brussels or in Downing Street, can now trust a word that comes out of Washington? Its bond is broken, its honour in shreds.Trump’s betrayal follows a pattern of lesser treacheries: arbitrary tariff wars waged against trading partners, the traducing of loyal allies, threats against Canada and Greenland,abandonment of a two-state solution in Palestineand most recently, his disastrouswar against Iran – the real reason why US midterm voters, facing inflated fuel prices, are turning against him and his Republicans. But his Russian folly may be the most egregious and consequential. AsMI5 has warned, Britain and Europe are under daily attack from Russia, its spy networks, saboteurs, cyber warriors and paid agents. Reports this week suggest it ismenacing western space satellites, too. Don’t look to turncoat Trump for help. He’s on the other side.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe can stop Trump’s assault on the international criminal court | Kenneth RothRead moreTrump’s Munich moment is a disaster in the making for Europe’s security and defence. A Putin victory, accepted and facilitated by the US, would fatefully damage respect for international law and sovereign borders. Untold numbers of war crimes and crimes against humanity would go uninvestigated and unpunished in a partitioned, fractured Ukraine. China and others might soon follow the precedent established by successful Russian aggression. For all these reasons, Britain and its European allies can no longer afford to hold back. Indignant speeches at the UN, off-the-record murmurings and carefully calibrated verbalslaps on the wristwill not suffice, if they ever did. Andy Burnham, France’s Emmanuel Macron, Germany’s Friedrich Merz and Canada’s Mark Carney must lead the way in confronting Trump head-on, even at the cost of a definitive break with Washington.Tell Trump publicly to knock it off. Take concrete steps to punish him for rewarding Putin and prove that the democracies of the world will not be bullied and sold out. Tell him if he really wants to be remembered as the US president who shattered the western alliance and ensured the triumph of authoritarianism, then keep on licking Putin’s boots – but he will be on his own. The UK, EU andNatomember states, Japan, South Korea and other like-minded countries, are far from powerless, economically, militarily and in numerous other ways. And despite what polls may suggest, healthy majorities of their citizens reject the hateful far-right lies and sick populist myths on which Trump and his pitiful emulators feed.The US ultimately leads the west by consent, not by right. Consent can be withdrawn. Burnham could start by ordering the closure of US military bases in Britain, offensive symbols of a hostile occupying power. At all costs, Trump’s treachery must not stand.Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentatorExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionRussiaVladimir PutinUkraineNatoEuropeVolodymyr ZelenskyycommentShareReuse this content

title: The internet has broken – again. Shouldn’t the tech firms that make billions from it pay to fix it? | Chris Stokel-Walker | The Guardian
description: I’ve been banging the drum about these vulnerabilities for years. It will take more than a handful of exhausted developers to keep us safe, says author and journalist Chris Stokel-Walker
Author: Chris Stokel-Walker
Headline: I’ve been banging the drum about these vulnerabilities for years. It will take more than a handful of exhausted developers to keep us safe, says author and journalist Chris Stokel-Walker
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/GettyOpinionData and computer securityThe internet has broken – again. Shouldn’t the tech firms that make billions from it pay to fix it?Chris Stokel-WalkerI’ve been banging the drum about these vulnerabilities for years. It will take more than a handful of exhausted developers to keep us safeThu 22 Oct 2026 09.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.13 EDTShareParts of the internet are going dark. In the Netherlands, government websites, including its digital ID login service, have become unavailable. Finland has taken public services offline, and Wikimedia, the organisation behind Wikipedia, has switched off some of its systems too.This sounds like the results of a cyber-attack. In most instances, however, the people running the sites deliberately switched them off because the alternative – keeping them online – was too risky. The future is here, and suddenly much of our digital infrastructure is looking very fragile.The websites were turned off because oftwo serious security vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language that is used by about 70% of websites that we can track. Those vulnerabilities in effect gave hackers an open window through which to climb and loot everything within. That could mean an attacker getting into an online shop, stealing customers’ addresses and passwords, or changing its checkout page to harvest card details. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centreadvised organisationsthat were unable to update immediately to consider taking their systems offline.It’s very tricky to get people to care about something quite so techy. PHP is a tricky abbreviation – even explaining what it stands for (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) is complicated, because it’s recursive. And how it helps the web work is also difficult to explain: a good analogy is it’s like the back-of-house team in a restaurant: your browser puts in an order, and PHP handles the cooking and delivers the meal. In any case, what matters is that you’ve almost certainly used websites powered by it this week.I’ve been reporting on scares like these in our digital architecture for more than a decade, and the underlying problem barely changes. In 2014, Iwrote about Heartbleed, a vulnerability in OpenSSL, the software that helps keep communications across the internet secure. It was up to two men named Steve – working for OpenSSL on a shoestring budget and shouldering an awful lot of responsibility – to keep us from disaster. Twelve years later, it feels like we’re still having the same conversation.Heartbleed wasn’t the end of it. In 2021 I reported on adangerous flaw in Log4j, a seemingly mundane tool that records what happens inside computer systems. Then three years later we hadXZ Utils, a tool for shrinking file sizes used on Linux computers into which someone had deliberately planted a backdoor. In each of these incidents, small teams working for the public good recognised the problem, acted, and averted disaster.Each one of these incidents underscored how we rely on a handful of under-resourced individuals to keep vital parts of the web secure.ThePHP Foundation made that point itself this week. Its developers first identified the issue that could bring the internet to a halt in 2024, but it was seen as too expensive and too tricky to fix. The foundation has since admitted the delay was a “structural failure” owing to poor resource levels.This is where AI comes in. In August, researchers working with Calif, OpenAI and Wiz identified how easily the PHP issue could be exploited by using AI tools. And hackers quickly did too.Cloudflare’s chief executive, Matthew Prince, saidhis company had seen millions of attempts to exploit it already.Automated systems powered by AIcan hammer away at weaknesses in an instant, bombarding their human guards with reports that they have to sift through. Researchers documentedabout 48,000 vulnerabilitiesacross the internetin 2025. We’ve already passed 84,000 in 2026, with more than two months of the year still to go. That’s one every five minutes. Not every one will be as serious as this latest one, which scored 9.2 on a 10-point scale used to measure these things. But we’re facing an onslaught.Which all makes for an uncomfortable reality: we’re going to have more days like these. AI makes it inordinately cheaper to find weaknesses in vast volumes of old code, and repairing them is difficult. A 2025review by the UK government foundthat about 28% of central government technology was classed as “legacy” – meaning out of date – while some organisations couldn’t even estimate how much old software they had. In April,ministers admittedthey couldn’t give a comprehensive account of what had since been fixed or retired.So we need to fix that. Companies need to know what software they’re using, including the obscure elements they rely on, and who’s responsible for fixing it. That documentation is boring work, which is probably why it’s overlooked. But we’re in a different world now, and it needs to be done. Paradoxically, AI can help with it. But companies and the organisations protecting us also need adequate funding.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere are some things to be optimistic about. The OpenSSL Foundation, the not-for-profit company that fell victim to the Heartbleed vulnerability in 2014,received more than €400,000from Germany’s sovereign tech fund last year to bolster its resources. The PHP Foundation has hired more staff and is using AI to help triage what’s important and what’s not. And a number of organisations deployed fixes before the current issue went public.But more is needed. The solution is the same one we keep talking about, but rarely actually do anything about: the big tech companies making billions from software they get for nothing (because of its open-source nature) should contribute properly to maintaining it. Governments ought to do the same, rather than hoping a handful of exhausted developers will keep things ticking over indefinitely.I’m growing sick of reporting on, and explaining why, the internet repeatedly breaks. I’ve covered Heartbleed, Log4Shell and XZ Utils – and am now documenting the fallout from PHP. I don’t particularly want to keep doing it. Yet I fear unless we start properly valuing those who keep our internet safe, I will be.Chris Stokel-Walker is the author of TikTok Boom: The Inside Story of the World’s Favourite AppExplore more on these topicsData and computer securityOpinionHackingInternetAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Strongmen like Trump would destroy the planet out of pure spite – and Brazil shows we’re all in peril  | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: If Flávio Bolsonaro is elected, Brazil’s ecosystems will face collapse. The ruling class would rather burn the world than share it with the poor, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: If Flávio Bolsonaro is elected, Brazil’s ecosystems will face collapse. The ruling class would rather burn the world than share it with the poor, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro after voting in Brazil’s general election, Rio de Janeiro, Sunday 4 October.Photograph: Lucas Landau/APView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro after voting in Brazil’s general election, Rio de Janeiro, Sunday 4 October.Photograph: Lucas Landau/APOpinionBrazilStrongmen like Trump would destroy the planet out of pure spite – and Brazil shows we’re all in perilGeorge MonbiotIf Flávio Bolsonaro is elected, Brazil’s ecosystems will face collapse. The ruling class would rather burn the world than share it with the poorThu 22 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.40 EDTShareHowever grim the trajectory might seem, I’ve always believed that sense will ultimately prevail. As the great perils of dismantling the living world become increasingly obvious, even the most rapacious exploiters must come round. Nobody wants to live on a dead planet, do they?There are – orwere– signs that this wasn’t just wishful thinking. Since 2015, mostly thanks to China, the area of the planet being reforested hasincreased, while thanks in large part to Brazil, the global rate of forest destruction has declined. The area of the Brazilian Amazon forest cleared each year isone-sixth of what it waswhen records began in 1988. In the past four years, as a result of Brazilian government policy, the deforestation rate hasfallen by 71%. IfLuiz Inácio Lula da Silvais re-elected president on Sunday, the country could reach zero deforestation by 2030. The arc of the moral universe seems to have bent towards justice.But what my faith in human nature failed to account for was a perverse delight in destruction among a small cohort of the economic elite. There are people who appear to hate life and love death. Donald Trump’sremoval of protections on public lands, the small bite – doubtless the first of many – he wants totake out of Yosemite, hisassaultson the US National Park Service and theUS Forest Service, his trashing of theEndangered Species Act: all are partly a response to lobbying by ranchers, loggers, frackers and miners. But this, I think, is not the primary driver.More important to him, I’ve come to believe, is a vengeful desire to hurt. I doubt Trump hates the monarch butterfly. I’d be surprised if he knows what it is. But he does appear to hate people who love the monarch butterfly.Destroying the habitatson which this and many other endangered species in the US depend seems to be part of the“retribution”he promised. The New York Times wasunable to find evidencethat Trump has ever visited a national park. He probably doesn’t hate them either. But seemingly anything valued by the enemy – greens, liberals, socialists, feminists, anti-racists, “bureaucrats” and “blockers” – should be attacked on principle.Wiping ecosystems off the map is an obvious demonstration of power. Extinction leaves a permanent mark, which is every dictator’s dream. It’s also a highly effective means of hurting those who resist him: the Indigenous people and other people of colour so often on the receiving end of environmental destruction; the regulators; the scientists and the rest of the intelligentsia; above all, people whocare.Caring could be seen as the far right’s meta-target. The“suicidal empathy” themenow crops up repeatedly in videos, newspaper columns and speeches: a professed belief that those who care about other people or species should be destroyed by those who don’t. This belief, by definition, is psychopathic. What exhausts my optimism is that, conned by shallow promises such as the use of brutal methods to address crime, people keep electing those who subscribe to it.View image in fullscreenInspector with logs seized from the Amazon rainforest during an operation to combat deforestation, at a sawmill in Nova California, Rondonia, February 2025.Photograph: Ueslei Marcelino/ReutersPhysically and politically, Flávio Bolsonaro is the spitting image of his father, thejailed coup-plotter, Jair. When Jair Bolsonaro was president of Brazil, he appeared to see ecological destruction as a kind of a holy duty. The deforestation raterose by 59%in his four years, andattacks on Indigenous peopleand other forest defenders, as well as invasions by illegal ranchers, loggers and goldminers rocketed. The crudest forms of extractivism – regardless of their costs, or how they might hold back all kinds of progress – were a matter of policy.The ideology of the far right in Brazil has been described as “beef, Bible and bullets”: violence against those who resist the seizure of their resources, anultra-conservative evangelismand the expansion of cattle ranching, which is both a potent symbol offar-right machismoand theprimary driverof deforestation in the Amazon.Jair Bolsonarolooked backwith nostalgia to the military dictatorship of 1964 to 1985 – which wasactively supportedby the US government – during which local oligarchs could do as they pleased, and those who opposed them weretortured and disappeared. The warnings couldn’t be clearer, but Brazil seems determined to revisit its nightmares. Flávio Bolsonarowon the first roundon 4 October, and is likely to become president.If he wins the second round this week, the gleeful rampage of his supporters,catalysed by government policy, threatens not only the Amazon but the Atlantic forest in the south, the Pantanal wetlands, the Pampa grasslands and the savannah habitats of the Cerrado. This is politics as an orgy of destruction. Let’s eradicate our life support systems – that’ll teach the liberals!Brazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote loomsRead moreTrump has been using all possible means tohelp Bolsonaro win. He gives the impression of seeing Latin America as theconquistadoresdid – one big heap of treasure, ready for looting. The region’s far-right demagogues are only too happy to help. Mass deforestation and thesudden ecosystem collapsethat is likely to result offers a finality to their politics: there’s no coming back from this. You Indigenous people, you greens, you carers: you’ll have nowhere left to hide. The world will be ours, even if it is a world of ashes.What mightBolsonarismoteach us? First, it appears there is no limit to the perversity of the ruling class, which would rather there was nothing left to share than cede any fraction of the planet to the poor.Second, that it possesses all the tools – social and traditional media, the pulpit and the gun – required to make its perversity look like common sense, or at least irresistible, as force is deployed. Third, that the only defence we have against suicidal gullibility is what the Brazilians callconscientizaçao: raising awareness about the relations between exploiters and exploited, and the violence that underpins them. Otherwise all that is good, trusting and hopeful in humanity can be harnessed for a war against everyone and everything.As for the idea that nobody wants to live on a dead planet, Elon Musk, with hispreposterous plans for living on Mars– “Fuck Earth! Who cares about Earth?” – has killed that too. Extending the frontier of destruction, even to the point of human extinction, comes across as a matter of pride. The four horsemen ride again, not in cloaks but in stetsons and denim shirts, driving their cattle before them.George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsBrazilOpinionDeforestationConservationTrees and forestsAmazon rainforestThe far rightBiodiversitycommentShareReuse this content

title: Is this Prince Harry or David Brent in The Office? Either way, we’re watching a masterclass in awkwardness | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: The wayward prince and his wife seem to be aiming for a reboot – searching for purpose, but not self-awareness, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: The wayward prince and his wife seem to be aiming for a reboot – searching for purpose, but not self-awareness, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Content: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex in Nottingham on 15 October 2026.Photograph: FD/Francis Dias/NEWSPIX INTERNATIONALView image in fullscreenThe Duke and Duchess of Sussex in Nottingham on 15 October 2026.Photograph: FD/Francis Dias/NEWSPIX INTERNATIONALOpinionPrince HarryIs this Prince Harry or David Brent in The Office? Either way, we’re watching a masterclass in awkwardnessEmma BrockesThe wayward prince and his wife seem to be aiming for a reboot – searching for purpose, but not self-awarenessThu 22 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.39 EDTShareYears ago, I was in Washington DC when Prince Harry blew through on an official engagement. He was 28, with a full head of hair, a slightly louche gait and a public image that,on a tour of the Senate led by a baffled-looking John McCain, caused people to lose their minds.Senate staffers stood five deep to get a glimpse; women materialised from every corner, more glamorously dressed for the office than usual. The excitement was so great that there were actual screams from behind the security line. I remember noting the prince’s prominent ears, the high colour in his cheeks and his habit, when addressed, of bowing his head, as if humbled by what he was hearing. Aw, I thought. Bless him.But that was a long time ago. This week, Harry, now 42, appeared on camera in aninterviewin New York with GQ, playing to a very different audience. He looked older and schlubbier – don’t we all – the diffidence of youth replaced by something more pompous and belligerent, undergirded by what, in recent years, has appeared to be his bottomless well of hurt feelings. Harry was promoting something – amasterclasson “grief science”, which he has undertaken with Dr Mary-Frances O’Connor. But the question of why on earth he would double down on previous US media appearances, none of them successful, sat alongside the bigger royal question of the season: namely, what are he and his wife, Meghan, going todo?Since the pair arrived back in the UKthis summer after a six-year absence, watching them try to settle on a role has been a veritable festival of awkwardness, not least because it’s not entirely obviouswhere they have left to go. In March, Netflix ended its partnership with Meghan’s lifestyle brand, As Ever, less than a year after it replaced the pair’s $100m mega-contract with a first-look deal. These well-publicised failures were compounded by the previousdeath of Meghan’s podcast,the couple’s parting with Spotifyand what might politely be called their low productivity metric when it comes to anything not immediately related to the royal family.In this, the Sussexes are no different to any other creators endlessly raking over their own lives for content. The difference, of course, is that Harry, with a lofty mindset inculcated from birth and which is presumably incredibly hard to shake, presents his every gesture as automatically belonging to that higher calling, public service. “I don’t do it for myself,” he says in the interview in New York when explaining the venture with MasterClass. (Side note: the real masterclass here is in watching the GQ hack trying to use Harry’s grief project as a Trojan horse for questions about the royal family, among them: “Do you grieve that?” in relation to Harry’s fallout with King Charles, and a sleight of hand reference to “anticipatory grief” in a reach to get his father’s health on the table. Honestly, I tip my hat).View image in fullscreenRicky Gervais as David Brent in The Office, 2001.Photograph: BBC“Trying to make an impact in the world, that is genuinely what energises me,” says Harry, sinuously pivoting away from the awkward questions. And if he stuck to harmless banalities about grief and, oh God, what he calls his mission as a storyteller, one might be inclined to say good luck to him. Harder to stomach is what appears to be his and his wife’s need for the public to participate in their grandiose delusions.Witness the Sussexes in Nottingham last week, going on a walkabout under the auspices of a charity event that, to me, looked more like an exercise in self-gratification. As theking had already sternly warned the pair: they’re private citizens, now, with no officially sanctioned public engagements, and yet here they were, working a crowd like any active-duty royals. While Meghan smiled excessively with her “hello, little people!” act, her husband alternated between mild engagement with the well-wishers and sending category-five death stares to the hacks, poor sods, who’d turned up to cover this non-event. It was embarrassing, and awkward, and as someone pointed out on the internet, like watching David Brent return to the office after being fired.And so, while the top line from the interview in New York focused on Harry’s indirectcall for reconciliation with his family, it was another takeaway that struck me more forcefully. More than once, the prince talked about the importance of knowing yourself, adding that he had “put in the work” and clearly positioning himself as more evolved than his father and brother. I would suggest Harry’s journey of self-awareness has a way to go yet.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEmma Brockes is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: A violent and coordinated youth uprising? That’s exactly the picture Europe’s enemies want to paint | Alberto Alemanno | The Guardian
description: Each country’s protesters have distinct grievances. Listen to them, not the voices telling us Europe is ungovernable, says law professor Alberto Alemanno
Author: Alberto Alemanno
Headline: Each country’s protesters have distinct grievances. Listen to them, not the voices telling us Europe is ungovernable, says law professor Alberto Alemanno
Content: Students in Paris protest against under-resourced schools, 8 October 2026.Photograph: Aurélien Morissard/APView image in fullscreenStudents in Paris protest against under-resourced schools, 8 October 2026.Photograph: Aurélien Morissard/APOpinionProtestA violent and coordinated youth uprising? That’s exactly the picture Europe’s enemies want to paintAlberto AlemannoEach country’s protesters have distinct grievances. Listen to them, not the voices telling us Europe is ungovernableThu 22 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 05.34 EDTShareLast Saturday night, the town hall of Limoges in west-central Francewas set ablaze. By Sunday, images of the fire destroying a symbol of the French republic, andother scenes of unrest across France, were everywhere, but being used to tell very different stories about what is happening in Europe.For some, the flames announced a pan-Europeanyouth revolt, proof that a single movement was sweeping the continent. Donald Trump, who had already insisted that the French schools protests were not about schools but aboutmigration and Islam,urgedEuropeans to “close the borders”.The mayor of Limogessaw the fingerprints of an alleged ultra-left insurrection.I lost count of how many mainly rightwing media outlets were contacting me suddenly. Most were based in India, China, Singapore and the US. They sought voices to validate the idea of a “teen revolt” spreading acrossEurope, driven by the same grievances and violence.None of these narratives, each serving a different political agenda, adequately explains what is happening. Europe’s protests have different causes, constituencies and demands. Portraying them as a Europe-wide rebellion erases those differences and makes Europe look ungovernable. That picture is a gift to anyone who wants to exploit the unrest.What set off the protests varies from country to country. In France,the mobilisation beganin schools in mid-September in frustration over longstanding failures to address overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated buildings and facilities. By the time of the huge demonstration on Saturday, public-sector workers had joined, and the grievances hadwidened to encompass the cost of living.InBelgium, meanwhile, students have challenged tuition-fee increases in the country’s French-speaking region and demanded additional teaching hours.Greek studentshave mobilised over housing costs and access to accommodation, whileGerman pupilshave protested against the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service.View image in fullscreenThe city hall in Limoges, central France, on fire after protests turned violent, 17 October 2026.Photograph: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP/Getty ImagesLook beyond western Europe, and the differences become even more distinct. InAlbania, student unrestbuilds on a pre-existing anti-government mobilisation, rather than a standalone youth revolt. InSerbia, students have led nearly two years oflargely peaceful protestsfollowing theNovi Sad railway station disaster. Their movement centres on demands for an end to corruption, a lack of institutional accountability and political inaction. Now the students arerunning in this weekend’s electionon their own list. This is a battle over power and accountability, and goes well beyond education or generational frustration.Italian students may occupy schools and shout slogans in French, but the cross-border spread of images,slogansand tactics does not prove a shared organisation. Rather, 24-hour news coverage can turn separate protests into a single story of youth rebellion, creating, deliberately or not, the illusion of a common movement and programme where neither exists.Rejecting the idea of a single European youth revolt does not mean denying the existence of a shared generational anxiety. Housing has become increasingly unaffordable, public services are under pressure, and the transition into secure employment is uncertain.Eurostat reportsthat EU house prices rose by 55.4% and rents by 26.7% between 2010 and the fourth quarter of 2024. The 2026TUI Foundation Youth Study foundthat 52% of young people aged 16–26 across seven European countries expected to be worse off than their parents, compared with just 25% who expected to do better.Youth unemployment in the euro arearemains substantially higherthan overall unemployment. Onestudy of French firms founda sharper decline in permanent hiring among workers aged 21–29 in occupations exposed to artificial intelligence. TheEuropean Central Bank cautionsthat the evidence does not yet establish generative AI as the cause. But the uncertainty itself can create a shared sense of insecurity across national borders.Such anxieties help explain why protests in one country resonate with young people in another, and why images of school sit-ins or street demonstrations can inspire imitation. But they don’t translate into common demands, let alone a coordinated political movement.France’s demonstrations last Saturday exposed another danger: how quickly violence can overshadow a protest’s message. Most demonstrators marched peacefully, but a minority resorted to violence. Their actions should not define hundreds of thousands of demonstrators, just as peaceful protest should not provide cover for criminal acts.What happened in Milan showedhow the two can blur. A peaceful cost of living march alongside protests over education cuts and race-based reform,was followed by lootingcarried out by hooded, mostly teenage groups organised partly via TikTok. More than 200 were detained, most of them minors, and the march’s organisers disowned them. Defending public order must go hand in hand with accountability for violence andscrutiny of police conduct.But when images of burning buildings and looting dominate coverage, peaceful protest and criminal violence become harder to distinguish in the public mind. A single incident can come to define an entire mobilisation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe misleading narrative of a pan-European revolt has consequences, because it allows images of unrest to be taken out of their national contexts and presented as proof that a chaotic Europe is ungovernable.This is particularly useful to those seeking to deepen divisions and undermine European democracy: it turns distinct national problems into a sweeping story of European failure.For the radical right, the idea of a continent in flames proves that open societies cannot protect their citizens, hence the call to “close your borders”. For those on the radical left who celebrate every burning building as the dawn of a continental uprising, the flames prove that liberal democratic institutions are beyond repair. Both need Europe to look ungovernable but neither offers an answer to the disorder it complains about. And both serve the interests of those beyond Europe’s borders who gain from a divided union, fromthe Trump administrationto Vladimir Putin.President Macron had a point when he lashed out at the “stupid” comments of foreign leaders about events in France. AI-generated images of scenes that never took place in France had been circulating, he said. Macron is hardly neutral, but certain forces clearly have an interest in amplifying images of chaos.Governments should neither romanticise protest nor use violence as a pretext to dismiss legitimate grievances. They must protect peaceful demonstrators, hold perpetrators accountable and address the pressures that leave many young people uncertain about their future.Europe’s democracies will be judged not by how they withstand these protests, but how they address the distinct grievances behind them and restore confidence in the future. That is how generational anxiety can become a force for democratic renewal rather than fuel for those seeking to portray democracy as broken.Alberto Alemanno is the Jean Monnet professor of EU law at HEC Paris and the founder of The Good LobbyFrance readers Q&A: Guardian Europe columnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst will be live taking questions from our readers about the unrest in France from at 1500 BST / 1600 CEST on Friday 23 October. Send your questions by email now toconversations@theguardian.comor post questions in the comments from 0900 BSThere.Explore more on these topicsProtestOpinionFranceEuropeSerbiaItalyAlbaniaGreececommentShareReuse this content

title: In You Can See Everything, it’s Elizabeth Holmes’s partner who makes for 2026’s timeliest villain | You Can See Everything | The Guardian
description: Nathan Fielder’s conversation-igniting film on the Theranos founder finds its darkest moments in her deceptive, Charlie Kirk-loving fiance Billy Evans
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: Nathan Fielder’s conversation-igniting film on the Theranos founder finds its darkest moments in her deceptive, Charlie Kirk-loving fiance Billy Evans
Content: Billy Evans in You Can See Everything.Photograph: A24View image in fullscreenBilly Evans in You Can See Everything.Photograph: A24You Can See EverythingIn You Can See Everything, it’s Elizabeth Holmes’s partner who makes for 2026’s timeliest villainJesse HassengerNathan Fielder’s conversation-igniting film on the Theranos founder finds its darkest moments in her deceptive, Charlie Kirk-loving fiance Billy EvansSecrets, lies and a shock A-list cameo: how You Can See Everything became the film of the year‘You can’t make this stuff up’: why we remain fascinated by Elizabeth HolmesThu 22 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.45 EDTShareIt’s likely that most audiences going into the surprise documentary smashYou Can See Everythingare familiar with either its nominal subject (and literal poster gal with an intense stare) Elizabeth Holmes, the tech founder serving a prison sentence for defrauding investors; or the film’s on-camera co-director Nathan Fielder. Holmes, as the movie points out, was all over the media as her company Theranos was hyped to the moon and then spectacularly imploded; she was also played by Amanda Seyfried in the well-regarded Hulu miniseries The Dropout. Fielder, meanwhile, may not have graced as many magazine covers, but is similarly familiar to prestige-TV acolytes from his comedy-reality series Nathan for You and its successor, the more reality-bending series The Rehearsal. A third figure not included in the film’s ad campaign becomes a key part of the film in the second half, and will also be familiar to many viewers.Secrets, lies and a shock A-list cameo: how You Can See Everything became the film of the yearRead moreThis should leave Billy Evans as the odd man out. Evans, Elizabeth Holmes’s partner (she has said they’re not legally married, though they did get engaged in 2018, have two children and seem to treat each other as spouses), is a not-particularly-famous guy whose screen time competes with the other three well-known faces in what is essentially a four-character drama. But while Evans isn’t boxed out in terms of screen time or memorability, he does remain the odd man out in the sense that in all the discussionYou Can See Everythinghas prompted about manipulation, shifting sympathies and who can or cannot be trusted, everyone seems to agree on one crucial point: Billy Evans sucks.Well, everyone except Holmes, who never indicates so much as a moment of doubt or hesitation toward her common-law husband, at least so far as Fielder or co-director Lance Oppenheim show us. But the movie does show Fielder appearing baffled by Holmes – her absurd claims to have never lied in her adult life; her tautological and nonsensical explanation of how her blood-testing device does actually work (which basically amounts to “if everything about it worked, it would work”); her inability to understand Abbott and Costello’s most famous comedy routine – to the point of having trouble discerning whether she’s consciously scamming him or just, let’s say, reality-divergent. By comparison, Evans comes across as more of a slightly puzzling but recognizable nuisance.When he calls a meeting to demand a percentage of the film’s profits – the kind of arrangement that might be typically reserved for a promotional piece commissioned by a musician, not a nonfiction film extensively interviewing a notorious subject – Fielder and Oppenheim zero in on the question of whether Holmes knew about this request and what became of it, but Evans is the one who violates documentary norms by asking for profit participation (and getting it, at least temporarily). Earlier on, he demands privacy when he grows visibly uncomfortable with questions asked of Holmes while also appearing fully, frontally nude in the film. In a small but underlined moment, he casually relieves Holmes of egg-scrambling duty because he believes she’s not stirring vigorously enough.You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead moreAnd those are just some of his antics before the film’s two-year time jump, after which Evans seems to exert even more control over his partner. Given Holmes’s reputation as a Silicon Valley scam artist, it would make sense enough to categorize Evans as a real-life version of Hollywood’s favorite go-to villain:the evil tech bro. The film even refers to Holmes’s turn in that particular hot seat as the subject of The Dropout, which is not a story of heroes and villains, exactly, but certainly exists adjacent to narratives about tech-forward monsters.Evans has plenty of grimly hilarious signifiers, before and after his partner’s incarceration. Beforehand, he can be seen listening to podcasts at double speed like a true #content consumer/wannabe timemaxxer. Afterward, he shows repeated signs (uncommented upon by Oppenheim or Fielder) of posturing but increasingly intense post-“woke” radicalization: he spends time at a shooting range, claims to carry a gun everywhere, volunteers that he’s a fan of Charlie Kirk and brags about his own supposed vindictiveness. He uses his sketchy control of Holmes’s social media to engage in petty clapbacks that seem entirely out of character for her; he uses his sketchy control of her AI likeness to side-boast about how much healthier she looks as a prisoner than she did immediately postpartum.View image in fullscreenBilly Evans and Nathan Fielder in You Can See Everything.Photograph: YouTubeWith paranoia, delusions of grandeur, lofty-sounding projects that don’t amount to anything and a seeming possessiveness of the woman in his life, Evans checks plenty of tech-bro boxes – only without even a modicum of demonstrated tech expertise, seemingly not even in his fevered imaginings. Yes, Elon Musk propped himself up as a genius on the basis of other people’s companies and his vast fortune; Mark Zuckerberg is a dead-eyed egomaniac whose famous invention is a Friendster clone that bought up a bunch of other already-successful websites and Sam Altman’s career is littered with failures that in no way qualify him to order us all to treat AI as the future. But even if you see these guys as scammers nearly on par with Holmes, they have the distinction of having successfully made money and, in the case of Musk and Zuckerberg, placing some of their might behind products that people do actually use (in some cases, whether they really want to or not). One reason they’re villainized in fictionalized true stories like those poweringThe Social Reckoning(with Jeremy Strong as Zuck) or the upcomingArtificial(with Andrew Garfield as Altman and Ike Barinholtz as Musk) is that they have actually accrued power in the first place. There are stakes to their existence.‘You can’t make this stuff up’: why we remain fascinated by Elizabeth HolmesRead moreEvans has no such claims to fame or even big-canvas notoriety that could inspire something like the four-hourMuskdocumentary by Alex Gibney, released concurrently with You Can See Everything. It seems notable, too, that the similarly lengthy You Can See Everything has seemingly stolen focus from the more traditionally rigorous piece on Musk, a far more influential individual compared to either Holmes or Evans. Holmes was certainly a destructive force for the cancer patients whose hopes she raised, and Evans comes across like a restless creep, but it feels telling, and a little discomfiting, that the gossipy nervous laughter provoked by You Can See Everything is proving a vastly more headline-grabbing draw than a movie laying out the case against a maniacal on-again, off-again trillionaire who has done genuine damage to the world, and is poised to do plenty more. Does someone need to be as petty, strange and blatantly unsuccessful as Evans to be truly finished off in public?Then again, Evans does make a compelling villain for precisely that restless lack of achievement. He will never be as influential as someone like Musk or Zuckerberg, but apparently aspires to that kind of overlord-level bravado (why else would you use your wife’s social media to pick fights?). He’s a fake-it-til-you-make-it-and-then-keeping-faking-it type, more akin to erstwhile reality star turned pretend mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt or any number of filibustering podcasters. Instead of Facebook or Tesla or a portfolio of Donald Trump-style scams, he can simply puppeteer the damaged brand that isElizabeth Holmes– near-literally, when he shows off his AI version. Holmes is clearly manipulative (and based on available information about Theranos, an unambiguous liar), yet Fielder does locate, or maybe even manufacture, some kind of humanity through her inscrutability. There’s something haunting about her, sometimes in spite of herself. Evans is the odd man out in You Can See Everything because he seems to lack that kind of turmoil. He’s hustle-and-grind culture in its final dehumanizing form. The world is just something for him to absorb and scan for advantages at 2x speed.Explore more on these topicsYou Can See EverythingElizabeth HolmesNathan FielderDocumentary filmsSilicon ValleyCharlie Kirk shootingElon MuskcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on England’s north-south divide: Burnham must deliver more than devolution | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The prime minister promises to repair decades of regional damage. His government must redistribute wealth to close deadly inequalities
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The prime minister promises to repair decades of regional damage. His government must redistribute wealth to close deadly inequalities
Content: Andy Burnham speaks to employees during his visit to the King’s Trust centre in Manchester on 15 October 2026.Photograph: WPA/GettyView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham speaks to employees during his visit to the King’s Trust centre in Manchester on 15 October 2026.Photograph: WPA/GettyOpinionInequalityThe Guardian view on England’s north-south divide: Burnham must deliver more than devolutionEditorialThe prime minister promises to repair decades of regional damage. His government must redistribute wealth to close deadly inequalitiesThu 22 Oct 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 13.27 EDTShareAndy Burnham’s call to abandon “40 years of neoliberalism” rests partly on the damage that he says it has done to northern England. A new study – published in theLancetthis week – adds weight to his argument. It found that for adults aged 25 to 49, death rates in the north were 13% higher than in the south in 1981. By 2024, that gap had more than tripled to 42%. What happened in the four decades that left younger adults in northern England with so much worse chances of survival?The answer lies in the lives and jobs that people have, and the homes they can afford, as well as the state of the public services, like the NHS, that they rely on.Deindustrialisationstripped secure employment from many communities in the north of England – as it did in Scotland and Wales.Austeritythen weakened support systems. These reasons also underscore Mr Burnham’s analysis that Britain’s economic model and concentration of power in London have failed its regions.View image in fullscreenFriedrich Engels.Photograph: Print Collector/GettyThe question for the budget is what will it do about these inequalities. The north has substantial levels ofdeprivation, lower rates ofpayand fewerhealthyyears of life for its people. Among people under 75, the Lancetstudyfound that mortality in northern England was 26% higher than in the south. To close these gaps means helping poorer households with the rising cost of essentials and sending more resources to deprived areas. Investment in, say, early years education and council budgets would help to deal with the social conditions underlying ill health.Reducing regional inequalities requires redistribution – not just devolution alone. Giving a poorer area more control over an inadequate budget does not increase the cash it can spend. Mr Burnham’s idea to let mayors retain locally raisedtaxesmay help. But without a way to ensure each region gets enough resources to meet their needs, such a policy might simply preserve existing disparities. Researchers at Manchester and Liverpool universities and Health Equity North divided England into two roughly equal populations along a line from the Wash to the Severn Estuary. Closing the north’s health gap, they claim, could add£18bna year to its economy.Regional policy plays a complementary role to redistribution by aiming to change where wealth is produced. However, in a recent paper, Steve Fothergill of the Industrial Communities Alliancewarnedthat “the UK has moved away from a long‑established framework that explicitly sought to promote jobs and growth in its less prosperous places … the UK now deploys a weaker set of tools for regional economic development than at any point since the mid-twentieth century”. Mr Burnham needs to reverse this trend.The chancellor, John Healey, says that he wants a budget for “bloody-minded entrepreneurs”. But a richer northern England would not necessarily be a healthy or more equal one. During the 19th century, when Manchester became known as “Cottonopolis”,Friedrich Engels– bemoaning the city’s “disgraceful unhealthy slums” – was shocked to be told by a local businessman: “And yet there is a great deal of money to be made here.” Bringing investment and good jobs to economically weaker regions matters. But whether the resulting prosperity translates into secure incomes, decent homes, good public services and longer lives is just as important. Mr Burnham’s ambition needs to meet twin challenges: where wealth is created and what life it lets people enjoy.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on AI safety: the push for global regulation must advance | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The current US administration is an obstacle, but public demand for protection will ultimately prevail
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The current US administration is an obstacle, but public demand for protection will ultimately prevail
Content: The PHP Foundation website with an update to the latest version of PHP.Photograph: ANP/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe PHP Foundation website with an update to the latest version of PHP.Photograph: ANP/ShutterstockOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)The Guardian view on AI safety: the push for global regulation must advanceEditorialThe current US administration is an obstacle, but public demand for protection will ultimately prevailThu 22 Oct 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 13.39 EDTShareOrganisations around the worldscrambledon Thursday to fix critical flaws in PHP, the software that powers much of the web. The vulnerabilities could allow attackers to take control of affected servers. Some websites were taken offline as a precaution while fixes were installed. The paradox is that while AIhelpedresearchers uncover the flaw, it also threatens to accelerate the ability to exploit it. Amazonsaidthat it had detected an attempt before the public disclosure of the PHP flaws.What the episode highlights is AI’s central role in security – and not always for the right reasons. OpenAI’s models have also been responsible for two alarming hacks this year – a security breach of an Australian health department website and a raid by aswarm of AI botson Hugging Face, an AI services platform. Citing those incidents, the AI minister, Kanishka Narayan,warnedthat a similar cyber-attack on the UK is “likely, if not inevitable”.Britain is not uniquely vulnerable. In some respects it is more advanced than many countries in grasping the scale of the challenge. The London-basedAI Security Instituteis internationally recognised as an authority in a rapidly evolving field. A cybersecurity bill to protect critical digital infrastructure is going through parliament.View image in fullscreenKanishka Narayan.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockAs Mr Narayan concedes, national governments face limits in protecting their citizens from a global threat. Having Donald Trump in the White House makes the international challenge harder. The US president hasrejected callsfor international negotiations on AI regulation. He is even dismissive when the bosses of US technology companies recognise the need for external monitoring and ask for statutory guardrails on their own activities.Mr Trump takes the view that America’s lead at the most advanced frontier of AI is a national strategic asset that would be compromised if other nations, and China in particular, were allowed to set the pace of advancement. In the president’s eyes it is a race for global supremacy and only losers urge caution. “Whoever wins AI, wins,” he has said.That is a disturbingly reckless approach to technology that, in some of the more apocalyptic prognoses, has thepotential to destroy humankind.Even in more circumspect scenarios, the risk of some catastrophic incident or severe economic shock caused by the malicious or accidental use of AI is growing at a rate that more responsible leaders than Mr Trump cannot afford to ignore.Andy Burnham has said that he intends to put AI at the top of the agenda when the UK holds the G20 presidency for the first half of next year. Inhis speechat the Labour party conference earlier this month, the prime minister compared his role to the global leadership position that Gordon Brown took on as the chair of the G20 in early 2009, coordinating a response to the financial crisis.But the world looks very different in 2026. Mr Burnham’s convening power will not move a US administration that treats historic allies and multilateral institutions with contempt. That is not a reason to abandon the ambition. The drive to build some global regulatory architecture has to advance. If Mr Trump cannot be moved by care for humanity, this week’s PHP emergency should remind him that America’s technological lead offers no protection from disruption. Shielding US citizens and businesses from such turmoil requires international cooperation that arace for AI supremacyputs at risk.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: What would make neonatal units safer for babies? | Lucy Letby | The Guardian
description: Letters: Dr Pamela S Melding highlights how New Zealand has created a healthcare culture where patient safety, interests and consent are the overriding principles. Plus letters from Mark Hanson, Paul Whiteing and a reader who lost her baby
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Dr Pamela S Melding highlights how New Zealand has created a healthcare culture where patient safety, interests and consent are the overriding principles. Plus letters from Mark Hanson, Paul Whiteing and a reader who lost her baby
Content: ‘Destroy candour and you destroy one of the most powerful tools of patient safety.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Destroy candour and you destroy one of the most powerful tools of patient safety.’Photograph: AlamyLucy LetbyLettersWhat would make neonatal units safer for babies?Dr Pamela S Meldinghighlights how New Zealand has created a healthcare culture where patient safety, interests and consent are the overriding principles. Plus letters fromMark Hanson,Paul Whiteingand a reader who lost her babyThu 22 Oct 2026 11.27 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.29 EDTShareI support Mark McDonald’s submission that the Thirlwall recommendations will lead to more blame and suspicion in the NHS (17 October). We often hear of hospital scandals where trusts are intent on preserving their reputations, internal inquiries go nowhere, defensive clinical staff deflect blame on to others, non‑disclosure to patients of errors and “lessons learned” rhetoric that is quickly forgotten. There is also an industry of ambulance-chasing lawyers. None of this is conducive to a no-blame, honest, open culture in healthcare. The Thirlwall recommendations of more surveillance will make it worse.There is an alternative. Most of my professional life as a hospital consultant, clinical director and deputy chief medical officer has been spent in New Zealand, whose publicly funded NHS is the same model as the UK’s – but with a major difference. In the 1970s, New Zealanders lost their right to sue for damages for medical accidents or injury through the public court system with theAccident Compensation Act. This got rid of the grievance culture and ambulance-chasers, and the system provided remedial care for any injury. In the 80s, after a huge scandal regarding medical investigations, theCartwright inquiryushered in the creation of the independentHealth and Disability Commissioner(HDC) and overriding principles of patient safety, interests and consent.All complaints – from patients, public and staff – about any health facility, organisation or practitioner go first to the office of the HDC for investigation. If the HDC deems it necessary, it goes to the various professional disciplinary bodies or to the Medical Council ofNew Zealand. HDC reports on complaints are publicly available.In 2005, the government passed its “no fault, no blame” legislation. This brought in a duty to report “any risk of harm to the public from authorities responsible for patient safety”. This freed clinicians to engage with any compensation cases with openness. The system has its critics, but overall works well.Dr Pamela S MeldingSt Helens, MerseysideMark McDonald’s column is a breath of common sense. The Criminal Cases Review Commission isstill consideringLucy Letby’s convictions, yet Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall has constructed a programme of reform on the assumption that the central conclusion of the case is beyond question. Meanwhile, barely enough time has passed for reflection on what would actually make neonatal units safer.Thirlwall’s answer appears to be surveillance, suspicion and blame: cameras in cots, encouragement to report colleagues and an explicit retreat from the “no blame” culture developed precisely to make organisations safer.But what makes a hospital safe? Is it a nurse wondering whether a colleague is about to report them, or a nurse confident enough to admit that they have made a mistake? Is it a doctor practising defensively, or one willing to report a near-miss before it becomes a tragedy?Destroy candour and you destroy one of the most powerful tools of patient safety. A frightened workforce will hide mistakes, keep quiet about doubts and practise defensively. Patients will pay.Mark HansonHitchin, HertfordshireIn March this year my daughter was born and died in the neonatal intensive care unit seven days later. I believe her death was preventable and one key mistake was made that resulted in her death. But I don’t blame the consultant who made (what I consider to be) the error. She was doing the best she could in a difficult situation.What I find concerning is the follow-up from the trust’s management. They have bent over backwards to try to hide their tracks rather than discussing it openly and using it as an opportunity to learn and ensure other babies don’t suffer a similar fate. The response has been so heavy-handed that it’s an insight into the fear and blame culture doctors face, which I find so concerning. Mistakes are an opportunity to learn.Name and address suppliedMark McDonald makes many good points. But sadly he overlooks the role that patients and families play in their healthcare and safety. The NHS needs staff who can speak up without fear. But it also needs patients who are listened to, informed, supported and involved. Some of the most important safety signals come not from systems, but from the people experiencing care. If there is one lesson from theLucy Letbycase, it is that patients and families must be recognised as partners in identifying risk, seeking answers and driving improvement.Paul WhiteingCEO, Action Against Medical AccidentsHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Carers can’t live on 51p an hour | Carers | The Guardian
description: Letter: Emma Sainsbury questions whether government policy takes sufficient account of people whose caring responsibilities shape their finances and ability to keep a home
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Emma Sainsbury questions whether government policy takes sufficient account of people whose caring responsibilities shape their finances and ability to keep a home
Content: ‘Unpaid carers save society enormously, often at the expense of their own earnings, pensions and financial security.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Unpaid carers save society enormously, often at the expense of their own earnings, pensions and financial security.’Photograph: AlamyCarersLettersCarers can’t live on 51p an hourEmma Sainsburyquestions whether government policy takes sufficient account of people whose caring responsibilities shape their finances and ability to keep a homeThu 22 Oct 2026 11.26 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.35 EDTShareFor 13 years, I have cared for my lovely 101-year-old adoptive mum who requires round-the-clock care. I feel blessed to care for her and have no regrets. But love does not pay the bills.Carer’s allowance is£86.45 a weekfor 2026-27. Spread across 168 hours, that is roughly 51p an hour. As a sole carer, I have no downtime. I still work part-time as a self-employed therapist when Mum’s health allows, but when she is poorly, my work stops while the bills continue.I do not claim carer’s allowance as the frequent paperwork required to report changes in my self-employed earnings is difficult to manage alongside my caring responsibilities.Last winter, our electricity bill exceeded £400 a month because Mum needs heating round the clock. This is the reality of caring in a cost of living crisis. I worked hard to buy and pay off my own home. But it had no downstairs bedroom or bathroom, and was unsuitable for Mum. I had to rent it out, hoping one day to live there. Eventually, caring and the costs of maintaining the property forced me to sell, and I faced a capital gains tax bill.I do not blame HMRC for applying the rules. I question whether government policy takes sufficient account of people whose caring responsibilities force them to make difficult decisions about their homes. Unpaid carers save society enormously, often at the expense of their own earnings, pensions and financial security. We need more than praise: we need practical support and a system that recognises the real cost of caring. Loving someone should not mean years of essential care leave you financially vulnerable.Emma SainsburyAuthor, Love, Laughter and the Hidden World of Unpaid CarersHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Do Stormont politics stifle the non-sectarian parties? | Northern Ireland | The Guardian
description: Letters: Responding to an editorial, Boyd Black deplores Labour’s policy of not fielding candidates in Northern Ireland. Plus a letter by Declan O’Neill
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Responding to an editorial, Boyd Black deplores Labour’s policy of not fielding candidates in Northern Ireland. Plus a letter by Declan O’Neill
Content: Parliament Buildings at the Stormont estate, Belfast.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAView image in fullscreenParliament Buildings at the Stormont estate, Belfast.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PANorthern IrelandLettersDo Stormont politics stifle the non-sectarian parties?Responding to an editorial,Boyd Blackdeplores Labour’s policy of not fielding candidates in Northern Ireland. Plus a letter byDeclan O’NeillThu 22 Oct 2026 11.25 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.26 EDTShareYour editorial on the dysfunction in Northern Ireland politics (15 October) does not mention the main cause: the denial of basic democratic rights to the people by the Labour party.The party national executive committee refuses to run Labour candidates in anyNorthern Irelandelection, whether to district councils, the Stormont assembly or the Westminster parliament.This means people here, including affiliated trade unionists, are denied the basic democratic right to vote for ourLabourgovernment, which is setting our taxes and winding us up for war.This undemocratic stance by Labour is not an act without consequences. By suppressing cross-community Labour party electoral politics, it forces the electorate into their ethnonational blocs and incentivises the sort of communal sectarian politics and stalemate that we are well used to.Boyd BlackSecretary, the Labour party in Northern IrelandIt is undoubtedly true, as your editorial says that “Northern Ireland’s voters currently do not have the politics they deserve”. However, there are problems with your assertion that the current model of power-sharing “designed to reassure nationalist and unionist communities remains indispensable”. In fact, it plays a part in maintaining the current “cycle of dysfunction”.I have family in Northern Ireland who would prefer to vote for parties that do not fit into this category, but doing so under the current rules would be pointless. They are part of a growing number of voters who do not primarily identify as being part of either “community”.However, even if parties such as the Alliance, the Greens, People Before Profit were to win a majority at Stormont, they would under the current rules not be allowed to form an administration. In fact the current system reinforces sectarian division by stipulating that only those parties self-identifying as nationalist or unionist can “power-share”. Ireland needs real change. The current system cannot deliver it.Declan O’NeillOldham, Greater ManchesterHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Storm names should tell a story or two | UK weather | The Guardian
description: Brief letters: Storm Austen | Interpreting Hokusai | NI for pensioners | Creative car names | Queue for the Bayeux
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Brief letters: Storm Austen | Interpreting Hokusai | NI for pensioners | Creative car names | Queue for the Bayeux
Content: A pedestrian on Westminster Bridge, London, braves Storm Austen.Photograph: ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA pedestrian on Westminster Bridge, London, braves Storm Austen.Photograph: ShutterstockBrief lettersUK weatherLettersStorm names should tell a story or twoStorm Austen | Interpreting Hokusai | NI for pensioners | Creative car names | Queue for the BayeuxThu 22 Oct 2026 11.24 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.25 EDTShareI was delighted to see that the first storm of the season is called Austen (Report, 20 October). I envisaged that its successors might be named after the Brontë sisters, Dickens and other notable British novelists. But my excitement soon subsided when I read that Storm Austen has been named not for Jane, but Austen Nagle, the first director of the Met Office.Christine ShuttleworthLondonJonathan Jones rightly praises the new exhibition of Hokusai’s work in Dulwich (Hokusai: Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji review, 19 October). But in Japan the work is read from right to left. We go with the power of the wave, but if you reverse the print, the wave appears even more dangerous.David CockayneWarrington, CheshireRe paying for sociall care (Letters, (19 October), national insurance currently ceases at pensionable age. A simple way to raise funds for social care would be to reinstate NI for well-off pensioners. It could then be renamed social care insurance.Peter McCartneyBristolIt’s not only placenames that can be hijacked for other uses (Letters, 16 October). The current crop of Chinese cars is a veritable seam of rich pickings: Jaecoo (cleaning cloths); Omoda (washing powder); Chery Tiggo (fruity gobstoppers). Struggling with Ora Funky Cat…Phil ThomasFrodsham,CheshireWhen my husband tried to buy tickets to see theBayeux tapestry, he was told that he was 233,600th in the queue. It puts waiting for the doctor to call back into perspective.Sandy CowlingLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
