title: Emery and Nagelsmann are top targets if Manchester United sack Carrick | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Unai Emery and Julian Nagelsmann have emerged as leading targets to replace Michael Carrick as Manchester United’s manager
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Unai Emery and Julian Nagelsmann have emerged as leading targets to replace Michael Carrick as Manchester United’s manager
Content: Unai Emery (left) and Julian Nagelsmann are in the frame if the Manchester United job becomes available.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUnai Emery (left) and Julian Nagelsmann are in the frame if the Manchester United job becomes available.Composite: Getty ImagesManchester UnitedEmery and Nagelsmann are top targets if Manchester United sack CarrickCarrick expected to be in charge for Bournemouth gameCompensation could be obstacle for Aston Villa’s EmeryJamie JacksonThu 22 Oct 2026 11.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 14.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnai Emery and Julian Nagelsmann have emerged as leading targets to replace Michael Carrick as Manchester United’s head coach should the board decide on a change after the club’s poorest start to the season since 1986.Carrick is expected to remain in place for Sunday’s visit of Bournemouth – he is due to hold his pre-game media conference on Friday – but the 45-year-old’s job is in the balance after two wins from 11 games this season.Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation at Comoin the Champions League has focused attention at United on a potential candidate to succeed Carrick should he be removed. Emery and Nagelsmann have admirers at board level.Carrick joins Wilcox under the bus after Manchester United’s latest night in crisis | Max RushdenRead moreEmery is contracted to Aston Villa until 2029, and Nagelsmann is unemployed after leaving his position as Germany’s manager in the wake of the team’slast-32 World Cup exitin the summer.Emery has impressed since taking over Villa in 2022, last season winning the Europa League, the club’s first major trophy since 1996, and finishing fourth, one place behind United.But Emery earns between £10m and £12m a year, so the compensation package United would have to pay Villa may be a stumbling block. He has also won trophies with Sevilla, Paris Saint-Germain and Villarreal and had a less successful spell with Arsenal.Nagelsmann has managed Hoffenheim, RB Leipzig and Bayern Munich, with whom he won the Bundesliga in 2022 before being sacked in March 2023. He is highly regarded by United’s head of recruitment, Christopher Vivell.The 39-year-old Nagelsmann guided Germany to the Euro 2024 quarter-finals, where they were knocked out by the eventual winners, Spain. It is understood Nagelsmann would be interested in an approach from United.Other potential candidates who may be considered include Antonio Conte, Eddie Howe and Kieran McKenna. They are out of work after leaving jobs with Napoli, Newcastle and Ipswich respectively. It is understood Fabian Hürzeler is not open to leaving Brighton at this stage.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBruno Fernandes’s house was the target of a break-in while United’s captain was away with the team at the Como defeat. His family were not at home, it is understood, and the intruders were inside for less than five minutes before the police arrived.The club is supporting Fernandes and his family and have asked for privacy regarding what it said was a difficult time.Meanwhile, the 32-year-old midfielder is not expected to face any disciplinary action for his criticism of Carrick on Wednesday.Fernandes questioned the head coach’s tacticsfollowing the Como defeat.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedUnai EmerynewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Max Dowman may get a chance, Spurs need to find balance at Stamford Bridge and Axel Disasi must make amends
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Max Dowman may get a chance, Spurs need to find balance at Stamford Bridge and Axel Disasi must make amends
Content: Arsenal’s Max Dowman, Rio Ngumoha of Liverpool and Aston Villa’s Emi Buendía.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenArsenal’s Max Dowman, Rio Ngumoha of Liverpool and Aston Villa’s Emi Buendía.Composite: Getty ImagesPremier LeaguePremier League: 10 things to look out for this weekendMax Dowman may get a chance, Spurs need to find balance at Stamford Bridge and Axel Disasi must make amendsPremier League top scorersGuardian sportThu 22 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 19.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1Glasner needs to fix Forest, fastAfter seven games, Nottingham Forest’s record is eerily similar to last season: five points, five goals scored. A year ago Forest’s eighth game was a 3-0 home loss to Chelsea thatmarked the end for Ange Postecoglou, the second of four managers to occupy the dugout last term. There is no suggestion that Oliver Glasner is under similar scrutiny yet, but the Austrian needs to find solutions for the league’s lowest scorers. Morgan Gibbs-White is available after missing thenarrow defeat by Arsenal, while Liam Delap may benefit from a return to familiar surroundings – 12 of his 14 career Premier League goals were scored for Ipswich, six of them at Portman Road. “What we need to improve is getting [Delap] into more positions where he can score,” Glasner said before Friday evening’s game. “He’s one of our best finishers.” Gary O’Neil also lacks a standout scorer, but he is squeezing goals out of his side. Eight different Ipswich players have scored in seven games; only Brighton and Brentford can better that total this season.Niall McVeighIpswich vNottingham Forest, Friday 8pmBSTNottingham Forest’s false start places early focus on Glasner and DelapRead more2New-look Villa host Maresca’s defiant CityIt was five months ago but it feels a lot longer. When these two sides met in May to finish the season, the contest doubled as Pep Guardiola’s leaving party after 10 years in the job and twice as many trophies, an era now laden with asterisks. It must be surreal for Aston Villa supporters, too.Their 2-1 victoryat the Etihad Stadium, inspired by two goals from Ollie Watkins to complete a league double over City, came only four days after theirEuropa League triumphin Istanbul, where Youri Tielemans, Morgan Rogers and Emi Buendía were the scorers. Buendía is the only one left in claret and blue as Unai Emery builds a new side, one that has picked up in form after a single point from their first four league games. City, meanwhile, are thriving on the pitch: victory would make them just the third side to win their first eight games of a Premier League season.Taha HashimAston Villa vManchester City, Saturday 12.30pm BST3Saka injury may benefit DowmanMax Dowman became the youngest goalscorer in Premier League history withhis dazzling solo strike against Evertonat the Emirates in March. But the supremely talented 16-year-old has found opportunities limited this season. Dowman has played only nine minutes in the Premier League despitescoring twice against Ipswichin the Carabao Cup last month as Arsenal have tried to protect their rising star. Yet thesuspected quad muscle injurysuffered by Bukayo Saka inWednesday’s 2-2 Champions League draw at Bayern Munichmeans Mikel Arteta is short of attacking options. With David Moyes’s side back in north London, it could be the perfect chance for Dowman to step up in his favoured position on the right flank.Ed AaronsArsenal vEverton, Saturday 3pm BST4Lampard wants Coventry to toughen upCoventry and Fulham have only met twice in the English top flight – back in 1967-68, when the promoted Sky Blues took a single point from two meetings, but stayed up by a point while Fulham went down. It is too early to call Saturday’s game a six-pointer in the relegation battle, but the two teams sit either side of the dreaded dotted line after shaky starts. Coventry have shown glimpses of their Championship swagger, particularlyin the 4-1 rout of Newcastle, but Frank Lampard wants his players to start thinking like a Premier League team. “I can’t keep applauding the players, believing they deserve to be here,” the Coventry manager said. “Now we have to get over that. We can’t be too soft.” Sunderland, Crystal Palace and Ipswich all visit the CBS Arena in the coming weeks, so there is an opportunity to consolidate. Fulham were linked with Lampard in the summer, and questions remain over whether Álvaro Arbeloa is pragmatic or flexible enough to succeed. Will these sides meet in the Premier League again next season? The jury is out.NMCoventry vFulham, Saturday 3pm BSTView image in fullscreenÁlvaro Arbeloa: still under pressure despite Fulham’s win over Hull.Photograph: Javier García/Shutterstock5De Zerbi needs balance for Chelsea challengeTottenham’s recent record against Chelsea is miserable. They are on a six-match losing streak against their London rivals and have collected a paltry two points at Stamford Bridge since last winning therein April 2018. Tottenham finally have a league win –they beat Coventry 3-1on Monday – but remain unconvincing. Roberto De Zerbi used a 3-4-2-1 system against Coventry. He had problems in midfield but now has to work out whether to change a winning team. Does he stick with James Maddison after the No 10’s excellent goal against his boyhood club? Spurs still looked short of energy at times. There is an argument to bring back Conor Gallagher’s dynamism, but would that hurt the side’s quality on the ball? Mateus Fernandes is another option but is yet to establish himself since joining from West Ham. Spurs’ approach remains hard to decipher. De Zerbi likes possession, but Chelsea want teams to open up as the Blues have searing pace on the break. Given their history in this fixture it seems Spurs should focus on tightening up. Equally they can’t be passive and need a threat on the break. De Zerbi will be searching for the right balance.Jacob SteinbergChelsea v Tottenham, Saturday 5.30pm BST6Iraola waiting for Anfield breakthroughTalk of Brighton achieving Champions League qualification for the first time will gain more credence, even at this early stage, should Fabian Hürzeler’s confident side extend their winning streak to seven matches in all competitions. There have been five clean sheets and 22 goals scored in their six-game winning run and the Premier League’s highest scorers will take encouragement from Liverpool’s defensive problems inthe comeback against Villarreal, which were not limited to Virgil van Dijk’s early lapses. Andoni Iraola is yet to savour a first home league win as Liverpool head coach – Anfield has seen only four home wins in 13 league games this year – and he will be wary of Brighton’s various threats. But with Rio Ngumoha electric in the Champions League win, Florian Wirtz improving and Alexander Isak increasingly decisive, the ingredients are in place for another enthralling spectacle.Andy Hunterskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLiverpool v Brighton, Sunday 2pm GMT7Who can rouse Carrick’s rabble?Who can or will lift Manchester United after the latest dismal/embarrassing week?Bruno Fernandes’s abdication of captaincy duties– accusing his manager of being tactically inept – showed what a rabble the team has become under Michael Carrick; and beyond the double footballer of the year, is there another star act who can win a game? Bournemouth will hope to take advantage, register only a second league win of the season, and deepen the misery for their hosts and fans. If his side goes down to the Cherries, Carrick will surely follow: the latest victim of the United circus.Jamie JacksonManchester United v Bournemouth, Sunday 2pm GMTView image in fullscreenBournemouth are coming off a 3-0 win against Milan on Thursday.Photograph: MB Media/Getty Images8Disasi must make amends at PalaceIt’s been six months since Crystal Palace recorded a clean sheet in the Premier League at Selhurst Park and the pressure will be on Pierre Sage against Newcastle on Sunday. Palace have conceded eight goals in four home league games this season, although they welcome back Axel Disasi from suspension afterhis reckless red card against Ipswich. The French defender was brought in on loan from Chelsea to add experience but cost Palace in the defeat by the newly-promoted side and had to watch from the sidelines as the Eagles werehumiliated against Brightonlast weekend. Disasi owes Sage a favour and he will be desperate to make up for his poor start to life in south London.EACrystal Palace v Newcastle, Sunday 2pm GMT9Hull and Brentford thrive off the ballSomething unusual will happen at the MKM Stadium on Sunday; either Hull City or Brentford will register more than 50% possession. In seven league games, Brentford only had more of the ball intheir 1-1 draw at Leeds. The hosts, meanwhile, are comfortably the most possession-averse team in the top flight so far this season, at an average of just over 30%. Both teams have been effective on the break and successful at set-pieces, with three goals apiece from dead balls. This may prove to be a match for the purists, where one clinical moment makes the difference. The Bees head coach, Keith Andrews, will hope it comes from Igor Thiago, yet to recapture the prolific form of last season. “Thiago at the moment is a very marked man, but we’ve got goalscorers throughout the team,” Andrews said of the Brazilian forward, who has scored one goal in seven this season. “Thiago being Thiago wants to score more goals, and he’s certainly not far away.”NMHull vBrentford, Sunday 2pm GMT10Mukiele issues war cry to SunderlandNordi Mukiele ranks among Sunderland’s best players and most influential dressing-room figures. Tellingly the former Paris Saint-Germain defender has been scathing about his team’s dismal start to thePremier Leaguecampaign and expects a reaction when Leeds visit Wearside on Sunday. “Leeds will be the right moment to show everyone we are not dead,” says Mukiele, well aware that Régis Le Bris’s side start this weekend on the bottom of the table. “We have not been good enough. Right now it’s not us; we are not Sunderland. I believe we can go back to the top. I believe in this team and this staff. We have quality.” Sunderland must use their three league fixtures before the international break – Leeds, Coventry away and Chelsea at home – to remind everyone why they finished seventh last season.Louise TaylorSunderland v Leeds, Sunday 4.30pm GMTPosTeamPGDPts1Man City712212Arsenal76183Brighton718164Chelsea74135Liverpool71126Brentford75107Leeds73108Everton71109Hull71910Ipswich7-4911Newcastle7-4812Aston Villa7-4813Man Utd70714Crystal Palace7-8715AFC Bournemouth7-4616Tottenham Hotspur7-4617Coventry7-8618Fulham7-3519Nottm Forest7-4520Sunderland7-84Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueManchester CityArsenalBrighton & Hove AlbionChelseaLiverpoolBrentfordfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Bournemouth enjoy night to remember as 10-man Milan fail to weather storm | Europa League | The Guardian
description: When it rains, it pours for Ruben Amorim as his Milan side were beaten 3-0 by Bournemouth after Mike Maignan’s mad red card
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: When it rains, it pours for Ruben Amorim as his Milan side were beaten 3-0 by Bournemouth after Mike Maignan’s mad red card
Content: Bournemouth’s Amine Adli adds gloss to the scoreline with his late free-kick.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBournemouth’s Amine Adli adds gloss to the scoreline with his late free-kick.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesEuropa LeagueBournemouth enjoy night to remember as 10-man Milan fail to weather stormNick Amesat the Vitality StadiumThu 22 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 18.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis was a momentous night in Bournemouth’s history, although the truth is they would have been given a far sterner examination by Coventry or Hull. Whatever this rotten impersonation of a Milan side was, it bore no relation to those that forged such a celebrated history. The visitors resembled holograms even before their goalkeeper Mike Maignan, with an extraordinary rush of blood resulting in a penalty and red card, rendered their task impossible. They never showed the slightest hint of putting up a fight.Bournemouth simply swamped the seven-time European champions and, amid a swirling south coast storm that rarely let up, could depart singing in the rain. Amine Adli’s sumptuous late free-kick, curled left-footed from 22 yards, meant they could finish the evening with the flourish they deserved. Their joy was clear at full time and met disapproval from some of Milan’s staff, who appeared to take umbrage in a short-lived fracas near the tunnel afterwards.Europa League: Sunderland held in Poznan as Juventus denied comeback winRead moreIt was certainly an abject return to English soil for Ruben Amorim, who could have been excused in seeing this particular week as the opportunity to prove a point. Amorim may view Bournemouth as kryptonite given they beat his Manchester United side by an identical scoreline at Old Trafford in December 2024. As it happens that is where the Cherries head on Sunday. On this damning evidence the modern version of Milan share more than a few similarities with his former employers.“A difficult night in every aspect,” Amorim said. It began with a downpour and waves of Bournemouth pressure, an incisive move ending with Justin Kluivert missing his kick and Ben Gannon-Doak’s drive deflecting wide. Milan failed to clear their lines from the resulting corner and were punished when VAR found Koni De Winter had deflected Evanilson’s header wide with his arm. Kluivert converted the spot kick coolly and the die was firmly cast.Amorim’s attempt to divide the match into two parts, before and after Maignan’s 27th-minute dismissal, cut no ice. Bournemouth’s tempo had been far too much for Milan before that, Maignan saving untidily from Ryan Christie after Yunus Musah’s pocket had been picked. “We just suffocated them, we didn’t give anything to them,” said a satisfied Marco Rose. “The way they did it today was just brilliant from the first minute until the last.”View image in fullscreenTyler Adams hits the deck after Mike Maignan pushes him in the face at a corner, resulting in a red card for the Milan goalkeeper.Photograph: Alex Pantling/Uefa/Getty ImagesWhen Maignan clawed James Hill’s deflected shot wide, everybody on view set up for a left-sided corner. Nobody was prepared for Maignan, who perhaps expected to be manhandling a taller opponent, to shove Tyler Adams in the face as the ball was sent in. It was a moment of supreme idiocy from the captain; the penalty award was inevitable and so, even before confirmation via VAR, was his departure. This time Marcus Tavernier did the honours, beating the replacement keeper Lorenzo Torriani.Barely half an hour in, the outcome had been settled. Bournemouth could hardly have imagined, in making their “great escape” from the fourth-tier trapdoor in 2009, that they might land in such a position against Italian royalty. Past luminaries looked on from the stands, Harry Redknapp among them, while their polished successors turned the screw down below.The relentless Gannon-Doak, called “a special player” afterwards by Rose, thrilled and frustrated in equal measure; the substitute Rayan almost set up a goal for Christie with a delightful piece of skill. It was Adli, another replacement, who applied a delicate garnish.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQuick GuideConference League: Salah breaks Hearts and Brighton held by JablonecShowInjury-hitHeartsproduced a spirited display in Turkey but ultimately went down to a 2-0 Conference League defeat at the hands of Mohamed Salah-inspiredTrabzonspor.The Scottish side acquitted themselves well amid a hostile atmosphere before going down to Salah’s first-half penalty and a second-half strike from Franculino, laid on by the former Liverpool star (pictured).The defeat leaves Wouter Vrancken’s side with one point from two matches ahead of their trip to Swiss champions Thun in a fortnight. Their visit had started in painful fashion after left-back Harry Milne suffered a suspected anterior cruciate ligament injury during training.Brightondrew a rare blank as they were held to a goalless draw by Czech minnowsJablonec. The Premier League’s top scorers, who have scored 23 goals across their first seven matches, misfired badly in the foothills of the Jizera Mountains in northern Czechia.Brighton head coach Fabian Hürzeler, in his 100th match in charge, made eight changes from that memorable win with only Bart Verbruggen, Olivier Boscagli and Pascal Gross keeping their places. The visitors squandered a host of chances, the best falling to Jack Hinshelwood, Georginio Rutter and Ibrahim Osman, and Jablonec were looking the likelier to score towards the end.Antonín Rusek almost capitalised on a mistake by Joao Costinha before Verbruggen had to make a spectacular fingertip save to prevent Jiri Slama’s drive from hitting the top corner.Press AssociationPhotograph: Hasan Tascan/AnadoluWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.What a night, then, for a club that knows what it is to gaze into the abyss. “How did we end up here?” asked the public address announcer before kick-off, a question repeated on a banner hoisted by the Steve Fletcher Stand, but it was worth posing in a different sense too. The sizable elephant in the room was how the Premier League’s 15th-placed team could face down one of Serie A’s most decorated institutions, unbeaten domestically this season, and simply sweep them off the park.In truth nobody could feign too much surprise; certainly not the bookmakers, who deemed Bournemouth the pre-match favourites. Scoffing at Milan’s inadequacy is, up to a point, simply plucking low-hanging fruit. Football’s ecosystem has arrived in a glum place where outwardly fairytale occasions like this are packaged with caveats: even the English top flight’s relative minnows are, through financial and physical power, playing on a different pitch to representatives of leagues once deemed its equals.For those understandably immersed in the here and now, Rayan came close to a superb fourth. “I’m happy for our fans especially,” Rose said. It is unlikely to be Bournemouth’s last European gala show.Explore more on these topicsEuropa LeagueBournemouthMilanmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Europa League: Celtic lose to Celta after leading, Mateta returns in Palace draw | Europa League | The Guardian
description: Celtic fell to another defeat after taking the lead against Celta Vigo, while Jean-Philippe Mateta scored on his first start for Crystal Palace since the opening day in a 2-2 draw at Besiktas
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Celtic fell to another defeat after taking the lead against Celta Vigo, while Jean-Philippe Mateta scored on his first start for Crystal Palace since the opening day in a 2-2 draw at Besiktas
Content: Celta Vigo's Javi Rodríguez shows his delight after giving his side the lead at Celtic Park.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAView image in fullscreenCelta Vigo's Javi Rodríguez shows his delight after giving his side the lead at Celtic Park.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAEuropa LeagueEuropa League: Celtic lose to Celta after leading, Mateta returns in Palace drawSunderland drop points in 1-1 draw but stay unbeatenVAR rules out Juventus winner in draw with RennesAgenciesThu 22 Oct 2026 17.41 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 15.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCelticsuffered moreEuropa Leaguepain as Spanish sideCelta Vigocame from behind to win 2-1 at Parkhead. After defeats by Ferencvaros and Benfica in their first two league phase fixtures, Martin O’Neill’s side struggled to impose themselves on the visitors who were neat and tidy without really testing Hoops keeper Sam Johnstone.Germany midfielder Mika Baur fired the home side in front just over a minute into the second half to thrill theCelticfans but Spain defender Javi Rodríguez scored twice in three minutes – a header then an unstoppable drive – to stun the home side who could not find a way back.Bournemouth enjoy night to remember as 10-man Milan fail to weather stormRead moreIt was another damaging Euro night for the Scottish champions, knocked out of the Champions League qualifiers by LASK on a 5-4 aggregate after being 4-0 up at one stage earlier in the season.Celtic’s ultras group, the Green Brigade, boycotted the game in protest at the running of the club, albeit there appeared to be only a couple of hundred empty seats, while 3,000 raucous Celta Vigo fans helped the noise.Jean-Philippe Mateta scored on his first start since the opening day butCrystalPalacecould not capitalise on aBesiktasred card to produce a winner in their 2-2 Europa League draw in Istanbul.Palace were looking to bounce back from Sunday’s humiliating 5-0 defeat at Brighton, and were the superior side before Wilfred Ndidi opened the scoring for the hosts in first-half stoppage time.Yéremy Pino drew the sides level six minutes after the restart and Mateta – who had a first-half goal chalked off by the video assistant referee – fired Palace to a first-time lead four minutes later.Junior Olaitan netted a 73rd-minute equaliser, and Palace could not find a winner after Umit Akdag was sent off for a clumsy 77th-minute challenge on Jørgen Strand Larsen, who was subsequently forced off.Sunderland’s winning start in the Europa League was ended with a 1-1 draw away toLech Poznan. The point keeps Sunderland unbeaten in Europe this season after back-to-back victories over AZ Alkmaar and Torreense.In a thrilling openingSunderlandwent in front early through Timur Tutierov, who was making only his third competitive start since arriving at Sunderland’s academy in 2023.The visitors had opportunities to extend their lead when Malick Fofana hit the post and Nordi Mukiele forced a strong save from Mateusz Lis, but Lech responded in the 70th minute through the substitute Leo Bengtsson’s low strike.Bournemouth v Milan, Celtic v Celta Vigo, and more: Europa League – liveRead moreRégis Le Bris made six changes fromSunday’s Premier League defeat to Bournemouth, including a first start of the season for Habib Diarra following his return from injury.Sunderland took the lead in the second minute when Nilson Angulo pounced on a tame pass from Lis, and the winger crossed into Tutierov in the middle of the box to comfortably nod home for his first Sunderland goal.Robin Roefs was called into action at the opposite end with a double save to deny Patrik Wålemark and palm away Antoni Kozubal’s header before Diarra charged up the pitch and fired into the side netting.The hosts had two good chances to level when Pablo Rodríguez blasted just past the post and Daniel Håkans was played through in a one-on-one with Roefs but flicked his shot wide.Sunderland enjoyed a good spell of possession during which the skipper, Granit Xhaka, had a strike parried away by Lis and the rebound fell to Fofana, who rattled the woodwork. Moments later Dayann Méthalie was denied at the near post by Lis as the visitors pushed for a second goal.View image in fullscreenTimur Tutierov scores his third goal for Sunderland’s first team since joining the academy in 2023.Photograph: Wojtek Radwański/AFP/Getty ImagesEarly in the second half, Fofana cut into the box but could only send his effort over and Poznan looked to strike when Wålemark scuffed a shot wide following a good solo run.Diarra fired wide for and Angulo’s low strike was scooped up by Lis, who moments later made a great save to tip Mukiele’s shot over the bar.Bengtsson looked to make an instant impact from the bench when his effort from Wålemark’s cross was sent wide. However, the midfielder made no mistake when next presented with an opportunity as a corner rebounded towards him just inside the area and he fired into the bottom corner with 20 minutes to play.Poznan almost took the lead moments later when Roefs made a brilliant point-blank stop from Michal Gurgul. Fofana skewed an effort wide as Sunderland looked to restore their advantage and the substitute Chris Rigg’s powerful shot landed on the roof of the net, but the spoils were shared.Quick GuideConference League: Salah breaks Hearts and Brighton held by JablonecShowInjury-hitHeartsproduced a spirited display in Turkey but ultimately went down to a 2-0 Conference League defeat at the hands of Mohamed Salah-inspiredTrabzonspor.The Scottish side acquitted themselves well amid a hostile atmosphere before going down to Salah’s first-half penalty and a second-half strike from Franculino, laid on by the former Liverpool star (pictured).The defeat leaves Wouter Vrancken’s side with one point from two matches ahead of their trip to Swiss champions Thun in a fortnight. Their visit had started in painful fashion after left-back Harry Milne suffered a suspected anterior cruciate ligament injury during training.Brightondrew a rare blank as they were held to a goalless draw by Czech minnowsJablonec. The Premier League’s top scorers, who have scored 23 goals across their first seven matches, misfired badly in the foothills of the Jizera Mountains in northern Czechia.Brighton head coach Fabian Hürzeler, in his 100th match in charge, made eight changes from that memorable win with only Bart Verbruggen, Olivier Boscagli and Pascal Gross keeping their places. The visitors squandered a host of chances, the best falling to Jack Hinshelwood, Georginio Rutter and Ibrahim Osman, and Jablonec were looking the likelier to score towards the end.Antonín Rusek almost capitalised on a mistake by Joao Costinha before Verbruggen had to make a spectacular fingertip save to prevent Jiri Slama’s drive from hitting the top corner.Press AssociationPhotograph: Hasan Tascan/AnadoluWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Juventusdropped their first points of the Europa League campaign after coming ⁠from behind to draw 2-2 with visitorsRennes.Zeki Celik gave Juventus a fifth-minute lead, but ⁠the French side ⁠kept their ​composure and were level 10 minutes later when the Jordan international Musa Al-Taamari finished from close range for ⁠his first goal in the competition.Rennes then stunned the hosts with a Boulaye Dia penalty two minutes before the ⁠break as the Italians struggled to create chances until Nick Woltemade equalised ​from the spot in the 67th ‌minute.View image in fullscreenNick Woltemade equalises from the spot for Juventus in their 2-2 draw with Rennes.Photograph: sportinfoto/DeFodi Images/ShutterstockThe Germany forward ‌twice went close to scoring again as Luciano Spalletti’s team upped the ‌pressure, and Juve thought they had won it in the 88th minute when Jhon Lucumí found the net from close range, but his effort was ruled out for offside.The draw at least spared Juventus a second successive defeat following Sunday’s 3-0 home loss to Lazio ‌in Serie A.Jonas Hofmann made the most of his surprise start forBayer Leverkusen, scoring twice in three minutes ​to give the Bundesliga side a 2-0 victory atOFI Creteto go top of the table with their third straight win.Crete, who stunned Hoffenheim 2-0 in their opening league-phase match, were twice caught napping by Hofmann, ⁠who was added to the side following an injury to ​Martin Terrier. title: Sri Lanka stun England with second-highest ODI chase despite Brook’s 202 | Harry Brook | The Guardian
description: Sri Lanka beat England by two wickets despite Harry Brook’s record 202 with the second-highest successful ODI run chase
Author: Taha Hashim
Headline: Sri Lanka beat England by two wickets despite Harry Brook’s record 202 with the second-highest successful ODI run chase
Content: Sri Lanka's Janith Liyanage is hugged by his teammates after hitting the winning runs.Photograph: Akhtar Soomro/ReutersView image in fullscreenSri Lanka's Janith Liyanage is hugged by his teammates after hitting the winning runs.Photograph: Akhtar Soomro/ReutersHarry BrookSri Lanka stun England with second-highest ODI chase despite Brook’s 202Liyanage hits six for win with one ball to spareEngland captain’s record innings not enoughTaha HashimThu 22 Oct 2026 12.37 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 18.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHarry Brook pulverised his way to the fastest double hundred in ODI history and still ended up on the losing side. This was an absurd contest, with Sri Lanka hauling down a target of 430 in Rawalpindi, the second-highest successful chase in the history of the format. Only that magical 438 game, 20 years ago, trumps it.Pavan Rathnayake, Dasun Shanaka and Avishka Fernando were the headliners, turning it around for Sri Lanka after they were reduced to 24 for two. Rathnayake top-scored with 130, Fernando struck 97, and Shanaka, with 97 of his own, was the most brutal of the lot. After being taken apart with the ball, his revenge act included eight sixes.England v Sri Lanka: Brook makes history in men’s tri-series cricket ODI – liveRead moreNone of the trio were there at the close as England suddenly found themselves back in it, eight needed by Sri Lanka off the final over. Josh Tongue rattled the stumps of Dunith Wellalage and Eshan Malinga with consecutive deliveries, but Janith Liyanage walloped a six down the ground to close the night, finishing his stay on 61 with a ball to spare.So a sublime piece of work, even by Brook’s high standards, came in vain. His footwork was the standout during his 202, tap-dancing across the crease as he ramped, scooped and sliced the ball behind both sides of the wicket with remarkable ­consistency. It took him 114 balls to reach 200, beating Shubman Gill’s 117-ball effort for India against West Indies three weeks ago.“It was a nice innings; unfortunately it doesn’t mean anything now,” he said. “Being on the losing side, it has no value whatsoever in my eyes.”England’s captain will also have to reflect on the makeup of his side for the next two games of this tri-series after back-to-back defeats. A ­notable selection call could so easily have been forgotten in victory. Adil Rashid,expensive against Pakistan on Tuesday, was left out for Liam Dawson as England opted for the skiddier left-arm option.Tom Banton punched his way to 50 for the fourth game in a row, but the first major act was the third-wicket stand between Joe Root and Brook. The pair hopped into the DeLorean and went back to January in Colombo,when they put on 191in a series decider against Sri Lanka. Brook began slowly, just 13 off his first 24 deliveries, but took advantage of the part-timers, thumping Kamindu Mendis and Liyanage to reach his half-century off 42 balls.Quick GuideA record-breaking ODI: in numbersShowHarry Brook’s 202 was England’s highest ever one-day international score, beating Ben Stokes’ 182 against New Zealand in 2023.• It was the highest ever score and first double century by a batter in an ODI defeat,the previous record being Charles Coventry’s 194 not outfor Zimbabwe against Bangladesh in 2009.•429 for fourwas England’s fourth-highest ODI total, the record being498 for fouragainst the Netherlands in 2022. It was their highest outside England against a Test-playing nation.• The859 runs scored in totalwas the second highest ODI aggregate and the highest in a game involving England, beating the 807 in a February 2019 win over the West Indies.•Brook’s 144 runs in boundaries– 21 fours and 10 sixes – surpassed Jos Buttler’s England record of 124 in that game. The two teams combined for93 foursand552 runs in boundariesin Rawalpindi, both records for a one-day international match.• Sam Curran broke his own England record for the most runs conceded in an ODI innings.Curran's two for 103from nine overs exceeded the 98 runs he gave up in a 2023 loss to the Windies.• There were an ODI record-equallingfour century partnerships– Brook with both Joe Root and Will Jacks for England, and Sri Lanka’s Pavan Rathnayake with both Avishka Fernando and Dasun Shanaka. It was the fifth ODI with four such stands, the most recent coming in July as England beat India at Lord’s.PAHighest successful run chases in men's ODIsSri Lanka's astonishing effort on Thursday slots in as the second-highest successful chase in men's one-day international history …438-9South Africa v Australia, Johannesburg 2006430-8Sri Lanka vs England, Rawalpindi 2026406-2India v West Indies, Guwahati 2026374-6Netherlands v Scotland, Dundee 2025372-6South Africa v Australia, Durban 2016364-4England v West Indies, Bridgetown 2019Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Milestones follow Root every time he bats nowadays and this time it was the mark of 8,000 ODI runs. He quietly accumulated as Brook began to torment Sri Lanka’s frontliners as well. While Root miscued on 69, Brook reached his hundred from 75 balls.As Will Jacks joined in and bashed a few himself, it became clear that an enormous total was on, as was the double for Brook. He moved from a ton to 150 in 22 balls; he took 17 more to reach 200. A cute ramp off Liyanage was a fitting stroke to get there. The only thing missing was a red-inker, with Brook perishing off the final ball of the innings.View image in fullscreenHarry Brook guides the ball to the off side during his record-breaking 202 off 116 balls.Photograph: Sameer Ali/Getty ImagesLost within Brook’s genius was Jacks’s power, his unbeaten 66 ­taking 30 balls. Wellalage was the only bowler to escape Brook’s wrath, not conceding a boundary off the 27-year-old. Two for 56 has never looked so good.Sri Lanka lost two wickets quickly. Tongue bowled Kamindu with a corker and Kusal was gone before facing, run out by Gus Atkinson’s fingertips at the non-striker’s end. But Rathnayake and Avishka refused to collapse.Quick GuideWho else scored a double century and ended up on the losing side?ShowHarry Brook is far from the first player to score more than 200 runs in an international innings and end up on the losing side – it happened to West Indies legend Brian Lara on three occasions. Azhar Ali and Len Hutton shared the feeling of scoring a double ton and ending up losing a Test by an innings.The Englishman is, however, the first to endure the feeling in a one-day international.242Ricky Ponting (Aus) Lost by 4 wkts to Ind, Second Test 2003226Brian Lara (WI) Lost by 7 wkts to Aus, Third Test 2005222Nathan Astle (NZ) Lost by 98 runs to Eng, First Test 2002221Brian Lara (WI) Lost by 10 wkts to Sri Lanka, Third Test 2001217Shakib Al Hasan (Ban) Lost by 7 wkts to NZ, First Test 2017214Victor Trumper (Aus) Lost by 38 runs to SA, Third Test 1911209Graeme Pollock (SA) Lost by 6 wkts to Aus, Second Test 1966-7206Paul Collingwood (Eng) Lost by 6 wkts to Aus, Second Test 2006205Neil Harvey (Aus) Lost by 6 wkts to SA, Fifth Test 1953205Azhar Ali (Pak) Lost by innings and 18 runs to Aus, Second Test 2016204Aubrey Faulkner (SA) Lost by 89 runs to Aus, Second Test 1910-11203Dennis Amiss (Eng) Lost by 231 runs to WI, Fifth Test 1976203Matthew Hayden (Aus) Lost by 2 wkts to Ind, Third Test 2001203Kumar Sangakkara (Sri Lanka) Lost by 193 runs to NZ, Second Test 2015202Len Hutton (Eng) Lost by innings and 56 runs to WI, Fourth Test 1950202Brian Lara (WI) Lost by 189 runs to SA, First Test 2003202Harry Brook (Eng) Lost by 2 wkts to Sri Lanka, ODI Tri-Series 2026201Syd Gregory (Aus) Lost by 10 runs to Eng, First Test 1894201Virender Sehwag (Ind) Lost by 168 runs to Pak, Third Test 2005Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.This was still a flat pitch to enjoy and Sri Lanka, hours earlier, had ­chosen to chase. The third-wicket pair put on 166, with Rathnayake particularly brutal when the ball went short. Avishka fell just shy of a hundred, returning a catch to Jamie Overton, but Shanaka kept up the rhythm. All while England’s great leg-spinner sat on the bench.At 250 for three, with 16 overs left, Sri Lanka were far better placed than England had been at the same stage, but it still felt so very far away. Rathnayake reached his century off 87 balls, thriving with that low-hands setup at the crease, and England failed to find a quiet over or two.Shanaka blitzed Sam Curran’s moon ball as he passed 50 and with 109 needed off 60 Sri Lanka finally looked the more likely victors. A tiring Rathnayake could not beat long-on against Curran and Shanaka fell on the boundary against Dawson. But Liyanage remained, keeping England winless in the series. Just staggering.Explore more on these topicsHarry BrookEngland cricket teamSri Lanka cricket teamCricketmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: South Africa beat Boland and weather to force series decider against Australia | Cricket | The Guardian
description: Scott Boland batted for more than three hours but South Africa beat Australia by an innings and 31 runs in the second Test in Gqeberha
Author: Geoff Lemon
Headline: Scott Boland batted for more than three hours but South Africa beat Australia by an innings and 31 runs in the second Test in Gqeberha
Content: South Africa won despite losing nearly two days to rain and a bowler to injury, and being 110 for 6 in their first innings.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSouth Africa won despite losing nearly two days to rain and a bowler to injury, and being 110 for 6 in their first innings.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesCricketSouth Africa beat Boland and weather to force series decider against AustraliaRabada and Mulder lead hosts to victory in second TestBoland bats for more than three hours as nightwatchmanGeoff LemonThu 22 Oct 2026 11.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 18.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt took time, it gently frayed nerves, but South Africa sealed the second Test in Gqeberha deep into the final day, clear by an innings and 31 runs, levelling the series with one to play. Although Australia made 295 and got within 28 overs of safety, they did not deserve to save this game, even if Scott Boland and Travis Head did.Letting South Africa escapefrom 40 for four to pass 400 was the first offence, then cameAustralia’s capitulation for 99to be forced to follow on. The salvage operation was in waters too deep.South Africa beat Australia by innings and 31 runs: second men’s cricket Test, day five – as it happenedRead moreAustralia got an early boost from a washed-out morning session that cut the day’s ration from 98 overs to 82. The next boost came from Boland: havingdone it all with the ballwhile nobody else could match him, he then led with the bat. He had the nightwatch job in the first innings, batting briefly on the fourth morning, then had to do it a second time that evening, taking Australia to stumps at 156 for four.On day five, though, his stay was anything but brief. With his team four wickets down and 170 runs behind, Boland settled in for the most substantial innings of his Test career, a personal best of 166 balls, while his 40 runs nearly doubled his previous best. He outlasted century-maker Head, outlasted Steve Smith and passed the tea break after an extended session.There was the odd dabble at the wrong ball, the odd bit of luck with an edge, but the rest was an exercise in careful defence on the front foot, evasion on the back, batting out maidens with relative ease and taking rare chances for a stylish cut.At the other end, Head did not tarry in the 90s with a few carved boundaries through the off side, then settled right down after raising his first official hundred in an away Test – hisWorld Test Championship final tonagainst India at the Oval in 2023 being defined as neutral in venue. By his standards it was a sedate 121 from 190 balls and while it continued the spectre of the draw became a little more material, even though change hovered one wicket away.View image in fullscreenWiaan Mulder took three key second-innings wickets, including the nightwatchman Scott Boland.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesIt was fitting that the day was defined by Wiaan Mulder, the shortest, least rapid and least celebrated member of South Africa’s fast-bowling stocks. Humility is at Mulder’s core, the man whodeclined a shot at breaking the world record score, the man who does whatever job his team asks of him: new ball in Durban with two spinners, old ball when Kagiso Rabada returns, stepping up for more overs when Anrich Nortje is injured, bowling into a serious wind, batting three when nobody else wants it, batting seven when they do, attempting to bat time when Australia were bowling for victory, stopping them from batting time when the tables had turned.Here, his approach was simple and skilful: hit the seam, wait for jag. Head got plenty, shorter and faster than expected, making him jump, forced to glove down on to his stumps. Boland got a better one, fuller and decking into the gap for the right-hander, even his set defence no chance of keeping it out.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSri Lanka stun England with second-highest ODI chase despite Brook’s 202Read moreAn over later, Mulder repeated the dose to Pat Cummins, the ball moving a little less this time to make him play inside the line. Mulder’s three for 64 will not be written on any walls, but it won the match.That left the score 262 for eight, with Smith already gone, and while reputation would suggest that he was the most important wicket, that belies his long record of having no effect on fifth days. Showing no sign of the stiff neck that had hampered him the previous day, Smith nonetheless torpedoed his brief innings with an atrocious shot, trying to pound a pull shot off Rabada from outside off stump, hitting a catch up in the air.With nothing needed but to bat time, it was a decision as poor as Marnus Labuschagne’s attempted six off Simon Harmer’s spin the previous day. The comparison of either to Boland’s determination is catastrophically unflattering. While the lower order is not primarily to blame, you could equally ask why Mitchell Starc tried swinging Rabada over the leg side, instead finding fresh air and losing leg stump. Or why Josh Hazlewood tried a booming drive through cover to nick to slip, stranding Alex Carey on 37 not out. Marco Jansen got that last wicket, Rabada finished with four.With so few overs to go, and with heavy cloud starting to roll in, this was a match that could have been saved with more application from one or two players. It concluded an Australia performance riven with fundamental failures of decision-making, from players whose celebrated wealth of experience gives them no excuse for that shortfall.For South Africa, it is a dramatic comeback fromtheir own heavy loss at Durbanand a reminder that all revelry and disappointment is temporary. There will be another portion of each, however, to be doled out next week in Cape Town. The decider beckons.Explore more on these topicsCricketAustralia cricket teamAustralia sportSouth Africa cricket teammatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Lewis Hamilton aims to extend career till early 2030s so he can race in African Grand Prix | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: The 41-year-old is set on fulfilling his ‘dream to be able to race in Africa’, specifically Rwanda which will host despite criticism of its human rights record
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: The 41-year-old is set on fulfilling his ‘dream to be able to race in Africa’, specifically Rwanda which will host despite criticism of its human rights record
Content: Lewis Hamilton believes that the race in Rwanda will be a force for good rather than sportswashing.Photograph: Brett Farmer/LAT ImagesView image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton believes that the race in Rwanda will be a force for good rather than sportswashing.Photograph: Brett Farmer/LAT ImagesFormula One 2026Lewis Hamilton aims to extend career till early 2030s so he can race in African Grand Prix41-year-old set on ‘dream to be able to race in Africa’Rwanda to host despite criticism of human rights recordGiles Richardsin AustinThu 22 Oct 2026 17.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 18.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLewis Hamilton has said he hopes to remain racing in Formula One until he can take part in the African Grand Prix which isset to take place in Rwanda in the 2030s. The seven-time world champion believes it is right that F1 is to hold a race there despite criticism of the country’s human rights record.Last week F1 confirmed Rwanda was to host the African Grand Prix having concluded a 10-year agreement for the meeting on a purpose-built circuit, with the first race set for the early 2030s. It is lined up to be held on a circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital, Kigali, which has yet to be constructed and marks a return to the African continent for the first time since it last held a race at Kyalami, SouthAfricain 1993.Austin GP is about much more than potential for Antonelli’s first F1 world title | Giles RichardsRead moreHamilton has beenchampioning a race in Africafor some time. The 41-year-old is understood to be currently contracted with Ferrari until the end of the 2027 season, and speaking before this weekend’s US Grand Prix he said he would like to continue racing for at least another four years in order to make it to the meeting in Rwanda.“I’m now forced to have to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa andthat’s been my dreamto be able to race in Africa,” he said. “So, I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit if I can. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we’ll keep it going.”Hamilton would be at least in his mid-40s if he was to continue until 2030. F1’s current oldest driver is 45-year-old Fernando Alonso.F1’s deal withRwandais for a 10-year period but because of the country’s human rights record the award of the race has been criticised as an act of sportswashing.Quick GuideBritain's Slater, 18, to make F1 practice debut for AudiShowBritain’s 18-year-old Freddie Slater will make his Formula 1 free practice debut for ⁠Audi at next week’s Mexico City Grand Prix.Audi entered Formula 1 this year ⁠after taking over ⁠the ​Sauber team, and Slater was the first driver signed to the team’s new driver academy.Slater ⁠finished second in the Formula 3 standings to Ugo Ugochukwu in his debut season while ⁠racing for Trident Motorsport. He is slated to move ​to Formula 2 with Invicta ‌next year."Getting behind the wheel of an F1 car at a grand prix weekend is a big moment for me and something I’ve been dreaming of since I was a kid," Slater said. “I’ve learned a ‌lot this year, and these Free practice outings with Audi F1 Team will be another opportunity ​to keep gaining on-track experience."Slater is also slated to drive in the first practice session at next month’s Sao Paulo Grand Prix."We have seen Freddie making great progress ⁠throughout recent years, both on and off the track; ​it is ​the right time for ​Freddie to step up," Audi racing director and ​academy director ‌Allan McNish, a former F1 driver himself, said."These ​appearances ​in Mexico and Brazil will give him valuable experience of a Formula 1 race weekend, and another chance to continue his development."ReutersWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“A 10-year grand prix ‘presented by Visit Rwanda’ is a sportswashing prize for the Rwandan authorities,” said Felix Jakens, Amnesty UK’s head of campaigns. “Rwanda isbuying into the world’s biggest sportsto polish its image and deflect from ⁠its appalling human rights record. Formula One says sport can be ‘a positive force for good’. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with. Rwanda’s authorities are prolific in arbitrary detention, torture and the repression of free speech.”View image in fullscreenRwanda’s investment in sports sponsorship has led to accusations that it is attempting to sportswash its human rights record.Photograph: SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesHamilton nonetheless felt the meeting would serve as a force for good in Africa and that there also should be more education about the continent.“I’m really, really hopeful for that grand prix,” he said. “Of course, I don’t get to choose where we go, and naturally there’s problems all over the world today, so I’ve seen many of the stories but I think we really have to approach it with humility.“There’s a lot that we don’t know. I mean, growing up in England, they never ever taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum. A lot of the problems they have there are still results of colonialism, and the West intervening.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I really hope, and I still have hopes, that Africa unites. I know there’s many people that don’t want that to happen, because they would be so powerful if they did, but I’m still hopeful that at some stage they will.”The new race is being backed by the government of Rwanda and the Rwanda Development Board, who intend to develop the venue as a destination not only for motorsport but for promoting economic growth. The country has recently invested heavily in hosting sporting events, including cycling’s road world championships, cricket’s Women’s Challenge Trophy, the 2023 Fifa congress andthe Basketball Africa League.Hamilton felt that at least the race would present an opportunity for people to take a greater interest in Africa.“Going doesn’t mean that you neglect the things that are happening there,” he said. “Hopefully many people start to educate themselves a little bit more of what is happening there, what has happened there for hundreds of years and I hope that does spark the conversation. Then I guess I’ll finish it off with, I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping that at some stage we get to.”Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli goes into this weekend’s US Grand Prix in a position to clinch his first F1 title. The 20-year-old holds a 102-point lead over his teammate George Russell and will become Formula One’s youngest world champion if he wins, Russell finishes ninth or lower and Hamilton is fifth or lower.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Lewis HamiltonFerrariFormula OneMotor sportRwandaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Tour de France 2027 routes revealed with British stages, time trials and a volcano | Tour de France | The Guardian
description: Edinburgh will host the most northerly Tour de France start in 2027 while the Pyrenees will provide the competitive finale of next year’s route
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Edinburgh will host the most northerly Tour de France start in 2027 while the Pyrenees will provide the competitive finale of next year’s route
Content: Tour de France race director Christian Prudhomme unveils the map of the stages during the presentation of the Tour de France 2027 in Paris.Photograph: Christophe Petit-Tesson/EPAView image in fullscreenTour de France race director Christian Prudhomme unveils the map of the stages during the presentation of the Tour de France 2027 in Paris.Photograph: Christophe Petit-Tesson/EPATour de FranceTour de France 2027 routes revealed with British stages, time trials and a volcano‘Britain offers us a symbol that ties the races together’Tour de France Femmes will conclude on Puy de DômeJeremy WhittleThu 22 Oct 2026 07.11 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 15.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe most ambitious Grand Départ in the long history of theTour de Francewas unveiled in Paris on Thursday as the race organisers fleshed out the details of next summer’s men’s and women’s race starts in Edinburgh and Yorkshire.Over six days of racing, Scotland, England’s Lake District and Peak District, Lancashire and Yorkshire, Wales and central London will be taken over by the snaking race caravan on a route that is expected to lure millions to the roadside.Christian Prudhomme, the men’s Tour director, said he expected “a warm and massive welcome for the champions”. “From the start at the foot of Edinburgh Castle – the northernmost in the history of the Tour – to a team time trial in London, Great Britain offers us a symbol that further ties the two races together,” he said.The sports minister, Stephanie Peacock, confirmed that £65m has been allocated to fund the six stages and said the Tour’s visit would “shine a spotlight on women’s cycling like never before”.View image in fullscreenChristian Prudhomme at the route unveiling in Paris.Photograph: Christophe Petit-Tesson/EPAThe men’s race starts in Edinburgh on 2 July and finishes in Paris on 25 July, with a final stage that maintains the tradition of racing up and over the cobbled streets of Montmartre.Paul Bush, the managing director of Grand Depart GB, has big ambitions of his own for the race. “One of my aspirations will be to turn the UK yellow next year, for two weeks, so everybody is in yellow,” he said. “Now that would be pretty special.“Now that would beat 2014. Not that I’m looking to beat 2014, because it’s not a competition. But if we could encourage everybody, workplaces, communities, old age pensioners’ homes, schools, everything to become yellow, I think that would really embrace the thing.”In fact, the men’s Tour will begin and end on cobblestones. From the Royal Mile to the Champs-Élysées, the peloton will cover 3,479km of racing and take in two individual time trials, three summit finishes and a potential decider in the climbs of the Pyrenees.The first British stage, from Edinburgh to Carlisle, will head through Midlothian and the Borders, while stage two, from Keswick to Liverpool, will cover 223km and take in Lancashire’s Trough of Bowland before finishing on Liverpool’s waterfront.View image in fullscreenA view of the route for stage one of the 2027 Tour.Illustration: TdFView image in fullscreenStage two of the Tour will take riders from Keswick to Liverpool.Illustration: TdFThe final British stage will include eight climbs on the winding road from Welshpool to Cardiff, and is likely to be one of the hardest stages of the race.View image in fullscreenThe challenge awaiting riders in Wales on stage three.Illustration: TdFAfter the transfer across the Channel, the peloton races across central France, from Cherbourg to the Jura, for the first summit finish on the Grand Colombier, followed by mountain stages to Sallanches and Les Saisies.From the Rhone Valley, wherethe furnace conditionsthat characterised this year’s race are likely to return, the convoy heads into the Cévennes and the Tarn for finishes in Mende and Albi.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe second time trial is centred on Toulouse and comes before two brutal Pyrenean stages, the first crossing the fearsome Col du Tourmalet before a finish on the Col du Portet, and the second, to Laruns, taking in four major ascents and 4,300m of climbing.The Tour de France Femmes begins in Leeds on 30 July, 13 years after the men’s race staged its Grand Départ there, with an opening stage from the Headrow to a likely sprint finish on Deansgate in Manchester.The next day’s challenge, from Manchester to Sheffield, includes both Winnats and Snake Pass on a route which features almost 3,000m of climbing and which the race director, Marion Rousse, called the cornerstone of “the hardest opening in the history of the women’s race”.But the showpiece stage will be in central London, with an 18km team time trial, routed from Westminster to The Mall, taking in Tower Bridge, St Paul’s Cathedral, Trafalgar Square and Buckingham Palace.London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, said the Tour’s visit would “not only cement London’s status as the undisputed capital of women’s sport, but also inspire more people to take up cycling, as we build a better, greener London for everyone.”After the transfer to northern France, the women’s peloton heads south, via Calais, Magnanville and Bourges, to a first mountain finish at La Loge des Gardes before a penultimate mountain stage through the Auvergne to Clermont-Ferrand. The nine-day race climaxes on the steep volcanic Puy de Dôme, after a stage that climbs almost 4,000m.View image in fullscreenTour de France Femmes race director Marion Rousse confirms the 2027 route.Photograph: Billy Ceusters/Getty ImagesBoth routes were unveiled at Porte Maillot even as curfews remained in place in some parts of central Paris, including Place de la République and Les Halles. The French media described the nation as sinking “deeper into crisis”, but in the aftermath of the Covid pandemic and the controversies of climate change, the Tour has become well-versed in puffing out its chest in the face of adversity and threats.However, disruption, due to both civil unrest and extreme temperatures, remains possible. Race organisers ASO faced a similar situation in July 2023, when climate activists and rioting threatened the race. That year, Prudhomme said the Tour was “in constant liaison with the state” and would “adapt if needed”.Explore more on these topicsTour de FranceCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Surfing faces a cultural reckoning as women’s voices grow louder over sexual abuse allegations | Surfing | The Guardian
description: A culture of silence has buried the stories of women who allege sexual assault in surf industry settings
Author: Lucy Small
Headline: A culture of silence has buried the stories of women who allege sexual assault in surf industry settings
Content: ‘For the first time since I joined the surfing community, I have seen the rumours written down, albeit so far in comment sections and Instagram posts,’ Lucy Small says.Photograph: Ed Sloane/World Surf League/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘For the first time since I joined the surfing community, I have seen the rumours written down, albeit so far in comment sections and Instagram posts,’ Lucy Small says.Photograph: Ed Sloane/World Surf League/Getty ImagesSurfingSurfing faces a cultural reckoning as women’s voices grow louder over sexual abuse allegationsLucy SmallA culture of silence has buried the stories of women who allege sexual assault in surf industry settingsThu 22 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 10.01 EDTShareWhen news broke last week that a surfer had been provisionally suspended from international competition, after what the InternationalSurfingAssociation (ISA) described as “recent reports of serious allegations of abuse within the surfing community,” the response online was unprecedented in the world of surfing.While investigations into those allegations are ongoing, the story prompted a deluge of comments detailing other alleged experiences of sexual misconduct and assault in surf industry settings, ranging from corporate brand houses in Hawaii to organised surf trips. While horrifying, for women who have existed in this subculture across the decades, those broader stories are sadly no surprise.Climate crisis is coming to crush many of world’s best surf breaks, study warnsRead moreIn 2019, as I stood in a bar in New York City at the afterparty of a World Surf League (WSL) Longboard Tour contest, I took stock of my surroundings. It was after midnight and the bar was packed with competitors who had just wrapped an event on a windy North Atlantic Ocean earlier that day. From the women’s side of the tour, teenagers gathered; nearby, other competitors and event staff, many well into their 40s, were dotted across the room. Alcohol flowed freely; the event was private, so there was no one checking IDs. In fact, surfers themselves could be found behind the bar pouring drinks. I reflected on the moment: who was tasked with keeping these young women safe while in a setting like this? And if something were to happen, how would we report it, and to whom?Over the years, the stories between women working and competing in the industry have accumulated in private. Ranging from sexual harassment to assault, none of these stories ever ended in accountability. When I raised this issue with Surfing NSW a few years ago, I was told the process for something that happened at a Surfing NSW event would be to make the complaint to the event director, and it would then be passed on to the state body’s CEO. At the time, Surfing NSW said they had never received any such complaint. It’s not difficult to understand why.In the WSL context, while I have competed in sanctioned events for more than a decade, I have never received any information about how to report an incident of sexual abuse to the WSL, or how that report would be treated. And in a male-dominated industry that is tight-knit and insular, where the same people move from institution to institution, where work is often contract to contract, and sponsorship decisions and other opportunities are relationship-based, trying to act against these ranks in search of accountability carries potentially career-ending risk.Without any clear independent reporting mechanism or track record of taking these reports seriously, these institutions create a culture of silence that protects the accused and buries the stories of women who may have faced sexual violence while competing or working at surfing events.What was most surprising about the recent allegations that prompted a statement from the ISA was not that they are being made, but that there has actually been a response. A surfer has been suspended, pending investigation, in a culture that had previously glorified a lifestyle where women’s bodies were sacrificed in favour of surfing talent.Australian surfer Nat Young, who was the 1966 world champion and is credited with being one of the pioneers of the shortboard revolution of the 1970s, described a disturbing scene in the opening chapter of his memoir Nat’s Nat and That’s That. Young writes in the book published in 1998 that a friend “had strategically positioned the girl so that she was lying on her back with her head facing away from the youthful group of lechers and so was able to give the nod over her shoulder”. He adds that when the friend “slipped out”, another “slipped in”, then a third person and Young “had our turn in the same manner”.“The Grunter”, as Young describes the girl in the book, “was really into group sex and we all greeted her with open flies every time we saw her getting off her school bus”. “The scene was starting to get a bit out of hand, the line getting longer and longer as friends and acquaintances from other beaches joined in,” he writes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toAustralia SportGet a daily roundup of the latest sports news, features and comment from our Australian sports deskEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYoung’s account is not the only one of its kind that exists in the pages of surfing’s magazines and memoirs that have been published over the years, serving as a tool to not just validate and normalise such experiences but laud them, weaving them into the central fabric of the industry.Now it appears that wind has started to blow under the cladding that has kept this conversation confined to the private spaces of women, spoken in secret for fear of professional or social reprisal. For the first time since I joined the surfing community, I have seen the rumours written down, albeit so far in comment sections and Instagram posts. But will this be a reckoning beyond a passing moment of outrage? Will it lead to actual reform of the structures that have maintained this culture?Lucy Small is a professional surfer, journalist and film-maker from Sydney, with a special interest in women’s sportExplore more on these topicsSurfingAustralia sportcommentShareReuse this content

title: Downing Street rejects Witkoff’s description of Putin as a ‘humanitarian’ | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: No 10 says Russian president ‘has killed thousands of people, both innocent Ukrainians and his own people’
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: No 10 says Russian president ‘has killed thousands of people, both innocent Ukrainians and his own people’
Content: Steve Witkoff and Vladimir Putin met at the Constantine Palace in St Petersburg on Wednesday.Photograph: Kristina Solovyova/ReutersView image in fullscreenSteve Witkoff and Vladimir Putin met at the Constantine Palace in St Petersburg on Wednesday.Photograph: Kristina Solovyova/ReutersUkraineDowning Street rejects Witkoff’s description of Putin as a ‘humanitarian’No 10 says Russian president ‘has killed thousands of people, both innocent Ukrainians and his own people’Aletha AduPolitical correspondentThu 22 Oct 2026 12.33 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 13.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDowning Street has rejected the description ofVladimir Putinas a “humanitarian” made by Donald Trump’s chief negotiator on the Ukraine war.Steve Witkoff met the Russian president in St Petersburg on Wednesday as he sought to make a new push to end the invasion ofUkraine, with the US putting pressure on Kyiv to agree to a settlement.In a Russian state media video clip posted on X, Witkoff told Putin: “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also sir, and I salute that. I commend you.”1:13Witkoff calls Putin a ‘humanitarian’ after release of jailed American – videoWhen asked about Witkoff’s description of Putin, a Downing Street spokesperson said: “We certainly do not recognise that characterisation, and President Putin has killed thousands of people, both innocent Ukrainians and his own Russian people, who he has sent to their deaths on the frontline.“He is starving children and the elderly of the heat and warmth, and systematically targeting critical national infrastructure. Ukraine’s foreign minister summed it up well this morning when he said: ‘This night, the residents of Kyiv heard what Russian humanitarianism really sounds like.’”View image in fullscreenFirefighters amid the wreckage left by Russian strikes on Kyiv on Thursday.Photograph: Ukrinform/ShutterstockAsked if the government would make this argument directly to the US administration, the spokesperson said: “We engage regularly at a range of levels with a range of partners on Ukraine, and I’m sure we will continue to do so.”Downing Street’s remarks came after the Scottish secretary,Douglas Alexander, told LBC that Britain viewed Putin as “somebody who illegally invaded Ukraine at the start of this conflict, who has been responsible for conduct by his government that included attempted assassinations on UK soil”.Alexander added: “We simply do not recognise the description of Vladimir Putin as a humanitarian.”‘You are a humanitarian also, sir’: the US feeds Putin with lies as Ukraine’s children take cover and die | Andrew RothRead moreAfter Witkoff met Putin, Russia agreed to resume peace talks with Ukraine and the US in principle. Trump has suggested Russia and Ukraine are “maybe now the closest we’ve been” to ending the war.Despite this, Russia has continued to launch missile attacks at Ukraine, including a drone strike on Kharkiv as Putin and Witkoff spoke.Last week, Andy Burnham welcomedVolodymyr Zelenskyyto Downing Street and backed the Ukrainian president amid Trump’s attacks.Trump had suggested Zelenskyy should be replaced and declined to say whether Russia was responsible for the war.Explore more on these topicsUkraineVladimir PutinVolodymyr ZelenskyyDonald TrumpAndy BurnhamDouglas AlexanderRussianewsShareReuse this content

title: King Charles urged ‘as human brother’ to support reparations talks at Caribbean summit | King Charles III | The Guardian
description: Caricom commission chair Hilary Beckles wants king to ensure Commonwealth becomes a ‘moral institution committed to human justice’
Author: Natricia Duncan
Headline: Caricom commission chair Hilary Beckles wants king to ensure Commonwealth becomes a ‘moral institution committed to human justice’
Content: Hilary Beckles gives a speech during a plenary session at the high-level consultative conference on the next steps to the landmark UN resolution on the trafficking of enslaved Africans on 18 June 2026.Photograph: Ernest Ankomah/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHilary Beckles gives a speech during a plenary session at the high-level consultative conference on the next steps to the landmark UN resolution on the trafficking of enslaved Africans on 18 June 2026.Photograph: Ernest Ankomah/Getty ImagesKing Charles IIIKing Charles urged ‘as human brother’ to support reparations talks at Caribbean summitCaricom commission chair Hilary Beckles wants king to ensure Commonwealth becomes a ‘moral institution committed to human justice’Natricia Duncan, Caribbean correspondentThu 22 Oct 2026 19.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 19.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe head of the Caribbean’s reparations commission has appealed toKing Charles IIIas a “human brother” whose family he said had benefited from slavery to support reparations talks at next month’s Commonwealth leaders meeting in the Caribbean.Speaking at a press conference ahead of the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda next month, professor Hilary Beckles urged the king to use his influence to advance slavery reparations talks between Britain and the Caribbean.Beckles, the chair of theCaribbeanCommunity (Caricom) Reparations Commission, said: “My personal appeal to King Charles III, not so much in his role as head of the Commonwealth, not so much in his role as the constitutional monarch of the United Kingdom … I’m appealing to Charles Windsor, a parent, a grandparent, a man today who reflects upon the history of his family, and he can see the enrichment that slavery has presented to his family.”He declared that he believed the king was aware that the wealth he is passing on to his children and his grandchildren came from chattel slavery.Referring to the king as “a man, as a human brother”, he urged Charles to ensure the Commonwealth, historically “the site of this crime”, becomes a “moral institution committed to human justice”.Beckles’s appeal comes amid growing calls from Caribbean leaders and groups for Charles to formally apologise for slavery when he visits Guyana and the Bahamas next week ahead of Chogm, which he will attend in Antigua.On Thursday, Commonwealth secretary-generalShirley Ayorkor Botchweytold Sky News that a formal apology for slavery from King Charles “wouldn’t hurt” and that the “time has come” for a serious conversation regarding reparations.Jamaica says slavery reparations petition to be heard by UK privy council in March 2027Read moreEric Phillips, head of Guyana’s reparations committee and vice-chair of the Caricom Reparations Commission, joined the calls for an apology from the king.“The king is a decent monarch based on his lifelong commitments to the world in which the environment for him is sacred. We Africans are also part of that sacred environment. As an enlightened monarch, I strongly believe King Charles will want to promote a conversation of decency that reflects his character and values,” he said.“The citizens of the United Kingdom say, long live the king. We in Guyana say, long live the king, so he can apologize and call for reparations,” he added.Last month, when Jamaican officials lodged a landmark petition to King Charles for legal advice on its claim for slavery reparations, which will be heard by the privy council in March, a palace spokesperson said Charles “has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today”.But David Comissiong, the deputy chair of theBarbadosNational Task Force on Reparations, said he was concerned about a lack of unanimous agreement on commitments on reparations in a draft of the 2026 Chogm communique, which records agreements made by leaders.Comissiong said a paragraph that referenced the commitment to dialogue made at the previousCommonwealth summitin Samoa and highlights subsequent developments at the UN, African Union and Caricom, was confirmed, but there was disagreement about a second paragraph mandating Commonwealth foreign ministers to advance discussions on historical harms from the transatlantic slave trade through “structured, inclusive, and good faith dialogue”.“It is very peculiar, to say the least, that the second paragraph which speaks about the Commonwealth foreign affairs ministers coming together to engage in these discussions … has not been unanimously agreed upon,” he said.Dorbrene O’Marde, chair of the Antigua and Barbuda reparations commission, said that campaigners are expected to raise the issue of reparations during the conferences’ major forums, and that discussions between governments are expected to take place at their meetings.He said the reparations movement will launch a “Global Reparations Caravan”, described as an international movement combining reparations advocacy, demonstrations and culture, at a separate event on 3 November.O’Marde added that, while there will be stringent security measures around the event, he expects physical demonstrations from groups who are “inflamed” by the blanket statements of no apology coming out of the UK.“Blanket no apologies from both government and monarchy reek of gross insensitivity to the demands of the citizens of the Caribbean,” he said.Beckles stressed that the absence of a dedicated official event at Chogm does not mean that reparations would remain peripheral to the summit. He described the meeting as “the Chogm of reparations” and the “first round of reparations negotiations”.“This is the meeting of the Commonwealth in the Caribbean, and the number one item in the Caribbean as far as this gathering is concerned is reparatory justice,” he said.“I can assure you that [for] everyone in the Caribbean right now, everyone who’s going to be at that meeting from the Caribbean, with an interest in the Caribbean, from Africa, and an interest in the global African movement, this will be the number one item on the table.”Explore more on these topicsKing Charles IIICommonwealth summitCaribbeanReparations and reparative justiceCommonwealth of NationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK to relax post-2008 rules that hold City bosses accountable for wrongdoing | Financial sector | The Guardian
description: Regulators say removing ‘unnecessary burdens’ will save businesses about £2bn over 10 years
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Regulators say removing ‘unnecessary burdens’ will save businesses about £2bn over 10 years
