Content: The new requirements will mean only ‘serious misconduct’ and cases where City staff are given final warnings or fired need to be reported.Photograph: Gary Yeowell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe new requirements will mean only ‘serious misconduct’ and cases where City staff are given final warnings or fired need to be reported.Photograph: Gary Yeowell/Getty ImagesFinancial sectorUK to relax post-2008 rules that hold City bosses accountable for wrongdoingRegulators say removing ‘unnecessary burdens’ will save businesses about £2bn over 10 yearsKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentThu 22 Oct 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK is watering down rules introduced in the aftermath of the financial crisis that were designed to hold City bosses accountable for wrongdoing.The plans, put forward by the financial industry’s two top regulators, the Bank of England and theFinancial Conduct Authority(FCA), include a reduction in reporting for “lower-level misconduct” and would also free 140,000 managers from extra checks.The proposals were announced as regulators hosted a dinner for City executives at the Mansion House in central London. They are meant to“significantly” reduce the number of roles that will be required to undergo enhanced checks and would require only the most senior executives – such as chief executives and chief financial officers – to be forced to prove they are “fit and proper” each year, and before taking new jobs.This will free about 140,000 staff from having to illustrate they are operating with “integrity” and following regulators’ conduct rules. It would be a watering down of measures thatcame into force in the mid-2010s, in response to widespread public anger over the 2008 banking crash.Cyprus police investigate financial and tax affairs of ex-Chelsea owner Roman AbramovichRead moreThe senior managers regime was meant to address the fact that few bank bosses were held to account for actions that contributed to the ensuing financial crisis. While the regime originally covered banks, itwas later expandedto cover all financial services companies including asset managers and hedge funds.It is the latest set of City rules to have been scaled back since the government gave regulators a new objective: ensuring UK firms are competitive on the world stage. Those efforts have already helpedlift the cap on banker bonuses, which were previously limited to two times a banker’s salary.The new changes will also lead to the loosening of rules around how often firms report bad behaviour by lower level staff. It means they will no longer have to report first warnings or “lower-level misconduct of limited relevance” to regulator’s targets, such as if staff are showing up late or dropping calls.Instead, they only want to hear about “serious misconduct” and cases where staff are given final warnings or fired. Any initial cases of misconduct will still have to be flagged for top brass, including chief executive and chief financial officers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe regulators said removing these “unnecessary burdens” would save businesses about £2bn over 10 years while cutting the Bank of England’s and FCA’s costs by £11.5m and £229m each year, respectively.The Bank of England and FCA said that this would not mean bosses would get away with bad behaviour. They said in a joint statement that the “high standards of individual accountability and conduct will remain unchanged, including the regulators’ commitment to ensuring that individuals are accountable for misconduct that affects society as well as their employers”.Explore more on these topicsFinancial sectorBankingCorporate governanceFinancial Conduct AuthorityRegulatorsBank of EnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Websites across world hit by millions of attempts to exploit PHP code flaw | Internet | The Guardian
description: Problem in language that underpins 70% of sites has led governments and companies to pull sites offline to patch fault
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Problem in language that underpins 70% of sites has led governments and companies to pull sites offline to patch fault
Content: A page on the BBC website temporarily unavailable due to the issue.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenA page on the BBC website temporarily unavailable due to the issue.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAInternetWebsites across world hit by millions of attempts to exploit PHP code flawProblem in language that underpins 70% of sites has led governments and companies to pull sites offline to patch faultTell us: have you been affected by the PHP code flaw?What is PHP, and how bad is the computer language flaw causing website shutdowns globally?Robert BoothandAisha DownThu 22 Oct 2026 12.42 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 07.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWebsites around the world have been hit by millions of attempts to exploit a recently discovered vulnerability in their code, cybersecurity companies have said, as the US warned the flaw could allow attackers to take control of web servers, steal data and disrupt services.The problem in the PHP programming language, which underpins about 70% of the world’s websites,emerged on Wednesdaycausing governments and companies to pull their websites off the internet before they could be attacked and so they could patch the fault.What is PHP, and how bad is the computer language flaw causing website shutdowns globally?Read moreIn the UK, 32 government services had been taken offline, the cybersecurity minister, Liz Lloyd, told parliament. She said this “largely resulted from precautionary measures” while updates were applied. Downing Street said no public-facing critical services had been affected and “some limited services may be temporarily offline” but this did not mean they had been hacked.9:23The race to fix huge PHP flaw at the heart of the internet - The LatestThe website for the BBC’s Traitors was one of those that was down on Thursday, while the government declined to name the affected sites, saying services were being reviewed, updated and coming back online. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) sent out 50,000 alerts to affected organisations, but said it had no reports of successful hacks as a result of the flaw. Other sites reportedly temporarily affected included theInternetArchive, Wikipedia and 4Chan.The vulnerability sparked particular concern about the ongoing vulnerability of systems used by schools, local governments and charities, which may not have dedicated cybersecurity support to execute the fix. The NCSC said the scale of the vulnerability was “unprecedented” and the patch would not work for some organisations running older systems, and these would have to be replaced. The British Chambers of Commerce, which represents thousands of employers, said it was not yet causing firms any significant difficulties.Ciaran Martin, the former chief executive of the NCSC, described the flaw as “very bad”, saying that while most internet software vulnerabilities did not matter, this was “the most serious vulnerability discovered for five years”. The former GCHQ chief David Omand warned that Russia and China could look to exploit the bug.However, Ryan Austin, a researcher at the cybersecurity company Calif, who was key to discovering the flaw, said: “At the moment it doesn’t look like exploitation has taken off or been widespread.”View image in fullscreenA notice on the National Cyber Security Centre website warned of a critical security issue affecting PHP.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAThe flaw prompted governments into action, with the US National Security Agency saying it could allow attackers to seize control of web servers, steal sensitive data, disrupt services and move deeper into a network. Government websites were quickly taken down so the patch could be installed with many coming back on line soon afterwards.In an update overnight on Wednesday, and into Thursday, Matthew Prince, the chief executive of the cybersecurity business CloudFlare, said the company encountered tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the weakness in the 45 minutes after the problem was announced, rising to “hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now”.Amazon Threat Intelligence, another cybersecurity company, said PHP2Shell, as the vulnerability is known, was “now being broadly exploited in the wild” and it had identified several attempts from multiple actors to test ways to capitalise on the vulnerability before the fix was released by the PHP developers on Wednesday.CloudFlare also said that in the 10 hours before the vulnerability was publicly announced, it saw thousands of attempts to exploit it, amid concern over the handling of the alert. One cybersecurity expert, Prof Alan Woodward, said the flaw was revealed a day before the patch was released, and that “somebody let the cat out of the bag”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe PHP vulnerability could allow hostile actors to “grab the resources” of exposed sites, said Michał Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert. A website, such as Slack or Wikipedia, has access to computing power, servers, and IP addresses which locate it on the internet. In many cases, this infrastructure is managed and mediated by PHP.Criminal groups, state-sponsored hackers, or crypto miners might “nest” themselves into exposed sites using this PHP vulnerability, and then exploit those resources for their own aims. A hacking group could use an exposed site’s IP address to launch attacks that could not then be traced back to it. Crypto miners could use a server’s computing power to run their energy-intensive calculations for free.It was unclear at what scale this has been done, said Woźniak, and many sites would not even be aware of it.Wiz, one of the research organisations that uncovered the vulnerabilities, said it was arguably among the most severe software vulnerabilities ever discovered. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” itsaidin a blogpost. “Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”“Cyber-actors are likely to weaponise PHP2Shell,” theNSAsaid. “These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across US government departments and agencies.”The government of South Korea said on Thursday it was activating emergency response measures, raising its private sector cybersecurity alert level and issuing guidance to tens of thousands of companies on how to fix the problem.China’s industry ministry urged organisations to immediately inspect their systems and upgrade to the latest secure version of PHP, and recommended strengthening cybersecurity monitoring, changing passwords and keys. The prime minister of Japan encouraged businesses and organisations to patch the vulnerability – or shut down their sites.Explore more on these topicsInternetData and computer securityHackingProgrammingComputingNSACybercrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham vows UK will hit net zero target despite Jackdaw gasfield approval | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: PM pledges commitment to address climate crisis, saying in Guardian article that his ‘determination is unwavering’
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: PM pledges commitment to address climate crisis, saying in Guardian article that his ‘determination is unwavering’
Content: Activists from Fossil Free London stage protest outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenActivists from Fossil Free London stage protest outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockClimate crisisAndy Burnham vows UK will hit net zero target despite Jackdaw gasfield approvalPM pledges commitment to address climate crisis, saying in Guardian article that his ‘determination is unwavering’Andy Burnham: We will make the net-zero transition work for BritainJessica ElgotandAlexandra ToppingThu 22 Oct 2026 17.34 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 13.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has said he will not “abandon the responsibility” of fighting the climate crisis after the government approved the Jackdaw gasfield, pledging to block new North Sea licences and keep Britain on track for net zero by 2050.We will make the net-zero transition work for Britain – approving the Jackdaw gasfield is part of the plan | Andy BurnhamRead moreThe comments are the prime minister’s most forthright yet on net zero, after many MPs have privately cast doubt on the authenticity of his commitment to tackling the climate crisis.The energy secretary,Miatta Fahnbulleh, insisted that she alone would make a decision on whether to approve the Rosebank oilfield – a decision sources say she is minded to block.Burnham has been under pressure from industry and political opponents, as well as some Labour MPs, to water down Labour’s manifesto promises on new oil and gas licences and the net zero targets.“There has been much speculation about what this announcement means for Britain’s commitment to addressing the climate crisis. I want to be clear that our determination is unwavering,”the prime minister said in an article for the Guardian.He said he was conscious of the “acute global instability” affecting energy security and wanted to treat oil and gas workers with more dignity.Burnham said that would not stop the government from abiding by its climate targets, saying he was “personally committed to confronting” the challenges of the climate crisis.“Britain has just emerged from its hottest summer on record, during which we had nurses collapsing on hospital wards, bus drivers working in intolerable conditions and families losing everything to wildfires,” he wrote.“More extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead. The climate crisis is no distant threat. It is here, on our doorstep, affecting people’s lives and livelihoods. I am personally committed to confronting it, and I will not abandon the responsibility we have to future generations.”View image in fullscreenMiatta Fahnbulleh: ‘It has been really painful to watch the consensus burn at a time when we’re seeing the impact of climate change.’Photograph: Imageplotter/AlamyMeanwhile, Fahnbulleh doubled down on her insistence that she would not be influenced by other departments on whether to approve the Rosebank oilfield, setting up a potential standoff with the Treasury.The chancellor, John Healey, has said he expects “oil and gas” revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, but Fanhbulleh said “only I can make that decision”, insisting that she bore the legal responsibility to ensure the UK did not violate its climate commitments.Dismissing speculation that Burnham, or his chancellor, would make the final call, she said: “[It] sits heavy for such a big controversial decision because, in the end, only I can make it. And if it is overturned by other colleagues, all that means is we’re going to be overturned in the courts. So we will do the process and we will do it properly.”Fahnbulleh said she was “really concerned” and “quite sad” about the breakdown in consensus about the climate crisis. She said: “I think it’s a sad place where Reform has gone and got to. But I’m even sadder about the Tories because they know better, and they’ve had a long tradition, including Boris Johnson, of working cross-party on climate action.“It has been really painful and tragic to watch that consensus burn at a time when we’re seeing the impact of climate change this summer.”The climate crisis was having a real impact on communities, she added. “It’s people’s livelihoods, it’s their jobs, their communities. Even if you don’t care about climate – care about that, you’ve got to take action.”Reflecting on the decision to approve the Jackdaw gasfield, Burnham said he wanted to make the transition to a greener future “on our terms”, saying that meant giving oil and gas workers a path to new jobs and using homegrown rather than imported gas.“At a time of acute global instability, it makes sense to responsibly use our resources here at home.Gasfrom this field will begin heating our homes and powering our businesses this winter.”He said he had been moved by the plight of oil and gas workers in Aberdeen, adding that it was an industry that had suffered from deindustrialisation “with too little thought given by politicians to the places left behind. I will not be so careless with people’s lives.”Fahnbulleh echoed the prime minister’s words, saying the private sector had invested £100bn in clean energy in the last two years. “It’s a huge opportunity for parts of our countries that have been left behind,” she said. But that investment had to have a real-world impact, she added. “When you say jobs are going to be created, don’t say it. People need to see it.”Burnham said the energy wealth fund that was being created to convert North Sea oil and gas tax revenues to clean energy programmes was long overdue – “something that, frankly, should have happened more than 40 years ago”.It comes as Burnham announced that military planes and helicopters would fight wildfires for the first time, ahead of a major wildfire summit with fire chiefs, local leaders and experts.The RAF’s chinook helicopters and A400M aircraft will fight fires and help crews across the UK tackle blazes on remote moorland, steep hillsides and other hard-to-reach terrain.“Heroes shouldn’t have to fight with one hand tied behind their backs,” said the prime minister.Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisFossil fuelsEnergyMiatta FahnbullehAndy BurnhamOilOil and gas companiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentre | Environment | The Guardian
description: Company ordered to stop work at two sites in country, which has found itself at forefront of tech firms’ latest push
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Company ordered to stop work at two sites in country, which has found itself at forefront of tech firms’ latest push
Content: Finnish forest cleared for data centre developmentEnvironment‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentreCompany ordered to stop work at two sites in country, which has found itself at forefront of tech firms’ latest pushMiranda Bryantin Muhos and OtanmäkiThu 22 Oct 2026 07.22 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.08 EDTShareBehind a wire fence lies a vast gaping wound of earth. Before Google’s arrival a few months ago, an estimated quarter of a million trees occupied the 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest near the town of Muhos in rural northernFinland. Now they are all gone.After the tech company illegally stripped the entire area to build a datacentre – taking even the top soil with it – all that remains is a vast expanse of mud indented with the trail marks of machinery, puddles and mounds of earth, roots and branches. Residents say that brown water flowing off the site is going into a stream that feeds the Oulujoki River.“It doesn’t end. It goes on and on,” says Mari Annala, an ecologist from the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation (SLL), looking at drone footage of the former forest from the perimeter.View image in fullscreenMari Annala is a Finnish environmental expert, researcher and board member of the Oulu region district of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation.Photograph: Jarno Artika/The GuardianWith 145 new datacentres at various stages of planning, Finland has found itself at the forefront of the tech companies’ latest push. As well as its relative geopolitical and geological stability and abundance of land, the cool climate makes it especially attractive for saving on energy costs.MapEarlier this month,Googlewas ordered by the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) to temporarily stop work on Muhos and another site about 100km south-east in the village of Otanmäki after it failed to complete the necessary environmental impact assessments before clearcutting the land. The news has prompted widespread outcry and a national reckoning over what role, if any, the country should play in the global rush to build datacentres to keep up with rapid AI development.Last week, Google’s Finland country manager, Antti Järvinen, apologised for the forest clearings but claimed the company had acted “on the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time”.View image in fullscreenIn the northern Finnish town of Muhos, the forest has already been cut down on land acquired by Google, with excavators now clearing the ground and rumbling trucks shuttling back and forth to the construction area located next to major power lines.Photograph: Alessandro Rampazzo/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn aerial view of the site where Google’s data centre was set to be built in Muhos.Photograph: Alessandro Rampazzo/AFP/Getty ImagesMuhos and Otanmäki are part of a €13bn AI infrastructure project by Google that has attracted criticism from Donald Trump, who would rather the centres were built in the US and has publicly called for the company to reconsider. It is the biggest ever project of its kind in the Nordic country.The Finnish government, which has presided over deep spending cuts, has encouraged the investment. Last month, when the Google plans were announced, the country’s prime minister, Petteri Orpo, said attracting investment was a “top priority” and “the value of the data economy extends far beyond direct investment”. He said the Google deal would “deliver lasting benefits for both parties”.But the revelations over Google’s misconduct have prompted public concern over what these deals mean for nearby communities, energy prices for Finnish households and Finland’s natural environment, a national source of pride. The datacentre push is likely to become a key election issue when Finns go to the polls in April.View image in fullscreenGoogle’s clearcut area is 3km long and 2km wide, 330 hectares in total, and 400 metres from the Oulujoki River.Photograph: Jarno Artika/The GuardianIn addition to the 250,000 trees felled at Muhos, Annala estimates that an additional 150,000 trees were felled at Otanmäki. Because the trees have been felled illegally, she says wood from the two sites cannot be sold to wood-processing plants.The move has also prompted questions over why Finland’s renewable energy sources are being used to power international corporations.More than 93,000 people have signed a petition demanding more datacentre regulation and a fee to compensate local communities for environmental damage. Since the scandal broke, Orpo has described what happened in Muhos as a “cold shower”.Hanna Halmeenpää, chair of SLL’s board, said she had been incredulous when she discovered Google’s law breaking. “At first I couldn’t believe it,” she said. “I have never heard that any company has done anything like this in Finland.” She said the system depended a lot on trust, which she believes Google took advantage of. “They bought the vast land area and they just started to cut it, just like that,” she said. “It’s pure arrogance and it’s amazing.”View image in fullscreenThree electrical pylons next to the Google clearcut.Photograph: Jarno Artika/The GuardianThe speed of developments had shocked the country, she said. “Many people are just watching the news and asking each other: ‘What’s happening now? What can we do about it? And do we have to take all these datacentre projects in Finland?’”Jussi Kangasharju, head of computer science at the University of Helsinki, said that while datacentres brought a limited number of jobs, potentially boosting the local economy, the benefits on a national level were minimal. “Really, for Finland, there are no benefits,” he said. “They are international companies serving international customers. Very little corporate taxes go to Finland.Datacentresultimately have very little benefit for others except the datacentre operator.”View image in fullscreenHanna Halmeenpää, chair of the board of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, near the site where Google’s new datacentre is to be built in Muhos.Photograph: Alessandro Rampazzo/AFP/Getty ImagesWith legislation still playing catchup, there is a rush to get projects under way as fast as possible.Some are calling for a centralised body to coordinate datacentre projects, rather than leaving so much of the decision-making down to municipalities that are likely to prioritise the immediate needs of the local area.In Muhos and Otanmäki, there are people who support the projects, along with the jobs and land taxes they will bring into the local area. But many believe they have been sold short by municipalities.View image in fullscreenGoogle has illegally stripped the entire area, removing even the top soil.Photograph: Jarno Artika/The GuardianAntti Jakonen, who lives in Muhos, said that, although the trees felled represented a small fraction of Finland’s overall forests, he objected to the manner in which it had been carried out. “It has been done in the wrong way. American style. No sense. No sense at all,” he said. The former entrepreneur and fisher wants Google to compensate by helping to restore the local salmon population destroyed decades ago by hydropower.In Otanmäki, the disruption to nature and to residents’ daily lives is being vividly felt. When the trees were felled, the wolves who had lived there came to the village, said Anni Ranta, 53, whose family has lived there for generations.View image in fullscreenPentti Korhonen, a wilderness guide, has lived in Otanmäki for 12 years.Photograph: Jarno Artika/The GuardianA former mining village, the area is known for its rare earth elements. Ranta’s family live at the centre of the village next to a triangular church spire and a former bar that has been empty for years. The peaceful forest used to extend for miles from the village. Now the sound of building work next to the clearcut Google site reverberates.“We had wolves coming into the village because all the wild animals moved out of the forest,” said Ranta. “They fled. What worries me about the datacentres is also the noise because this is hardrock soil. Even when we are standing here talking,” she added, stamping her feet, “it’s like a drum.”Such is her strength of feeling against the arrival of Google that she is thinking of moving out. She also fears the datacentre could make the village a target for Russia, with whom Finland shares a long border. “I don’t want them here,” she said of Google. “I don’t want them in Finland at all. I don’t like the whole idea of AI and the world changing and the way it’s changing. It’s going too fast, too soon.”View image in fullscreenVesa Hyyryläinen, a biologist, drives past the construction area next to the Google clearcuts in Otanmäki.Photograph: Jarno Artika/The GuardianHer father, Pentti Korhonen, a retired wilderness guide, said that since the forest was destroyed, the water in the stream has turned brown. “There is no need at all for datacentres in Finland. No need for datacentres at all,” he said.Vesa Hyyryläinen, chair of the local SLL district, said three-toed woodpeckers nesting in the forest had been pushed out. “All of us nature conservationists are very worried about our Finnish political situation and politics,” said the biologist and osprey expert. “I wonder why we have to sacrifice so much of our nature. They give everything away too easily.”He said, however, that he understood why authorities were trying to bring in new sources of investment and jobs, given the region’s ageing population. “Young people go to Helsinki and Berlin and Paris,” he said. “There are so few people. We have to sacrifice.”View image in fullscreenHyyryläinen said: ‘I wonder why we have to sacrifice so much of our nature. They give everything away too easily.’Photograph: Jarno Artika/The GuardianVeli-Matti Uski, director general of the ministry of environment, said the government was “monitoring the general development of the [datacentre] sector, [and the] application of its legislation, and is prepared to propose legislative amendments as necessary”.Google said it was working to protect water quality at the Muhos site, and that it planned to plant trees across 130 hectares there. Conservationists say that figure is too low to have any real impact in comparison to the damage done by the tree felling.A spokesperson said: “We have operated in Finland for 15 years and have always worked to meet or exceed zoning, environmental, health and safety requirements.“After receiving the LVV letters on 6 October, we stopped preparatory works at Muhos and Kajaani [where the Otanmäki site is located] and have submitted a formal response to LVV confirming this.“We will fully comply with LVV’s requests in this matter. We look forward to maintaining an active, open dialogue with all authorities to strengthen our partnership with Finland and local organisations.”Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentFinlandEuropeAI (artificial intelligence)GoogleAlphabetDatacentresShare

title: Have scientists finally found a way to save the banana from disaster? | Food security | The Guardian
description: With the climate crisis and diseases threatening one of the world’s most popular fruits, researchers are hoping a breakthrough in breeding techniques could give the Cavendish banana a certain future
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: With the climate crisis and diseases threatening one of the world’s most popular fruits, researchers are hoping a breakthrough in breeding techniques could give the Cavendish banana a certain future
Content: Fernando García Bastidas, KeyGene’s TR4 expert, at work on the banana-breeding programme.Photograph: Courtesy of KeyGeneView image in fullscreenFernando García Bastidas, KeyGene’s TR4 expert, at work on the banana-breeding programme.Photograph: Courtesy of KeyGeneFood securityHave scientists finally found a way to save the banana from disaster?With the climate crisis and diseases threatening one of the world’s most popular fruits, researchers are hoping a breakthrough in breeding techniques could give the Cavendish banana a certain futureSupported byAbout this contentNicola DavisScience CorrespondentThu 22 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLove them or loathe them,bananas are one of the world’s most popular fruit. But a combination of the climate crisis and new killer diseases have had growers concerned over thebanana’s threatened extinction, something that would impose a huge toll on farmers in countries from Guatemala to Malawi, alongside eradicating a staple food.Now researchers say they have made fresh advances in the race to save them from disaster. This month, Yelloway – a research collaboration between Chiquita, theworld’s largest banana company, and the crop-improvement company KeyGene – announced it had developed a fully fertile Cavendish banana, meaning it may be possible, through cross-breeding, to create new banana varieties that are commercially viable and resistant to disease.Second only to the tomato in terms of fruitconsumption globally, the world grows about139m tonnes of bananas a year. While there are more than 1,000 varieties, it is the Cavendish that is now found in most fruit bowls, taking over from the Gros Michel cultivar, which fell victim to Panama disease from the 1950s.View image in fullscreenA Cavendish banana plantation in the Canary Islands.Photograph: Dominik Spalek/AlamyBut the Cavendish itself is under threat from diseases including a strain of Panama known asTropical Race 4(TR4). Dr Jose De Vega, an expert on crop genomics at the Earlham Institute in Norwich, said TR4 had spread from south-east Asia to Australia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America.“The most worrying recent report came in December 2025 from Ecuador, the world’s largest banana exporter,” he said, noting that the disease threatened both global supply chains “and the food security of millions of people in the tropics for whom bananas and plantains are a staple food and a source of income”.Cavendish bananas have three sets of chromosomes, meaning they are typically sterile. “Combined with the ability to set fruit without pollination, this gives us the seedless banana,” said De Vega.View image in fullscreenSymptoms of yellowing and necrosis on a banana plant affected by Tropical Race 4, a strain of Panama disease.Photograph: emarys/Getty ImagesThere are several different types of Cavendish, including dwarf versions, which have arisen as a result of random mutations in the Cavendish genome.But in each case new plants are grown from offshoots, so they are virtually genetically identical to the plant from which they came. While this results in uniform fruit, it also means they are vulnerable to the same diseases.Peter Stedman, Chiquita’s sustainability director, said: “We are not trying to preserve Cavendish. We’re trying to replace Cavendish because we believe at the core of any sustainable farming system is biodiversity and genetic diversity.”View image in fullscreenProf James Dale with young banana plants at a field trial site in Australia’s Northern Territory.Photograph: Anthony Weate/QUTOther researchers have taken different approaches. In Australia, a team at Queensland University of Technology led by Prof James Dale has created agenetically modified Cavendishby using a bacterium to introduce a gene from a wild banana that produces resistance to TR4.The upshot, a type of Cavendish called QCAV-4, has beenapproved for human consumptionin Australia and New Zealand, with researchers confirming that ittastes like the traditional banana.De Vega, by contrast, is collaborating with other researchers to explore gene-editing techniques. These involve using “molecular scissors” to cut parts of the Cavendish’s DNA and replace them with genes from other banana cultivars.His team have been sequencing the genomes of banana varieties that have different responses to TR4. “We are looking for the [immune genes] that resistant varieties have and that the Cavendish lacks, carries a broken version of, has too few copies of, or doesn’t switch on strongly enough,” said De Vega.“Once we identify a candidate gene, the idea is to edit the Cavendish’s own copy so it matches the copy in the resistant cousin. That keeps everything that makes a Cavendish a Cavendish.”View image in fullscreenYelloway is a partnership between Chiquita, the world’s largest banana company, and KeyGene, a crop improvement business.Photograph: Courtesy of ChiquitaIn England and elsewhere in Europe, De Vega added,gene-editing was seen as precision breedingrather than genetic modification.“That is because the change is one that could happen naturally or through conventional breeding,” he said. “The catch is that with a sterile Cavendish, conventional breeding has never really been an option, which is exactly why editing is so attractive for bananas.”Australia’s first genetically modified fruit is ripe for a taste test. Could it avert a global banana apocalypse?Read moreBut Stedman said there were drawbacks to such approaches. “Every time you are editing or improving Cavendish, you’re not creating a new variety, you’re not creating biodiversity – you’re just maintaining a monocrop,” he said, noting that brought susceptibility to disease.Yelloway’s production of a fully fertile Cavendish line – known as “Yellowdish” – using non-GM technologies potentially opens up a new route.Dale and De Vega noted that details on exactly how Yellowdish was produced, and with how many chromosomes, had not been revealed – meaning questions remained.Dale said the approach with Yelloway of crossing a fertile Cavendish with other types of fertile banana resistant to TR4 – and potentially other diseases–could have benefits, including in the regulatory environment and in public perceptions.View image in fullscreenA customs warning sign about the spread of  the TR4 fungus that affects bananas and plantains at Bogotá airport in Colombia.Photograph: Jeff Greenberg/Universal Images/GettyBut while it may result in disease-resistant progeny, he noted it could also yield a very different type of fruit.“Whatever they generate is going to be different to Cavendish,” Dale said, pointing out that crosses could produce a huge range of types but any new variety needed not only to be resistant to disease but also produce high yields and taste good.For Stedman, the challenge boils down to a numbers game. “If you have enough progeny, if you have enough children, the chances of one of them having … the traits that you want is much, much higher,” he said.Explore more on these topicsFood securityFruitFood (global)Food (Environment)GeneticsBiologyGene editingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Almost every shallow-water coral reef on the planet faces ecosystem collapse by 2075, UN advisors say | Coral | The Guardian
description: Assessment finds global heating is endangering 96% of coral reefs across 80 countries – a figure scientists say should serve as a ‘wake-up call’
Author: Graham Readfearn
Headline: Assessment finds global heating is endangering 96% of coral reefs across 80 countries – a figure scientists say should serve as a ‘wake-up call’
Content: Papa Bay, Hawaii. Scientists say findings that 96% of all shallow-water reefs face collapse due to global heating should serve as a wake-up call to rapidly cut the use of fossil fuels.Photograph: Lindsey Kramer/Hawaii Wildlife Fund/IUCNView image in fullscreenPapa Bay, Hawaii. Scientists say findings that 96% of all shallow-water reefs face collapse due to global heating should serve as a wake-up call to rapidly cut the use of fossil fuels.Photograph: Lindsey Kramer/Hawaii Wildlife Fund/IUCNCoralAlmost every shallow-water coral reef on the planet faces ecosystem collapse by 2075, UN advisors sayAssessment finds global heating is endangering 96% of coral reefs across 80 countries – a figure scientists say should serve as a ‘wake-up call’Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter hereGraham ReadfearnEnvironment and climate correspondentThu 22 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 17.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlmost every shallow-water coral reef on the planet, including Australia’sGreat Barrier Reef, faces a high risk of ecosystem collapse before 2075 because of global heating, according to an assessment by United Nations nature advisers.About 24% of the planet’s reefs across more than 80 countries are already critically endangered, the assessment said, but when the expected impacts of global heating were added this rose to 96%.Coral reefs are known as the rainforests of the sea. A quarter of all known marine species are found in and around them and they support hundreds of millions of people with food, as well as protecting shorelines and supporting tourism.The Great Barrier Reef isn’t dead yet. According to News Corp that makes climate science a ‘pseudo-religion’ | Temperature CheckRead moreOverfishing, pollution, coastal development and global heating have already caused declines in the ecosystems over the past 50 years, measured by the loss of live coral as well as changes in fish populations, the assessment said.But the scientists said while the prognosis was dire, the findings should serve as a “wake-up call” because reefs could survive with rapid cuts to fossil fuel use and strong conservation action at local levels.Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter“The risk is real and very concerning,” said Dr Mishal Gudka, research director at Cordio (CoastalOceansResearch and Development in the Indian Ocean) East Africa and the scientific lead for the assessment.“We stand to lose one of the most valuable ecosystems we have – the impacts of which will affect millions of people around the world.”The assessment analysed the current status and future threat levels of 127 coral reef regions and was coordinated by the International Union forConservationof Nature (IUCN), an international group that advises the United Nations.The assessment assumed greenhouse gas emissions – mainly from burning fossil fuels – would follow a “middle-of-the-road” pathway, causing about 2.7C of global heating by the end of the century when compared with temperatures before the Industrial Revolution.Current climate policies and targets adopted by countries around the world are likely to cause about 2.6C of global heating,one assessment finds.The share of coral eco-regions considered critically endangered would likely be even higher, the IUCN said, but four regions did not have enough data to assess them and the coral reefs of the western Galápagos had already collapsed.View image in fullscreenExtensive coral bleaching occurred at the Ningaloo Reef, Western Australia, in February 2025.Photograph: Brooke PykeThe critically endangered classification meant an “extremely high risk” of ecosystem collapse before 2075.The group considers a coral reef ecosystem to have collapsed if the reef could not maintain itself because of a near or complete loss of living reef-building corals.The assessment did not fully account for the impacts of the fourth global mass bleaching event from early 2023 to mid-2025 – the most widespread global mass bleaching event on record,the US government’s Coral Reef Watch has confirmed.That global event was bookended by the worst mass bleaching eventon record for reefs in Western Australiawhere a heatwave killed corals across 1,500lm (930 miles).Marine heatwaves can cause corals to separate from the symbiotic algae that provides them with colour and nutrient. While not always deadly, bleaching can weaken corals and make them more susceptible to disease.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When he publishesSign up toClear Air AustraliaAdam Morton brings you incisive analysis about the politics and impact of the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGudka said the results were a “wake-up call” and were “alarming, but certainly not hopeless”.He said: “They should be seen as a call to action – an early warning sign before the worst outcomes eventuate.”Dr Grethel Aguilar, the director general of the IUCN, said: “It is not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover, but it requires decisive action to tackle climate change and halt further ocean warming.Carbon pollution has fuelled ‘massive expansion’ of marine heatwaves in Europe, study findsRead more“We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them.”Four of Australia’s 17 reef regions were considered critically endangered. Five were endangered and five more were classed as vulnerable.But all 17 regions, including the Great Barrier Reef, were critically endangered once the expected impacts of climate change were accounted for.Dr Ben Fitzpatrick of the University of Western Australia Oceans Institute led the Australian assessment. He said even after accounting for the ability of some corals to adapt to warmer water, the rising heat “overwhelmed everything”.“Reefs are like Picasso paintings under water,” he said. “They have all these wonderful inhabitants in their millions. You can spend a lifetime trying to understand how all these weird critters go about their daily lives.“To think we might lose that is devastating. There’s one message. We have to stop burning fossil fuels.”This story was amended on 23 October 2026. An earlier version misstated Mishal Gudka’s organisation name.Explore more on these topicsCoralClimate crisisMarine lifeWildlifeGreat Barrier ReefOceansConservationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Woman charged over shooting of police officer in Nottingham | UK news | The Guardian
description: Aisha Zaman, 27, charged with two firearms offences after incident in city centre on Sunday
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Aisha Zaman, 27, charged with two firearms offences after incident in city centre on Sunday
Content: Forensics officers at the scene of the shooting of a police officer in Nottingham city centre on Sunday.Photograph: Ben Booth/Sopa Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenForensics officers at the scene of the shooting of a police officer in Nottingham city centre on Sunday.Photograph: Ben Booth/Sopa Images/ShutterstockUK newsWoman charged over shooting of police officer in NottinghamAisha Zaman, 27, charged with two firearms offences after incident in city centre on SundayNadeem BadshahThu 22 Oct 2026 17.31 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 15.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 27-year-old woman has been charged after a police officer was shot while attending an incident in Nottingham.Aisha Zaman, from the Hyson Green area of the city, has been charged with possession of a prohibited firearm and possession of that firearm with intent to commit an indictable offence.She has been remanded into custody and will appear before Nottingham magistrates court on Friday.The officer, who is in a stable condition in hospital, had approached two people at a bus stop at 4.50am last Sunday when he was shot in the foot, Nottinghamshire police said.A weapon was recovered and a large crime scene cordon put in place around Angel Row in the city centre.Several other people have been arrested in connection with the incident including two men, aged 24 and 30, and two women, aged 25 and 21, on suspicion of assisting an offender.A 35-year-old man and a 33-year-old woman have also been arrested on suspicion of possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life and assisting an offender. Both suspects remain in police custody, the force added.DCS Rich Bull said: “We would just like to take this moment to thank the public. The outpouring of support for the injured officer has been greatly appreciated.“We continue to support him as he undergoes further treatment in hospital and are keeping him and his family fully informed of the developments in this investigation. He has asked for privacy during this incredibly difficult time.”The Police Federation sent its best wishes to the officer and said it was a “stark reminder of the dangers police officers face every day”.Following the incident, Neghat Khan, the leader of Nottingham city council, said she was “deeply shocked and saddened”.She said Nottingham was a “safe city” and praised the bravery of police and community protection officers, adding: “My thoughts and full support are with the injured police officer, their family and their colleagues across Nottinghamshire police.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tommy Robinson tells court he had photos taken of journalists’ homes to pressure them | UK news | The Guardian
description: Far-right activist says he used private investigators to track down journalists but denies trying to intimidate them
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Far-right activist says he used private investigators to track down journalists but denies trying to intimidate them
Content: Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, arriving at Southwark crown court.Photograph: James Manning/PAView image in fullscreenTommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, arriving at Southwark crown court.Photograph: James Manning/PAUK newsTommy Robinson tells court he had photos taken of journalists’ homes to pressure themFar-right activist says he used private investigators to track down journalists but denies trying to intimidate themBen QuinnThu 22 Oct 2026 13.23 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 14.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe far-right activist Tommy Robinson has told his harassment trial that he used private investigators to track down journalists who had written about his alleged role in the 2024 riots, and had photographs taken of their homes “to put pressure” on them.Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, denied in court that his actions, which included sharing photos of the wife and daughter of one of the journalists, were designed to intimidate and bully.“I’m not coming to beat [them] up … they know that,” he said, referring to messages and telephone calls, including a voicemail message left for the editor of the Daily Mail after Robinson had paid to get his personal number.Robinson is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two MailOnline journalists, Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber, in 2024. He denies the charges.Robinson, 43, gave evidence and was cross-examined on Thursday, when he claimed he “felt it was totally reasonable” to publish a photo of Dirnhuber at his home because he was “in a race against time” to get the Mail to remove a photo of his ex-wife, which the Mail published in a story about him being in Cyprus, with the headline: “Stoking race riots from his sunbed”.However, he conceded that when he sent messages to the journalists, spoke to one on the phone, and left a message on the voicemail of the Mail’s editor-in-chief, Ted Verity, he had not asked for the Mail to remove the image.Robinson said he believed he was “restrained” in the voicemail he left for Verity, in which he said he would make him and his family famous, and went on to say he told the journalists involved that he would get their addresses because he was “using it as a play card”.The prosecutor Ben Holt asked him about Dirnhuber and his partner having to leave their home as a result of threatening emails he allegedly received, and about Young’s family having also considered leaving their home.“The entire situation, I wish didn’t happen, I wish that none of that had happened,” said Robinson. “I was unfortunately in a situation where I was panicked.”Referring to the journalists and how they felt about messages he sent to them, he told Southwark crown court: “They know I’m not going to come and beat them up. They know that.”Holt continued: “They are scared of you, Mr Lennon,” to which came the reply: “They are not scared of physical violence from me.”Robinson was also asked about messages and online posts directed at the journalists by others after he had started using his own X account to tweet about them, including one post from an X user who told Dirnhuber they would beat the “fuck” out of him.Asked by Holt if he appreciated that messages such as this had been “generated” by his own output, Robinson said: “I don’t agree with any of these messages … I don’t know who sent these messages. I don’t know, I don’t know, I don’t know.”Robinson had been in Cyprus in early August 2024. At the time, violence was breaking out across England in the wake of the murder of three girls in Southport. He told the jury he was with “my ex-wife, my three children and three other families and their children”.In the witness stand, Robinson claimed he had not “stoked” the riots, but tried to calm things.The first day of the trial was told on Monday that journalists and their family members had to flee their homes after Robinson deployed “bullyboy, intimidatory tactics”.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to become first PM to appear on Gogglebox in episode filmed at No 10 | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: The PM is heard having a long discussion about crisps in the trailer to the show, which is in aid of Stand Up To Cancer
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: The PM is heard having a long discussion about crisps in the trailer to the show, which is in aid of Stand Up To Cancer
Content: Andy Burnham and Steve Rotheram on the special episode of Gogglebox, which will air on Friday.Photograph: Simon Dawson/No 10 Downing StreetView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and Steve Rotheram on the special episode of Gogglebox, which will air on Friday.Photograph: Simon Dawson/No 10 Downing StreetAndy BurnhamBurnham to become first PM to appear on Gogglebox in episode filmed at No 10The PM is heard having a long discussion about crisps in the trailer to the show, which is in aid of Stand Up To CancerHelena HortonThu 22 Oct 2026 12.07 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom ranking his favourite crisps in the pub to complaining about people watching TikToks out loud on the train,Andy Burnhamhas made efforts to show he has the common touch.Now he will become the first prime minister to appear on the TV showGogglebox, in a special charity episode on Friday.He will review the television shows of the week alongside the mayor of Liverpool city region,Steve Rotheram– a close friend. Others featured in the episode will include the pop band Sugababes and the comedian Joe Lycett.The show was filmed inside No 10. In the trailer, viewers are introduced to “good friends Andy and Steve” and Burnham can be heard saying: “Might have some crisps out here, do you want any?” They then have a long discussion about crisps.Rotheram responds that he has brought Quavers with him. Burnham offers his friend Skips, pork scratchings, Twiglets or bacon fries to go with a beer. He is heard throwing the packet to Rotheram and it appears to drop on the floor, after which both laugh uproariously.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueChannel 4 said: “Nothing is off limits as Gogglebox continues to celebrate the simple joy of watching television together. They’ll be sharing hilarious, honest and often unexpected reactions to the week’s biggest television moments as well as poignant stories, all in aid of Stand Up To Cancer.”A source close to Burnham told the Guardian he liked Gogglebox and had enjoyed watching the show. No 10 said he had a longstanding commitment to supporting charities, building on his work as the mayor of Greater Manchester and continuing in office as prime minister.In 2017, Jeremy Corbyn, then the Labour leader, appeared on the show. During his episode he shared his recipe for coddled eggs while watching a Nigella Lawson cookery programme.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStand Up To Cancer is a joint national fundraising campaign from Cancer Research UK and Channel 4 that brings Britain together to speed up progress in cancer research. More than £127m has been raised to date, funding 73 clinical trials and research projects involving more than 13,000 cancer patients.More celebrity TV critics are to be announced. The show airs this Friday on Channel 4 at 9.05pm.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamGoggleboxSteve RotheramChannel 4TelevisionEntertainment TVnewsShareReuse this content

title: Republican leader embarrassed by Ali G film says he plans to sue Sacha Baron Cohen: ‘A liar and a pervert’ | Movies | The Guardian
description:
Exclusive: Michael Aboud, whose actions in what he believed to be a documentary are likely to come under considerable scrutiny, has expressed anger at the film-maker

• This article contains substantial spoilers for Ali G: Who Iz I?
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: Exclusive: Michael Aboud, whose actions in what he believed to be a documentary are likely to come under considerable scrutiny, has expressed anger at the film-maker• This article contains substantial spoilers for Ali G: Who Iz I?
Content: ‘He taught me soooo much’ … Sacha Baron Cohen at the world premiere of Ali G: Who Iz I?, 14 October.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘He taught me soooo much’ … Sacha Baron Cohen at the world premiere of Ali G: Who Iz I?, 14 October.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersMoviesRepublican leader embarrassed by Ali G film says he plans to sue Sacha Baron Cohen: ‘A liar and a pervert’Exclusive:Michael Aboud, whose actions in what he believed to be a documentary are likely to come under considerable scrutiny, has expressed anger at the film-makerThis article contains substantial spoilers for Ali G: Who Iz I?Review: Ali G: Who Iz I?Catherine ShoardThu 22 Oct 2026 11.10 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 14.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe chair of the El Paso County Republican Party has said he intends to sueSacha Baron Cohenover footage of the local politician used in new satirical comedy Ali G: Who Iz I?Ali G: Who Iz I? review – Sacha Baron Cohen’s high-stakes satire punches up and down with spectacular bad tasteRead moreIn the film,Michael Aboudis shown taking part in a training programme with another Cohen character, ex-Mossad terrorist expert Col Erran Morad, who instructs Aboud and fellow Maga sympathisers in self-defence techniques including the wearing, over clothes, of protective plastic buttocks. He also schools them in how to fire bullets from the middle of these buttocks by the repeated up and down manipulation of a rubber penis.Aboud and a fellow student, former preacher and aspirant actor Joshua Loudermilk, are then recruited by Morad to help in a mission to prevent the birth in the US of the baby of a (fictional) South American drugs kingpin.This involves Aboud and Loudermilk abducting his heavily-pregnant girlfriend and driving her in a phoney ambulance to a remote unstaffed medical facility, where she gives birth (to a lifelike prosthetic).View image in fullscreenMaga sympathisers … Joshua Loudermilk and Michael Aboud in Ali G: Who Iz I?Photograph: Ali G: Who Iz I?‘A vehicle to expose prejudice, bias, and stupidity’: Sacha Baron Cohen defends Ali G as satireRead moreThey then abandon her, Morad having placed her live baby in a zipped bag, and drive with it towards Mexico. Loudermilk is later seen attempting to discharge fire from his fake buttocks, while Aboud takes the decision to drop the baby – at that point being dangled from a drone at a substantial height – to the ground to prevent it touching US soil. The actions could not be anything other than extremely serious for a real infant.Until the Guardian contacted Aboud on Tuesday, the businessman was unaware of his participation in anything other than what he believed to be a nonfiction film. In a statement, Aboud called Baron Cohen “and his entire film crew … a bunch of liars [who] deceive people to benefit themselves. They claimed that this would be a documentary about the illegals crossing the border. Then they said they were adding in this self-defence guy from Israel.”He added: “It is my opinion that Sasha Cohen [sic] is a pervert. Plus he talked about how Muslims are all gay because they follow the sex practices of Mohamid [sic]. No one should spend one penny watching anything he produces or appears in. I plan to sue him.”Pressed further on whether he stands by his actions in the film, Aboud declined to comment.The film repeatedly stresses that neither Aboud nor Loudermilk are “in on it”. Loudermilk has not responded to requests for comment, but his social media feed suggests a level of understanding about the project not shared by most of his fellow participants.Earlier this week, Loudermilk posted on Facebook that “I got to spend 12 hours one on one with Sasha [sic] and he taught me soooo much about the fun of making others laugh” as well as a link to a video promo for the film, saying, “I am in the trailer.” On 10 January, he also posted a headshot of himself, saying: “Howdy. Done with Sasha Cohen movie and ready for more.”Representatives for the film have told the Guardian that Loudermilk was unaware of the true nature of the film.Aboud’s shock at his involvement is particularly surprising given that he, along with Loudermilk, features in the second trailer for the film, which was released a fortnight ago.That clip alone contains considerable clues to those involved that all is not what it seems. In his address to the recruits, Morad, who was a fixture of Baron Cohen’s 2018 show Who is America?, advises the group that they should not be fooled, for the immigrants they are set against “are not coming here to mow your lawn, trim your trees, rake your leaves, clean your house, care for your babies, bus your tables, wash your cars, paint your houses, build your fences, install your roofs, drywall, plumbing or electric. They are coming to kill you.”Can Ali G: Who Iz I? save character comedy cinema?Read moreAnother section of the film involves Ali G hosting a “free speech” web show in which he is given a questionable script to read by South African producer Dirk Visser, who could not be contacted for comment.The character also presides over a gameshow of Visser’s invention in which contestants, against the clock, must stuff mannequins depicting “undesirables” including rappers, gay people, Muslims and Mexican babies into pretend shower cubicles, before pressing a button to seemingly activate the release of the poisonous gas Zyklon B. The segment ends with a mass Nazi salute.One of those who takes part is the disgraced former Republican congressman George Santos, who tells the camera his takeaway from playing the game is that next time he would try to grab more babies, as they’re easier to fit in the shower. In correspondence with the Guardian, Santos also suggested he was unaware of the true nature of the film, “as me and my team had no involvement”, and declined to justify his behaviour.Ali G: Who Iz I? opens in the UK, US and Australia on FridayExplore more on these topicsFilmRepublicansSacha Baron CohenAli G: Who Iz InewsShareReuse this content

title: Tom Skerritt, Alien and Top Gun actor, dies aged 93 | Movies | The Guardian
description: Actor also had roles in M*A*S*H, A River Runs Through It and Picket Fences in career spanning 60 years
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: Actor also had roles in M*A*S*H, A River Runs Through It and Picket Fences in career spanning 60 years
Content: Tom Skerritt in 2010.Photograph: Reed Saxon/APView image in fullscreenTom Skerritt in 2010.Photograph: Reed Saxon/APMoviesTom Skerritt, Alien and Top Gun actor, dies aged 93Actor also had roles in M*A*S*H, A River Runs Through It and Picket Fences in career spanning 60 yearsBenjamin LeeThu 22 Oct 2026 16.19 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 16.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTom Skerritt, the actor known for roles in Alien andTop Gun, has died at the age of 93.His publicist confirmed toVarietythat he died from natural causes.“While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity, and the love he brought into our lives,” a family statement shared withPeopleread.In a career spanning more than 60 years, the actor had more than 170 big and small screen credits, winning an Emmy and receiving Golden Globe and Screen Actors Guild award nominations.After serving a four-year tour of duty in the US air force, Skerritt made his big-screen debut in the 1962 war film War Hunt alongside Robert Redford and Sydney Pollack, but his breakout came in 1970 with a role in Robert Altman’s hit satire M*A*S*H. The film was a major box office hit and was nominated for the best picture Oscar.The 1970s saw Skerritt follow the film with roles in the cult black comedy Harold and Maude, Altman’s crime drama Thieves Like Us, Roger Corman’s sexploitation comedy Big Bad Mama and the Oscar-nominated ballet drama The Turning Point.View image in fullscreenSigourney Weaver, Yaphet Kotto, John Hurt, Tom Skerritt and Ian Holm in Alien.Photograph: Ronald GrantThe decade closed out with a role in Ridley Scott’s smash hit Alien, a film he had earlier turned down due to the low budget. “At two million bucks and with other actors that I don’t know about, this is a film that could have been directed by Ed Wood,” he said ina 2019 interview. “I was uncertain about it because my training with Altman and Ashby had proceeded me, so I had that approach that I had absorbed from watching those two guys going about their work.”The following decade saw him feature in David Cronenberg’s The Dead Zone, the sci-fi adventure SpaceCamp, horror sequel Poltergeist III and female-led comedy drama Steel Magnolias.Skerritt also worked with Tony Scott in the 1986 blockbuster Top Gun, a role he almost didn’t get. “There was some question about me playing that role because I was … I think they used the word, laconic,” he said in a 2021 interview withVulture. “It pissed me off. I went into it with [producer] Don Simpson, who was still alive at that point … don’t tell me, as a producer, what you think I’m going to be doing. You’re going to get what you need.”In the 1990s, he reunited with Robert Redford for A River Runs Through It and also starred with Jodie Foster in Contact, Drew Barrymore in Poison Ivy and Diane Keaton in The Other Sister.Skerritt also received an Emmy for his role in David E Kelley’s family drama Picket Fences, a show that ran for four seasons.The 2000s saw him star with Bruce Willis in Tears of the Sun, Kate Beckinsale in Whiteout and on the small screen he had roles in Will & Grace, The West Wing and Brothers & Sisters.His last film role was in the western drama Broke in 2025 with Dennis Quaid.In 2012, he also co-founded an initiative called the Red Badge Project, which aimed to help veterans process their PTSD through storytelling. “It starts with that wanting to help someone else rather than talking about it,” Skerritt said toCBS News. “I just got tired of talking about this if I could do something about it.”“I’m just a lucky guy, man,” he said in 2021. “Strength is measured in how you confront your weaknesses. I have had a lot of weaknesses. I still have them.”Explore more on these topicsFilmAlienTop GunUS televisionTelevisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Teacher wounded in Oregon school shooting played dead after she was shot | Oregon | The Guardian
description: Becky Drury says she was hit by gunfire before she could intervene in attack that killed four, including three children
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: Becky Drury says she was hit by gunfire before she could intervene in attack that killed four, including three children
Content: Becky Drury, a teacher wounded in a shooting at Silver Rail elementary in Bend, Oregon.Photograph: Zack Hall/Drury family/APBecky Drury, a teacher wounded in a shooting at Silver Rail elementary in Bend, Oregon.Photograph: Zack Hall/Drury family/APOregonTeacher wounded in Oregon school shooting played dead after she was shotBecky Drury says she was hit by gunfire before she could intervene in attack that killed four, including three childrenDani AnguianoThu 22 Oct 2026 16.12 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 17.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOregon shooting victims: three boys and female teacher killed at elementary schoolRead moreA teacher wounded inlast week’s shootingat a Bend, Oregon, elementary school shared her account of the incident, and how she was shot before she could intervene and “[pretended] to be dead”.Becky Drury was seriously wounded at Silver Rail elementary when Griffin J John II, a 16-year-old former student at the school armed with a shotgun, broke in and headed toward a special education classroom. He shot six people, killing Megan Lambert, a 25-year-old teacher, and three children, including five-year-old Rhoam Summer.Drury and Saylor Graham, a seven-year-old student, were also shot. Another teacher threw her phone at John and tackled him beforea parent fatally shotthe teen gunman.Drury, who is still hospitalized, released a statement on Wednesday.After the unimaginable happens, an Oregon town mourns: ‘You can’t stop thinking about the kids’Read more“Here is what I remember: Once I realized something was happening outside, I ran to see what was going on. I then saw the shooter and immediately ran back into the classroom. I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there. Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground,” Drury said.Her left hand was almost completely severed, and her other arm was also badly injured, Drury said.“I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else. So, I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again,” she said. “I know there has been contradictory reporting about my actions that day, but the truth is I was shot before I had any chance to act.”Bystander who killed Oregon shooter identified as father of girls at elementary schoolRead moreDrury’s account contradicted some reporting that she had thrown herself on top of a student in an effort to protect her, and the 54-year-old said she wanted to ensure “the events of that day and my actions in particular are reported accurately”.She described the violence as “unimaginable” and said: “My heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy.”Public schools in the centralOregoncity began reopening this week. Dozens of officers have welcomed students as they return to their classes.The shooting remains under investigation. The Bend police department said this week that the shotgun used in the incident was purchased legally.Explore more on these topicsOregonUS school shootingsUS crimeWest CoastGun crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Rebel Wilson secures another Australian court win as co-producers of The Deb awarded just $10  | Rebel Wilson | The Guardian
description: NSW supreme court judge otherwise dismisses case brought by film’s co-producers and awards Wilson almost $400,000 after star countersued
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: NSW supreme court judge otherwise dismisses case brought by film’s co-producers and awards Wilson almost $400,000 after star countersued
Content: Rebel Wilson in Sydney in April 2026. Wilson countersued producers, claiming their involvement in The Deb was marked by a pattern of illicit and egregious behaviour.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPView image in fullscreenRebel Wilson in Sydney in April 2026. Wilson countersued producers, claiming their involvement in The Deb was marked by a pattern of illicit and egregious behaviour.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPRebel WilsonRebel Wilson secures another Australian court win as co-producers of The Deb awarded just $10NSW supreme court judge otherwise dismisses case brought by film’s co-producers and awards Wilson almost $400,000 after star countersuedAustralian Associated PressThu 22 Oct 2026 19.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 20.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralian A-listerRebel Wilsonhas secured a major court victory after co-producers of her debut film accused her of sabotage, lying and breaching contracts.The Pitch Perfect star directed,co-produced and starred in The Deb, a musical comedy that became the battleground for multiple legal battles in Australia and the US.It had a budget of A$22m (US15.4m, £11.5m) but made just $335,000 (US$235,000, £175,284) at the local box office, which Wilson’s co-producers allege could be traced to her false and derogatory statements about them online.Rebel Wilson wins defamation case brought by co-star after bitter disputeRead moreThe Bridesmaids star claimed in posts from July 2024 that producers Amanda Ghost, Gregor Cameron and Vince Holden tried to block The Deb’s release, embezzled money and behaved inappropriately towards the film’s star.The producers alleged Wilson caused their company financial and reputational damage in an attempt to devalue her debut film so she could purchase it from them.On Friday, Justice Elisabeth Peden in the New South Wales supreme court awarded the trio $10 (US$7, £5) in damages and otherwise dismissed the summons.Wilson had denied her co-producers’ allegations and countersued, claiming their involvement in the film was marked by a troubling pattern of illicit, egregious behaviours, including theft, bullying and sexual misconduct.The judge awarded her $359,000 (US$251,830, £187,868) plus interest in a brief decision, which will be followed by a written judgment.It was the second victory for Wilson after she wascleared of defaming her debut film’s star Charlotte MacInnesearlier this year following a fiery federal court hearing.MacInnes claimed Wilson defamed her in four social media posts that implied she was a liar and a sellout who walked back a sexual harassment complaint to further her career.The posts alleged the young actor confided in Wilson – and later recanted – that she felt uncomfortable when the film’s co-producer Amanda Ghost asked to have a shower and a bath together.MacInnes denied making or retracting a complaint, insisting she had not been uncomfortable when the pair shared a bath in their swimwear after Ghost suffered a medical episode in September 2023.The federal court found none of Wilson’s posts were defamatory.Explore more on these topicsRebel WilsonAustralian filmAustralian lawMusicalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Macron bans ‘illegitimate’ protests in France as he tries to get a grip on unrest | France | The Guardian
description: French president also says he will decide on concrete ‘next steps’ for the next nationwide demonstrations
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: French president also says he will decide on concrete ‘next steps’ for the next nationwide demonstrations
Content: Student protesters in Paris on Thursday after an initial police ban on their demonstration was overturned by a court.Photograph: Ibrahim Ezzat/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStudent protesters in Paris on Thursday after an initial police ban on their demonstration was overturned by a court.Photograph: Ibrahim Ezzat/Anadolu/Getty ImagesFranceMacron bans ‘illegitimate’ protests in France as he tries to get a grip on unrestFrench president also says he will decide on concrete ‘next steps’ for the next nationwide demonstrationsAngry lawyers and bewildered defendants: the fallout from fast-tracking French rioting casesJon Henleyin ParisThu 22 Oct 2026 11.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 14.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmmanuel Macron has said “illegitimate” demonstrations will be banned over the coming days as France seeks to get a grip on civil unrest aftersome of its worst street violence in yearserupted on the fringes of cost of living protests at the weekend.Speaking after a ​meeting with intelligence officials and senior ministers, the French president said on Thursday that demonstrations organised by recognised groups would be allowed to go ahead, although their routes could be changed.View image in fullscreenEmmanuel Macron chairs a security council meeting at the Élysée Palace.Photograph: Suarez Teresa/ABACA/ShutterstockProtests requested by “individuals or groups with no legitimate authority” would be banned, Macron said. Requests by organisations such as trade unions would be “examined in accordance with the law” but they might have to use alternative routes.The measures were necessary to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings, he said, adding: “The rules are simple and I think they’re commonsense. The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days.”Macron blamed much of last weekend’s unrest and looting on rioters who came expressly to loot, but said the worst of the violence was due to “political and seditious acts by ultra far-left groups who aimed to bring down the republic”.View image in fullscreenProtesters in Paris hold a banner reading “high school students target the Bac. The Bac target the head.” The Bac refers to the baccalaureate exam and also the French police’s anti-crime brigade.Photograph: Teresa Suárez/AP“The priority is a return to calm,” he said, adding that he would chair a defence council meeting of key ministers on Friday to decide concrete “next steps” for new nationwide demonstrations called for Saturday and afterwards.An initial police ban on a student protest planned inParisfor Thursday was overturned by a court, but marches also scheduled for the day in Grenoble, Rouen, Le Havre and Toulon were halted.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMacron accuses Trump and other foreign leaders of ‘stupid comments’ about France unrestRead moreAuthorities have already declared a ban on “all protests” on Saturday in the centre of Lyon, France’s third-biggest city, where between 200 and 300 shops were ransacked and looted last weekend and the tourist office was set ablaze.Authorities in Marseille, Nice and Toulon announced similar bans for Saturday. In Paris, a march planned for Saturday to be held in the east of the capital, starting at the Place de la Bastille, was authorised but banned from heading into the city centre.However, a separate march through the capital planned for Saturday by students and some members of thegilets jaunes(yellow vests) movement, whose protests over fuel prices rocked France in 2018 and 2019, would not be permitted, authorities in the capital said.View image in fullscreenA demonstration involving members of the gilets jaunes on the capital’s Place de la République on Saturday.Photograph: Giulia Morici/NurPhoto/ShutterstockFrance’s main student union, UNEF, has also called ‌for rallies on Saturday. Businesses in central Paris and other cities had already begun boarding up their windows and hiring private security in preparation for violence, French media reported.The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, said 174 of the 2,500 people arrested since last weekend’s rioting had been remanded in custody and more than 900 were being prosecuted. Two people have been arrested after Limoges town hall was set on fire.‘America, this is a warning’: pro- Trump Maga media in a froth over Europe protestsRead moreThe prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, was hosting a meeting of key figures from France’s main political parties on Thursday to hear their views and seek cooperation, and was due to meet several big-city mayors later in the day.The tough security response has included partial night-time curfews in parts of several cities including Paris, as well as bans on gatherings in areas such as around the Élysée presidential palace, the parliament and the city’s main train stations.The demonstrations began last month in a high school in Créteil, south-east of Paris, over staff shortages and dilapidated buildings, and spread nationwide, with strikes, blockades and demonstrations by high-school pupils around the country.Those demonstrations have morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, six months before next year’s presidential elections, which will choose Macron’s successor.Explore more on these topicsFranceEmmanuel MacronParisProtestEuropeCost of living crisisGilets jaunes protestsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sharp drops for AI stocks overwhelm markets worldwide as oil prices jump | US markets | The Guardian
