description: Datacenter and chip costs fueled sharp decrease in AI sector although non-AI stocks still had a strong showing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Datacenter and chip costs fueled sharp decrease in AI sector although non-AI stocks still had a strong showing
Content: An options trader works on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on 7 January 2026.Photograph: Richard Drew/APView image in fullscreenAn options trader works on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on 7 January 2026.Photograph: Richard Drew/APUS marketsSharp drops for AI stocks overwhelm markets worldwide as oil prices jumpDatacenter and chip costs fueled sharp decrease in AI sector although non-AI stocks still had a strong showingAssociated PressThu 22 Oct 2026 17.50 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 18.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe latest shudder for stocks in theAIindustry pulled markets lower worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about thewar with Iran.TheS&P500 fell 1.2% for its worst day since July, while theNasdaqcomposite tumbled 2.6%. The weakness for tech stocks was so overwhelming that it masked strength for the rest of the US market, in which the majority of stocks actually rose. TheDow JonesIndustrial Average added 11 points, or less than 0.1%.AI-related stocks have been swinging on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build datacenters and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that their prices shot too high following a years-long frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.Oil prices jump to five-month high as attacks threaten global supplyRead moreLam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 11.8%.Other big tech stocks likewise fell following quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets.Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7% after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, shedding tens of billions in market value, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it was creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses.Tesla fell 3.1% after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast.The global tide against AI stocks knockedNvidiadown 4.4%. Because the chip giant is the largest company on Wall Street by total value, movements for its stock carry more weight on the S&P 500 than any other, and it was the single strongest force pulling the index lower.CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 10.1%.The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where indexes are full of players in the industry. South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5%, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3% and Japan’sNikkei225 sank 2.7%.Also weighing on global stock markets was a jump in oil prices.The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil leaped 4% to $113.17 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s shot up from less than $97 at the start of the month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1.4%. It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or US indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds.Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWorries about big government debt are weighing on almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong US economy and other factors, have pushed yields in the US bond market recently to their highest levels in decades.But US yields nevertheless fell sharply on Thursday in a signal that investors were buying US government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled.The yield on the 10-year treasury tumbled to 4.97% from 5.13% late on Wednesday and from more than 5.30% earlier this month. That’s a major move for the bond market.Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the US economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could signal that layoffs remain low across the country.That solid economy has helped US companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the US stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. Two out of every three stocks within the S&P 500 rose on Thursday, only to get drowned out by the drops for more influential tech stocks.Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses on Thursday.CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expected “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 5.6%.All told, the S&P 500 fell 93.74 points, to 7,663.43. TheDow JonesIndustrial Average added 11.89, to 52,867.98, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 694.00, to 26,008.86.Explore more on these topicsUS marketsStock marketsDow JonesNasdaqStandard & Poor'sNikkeiMetanewsShareReuse this content

title: You be the chancellor: play our budget game to see if you can balance the books | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: See if you can do a better job than John Healey at creating a budget that keeps MPs and the bond markets onside
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: See if you can do a better job than John Healey at creating a budget that keeps MPs and the bond markets onside
Content: John Healey will announce his budget on 28 October.Composite: Prina Shah for the Guardian / ReutersView image in fullscreenJohn Healey will announce his budget on 28 October.Composite: Prina Shah for the Guardian / ReutersBudget 2026You be the chancellor: play our budget game to see if you can balance the booksSee if you can do a better job than John Healey at creating a budget that keeps MPs and the bond markets onsideRichard PartingtonandSeán ClarkeThu 22 Oct 2026 04.04 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 04.52 EDTShareThe challengeOn 28 October,John Healeywill announce the autumn budget to parliament. As in all years, the chancellor has to strike a balance between the following:Raising the money needed to fund the services that voters demand.Keeping taxes at levels that are acceptable to voters.Persuading the government’s creditors in the bond markets that it will continue to be able to pay its debts.The gameIn our game you get to try your hand at designing a successful budget. Can you keep backbenchers happy without upsetting the bond markets? And can you do it all while keeping the books balanced?Just like the real chancellor, you begin in the red.At the spring statement, Healey’s immediate predecessor, Rachel Reeves, had left herself £23.6bn of “headroom” against the fiscal rules, which require day-to-day spending to be matched by receipts by the end of this parliament.However, the buffer is widely expected to have been slashed by a surge in debt interest costs, as the war in the Middle East triggers a global inflation shock that is rattling the bond markets.Taken together, the Resolution Foundation thinktank predicts the headroom against the government’s fiscal target will be halved, to about £12bn.Healey is thought to be willing to allow the buffer to take a hit. However, jittery bond investors are looking for him to retain a degree of headroom to guard against further negative shocks, with at least £14bn thought to be needed to avoid provoking a bond market reaction.The chancellor is also under pressure to find space in the public finances for three things: a cost of living support package; a boost in defence spending; and financing Andy Burnham’s long-term priority to spread “good growth” to every postcode.TipsSolving the above is all part of your task. You’ll see the headroom grow or shrink, or – most worrying – become negative in response to your policy decision. But keep an eye on the alerts on how the markets – which may not be convinced – and the opinion polls are responding as you go. Good luck.If you get stuck tap or click for Treasury briefings –chart icon– and wry notes from Burnham –note icon– for guidance.{{ html }}Sources and notes: the estimates of income from each of the measures and for the current government balance come from a variety of economists and thinktanks and the government’s own assumptions. The core fiscal impacts are from HM Revenue and Customs, and the estimates for other measures are sourced in the descriptions. These estimates are often based on those economists’ own assumptions about future growth, inflation, collection rates and other variables. So this game should be seen as illustrative of the relative sizes of the impacts of measures. Do not buy or sell gilts on the basis of this game, in case you were thinking of it.Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026John HealeyAndy BurnhamTax and spendingLabourShare

title: BBC News to axe education editor role in cost-cutting move | BBC | The Guardian
description: Fears over lack of scrutiny for key sectors as health editor position also to go in cuts aimed at saving £5.5m
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Fears over lack of scrutiny for key sectors as health editor position also to go in cuts aimed at saving £5.5m
Content: An editing suite at the BBC newsroom at British Broadcasting House, London. About 100 jobs are being cut at BBC News.Photograph: Jeff Gilbert/AlamyView image in fullscreenAn editing suite at the BBC newsroom at British Broadcasting House, London. About 100 jobs are being cut at BBC News.Photograph: Jeff Gilbert/AlamyBBCBBC News to axe education editor role in cost-cutting moveFears over lack of scrutiny for key sectors as health editor position also to go in cuts aimed at saving £5.5mMichael SavageMedia editorThu 22 Oct 2026 08.21 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 08.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe BBC will no longer have a dedicated education editor as part of acost-cutting drivein which 100 jobs are to go across BBC News under a plan that school leaders described as “deeply regrettable”.BBC staff have been told that the roles of education editor and social affairs editor are to be combined into a single position as part of a round of changes that will save £5.5m. However, prominent unions and campaigners are saying the reform will dilute scrutiny of two specialisms that are too important to go without a dedicatedBBCrole.The education editor at BBC News is Branwen Jeffreys and the social affairs editor is Alison Holt.In a message to staff seen by the Guardian, Richard Burgess, the director of news content, said he was proposing the change after a review of on-air editor roles. He said the review looked at “audience demand, editorial requirements and how we ensure these roles remain relevant in a changing news environment”.There will also be no health editor title at the BBC when the current incumbent, Hugh Pym, leaves in the spring. That job will be incorporated into the role of medical editor, currently held by Fergus Walsh.“These are difficult decisions, but I have given the changes careful consideration, taking into account levels of audience interest and editorial demand, as well as how we can work as efficiently as possible across the department,” Burgess said.It appears BBC executives have opted to combine the education and social affairs jobs as they attempt to reduce duplication and cut wage costs. Sources said experienced education and social affairs specialists would remain at the BBC, but others inside the corporation have been left puzzled by a change that will leave the world’s oldest national public service broadcaster without a dedicated education editor.BBC Three and BBC Scotland TV channels to be shut down next yearRead moreSchool leaders and teaching unions questioned the move. “On the face of it, this announcement suggests that the BBC is proposing to dilute leadership of its education coverage,” said James Bowen, the assistant general secretary at the school leaders’ union NAHT. He urged the BBC to rethink the plan.He said: “This would be a deeply regrettable move by our national broadcaster, which plays a vital role in shining a light on important issues affecting the education sector and holding the government and Department for Education to account.”Daniel Kebede, the general secretary of the National Education Union, said the move would “diminish the public’s understanding of education matters in this country”. Matt Wrack, the general secretary of the NASUWT teachers’ union, said: “At a time when schools are grappling with rising child poverty, crumbling buildings, teacher shortages and major funding cuts, the public needs to hear from strong public interest reporting in the sector.”Nadra Ahmed, the co-chair of the National Care Association, said she was concerned that the lack of a social affairs editor meant the sector could lose attention at a critical time with the prime ministerdrawing up social care reforms.One BBC insider said combining the education and social affairs editor roles “further erodes our ability to give sufficient coverage to the breadth and depth of two materially distinct topics”.However, others inside the BBC said the issues of education, social affairs and health all had dedicated teams of journalists that would ensure proper coverage. A BBC spokesperson said: “The BBC remains committed to covering education, and will continue to do so both at editor level, and with its team of expert reporters and producers.”Burgess said that alongside the editor role changes the job requirements of on-air editors would be reviewed to place “greater emphasis” on making an impact on social media and digital platforms such as YouTube and TikTok.The BBC is making renewed efforts to boost its presence on those platforms as it attempts to reach younger audiences who are increasingly using the sites for news.The new head of BBC News,Rachel Jupp, used one of her first memos to staff to tell them that the department’s target of finding £51m in savings could be increased “given the BBC’s financial pressures”.Explore more on these topicsBBCPublic service broadcastingHealthTrade unionsTeachingTV newsPublic service reportingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Barclays to cut 5,000 jobs as bank’s bosses hail AI productivity advances | Barclays | The Guardian
description: Equating to the loss of 5% of its 93,000 global staff, job cuts come as bank announces jump in quarterly profits
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Equating to the loss of 5% of its 93,000 global staff, job cuts come as bank announces jump in quarterly profits
Content: Barclays’ strong performance included a 6% rise in net interest income at its UK retail banking operations, to £2bn.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBarclays’ strong performance included a 6% rise in net interest income at its UK retail banking operations, to £2bn.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesBarclaysBarclays to cut 5,000 jobs as bank’s bosses hail AI productivity advancesEquating to the loss of 5% of its 93,000 global staff, job cuts come as bank announces jump in quarterly profitsKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentThu 22 Oct 2026 10.39 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 03.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBarclays is cutting 5,000 jobs as part of wider cost-saving plans that its bosses say are being driven by advances in AI.The job cuts will mean losing about 5% of the bank’s 93,000 global staff, with executives confirming they had already cut 1,000 workers since the start of the year.The bank’s chief financial officer, Anna Cross, told reporters on Thursday that the job cuts were part of plans to save more than £1.1bn in 2027. “These actions involve an expected reduction of circa 5,000 full-time employees. Around 60% of the group actions relate to support functions, including fewer developers, as AI makes our people more productive.”When asked how many of the total job cuts would be directly linked to advances in AI, the chief executive, CS Venkatakrishnan, said the bank had been making “deep investments” in technology and simplifying its processes.“That is driving the bulk of the efficiency gains that you’ve seen so far. AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future,” Venkatakrishnan said, calling AI the “icing on the cake” to modernising the bank’s technology.Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the Unite union, said Barclays workers “deserve better”.She added: “The company is using AI as an excuse to discard its loyal and long-suffering workforce. Employers should be focused on upgrading employees’ skills so that they remain employed as new technology changes the workplace. Instead, Barclays is guilty of taking a short-term, kneejerk approach.”The news comes months after another UK-headquartered bank, Standard Chartered, announced plans to cut more than 7,000 jobs in the next four years as it ramps up the use of AI. It will mean slashing about 15% of its back-office roles by 2030.Barclays also announced plans to hand a further £500m to investors, taking the total amount given to shareholders since January – through buybacks and dividends – to £2.8bn.It came as the lender reported £2.3bn in pre-tax profits over the July to September quarter, up 12% from £2.1bn during the same period last year.The strong financial performance will probably to be used to justify the expectedincrease in bank taxesin the 28 October budget, as Andy Burnham’s government looks for ways to raise revenue to help fund cost of living support programmes.When asked whether the bank might consider tilting assets or investment out of the UK and to the US – where it also has operations – as a result of higher levies, Venkatakrishnan said Barclays would be able to absorb them.“I recognise that the chancellor and the government … have to balance a host of considerations,” he said, adding that Barclays shared their goal to prompt growth.“This is not a question of a financial hit to us. It’s bearable. It is a question of proportion and it’s a question of market signalling. But … I deeply respect the responsibility that the chancellor has and he has our full support and backing.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBarclays’ strong performance included a 6% rise in net interest income at its UK retail banking operations, to £2bn. The figure has become a flashpoint for campaigners pushing for a bank tax.It accounts for how much money banks make from loan charges, minus what they pay on deposits, and is linked to interest rates, which have been rising as the Iran war has driven up inflation expectations.The Trades Union Congress, which has been campaigning for a bank tax increase, said lenders needed to contribute more at a time when people were struggling with household bills.TheTUCgeneral secretary, Paul Nowak, said: “Barclays’ bumper profits aren’t an anomaly. All the big banks are doing exceptionally well … Britain’s big four banks have made £200bn in profit since 2021. They can – and should – pay more tax.”Healey has promised that next week’s budget will support Britain’s entrepreneurs, and focus on cutting the “cost of business”.Hetold the Times: “I want to be a chancellor who backs business in Britain making a profit, those entrepreneurs who in the end are the ones who challenge the status quo, come up with innovative ideas and are trying, some of them through sheer bloody-mindedness, to keep going through these sorts of pressures, which is what they’ve done.”Explore more on these topicsBarclaysBankingBudget 2026John HealeyBudgetTax and spendingTUCnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘If my brother hadn’t died, my life would be so different’: Olympic boxer Ramla Ali’s incredible journey | Movies | The Guardian
description: From fleeing the Somali civil war to fighting at the Tokyo Olympics, Ali’s life has been remarkable – and now she is being played by Top Boy’s Jasmine Jobson in a new biopic. We hear from both on this ‘positive migrant story’
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: From fleeing the Somali civil war to fighting at the Tokyo Olympics, Ali’s life has been remarkable – and now she is being played by Top Boy’s Jasmine Jobson in a new biopic. We hear from both on this ‘positive migrant story’
Content: Star power … Jasmine Jobson, left, and Ramla Ali at the premiere of In the Shadows at the London film festival.Photograph: Phil Lewis/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenStar power … Jasmine Jobson, left, and Ramla Ali at the premiere of In the Shadows at the London film festival.Photograph: Phil Lewis/SOPA Images/ShutterstockMoviesInterview‘If my brother hadn’t died, my life would be so different’: Olympic boxer Ramla Ali’s incredible journeyCath ClarkeFrom fleeing the Somali civil war to fighting at the Tokyo Olympics, Ali’s life has been remarkable – and now she is being played by Top Boy’s Jasmine Jobson in a new biopic. We hear from both on this ‘positive migrant story’Thu 22 Oct 2026 09.28 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 10.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBoxer Ramla Ali sweeps into the green room of a West End cinema, tiny in a frothy dress with a huge skirt of cascading black feathers. It’s an absolute showstopper. She’s just introduced the premiere of a new film about her life. There are messages on her phone from Bear Grylls and Malala Yousafzai, who are in the audience watching.But the person who matters most is her mum, who is seeing it for the fourth time. What does she think? “She loves it,” says Ali quietly. The film is In the Shadows, directed by Anthony Wonke and stars Top Boy actor Jasmine Jobson. It tells the story of Ali’s journey to the 2021 Olympics in Tokyo.And what a journey. Ali was born inSomalia. When she was a baby, her older brother Abdulkadir was killed in an explosion while playing. The family fled Somalia, making the perilous crossing by boat to Kenya, finally arriving in the UK as refugees.Ali grew up in east London, joining a boxercise class at the local gym after being bullied at school about her weight. When she started boxing seriously, she kept it hidden from her family. As a Muslim girl, it would not be allowed. And she knew that her mother, having moved heaven and earth to get the family away from violence, would be devastated seeing her in harm’s way. These days, her mum is the first person Ali calls after a fight.It was eight years ago that the idea of a film first came up. Ali’s husband Richard Moore has just walked into the room. He used to be her coach and is also an executive producer on the film. He explains that one of the biggest reasons for pitching it back in 2018 was practical: they were broke. “We were down to our last hundred quid. We were lucky at that time, we had friends who took us in and housed us.” For a while they were a living in a home owned by Idris Elba and his wife, Sabrina. “They were our saviours. Then we got Covid and had to stay for ages,” giggles Ali.View image in fullscreenIn the ring … Ramla Ali lands a punch on Crystal Garcia Nova, 2022.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/ReutersDid she have any doubts about making the film? She nods: “Yes. I wasn’t sure I wanted to be so vulnerable, to sit down with a writer and tell her everything about my life, things I haven’t shared before.” There was her family’s trauma to consider, too: “I remember thinking, how is it going to affect my mum? It’s my story, but it’s her story as well. When I talked to my family, none of them were really up for it.” In the end, unexpectedly, it was her mother who came round first. And she had strong opinions about the script too: “My mum was adamant that the scene when my brother got killed be included. It had to be in.” Moore thinks it was a way of keeping him alive: “Remembering him, and making his death mean something bigger.”Ali has gone quiet. After a moment she says that Abdulkadir being killed set in motion a sequence of events that changed all their lives in her family: “His death is the ripple effect. If my brother hadn’t died, we wouldn’t have come to the UK. I wouldn’t have taken up boxing. I wouldn’t have met Richard. My life would be so different.”She says the film is not a pro-immigration statement. But it does offer another point of view to the fearmongering about migrants arriving on boats and stealing British jobs. “It’s depicting a human migrant story. Immigration has been weaponised politically to drive division in this country. Positive migrant stories don’t sell newspapers in the same way, so they rarely get told. But they are far more representative of the people who come here and build lives, families and careers. If audiences walk out seeing a person rather than a headline, the film has done its job.”She is the living proof of a positive migration story. In 2015, Ali became the first Muslim woman to win an English amateur boxing title. Six years later, she competed at the Tokyo Olympics as the first boxer in history to represent Somalia. She has modelled, appearing on the cover of British Vogue guest edited by the Duchess of Sussex. In 2018, she set up Sisters Club, a charity providing free boxing classes to vulnerable women. She is a Unicef ambassador.View image in fullscreenKnockout performance … Jasmine Jobson as Ali and Gershwyn Eustache Jr as Clinton in In the ShadowsPhotograph: Gavin Bond/True Brit Entertainment LtdAli tells me she worked hard behind the scenes of In the Shadows, reading every draft of the script, on set every day of the shoot. “Some exec producers just write their names on the film. But Iworkedfor that title. Iearnedit.” She even body doubled in the boxing scenes.Ali has been thinking lately about life after boxing. She and Moore have written and directed a comedy film together, Not Like Us, and she’s dipped her toe into acting too. “Boxing’s not for ever. There comes a day where you think: It’s time. Everyone laughs at me, but I keep saying it’s very similar to boxing. The dedication you’ve got to put into your boxing will show on the night in the ring. It’s the same with film-making. The level of dedication you’ve got to put in will show on screen.”What kind of films does she want to make? “I feel like in America there are so many films made for black people. I would love to be able to be in a position to tell more stories focused on the Black British experience.”It’s a sunny afternoon when I catch up with Jasmine Jobson, who plays Ali in the film. She took over from Letitia Wright, who was initially attached to the project. Jobson arrives at the BFI Southbank with a full entourage – publicist, makeup and hairdresser. “There’s not one part of my team that can be missing,” I hear her say as she strides across the room in Louboutin heels.She looks in fabulous shape. Is that the boxing? “Thank you. No. I haven’t continued boxing. I do need to get back into it.” She is focused on physio for an old shoulder injury, picked up years ago at the gym. “At college, I was training to be a personal trainer. I just pulled a bit too much weight down on a lat-pull.”Did she get into the swing of the boxing easily? “Yeah. Straight in. When I was young, I did karate, kickboxing, things like that. But I only had two weeks to prepare for this job. Literally two weeks to become a champion.” She spent eight hours a day training: “I absolutely loved boxing. I just don’t like getting my face touched. No one’s allowed to get my face. This is my money maker.”View image in fullscreen‘She’s overcome so much’ … Ramla Ali and Jasmine Jobson.Photograph: Tom CockramJobson says she fell in love with Ali the moment they met for coffee. “We had a nice little chat and got to know each other on a bit more of a deeper level. She’s overcome so much. To come out the other side, and to be an international success, to be able to change perceptions …” Jobson pauses. “Something might feel distant, or not necessarily accepted. But if you are passionate about it, and you are very good at it, if it’s your talent, go for it. You can be a success story no matter what your dream is. She’s a testament to that. Kudos to her, man.”Did it feel intimidating taking on the part of a real-life person, I ask. “No. Not all. Any role I’ve played, I’ve incorporated myself into it.”Like Ali, her experience of childhood adversity makes her achievements doubly impressive. As a young child, Jobson’s parents encouraged her talent for performing. But when she was in secondary school, social services became involved with the family. Jobson moved out of her mother’s house to live with her grandmother. Then, aged 14, she took the decision to place herself in foster care: “I had to do a very very deep dive within myself and take myself away from bad crowds, and figure out what my destiny was. My brain got a little bit clouded, and I had to find Jasmine again.”A family friend suggested she try out for The Big House, a theatre company in north London that works with care leavers, and there she got an agent. Like Ali, she is a grafter, and learned lines in Somali for In the Shadows. She gives me a phrase in Somali: “It means: ‘I just want you to be proud of me.’ That’s all I’ve ever wanted – for my family and everybody to be proud of me.”It sounds as if she put a lot of herself in the role. “Oh, 100%. But at the same time, I had to make sure it was authentically Ramla.” She can see the similarities, she admits: “It’s not that we’ve had the same life experiences, but we both had struggles and we both had a dream.”In the Shadows is in UK and Irish cinemas from 30 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmBoxingSomaliaBiopicsRefugeesAfricaMiddle East and north AfricainterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Shovel Dance Collective: Everything in Readiness review – ecstatic, dissonant folk music fighting for sonic and spiritual freedom | Music | The Guardian
description: The nine-piece London-based group take a radically fresh approach to traditional music, sounding raging, lo-fi and joyful as they link Britain’s violent past to its present
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: The nine-piece London-based group take a radically fresh approach to traditional music, sounding raging, lo-fi and joyful as they link Britain’s violent past to its present
Content: Uninterested in breaking in newcomers gently … Shovel Dance Collective.Photograph: Brad GilbertView image in fullscreenUninterested in breaking in newcomers gently … Shovel Dance Collective.Photograph: Brad GilbertAlexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewShovel Dance Collective: Everything in Readiness review – ecstatic, dissonant folk music fighting for sonic and spiritual freedom(tak:til)The nine-piece London-based group take a radically fresh approach to traditional music, sounding raging, lo-fi and joyful as they link Britain’s violent past to its presentAlexis PetridisThu 22 Oct 2026 07.43 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 14.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThose thus far unaware of Shovel Dance Collective’s bracing approach to folk should probably note that their third album is not much interested in breaking newcomers in gently. Everything in Readiness kicks off with a three-song suite that lasts more than 10 minutes and takes you, via a series of dramatic sonic jump-cuts, from a grinding one-note drone to a reel that seems to split the difference between trad folk fiddle-playing and the punishing squall of the Velvet Underground’s Black Angel’s Death Song. It then leaps to Tally Ho! Hark Away!, which sets a hunting song first collected in the late 1940s over a blast of what might best be described as ecstatic noise. It’s genuinely hard to work out what instruments are involved in the clattering arrhythmic chaos behind the vocal – there’s definitely a heavily distorted guitar in the mix – but the effect is weirdly euphoric rather than claustrophobic: a kind of purgative release after the mounting weirdness of the preceding reel.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Shovel Dance Collective’s Everything in Readiness.Photograph: PRIf you’re looking for evidence that the nine-piece London-based group take a radically fresh approach to folk music, then there it is. The glib shorthand is that they’re doing for traditional English music what Lankum have done for its Irish equivalent – joining the dots with the kind of out-there experimentation that fills the pages of the Wire magazine – although it should be pointed out they sound almost nothing like Lankum. Anyone who already has an interest in leftfield explorations of British musical history might suggest their chaotic collage approach feels more akin to the fascinating collections of field recordings, folk song and avant garde composition released by Todmorden-based label Folklore Tapes. The music on Everything in Readiness careens unpredictably from gentle lo-fi recordings caked in distortion and tape hiss to the tumultuous, surging racket they serve up on their version of the traditional coalminer’s song Jowl, Jowl and Listen; from singing unaccompanied by anything but the sound of birdsong to the disquieting ambient shimmer of Who Killed Cock Robin? A Summoning (Kind Morning in our Fists), which sounds like it was recorded in a vast, echoing crypt.It’s an experience that leaves you feeling faintly punch-drunk and disoriented. Everything in Readiness ultimately doesn’t sound like anything else around, but perhaps it’s not so surprising that a bunch of experimental musicians – various members also serve in post-rock band Caroline, improv trio Sullow and the deeply unpredictable Gentle Stranger – have embraced traditional music. English folk in particular has a tendency to slip its standard moorings at times of crisis and find musicians and an audience outside the usual clubs and festivals. The electric folk wave of Fairport Convention, Pentangle and Steeleye Span took root between 1968 and 1972 as the optimism of 60s counterculture curdled into the dark reality of the early 70s. The indie-folk movement that begat folktronica and the founding of Green Man festival, repurposed traditional music’s more sinister overtones, its eerie bleakness, for the twitchy, post-9/11 years.Shovel Dance Collective: Jer the Rigger/The Foxhunter’s Reel/Tally Ho! Hark Away! – videoIt’s an impulse you could view as a retreat into “the certainties of a historical music that spoke of a more stable past”, as Rob Young’s peerless history of “Britain’s visionary music” Electric Albion called it. Equally, given folk’s visceral bloodiness and bursts of political radicalism, it could be a search for connection, a reaffirmation that this country has always been turbulent, violent and deeply strange. Shovel Dance Collective, with their loudly trumpted leftwing politics and willingness to dig out contemporary resonances in material hundreds of years old, clearly fit the latter category. You could view the closing I Wish There Was No Prisons as the 19th-century equivalent of those anarchist stickers that have proliferated during the cost-of-living crisis (“if you saw someone shoplifting, you didn’t”), although their approach is clearest on Bold Captain Avery, a 1694 broadside that hymned the “King of Pirates” as a bold freedom fighter, “disowned” by his native country but having at the foreigners and “heathens” in the name of St George. The reality is that Avery was a monster driven by the accumulation of wealth, whose most famous raid – on the Ganj-i-Sawai, a ship en route to Mecca – descended into an orgy of violence that seemed to shock even his own men. It doesn’t take a genius to grasp why Shovel Dance Collective might have repurposed it for 2026.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘A guy held a knife to my throat and said: play something normal!’ Richard Thompson on crazy crowds, his beloved beret and Sandy Denny’s driving skillsRead moreIt’s intended as no shade on the band’s political leanings to suggest all this feels less important than the way their third album sounds: it’s there if you want to find it and that’s undoubtedly a good thing, but the most immediate pleasure of Everything in Readiness lies in the head-spinning sonic surprises it delivers. As it lurches wildly around, you find yourself struggling to keep up, a sure sign that you’re in the presence of music that feels entirely fresh and different. It makes songs that are centuries old feel messily, hectically alive.This week Alexis listened toDarren Hayman – Close Your Eyes and Face the SunThe latest of singer/songwriter Hayman’s idiosyncratic DIY projects involves making an album using only the once-ubiquitous, now outdated DX7 synth. Here, it (and he) sound fragile and lovely in equal measure.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekFolk musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Audacity review – cracking TV packed with even more gloriously awful people than Succession | Television | The Guardian
description: This Silicon Valley satire follows a CEO in trouble after the collapse of an acquisition deal. Created by Succession writer Jonathan Glatzer, each character is more hideous than the next – and it is stuffed with twists and treacheries
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: This Silicon Valley satire follows a CEO in trouble after the collapse of an acquisition deal. Created by Succession writer Jonathan Glatzer, each character is more hideous than the next – and it is stuffed with twists and treacheries
Content: ‘Will fill the Succession-shaped hole in your life’ … Billy Magnussen as Duncan Park in The Audacity.Photograph: Ed Araquel/AMCView image in fullscreen‘Will fill the Succession-shaped hole in your life’ … Billy Magnussen as Duncan Park in The Audacity.Photograph: Ed Araquel/AMCTV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Audacity review – cracking TV packed with even more gloriously awful people than SuccessionThis Silicon Valley satire follows a CEO in trouble after the collapse of an acquisition deal. Created by Succession writer Jonathan Glatzer, each character is more hideous than the next – and it is stuffed with twists and treacheriesLucy ManganThu 22 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat if Mike Judge’s cult hit sitcomSilicon Valleywere remade as a dramedy and we had in the meantime come to appreciate tech and its titans as existential threats to humanity, I hear you ask. Well, wonder no more – the answer is here, and it is The Audacity. It comes at you in hour-long episodes, which rush past at breakneck speed and leave you panting and deeply unsettled in their wake. Rather like modern life itself, of course, except for the relief available while the credits roll, before the next chunk of horrors arrives.‘The tech bro fight club is real!’ The titans of AI get the Succession treatment in a wild new TV showRead moreThe Audacity has a sprawling cast (especially in the opening episodes, which really are frenetic) but the figure around which most of the narratives move is Duncan Park (Billy Magnussen). He is the part-bullish, part-neurotic and wholly unbearable CEO of Hypergnosis, a data brokerage company he founded with a friend, who has since been struck by tragedy.Duncan, who has not absorbed the key point of the Silicon Valley maxim and spends his time moving fast and breaking hisownstuff, is in trouble. Hypergnosis was in acquisition talks with Cupertino (named after the location of Apple’s real-world headquarters and just possibly meant to evoke the behemoth) until Duncan leaked the news to boost his share price before the company valuation. That brought the deal to a screeching halt. He is now on the hunt for a play that will enable him to avoid the humiliation and (relative) poverty that will occur once word of the cancelled acquisition gets out.Duncan’s wife, Lili (Lucy Punch), and daughters are weary of and maddened by him, and his therapist JoAnne (Sarah Goldberg) even more so. She is almost as gloriously hateful a character as Duncan, and that is before he gets the goods on her with an eye to blackmail. This feels like the right time to note that The Audacity’s creator, Jonathan Glatzer, was one of the writers on the first two seasons of Succession, the show that made “gloriously hateful characters” an art form.View image in fullscreenMaddened by her husband … Lucy Punch as Lili in The Audacity.Photograph: Ed Araquel/AMCJoAnne is married to Gary (Paul Adelstein), a slightly more ethical member of the same profession, though in the Valley this still means a lot of time spent administering ADHD tests to students in the hope that a diagnosis will buy them extra time on tests, and other such small corruptions. She shares custody of her son, Orson (Everett Blunck), with her equally unlovely ex-husband, and although she uses Orson’s birthday as her computer password, it’s not the right date.Like most of the younger characters – including the Parks’ older daughter, Jamison (Ava Marie Telek), whose weight and academic results are ceaselessly monitored by her mother – Orson is a sweet child. Heartbreakingly resigned to his fate as an afterthought in his parents’ lives, he forms a growing friendship with Jamison’s little sister, embryonic kleptomaniac Tess (Thailey Roberge). The younger characters’ quiet endurance of, and resistance to, the chaos, greed and narcissism that surrounds them gives emotional heft to the show’s satirical thrust. Is gen z a reservoir of hope, or is youth just a brief period in everyone’s lives before the venality of the world – especially in its tech-aggravated modern iteration – gets to work? The bleakness of the latter gives us pause.View image in fullscreenPotent … Zach Galifianakis  as Carl with Magnussen in The Audacity.Photograph: Ed Araquel/ AMC/HBOAdd to the mix a potent turn from Zach Galifianakis as Carl Bardolph, another self-obsessed tech titan (worshipped for inventing “Bardolph’s Law”, a principle of infinite growth and profit “based on the logic of a cancer cell” that he once scribbled on a napkin while high); a genius coder called Harper (Jess McLeod), whose new algorithm may save Park or destroy the last vestiges of society; Rob Corddry as a rep for the Veterans’ Association, begging for a morsel of aid from billionaires; and about 700 supporting characters, twists, treacheries, good deals, bad deals and ayahuasca trips, with no clear way to distinguish what is satire and what is reportage – and you have The Audacity.Once you’ve calmed down – and in later episodes, as the show gains confidence, it does too – it will fill both the Succession and Silicon Valley (sitcom)-shaped holes in your life. Unlike Hypergnosis, that’s an acquisition worth making.In the UK and the US, The Audacity is on HBO Max now, and in Australia on SBS on DemandExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’d consider replacing one of my children’: Taika Waititi on robot kids, his cheese-o-meter and Klara and the Sun | Movies | The Guardian
description: The director has turned Kazuo Ishiguro’s acclaimed novel about an ailing adolescent and her glitchy robot friend into a thought-provoking film. What do the pair think this story says about tech, love and grief?
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: The director has turned Kazuo Ishiguro’s acclaimed novel about an ailing adolescent and her glitchy robot friend into a thought-provoking film. What do the pair think this story says about tech, love and grief?
Content: Misreading social cues, crashing the family car … Jenna Ortega as artificial friend Klara.Photograph: Sony Pictures EntertainmentView image in fullscreenMisreading social cues, crashing the family car … Jenna Ortega as artificial friend Klara.Photograph: Sony Pictures EntertainmentMoviesInterview‘I’d consider replacing one of my children’: Taika Waititi on robot kids, his cheese-o-meter and Klara and the SunXan BrooksThe director has turned Kazuo Ishiguro’s acclaimed novel about an ailing adolescent and her glitchy robot friend into a thought-provoking film. What do the pair think this story says about tech, love and grief?Thu 22 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 07.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the wings of the London film festival, a group of young influencers are discussing their personal highlights. Klara and the Sun, says one, and her colleagues agree. It’s not just that the film is still so fresh in their memory, or that they have gathered today to meet its creators and stars. Klara is funny and moving; it’s their festival favourite so far. I relay this exchange toTaika Waititi, the film’s director, who is sipping bottled water in a room down the hall. His gaze widens. He almost chokes. “Thank God!” he exclaims with just a bit too much heat.Everybody has a perfect film, just as everybody has a perfect friend, and they vary because everybody is different. In the film, sick 14-year-old Josie loves her discontinued robot doll Klara, whereas most kids her age opt for brighter, shinier models. And the young influencers love Klara and the Sun – Waititi’s adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s acclaimed novel – while mostolder critics vehemently, violently disagree. All of which shows that there’s no accounting for taste, that people are confounding, and that our hearts and our brains are not always in sync. That keeps life interesting. It’s partly what the film is about. “The emotions that we give very simple labels to are really complex,” says Ishiguro, who is seated alongside the director. “The thing we call love, for example, is incredibly noisy and multifaceted. Nobody knows what the hell love is.”double quotation markI can't make a Schindler's List. That's not in my wheelhouseFor what it’s worth, I loved Ishiguro’sdistinctively spare and poignant source noveland am less convinced by Waititi’s screen version, which is certainly noisy. Jenna Ortega stars as Klara, the perky solar-powered AI who plays soulmate to adolescent Josie (Mia Tharia), at a remote country house. She’s a warm splash of sunshine in an otherwise frosty environment, a fish out of water in a tragicomic sci-fi caper. But there is a glitch in the matrix; the component parts don’t align. Waititi adds sugar and caffeine, pratfalls and one-liners. Klara misreads social cues and steers the family car off the road. She fears she’ll be shipped back to the factory and melted down for scrap.View image in fullscreen‘In another version of this movie, Klara could be a murder-bot’ … Mia Tharia as Josie with Ortega as her artificial friend.Photograph: Matt Grace/Sony Pictures EntertainmentPerhaps the perfect friend is independent, self-directed. Ishiguro has seen several of his Nobel prize-winning books – The Remains of the Day, Never Let Me Go, A Pale View of Hills – adapted for the screen. He feels that the best films break away and that the worst are too faithful. “Sometimes it’s not just loyalty but laziness,” he says. “You can’t just have the text there in front of you. You need to use your imagination to move it on. A film needs to step forward, out of my book on a journey to being something bigger.”Waititi agrees. “Why would you do a cover of a song with exactly the same instrumentation? You make the film because you love the book. But you at least want to bring some original ideas to the table.”The book and the film are so different, it follows that their creators would be too. Ishiguro is sober, soft-spoken and writes delicate dramas about the deep mystery of life. Waititi is voluble, peacockish and makes uproarious films such as Jojo Rabbit, What We Do in the Shadows andHunt for the Wilderpeople. He tends to view the world through a comic lens. “Yeah, that’s my instinct. I can’t make a Schindler’s List, that’s not in my wheelhouse. I want to push everything towards comedy and then reel it back.”View image in fullscreenTragicomic sci-fi caper … Waititi and Ortega shooting the film.Photograph: Matt Grace/Sony Pictures EntertainmentIt’s a defence mechanism, he admits, part of his cultural DNA. “I’m from New Zealand,” he says. “In New Zealand, my friends and I always had a very sensitive cheese-o-meter. We thought the Americans loved cheese and saw sentimentality as a good thing. But of course that’s also me being scared of it. Now I think there’s a way of being more emotional and dramatic. Hopefully that’s a sign of me maturing.”Waititi’s work, though, has always carried a pleasing eddy of sadness. His 2010 feature Boy was a comedy about child abuse, while What We Do in the Shadows reframed the vampire as a lost, lonesome immigrant. Klara and the Sun is a love story but it’s also about isolation: the gap between people; the limits of understanding. “Oh, I’m definitely interested in loneliness,” he says.Ishiguro chips in. “Yeah, I think you’re right, there’s a crossover between our preoccupations,” he says. “But this isn’t just everyday loneliness, it’s something more fundamental. It’s about the human experience. There is part of each of us that remains alone. There is stuff that we all have to face alone. Not least death.”View image in fullscreenIshiguro … surprised to hear that Google Deepmind is a fan of his story.Photograph: Chris Pizzello/Invision/APThat’s the other big looming topic of Waititi’s film: death. Klara works as an “artificial friend” while other robots serve as “bereavement dolls”, filling in for lost spouses, siblings and children. That’s a sound business model, the director insists. “As a father with two kids, I always fear I’ll lose one. The younger me would have thought, ‘Oh, you can’t replace someone special.’ But the older I get, and the more in love with my kids I get, I think, ‘Oh, eventually I’d believe it was them.’ The human brain is easily adaptable. A therapist will tell you that you can programme anyone to fall in love. Tell someone you love them 50 times a day and in a few months your brain will give up and believe it. So I’d definitely consider replacing one of my children.” He laughs. “They don’t even have to be dead. I’d just like a version that’s nice to me and doesn’t ask for money.”Kazuo Ishiguro: ‘AI, gene-editing, big data ... I worry we are not in control of these things any more’Read moreIshiguro once joked that he essentially writes the same story in a variety of guises. He is drawn to flawed eyewitnesses and a partial view of events; groping narrators who try to make sense of their places in the world. The Remains of the Day’s rigid butler doesn’t know he’s in love, nor that the stately home where he works contains Nazis. Never Let Me Go’s hothoused schoolgirl finds out she is held captive and being used in terrible ways. Ishiguro’s books are unique but each connects to the world, and sometimes in ways he could not have foreseen. Klara and the Sun, for instance, was recently cited as a potential handbook for the development of generative AI. Tom Lue, VP of global affairs at Google Deepmind, suggested it be used as an “ethical touchstone”, the centrepiece of a “human-centred” approach to the future of frontier AI.So the book has been co-opted. It has taken on another fresh life of its own. Waititi turns to the author. “It’s all your fault,” he says. “That’s incredible,” says Ishiguro. It’s the first he’s heard of it. “I know a lot of people within the AI industry are worried about its impact on society. It’s got to the point where they feel the need for a handbrake. So they are surprisingly keen to talk to creative people and road-test various ideas and scenarios.” He frowns. “But here I do become protective of both the book and the film. Because our story really isn’t about all that. If someone is trying to figure out the ethics of AI and where we should all be going, I’m not sure they’d be well-guided by this story. There are other, better places to go.”Waititi pipes up. “The Terminator’s a good one.”Klara has been built with a sweet, simple purpose: to provide friendship and support. But the human world is hazardous, unstable, which means she has to update her files and adapt her approach. Waititi’s film veers and darkens, riffing off its downbeat source novel, finally closing in towards death. “There’s another version of this story where Klara would turn into a murder-bot,” he points out.Robot dolls fill a need, plug a gap and ideally make life better. But artificial friends, by their nature, are replaceable too. In the press room next door, the influencers are still comparing notes, killing time between interviews. Klara and the Sun is receding; the conversation has already moved on. One says: “You have to see La Bola Negra. It’s my film of the year.”Klara and the Sun is in cinemas from 22 October in Australia, and 23 October in the UK and USExplore more on these topicsFilmTaika WaititiScience fiction and fantasy filmsAI (artificial intelligence)Kazuo IshiguroFilm adaptationsComputinginterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Nobody Wants This review – prepare to fall in love again … with a different couple | Television | The Guardian
description: Adam Brody and Kristen Bell’s hit romcom is still gorgeous as Noah and Joanne move in together. But if you’re thirsty for the fizz of new romance … their siblings might set hearts aflutter
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: Adam Brody and Kristen Bell’s hit romcom is still gorgeous as Noah and Joanne move in together. But if you’re thirsty for the fizz of new romance … their siblings might set hearts aflutter
Content: Phenomenal screen sparkle … Joanne (Kristen Bell) and Noah (Adam Brody) in Nobody Wants This.Photograph: Katrina Marcinowski/NetflixView image in fullscreenPhenomenal screen sparkle … Joanne (Kristen Bell) and Noah (Adam Brody) in Nobody Wants This.Photograph: Katrina Marcinowski/NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewNobody Wants This review – prepare to fall in love again … with a different coupleAdam Brody and Kristen Bell’s hit romcom is still gorgeous as Noah and Joanne move in together. But if you’re thirsty for the fizz of new romance … their siblings might set hearts aflutterJack SealeThu 22 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 08.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJust as you and your true love can’t have a second first date or another first kiss, romantic comedies can never go back. Nothing replaces the giddy spell of the movie’s opening act or the TV show’s debut season. Sure, there can be some joy and fulfilment in a fictional relationship settling down, but really we want the crackle of chemistry, the thrill of a connection that’s brand new.Nobody Wants This is now in its third season, so it has had to leave behind the days when it was powered entirely by the phenomenal screen sparkle between Adam Brody as Noah, the rabbi who can balance devotion to his faith with the mischievous instincts of a regular thirtysomething guy; and Kristen Bell as Joanne, the atheist co-host of a frank sex-and-relationships podcast who is not as cynical or shallow as people think, or as she pretends to be.Season one flew past in a whirl of meet-cute, kiss-cute, date-cute and continue-their-romance-despite-supposedly-unresolvable-cultural-divide-cute. While Brody and Bell traded pinging screwball one-liners as fluently as any screen couple ever have, the question of whether Noah’s place within his synagogue and his family could ever be compatible with his love for a woman outside the community gave the story weight. If he and Joanne were destined not to be together, it would be for reasons more substantial than the usual romcom misunderstandings.The second season leaned into what had become an unusually deep and nuanced portrayal of what it means to be a Jewish American in the 21st century, with the ongoing tension around whether Joanne would convert to Judaism enabling Nobody Wants This to repeat the trick of them splitting up during the final episode, then reconciling in a last scene where one or both of them sprints through the rain to say they made a mistake. It certainly can’t get away with that a third time.View image in fullscreenWill they or won’t they? … Morgan (Justine Lupe) and Sasha (Timothy Simons) in Nobody Wants This.Photograph: NetflixSo we rejoin Noah and Joanne as they move in together, opening with a gorgeous montage of them exclaiming “We live together!” in mundane domestic situations that have acquired new magic. The relationship comedy sinks into a comfortable rhythm, as Noah is destabilised by Joanne leaving the fridge door open and turning the dishwasher into a treacherous hellscape of upturned knife blades, while she chafes against his desire to take her for a dawn stroll, instead of respecting the ancient, sacred morning ritual of drinking coffee and checking celebrity gossip online.The stakes are lower and the old fizz has somewhat fizzled: the next step for a couple is usually marriage, which does bring its own difficult sensitivities, but nothing to compare to what Noah and Joanne have already overcome. One or two episodes in the middle of season three don’t really contain a significant event, and the new milieu Joanne is pitched into, as she attends classes at temple to educate non-Jews who are about to marry into the faith, is funny without bringing much edge.However, Nobody Wants This in safe mode still delights. The ensemble around the central couple stop it being a problem if nothing much is going on with them: we can just hang out with their parents, whose cartoon eccentricity still has plenty of comic juice in it, and particularly their siblings.If Brody and Bell are a classic romcom couple, Timothy Simons and Justine Lupe are arguably even better as Sasha (Noah’s brother) and Morgan (Joanne’s sister), – whose radically different personalities highlight the gap the central relationship has to overcome, but who share outsider status, which gives them something in common, which draws them together …Simons and Lupe have long been the show’s real stars as gangling manchild Sasha and self-absorbed fashionista Morgan, each ill-equipped for the adult world in their own way. Up to now Morgan has been a spectre haunting the jagged marriage of Sasha and Esther (Jackie Tohn), a couple who disagree fundamentally on how seriously to take life. Morgan’s dedication to consequence-free fun is a temptation Sasha cannot resist, while his refusal to judge her life choices and his total lack of preening self-regard, in contrast to the men Morgan normally picks, makes him a safe place for her to run towards.Season three finally sees Sasha and Esther split, which leaves more time for his tender bond with Morgan to become a proper will-they-won’t-they. Suddenly our heads are spinning and our hearts have resumed their fluttering. It may have put down roots, but Nobody Wants This knows how to make us fall in love with it all over again.Nobody Wants This is on Netflix now.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewTV comedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Black Bag by Luke Kennard audiobook review – brilliant Booker-shortlisted campus comedy | Books | The Guardian
description: The author reveals his mastery of comic timing in his narration of this novel about a cash-strapped actor paid to live inside a black leather bag
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: The author reveals his mastery of comic timing in his narration of this novel about a cash-strapped actor paid to live inside a black leather bag
Content: Sober reflections … Luke Kennard.Photograph: David Levenson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSober reflections … Luke Kennard.Photograph: David Levenson/Getty ImagesAudiobook of the weekBooksReviewBlack Bag by Luke Kennard audiobook review – brilliant Booker-shortlisted campus comedyThe author reveals his mastery of comic timing in his narration of this novel about a cash-strapped actor paid to live inside a black leather bagFiona SturgesThu 22 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe unnamed narrator of Luke Kennard’s novel is an out-of-work actor living in London. His last job was three months ago, he is behind with his rent and has “measured out my life in coffees I cannot technically afford”. So when he comes across an advert – “Male actor required for psychological enquiry. Non-speaking but discretion and devotion to restrictive performance requirements obligatory” – he offers his services.The job, he discovers, is at a university working under a psychology professor named Dr Blend. There he must strip to his underpants and zip himself into a black leather bag, in which there are two eyeholes and further holes for his feet. The actor is expected to sit silently in the bag during seminars while students contemplate his presence.The inspiration for Kennard’s Booker-shortlisted campus comedy is a 1967 social experiment, conducted at Oregon State University, where a student attended classes inside a black bag in a test to see whether other students would grow attached to his presence. It also nods to Yoko Ono’s 1964 conceptual artwork Bag Piece, in which gallery-goers were asked to climb inside a large black bag.Kennard, who is the reader, mines this surreal conceit for laughs as the protagonist does battle with revolving doors and tries to pay for coffee using a card taped to the inside of the bag at chest height. As with his prose, the author’s delivery reveals him as a master of comic timing and a mordantbon mot. Yet beneath Black Bag’s winningly oddball exterior are more sober reflections on human relationships and what it is to be a man.Available via John Murray, 9hr 12minFurther listeningBattle Axe: A MemoirMargaret Hodge, William Collins, 14hr 43minThe veteran Labour politician narrates her book detailing 50 years in frontline politics, from her early career as a leader of Islington council to her time as an MP during the Tony Blair and Gordon Brown premierships and her recent work as the UK’s anti-corruption champion.I Shoot Rock StarsTim Pope, Wildfire, 10hr 6minPope, a music video director, recalls wild moments with musicians of yore, from the time he dressed Freddie Mercury as a “giant Mediterranean prawn” to filming the Cure performing inside a wardrobe. Read by the author.Explore more on these topicsBooksAudiobook of the weekFictionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Bournemouth Symphony Orchestra / Wigglesworth review – phrasing with hospital corners | Classical music | The Guardian
description: BSO’s concert with their chief conductor Mark Wigglesworth mixed Tippett, Vaughan Williams, Adès and Sibelius. Best of all was the Tippett, and the Sibelius 5 had personality to burn
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: BSO’s concert with their chief conductor Mark Wigglesworth mixed Tippett, Vaughan Williams, Adès and Sibelius. Best of all was the Tippett, and the Sibelius 5 had personality to burn
Content: Detailed and sensitive conducting: Mark Wigglesworth with BSO at the Lighthouse, Poole.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreenDetailed and sensitive conducting: Mark Wigglesworth with BSO at the Lighthouse, Poole.Photograph: Mark AllanClassical musicReviewBournemouth Symphony Orchestra / Wigglesworth review – phrasing with hospital cornersLighthouse, PooleBSO’s concert with their chief conductor Mark Wigglesworth mixed Tippett, Vaughan Williams, Adès and Sibelius. Best of all was the Tippett, and the Sibelius 5 had personality to burnFlora WillsonThu 22 Oct 2026 09.26 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn paper, it was a curious programme: Tippett’s Concerto for Double String Orchestra and Vaughan Williams’s The Lark Ascending, followed post-interval byAdès’s Märchentänze and Sibelius’s Fifth Symphony. A calculated mix of more and less familiar works, certainly – but an otherwise unlikely foursome. The common preoccupations with folk music (threaded jauntily through the Tippett and the Adès) and the natural world (VW’s lark, Sibelius’s swans) only take us so far. In practice, the Bournemouth Symphony Orchestra’s performance under its chief conductorMark Wigglesworthrevealed a shared creative tussle with existing musical forms and with finding new means of expression without breaking entirely with the old ways.The Lark Ascending thus abandoned the Smooth Classics at Seven-mode for a covered, sometimes icy sound in the BSO’s world-class strings and a more risk-taking, more improvisatory approach from soloistAnthony Marwood. The tone of his Stradivarius was expensively sweet and his cool, no-vibrato opening compelling, though his performance was marred by intonation problems. Marwood fared better in Adès’s Märchentänze, which reworks folk tunes with unexpected timbral combinations and harmonies, and where the solo line tangles deliciously with the orchestra’s violins. But this work, written for theultra-charismatic violinist Pekka Kuusisto, was rather less interesting without such a compelling soloist.By contrast,Sibelius’s Symphony No 5had personality to burn in a performance that front-loaded its modernist strangeness. There were shadowy wind solos, creepy string tremolos and double basses that lurched nastily instead of settling comfortably into the finale’s swan business. There were also tuning difficulties in the wind and the BSO’s trombones were almost comically direct from where I was sitting. But Wigglesworth’s detailed, sensitive conducting came into its own in the work’s transitional passages, as he eased the weight out of dense textures and managed the journey to the symphony’s climax as a slowly, inexorably cresting wave.Best of all was the Tippett. Wigglesworth’s tempi were unhurried, even laid-back. Yet there was an angular neatness to Tippett’s neoclassical lines – this was phrasing with hospital corners – and the string sound was subtly malleable: from a striking, frosted tone in the first movement to the generous warmth that spread euphorically through the finale.The concert will be broadcast on BBC Radio 3 on 2 November.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Bartók: Miraculous Mandarin Suite, The Wooden Prince album review – vivid colours and astute pacing | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Edward Gardner and the LPO are taut and dramatically alert in fine performances of these two theatrical works
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Edward Gardner and the LPO are taut and dramatically alert in fine performances of these two theatrical works
Content: Revelling in a nature-inflected score  … Edward Gardner.Photograph: Chris Lobina/SkyView image in fullscreenRevelling in a nature-inflected score  … Edward Gardner.Photograph: Chris Lobina/SkyClassical musicReviewBartók: Miraculous Mandarin Suite, The Wooden Prince album review – vivid colours and astute pacingLondon Philharmonic Orchestra/Gardner(LPO)Edward Gardner andthe LPO are taut and dramatically alert in fine performances of these two theatrical worksClive PagetThu 22 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 09.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRecordings of The Miraculous Mandarin used to outnumber The Wooden Prince 10 to one, so it’s good to see Bartók’s earlier ballet getting equal billing here. Unlike the Mandarin with its grimy, urban, modernist vibe, the Prince is rooted in pungent Hungarian folk music, viewed, of course, through the composer’s unique 20th-century lens.View image in fullscreenLPO/Gardner: Bartók: The Miraculous Mandarin Suite and The Wooden Prince.It’s the story of a princess who falls in love with a decoy prince rather than the real thing and Edward Gardner revels in the vivid colours of its nature-inflected score. The London Philharmonic Orchestra is taut and dramatically alert throughout. There’s an unnerving sense of foreboding underpinning the Dance of the Trees; the Dance of the Waves churns with kinetic energy and the foot-stamping Dance of the Princess with the Wooden Doll cuts a rustic dash.The live recording is less clinical than Boulez’s crystalline 1991 studio performance (still essential listening), but Gardner’s astute pacing is more theatrically involving than recent accounts by Cristian Măcelaru or Susanna Mälkki.As for The Miraculous Mandarin Suite, this is as fine a performance as any, sleek and sinister in its evocation of the honeytrap antics of the sex worker and her thuggish pimps, swaggering or shy in her encounters with the old rake and the young man, and prickling with jagged pentatonic scales once the mandarin arrives on the scene. To open, Gardner paints a brutal portrait of the dystopian city with its honking car horns and concludes with a raw-nerved depiction of the desperate final chase.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com.
