title: Zadie Smith among authors letting public bid to name new characters for charity auction | Human rights | The Guardian
description: Other prizes at Freedom from Torture event include rare Mary Wollstonecraft book illustrated by William Blake
Author: Aamna Mohdin
Headline: Other prizes at Freedom from Torture event include rare Mary Wollstonecraft book illustrated by William Blake
Content: Zadie Smith, seen here in 2023, is one of several high-profile writers involved in the literary festival.Photograph: David Levenson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenZadie Smith, seen here in 2023, is one of several high-profile writers involved in the literary festival.Photograph: David Levenson/Getty ImagesHuman rightsZadie Smith among authors letting public bid to name new characters for charity auctionOther prizes at Freedom from Torture event include rare Mary Wollstonecraft book illustrated by William BlakeAamna MohdinCommunity affairs correspondentThu 22 Oct 2026 11.13 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMargaret Atwood, Zadie Smith and Ian McEwan are among a number of literary stars auctioning off the chance for readers to name characters in their next novels to raise money for survivors of torture.The auction is part of Freedom from Torture’s 10th anniversary literary festival, which brings together leading authors and survivors for a celebration of storytelling, featuring a poetry competition and live readings at the London Library on 11 November.More than 75 authors, poets, artists and illustrators are supporting the festival, with other prizes including original artwork by Quentin Blake, a rare book of Mary Wollstonecraft stories illustrated by William Blake, and a book club visit from the author Louise Doughty.A bookmark raffle will feature more than 30 original designs by authors, each paired with a signed copy of the book that inspired it. Contributors include David Nicholls, Mark Haddon, Felicity Cloake, Nathan Filer, Nikesh Shukla, Sathnam Sanghera and Jeremy Vine.The festival also features a poetry competition centred on the experiences of torture survivors, judged by the Booker prize-winning novelist Alan Hollinghurst and the poet Rachael Allen.It comes amid growing concern over asylum policies in Britain and across Europe, with the charity warning that changes to legal protections could put torture survivors at risk of being returned to the countries they fled.View image in fullscreenTracy Chevalier has taken part in several character-naming auctions.Samuel Morton, the special events and philanthropy manager at Freedom from Torture, said that the festival is inspired by their creative writing group, Write to Life, which is the UK’s longest-running refugee writers group, and believed to be the only one in the world for survivors of torture.“They meet weekly and put pen to paper, and it’s a brilliant way to support each other and to process the things that they’ve been through in their trauma, as well as their hopes for the future.”Four members from Write to Life will perform their own work at the London Library alongside acclaimed writers including Max Porter and the poet John Hegley.Tracy Chevalier, the bestselling author of Girl with a Pearl Earring and The Last Runaway, is another of the authors joining the auction. She has supported the charity’s literary auctions since 2006, but admitted she was initially nervous about letting strangers name her characters.“Names are important to me in my books,” Chevalier said. “What I choose to call a character, who I’m going to live with in my head for the next few years, they need to mean something to me.”To her delight, her first winning bidder was Laura Devine, whose name she gave to a circus performer in her novel Burning Bright. The pair have remained friends ever since.Chevalier has taken part in three more character-naming auctions, including one that saw her turn the name Dody Bienenstock into a “no-nonsense landlady” in San Francisco. She also praised the festival for giving survivors the opportunity to share their experiences in their own words.Iranian singer’s 74 lashes for performing without a hijab ‘a form of torture’, say rights groupsRead more“The story of your life is inside of you and for a lot of people it’s not great,” she said.“They’ve had really terrible experiences and that pressure builds and to not only let it out, but control how you let it out. [To say] this is my story and I’m going to tell it. I’m not going to have a journalist tell it for me or a famous writer. I’m speaking.“And the incredible power of that, of writing it down, so that it gets out of you and on to the page, and then you can shape it and do with it what you will, or throw it away if you want.”Chevalier said many authors were drawn to the cause by concerns over the worsening treatment of asylum seekers in Britain. “I’m an immigrant myself, but nobody’s ever questioned my right to be here. And that’s because I’m white and American,” she said.Morton criticised thegovernment’s proposals to weaken the appeals systemand raised concerns over the growing appetite across Europe to weaken legal safeguards, such as Article 3 of the European convention on human rights.“Poor-quality asylum decisions risk sending survivors back into the hands of their torturers,” Morton said. “These protections are fundamental and must not be weakened for political convenience.”Explore more on these topicsHuman rightsZadie SmithMargaret AtwoodIan McEwanTorturenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Jane Austen is for everyone’: novelist Diana Reid on adapting Sense and Sensibility – and surprising Brits with her accent | Jane Austen | The Guardian
description: The Australian author of Love and Virtue says her nationality didn’t give her pause when she wrote the script, but Ang Lee’s ‘perfect’ 1995 film did
Author: Katie Cunningham
Headline: The Australian author of Love and Virtue says her nationality didn’t give her pause when she wrote the script, but Ang Lee’s ‘perfect’ 1995 film did
Content: Diana Reid: ‘I love the 1995 film, and my initial instinct was that there was a reason it hadn’t been [adapted] for 30 years.’Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDiana Reid: ‘I love the 1995 film, and my initial instinct was that there was a reason it hadn’t been [adapted] for 30 years.’Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianJane Austen‘Jane Austen is for everyone’: novelist Diana Reid on adapting Sense and Sensibility – and surprising Brits with her accentThe Australian author of Love and Virtue says her nationality didn’t give her pause when she wrote the script, but Ang Lee’s ‘perfect’ 1995 film didKatie CunninghamThu 22 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 19.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe summer Diana Reid spent writing her film adaptation ofSense and Sensibility, she found herself having some oddly formal conversations down at the pub. The Australian author used only about 25 lines from Jane Austen’s first published novel for her screenplay, inventing most of the dialogue herself. To be able to mimic that very distinctive voice, Reid had to dive headfirst into studying Austen’s rhythm and sentence structure.“I got so immersed in the language it infected my own speech. I would be describing someone I just met, and I’d be like, ‘Oh, he was most amiable!’” Reid says, laughing. “It was a kind of insanity.”Until now, Reid has been best known as the novelist behind bestsellers such as 2021’sLove and Virtueand 2025’sSigns of Damage, which are set among the university campuses and Euro holiday destinations of the modern world. Adapting a book published in 1811, then, was a very different job – but one that became oddly freeing.“So much of writing contemporary dialogue is trying to make it sound believable, which often involves making people inarticulate,” Reid says. “Writing this, I got to sit at my computer and be like, ‘What is the most elegant way this sentiment could possibly be expressed?’ … It was actually a joy.”Reid is speaking to me via Zoom from a chandelier-clad hotel room in Santa Fe, New Mexico, where she has been flown to promote the film (one of the perks of screenwriting is that the film industry has much “deeper pockets” than publishing, she says).Her adaptation, directed by Georgia Oakley and released in Australia and the US this month, retells the story of Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, who are forced out of the landed gentry and into more precarious financial circumstances after the death of their father. Elinor falls for Edward Ferrars, a man who can’t seem to articulate his obvious reciprocal feelings for her, and Marianne is soon swept off her feet by the roguishly charming John Willoughby – but neither romance is what it first seems.View image in fullscreenEsmé Creed-Miles (left) and Daisy Edgar-Jones in Sense and Sensibility.Photograph: Courtesy of Focus Features/APReid and producer India Flint pitched the idea of a new adaptation because they wanted to tackle something by Austen, who Reid loves and considers a “genius”.Pride and Prejudice had been very successfully remade in 2005andEmma more recently in 2020– but the Dashwood sisters hadn’t been revisited on film in 30 years, when Ang Lee delivered his beloved 1995 take on the tale.The Oscar-winning screenplay for that adaptation was penned by Emma Thompson, who also played Elinor. Unlike that thoroughly British star, Reid’s Australian accent has been tripping up some British fans and media.“In recent weeks it’s almost felt like in Britain, perhaps [Austen] is viewed as a piece of cultural inheritance and that there are worthy and unworthy successors – and it seems striking or hubristic that an Australian would think themselves worthy,” Reid says. “But I never thought ofJane Austenas a possession. I just thought that she was something for anyone who was interested … if you don’t think of her as a possession, then it doesn’t occur to you to worry about whether it’s your right to receive it.”Whatdidgive Reid pause, though, was how high a bar Ang Lee’s adaptation set.View image in fullscreenEmma Thompson and Kate Winslet in Ang Lee’s Oscar-winning 1995 adaptation.Photograph: AJ Pics/Alamy“I love the 1995 film, and my initial instinct was that there was a reason it hadn’t been [adapted] for 30 years, and that was because the 1995 film was perfect,” Reid says. “But then I read the book and I rewatched the movie, and I felt that I did find something to say that I didn’t think had been said on screen before.”Reid believes the main love story of Sense and Sensibility isn’t between Elinor and Edward or Marianne and Willoughby (or Colonel Brandon), but between the two sisters themselves – one logical and level-headed, the other utterly free-spirited.Sense and Sensibility review – Daisy Edgar-Jones leads sober-minded next-gen do-over of Austen romcomRead more“The spine of the story was about how these two women depend on each other, challenge each other and ultimately change each other,” Reid says. “And while there are romances in it, it’s almost as if the men are the rewards that the two women get for having gone on this journey of growth together.”So in structuring the script, Reid tried to approach it almost as a romantic comedy but with the story arc plotted along tension between the sisters, not two love interests: the film’s climax comes when Elinor and Marianne are at odds, and their happy ending requires each to adapt qualities from the other. “Which is a very typical romcom structure,” Reid says.View image in fullscreenReid says Austen’s work possesses ‘a generosity about the possibility of love’ that is both romantic and timeless – and why it’s perennially reinvented.Photograph: Alex Bailey/Focus Features/APPurists will be pleased to hear that Reid’s adaptation is a fairly faithful one –Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heightsthis is not. But she did make some tweaks to the romantic fate of the younger Dashwood sister, feeling that Austen’s original ending wouldn’t sit well with modern audiences, who “respect what Marianne represents” – a bold, headstrong woman who goes for what she wants in life and accepts no substitutes.Instead of “scene after scene of women sitting down in the parlour drinking tea, as Austen can sometimes feel”, she and Oakley opted to depict the Dashwood sisters cooking, chopping firewood and tending the veggie patch. Aesthetically, the film feels far drearier than the 1995 film, too, as the typical aestheticisation of Austen’s work – “very floral and bonnets; cosy, comfy escapism” – didn’t sit right with Reid, who considers her work very dark and imbued with an often cruel sense of humour.What hasn’t changed is the heart of Sense and Sensibility. As Reid sees it, Austen’s work possesses “a generosity about the possibility of love” that is both romantic and timeless – and why it’s perennially reinvented.“I don’t feel like Austen is, like, my cultural property now as a result of having written it,” Reid says. “I just feel like it is this thing that’s endlessly adaptable – there’s probably someone else doing their Sense and Sensibility adaptation right now. It is for everyone, and it’s still for everyone.”Sense and Sensibility is in cinemas now in the UK, Australia and the USExplore more on these topicsJane AustenFilm adaptationsRomance filmsDrama filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort review – Wii Sports lives on in this effortlessly appealing collection of games | Games | The Guardian
description: Bringing a holiday vibe and a generous selection of sport-themed games, this is exactly what you want from a family video game
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: Bringing a holiday vibe and a generous selection of sport-themed games, this is exactly what you want from a family video game
Content: Guaranteed strike … Nintendo Switch Sports Resort.Photograph: NintendoView image in fullscreenGuaranteed strike … Nintendo Switch Sports Resort.Photograph: NintendoGamesReviewNintendo Switch Sports Resort review – Wii Sports lives on in this effortlessly appealing collection of gamesNintendo Switch 2; Nintendo/NintendoBringing a holiday vibe and a generous selection of sport-themed games, this is exactly what you want from a family video gameKeza MacDonaldThu 22 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 07.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the first Nintendo Switch Sports brought the effortless fun of Wii Sports back into my living room in 2022, I wasfrankly delighted. My small children discovered the pleasure of waving a controller around in enthusiastic imitation of a tennis player, and the surprising subtlety of virtual bowling, working out how to twist the wrist just right to guarantee a strike. I did not expect this game to become a family fixture for the next several years as my kids got older and climbed up the online ranks in all six of its sports (plus the two that were added as free updates). Switch Sports is so beloved in my household that the release of Switch Sports Resort this week is the most anticipated gaming event of the year. To be fair, my children are a bit young for Grand Theft Auto.Nintendo Switch Sports Resort brings three of the six sports back – tennis, bowling, and volleyball – alongside golf and basketball. Then there are seven entirely new sports: boxing, table tennis, archery, thumb wrestling, skateboarding, jetski, and piloting a little prop plane. They are all intuitive, easy to get the hang of on the first or second attempt – some have more legs than others, in the long run – and all of them, crucially, are a little bit silly. Thumb wrestling in particular is cheerfully absurd, giving your characters gigantic thumbs on hands the size of their heads.View image in fullscreen‘One two three four let’s have a thumb war’ … Nintendo Switch Sports ResortPhotograph: NintendoEvery sport here is fun. In skateboarding you use the controller like a mouse, pulling it towards you to propel yourself forwards on the board and tilting it to steer through surprisingly challenging courses, lifting it into the air to jump and spin for tricks. Archery is perfectly intuitive, boxing enjoyably frenetic (especially when played with a seven-year-old), table tennis energisingly competitive, letting you spin and smash the ball with nuanced wrist movement. Almost all of these sports work exactly as you’d expect, with the exception of basketball, whose real-world speed and flashiness are replaced here with methodical turn-taking.Touring the resort on a jetski or in a plane is more peaceful, reminiscent of Wave Race and Pilotwings, two long-dormant Nintendo series whose DNA is clearly evident in the Wii Sports lineage. On the jetskis, you can follow pink dolphins leaping through the waves. As you pass over the island’s stadiums, cafes and beaches in the plane you will see that they are busy with tiny people, watching a match or lazing on the sand. When you’re skating or soaring around you realise just how big and lively it actually is.This gloriously unnecessary attention to detail gives this collection of sports games a sense of place and a holiday atmosphere that’s irresistibly appealing. The music is a sunny as the setting, full of guaranteed earworms. I spent a bunch of time dressing up my little character in outfits that you win by ranking up in the island leagues for each sport, a welcome addition that gives some structure to playing by yourself when you aren’t handing controllers around to friends and family. Variants on every sport also up the longevity: obstacle courses in bowling, for instance, or a three-pointer shooting contest in basketball.After a week of daily play, it has become clear that Switch Sports Resort will not be going back on the digital shelf for some time yet. It is perfect for a Saturday afternoon with friends, but it also has enough going on beneath the surface to sustain the long-term attentions of an enthusiastic child. In other words, it is exactly what you want from a family video game – and as a bonus, it gets everyone off the sofa.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNintendo Switch Sports Resort is out, 22 October; £41.99/$49.99/€49.99Explore more on these topicsGamesNintendo Switch 2NintendoreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The joy of strap-ons, Sherman’s plump pearls and a hypnotic apocalypse: five free exhibitions to see | Art | The Guardian
description: An inflatable Lady Godiva is just one of the thrills in a Pia Camil’s ode to lust. But why is Mark Leckey feeling so doomy and Cindy Sherman so bougie?
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: An inflatable Lady Godiva is just one of the thrills in a Pia Camil’s ode to lust. But why is Mark Leckey feeling so doomy and Cindy Sherman so bougie?
Content: Pump it up … the inflatable Lady Godiva in Pia Camil’s liberating Bestia show.Photograph: Elizabeth Xi Bauer, 2026. Photograph: Richard Ivey. Courtesy of the Artist and Elizabeth Xi Bauer, London.View image in fullscreenPump it up … the inflatable Lady Godiva in Pia Camil’s liberating Bestia show.Photograph: Elizabeth Xi Bauer, 2026. Photograph: Richard Ivey. Courtesy of the Artist and Elizabeth Xi Bauer, London.Eddy Frankel's gallery crawlArtThe joy of strap-ons, Sherman’s plump pearls and a hypnotic apocalypse: five free exhibitions to seeAn inflatable Lady Godiva is just one of the thrills in a Pia Camil’s ode to lust. But why is Mark Leckey feeling so doomy and Cindy Sherman so bougie?Eddy FrankelThu 22 Oct 2026 07.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 07.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePia Camil: Bestia★★★★☆All sorts of secret, shocking things happen behind closed doors, but they probably pale in comparison to what’s happening behind the saloon-style screens in Mexican artist Pia Camil’s debut UK exhibition. Swing them open and you’re greeted with eye-popping paintings of lust and sexual freedom. A demonic, fanged creature humps away at a blindfolded woman in one, a blue-skinned being with a curly little pig’s tail performs cunnilingus on another. Everywhere you look there are bodies writhing in ecstasy, hair being pulled, stilettos being pressed into bare skin. Most of the time when you see sexual art these days it carries a big political message about exploitation and abuse, but this is the opposite: this is about the joy of sex, about liberation through desire, about a feminist reclamation of eroticism. In the middle of the room, a huge inflatable sculpture of Lady Godiva inflates and deflates, rises and falls, over and over.The whole show is like all your favourite erotic surrealists put through a Mexican art filter. It’s shocking art, not because of the strap-ons and genitalia, but because it’s so rare to see a painter this fun, an artist so obviously and totally devoted to pleasure, hedonism and joy.Elizabeth Xi Bauer, until 22 NovemberMark Leckey: The Last Leg of the Final Eschaton★★★★☆View image in fullscreenPretty mesmerising … Mark Leckey: The Last Leg of the Final Eschaton at St Chads.Photograph: Mark LeckeyThe end is nigh in Mark Leckey’s latest video work. The influential English conceptualist has gone all apocalyptic, with a wild found-footage video that draws parallels between medieval cultists, 60s hippy freak-out gigs and millennial raves. It all starts with a renaissance painting by Uccello, which sends Leckey’s brain tripping across doom-mongering conspiracy theories, biblical prophecies and stock market crashes. It’s freeform and weird, almost unfollowable, but also pretty mesmerising. The film is unfinished, and it’s housed in a barren gallery in an abandoned former hospital, but this is exactly what you want from this kind of project space: challenging, strange, totally uncompromising and blatantly uncommercial art. These kinds of places give room for art and ideas to bloom and evolve, and are becoming rarer and rarer. The shows here are by appointment only – you message them through their Instagram – but you have to take advantage of experimental art spaces while they’re still around. Doom and gloom never felt so hypnotic.St Chads Projects, until 28 NovemberMarcin Dudek: Pawilon★★★★☆View image in fullscreenDystopian abstraction … Marcin Dudek, Pawilon, installation view Edel Assanti.Photograph: Tom Carter Photography LtdMarcin Dudek has become an archaeologist of the self, digging through his past, his memories, trying to figure out how it all came to this.His work has always been largely based on the Polish housing estate he grew up in: the basement gyms and football violence that marked his childhood and youth. But this show takes us into something a little more mundane: the local supermarket. He has recreated its metal walls here, rusted and filthy, a dead mouse petrified against the corrugated steel. Inside, he has laid out bottle caps, stones and torn cigarette packets excavated from outside the shop itself. Proper archaeological stuff, but useless, worthless, and meaningless except to him.The metal collages on the wall are covered in burn marks and images of crowds and police vans. In the communist 1980s, the supermarket was a hub, a sanctuary. But by 1989, capitalism had arrived, bringing with it abundance – and crime.Dudek’s whole look is dystopian abstraction, taking all the wreckage of his past and reassembling it into fractured grey images and threatening installations. All the rusted and twisted metal here is full of anger and incomprehension, but you get the sense that if he keeps digging, keeps uncovering and excavating the past, it might eventually start making sense.Edel Assanti, until 12 DecemberCindy Sherman★★☆☆☆View image in fullscreenAhead of the curve … Cindy Sherman, Untitled #710.Photograph: Cindy ShermanCindy Sherman has always been way ahead of the curve. Her photographic playacting has seen her dealing with ideas of identity, fiction and reality for decades, way before every young artist with an internet connection started doing the same thing. She’s brilliant, influential and important.And this new exhibition is more of what you’ve come to expect from her. This time, her characters are lounging, they are draped over sofas, reclining in bed. These are wealthy, elderly, powerful women in moments of repose. They all wear extravagant undulating fabrics, their wrists and necks weighed down with the thickest gold chains, the plumpest pearls.How do the rich construct their identities? How do once-young, once-beautiful women continue to project their importance and vivacity into old age?It feels like a bit of an in-joke, as if she’s taking aim at the kind of people who can afford to buy her work. I don’t mind that: it’s neatly ironic watching ladies with expensive facelifts staring right into these works as they walk around the gallery, unaware that Sherman is holding up a mirror.They are neurotic, vulnerable ruminations on ageing. But they’re not Sherman’s best work, not by a long shot. What makes it uncomfortable though is that it was all made at Chanel’s invitation, and a lot of the jewels and clothing the characters are wearing come from the fashion house’s archive. It makes the whole thing feel like an ad instead of an artwork. Selling out comes at a price, and this time it might be too high.Hauser & Wirth, until 23 DecemberNicola Turner: I Tear Secrets from Your Yielding Flesh★★★☆☆View image in fullscreenHair-raising … Nicola Turner, I Tear Secrets from Your Yielding Flesh, at Annely Juda.Photograph: Maxwell AttenboroughFor people like me who are cursed to forever ask the universe where our hair has gone, the answer might be Nicola Turner’s exhibition. There are massive, curling, dreaded coils of the stuff tumbling out the front of the building, and things just get hairier inside. Big mounds of twisted wool and horse hair have grown out of the floor, reaching up the walls. Hair has coalesced into strange beings with tripods and shears for legs, stomping through the gallery.The whole thing is half repulsive, half attractive, part kink weirdness, part psychological horror. Turner is talking about medical procedures and grief, about fashion and the body, about how we cover ourselves and expose ourselves at the same time. It’s good: unsettling, theatrical, but you get a bit too lost in gawping at the giant hair installations to feel much warmth from any of it.Annely Juda, until 7 NovemberExplore more on these topicsArtEddy Frankel's gallery crawlExhibitionsCindy ShermanMark LeckeyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Martin Guerre review – return of Les Mis duo’s melodrama reveals a surprise new hero | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Matthew Warchus directs a radical and intimate revival of Alain Boublil and Claude-Michel Schönberg’s musical about a Frenchman who flees home
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Matthew Warchus directs a radical and intimate revival of Alain Boublil and Claude-Michel Schönberg’s musical about a Frenchman who flees home
Content: Twists and surprises … Liv Andrusier and Shane O'Riordan in Martin Guerre.Photograph: Helen MaybanksView image in fullscreenTwists and surprises … Liv Andrusier and Shane O'Riordan in Martin Guerre.Photograph: Helen MaybanksTheatreReviewMartin Guerre review – return of Les Mis duo’s melodrama reveals a surprise new heroOld Vic theatre, LondonMatthew Warchus directs a radical and intimate revival of Alain Boublil and Claude-Michel Schönberg’s musical about a Frenchman who flees homeArifa AkbarThu 22 Oct 2026 04.47 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 04.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome revivals overstate their revisionism but Alain Boublil and Claude-Michel Schönberg’s musical, which premiered 16 years after their 1980 hit Les Misérables, has had a radical overhaul here.The story, set in 16th-century France, has been restructured with new lyrics by Boublil, Annabel Mutale Reed and Paul Hodge and folkier orchestrations. It has been cut down to be performed in an hour and a half without an interval, on the floor of the theatre’s returning show, A Christmas Carol. A miniature Les Mis in spirit, it is filled with the same booming melodrama and preoccupations with crime and disguise.Based on the real-life story of a Frenchman who fled his home after getting married and returned, years later, to face claims of deception and false identity, it keeps you guessing. There are similarities with the Austrian filmRose, selected for the London film festival, and Anjet Daanje’s novelThe Remembered Soldier, published in English last year.View image in fullscreenBooming … the company of Martin Guerre.Photograph: Helen MaybanksAmong the twists and surprises, the real fireworks come from Matthew Warchus’s ingenuity as director. His in-the-round production creates intimacy between Martin and his wife, Bertrande (Liv Andrusier), but also brings a frothing sense of mob rule as the villagers brand her a witch and punish her for his desertion.Warchus, as deft as he is, cannot override all the problems of the musical and the reworking feels simultaneously fast and slow, the sleeker shape bringing momentum but the songs – operatic, emotional, too tonally similar – slowing everything down again. At least the titular number is distinctive, swooping and swooning infectiously.View image in fullscreenOddball … Colin Ryan in Martin Guerre.Photograph: Helen MaybanksPerhaps the production could do more to flesh out the return of Martin. There are a few scenes from the intervening years, in which we see him take part in France’s religious war to fight the Protestant Huguenots. For these brilliantly quicksilver flashbacks, Rob Howell’s set design transforms from courtroom to battlefield and back so cleanly it leaves you gasping with admiration. But the context is bare-boned, the war vague, some characters indistinct. The village oddball, Benoit (Colin Ryan), carries a puppet representing the scarecrow Louison, an underexplained figure who may create confusion for those unfamiliar with the story. You want more of Guerre’s relationship with a fellow soldier too, which proves key within the deception.High School Musical review – Disney fave is sweet, slick and as squeaky clean as everRead moreIt does develop an emotional pull as the plot speeds up and your sympathies lie with the man the town brands an impostor. There is a keen sense of Christian zeal about curses and demons, captured by Lizzi Gee’s choreography of a baying mob carrying weapons. The melodrama comes with the thunder and rumble of Fergus O’Hare’s sound design and blasts of sharply contrasting lighting, designed by Hugh Vanstone, Luca Panetta and Toby Ison.The story’s restructuring has a curious outcome on character and the underlying protagonist becomes Guerre’s abandoned wife, who stands unerringly by him. Andrusier is such a powerful performer, her rendition of one of the show’s new songs, Someday, is a blast of such passion, that it is as if a new hero has arisen to take claim of this story.AtOld Vic theatre, London, until 31 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMusicalsOld Vic TheatreMatthew WarchusWest EndreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Female Life on Planet Earth by Laleh Khadivi review – a mother’s secret past in the Iranian revolution | Fiction | The Guardian
description: A woman living in California discovers her mother may have been a merciless enforcer of the Islamic revolution, in an intriguing novel of inheritance and identity
Author: Shahidha Bari
Headline: A woman living in California discovers her mother may have been a merciless enforcer of the Islamic revolution, in an intriguing novel of inheritance and identity
Content: Cosmic sensibility … Laleh Khadivi.Photograph: Jesse DittmarView image in fullscreenCosmic sensibility … Laleh Khadivi.Photograph: Jesse DittmarBook of the dayFictionReviewFemale Life on Planet Earth by Laleh Khadivi review – a mother’s secret past in the Iranian revolutionA woman living in California discovers her mother may have been a merciless enforcer of the Islamic revolution, in an intriguing novel of inheritance and identityShahidha BariThu 22 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 03.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“It’s a little scary, isn’t it, inheritance?” That’s what Heti, the protagonist of Laleh Khadivi’s latest novel, remarks to a “soccer mom” as they watch their daughters play. “We don’t get to choose what we inherit. Or what we pass on.” Heti, who lives in Los Angeles, is Iranian-American and works for an accountancy firm. She has two daughters, Ava and Zora, and her mother has recently died. When Ava scores a goal, the soccer mom asks, “Did she get that from you?”, but Heti is less interested in the skills that parents pass to their children than the secrets they keep from them.Khadivi’s novel is about mothers and the mysteries they contain. In Female Life on Planet Earth she asks what happens when the people closest to us turn out to be strangers. How do we manage our grief and memorialise our loss when those we love have hidden awful parts of their lives? At the beginning of the book, Heti receives strict instructions from an Iranian aunt about the correct way to mark her mother’s passing. “One year after the death you throw a party,” she is told, “so that [people] can think about your mother, really remember and mourn her.” But then Heti receives a startling set of photographs from an unknown sender. In one image, a younger version of her mother stands veiled in black, a machine gun slung over her shoulder. In a second image, the weapon is extended towards a group of handcuffed women, “their miniskirts uneven on their hips, rips in their tight sweaters”, some crying before the camera, another lying prone, “face pressed into the concrete floor”.double quotation markThe protagonist puzzles through her uncertain feelings in a novel that’s serious and sardonic, analytical and droll by turnsCould her mother have been a merciless enforcer of the Islamic Revolution in Iran? Khadivi doesn’t pose the question so bluntly. Instead, she allows the impact of the images to reverberate for Heti. The pictures with the gun are disturbing, but it is the “shock of affinity” that startles her most of all. “Even though I’m terrified by these pictures, I understand her urge to have control … For the tiniest second I was weirdly reassured that my mother wasn’t all manners and sweetness and that maybe we had more in common than I thought.”Later, she visits her local library and reads about all-female militias, women who in “their newfound zeal … found the punishment of their sisters, the task assigned them by the revolutionaries, to be a satisfying outlet of power”. It’s a grimly fascinating history, but Khadivi is less interested in raking over the political complexities than in attending to the dissonance it stirs in Heti. She allows Heti to puzzle through her uncertain feelings in a novel that fluctuates in tone, serious and sardonic, analytical and droll by turns.The drollery is partly an effect of the book’s structure – a series of vignettes dotted over the course of a year in which Heti wrestles with big issues in incongruous places. On the soccer pitch, she is bemused by the mom who complains, “You can’t believe all that Barbie feminist crap.” At the wholesale supermarket, with its “maze of open freezers filled with thirty pound turkeys”, she wonders if she is remembering her mother “as she really was or as I want her to be”. Doing the accounts on the set of a soft porn film, she decides that what “happens in these shoots is a kind of freedom … Where I came from, where my mother and I were born, a woman’s pleasure can destroy her.”Standing in contrast to the comic parts of Heti’s suburban life is Khadivi’s more cosmic sensibility – suggested by the book’s title. Chapters are named for planets or taken from terms in physics, but the shift between the domestic and the metaphysical can make reading an uneven experience. Khadivi can be grandiose: “At night, Heti’s soul ranged and she followed. Without direction or orientation her thoughts spread into undefined time and limitless space.” At other times, the cosmos is an effective analogy: the “emotional gravity” of Heti’s experience pulls her “into a freefall” that feels like grasping at Jupiter’s vaporous atmosphere. In such circumstances, as Heti tells her daughters, “either you fall and fall or you figure out how to fly …”When Zora later expresses her determination to act on the climate crisis, she tells her mother that “it’s going to be our job to do the extreme things, like take hostages, or destroy oil tankers, or stop eating meat just to get people to care. I’m ready to do any of those.” Khadivi positions Zora’s radicalism as an intriguing mirror to that of her grandmother, quietly challenging any easy assumptions a reader might have about the rights of one and the wrongs of another. If mothers can conceal their lives from their daughters, Khadivi is right to point to how daughters can carry forward, resist or remake the legacies they inherit. As Heti comes to understand in this intriguing and unusual novel, perhaps the more important question may be not what we inherit, but what we choose to become.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsFictionBook of the dayreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Zach Braff: ‘You can be talented and good-looking, but acting success is still like winning the lottery’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Scrubs and Garden State star answers your questions about working with megastars, getting his hair to look good and being brutally killed on BoJack Horseman
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The Scrubs and Garden State star answers your questions about working with megastars, getting his hair to look good and being brutally killed on BoJack Horseman
Content: Zach Braff ... ‘I started auditioning at 14 and barely got anything for years.’Photograph: Robby Klein/Getty Images for SCADView image in fullscreenZach Braff ... ‘I started auditioning at 14 and barely got anything for years.’Photograph: Robby Klein/Getty Images for SCADFilm & Music reader interviewMoviesInterviewZach Braff: ‘You can be talented and good-looking, but acting success is still like winning the lottery’As told toRich PelleyThe Scrubs and Garden State star answers your questions about working with megastars, getting his hair to look good and being brutally killed on BoJack HorsemanThu 22 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow do you manage not toact starstruck when directing people like Morgan Freeman, Michael Caine and Harrison Ford?TopTrampThat’s where my acting comes in – I pretend that I don’t know how famous they are. Every actor really wants a leader. They want someone who knows the script really well, has a plan for how the scene is going to be executed, and – in the case of comedy – knows how to make it funny. The last thing any of those guys wants is someone coming in starstruck and wide-eyed. So I use my acting skills to pretend I’m not starstruck and treat them like normal people.View image in fullscreenBraff (right) on the set of his 2017 film Going in Style, with Alan Arkin (left) and Morgan Freeman (centre).Photograph: THA/AlamyYour Fake Doctors, Real Friends podcast was a real help through lockdown.You were very emotionally open and personal; it was like catching up with friends.I still think about your line that making it in acting, even if you’re talented and good-looking, is like winning the lottery. Do you think that early 00sZach Braffwould make it in the present day the way you did?KamesJBack then, the broadcast networks were making so many pilots, at least it was work for people. Now, I think it’s a much harder landscape to break through. I firmly believe that you can be talented and good-looking, but success is still like winning the lottery. I know plenty of brilliant actors whose lottery ticket hasn’t come up yet. I started auditioning at 14 and barely got anything for years, so I’ve always felt very lucky.And as far as the podcast, that’s so great to hear. We didn’t plan to start it during Covid, but it became a nice sort of warm hug for people who wanted a little bit of nostalgia. Donald [Faison, who plays Dr Turk] and I loved getting together, making each other laugh and reminiscing. So much so that we’re actually bringing it back.View image in fullscreenRipe for a musical? Garden State, from 2004, with stars Natalie Portman and Zach Braff.Photograph: Miramax/Sportsphoto/AllstarHave you thought about Garden State 2?HaggisneepsnfattiesWe did an anniversary concert for the soundtrack last year – we got most of the bands together and did a charity show for the Midnight Mission in Los Angeles – and that was really cool. Natalie Portman was there. I had told her that people have come to me about doing a musical of the movie. I love musicals, but I’ve always thought: “I don’t know if that I want to do that.” Then she said: “Why don’t you do it with the songs from the soundtrack?” It’s funny, because I never thought of that. I haven’t taken any steps to make it a reality, but I do daydream of somehow using the music that people love so much from the soundtrack to make it into a musical.When you agreed to join the cast ofBoJack Horseman, how did you feel about your character having such a grisly end?topfootI love the show, so it was so fun to play a cartoonish version of myself, and I just did whatever they said. I never said: “Don’t kill me that way. Don’t have Jessica Biel feast on my carcass,” or whatever the hell it was.How much fun was it playing a small role inArrested Development– to my mind the funniest, cleverest and silliest of all the US sitcoms?ManofthesouthIt was amazing, especially because I didn’t know I was going to be a never-nude until I got the script. In the world of Arrested Development, a never-nude is someone – mainly Tobias – who can never be fully naked, even in the shower, so he wears denim short-shorts.Scrubs and Arrested Development were both doing really well. Jason Bateman and I were at some big event with the heads of both networks – we were NBC, they were Fox. We were laughing, saying: “It’d be fun if we each guested on each other’s show, but the networks would never let us do that.” Then we realised: “They’re all here. Let’s just go ask them.” They said “Sure,” so I guested on Arrested and Jason did an episode of Scrubs as an ostrich farmer.View image in fullscreenConspiring with Dr Turk (Donald Faison) on Scrubs.Photograph: Sergei Bachlakov/Disney/Getty ImagesWho would you most like to cast inDr Acula: The Movie – JD’s vampire-doctor screenplay in Scrubs?PickleManMichael B Jordan and Leonardo DiCaprio, if we’re in the fantasy where we’re going to make an amazing, huge-budget version. Remember at the end of Pee-wee’s Big Adventure when they make the movie of his life and cast beautiful movie stars, and Pee-wee ends up as a bellhop? That’s the version of Dr Acula I want: megastars, while Donald and I are just in the background.You’ve had huge success whether you’re acting, writing or directing. If you were to pick one standout pinch-me moment, what would it be?TurnipsnitzelMorgan Freeman saying yes to my film was one of those great moments. So was standing in the back of the Eccles theatre in Park City when Garden State premiered, thinking: “Holy shit, how did this happen?”When I got Scrubs, I was waiting tables. I put my Motorola StarTAC phone on the passenger seat as I was driving home from the final callback, and was just eyeing it to see if it was going to ring. Then it rang, I pulled over, called my parents, then I called the manager of the restaurant. She said: “I’m so happy for you, babe, but you got to work tonight still.” I said: “Oh, don’t worry, I’m coming in.” So I worked the whole shift knowing I probably wouldn’t be waiting tables for a couple of years.If you were on a plane and there was an announcement asking if there’s adoctor on board,would you put your hand up?MrSOBaldrickAbsolutely not. I don’t know anything. I really don’t. We have the most amazing consultants on set, including this wonderful nurse who’s just a badass. She shows us what to do and tells us what the hell we’re saying. Anyone who thinks we know anything for real is crazy.Scrubs taught me a lot about illness, life and death. Did it do the same for you?waydgroodsI was so young when we did the original series that I don’t think I had any experience with loss and being in hospitals and grief. In the years since, I’ve lost so many people. I’ve sat in hospital and ICU waiting rooms, waiting with bated breath for the doctor to come in with good or bad news. I’ve seen how the nurses run the whole hospital. I’ve witnessed it first-hand in a way I hadn’t as a young man. So I think now I have even more respect. I feel more like I’m playing a superhero as the guy who’s the chief of medicine at an underfunded hospital who’s meant to be a particularly badass doctor.Does your hair have its own agent?Dr_J_A_ZoidbergMy hair’s agent is that I take a shower at night and then I go to sleep on it and you get magical bedhead.Clean Hands is released in the US on 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmFilm & Music reader interviewZach BraffTelevisionArrested DevelopmentComedyTV comedyUS televisioninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: This mighty cry for a goddess to help Earth proves Dickson Mbi is a bold force in dance | Stage | The Guardian
description: The Olivier-winner draws on his Cameroonian heritage in a visceral show, with music and movement that speak as one
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: The Olivier-winner draws on his Cameroonian heritage in a visceral show, with music and movement that speak as one
Content: Flashes of brilliance … Harvey Burke-Hamilton (centre, floor) in Tellus by Dickson Mbi at Sadler's Wells East, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFlashes of brilliance … Harvey Burke-Hamilton (centre, floor) in Tellus by Dickson Mbi at Sadler's Wells East, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianStageReviewThis mighty cry for a goddess to help Earth proves Dickson Mbi is a bold force in danceSadler’s Wells East, LondonThe Olivier-winner draws on his Cameroonian heritage in a visceral show, with music and movement that speak as oneLyndsey WinshipThu 22 Oct 2026 09.48 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDickson Mbi won an Olivier award for his last major dance piece,Enowate, a result that surprised some of us who saw a talented artist still mastering the craft of choreographing a full-length work. But his new one, Tellus, is a much more sure and expressive work that creates a confident, textured world. Plus, Mbi is now not only a choreographer, but also a composer – a skill he honed during the pandemic – and the score is an essential part of the choreography (there are musicians on stage behind the eight performers), full of haunting melody and emotional pull. The music effectively shapes and enhances the action and speaks with the dance.View image in fullscreenRousing … Hannah Joseph (centre) in Tellus by Dickson Mbi at Sadler’s Wells East, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTellus is a kind of folk tale about finding hope in a world that’s in environmental turmoil. The gist of the story (you may need to refer to the programme) is of a lost and stumbling central figure, a community struck by fire and drought, and an appeal to a goddess, Mami-Wata, for help. It draws on Mbi’s Cameroonian heritage, as does the music and the movement, which also takes in Mbi’s roots in hip-hop, with contemporary, South Asian and classical dance seemingly all in the mix. There are flashes of brilliance in the choreography, rousing ritual movement for the group and individuals with strong movement signatures: a spinning, leaping Nathan Goodman; an imperious, tottering Hannah Joseph.Mbi has brought in some expert collaborators, including video designers YeastCulture, who provide a little magic in the visuals. He has been mentored by Complicité’sSimon McBurney, and worked with poet Nick Drake on the scenario; however, the result is a work of instinct and visceral impact rather than detailed narrative, although the message of reconnecting with our precious Earth is a simple and essential one.AtSadler’s Wells East, London, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageDanceSadler's WellsSimon McBurneyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Helen Fielding launches Bridget Jones prize for northern comedy writing | Books | The Guardian
description: The Yorkshire-born author says that the 1,000 word competition is for people ‘just living their lives being quietly hilarious’
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: The Yorkshire-born author says that the 1,000 word competition is for people ‘just living their lives being quietly hilarious’
Content: Dream team … Renée Zellweger and Helen Fielding.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDream team … Renée Zellweger and Helen Fielding.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty ImagesBooksHelen Fielding launches Bridget Jones prize for northern comedy writingThe Yorkshire-born author says that the 1,000 word competition is for people ‘just living their lives being quietly hilarious’Emma LoffhagenThu 22 Oct 2026 07.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBridget Jones authorHelen Fieldinghas launched a comedy writing prize in the name of her most famous creation, aimed at unearthing funny new voices from the north of England.TheBridget Jones prizefor northern comedy writing will go to the funniest self-contained, first-person prose of 1,000 words. The format echoes the anonymous diary columns in the Independent that first brought Bridget to readers in the mid-1990s.Fielding, who grew up in Yorkshire, wrote the original columns andfour Bridget Jones novels, as well as co-writing the blockbuster film adaptations starringRenée Zellweger.She said Bridget’s humour was drawn from the people she grew up with: “laughing together at our mess-ups; bringing the fancy and pretentious down to earth”.“There are lots of famous northern comics,” she said. “But this prize is for the comic voices of people who aren’t famous: just living their lives being quietly hilarious.”Writers living in the north who have neither been published nor signed with an agent are eligible to enter. There is no entry fee and the winner will take home £2,000, plus a session with Aitken Alexander Associates, the agency that represents Fielding, and tailored support from the charity New Writing North. One runner-up will get £1,000.Fielding was strict about the word limit. “I always tried to make the Bridget columns exactly 1,000 words long – like making the petrol pump stop at exactly 20 quid,” she said. “If it’s slightly under you won’t be punished. Just DON’T MAKE IT ANY LONGER!”Fielding will judge alongside an Aitken Alexander agent and a representative from New Writing North, and the winner will be revealed at next summer’s Northern Writers’ awards in Newcastle, with the prize presented by Fielding. The prize will be given out each year until 2029.Will Mackie from New Writing North said: “This is the first time the Northern Writers’ awards have featured an award exclusively for comedy writing.“There is no one more fitting to identify an original comedy voice than Helen, who created one of the nation’s most beloved comic characters of the last 30 years.”Fielding cited Victoria Wood, Alan Bennett, Les Dawson, Thora Hird and Morecambe and Wise as inspirations.Submissions open on 23 November and close on 1 February 2027.Explore more on these topicsBooksHelen FieldingAwards and prizesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Judi Dench says sight loss means she can no longer perform but she is still ‘besotted by’ Shakespeare’s sonnets | Judi Dench | The Guardian
description: Age-related macular degeneration has also left actor, 91, unable to read or recognise faces any more
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Age-related macular degeneration has also left actor, 91, unable to read or recognise faces any more
Content: Judi Dench was speaking before the publication of her memoir, Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It?, written with the theatre director Brendan O’Hea.Photograph: Paul StuartView image in fullscreenJudi Dench was speaking before the publication of her memoir, Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It?, written with the theatre director Brendan O’Hea.Photograph: Paul StuartJudi DenchJudi Dench says sight loss means she can no longer perform but she is still ‘besotted by’ Shakespeare’s sonnetsAge-related macular degeneration has also left actor, 91, unable to read or recognise faces any moreNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentThu 22 Oct 2026 09.19 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 09.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJudi Dench has said she can no longer perform on stage or in films because of her deteriorating eyesight, more than a decade after revealing she had been diagnosed with age-related macular degeneration.“I can’t be on stage. I can’t do a play any more. I can’t do a film any more. I can’t read any more,” the 91-year-old actor told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Thursday.Dench, one of Britain’s most celebrated actors, was diagnosed withage-related macular degeneration(AMD) in 2012. The condition causes progressive sight loss and has increasingly affected her ability to work, as well as her independence in everyday life.She described how she can no longer read or recognise faces. “I go up to lots of the wrong people and give them an almost hug and say: ‘Oh sorry, didn’t realise’,” she said. She also told the presenter Emma Barnett: “I can’t see your face at all.”Dench’s comments mark a stark development in a gradual deterioration that has affected her ability to work for years. In 2014, she said her failing eyesight made reading difficult, but insisted she would continue working for as long as she could.By 2023, she said shecould no longer see on film setsand relied on friends to teach her scripts, learning lines through repetition. Last year, she revealed that shecould no longer go out alonebecause she feared walking into objects or falling over.The actor also told Barnett of her sadness at no longer being able to see bluebells. “They said this summer was absolutely sensational with bluebells; I couldn’t see one,” she said. “But I know what my trees look like, and part of it is in my memory and part of it is about hopefully what I can make out.”‘Oh God, I can’t bear it’: Judi Dench says Cats film was ‘a waste of goodwill and talent’Read moreAsked about ageing, Dench replied: “There’s nothing to say for it at all. [I] don’t think about it too much.”Despite the impact of her sight loss, she spoke warmly ofher enduring love of Shakespeare’s poetry. “I am besotted by the sonnets, I just love them,” she said, describing their ability to capture human feelings simply. “It’s the rhythm of it. It’s the rhythm of your heart. It’s the way he’s summed up so simply the way that any of us feel about, well, anything.”Dench was speaking before the publication of her memoir, Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It?, written with the theatre director Brendan O’Hea.Dench’s career spans more than seven decades. She won an Oscar for playing Queen Elizabeth I in Shakespeare in Love and became internationally renowned as M, James Bond’s boss, appearing in eight films in the franchise. Her stage work included celebrated Shakespearean roles such as Juliet, Lady Macbeth and Cleopatra.Explore more on these topicsJudi DenchRadio 4Blindness and visual impairmentDisabilityBBCActingTheatrenewsShareReuse this content
