title: 18 again: I returned to my life in 1983 – to reckless adventures, in a world soaked in alcohol | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Sundays were deadly, the generation gap between parents and their kids was enormous, and a pint cost 50p. The frisson of casual violence was everywhere. When I left school and set off to travel, I had no sense at all of where I was going or what I would find
Author: Rick Williams
Headline: Sundays were deadly, the generation gap between parents and their kids was enormous, and a pint cost 50p. The frisson of casual violence was everywhere. When I left school and set off to travel, I had no sense at all of where I was going or what I would find
Content: Rick Williams, pictured in the 1980s.Photograph: Courtesy of Rick WilliamsView image in fullscreenRick Williams, pictured in the 1980s.Photograph: Courtesy of Rick WilliamsThe year I turned 18Life and style18 again: I returned to my life in 1983 – to reckless adventures, in a world soaked in alcoholSundays were deadly, the generation gap between parents and their kids was enormous, and a pint cost 50p. The frisson of casual violence was everywhere. When I left school and set off to travel, I had no sense at all of where I was going or what I would findRick WilliamsThu 22 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIam wandering down a steep and unfamiliar street in Saint Peter Port, Guernsey, a force seven gale blowing in my face, when I look up to cross the road and see a back garden running up the hillside opposite. It ends in a granite rock face about 30ft high, and in that moment, I have a vivid flashback to being sat on top of it, watching a group of people in the garden below. I can’t conjure their faces, but the memory is all too real: the sun on my face, a woman calling up: “Don’t break your neck!” I can tell she’s not worried and neither am I. Nobody is. It’s a party and we’re young and we’re drunk and we’re carefree, without a worry in the world. Or at least, that’s how I remember it.I continue down the street, spooked by the power of the recollection, how it has ambushed me. I stand outside the house. I could swear I’ve never seen it before. Did I come to the party over the cliff? Should I knock on the door? Hi, this is going to sound weird but I was in your back garden about 42 years ago and I haven’t a clue why but I’ve just remembered it like it was yesterday …There are no lights on, no car outside. I carry on down to the coast, where huge waves crash against the sea wall.“A single person’s memory, uncorroborated and unsubstantiated by other evidence, is a feeble guide to the past,” the novelist, Julian Barnes, wrote in the Guardian last year. I am in Guernsey because it’s where I lived when I turned 18, even though I spent most of that year working and travelling abroad. I’m trying to recapture what my life was like then and it’s a good place to start. In Back to the Future, Michael J Fox’s Marty McFly gets in a DeLorean time machine. I have flown in an ATR 72-600 turboprop, and it is only my second time on the island in 35 years.On 26 May 1983, a 7.8 magnitude earthquake in the Sea of Japan triggered a tsunami that devastated Honshu. Across the Pacific, the US conducted a nuclear test in Nevada, while Candy Girl by New Edition topped the UK charts. Manchester United beat Brighton & Hove Albion 4-0 in the replay of the FA Cup final (a painful fact to write as a Liverpool fan and now Brighton resident) and Star Wars: Episode VI – Return of the Jedi was bossing it at the box office. It was also my 18th birthday. Two weeks later, on 9 June, the Tories had a landslide general election victory that cemented Thatcherism for the next decade, a far more unpleasant detail to recall than the football result.View image in fullscreenOn the bus … Rick Williams at 18.Photograph: HandoutI don’t remember any of that – a quick internet search has filled me in. But it can’t tell me whatIdid that day. A Thursday in the middle of my A-levels, I would have probably been revising in my bedroom (although I remember spending more time doing keepy-uppies in the garden, struggling to focus), eager for the exams to be over, to leave school and home and go travelling. Top of the Pops was on that evening but it was no longer the weekly ritual of my earlier teens. Apparently the Police performed Every Breath You Take, today the most-streamed track of the 80s. I didn’t like it back then. The month before, Bowie’s Let’s Dance had been No 1 for three weeks. I loved Bowie and bought the album, but was disappointed: it was too polished, too commercial, a new direction for him I disapproved of, all tan and white teeth, a sign of much of the 80s to come.When I was 11, my family moved from Wirral (or the metropolitan county of Merseyside, which it became part of in 1974) to Guernsey. My dad worked for the Midland Bank on Dale Street in Liverpool and was being transferred. Five days before I was due to start secondary school in Birkenhead, we drove south and caught a ferry. I’d never been on one before, never been abroad (neither had my parents). I told my mates I was going to live on the equivalent of a Caribbean island. It was the heatwave of 1976; the sun had clearly gone to my head. That first winter in Guernsey it seemed to rain incessantly and as a family we struggled to adapt to a very different way of life in a rented bungalow. My sister, Sue, who was two years older than me, never adjusted. When she was 16, three years after our move, she went back to Birkenhead to finish her education, living with the family of a friend of hers, only returning to the island for holidays. Which meant that from the age of 14, I was essentially an only child.View image in fullscreenSound and rhythm … Williams’ records from the 80s.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianI had a troubled relationship with my parents, as did my sister; it was a big reason she left. The generation gap was huge. My parents had no experience of being a teenager. Born in the 1930s, they grew up in north Wales before youth culture. My father had a motorbike, but he wasn’t a biker. He couldn’t understand why I had to question and challenge everything. Because I did. I struggled with authority and I saw him as compliant. We were chalk and cheese. Even my being left-handed, which he jokingly called “cack-handed” when I laid the table with the fork on the right, was further evidence of our difference. A friend said once: “Everything we did was a way of saying to them: ‘I don’t want to be like you.’” Their politics, their clothes, their music, the TV they watched and the jobs they did (my mother was a housewife) were anathema. Such rejection must have been difficult, but perhaps not that unusual. Late 70s punk shocked not only my parents’ generation but its own. Rebellion was in the air. Another friend, who had a similarly difficult relationship with his conservative father around the same time, puts it: “He didn’t have the tools to deal with me.”There was also the growing disparity in our educations. My parents left school at 16 but their ambition was for me to go to university (about 7% of 18-year-olds in the UK went to university in 1983, compared with 40.6% in 2025, despite there being grants and not crippling loans). English was my favourite subject (I was a big reader) and two books I studied for A-level helped broaden my horizons: As I Lay Dying by William Faulkner introduced me to stream of consciousness and more experimental writing, while Strait is the Gate by Andre Gide for my French A-level got me reading Sartre, Cocteau, Camus and Kafka – and opened the door to a morally ambiguous and transgressive world that I embraced for its essential absurdity. This was perhaps not the education my parents had in mind.View image in fullscreenWilliams in the Dorset Arms in Guernsey with old friends, from left: Steve, Jay and Paul.Photograph: Paul Chambers/The GuardianBefore going to Guernsey, I arrange to meet my old friends Paul, Jay and Steve, who still live there. In the pub, as we chat about the past, I am initially struck – and a little alarmed – by how much more they remember than I do: people, pubs and clubs, parties and incidents. I tell myself it’s because they still live there, the constant reminders, but I also wonder if it is more about what we choose to remember.Over dinner, we talk about how we understood the world in 1983 and what shaped us, with no internet and only four TV channels. Apart from our peers, we agree that NME and other magazines such as the Face were hugely influential, along with the John Peel show and Radio Caroline. I first started reading NME when I was 14 from cover to cover (the classified ads were as fascinating as the editorial). A review or interview might mention an older band or influence, and at the record shop (No.19 in Saint Peter Port, today a White Stuff), you’d search through the racks for them. Did the Teardrop Explodes and Echo and the Bunnymen trigger an interest in the Doors and 60s psychedelia, acid and Carlos Castaneda, the beats and counter culture?You often had to take a punt on a record, parting with your hard-earned cash (I had a job as a milkman on a Sunday and in the holidays throughout my school years). Did I buy Thermonuclear Sweat by Defunkt in 1983, a band I’d never heard of, because I picked it up in No.19, drawn to the title, and saw a Joseph Bowie in the lineup and I was a Bowie fan? Its punk-jazz threw me, but I grew to love it, learned that Joseph was the brother of Lester Bowie, co-founder of The Art Ensemble of Chicago, my hardcore introduction to jazz. In that random way, one thing could lead to another, so slow compared with today, when we have a world of knowledge at our fingertips.View image in fullscreenEcho and the Bunnymen.Photograph: Gunter W Kienitz/ShutterstockThe early 80s were tribal: punk, mod, skin, rude boy, new romantic, indie: you dressed like the bands you listened to (on Saturday afternoons, we would go to jumble sales and find clothes to customise). The music you bought spoke volumes. Talking to my own three children, Connor, 27, Ella, 23 and Jake, 21, I get the impression that they didn’t listen to music with the same prejudices when they were 18. Fleetwood Mac, Genesis, Led Zeppelin and all those 70s “rock dinosaurs” would never have darkened my turntable (or increasingly, my cassette player; although I still have a lot of my records, not a single cassette has survived, all those cherished mixtapes, often painstakingly recorded off the radio, gone).I remember being interested in the news, what was happening in the world (it was easy to feel cut off on an island). I read the Guernsey Evening Press (I liked the crime pages) and the Times, which my parents got, every day. They listened to BBC Radio 2 at breakfast, Terry Wogan to start the day, and watched The Nine O’Clock News in the evening. The news events that I remember were acid rain destroying the forests of northern Europe, high unemployment of 11.5% in the UK (though in Guernsey the rate was negligible), the Soviet Union invasion of Afghanistan and the tensions of the cold war growing with Reagan in the White House. There had been the Falklands war in 1982, a 74-day conflict that saved Thatcher’s premiership but seemed a world away. (The landlady of Taylor’s Long Bar in Saint Peter Port didn’t like serving groups of young men, but made an exception for servicemen. My friends and I happily told her we were back from the Falklands and she served us underage.)The biggest threat was nuclear Armageddon. In September 1983, only the quick thinking of a Soviet officer averted catastrophe, when he interpreted a reported US nuclear strike as a false alarm and didn’t push the button – the closest the world has come to nuclear war since the Cuban missile crisis.We all knew the name of Greenham Common, but I didn’t fully understand what was happening there. We would laugh about the advice of hiding under a table, in the case of a nuclear attack. Yeah, right.View image in fullscreenProtesters outside the gates of Greenham Common air base in 1983.Photograph: Dave Caulkin/APAlcohol played a massive part in my life when I was 18, as it had done throughout my teens. It was easy to get served underage, so turning 18 wasn’t a landmark moment in terms of legally buying a drink (no one carried ID). Alcohol and tobacco were cheap on Guernsey: we all drank and smoked. You could go out with a fiver and have a night of it at about 50p a pint, the same for a packet of cigarettes. (It’s no longer cheap there, more or less the same as the UK.) During my visit, I pop into a pub at lunchtime that we used to frequent. It has seen better days. There is one customer, a woman at the bar having a large glass of wine. While I am chatting to the barperson about why I am on the island, the woman turns and says: “Love, all you’ve got to write about Guernsey is: 70,000 alcoholics clinging to a rock in the middle of the sea.”There is certainly a wild and reckless alcoholic haze to a lot of my memories. A time and a pub would be agreed and the night would go on from there. Afterwards, we might go to a club or a house party, invited or not. We were all sexually active, quite promiscuous. Aids was still a few years off from being widely reported and we took few if any precautions. We drank and drove, motorbikes when we were younger (my friend Paul was a mod and we went round on his Lambretta), cars once we were 17. Guernsey didn’t have breathalysers at the time. If you were pulled over, you had to walk toe to heel for about 10ft, bend down and pick up a coin, and toe to heel back. If you didn’t lose your balance, you were fit to drive. I got away with it several times.View image in fullscreenAn important place of discovery … inspirational reads from the local bookshop.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianApart from the record shop, the bookshop was another important place of discovery. It was there that I bought Jean Genet’s Miracle of the Rose when I was 17 and got chatting to the owner about literature. He invited me to his house for a cup of tea and showed me around the place. The last room was the cellar, which turned out to be a sex dungeon: handcuffs on the wall, whips and masks. He casually explained that he threw parties down there and if I ever fancied coming to one … I declined as casually as I could. Maybe we’d talked about De Sade earlier in the bookshop. The next time I saw him we chatted as if it had never happened. He must have trusted me not to tell anyone, which I didn’t (it would have been scandalous in such a conservative place). But it seemed like confirmation of the edgy and exciting world that books could lead to.It’s hard to say if our lives were better or worse than they are for 18-year-olds today. We experienced boredom more – Sundays were deadly, everything closed. Sexism and racism and homophobia were commonplace, as was casual violence; parents physically disciplined their kids and corporal punishment wasn’t banned in state schools until 1986, so it’s perhaps no surprise that, with a few drinks, punches got thrown. Football hooliganism was rampant, making headlines. On a night out, there was a mild expectation of trouble.We would occasionally go to London to see bands (in my early teens, bands came to Guernsey – Elvis Costello, the Jam, Depeche Mode, Adam and the Ants – but then stopped. I’m not sure why, but logistics, costs and the island not having a big enough venue were all probably part of it). There was a world out there – and I was desperate to explore it.Three months after my 18th birthday, my friend Joel and I set off travelling. I had saved £400 from working all summer in a greenhouse that was pioneering the cultivation of kiwifruit on Guernsey, to replace the dying tomato industry (it never took off). Our vague plan was to work our way across Europe, maybe end up on a kibbutz (which still had a reputation as socialist paradises), then travel further. A gap year before university. In the bookshop I had chanced upon Work Your Way Around the World, which was in its first edition; we’d never heard of Lonely Planet and were perhaps as informed by the spirit of On the Road and Genet. Our only map was of all of Europe, taking in the top of north Africa and some of the Middle East. It was somewhat lacking in detail. No one else we knew was going travelling or had been. Looking back, Joel and I agree that naivety was as much our guide.View image in fullscreenAn indispensable guide.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianAfter grape picking in the Champagne region, we hitchhiked to the south of France. Often, no one would pick us up (including Björn Borg, who drove past us twice in his black Porsche near Monaco) and we would walk for miles, sleeping rough. On the French riviera, we bought a cheap summer tent and crossed northern Italy, sleeping in railway stations. In Venice, a guy tried to rob us in the middle of the night. When I woke, he threatened me and carried on going through my bag so I pulled out my knife to scare him off. I’d had it since I was 14, when I saw it glinting at the bottom of the marina in Saint Peter Port and dived down to retrieve it, a British second world war Fairbairn Sykes stiletto fighting knife; no plaything. He looked at it and laughed, whipped out a switchblade and waved it in my face, to show I didn’t stand a chance, before strolling off. I vowed to never pull a knife on anyone again. But what amazes me now is that I carried that knife through dozens of border checks and on numerous flights, and it was never an issue.View image in fullscreenChristmas Day 1983 in Kalamata. Williams, left, with Gilles.Photograph: Courtesy of Rick WilliamsWe continued through Yugoslavia and into Greece, where Work Your Way Around the World said there was orange picking on the Peloponnese. We met a few other northern Europeans, older than us, also looking for work. They told us the harvest was late. We wandered around Greece for weeks, ending up in the small town of Gargalianoi, where we stayed for three months, helping with the olive harvest, working in construction and an olive oil factory. Most of the time we slept in woods on the edge of town, our own little squatter camp that the locals turned a blind eye to, once a week going to the fleapit hotel in town, for a cold shower and the comfort of a bed. We were the only foreigners, apart from a couple of French guys, Gilles and Eric. They were recovering heroin addicts (Gilles had done nine months in Paris’s notorious La Santé prison for possession) and were planning to stay out of France for seven years to avoid military service, that length of absence granting exemption. We became friends and also increasingly aware that being British, we were the envy of European youth for not having national service: a Greek friend we were working with, Tomas, was about to start his two-year military conscription, a bleak posting on the troubled Turkish border.That eight-month journey sometimes feels like a fever dream. It defines being 18 for me: freedom and adventure, living on your wits, never knowing what the next day might bring. From Greece we went to Egypt and across north Africa, back up through Spain and France and home. There were tough times, but no question of turning back. People on the whole were kind – we were kids and they wanted to help us. Our map was so basic, we had little idea where we were going, following the setting sun. For a time, we used a copy of David Copperfield we picked up in a hotel in Cairo as toilet paper, each reading the same 20 or so pages a day and then tearing them out.There were two threatening periods: in Tunis, we became the target of unwanted sexual attention, followed night and day, men waiting outside our hotel room, every invitation for coffee turning into aggressive attempts at seduction; and in Tétouan in Morocco, we were hounded by dealers for days, sold hash and then told we would be shopped to the police unless we bought more. They were still threatening us as we left on the bus.View image in fullscreenVisiting Aswan High Dam, Egypt.Photograph: Courtesy of Rick Williams“The stories we tell most often about our lives are likely to be the least reliable, because we will have subtly amended them in every retelling down the years,” Barnes wrote in the same article. “It’s salutary to discover, from time to time, how other people’s memories are often quite different from our own – not just of events, but of what we ourselves were like back then.” Joel had forgotten the use of Dickens as toilet paper; I’d forgotten the level of hassle in Tétouan. Maybe I was too stoned. The truth is there, somewhere, among the stories.View image in fullscreenFive forgotten letters to home.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianIn 2019, when my mother went into a home, I was clearing my parents’ house with my sister when I came across a folder of old documents and papers of mine that they’d kept. Looking through them for this article, I found five letters I wrote during my time away – I’d forgotten they existed, this was the first time I’d read them since I wrote them 42 years ago. Would they corroborate what I wasreallylike as an 18-year-old? The fact that I sent only five letters and made no phone calls in eight months shocks me now as a parent (my sister says she asked my mum if she worried about me when I was away and she said she did, but that she felt there would have been disapproval, possibly from my father and no doubt from me,if she had expressed it).View image in fullscreen‘The truth is there, somewhere, among the stories’ … Rick Williams.Photograph: Paul Chambers/The GuardianTo be honest, I’m surprised I wrote any letters at all, from how I remember our relationship. Instead, I find myself joking to them about being hungry, about roughing it, my hair getting longer, losing weight. There are things I had forgotten – our plan to go to a kibbutz in Israel thwarted by “war and conflict”; another plan to take a two-week boat trip from Athens to Alexandria (why would it take so long?!); our intention to cross the middle of the Sahara, only to find out in Egypt it would take three months to get a visa to enter Sudan and continue into Chad. I can see I am trying to shock them at times, but not too much. I tell them about Gilles and Eric and getting drunk on New Year’s Eve with them, Gilles throwing up in our hotel room, but I don’t mention their heroin addiction or the pills we took that had me hallucinating large insects crawling over my body, something that I thankfully found hilarious rather than terrifying. I say how beautiful Venice is, being kicked awake by Italian cops at dawn, but I don’t mention the incident with the knife. I complain about being sexually harassed in Tunis, but brush it off.View image in fullscreenBack to the future … Williams in Guernsey, 2026.Photograph: Paul Chambers/The GuardianWhat surprises me most though is a warmth I hadn’t allowed for. Maybe distance did. Letters tell their own stories.Most of us look back at our 18-year-old selves and do a little editing. As F Scott Fitzgerald wrote: “At 18, our convictions are hills from which we look; at forty-five they are caves in which we hide.” What were my convictions? Is the unheralded memory of being sat on that rock face – acting fearless, reckless, carefree, about to leap into the unknown – as accurate a picture as any? I spent most of my 20s after university travelling, living abroad. I still love to travel, even if kids and a career and the realities of adult life have restricted the opportunities. I still love the feeling of the bag on my back containing all I need. My kids love to travel too; I like to think my wife and I have given them that sense of adventure. We plan to go travelling for a year when we stop working. I like to think that 18-year-old is still with me.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe year I turned 18Young peopleGap year travelfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best bread makers in the UK for easy homemade loaves – tested | Bread | The Guardian
description: Want fresh bread without the hard work? Our expert baked her way through nine machines to find the best for white, wholemeal and gluten-free loaves
Author: Danielle Amato
Headline: Want fresh bread without the hard work? Our expert baked her way through nine machines to find the best for white, wholemeal and gluten-free loaves
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterBreadThe best bread makers in the UK for easy homemade loaves – testedWant fresh bread without the hard work? Our expert baked her way through nine machines to find the best for white, wholemeal and gluten-free loavesEverything you need to make great sourdoughDanielle AmatoThu 22 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs a bread-loving lazy person, easy access to plump, airy loaves is always appreciated. And while buying it from a shop might be considered the laziest way to acquire it, I think making it at home can be just as convenient, especially with a decent bread maker to do all the hard bits for you.Bread machines mix, knead, prove and bake your loaf at the touch of a button and most, including the ones I’ve tested here, produce loaves that are above and beyond your standard sandwich bread.This is a real treat if, like me, you enjoy letting your imagination run wild with all the different loaves you can make. Sweet chocolate-chip breads, Italian pesto loaves, super-seeded high-fibre slices for your lunchtime toasties – the possibilities are almost endless. Making bread from scratch also means you can cater to dietary preferences – and most of the models here make an outstanding gluten-free loaf.To find the best bread makers, I put nine machines through their paces – munching my way through an unimaginable amount of white, wholemeal, gluten-free and olive loaves in the process. These are the models that proved to be worth their salt, and more importantly, worth your money.At a glanceBest bread maker overallPanasonicSD-PMC100NXC mini bread and ice-cream maker£199.99 at AmazonBest budget bread makerMorphy RichardsFastbake£69 at AmazonEasiest bread maker to useLakelandDeluxe bread maker£109.99 at LakelandBest for gluten-free breadSageThe Custom Loaf£229.95 at John LewisBest bread maker for varietyGraefBread maker£284.95 at Harts of SturWhy you should trust meHaving spent almost 10 years testing and writing about kitchen appliances and cooking gadgets, I’ve built a wealth of knowledge on just about every cooking tool out there. From emerging trends to tried-and-true chef favourites, I’ve seen it all.All of this experience means I can spot a worthwhile product a mile away, but also know when something might not quite hit the mark. I’m also dough-obsessed, making pizza and bread from scratch most weeks, which makes the pursuit of finding the perfect bread machine all that bit easier.How I testedView image in fullscreenThe slice is right: Danielle tested a range of recipes in each bread maker.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianWhen it comes to bread, consistency is key. A good bread maker should be as adept at making a basic white loaf as a crusty wholemeal or gluten-free variant. This is why I made and taste-tested multiple such loaves (36 in total) across nine bread makers, using the same recipes each time.For machines with a mix-in function, I also made an additional olive loaf to assess the reliability of the mechanism that drops ingredients into the loaf. Testing the various flours gave me a good indication of how well each bread maker is suited to specific tasks, as well as how well they perform in general.Most bread makers allow you to use any recipe, as long as the weight is correct for the bread pan you’re using. As they’re automated, they are, however, a little more slapdash with the mixing, so if you’re used to making your favourite loaf by hand, you might find a little trial and error is involved to get it right in a bread machine.I also measured the energy consumption of each bread maker using a power meter, noting the result in the specs below. Functionality and how easy each machine was to use and clean were also factored into my testing and reviews.All the bread makers sourced for this article will be sent back to their manufacturers after testing.The best bread makers in 2026View image in fullscreenRise and shine: some of the bread makers put to the test.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianBest bread maker overall:Panasonic SD-PMC100NXC mini bread and ice-cream makerPanasonicSD-PMC100NXC mini bread and ice-cream makerfrom£199.99£199.99 at John Lewis£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveFantastic all-round performance, including gluten-freeWhat we don’t loveCompact design means only one loaf sizeView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£199.99 at John Lewis£199.99 at AmazonAs well as being the best all-round performer in my tests, the Panasonic is a great choice for anyone looking for a compact machine that doesn’t take up too much worktop or cupboard space.Why we love itThe mini bread maker offered some of the most consistent and impressive results in my tests, alongside Sage’s the Custom Loaf. The shape, crumb and crust on every loaf I made were consistent, while white bread was soft but easy to cut and wholemeal was moist with a slight denseness.This bread maker even does a great job of producing a small gluten-free loaf with a lovely crust and texture that toasts well. There was a little uncooked mixture on the outside of the bread after baking, but this could be scraped off. It’s also worth noting that this happened with every gluten-free test due to the paddle struggling with the extra-wet dough. After baking, I was pleased that the ungreased stirring paddle released cleanly from every loaf. Cleaning is easy too – a quick soak in warm water helps loosen any baked-on crumbs around the paddle.This machine can only make one loaf size, with a maximum weight of 500g, compared with the choice of at least two sizes you get with some other bread makers on this list. However, the loaves it produces are plenty big enough for two people to enjoy over a few days. Homemade bread is also best eaten fresh, due to the absence of preservatives or stabilisers, meaning the loaves are the ideal size if you’re making a new one every couple of days.There’s an automatic ingredient and yeast dispenser at the top of the machine, and it has 34 settings – I particularly like the functionality for making panettone and pasta dough. A few recipes are included in the manual, but Panasonic also has adedicated appwith about 50 additional recipes.Interestingly, this bread maker also doubles as anice-cream makerand comes with a small, freezable bowl that churns up to 400ml of ice-cream.It’s a shame that …it offers only one loaf size.Dimensions:24.1 x 30.4 x 34.7cm (WDH)Loaf sizes:400-500gAverage slice height:15cmTime for a white loaf:4hrsEnergy cost per loaf:4p(0.167kWh)Spare parts and repairs:spares available from thePanasonic accessories store, and repairs available via thesupport siteWarranty: up to two years (depending on retailer)PanasonicSD-PMC100NXC mini bread and ice-cream makerfrom£199.99£199.99 at John Lewis£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveFantastic all-round performance, including gluten-freeWhat we don’t loveCompact design means only one loaf sizeBest budget bread maker:Morphy Richards FastbakeMorphy RichardsFastbakefrom£69£69.99 at Morphy Richards£69 at AmazonWhat we loveEasy bread in under three hours, or one hour with FastbakeWhat we don’t loveCan’t make a good gluten-free loafView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£69.99 at Morphy Richards£69 at AmazonThe Morphy Richards Fastbake might be more than a decade old, but it’s still a good budget machine with a useful quick-bake setting for easy, simple sandwich bread. Just don’t expect miracles at this price.Why we love itSimplicity is the name of the game here. There are no unusual settings for breads you’ve never heard of and no fancy extras; it simply makes bread (and, like most bread makers, dough, cake and jam). Initially, I wasn’t won over by the Fastbake as it felt lightweight and a little cheap, but then, this is a budget bread maker, and performance is what really counts.The Fastbake really proved itself (no pun intended) when making classic white loaves and 50/50 bread. The crumb was nice and airy, while the crust was perfectly done on the medium setting. It also produced a nice 100% wholemeal loaf, but I felt that other machines, such as Sage’s the Custom Loaf, performed better. I also tested the Fastbake programme on this machine, which mixes, proves and cooks a loaf in under an hour. The bread produced definitely isn’t as light and fluffy as the regular white loaf, but it does the job if you’re short on time. It’s worth noting that the standard white bread setting is a speedy 3hrs.It’s a budget model, so I wasn’t surprised about the lack of an add-in ingredient or yeast dispenser for seeded breads or more niche recipes, but it’s important to note that it also doesn’t have a dedicated gluten-free setting. Morphy Richards suggests using the basic loaf programme for this, which gave fairly average results in testing, so it’s not ideal for gluten-free bakers. The paddle does tend to stick in the bread with this one as well, but if you let it cool, you can then pull it out fairly cleanly.Generally, it’s easy to use and features old-school buttons and a basic screen. I found this quite intuitive to use compared with some others I tested. Cleaning isn’t too bad either. Like all the bread maker pans, I gave this one a quick soak in warm water and found that it lifted any stuck dough or crust.It’s a shame that …it can’t make a good gluten-free loaf.Dimensions:40.5 x 28.5 x 30.5cm (WDH)Loaf sizes:1.5lb (680g), 2lb (907g); 1lb (454g) possible for some recipes using the 1.5lb settingAverage slice height:17cmTime for a white loaf:3hrsEnergy cost per loaf:6p (0.211kWh)Spare parts and repairs:spare parts available fromMorphy Richards website, repairs available viasupportWarranty: three years, withregistrationMorphy RichardsFastbakefrom£69£69.99 at Morphy Richards£69 at AmazonWhat we loveEasy bread in under three hours, or one hour with FastbakeWhat we don’t loveCan’t make a good gluten-free loafEasiest bread maker to use:Lakeland Deluxe bread makerLakelandDeluxe bread makerfrom£109.99£109.99 at Lakeland£109.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIt’s easy to use and produces good loavesWhat we don’t loveThe touchscreen is quite sensitiveView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£109.99 at Lakeland£109.99 at AmazonIn my time reviewing bread makers, I’ve found the interfaces are not always the most intuitive. Thankfully, the Lakeland Deluxe bread maker is easy to use, and it makes a great loaf.Why we love itThere’s a lot to like here: it’s affordable, performance is good, and unusually, it has a colour touchscreen with pictures of each of the 12 preset baking programmes. That makes it easy to navigate without having to pore over pages of instructions.This machine makes a cracking white sandwich loaf that’s light, airy and evenly baked. Wholemeal was even better, with a rich, slightly denser crumb that still had plenty of bounce. The gluten-free loaf was also good, with a nice rise and airy crumb.The bread mixture was well kneaded and, as with other machines, I only experienced a little unmixed flour with the gluten-free loaf – though this didn’t spoil the bread and could be easily wiped off once the loaf had cooled. The paddle also stays in the pan after cooking and doesn’t leave too much of a gap in the bottom of the loaf.There’s no ingredient dispenser, but I found it easy to open the machine and add things as it was kneading, so it’s possible to include olives, nuts or chocolate chips, for example, in recipes. The Lakeland Deluxe comes with a measuring pot and spoon, as well as the bread pan and paddle. All these parts are dishwasher-safe, but I’d recommend hand-washing the pan, as baked-on crumbs can sometimes stick to the paddle attachment and these don’t come off in the dishwasher.It’s a shame that …it’s a tad noisy, and the touchscreen is sensitive, so you need to take care not to accidentally turn it off.Dimensions:36 x 22.5 x 33.5cm (WDH)Loaf sizes:500g, 750g, 900gAverage slice height:16cmTime for a white loaf:2hrs 53minsEnergy cost per loaf:8p (0.299kWh)Spare parts and repairs:spares available via theLakeland websiteWarranty:three years (if bought from Lakeland)LakelandDeluxe bread makerfrom£109.99£109.99 at Lakeland£109.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIt’s easy to use and produces good loavesWhat we don’t loveThe touchscreen is quite sensitiveBest for gluten-free bread:Sage the Custom LoafSageThe Custom Loaffrom£229.95£229.95 at John Lewis£229.95 at SageWhat we loveConsistent loaves and plenty of bonus featuresWhat we don’t loveA tad large, and the retractable paddle is temperamentalView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£229.95 at John Lewis£229.95 at SageSage’s the Custom Loaf is a standout machine, giving consistent results across a wide range of loaves.Why we love itSage’s bread machine really shines when it comes to consistency. In testing, it performed admirably with loaves that looked and tasted good. I made two lots of white, wholemeal and gluten-free bread, as well as an olive loaf to test the automatic ingredient dispenser.The dedicated gluten-free and custom dough settings make this an ideal choice for people with gluten sensitivity or coeliac disease, but the machine made some really tasty loaves across the board. The breads all held their shape well – the white loaf was light and fluffy with a fine, well-hydrated crumb, and the 100% wholemeal was denser but still very moist. I also found the custom bread setting easy to use, and the ingredient dispenser made sure the olives I added were evenly distributed throughout the dough.The shape and density of the gluten-free loaf were outstanding, similar to the results of the Panasonic mini bread maker. Gluten-free breads can have a tendency to be crumbly or flaky, and while this is partly down to finding the right recipe, it’s also important that the dough has the additional time it needs to prove and crisp. Sage provides the flexibility to tweak the settings even further if needed.This machine is also surprisingly quiet. While some have noisy mixing cycles, I barely noticed the Sage whirring away. Its size means it’s a tad intrusive on the worktop, but I can forgive that due to the variety of thoughtful features. These include cord storage at the back, and it’s the only bread maker I tested with an internal light. I also found the Custom Loaf’s screen easy to understand and navigate, something that can’t be said for many bread makers.It’s a shame that …the retractable paddle doesn’t always work as intended, sometimes staying in the up position.Dimensions:41.7 x 24.4 x 33.8cm (WDH)Loaf sizes:500g, 750g, 1kg, 1.25kg (1kg, 1.25kg for gluten-free)Average slice height:15cmTime for a white loaf:3hrs 5minsEnergy cost per loaf:8p (0.311kWh)Spare parts and repairs:available via theSage websiteWarranty: two-yearmanufacturer’s guaranteeSageThe Custom Loaffrom£229.95£229.95 at John Lewis£229.95 at SageWhat we loveConsistent loaves and plenty of bonus featuresWhat we don’t loveA tad large, and the retractable paddle is temperamentalBest bread maker for variety:Graef bread makerGraefBread makerfrom£284.95£284.95 at Harts of Stur£285 at GraefWhat we loveLovely loaves and an impressive 36 preset recipesWhat we don’t loveOne of the more expensive optionsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£284.95 at Harts of Stur£285 at GraefThe German-designed Graef bread maker is one for the enthusiasts, thanks to its eclectic mix of presets for basic white bread and more unusual loaves.Why we love itFor those who want a bread maker that goes above and beyond the standard loaf, Graef’s is the one. It has all the standard programmes for white, gluten-free and wholemeal bread, plus interesting additions such as yoghurt-honey bread, spelt buns and protein bread among its whopping 36 presets.I tested the Graef bread maker the same way as others on this list: by making my three test recipes for white, wholemeal and gluten-free bread. All three came out well, but I was particularly impressed with the shape and density of the robust-yet-bouncy wholemeal loaf. The gluten-free bread had a little unmixed flour on the outside, but almost all the bread makers I tested struggled with this. I also made an olive loaf to test the machine’s dispenser setting, and used the grain bread preset to try something a little different. I was impressed with the results, and making breads less common in the UK but popular elsewhere in Europe was fun.It’s worth mentioning that the more compact bread pans, such as those found in the Graef and Panasonic, seemed to produce more consistently shaped loaves in my tests, so consider this machine if that’s important to you. Unlike the Panasonic, the Graef bread maker does offer two loaf sizes: 500g and 750g.To my surprise, I found that the recipe presets printed on the machine’s inner lid are in German. Thankfully, waterproof stickers with corresponding English translations are included in the box. This means you won’t need to whip out Google Translate if you can’t tell your bauernbrot from your weizenbrot.It’s a shame that …it’s pricey.Dimensions:24.3 x 36.1 x 31.8cm (WDH)Loaf sizes:500g, 750gAverage slice height:15cmTime for a white loaf:3hrs 35minsEnergy cost per loaf:7p (0.274kWh)Spare parts and repairs:noneWarranty:up to two years (depending on retailer)GraefBread makerfrom£284.95£284.95 at Harts of Stur£285 at GraefWhat we loveLovely loaves and an impressive 36 preset recipesWhat we don’t loveOne of the more expensive optionsThe best of the restView image in fullscreenNot every loaf went to plan …Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianRussell Hobbs Compact Classics bread makerRussell HobbsCompact Classics bread makerfrom£79.99£100 at Argos£79.99 at AmazonWhat we loveEasy to use and makes a good white loafWhat we don’t loveNot as consistent as other models on this listView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£100 at Argos£79.99 at AmazonBest for:classic white breadWhile the Russell Hobbs machine produced some good loaves, I found the bakes weren’t as consistent as the machines featured above. It made a perfectly nice white sandwich bread with a slightly soft crust and airy crumb, but I had mixed results with the other settings. None were verging on inedible, they were just not quite as good as they could be. Nonetheless, this machine is still worth considering if you’re looking for a more affordable option that does the basics well.It’s also very easy to use. The interface has simple buttons, and it doesn’t have an overwhelming number of presets. The fast bake programme produces a loaf in about 1hr 15mins, and there’s a preset for gluten-free loaves. This is also one to consider if you prefer a larger loaf, as its two standard sizes are 750g and 1kg.It didn’t make the final cut because …results were inconsistent, despite using the same recipe.Dimensions:32.8 x 28.2 x 27.7cm (WDH);loaf sizes:750g, 1kg;average slice height:17cm;time for a white loaf:3hrs;energy cost per loaf:7p (0.271kWh);spare parts and repairs:available via theRussell Hobbs website, repairs and replacements available via support if under warranty;warranty:three-year manufacturer’s guarantee ifregistered(depending on retailer)Russell HobbsCompact Classics bread makerfrom£79.99£100 at Argos£79.99 at AmazonWhat we loveEasy to use and makes a good white loafWhat we don’t loveNot as consistent as other models on this listTefal Pain & Délices bread makerTefalPain & Délices bread makerfrom£89.98£99.99 at John Lewis£89.98 at AmazonWhat we loveGood range of loaf sizes and nice gluten-free breadWhat we don’t loveUneven browning and hot spots on crustView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£99.99 at John Lewis£89.98 at AmazonBest for:loaf sizesTefal’s compact bread maker produces a range of good loaves in three different sizes – 500g, 750g and 1kg. It made a particularly good gluten-free and white loaf, both of which had a nice shape. The main issue I faced was noticeably uneven browning on each loaf’s crust, though the insides had no signs of overcooking. Internally, the crumb was light and airy, particularly in the white loaf. The paddle does get baked into the bread if it’s not greased beforehand, but this isn’t uncommon with more affordable bread makers.The machine has a reasonable number of baking presets, and like many others on this list, can also make jam, yoghurt and pasta dough. More unusually, Tefal’s bread maker also comes with a special pot and strainer basket for making curd cheeses. If you can pick it up on offer, I’d still be tempted by this one.It didn’t make the final cut because… most of the loaves I made had uneven browning.Dimensions:29 x 31.8 x 29.8cm (WDH);loaf sizes:500g, 750g, 1kg;average slice height:16cm;time for a white loaf:3hrs 2mins;energy cost per loaf:5p (0.199kWh);spare parts and repairs:available via theTefal accessories store, repairs and replacements available through Tefal customer service;warranty:two-yearmanufacturer’s guaranteeTefalPain & Délices bread makerfrom£89.98£99.99 at John Lewis£89.98 at AmazonWhat we loveGood range of loaf sizes and nice gluten-free breadWhat we don’t loveUneven browning and hot spots on crustWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenWorth your dough: bread makers take care of the kneading, proving and baking, but finding the right recipe is key.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianHow to use a bread makerMost of the bread makers on this list offer a range of programmes for different types of bread, including white, wholemeal and gluten-free, as well as rapid settings for baking a white loaf in about an hour. You can also choose the crust colour – usually light, medium or dark – and the best bread makers have a delay timer if you want a fresh loaf ready by a specific time.Ultimately though, the most important part of using a bread maker is finding a recipe you like. Most bread makers come with a couple of basic recipes included as part of the manual and occasionally a recipe app. If they don’t, there are lots of bread-maker-specific recipes online. Just ensure the recipe size matches the loaf sizes your bread machine can make. For example, to find a good gluten-free recipe for my testing benchmarks here, I searched for a “500g and 1kg gluten-free bread maker recipe” and found theFreee Gluten Free bread recipeto be most consistent. I used the quantities for the 3-litre pan and halved them for 500g loaves.Once you have a recipe, the rest is relatively simple. For most bread makers, you add the wet ingredients first, but always check the manufacturer’s instructions, as the order can vary. Adding the wet ingredients first can help the bread paddle inside the maker mix more evenly and consistently, leaving no clumps around the edges of the pan.After this, the machine pretty much takes care of the rest, automating the mixing, kneading, proving and baking with no need to work the dough by hand or monitor the proving. You can, if manufacturer instructions permit, remove the bread maker’s paddle before the baking starts to minimise the hole in the bottom of your loaf.Once the full cycle finishes, remove the loaf from the pan and leave it to cool before slicing. If you try to cut into it while it’s still hot, the structure can tear and collapse, leaving you with broken slices and a sad-looking loaf.Can you make sourdough in a bread maker?You can make sourdough bread in some bread makers to speed up the process somewhat, but the crust and crumb structure won’t be the same as making it by hand. What’s more, as traditional sourdough relies on a live starter, which ferments dough more slowly than fast-action dried yeast, most basic bread maker presets don’t allow enough time for the dough to rise.More advanced bread makers, such as the Graef model reviewed above, have dedicated sourdough settings that automate the process and allow more proving time (although the sourdough recipes provided by Graef also use yeast and require a separate fermentation stage). You can also consider a bread maker with a custom setting, such as Sage’s the Custom Loaf, as this will allow you to set your own longer proving and bake times.What else can you make in a bread maker?Bread makers are surprisingly versatile machines once you get to know them. As well as kneading, proving and baking your bread, many models have programmes for other food prepping tasks. Most machines have presets for various mixing and cooking tasks, including anything from yoghurt and cheese to pasta dough and compote.How to buy a refurbished bread makerIf you’d rather give an old bread maker a new lease of life and save yourself a bit of money, there are plenty of refurbished and secondhand bread makers available online if you know where to look.Good places to look includeeBayandDirect Vacuums. I found arefurbished Tefal bread maker, featured in our best of the rest list, for £64.99 on the latter. You can also searchAmazon ResaleorAmazon Renewedfor secondhand and refurbished options. It’s also worth paying your local charity shops a visit, as larger ones, such as the British Heart Foundation’s, tend to sell used and tested electrical goods. Before buying secondhand, check that the appliance hasn’t been recalled, that the plug and cable are undamaged, and that all the parts are included.For more, readeverything you need to make great sourdoughand thebest stand mixers to make baking easierExplore more on these topicsBreadThe FilterBakingFoodHomesGadgetsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Low-alcohol, high-calibre: the best super-session ales | Food | The Guardian
description: Increasingly full-bodied and flavourful, low-strength British pale ales are growing in popularity, especially on the dinner table
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: Increasingly full-bodied and flavourful, low-strength British pale ales are growing in popularity, especially on the dinner table
Content: Low-alcohol session beers work really well with food.Photograph: Cavan Images/Getty Images/Cavan Images RFView image in fullscreenLow-alcohol session beers work really well with food.Photograph: Cavan Images/Getty Images/Cavan Images RFFoodLow-alcohol, high-calibre: the best super-session alesIncreasingly full-bodied and flavourful, low-strength British pale ales are growing in popularity, especially on the dinner tableMina HollandThu 22 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 08.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is nothing like discovering something for yourself to engender a fierce sense of loyalty, and that’s exactly what happened a decade ago when I fell upon the Kernel Brewery’s TableBeer, a pale ale of roughly 3% ABV. This is a brew that never fails to meet me where I am as a working parent with multiple identities but one brain, who often craves a delicious little buzz without loss of function.Kernel brewer Evin O’Riordain tells me that sales have steadily increased over the past decade, and that 2026 has seen a tipping point. “For the first time ever, Table Beer became the thing we made the most,” he says. This is entirely consistent with the population’s collective interest in no-lo drinks, although, when it comes to beer, zero-alcohol examples are much better represented than low-alcohol ones (in the major retailers, at least). There are only a handful of the latter available in supermarkets, including Small Beer’s 2.3% IPA,Jiddler’s Tipple’s 3.8% Everyday Pale Ale(both Ocado), and Beavertown Satellite (2.8%) and Dark Star’s Hophead (3.4%), both at Waitrose.So what makes a good super-session beer? Flavour and body tend to be sacrificed when alcohol is reduced or removed, so maintaining those is key. With Table Beer, O’Riordain says he was trying to emulate traditional British cask beers, albeit using “clean and neutral” American yeasts instead of “spicier” English ones, so the bright, New World hops can shine through. The result is a citrussy flavour profile (in a classic IPA, says O’Riordain, the alcohol catalyses the flavour of the hops distinctly, often becoming more tropical).Texture, meanwhile, results from residual sugar. When he mashes the beer (the process of mixing crushed grain with hot water to activate the natural enzymes that convert starches into fermentable sugars), O’Riordain does so at very high temperatures, disabling the yeast from converting all of the sugar into alcohol. The result is a beer that has the satisfying body of something stronger. A second fermentation in bottle (rather than a forced carbonation, as many breweries do) “also adds a layer of depth”, he says, even though this does increase the alcohol, but only by about 0.2%.Beavertown describes its Satellite beer as a “super session”, and most beers in that group pitch themselves as supreme session beers – although the Table Beer moniker implies something to drink with food. Always one to refer to past examples, O’Riordain says his research revealed “a whole family of low-alcohol British beers made in the 1700-1900s that were grouped together less by style than by ABV”. These included “boys bitter”, “dinner ale”, “mild beer” and, yes, “table beer”. “Strangely, the lower-alcohol things were more appropriate with food,” he says. All my picks this week are great with flavourful foods; I drank them variously with fish tacos, mattar paneer and donburi. They aren’t just good low-alcohol beers, though; they’re really excellent beers full stop.Four beers for a proper sessionTable Beer£3.25 (330ml) The Kernel Brewery, about 3%. My go-to beer, day or night, food or none; for ever and ever, amen.Beavertown Satellite Super SessionIPA£6.50 (4 x 330ml) Waitrose, 2.8%. Refreshing and soft, fruity and swiggable; eke out the sunshine with one in hand.Dark Star Brewing Co Hophead Golden Ale£2.75 (500ml) Waitrose, 3.4%. The highest ABV here, which comes through in the body, plus there’s an amazing hoppy kick to finish.Small Beer IPA£3 (330ml) Ocado,2.3%. Golden, ultra-low ABV number from a brewery that specialises in “mid-strength” brews.Explore more on these topicsFoodBeerBritish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content
