title: ​Make the most out of the last spoonful | Food | The Guardian
description: ​Before you throw away that jar with only a bit left inside, turn it into a dressing, sauce, glaze or even a drink instead
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: ​Before you throw away that jar with only a bit left inside, turn it into a dressing, sauce, glaze or even a drink instead
Content: Get the most out of that jar … Rachel Roddy’s mixed leaf salad with gorgonzola and hazelnuts.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGet the most out of that jar … Rachel Roddy’s mixed leaf salad with gorgonzola and hazelnuts.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianFeastFood​Make the most out of the last spoonful​Before you throw away that jar with only a bit left inside, turn it into a dressing, sauce, glaze or even a drink insteadSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastRachel RoddyThu 22 Oct 2026 07.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 07.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has been almost three months now, and we still haven’t replaced the cupboards that fell off the kitchen wall. It is also disturbing how well we have adapted to the chaos and having half the room covered with plastic crates that once contained vegetables and that now contain the hundreds of items that used to fit in the three cupboards, the collective weight of said items explaining the incident. The lack of cupboards has put pressure on the fridge, too, which has become a depository. That’s why, when I finally looked inside it properly, I found three jars of honey, each with between 2mm and 2cm at the bottom, as well as two jars of peanut butter, and a pretty much scraped-out jar of chocolate spread. At least all of those jars provided inspiration for today’s newsletter.Making a dressing with the last inch of honey is perhaps the most efficient and satisfying way to deal with a near-empty jar. Pour in a bit of boiling water and some lemon juice, orange juice or red-wine vinegar, screw on the lid, then shake aggressively so the honey dislodges and dissolves into a syrup. Now add everything else – olive oil, a bit of mustard and whatever else you fancy – and shake again to emulsify. This dressing is great with one of the most useful, speedy and cheap salads in existence, namely shredded red and white cabbage, grated carrot, possibly with grated apple. Alternatively, use the same dressing ona seasonal salad of radicchio, hazelnuts and gorgonzola. And if the remnants in a jar happen to be mustard, do exactly the same as above, just inverting the order and adding honey later.Felicity Cloake also suggests a dressing inher four healing honey recipes, which also function as suggestions for using the stuff up. Her suggestion of a hot toddy is great – add hot water into a jar with a centimetre of honey left, shake, then pour the now syrupy liquid into a glass or mug and add a curl of lemon peel, a knob of ginger, a cinnamon stick, a few cloves and a large dose of whisky, too, for a really effective cure. Her honey peanut butter is another way: put two tablespoons of hot water in the peanut butter jar, shake, then add honey to make a dip for celery and carrot, or add the mixture to cake batter.View image in fullscreenHealing … Felicity Cloake’s warm hot toddy.Photograph: Brent Hofacker/Getty Images/iStockphotoIt isn’t just honey, either. The most efficient way to use up the end of any jar, and especially peanut or any other nut butter, is to add a little hot water, then shake the jar violently to turn its contents into a paste. And a good way to use peanut paste is in the base of a soup (especially one with pumpkin and white beans) orwith pasta or noodles.I used to think I was controversial (and therefore interesting), until an Italian friend rolled her eyes and said that she also often makes pesto with peanut butter – pesto being a generic word for “a pounded paste”. Let me explain. In a food processor, blend a large handful of herbs (basil or parsley are ideal), a clove of garlic, salt and enough olive oil to make a paste. Then, while the pasta boils in well-salted water, add a little of the cloudy pasta water to the end of a peanut butter jar and shake to make a thick paste. Add this paste to the herb paste, stir in some grated cheese (grana padano or parmesan), and mix the lot with the cooked, drained pasta, maybe including a handful of baby spinach, which will wilt in the heat.Fuchsia Dunlop does more or less the same thing for herspicy peanut butter noodles. While dried udon cook in water, she lifts a little of the hot water into the jar, shakes to make a thick paste, then adds two to six tablespoons of chilli oil, two teaspoons of sesame oil and a minced clove of garlic, and shakes again for a sauce the consistency of single cream (if necessary, add more water). Once the noodles are done, she lifts them into a bowl, pours on the dressing, tosses well, divides the now slippery noodles between plates and tops each serving with minced spring onion and toasted sesame seeds.Next up, jars with an inch of jam in them, which can also be used in a dressing, or to thicken gravy or to add to stews. More fun and slightly more work is to make a jam tart. Dan Lepard has good advice and an excellent shortcrust pastry recipe, which he suggests turning intoindividual jam tarts. I have also used his pastry to make a large tart filled with a mixture of leftover jams and marmalades, which I tried to keep in sections, but was not very worried when they blurred into a multicoloured mess. The last bit of jam can also be loosened with a little water and used as a glaze for roast vegetables or pork chops. It is also a reason to make semolina pudding.The jar of chocolate spread that looks empty, meanwhile, should be turned into a drink: add hot milk to the jar, shake, then pour into a mug, add a bit of sugar, if required, and a generous pour of rum. Now, does anyone have the number of a good handyperson in Rome?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy week in foodView image in fullscreenThe art of cooking … Still Life With Pumpkin Flowers and Vine Leaves by Giovanna Garzoni.Photograph: AlamyWhere the art is|The most exquisite cookbook of the year is Paola Gavin’sStill Life Cookbook, a collection of vegetarian recipes inspired by great paintings. An art expert and the editor-in-chief of Epoch Review, Gavin has written many cookbooks, including the excellentItalian Vegetarian Cooking. In this, her ninth book, her two worlds meet and still-life paintings from throughout the centuries are paired with recipes. So, Giovanna Garzoni’s 17th-century Still Life With Pumpkin Flowers and Vine Leaves sits next to a recipe for flowers stuffed with ricotta and spinach. The publisher must be praised for producing such a beautiful but practical edition: the images are breathtaking, the fonts fantastic and the recipes gorgeous.The Kei to my heart|Running down Wardour Street in London’s Chinatown the other day, on our way to seeMy Neighbour Totoro, the musical (go before it finishes in January), and desperate for something good and quick to eat, I saw a “CASH ONLY” sign in the window of a restaurant. “That has to beWong Kei,” I thought, rememberingan article by Angela Hui. As promised, the setting is stark but comfortable, the service fast and functional, and the vegetarian mapo tofu with mushrooms and peas, in a soft gravy warmed with chilli on a mound of sticky rice, was exactly what we needed.Go with the grain|Last week, I had the pleasure of cooking withchef Fatmata Bintaat the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN in Rome. Originally from Sierra Leone and now working in Ghana, Binta is an award-winning culinary innovator and advocate for African agri-food systems. A particular focus of her work and advocacy is a tiny, millet-like grain called fonio that is not only densely nutritious and gluten-free but also incredibly versatile: it can be used like couscous, rice or semolina, as well as in breads, cakes and biscuits. As part of the demonstration, she made a porridge from fonio, which was new as a taste while at the same time reminding me of creamy oat porridge and semolina – made even better with the last of the jam scraped from the jar.If you want to read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive Feast in your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFoodFeastItalian food and drinkPastaSauces and graviesHerbs and spicesnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for chicken with citrus and oregano | Italian food and drink | The Guardian
description: This dish has been handed down through generations of Roman restaurateurs
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: This dish has been handed down through generations of Roman restaurateurs
Content: Rachel Roddy’s chicken braised in citrus and herbs.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenRachel Roddy’s chicken braised in citrus and herbs.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The Guardian.A kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkRachel Roddy’s recipe for chicken with citrus and oreganoThis dish of chicken in a lipsmacking citrus and oregano sauce has been handed down through many generations of Roman restaurateursRachel RoddyThu 22 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you look through the window ofPiatto Romanobetween 10am and midday, there will almost certainly be two, maybe three people at the round table trimming vegetables: chicory, artichokes, poppy greens, amaranth. After midday, the crates and trimmings will have been cleared away and the table will now be home to trays of bright-green boiled vegetables and, maybe, baked salt cod. By 12.30pm, everything will have been moved into the small kitchen in time for service, which starts at 12.45pm.When I first moved to Rome in 2005,Via Bodoni 62was home to a restaurant called Da Rafaelle, which had white plastic chairs (inside as well) and served traditional Roman food with plenty of offal. We went to Da Rafaelle a few times before it closed in 2009. But, mostly, we went toLa Torricella,which is on the other side of Testaccio and serves mainly fish. The owner is Augusto D’Alfonsi and, during lunch one day, he mentioned that he was taking over via Bodoni 62, and that his daughter Francesca would run it. They’d serve traditional Roman food with plenty of offal and it would be called Piatto Romano. This was 2011. My son was born later that year and my memories are not unpleasantly foggy; of the vegetable trolley in the corner, of chicken with red peppers and of Francesca and her father negotiating strongly. I also remember Francesca’s brother, Andrea, starting to be around more, before he eventually took over in late 2013.Andrea grew up riding his bike along the pavement in front of La Torricella, which his parents had opened in 1973, a few years before he was born. If his lunch didn’t come out of the kitchen at La Torricella, it probably came out of the kitchen atDa Antonioon Via dei Pastini, where Andrea’s maternal grandma cooked, or from the kitchen of his maternal grandfather’s restaurant,Da Giovannion Via dei Barbieri. As a teenager, Andrea also ate at his paternal grandfather’s osteria,Gran Sassoin Trastevere, and in the various branches ofInsalata Ricca, a chain of salad restaurants opened by his entrepreneurial uncle Gino in the 1980s. All the various parts of the family have Abruzzese roots, but Andrea mentions Gino, eccentric and single-minded about history, vegetables and nutrition, as being a particular influence.The way Andrea continues to evolve Piatto Romano (which for many is the embodiment of an ideal Roman trattoria) would require several columns. For now, though, I will note his singlemindedness about the vegetables he picks up every day from his various sources. The other night, we had courgette greens – a little hairy and very succulent – with Leprino rabbit (typical of the Tuscia area of Viterbo) braised in wine and citrus, which produces a lipsmacking sauce/gravy. And head chef Umberto Mussato, who has worked with Andrea since 2021, has adapted his recipe for this column, but using chicken instead of rabbit. The dish is made even more tasty by the addition of three to five anchovy fillets mashed with a tablespoon of red-wine vinegar, plus a sprig of fresh thyme or oregano, which is then left to sit for at least half an hour before it’s served with greens and potatoes, if you wish.Chicken with citrus and herbsServes41.2kg skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs(or a mix of legs and thighs)Salt4tbsp olive oil100-150ml dry white wine1 tspdried thyme or oregano400ml fresh citrus juice– a mix of orange, lemon, grapefruit, mandarin3-5 anchovies mashedwith 1tbspgood-quality red-wine vinegarA few stalksfresh oreganoSeason the chicken with salt, rubbing it into the skin. Working in a heavy-based pan, warm the olive oil, then brown the chicken pieces in batches so as not to overcrowd the pan. Once all the pieces are brown, look at the amount of fat in the pan – I suggest leaving it all in there, but remove some, if you prefer.Return all the browned chicken to the pan, raise the heat and add the wine, which should sizzle and evaporate. Add the dried oregano or thyme, stir, then pour over the citrus juice. Lower the heat so the pan simmers, then cover.Leave the chicken to cook for 45 minutes to an hour, lifting the lid to turn the pieces every now and then, then lift off the lid and cook for another 20 minutes, so the sauce can reduce. By the end of the cooking, the chicken should be tender and the sauce thick. (If the sauce needs significant reduction, remove the chicken, simmer hard so the sauce reduces to your liking, then return the chicken pieces to the pan.)To finish, stir in the anchovies mashed in vinegar and a sprig of fresh thyme or oregano, then leave to sit for 30 minutes before serving.Explore more on these topicsItalian food and drinkA kitchen in RomeFoodChickenMain courseWineHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: A financially comfortable friend has set up a GoFundMe for vet bills. Is this socially acceptable? | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: Your friends may have had good intentions when making this request, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. But that needn’t dictate how you feel about it
Author: Eleanor Gordon-Smith
Headline: Your friends may have had good intentions when making this request, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. But that needn’t dictate how you feel about it
Content: ‘In [your friend’s] social circle, they may be the least well-off, which would change the dynamics of making this ask,’ writes Eleanor Gordon-Smith. Painting: Dog of the Havana Breed by Jean-Jacques Bachelier.Photograph: © The Bowes Museum, Barnard Castle/The Bowes Museum, Barnard CastleView image in fullscreen‘In [your friend’s] social circle, they may be the least well-off, which would change the dynamics of making this ask,’ writes Eleanor Gordon-Smith. Painting: Dog of the Havana Breed by Jean-Jacques Bachelier.Photograph: © The Bowes Museum, Barnard Castle/The Bowes Museum, Barnard CastleLeading questionsAustralian lifestyleA financially comfortable friend has set up a GoFundMe for vet bills. Is this socially acceptable?Your friends may have had good intentions when making this request, writes advice columnistEleanor Gordon-Smith.But that needn’t dictate how you feel about itRead moreLeading questionsEleanor Gordon-SmithThu 22 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA friend, who I believe is financially comfortable, set up a GoFundMe page to pay for vet bills for their sick dog while on holiday overseas.The family appears to be financially comfortable; both adults have good jobs, own two cars, have all the latest gadgets like expensive bikes and sporting equipment, take an annual holiday overseas and domestic holidays throughout the year, and live in a big house in a well-to-do area.Is it socially acceptable to ask for money publicly in these circumstances?Eleanor says:I’ll never forget someone posting their household expenses as proof it’s hard to get by on two six-figure incomes. By the time they’d paid for holidays, two cars, private school fees, insurance, extracurriculars, the mortgage and savings, there was nothing left!They really did think this was proof they weren’t well-off. I suppose in some sense they’re right. Once you use your money to secure your financial future and have a high quality of life, you don’t have a Scrooge McDuck pile left over.I have a crippling fear of being judged. How can I overcome this? | Leading questionsRead morePoint of story: moving up the wealth hierarchy moves your sense of what’s normal. Comparison looks up, not down, so people lose track of how many peoplethey’reabove. What they first experienced as an advantage slowly starts to seem like background. It’s possible your friends feel and are genuinely burdened – “we can’t cover this!” – in a situation other people would covet. And importantly, we don’t know their finances. They may not be liquid, precisely because of the holidays and the house and the equipment.But in the ethics of asking for and giving money, it’s important that money isn’t just money. It has social meaning. Money talks, in the sense that it says things.What it says isn’t always exhausted by how much people have. It may be important for the less well-off child to take their parents to dinner because that says“thank you”. Or for colleagues or dates to split the bill, because that meansneither owes a debt of gratitude. Or to help pay for your child’s wedding even though they could afford it themselves, because that feels significant as a parent.Where we go wrong is when our interpretations of what money says differ. Somebody thinks they’re being generous; others experience their largesse as domineering. Somebody – like a newlywed drafting the gift registry or, possibly, your friend – thinks they’re making it possible for people to give them money without any expectation of receiving it. Others experience that same action as tone-deaf and entitled.If money talks, what does their GoFundMe actually say?They might feelas if it says one thing: “Something unexpected happened, we’d be touched if anyone wanted to contribute.” You might feel as if it says another: “We expect you to cover our bills.” One is an appeal to friendship, the other is an appeal to need.In fairness, a GoFundMe isn’t means-tested. They can ask, and other people can say no. In their social circle, they may be the least well-off, which would change the dynamics of making this ask.They’re the authority on what they meant when they uploaded this, but they don’t get to be the authority on what everybody else hears. Meaning isn’t determined solely by our intentions. Their motivations might have been totally benign at the same time as their impact was gauche.Asking for money introduces a question that nobody had beforehand;why should I help pay for this?They may think that’s a mean-spirited question, if they intended this as an appeal to friendship. But it’s a question they’ve invited people to ask, and you’re allowed to decide your own answer.Ask Eleanor a questionShare your questionTell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.NameWhat is your question for Eleanor?Email addressYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.By submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreExplore more on these topicsAustralian lifestyleLeading questionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: You be the judge: should my husband stop letting our cat drink on the kitchen counter? | Pets | The Guardian
description: James says Tony leaving the cat’s water bowl where they prepare food is unhygienic. Should they feed their feline on the floor? You decide
Author: Georgina Lawton
Headline: James says Tony leaving the cat’s water bowl where they prepare food is unhygienic. Should they feed their feline on the floor? You decide
Content: Illustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianYou be the judgePetsYou be the judge: should my husband stop letting our cat drink on the kitchen counter?James says Tony leaving the cat’s water bowl where they prepare food is unhygienic. Should they feed their feline on the floor? You decideFind out how to get a disagreement settled or become a jurorInterviews byGeorgina LawtonThu 22 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheprosecution: Jamesdouble quotation markIt’s unhygienic. The cat will jump out of her litter box and on to the surface where we prepare foodI’ve been married to Tony for 10 years. We understand each other’s quirks, but he is a very intense person with many passions, and one of his passions is cats.We have three cats, adopted from Brazil. Growing up, I was a dog person, but I also used to rescue stray cats, so I love them too. But Tony is obsessed.We also had a dog, Jamie, but he died recently. He developed a digestive problem, aged 14, because he over-ate. He often ate the cats’ food, so we moved the cats’ bowls up on to the counter next to the kitchen sink to stop this. One cat, Juçara, got particularly used to eating and drinking up there.Now the dog isn’t around, but Tony will still leave the water bowl on the kitchen counter. I find it unhygienic. Juçara will jump straight out of her litter box and on to the surface where we prepare food. It’s too much.double quotation markTony has to try harder – he only left her water on the floor for three daysWe moved recently and I said to Tony I’d like things to change and that we should start feeding the cats on the floor again. Tony said that was fine, but during the first week he still left Juçara’s food and water on the counter. I realised then that it had become a habit and an expression of how much he cares for this cat.Tony also often lets all the cats eat on the table, and I don’t like that either. We live in an apartment, so the cats don’t go outside and are fairly clean, but there’s cat hair everywhere, even though we vacuum a lot. I’m not picky, but I’d like to reduce the amount of cat hair in my food.Tony says Juçara won’t drink water from the floor any more and he’s worried about her. I think the cat could be trained: she would drink from anywhere if she was thirsty, but she has to be given the opportunity to change. Tony only left her water on the floor for three days before moving it back up to the counter. He has to try harder.It’s funny, because Tony always says Juçara loves me more even though I am strict with her. Tony loves her, but she ignores him. Juçara is my bestie, but I need her off the countertop.You be the judge – send us your domestic disputesRead moreThedefence: Tonydouble quotation markThis is more about James wantinga tidy home than hygiene – he doesn’t like to see abowl out of placeI realise I’ve started a bad habit and I don’t deny anything James has said, except his claim that he doesn’t like cats on our table: I think he finds it cute. I also find the sound of the cats drinking water very relaxing.When the cat is drinking water, I’ll say to James: “Stop what you’re doing and just listen to her.” There are few things as relaxing as the sound of a hydrating cat. Only Juçara drinks water on the countertop. We can’t control that. Because James loves Juçara so much and she loves him, I think he should let it go. It’s a very small thing to concede.If he can’t, I like the idea of putting water bowls in different places around our home. We did that in our previous place, but Juçara only liked drinking at a certain height. I don’t know why; it’s just her personality.double quotation markI got a special water fountain for cats, but James didn’t like the buzzing noise it madeI am worried that she won’t drink at all if we only leave the water bowls on the floor. At the moment, Juçara will jump on to the counter and go to the sink to wait for her bowl of water, so I just give it to her. I got a special water fountain for cats, but I had to take it out of the apartment as James didn’t like the buzzing noise it made.We’ve been leaving bowls on the counter for ages: this is only a problem now because we’ve moved to a new place, and I said I’d change my ways. But I think the issue is more about how James organises our home than hygiene. He doesn’t like to see a cup or bowl out of place; he’s much tidier than me. But this is only a bowl filled with water on the counter. It’s not a big deal, but he doesn’t like to see a bowl left out.James is Juçara’s favourite, but she ignores me. I think that’s what love is: doing something for someone again and again even though it’s not reciprocated. James and I work in the same company, but I come home first and put the water out for the cat so he doesn’t see. I do the same in the morning at 7am, before James wakes up. I will always do this for Juçara and I will always defend her. If she needs me, I’m there.Names have been changedskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe jury of Guardian readersWhile I support Tony’s pet care, cat hair in food areas is unpleasant. The home belongs to James too. Tony could try leaving the water on the floor longer, or commit to cleaning the kitchen counters more regularly.Serrena, 31Tony saying “There’s few things as relaxing as the sound of a hydrating cat” makes me want to be on his side. But I can’t agree to kitties on counters. I’m a cat lover, but the idea of them pawing around food preparation or dining areas is a cardinal sin. Tony has to concede.Maddie, 28Tony shouldn’t view himself as defending Juçara against James. They need to work as a team, and not have Tony sneaking about while James is asleep. Try properly with the water on the floor. Or if a raised location is important (it makes some cats feel safer), perhaps try a windowsill.Imogen, 19Cats on worktops aren’t ideal, but Tony tries hard to strike a balance – keeping Juçara content and James happy. When clever Juçara asks for a drink (and Tony’s love, clearly), a countertop bowl is fine. But once she’s done, the bowl belongs on the floor. Sharing the dining table is downright unnecessary.Frank, 40Tony, Juçara respects James because cats are fur-natical about hygiene. Give Juçara a chance to form some new habits, which takes at least a month. So put the water somewhere hygienic where she will not contaminate her loving owners with parasites!Maria,49Now you be the judgeIn our online poll, tell us:should the cat be brought down to earth?The poll closes on Wednesday 28 October at 9amGMTLast week’s resultsWe asked whether Abdeen shouldstop looking up menus before eating outwith his wife.11%of you said yes –Abdeen is guilty89%of you said no –Abdeen is innocentExplore more on these topicsPetsYou be the judgefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I wanted to create the female version of a man’s suit’: how Roland Mouret’s Galaxy dress took over the world | Fashion | The Guardian
description: One the most famous dresses of this century, it was worn by royalty and A-list celebrities in the noughties. Its latest fans are Maga women. Here, the designer, and former mentor to Victoria Beckham, reveals the story behind it
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: One the most famous dresses of this century, it was worn by royalty and A-list celebrities in the noughties. Its latest fans are Maga women. Here, the designer, and former mentor to Victoria Beckham, reveals the story behind it
Content: Halle Berry, Beyoncé and Dita Von Teese in Roland Mouret Galaxy dresses.Composite: MediaPunch/Getty Images/WireImageView image in fullscreenHalle Berry, Beyoncé and Dita Von Teese in Roland Mouret Galaxy dresses.Composite: MediaPunch/Getty Images/WireImageFashion‘I wanted to create the female version of a man’s suit’: how Roland Mouret’s Galaxy dress took over the worldOne the most famous dresses of this century, it was worn by royalty and A-list celebrities in the noughties. Its latest fans are Maga women. Here, the designer, and former mentor to Victoria Beckham, reveals the story behind itMark C. O'FlahertyThu 22 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe story of one of the most photographed and ripped-off dresses of the last 50 years came together with a simple zip. It was 1998; the designer Roland Mouret had shown his first collection at London fashion week and was looking for a way to produce good clothes at speed. He connected with a small British atelier and it was there that some old-school industry wisdom would alter his course: he learned that a longer seam doesn’t actually cost any more than a shorter one.Despite his brilliantly instinctive approach to design, it was like cracking a code – and steered him towards the dress that would make his name. “My brain was buzzing!” he says. “I hadn’t thought about it before – if you extend a top by 50cm, it becomes a whole outfit. You just need accessories. Focusing on dresses gives you a signature piece at the right price.”The hyper-bodycon Galaxy dress, with its industrial zip on the back, was born, embedding itself in the public consciousness via the backs of Beyoncé, Halle Berry andVictoria Beckham. Creating a singular silhouette, it helped Mouret define the look of the late 90s and early 2000s in London as much as John Galliano or Alexander McQueen did a few years before him.View image in fullscreenNaomi Watts in the Galaxy dress in 2005.Photograph: James Devaney/WireImage“I really earned my two lines in the fashion bible,” says Mouret, whose new autobiography, I Am Roland Mouret – The Butcher’s Boy Who Dressed the World, documents the era. “It had what we call in French ‘the lunch neckline’, with the sharpness of a table, and a waistline cinched in like that of an iconic 1950s actress, but comfortable and not too girlie. It had masculinity.”While Elizabeth Hurley culturally ownedthatVersace safety pin dress after wearing it on the red carpet in 1994, leaving its second life solely to museums, the Galaxy reappeared in Mouret’s collections “in the colour and fabric of the season” for years – and continued to be seen on a who’s who of Hollywood, from Scarlett Johansson to Naomi Watts.“I always saw the people I was dressing from the back,” he says now over a video call from his home in London. “I wanted to position myself behind them so I could see their point of view. The zip was part of that – it was at the back of the dress. As soon as you see a face, your imagination stops and the real person is there.” It was a way of designing clothes that he would later impart as a mentor to Victoria Beckham; the Galaxy’s silhouette could be seen in her early collections.In the book, which is a candid and moving account of his life in rural France, Paris and London, Mouret writes about sexual exploration as a teenager. It would become part of the R&D for the Galaxy: “I had sex with women but knew I wasn’t straight,” he says. “It was a collaboration. I wasn’t trying to prove my masculinity, it was just an amazing experience, discovering a body in a carnal way. The dress was about equality. I wanted to create the female version of a man’s suit.” One of the celebrities who wore it, Dita Von Teese, who Mouret describes as “an athlete”, epitomised the woman who suited it best after a period of size zero ubiquity.View image in fullscreenDita Von Teese at the Elle Style awards in 2006.Photograph: MJ Kim/Getty ImagesThe way the Galaxy fastened was practical, but also part of the pleasure of wearing it. It was literally sensational. “It was lined in power mesh fabric,” says Mouret, “and when you unzip it at the back, whether yourself or with your partner, the flesh jumps out – it’s a rollercoaster of carnal experience, an explosion of emotion.”But while Mouret describes the zip as about “strength and choice”, some notable women chose to wear it minus the hardware. Catherine, Princess of Wales, had one made without it because, when faced with paparazzi, it was a weak spot. Ditto the female president on House of Cards, Claire Underwood. The actor Robin Wright, who played her, explained to Mouret that his usual gold zip needed to go. In the book she explains: “I love it as a woman but as a woman in charge, a female president … that part of me has to be invisible.”Perversely, some of Mouret’s Galaxy energy is now evident on podiums in Trump’s America. While the Galaxy is no longer being made new, similar sheath dresses by the Mouret label are still finding their way on to women including Ivanka, Melania and Lara Trump. And that bodycon silhouette,favoured by so many in the Trump administration, which has always been severe, now connotes a Trumpian aesthetic and style of politics, accented with extreme eyelashes, ironed hair and injectables.View image in fullscreenIvanka Trump, wearing a Mouret sheath dress, and husband Jared Kushner.Photograph: Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty ImagesDoes Mouret know why the look has been co-opted? “Fashion is just a reflection of the sociopolitics of its time,” he says. What “[Maga women] wear is extreme now. The clothes are so tight, and heels so high, that you couldn’t run from anything to protect yourself. The future is fear, and the look is decadent.”The past was a better-looking place, according to the memoir, which documents the optimism and subsequent collapse of possibilities in fashion for independent designers. But the book is a full stop on fashion as Mouret knew and lived it – it doesn’t define him today. He is no longer at the helm of his brand: after Covid depth-charged his niche of eveningwear and event dressing, the label went into administration in 2021 and then changed hands. Mouret now describes himself as a queer artist, and a lot of his imagery still harks back to being the rural butcher’s son who wanted to explore bodies regardless of gender.View image in fullscreen‘It was a dress born out of my collective consciousness’ … Roland Mouret.Photograph: Vianney Le CaerClothes are still made with Mouret’s name sewn into them, but they are not his. It’s unlikely lightning will be caught in a bottle again. As he says in the book: “The Galaxy proved to me that my signature was not my name, but my technique.”In 2015, 10 years after the dress first appeared, customers could buy one for £1,750 new. Now you can get one on resale sites for not much more than £200. Its time has passed, but it has also passed into fashion history, along with Mouret’s journey. It was autobiographical. As he writes in the book: “It was a dress born out of my collective consciousness; it was my mum getting dressed in the morning, it was my dad’s precision with meat, fat and bone.” It was the product of his biggest inspirations, Azzedine Alaïa and Yohji Yamamoto, filtered through his psyche. “Making it,” he writes, “was like the moment you find yourself speaking another language without thinking.”I Am Roland Mouret – The Butcher’s Boy who Dressed the World is published on 22 October by Quercus (£25). To support the Guardian buy a copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsFashionCelebrityVictoria BeckhamfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Some enchanted evenings: 10 of the best after-dark adventures for families in the UK  | Travel | The Guardian
description: The clocks go back this weekend, so embrace the longer nights with these family-friendly activities and events, from a stargazing festival to moonlit crazy golf
Author: Annabelle Thorpe
Headline: The clocks go back this weekend, so embrace the longer nights with these family-friendly activities and events, from a stargazing festival to moonlit crazy golf
Content: The Enchanted Forest in Faskally Wood, Pitlochry.Photograph:   Ian Georgeson/ Ian Georgeson PhotographyView image in fullscreenThe Enchanted Forest in Faskally Wood, Pitlochry.Photograph:   Ian Georgeson/ Ian Georgeson PhotographyTravelSome enchanted evenings: 10 of the best after-dark adventures for families in the UKThe clocks go back this weekend, so embrace the longer nights with these family-friendly activities and events, from a stargazing festival to moonlit crazy golfAnnabelle ThorpeThu 22 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 14.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Enchanted Forest, ScotlandLegend has it that Faskally Forest – the Pitlochry location of Scotland’s most famous sound and light show – steals an hour from time itself every 25 years. This year marks a quarter of a century since the first Enchanted Forest, and the theme taps into the legend: Stop the Clock: The 25th Hour. The trail is a mystical, atmospheric wander through jewel-hued woodland, with misbehaving clocks, time-themed installations and immersive soundscapes creating the sense of a dreamlike world. There are autism-friendly sessions and free carers’ tickets and an accessibility bus for those with mobility issues.Until8 Nov, adults from£28.50, kids from£15.50, family from£78.50,including shuttle bus to and from the eventNorth PenninesstargazingfestivalView image in fullscreenEven a beginner stargazer will find it easy to navigate an autumn night sky, when the stars are at their clearest and constellations such as Orion’s Belt and the Plough flicker and gleam with an iridescent glow. The North Pennines has some of thedarkest skiesin the country, along with the highest number of officialDark Skies discovery sitesin the UK – 16 – making the region’s stargazing festival one of the best. Choose from afamily astronomy eventat Grassholme Observatory (pictured), adark skies strollor stargazing onAlston Moor. All events need to be booked in advance.Until1 Nov, prices varyRiver of Light, LiverpoolView image in fullscreenPhotograph: TiltThe banks of the Mersey and some of Liverpool’s most iconic spots blaze with colour during this annual free outdoor light art festival, which brings together 13 original works on the theme of “together”.Installationsinclude 6-metre high peonies at the Cunard Building, which remain white by day but glow with ever-changing colours after dark, and Dream Herd, a floating cloud of sheep with interactive “legs” that trigger lighting and sound changes when touched. Over on Williamson Square, Pop! consists of five tall, colourful boxes that spring open like jack-in-the-boxes when people clap, sing or talk to them, revealing inflatable puppets. The installations will light up from 5pm–9pm each night, with quiet hours 4pm-5pm on 28 Oct and 1 Nov.23 Oct – 1 Nov,freeNocturnal wildlife adventures, across the UKView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Mick Durham FRPS/AlamyFrom badger banquets to batwatching safaris, many wildlife trusts and nature reserves run special late openings and events at this time of year to allow visitors to enjoy the nocturnal activities of their resident species. At RSPB Frampton Marsh in Lincolnshire you can look out for hunting owls, marsh harriers and starling murmurations on asunset walk(fortnightly on Saturdays, adults £19, adult members £15.50, children £10), while RSPB Mersehead in Dumfries and Galloway will be running its popularbadger banquets, where visitors can observe the shy mammals feeding through the glass windows of the reserve’s Sulwath Centre (24 & 30 Oct, 6, 14 & 20 Nov, adults £28, adult RSPB members £22.60, children £14.50). The Kent Wildlife Trust is hosting a familybat detecting eventat Sevenoaks Wildlife Reserve (29 Oct, £10pp) which includes hot drinks in the visitor centre and a guided night hike with bat detectors.Search for more eventson the RSPB’sDusk Discoveries pageMystical Marsh Lantern Experience, GloucestershireView image in fullscreenNature gets super-sized at this refreshingly un-Halloween-themed lantern trail at Slimbridge wetland centre, where giant frogs loom out of illuminated ponds, bats and kingfishers hover and swoop in the tree canopy and luminous giant bugs glitter between flaming scarlet fungi. Each creature is handmade and inspired by real wetland wildlife, with wings, fur and scales transformed into light sculptures. Arrive early to fuel up on street food at the Kingfisher Kitchen, or save yourself for toasted marshmallows around the firepit. Kids can make their own lanterns and the buggy-friendly trail takes about 45 minutes to explore.Until 1 Nov,£14.95ppLightpoolfestival, BlackpoolView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Gregg Wolstenholme/Bav MediaThe original (and some would say best) location for autumn illuminations, Blackpool is celebrating 10 years of the Lightpool festival, with interactive installations, illuminated artworks and live performances across the city. TheLight Art Trailincludes walk-through tunnels of light, glowing stone circles and glittering “sky orchards”. A specially designedVR arenaat the Winter Gardens conjures spectacular visuals, while the Firefly Field uses LEDs to creates the illusion of hundreds of beetles hovering and darting above the ground.Until31 Oct,6pm-9pm,freeskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGo ApeSundown Adventures,variouslocationsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Culture Manual LtdAs if scrambling across rope bridges and whizzing down from treetops isn’t challenging enough in daylight, every autumn more than 20 of the Go Ape high ropes courses open up for an evening adventure. This year, for the first time, there are adults-only sessions atselected locations, but the continuous belay harness system means the course is reassuringly safe for families and suitable for all children over six. The course is illuminated and takes about an hour to complete.Until 8 Nov, but dates vary according to location, from £31.95pp.Min height 1.2m;max weight 130kgAfter Darkat Heatherton, WalesView image in fullscreenPolish up your putting with a spot of moonlit golf at Heatherton World of Activities near Tenby, where the 18-hole Pirates of the Caribbean-themed course will take on a distinctly different feel, with atmospheric lighting and music. It’s just one of the After Dark offerings, along with climbing the Tree Tops tower before stepping off into the pitch black and whizzing down the 165-metre zipline, with the park illuminated below. For older kids, the Heatherton maze has been transformed into the full-on Institute of Terror – a not-so-abandoned asylum with live scare actors.Until31 Oct, prices vary according to activityGhosttrainadventure,SussexView image in fullscreenThis immersive rail adventure at the Bluebell Railway whisks passengers into the past to unravel a 100-year-old mystery of an engine explosion, a derailed train and a possible injustice as to who got the blame. The station platforms are peopled with characters from that fateful day in 1926, while clues about the real perpetrator wait to be discovered, and the air is thick with rumours of ghostly figures on empty platforms and the sound of a steam train that never appears. Spooky rather than properly scary, this is ideal for older children, with plenty of chances to interact with characters and explore independently.Until 1 Nov,adults from £42, children from £21Dinos After Dark, HertfordshireView image in fullscreenGet ready for a Jurassic Park-style adventure with an after-hours visit to the World of Dinosaurs, where 40 life-size, animatronic dinos roam and roar; all the more terrifying when they loom out of the darkness. The woodland trail winds past a pair of towering T rexes, stegosaurus and the startling, dome-headed pachycephalosaurus, with velociraptors springing out and flying reptiles swinging through the trees. Alongside the trail, UV-lit Halloween drummers provide a thrilling soundtrack, with face painting, a silent disco and glitter tattoos also on offer.23Oct–1 Nov,£18.99ppExplore more on these topicsTravelFamilyHalloweenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Thursday news quiz: Liz is absurd, Apu finds words and a bloke steals a bird | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Test yourself on topical news trivia, pop culture and general knowledge every Thursday. How will you fare?
Author: Martin Belam

Content: This pink flamingo has got some questions for you.Photograph: JackF/Getty/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenThis pink flamingo has got some questions for you.Photograph: JackF/Getty/iStockphotoThursday quizLife and styleThursday news quiz: Liz is absurd, Apu finds words and a bloke steals a birdTest yourself on topical news trivia, pop culture and general knowledge every Thursday. How will you fare?Martin BelamThu 22 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Thursday quiz is aware of standard international units of time, such as the Liz Truss (49 days) and the Scaramucci (11 days). Now a new unit of measurement has entered the chat: the Zacharia (five days). But whatever arbitrary length of time the world invents to measure chaos, political downfalls or social media meltdowns, the Thursday news quiz remains resolutely fixed. It is always seven days apart, unwavering, inescapable and ultimately reliable. Which means, once again, it is time for some questions on topical news, pop culture and general knowledge, with no prizes on offer except pride. Or shame.Allons-y!The Thursday news quiz, No 2701.Which province of Canada held a referendum this week on whether it should have a binding referendum on declaring independence from the country?OntarioNew BrunswickNova ScotiaAlbertaReveal2.Archaeologists believe they have solved the mystery of whose bones were buried in a Roman sarcophagus unearthed at Westminster Abbey. Who was it?A 9th-century Mercian princessAn 11th-century abbotCenturion Valerius Amandinus30-50 feral hogsReveal3.Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's film about Elizabeth Holmes (pictured) had the biggest documentary debut since 2004 in North America, taking in $15m. What is it called?One Single DropYou Can See EverythingBad BloodWould You Like To Invest Heavily Because I Have A Bridge I'd Like To Sell YouReveal4.The Thursday quiz loves trains and saw this lovely steam locomotive in Leicester the other day. But which city in the north of England is to get a brand new station as part of the Northern Powerhouse Rail scheme?Royston VaseyHalifaxYorkBradfordReveal5.Japan (pictured) has launched a space mission to gather rocks from which moon of Mars (also pictured)?PhobosDeimosAnterosDerekReveal6.A man has been found guilty of animal cruelty after he stole a 27-year-old flamingo from its enclosure at a Las Vegas hotel. What is the bird's name?PetalPeachyPinkyPeggyReveal7.Send Derren Brown today's collective noun. Use your psychic powers to let him know what, according to Grammar Monster, the collective noun for jaguars is (the animal, not the car).A stalkA prowlA slinkA confusionReveal8.This week's guest canine is Spanner, who the Thursday quiz met in Crouch End. She wants to know the name of the silly bomb-sniffing dog in Utah who accidentally broke several bones when he inexplicably leapt over the side of an overpass while out on a mission?AntonCraigLenBrunoReveal9.It is Jeff Goldblum's birthday today. Happy birthday, Jeff! Jurassic Park! What's the name of his character in the dinosaur-infused franchise?David LevinsonFitz KreinerSeth BrundleIan MalcolmReveal10.Apu has his voice back on The Simpsons. Who now voices the character?Utkarsh AmbudkarKaran SoniKunal NayyarSunil MalhotraReveal11.The Thursday quiz fondly remembers Keith Chegwin, so here is Cheggers plays population! According to the 2026 CIA World Factbook, what is the population of Algeria?27.7 million47.7 million67.7 million87.7 millionReveal12.England's lady egg chasers (pictured in training) lost their first rugby union match after four years and 41 games unbeaten. Who bested them?AustraliaNew ZealandCanadaSouth AfricaReveal13.A bear in California's Mono county wandered into where to raid the staff snacks and check out the new releases?A libraryA record storeA video game storeA book storeReveal14.On this day with Brian May! And his badger! 22 October is the anniversary of a war fought between Britain and Spain from 1739 to 1748, mostly in the Caribbean. The Thursday quiz imagines Queen's legendary guitarist wants you to tell him – and his badger – what it was called.The war of the stray dogThe war of the bucketThe war of Jenkins' earThe lobster warReveal15.The Thursday quiz regrets to inform you that Liz Truss is at it again, with a new book. What is it called?Inside JobBank JobOne-Woman JobHack JobReveal16.Bonus question: There is a new Doctor Who story that features a dachshund on the cover, and the writer, Jez Fielder, has posed you this question: In Anton Chekhov’s The Lady with the Little Dog, the lady’s dog is never named. Big Finish’s latest Doctor Who audio drama, The Beasts of Sakhalin Island, gives Chekhov a dog and finally supplies a name, the same as the lady herself. What is it?KaterinaNatashaAnnaSonyaRevealIf you really do think there has been an egregious error in one of the questions or answers – and can show your working and are absolutely 100% positive you aren’t attempting to factcheck a joke – you can complain about it in the comments below. title: Country diary: From Mexico’s Day of the Dead to a Shropshire allotment | Plants | The Guardian
description: The Marches, Shropshire: Symbolically a flower of the ancestor-honouring Mexican festival, the dahlia appeals to the British gardener’s appetite for the spectacular
Author: Paul Evans
Headline: The Marches, Shropshire: Symbolically a flower of the ancestor-honouring Mexican festival, the dahlia appeals to the British gardener’s appetite for the spectacular
Content: The dahlia in Paul Evans’ allotment ‘is the size of a plate and the brightest orange, like Mark Rothko’s painting No. 210/No. 211’.Photograph: Maria Nunzia @VarveraView image in fullscreenThe dahlia in Paul Evans’ allotment ‘is the size of a plate and the brightest orange, like Mark Rothko’s painting No. 210/No. 211’.Photograph: Maria Nunzia @VarveraCountry diaryPlantsCountry diary: From Mexico’s Day of the Dead to a Shropshire allotmentThe Marches, Shropshire: Symbolically a flower of the ancestor-honouring Mexican festival, the dahlia appeals to the British gardener’s appetite for the spectacularPaul EvansThu 22 Oct 2026 00.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGardeners are a deviant lot. Despite our passion for wildlife gardening and the drive to be sustained by, and share, our own fruit and veg, our appetite for novelty, aberrancy and even the spectacularly monstrous is insatiable.Take a look at this. The flower is the size of a plate and the brightest orange, likeMark Rothko’s painting No. 210/No. 211 (Orange), with a kind of vibrating stillness, maybe the colour of a sugar maple in autumn sunlight. The ray florets are a mass of long, pointed, half‑curled petals, wildly dancing, writhing away from the central boss of golden disc florets.This exotic vision is adahlia. We bought a bag of dahlia tubers from the supermarket and planted them in the allotment back in May. We lost the label and, anyway, they grew into three different varieties together, so we’d be none the wiser. One was a small white-tinged pink pompom that flowered in the heatwave, another was a larger white-orange-yellow ball and now this, a semi-cactus in audacious orange.These flower shapes are part of a dahlia culture that has flourished since their introduction from Mexico in the 18th century. The semi-cactus type originated from a single tuber ofDahlia juareziisent to Holland in 1872. Since then, hybridisation from all forms of dahlia seeds has resulted in 50,000 varieties.Although the dahlia’s position in gardening fashions waxes and wanes, dahlias are respectable again, but they have long been an allotment favourite as a cut-flower crop or grown competitively for shows. Our allotment neighbour has rows of gorgeous blooms and immaculate veg in the vernacular tradition.The stories dahlias have travelled with add to their exoticism. Their symbolic role as the flower ofDía de los Muertos(Day of the Dead) has made them the national flower of Mexico, and the festival’s link to Halloween is a potent folklore connection. Even so, the marigold is more historically correct as the primary flower of los Muertos.Much of what we read about dahlia history from the Aztec and Inca periods is myth, curated by European imperialists. Nevertheless, just like tomatoes, also fromMexico, funky and transgressive dahlias now have a special place in the traditions of British allotments and in our deviant little hearts.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsPlantsCountry diaryAutumnShropshireRural affairsMexicofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: US military failed to notify UK police of drink-driving allegation against airman based in England | Suffolk | The Guardian
description: British authorities were unable to investigate case of Christopher Mooty, who went on to commit another offence
Author: Rob Evans
Headline: British authorities were unable to investigate case of Christopher Mooty, who went on to commit another offence
Content: The failure to notify British police broke a longstanding formal agreement.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe failure to notify British police broke a longstanding formal agreement.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesBase justiceSuffolkUS military failed to notify UK police of drink-driving allegation against airman based in EnglandBritish authorities were unable to investigate case of Christopher Mooty, who went on to commit another offenceRob Evans,Emine Sinmaz,Harry DaviesandLouisa LoveluckThu 22 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 05.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUS militaryfailed to notify British police of an allegation that one of its airmen had been drink-driving in Suffolk, preventing the British authorities from being able to investigate the offence.The failure broke a longstanding formal agreement with British police that enables the UK to investigate alleged illegality by US military personnel who are stationed in Britain.The airman, Christopher Mooty, had spent the night drinking with two other American service personnel in a market town before driving them to buy a kebab in the early hours of the morning.The allegation of drink-driving was later reported to his commanders, who then used their own internal processes to discipline him.The case raises questions over how many other US military personnel based in the UK have committed crimes that have not been flagged to British police forces.Mooty went on to commit a second drink-driving offence a year later. This time he was prosecuted in a British court.The latest disclosures are part of the Guardian’s investigation into crimes carried out by American military personnel who are based in Britain.The series prompted the UK government and police chiefsto set up a high-level inquiryin the summer to establish whether US military personnel stationed in Britain are being brought to justice properly.View image in fullscreenThe airman was working at the USAF base at Mildenhall, Suffolk.Photograph: High Level/ShutterstockIn the latest case, Mooty, then a 21-year-old airman working at the huge United States Air Force (USAF) base at Mildenhall,Suffolk, went on a night out in March 2023.He met two other American airmen in a pub in Newmarket where he drank two or three bottles of beer in two hours, according to evidence heard at his disciplinary hearing. They then went to another Newmarket pub where he had two or three vodka Red Bulls over another two hours.They took a taxi to the home of one of the men in Bury St Edmunds. But they soon decided they were hungry and at around 4am Mooty drove them in his car to a kebab shop, according to evidence at the disciplinary hearing.While he was driving, Mooty received messages from a British woman who had been in a relationship with him. During the exchanges, the woman quickly suspected that he was drunk. Later that night, he went to her home. She said that Mooty was “the most drunk I’ve ever seen him” when he went to her house, adding: “I’m surprised he didn’t crash/get caught,” the disciplinary hearing heard.She reported him to his superiors at Mildenhall. “He is endangering the lives of the people in this country and should not be here,” she told them.Mooty was disciplined in a US court martial for being drunk in charge of a vehicle. A military judge convicted him, sentencing him to 20 days of hard labour and a demotion.However, under the terms ofan agreement that has been in force since the 1950s, the British police have the primary responsibility for investigating alleged wrongdoing by US military personnel, unless the offences were committed while the Americans were on duty, or against another member of their armed forces or property.View image in fullscreenUSAF aircraft at RAF Mildenhall.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAThere are now questions about why the US military prevented the possibility of Mooty being prosecuted in a British court.Suffolk police said they were “not notified of a drink-driving incident on 3/4 March 2023 involving a US airman from RAF Mildenhall. We understand that the incident was investigated and dealt with by the USAF.”In a statement, the USAF said: “While we do not have a specific written record of this notification occurring, there is no reason to believe that verbal notification was not provided in line with standard inter-agency coordination procedures.”Asked why it decided to investigate Mooty instead of handing the case over to the British police, the USAF said he “was not stopped by UK law enforcement while driving. Rather, the allegation was first reported to US military authorities well after the driving incident occurred.“Thus, no chemical testing (blood and breathalyser evidence) was available nor any first-hand observation of impairment by police forces, as typically desired by local UK prosecutors.”The USAF added that its military prosecutors could take Mooty to a court martial based on the testimony of witnesses and what it called “indicators of impairment”.The USAF said it had a policy of prosecuting as many of its personnel as possible within the boundaries of its agreement with the UK. It argues that this is amore effective way of maintaining disciplineand good order within its ranks. The USAF asks British police if it can take over the prosecution of cases, requests that British police often agree to.US military judges subsequently quashed the court martial verdict against Mooty and approved a rehearing of his case, but this has not been held, as he was dismissed from the USAF after he was caught drink-driving a year later.At 4.20am on 31 March 2024, he was arrested by a Suffolk police officer after driving a car while over the limit in Bury St Edmunds. He resisted being arrested.He was convicted at Ipswich magistrates court in August 2024 after pleading guilty to both offences. Mooty was banned from driving for a year and ordered to pay fines and penalties totalling £871.On this occasion, the USAF did not step in and request to take over the prosecution. It said it left it to the British police as it “understood prosecution of the case by local authorities to be perfectly appropriate” under the agreement with the UK.The USAF communicated with British prosecutors over the second drink-driving offence. It said it helped the British authorities gain access to another member of the US air force who rebutted Mooty’s defence that he was not driving that night.The conduct of American military personnel driving on British roads is contentious, as there has been a history of them committing offences such as speeding, drink-driving and driving without insurance.In one well-known case, it took a long campaign to bring to justice Anne Sacoolas, the American intelligence official who killed a 19-year-old motorcyclist, Harry Dunn, in a road accident outside a US base in Northamptonshire in 2019.Explore more on these topicsSuffolkBase justicePoliceUS militarynewsShareReuse this content

title: Lewis Hamilton aims to extend career till early 2030s so he can race in African Grand Prix | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: The 41-year-old is set on fulfilling his ‘dream to be able to race in Africa’, specifically Rwanda which will host despite criticism of its human rights record
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: The 41-year-old is set on fulfilling his ‘dream to be able to race in Africa’, specifically Rwanda which will host despite criticism of its human rights record
Content: Lewis Hamilton believes that the race in Rwanda will be a force for good rather than sportswashing.Photograph: Brett Farmer/LAT ImagesView image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton believes that the race in Rwanda will be a force for good rather than sportswashing.Photograph: Brett Farmer/LAT ImagesFormula One 2026Lewis Hamilton aims to extend career till early 2030s so he can race in African Grand Prix41-year-old set on ‘dream to be able to race in Africa’Rwanda to host despite criticism of human rights recordGiles Richardsin AustinThu 22 Oct 2026 17.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 18.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLewis Hamilton has said he hopes to remain racing in Formula One until he can take part in the African Grand Prix which isset to take place in Rwanda in the 2030s. The seven-time world champion believes it is right that F1 is to hold a race there despite criticism of the country’s human rights record.Last week F1 confirmed Rwanda was to host the African Grand Prix having concluded a 10-year agreement for the meeting on a purpose-built circuit, with the first race set for the early 2030s. It is lined up to be held on a circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital, Kigali, which has yet to be constructed and marks a return to the African continent for the first time since it last held a race at Kyalami, SouthAfricain 1993.Austin GP is about much more than potential for Antonelli’s first F1 world title | Giles RichardsRead moreHamilton has beenchampioning a race in Africafor some time. The 41-year-old is understood to be currently contracted with Ferrari until the end of the 2027 season, and speaking before this weekend’s US Grand Prix he said he would like to continue racing for at least another four years in order to make it to the meeting in Rwanda.“I’m now forced to have to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa andthat’s been my dreamto be able to race in Africa,” he said. “So, I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit if I can. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we’ll keep it going.”Hamilton would be at least in his mid-40s if he was to continue until 2030. F1’s current oldest driver is 45-year-old Fernando Alonso.F1’s deal withRwandais for a 10-year period but because of the country’s human rights record the award of the race has been criticised as an act of sportswashing.Quick GuideBritain's Slater, 18, to make F1 practice debut for AudiShowBritain’s 18-year-old Freddie Slater will make his Formula 1 free practice debut for ⁠Audi at next week’s Mexico City Grand Prix.Audi entered Formula 1 this year ⁠after taking over ⁠the ​Sauber team, and Slater was the first driver signed to the team’s new driver academy.Slater ⁠finished second in the Formula 3 standings to Ugo Ugochukwu in his debut season while ⁠racing for Trident Motorsport. He is slated to move ​to Formula 2 with Invicta ‌next year."Getting behind the wheel of an F1 car at a grand prix weekend is a big moment for me and something I’ve been dreaming of since I was a kid," Slater said. “I’ve learned a ‌lot this year, and these Free practice outings with Audi F1 Team will be another opportunity ​to keep gaining on-track experience."Slater is also slated to drive in the first practice session at next month’s Sao Paulo Grand Prix."We have seen Freddie making great progress ⁠throughout recent years, both on and off the track; ​it is ​the right time for ​Freddie to step up," Audi racing director and ​academy director ‌Allan McNish, a former F1 driver himself, said."These ​appearances ​in Mexico and Brazil will give him valuable experience of a Formula 1 race weekend, and another chance to continue his development."ReutersWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“A 10-year grand prix ‘presented by Visit Rwanda’ is a sportswashing prize for the Rwandan authorities,” said Felix Jakens, Amnesty UK’s head of campaigns. “Rwanda isbuying into the world’s biggest sportsto polish its image and deflect from ⁠its appalling human rights record. Formula One says sport can be ‘a positive force for good’. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with. Rwanda’s authorities are prolific in arbitrary detention, torture and the repression of free speech.”View image in fullscreenRwanda’s investment in sports sponsorship has led to accusations that it is attempting to sportswash its human rights record.Photograph: SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesHamilton nonetheless felt the meeting would serve as a force for good in Africa and that there also should be more education about the continent.“I’m really, really hopeful for that grand prix,” he said. “Of course, I don’t get to choose where we go, and naturally there’s problems all over the world today, so I’ve seen many of the stories but I think we really have to approach it with humility.“There’s a lot that we don’t know. I mean, growing up in England, they never ever taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum. A lot of the problems they have there are still results of colonialism, and the West intervening.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I really hope, and I still have hopes, that Africa unites. I know there’s many people that don’t want that to happen, because they would be so powerful if they did, but I’m still hopeful that at some stage they will.”The new race is being backed by the government of Rwanda and the Rwanda Development Board, who intend to develop the venue as a destination not only for motorsport but for promoting economic growth. The country has recently invested heavily in hosting sporting events, including cycling’s road world championships, cricket’s Women’s Challenge Trophy, the 2023 Fifa congress andthe Basketball Africa League.Hamilton felt that at least the race would present an opportunity for people to take a greater interest in Africa.“Going doesn’t mean that you neglect the things that are happening there,” he said. “Hopefully many people start to educate themselves a little bit more of what is happening there, what has happened there for hundreds of years and I hope that does spark the conversation. Then I guess I’ll finish it off with, I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping that at some stage we get to.”Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli goes into this weekend’s US Grand Prix in a position to clinch his first F1 title. The 20-year-old holds a 102-point lead over his teammate George Russell and will become Formula One’s youngest world champion if he wins, Russell finishes ninth or lower and Hamilton is fifth or lower.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Lewis HamiltonFerrariFormula OneMotor sportRwandaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Alberta welcomed migrant workers. Now, it wants to restrict their rights | Canada | The Guardian
description: ‘Scapegoating non-permanent residents is not going to lower the cost of living,’ Vanesa Ortiz says
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: ‘Scapegoating non-permanent residents is not going to lower the cost of living,’ Vanesa Ortiz says
Content: Albertans take part in a pro-Canada Rally, at the provincial legislature ahead of a non-binding referendum on Alberta sovereignty, in Edmonton on 18 October.Photograph: Todd Korol/ReutersView image in fullscreenAlbertans take part in a pro-Canada Rally, at the provincial legislature ahead of a non-binding referendum on Alberta sovereignty, in Edmonton on 18 October.Photograph: Todd Korol/ReutersCanadaAlberta welcomed migrant workers. Now, it wants to restrict their rights‘Scapegoating non-permanent residents is not going to lower the cost of living,’ Vanesa Ortiz saysLeyland Ceccoin TorontoThu 22 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Vanesa Ortiz came to Calgary fromMexico, she found herself in a city gripped by winter. Outside the airport, it was -15C (5F).“I would come to understand that this was not an extreme cold,” she said. “But in the moment it was terrifying.But she also found in those first moments an immense warmth. She was welcomed by elderly volunteers in white cowboy hats, and Ortiz soon felt that Calgary was a place she could one day raise a family. And yet when the teacher reflects on that moment a decade ago, she worries that the opportunities she had to put down roots could be soon closed to others.This week, Albertaheld a referendum, asking residents to weigh in on the province’s relationship with Canada – and the extent to which the province should restrict some newcomers’ access to healthcare, education and social support. It also asked about the need for constitutional reforms.While unofficial results show both the separation and constitutional questions will fail,the ones on immigration are likely to succeed.“I love Calgary and I love Alberta,” said Ortiz. “But when I hear people asking whether people should get access to these services – I mean, that was my daughter’s education. That was my family’s healthcare.”The referendum amplified thegrievances of fringe separatists,but it also exposed a central tension in Alberta’s approach to immigration. Even as the oil-rich province seeks newcomers to fill shortages in the job market, the provincial government wants to limit services available to some of those same workers.The governing United Conservative party blames the rapid population growth for overcrowded and underfunded hospitals and schools. But critics say the proposed solution – restricting access to healthcare, education and social supports – could leave workers and their families more vulnerable without fully addressing the underlying causes of the crisis.The referendum asked if the government should introduce a law ensuring only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and “individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status” can access healthcare and education. Another asked if newcomers should have lived in Alberta for 12 months before qualifying for certain social support programmes and allowing the province to charge some temporary residents fees for healthcare and education.Earlier in the year, the Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, blamed the immigration policy of Justin Trudeau’s Liberal government for the resource strains in classrooms, emergency rooms and social support systems. And in a social media post, Smithsaid: “For every $1 of taxes a guest worker generates, taxpayers are covering $10 in services. This is not sustainable.”‘This is not poker’: Alberta goes to polls in referendum that has exposed divisions, not least among separatistsRead moreCanada’s federal government has since trimmed immigration targets and placed restrictions on its temporary foreign worker program amid criticismsit was being abusedby large companies. But the western province’s economy relies on workers from abroad to fill jobs in sectors, like agriculture, food services and tourism, where employers struggle to recruit or retain enough staff.Ortiz, who works with the non-profit Asociación de Mexicanos en Calgary, worries mounting skepticism towards migrant workers will push workers into the shadows and make them more vulnerable to labor exploitation.“I can’t imagine the scale of the harm that a policy like this might create,” she said, noting that thousands of farm workers in the province don’t receive healthcare.Ortiz has seen views shift on immigration in recent years and says the results of the referendum reflect a population that is “squeezed” economically.“Scapegoating non-permanent residents is not going to lower the cost of living. That’s not going to fix our classrooms. They keep essential services open. In many cases, they are frontline workers. And now they’re being treated as disposable.”For some residents, the proposals represent a sharp reversal from Alberta’s earlier efforts to attract newcomers. The UCP government invested in recruitment and expanded its provincial immigration nomination targets to address labour shortages. But as a growing number of Albertanssour on immigration, the government position has shifted.Ximena González, a Calgary-based writer, said when the provincial government began its campaign to bring in more people, it “wanted more workers to exploit”, noting that most workers come from abroad on temporary permits.“Now, the message feels more out in the open: ‘We wanted you to come, to exploit you. And now, we don’t need you any more – so we will punish you.”The provincial government has claimed that temporary residents, who make up almost 6% of Alberta’s total population, contribute roughly $150m in tax revenues but cost the province more than $1bn annually in health, education and other social services.But Gonzálezargues that there is no data to back that claim.Economist Gillian Petitnotesthat temporary residents also remit taxes to the federal government, which helps fund Alberta’s healthcare, meaning those residents probably contribute far more than the province acknowledges. If they contribute less in total tax dollars than other Albertans, it is because they earn less than the median resident. They are also less likely to use healthcare and education resources than the average Albertan.“In all honesty, if I were a temporary resident and had to choose whether or not to stay, I wouldn’t,” said González, who came toCanada16 year ago as an international student. “I would not feel wanted, and I don’t want to be treated like a third-class citizen.”She says that media fixation on Alberta’s fringe independence movement meant the other questions in the referendum received little scrutiny and left voters uninformed.“The media failed to help people to make an educated vote – instead of just voting based on racism.”Economist Jim Stanford said hundreds of thousands of residents skipped over those questions on immigration, choosing to only answer the one on separation.“This cannot remotely be interpreted as a mandate for the government to crack down on immigration,” he said, adding the province didn’t have the power to “unilaterally” act on these proposals. “This was a symbolic ideological exercise and gives a cast of legitimacy to some of these very rightwing nativist sentiments that are bubbling in the far right of Alberta politics.”During a series of town halls over the years led by the government, more extreme views on immigration were clear. One residentreceived cheersafter suggesting a policy of mass deportations and another said immigrants “harm” children and suggested she might seek asylum in the US.For Ortiz, the government’s about-face reflects a “betrayal” of the workers who have helped build the province.“We’re asking people if we should remove the right to access healthcare and education from taxpayers who are, quite literally, building our communities,” she said. “But I also worry that what gets lost in this debate is these people. They are not just labour. They work, study and raise their children here. They need to know they deserve the chance to build a life with dignity and with respect to feel safe and to feel welcome.”Explore more on these topicsCanadaMexicoAmericasfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: North Korea prepares to restart propaganda loudspeakers as ties sour with South | North Korea | The Guardian
description: Kim Yo-jong, sister of Kim Jong-un, issues warning after inspecting border fortifications against backdrop of rising tensions
Author: Raphael Rashid
Headline: Kim Yo-jong, sister of Kim Jong-un, issues warning after inspecting border fortifications against backdrop of rising tensions
Content: Kim Yo-jong, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, visits frontline areas on Wednesday, as she warns that Pyongyang could restart propaganda loudspeakers on the border within days.Photograph: í©ëNí êMé–; 朝鮮通信社/KCNA/KNS/APView image in fullscreenKim Yo-jong, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, visits frontline areas on Wednesday, as she warns that Pyongyang could restart propaganda loudspeakers on the border within days.Photograph: í©ëNí êMé–; 朝鮮通信社/KCNA/KNS/APNorth KoreaNorth Korea prepares to restart propaganda loudspeakers as ties sour with SouthKim Yo-jong, sister of Kim Jong-un, issues warning after inspecting border fortifications against backdrop of rising tensionsRaphael Rashidin SeoulWed 21 Oct 2026 23.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 23.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePropaganda loudspeakers aimed atSouth Koreawill be ready to restart within days along the entire border, Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, has said amid a worsening of ties between the two countries.The statement, carried by the state news agency KCNA on Thursday, came a day after she said the loudspeakers would be in operation along the whole border from some time in October.Both North and South Korea havehistorically used giant loudspeakersto broadcast propaganda across the border, with the North in recent years playing haunting bestial howls, and the South opting for K-pop music ​and news criticising Pyongyang.If the broadcasts resume, they would be the first loudspeaker exchange across the border in 16 months.
