South Korean president Lee Jae Myung suspended broadcasts from the southern side just days into his presidency in June 2025 to ease tensions with Pyongyang, and the militarydismantled the speakersthat August.At a briefing on Thursday, a defence ministry spokesperson in Seoul said that ifNorth Koreawent ahead, “naturally there would have to be a proportional measure”, but made clear no decision had been made.View image in fullscreenA North Korean military guard post featuring loudspeakers, seen in February 2026.Photograph: Ahn Young-joon/APThe joint chiefs of staff said routine maintenance of the North’s loudspeakers had been observed before Kim Yo-jong’s statements.Tensions between the two Koreas have risen since September, when alandmine blast south of the military demarcation lineinjured three South Korean soldiers, two of them seriously.Seoul and the UN command – which oversees the 1953 armistice that halted but did not end the Korean war –concluded it wasa North Korean anti-personnel mine and an armistice violation. Pyongyang denied responsibility and called the incident a “self-staged farce”.The loudspeaker threat comes as North Korea continues to fortify its side of the border. SinceKim Jong-undeclared that the two Koreas were “two states hostile to each other” in December 2023, North Korea has laid mines, strung barbed wire and erected anti-tank barriers along the border.On Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong inspected several fortification points along the border with Pak Jong-chon, a marshal and adviser to Pyongyang’s defence ministry.The border had been “clearly blocked and turned into a fortress more thoroughly”, she said, adding that Kim Jong-un had told her it “should be a permanent line never to be crossed”.Seoul says North Korean troops have repeatedly crossed the military demarcation line, the 250km line dividing the two Koreas, during the construction work, prompting South Korean soldiers to issue warnings over loudspeakers and fire warning shots.North Korea has called the warning shots and broadcasts provocations by “armed rogues”.Explore more on these topicsNorth KoreaKim Jong-unSouth KoreaAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Australia offers astronaut Katherine Bennell-Pegg for space mission to International Space Station | Space | The Guardian
description: Australian of the Year would become the first astronaut in space to qualify under the Australian flag if she embarks on the 2028 mission
Author: Donna Lu
Headline: Australian of the Year would become the first astronaut in space to qualify under the Australian flag if she embarks on the 2028 mission
Content: Australian aerospace engineer Katherine Bennell-Pegg will go to the International Space Station in a 2028 missionPhotograph: Ina Fassbender/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAustralian aerospace engineer Katherine Bennell-Pegg will go to the International Space Station in a 2028 missionPhotograph: Ina Fassbender/AFP/Getty ImagesSpaceAustralia offers astronaut Katherine Bennell-Pegg for space mission to International Space StationAustralian of the Year would become the first astronaut in space to qualify under the Australian flag if she embarks on the 2028 missionGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastDonna LuAssistant editor, climate, environment and scienceThu 22 Oct 2026 19.51 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 19.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe federal government has sent an offer to the European Space Agency (ESA) to send the Australian of the Year, astronaut Katherine Bennell-Pegg, to theInternational Space Station.The mission, slated for 2028, will mark the first time a qualified astronaut has flown to space under the Australian flag.The ESA offer for Bennell-Pegg to join a future ISS mission garnered support from philanthropists and the Australian space industry, but has previously described by the office of the science minister, Tim Ayres, as “a very expensive undertaking” which no government alone could fund.Announcing the decision on Friday, Ayres said:“The government has been engaging extensively with the private sector, philanthropists, and other levels of government to raise funding to support a space flight – which is a significant cost.“We are grateful to the philanthropists who have committed over $6m in cash, plus in-kind support, and some indicative support from some state governments.”Australian taxpayers paid $466,000 for training of nation’s first female astronaut Katherine Bennell-PeggRead moreBennell-Pegg is director of space technology at the AustralianSpaceAgency (ASA) and completed astronaut training with the ESA in 2024.She is not the first Australian astronaut, but she is the first to qualify under the Australian flag. Dr Andy Thomas and Paul Scully-Power, both Australian-born, went to space as US citizens on Nasa missions. Elaine Hyde, a dual Australian and US citizen, last year took a suborbital flight aboard Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin NS-30.In May, the ASA announced it had entered into “treaty-level discussions” with the ESA, which “would establish a formal framework for enhanced cooperation between Australia and Europe”.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailIn August, Ayres and the assistant science minister, Andrew Charlton, wrote to state and territory leaders asking them to “partner” with the federal government to fund the mission. The letter, according toThe Australian, described it as a “complete Australian mission that includes locally developed experiments and ­technology”.South Australia, where the ASA is headquartered, has publicly committed to supporting Bennell-Pegg’s space bid.“South Australia stands ready to partner with the commonwealth in what should be a national endeavour,” the premier, Peter Malinauskus, said. “Katherine Bennell-Pegg has the potential to inspire a new generation to dream big and address the single biggest challenge to our economy which is productivity.“Australia has a massive shortage of young people taking up the fields of science, technology, engineering and maths, and we need more of it if we’re going to grow the nation’s productivity … Nothing would motivate young people more to take up these fields of endeavour than seeing Australia’s first ever flagged astronaut in space.”A campaign to secure Bennell-Pegg’s spaceflight mission was supported by entrepreneurs Dick Smith and Jim Whalley – who had each pledged $1m funding for the mission – and former prime minister Kevin Rudd, who said on social media that the “project makes long-term economic sense for Australia beyond the usual sensibilities of the Treasury bean counters”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRichard de Grijs, a professor of physics and astronomy at Macquarie University, said of Bennell-Pegg: “She is qualified, she has undergone significant training, so she is set to go up if a suitable mission can be found.“The government has actually contributed quite a lot of money to that education already,” he said. TheASA paid $466,000for Bennell-Pegg to complete her astronaut training at the European Astronaut Centre in Cologne, Germany.“There is an inspirational value in sending a citizen from your country to space who is also the Australian of the Year … but the question is, is that worth $100m?” De Grijs said.“It’s a lot of money, but on the other hand, it might actually lead to returns that are way more than the estimated number.”De Grijs pointed out that Australia was also involved in “inspirational spaceflight” by another means: an Australian-built lunar rover, namedRoo-ver, will be sent to moon on a Nasa mission in 2030.Darin Lovett, chair of the Space Industry Association of Australia, said the industry had “a strong track record of return on investment”.“For around $100m, less than the price of a single coffee for every Australian adult, this is not a ticket to space. It is a down payment on Australia’s future in one of the defining industries of this century.”In aspeech Bennell-Pegg deliveredearlier this month, she described space as “a gateway – a lure – into the full breadth of STEM fields. Especially for those that dream of going up there.”Explore more on these topicsSpaceEuropean Space AgencyInternational Space StationSouth AustraliaAustralian educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rebel Wilson secures another Australian court win as co-producers of The Deb awarded just $10  | Rebel Wilson | The Guardian
description: NSW supreme court judge otherwise dismisses case brought by film’s co-producers and awards Wilson almost $400,000 after star countersued
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: NSW supreme court judge otherwise dismisses case brought by film’s co-producers and awards Wilson almost $400,000 after star countersued
Content: Rebel Wilson in Sydney in April 2026. Wilson countersued producers, claiming their involvement in The Deb was marked by a pattern of illicit and egregious behaviour.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPView image in fullscreenRebel Wilson in Sydney in April 2026. Wilson countersued producers, claiming their involvement in The Deb was marked by a pattern of illicit and egregious behaviour.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPRebel WilsonRebel Wilson secures another Australian court win as co-producers of The Deb awarded just $10NSW supreme court judge otherwise dismisses case brought by film’s co-producers and awards Wilson almost $400,000 after star countersuedAustralian Associated PressThu 22 Oct 2026 19.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 20.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralian A-listerRebel Wilsonhas secured a major court victory after co-producers of her debut film accused her of sabotage, lying and breaching contracts.The Pitch Perfect star directed,co-produced and starred in The Deb, a musical comedy that became the battleground for multiple legal battles in Australia and the US.It had a budget of A$22m (US15.4m, £11.5m) but made just $335,000 (US$235,000, £175,284) at the local box office, which Wilson’s co-producers allege could be traced to her false and derogatory statements about them online.Rebel Wilson wins defamation case brought by co-star after bitter disputeRead moreThe Bridesmaids star claimed in posts from July 2024 that producers Amanda Ghost, Gregor Cameron and Vince Holden tried to block The Deb’s release, embezzled money and behaved inappropriately towards the film’s star.The producers alleged Wilson caused their company financial and reputational damage in an attempt to devalue her debut film so she could purchase it from them.On Friday, Justice Elisabeth Peden in the New South Wales supreme court awarded the trio $10 (US$7, £5) in damages and otherwise dismissed the summons.Wilson had denied her co-producers’ allegations and countersued, claiming their involvement in the film was marked by a troubling pattern of illicit, egregious behaviours, including theft, bullying and sexual misconduct.The judge awarded her $359,000 (US$251,830, £187,868) plus interest in a brief decision, which will be followed by a written judgment.It was the second victory for Wilson after she wascleared of defaming her debut film’s star Charlotte MacInnesearlier this year following a fiery federal court hearing.MacInnes claimed Wilson defamed her in four social media posts that implied she was a liar and a sellout who walked back a sexual harassment complaint to further her career.The posts alleged the young actor confided in Wilson – and later recanted – that she felt uncomfortable when the film’s co-producer Amanda Ghost asked to have a shower and a bath together.MacInnes denied making or retracting a complaint, insisting she had not been uncomfortable when the pair shared a bath in their swimwear after Ghost suffered a medical episode in September 2023.The federal court found none of Wilson’s posts were defamatory.Explore more on these topicsRebel WilsonAustralian filmAustralian lawMusicalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The great moth revival: how bogongs have bounced back | Insects | The Guardian
description: This animated map shows the insect’s population exploding in Australia’s eastern states, with the endangered species coming back from the brink
Author: Nick Evershed
Headline: This animated map shows the insect’s population exploding in Australia’s eastern states, with the endangered species coming back from the brink
Content: Bogong moths gather around a streetlight in Wollongong. The insects are back in big numbers on Australia’s east coast, including in Sydney and Melbourne.Photograph: Ken Griffiths/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenBogong moths gather around a streetlight in Wollongong. The insects are back in big numbers on Australia’s east coast, including in Sydney and Melbourne.Photograph: Ken Griffiths/Getty Images/iStockphotoThe CrunchInsectsAnalysisThe great moth revival: how bogongs have bounced backNick EvershedThis animated map shows the insect’s population exploding in Australia’s eastern states, with the endangered species coming back from the brinkThu 22 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 20.16 EDTShareIf you live anywhere on the eastern side of Australia, you’ve probably noticed that bogong mothsare back in a big way.While we don’t yet have figures from ecologist-led surveys to compare with previous years, there is a wealth of data on the great moth revival being generated by citizen scientists across the eastern states.In this animated map you can see bogong moth observations posted to the citizen science platformiNaturalistvia theBogong Watch project. Every dot is a sighting, which may include one or more moths.How Bogong Moths swarmed eastern AustraliaWhile there are some caveats to keep in mind with citizen science data (observation numbers over time can be skewed because of differences in effort and participation, for example), it does clearly show how the moth population has exploded this year.A rise from a great fallBogongs were once so commonthey numbered in the billions, according to researchers, with as many as 4 billion moths migrating to the Australian Alps in summer toaestivatein cool caves. The moths famouslycaused panic at the Sydney Olympics closing ceremonyin 2000, and were known to invadeParliament House in Canberra each year.But the bogong population declined slowly between 1980 and 2016, then crashed dramatically in the summer of 2017.View image in fullscreenGraph showing bogong moth abundance in summer at a site in Kosciuszko national park, NSWMoth numbers were so low the species was described as “undetectable” in the alpine regions.Ken Green, an ecologist who has been monitoring bogong moths for more than 40 years, previouslytold the Guardian that Australia’s drought through 2017, 2018 and 2019 was probably the largest contributor to the population crash, with pesticides and urban light pollution contributing to the slower decline from the 80s.After those years of catastrophic decline, the explosion of bogongs across the skies of eastern Australia this spring is great news for the plants the moths pollinate and the endangered species that rely on them for food, including themountain pygmy possum.Explore more on these topicsInsectsThe CrunchEndangered speciesAnimalsConservationWildlifeanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Reader Q&A: What’s next for France after a weekend of riots? Ask our Europe columnists | France | The Guardian
description: At 3pm BST/ 4pm CEST Friday 23 Oct, Guardian Europe columnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst will be live taking questions from our readers about the riots and protests in France. Send your questions by email now to conversations@theguardian.com, or join the discussion on Friday
Author: Rokhaya Diallo
Headline: At 3pm BST/ 4pm CEST Friday 23 Oct, Guardian Europe columnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst will be live taking questions from our readers about the riots and protests in France. Send your questions by email now to conversations@theguardian.com, or join the discussion on Friday
Content: 2d ago06.32 EDTWelcome to the ConversationView image in fullscreenThe Hôtel de Ville in Limoges, central France, on fire during a weekend of unrest.Photograph: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP/Getty ImagesAfter weeks of protests and a weekend of riots in which a town hall was set ablaze, 2,000-plus shops were looted, 2,300 people were arrested and 1,000 police injured, the repercussions for France – for its society and its economy – continue. Allegations of police brutality surfaced, and the violent protests unnerved investors,resulting in a debt sell-off, with borrowing costs rising higher than for Greece. All of this ahead of a hotly contested presidential election that’s now just six months away.The French government’s escalating financial problems were covered by the Guardian’s Europe correspondent Jon Henley who wrote: “France’s national debt, at 119% of GDP, is at itshighest level since 1946. Its budget deficit, at 5.1%, is also among the highest in the EU. There is just no money in the bank to ease the cost of living squeeze that brought 550,000 people on to the streets on Saturday.”Columnist Paul Taylor commented that “Last weekend’s violence has increased the likelihood of a law-and-order backlash among voters that could propel (Marine) Le Pen into the Élysée Palace. But if the financial situation worsens and the campaign turns on who can save the economy, she may yet lose out to a candidate who is firm on security and more orthodox on fiscal policy.”And theGuardian’s editorialnoted that “In an increasingly febrile atmosphere, France is heading towards a seismic reckoning in May. Alarmingly, the civil strife witnessed at the weekend may only be a foretaste of what is to come.”What are your views on the riots, their causes and their aftermath? Are they paving a path to the presidency for Le Pen? In his final months in charge, can embattled incumbent Emmanuel Macron meaningfully address the situation in whichFrancefinds herself?France-basedGuardian Europecolumnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst will be live here at 1500BST on Friday 23 October to answer your questions on what happened, why, and where France goes from here.Comments will open at 0900BST on Friday, but you can send your questions by email now toconversations@theguardian.comFerocious criticism from all sides underlines Macron’s isolationRead moreMacron bans ‘illegitimate‘ protests in France as he tries to get a grip on unrestRead moreAfter the violence and chaos in France, there’s only one beneficiary: Marine Le Pen | Paul TaylorRead moreFrom strife-torn France to the UK, rightwing populists win when they stir chaos while promising order  | Rafael BehrRead moreShareUpdated at12.54 EDT

title: Macron bans ‘illegitimate’ protests in France as he tries to get a grip on unrest | France | The Guardian
description: French president also says he will decide on concrete ‘next steps’ for the next nationwide demonstrations
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: French president also says he will decide on concrete ‘next steps’ for the next nationwide demonstrations
Content: Student protesters in Paris on Thursday after an initial police ban on their demonstration was overturned by a court.Photograph: Ibrahim Ezzat/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStudent protesters in Paris on Thursday after an initial police ban on their demonstration was overturned by a court.Photograph: Ibrahim Ezzat/Anadolu/Getty ImagesFranceMacron bans ‘illegitimate’ protests in France as he tries to get a grip on unrestFrench president also says he will decide on concrete ‘next steps’ for the next nationwide demonstrationsAngry lawyers and bewildered defendants: the fallout from fast-tracking French rioting casesJon Henleyin ParisThu 22 Oct 2026 11.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 14.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmmanuel Macron has said “illegitimate” demonstrations will be banned over the coming days as France seeks to get a grip on civil unrest aftersome of its worst street violence in yearserupted on the fringes of cost of living protests at the weekend.Speaking after a ​meeting with intelligence officials and senior ministers, the French president said on Thursday that demonstrations organised by recognised groups would be allowed to go ahead, although their routes could be changed.View image in fullscreenEmmanuel Macron chairs a security council meeting at the Élysée Palace.Photograph: Suarez Teresa/ABACA/ShutterstockProtests requested by “individuals or groups with no legitimate authority” would be banned, Macron said. Requests by organisations such as trade unions would be “examined in accordance with the law” but they might have to use alternative routes.The measures were necessary to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings, he said, adding: “The rules are simple and I think they’re commonsense. The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days.”Macron blamed much of last weekend’s unrest and looting on rioters who came expressly to loot, but said the worst of the violence was due to “political and seditious acts by ultra far-left groups who aimed to bring down the republic”.View image in fullscreenProtesters in Paris hold a banner reading “high school students target the Bac. The Bac target the head.” The Bac refers to the baccalaureate exam and also the French police’s anti-crime brigade.Photograph: Teresa Suárez/AP“The priority is a return to calm,” he said, adding that he would chair a defence council meeting of key ministers on Friday to decide concrete “next steps” for new nationwide demonstrations called for Saturday and afterwards.An initial police ban on a student protest planned inParisfor Thursday was overturned by a court, but marches also scheduled for the day in Grenoble, Rouen, Le Havre and Toulon were halted.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMacron accuses Trump and other foreign leaders of ‘stupid comments’ about France unrestRead moreAuthorities have already declared a ban on “all protests” on Saturday in the centre of Lyon, France’s third-biggest city, where between 200 and 300 shops were ransacked and looted last weekend and the tourist office was set ablaze.Authorities in Marseille, Nice and Toulon announced similar bans for Saturday. In Paris, a march planned for Saturday to be held in the east of the capital, starting at the Place de la Bastille, was authorised but banned from heading into the city centre.However, a separate march through the capital planned for Saturday by students and some members of thegilets jaunes(yellow vests) movement, whose protests over fuel prices rocked France in 2018 and 2019, would not be permitted, authorities in the capital said.View image in fullscreenA demonstration involving members of the gilets jaunes on the capital’s Place de la République on Saturday.Photograph: Giulia Morici/NurPhoto/ShutterstockFrance’s main student union, UNEF, has also called ‌for rallies on Saturday. Businesses in central Paris and other cities had already begun boarding up their windows and hiring private security in preparation for violence, French media reported.The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, said 174 of the 2,500 people arrested since last weekend’s rioting had been remanded in custody and more than 900 were being prosecuted. Two people have been arrested after Limoges town hall was set on fire.‘America, this is a warning’: pro- Trump Maga media in a froth over Europe protestsRead moreThe prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, was hosting a meeting of key figures from France’s main political parties on Thursday to hear their views and seek cooperation, and was due to meet several big-city mayors later in the day.The tough security response has included partial night-time curfews in parts of several cities including Paris, as well as bans on gatherings in areas such as around the Élysée presidential palace, the parliament and the city’s main train stations.The demonstrations began last month in a high school in Créteil, south-east of Paris, over staff shortages and dilapidated buildings, and spread nationwide, with strikes, blockades and demonstrations by high-school pupils around the country.Those demonstrations have morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, six months before next year’s presidential elections, which will choose Macron’s successor.Explore more on these topicsFranceEmmanuel MacronParisProtestEuropeCost of living crisisGilets jaunes protestsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia bombards Kyiv with missiles hours after agreeing to resume talks with Ukraine | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Experts say Russia is trying to destroy energy infrastructure before winter and US ‘appeasement and flattery’ will not achieve peace
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Experts say Russia is trying to destroy energy infrastructure before winter and US ‘appeasement and flattery’ will not achieve peace
Content: A woman looks at her damaged apartment on Thursday after a Russian missile attack in Kyiv, Ukraine.Photograph: Efrem Lukatsky/APView image in fullscreenA woman looks at her damaged apartment on Thursday after a Russian missile attack in Kyiv, Ukraine.Photograph: Efrem Lukatsky/APUkraineRussia bombards Kyiv with missiles hours after agreeing to resume talks with UkraineExperts say Russia is trying to destroy energy infrastructure before winter and US ‘appeasement and flattery’ will not achieve peaceLuke HardingandPjotr SauerThu 22 Oct 2026 11.46 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 06.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussia has carried out a massive “demonstrative” attack on Ukraine, bombarding Kyiv with ballistic missiles just hours after Vladimir Putin said he had agreed to resume trilateral negotiations aftertalks with the US envoy Steve Witkoff.Overnight, Moscow pounded the Ukrainian capital, killing at least two people and wounding 22, including four children. Targets included the southern bridge over the Dnipro River, civilian houses, energy infrastructure, an ambulance station, office buildings and a clinic.The Ukrainian president,Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said three of the missiles carried cluster warheads. One struck the Pecherskyi district, damaging several historic structures, including a monastery.“This is another extraordinarily revealing strike – revealing, because it was no accident,” Zelenskyy said. “The choice of weapon was deliberate; the choice of target area was deliberate, and so was the intent to inflict as much loss and damage on civilians as possible.”He said the strikes showedRussiawas not serious about peace, adding: “Almost immediately after another round of talks, Russia launched a pointed attack. This means there has been no real change in its attitude toward everything that is happening.”View image in fullscreenOvernight, Moscow pounded the Ukrainian capital, killing at least two people and wounding 22, including four children.Photograph: Vladislav Musienko/AFP/Getty ImagesDuring negotiations on Wednesday in St Petersburg, Witkoff lavished praise on Putin, who was sitting across the table. “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff said.In a social media post after the strikes in the early hours of Thursday, Zelenskyy issued a sardonic reply: “Three waves of ballistic missiles have been launched at Kyiv by Russian ‘humanitarians’ since yesterday evening. They used 21 missiles.”Zelenskyy said he was grateful to those among Ukraine’s western partners who saw “the situation for what it is” and “acknowledged the reality” that the Kremlin had little intention of stopping its war. He called for stronger air defences, Patriot interceptors that could bring down enemy missiles, and more sanctions against Moscow.‘You are a humanitarian also, sir’: the US feeds Putin with lies as Ukraine’s children take cover and die | Andrew RothRead moreUkraine’s foreign minister, ⁠Andrii Sybiha, ⁠added that “appeasement, ⁠servility ​and flattery” ‌would ‌not ‌stop Russian aggression.Downing Street said it did not recognise Witkoff’s description of Putin, pointing out that the Russian president had killed “thousands” of Ukrainians and his own frontline soldiers.On Wednesday, the Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said Putin had agreed “in principle” to resume three-way negotiations involving Russia, the US and Ukraine after 10 November, a week after the US midterm elections. In reality, Russia’s intention is to destroy Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in the coming weeks,leaving millions in the dark and cold, officials in Kyiv believe.According to Zelenskyy, the US hasresumed intelligence warningsof Russian missile attacks. The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Trump called Elon Musk to ask him to reverse the slowdown of Starshield, the military version of Musk’s Starlink internet satellite system, which had left Ukraine unable to intercept enemy drones or carry out mid-range battlefield strikes. Some Ukrainian officials reportedly told the Journal that the system had been working marginally better since the call, but others said it was still heavily restricted.The New York Timesreportedthat when the slowdown was imposed last week, dozens of armed drones heading to Russian military targets fell from the sky. The video feeds streaming their flight paths suddenly went fuzzy as the connection with Starshield was lost, the paper said.Vladimir, the commander of an air-defence unit protecting Kyiv, said the US restrictions had hampered his unit’s ability to intercept Russian drones. “Of course it’s hindering us. Our drones can no longer reach the speeds needed to intercept enemy targets,” he said, adding that he felt betrayed by Washington.The decision to cripple Ukraine’s successful drone programme came amid the most serious row between Washington and Kyiv since Russia’s full-scale invasion nearly five years ago. It began after Trump announced he waslifting sanctions on Russian diesel, to lower US fuel prices, a move that Zelenskyy criticised as “weak”.1:13Witkoff calls Putin a ‘humanitarian’ after release of jailed American – videoTheTrump administrationdenies it is deliberately helping the Russians. But European diplomats concede that the US appears to have switched sides. Ukrainian civilians are dying as a result, they say.Russia, meanwhile, said it had shot down hundreds of Ukrainian drones launched in overnight attacks. One man ⁠was ⁠killed ​and another was ⁠wounded as a ⁠result ​of ‌a Ukrainian aerial strike in Russia’s Belgorod region, local ‌authorities said.Details also emerged of a Ukrainian counterattack through a tunnel in the north-eastern city of Kupiansk, which Russia partly occupies. As part of Operation Veles, the Khartia corps carried out the world’s first underground counteroffensive, advancing 15km into enemy rear lines.“We observed how the enemy operates underground and studied their methods. The Russians intended to use gas pipelines to infiltrate the rear of our forces. So, we went underground ourselves,” Khartia’s commander, Brig Gen Ihor Obolienskyi, told Ukrainian media.The Ukrainian soldiers crawled 15km through tunnels – without communication, GPS or light – having developed their own navigation and life-support technologies in advance. About 100 Russians were killed in the operation, and 30 taken prisoner, the Khartia corps said.Luke Harding’sBetrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquestis published by Guardian FaberExplore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaTrump administrationUS foreign policyUS politicsVolodymyr ZelenskyyVladimir PutinnewsShareReuse this content

title: Shamonda virus detected in human for first time in France | France | The Guardian
description: Investigations under way to determine whether virus normally found in livestock contributed to man’s death
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Investigations under way to determine whether virus normally found in livestock contributed to man’s death
Content: The virus, which usually affects cattle, sheep and goats, was first detected in European livestock in the summer.Photograph: Pascal Rossignol/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe virus, which usually affects cattle, sheep and goats, was first detected in European livestock in the summer.Photograph: Pascal Rossignol/ReutersFranceShamonda virus detected in human for first time in FranceInvestigations under way to determine whether virus normally found in livestock contributed to man’s deathNicola DavisScience correspondentThu 22 Oct 2026 11.07 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 13.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man inFrancehas become the first human known to have contracted Shamonda virus, with investigations under way to explore whether it contributed to his death.Shamonda virus is a type of bunyavirus and is spread by bites from infected midges. According to theAustrian Agency for Health and Food Safety, in animals such as cattle, sheep and goats it can cause diarrhoea, lack of appetite and a decline in milk yield, “as well as abortions and congenital abnormalities in newborn calves, lambs and kids”.“In Switzerland and Germany, the presence of Shav [Shamonda virus] genetic material has also been reported in the brains of horses that died from neurological symptoms,” the agency said.The virus has previously been found in farm animals outside Europe, but was first detected in livestock on the continent in the summer. TheEuropean Centre for Disease Prevention and Control(ECDC) said the patient in France was the first recognised human infection.It also noted that he had already been seriously ill and had a compromised immune system, meaning it was unclear whether the virus played a role in his death this month.“Investigations into whether the virus caused or contributed to the patient’s death and how the infection was acquired are ongoing,” the ECDC has said.Prof Tom Solomon, the director of the pandemic institute at the University of Liverpool, said the risk to the general public appeared to be very low.“Shamonda virus has been circulating in animals, particularly cattle, but also sheep, goats, horses and alpacas, for many years, yet this is the first recognised human infection,” he said.“This suggests that transmission to humans is extremely unusual.”But unknowns remain, he said: “We don’t know whether healthy people can become infected without developing symptoms, what symptoms the virus might normally cause, or how frequently it might cause serious disease.“French authorities believe the neurological complications in this patient were very likely linked to the infection, although investigations are continuing.“This is clearly concerning, but one exceptional case does not necessarily mean the virus poses a significant threat to the wider population.”Dr Ben Brennan from the MRC-University of Glasgow’s centre for virus research, said there was currently no evidence of sustained transmission between humans.“While this discovery warrants further scientific investigation and continued surveillance, it does not currently suggest a significant new public health threat to the UK,” he said.“For most people, there is no reason to change their normal activities or take additional precautions.”Explore more on these topicsFranceHealthEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Revealed: billionaire Reform donor was in business with foundation linked to Iranian regime | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Sasan Ghandehari’s partnership with religious foundation raises questions about past dealings with republic criticised by Nigel Farage
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Exclusive: Sasan Ghandehari’s partnership with religious foundation raises questions about past dealings with republic criticised by Nigel Farage
Content: Nigel Farage (left) with Sasan Ghandehari, who says he runs a $10bn fund called HP Trust.Photograph: Jeff Gilbert/AlamyView image in fullscreenNigel Farage (left) with Sasan Ghandehari, who says he runs a $10bn fund called HP Trust.Photograph: Jeff Gilbert/AlamyReform UKRevealed: billionaire Reform donor was in business with foundation linked to Iranian regimeExclusive: Sasan Ghandehari’s partnership with religious foundation raises questions about past dealings with republic criticised by Nigel FarageRowena MasonWhitehall editorThu 22 Oct 2026 12.39 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 13.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage’s newest billionaire donor was in business with a powerful Iranian religious foundation under the authority of the country’s supreme leader, raising questions about his past dealings with the hardline republic.Hossein Ghandehari, also called Sasan, was little known in the UK until he pledged to give millions to Reform UK this summer anddonated £50,000 to Farageto cover the cost of two passes for the Davos World Economic Forum.He has said he is moving his tax residency from Switzerland to the UK in order to make “regular payments” of more than “one or two million” to the party.The 61-year-old Iranian-born British businessman, who says he runs a $10bn (£7bn) fund called HP Trust, has declined to give details about how his family made its money beyond saying the fund owns assets in Europe and North America.Now, a French arbitration decision unearthed by the Guardiansheds some light on Ghandehari’s past dealings with Iranian state-linked entities between 2013 and 2016.It also reveals Ghandehari’s further Iranian business links toanother Reform UK donor, John Richard Simpson, an administration professional and church warden from Potters Bar, north of London. Simpson’s design firm, Interior Architecture Landscape, counts the Ghandehari family as a client and gave £200,000 to Reform UK last year.Farage has been highly critical of Iran over the past year, and in March accused it of being abigger dangerto the UK than Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin.The French judgment reveals that Ghandehari was the major investor behind a deal to supply and build a fibre-optic cable to carry telecoms traffic across Iran in a joint venture with a state-linked Iranian partner.The businessman’s HP Trust was the ultimate owner of Ori Group, which took a 49% stake in the venture, called Omran Razavi International Co, in 2015.The other 51% of the venture was owned by Astan Quds Razavi (AQR), a multibillion pound religious foundation in Iran’s second city of Mashhad.AQR’s leader at the time was ayatollah Abbas Vaez Tabasi, who was appointed custodian of the foundation by the first supreme leader, Ruhollah Khomeini, and served from the 1979 revolution until his death in 2016. Vaez Tabasi had been an ally of some reformers but remained close to the next supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, and,according to the BBC, was reported by state media in 2009 to have said of opposition protest movements that those behind “sedition” in the country were “enemies of god” who deserved to be executed under sharia law.The joint venture ended in about 2016, with the Ghandehari-backed entities being pushed out of the deal as a hardliner was appointed to replace Vaez Tabasi.View image in fullscreenLawyers for Sasan Ghandehari said his involvement was intended to promote political change through greater access to information.Photograph: Jeff Gilbert/AlamyThe US imposed sanctions on AQR in 2021, saying it controlled “large swaths of the Iranian economy, including assets expropriated from political dissidents and religious minorities, to the benefit of supreme leader Ali Khamenei and senior Iranian government officials”. It describes it as abonyad, one of the “opaque, quasi-official organisations generally controlled by current and former government officials and clerics that report directly to the supreme leader”.Ghandehari’s lawyers said it would be misleading to characterise him as “working with Iran” without the context that, after 2016, he was targeted by Iran’s supreme national security council with the false allegation that he was working with hostile western powers. They also said his involvement was intended to promote political change through greater access to information, which he believed was why the US and French authorities authorised the project.Tom Keatinge, the director of the Centre for Finance and Security at Rusi, the foreign affairs thinktank, said dealing with Iran “has always been a risky business as a financial institution because of this blurring between kind of state and the private sector. The private sector is not free to operate. It’s just very hard to operate in that country without touching a live rail.”He said there was clearly a range of positions among ayatollahs but it would be “pretty difficult to operate in an industry like telecoms” without the acceptance of the core leadership.The judgment also revealed that, until 2016, Ghandehari’s HP Trust was the owner of Orico General Trading LLC, which was contracted to supply telecoms equipment from France’s Alcatel-Lucent and transport it from Dubai to Iran. After 2016, this company was transferred to Simpson, the administration professional, who was responsible for winding down Orico’s operations and taking hundreds of staff out of the region.Simpson told the Guardian he acquired the company after Iranian extremists took over AQR, when the project’s assets were seized and those involved faced political persecution on national security grounds, including accusations of working for hostile western governments. He said his plan was to wind down the business, adding that he carried out detailed checks before acquiring Orico.Ghandehari’s lawyers said AQR was independent and respected, and therefore the only viable choice for a joint venture in Iran. They said Ghandehari had never met Vaez Tabasi and that he did not regard him as an advocate for freedom or human rights but had believed him to be the only force in the Iranian hierarchy capable of holding back the hardliners in order for the project to go ahead.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe original contract for the deal was awarded to the Omran consortium in 2012 by the Iranian state-owned Telecommunication Infrastructure Company of Iran.According to Iranian corporate filings, Omran Razavi International Co also owned stakes in two majority state-owned banks, Bank Mellat and Bank Tejerat, in 2013. Both were subject to sanctions over involvement in Iran’s nuclear programme at that point.Ghandehari’s lawyers said Omran Razavi disposed of the small stakes in the banks before HP Trust’s Ori Group signed its agreement for a 49% stake in the venturein December 2014. They added that the deal was fully approved by authorities in France and the US.In 2016, AQR took over the whole of the joint venture. Around the same time, the project’s chair, Mohammed Reza Noory, ended up in Iran’s infamous Evin prison, serving an 18-year sentence.Ghandehari and Noory are both named on leaked judicial papers published by the hacktivist group Edaalat Ali as having being under investigation in Iran after the deal collapsed. Ghandehari’s lawyers say he first became aware of the “bogus allegations” during French court proceedings and that the intelligence services had not given him any further details. Ghandehari’s representatives said fabricating financial and social cases against its targets to discredit them was part of the Iranian regime’s playbook and had been widely documented and recognised by western governments, human rights organisations and independent journalists.Ghandehari’s lawyers said he had not been to Iran for 30 years and his wealth had no connection to the country, since his ancestral property and assets were confiscated in 2016.Farage has been highly critical of Iran’s government this year, supporting Donald Trump’s war against it, and attending a protest outside the Iranian embassy with pro-democracy activists in the spring. Last week he warned about Iranian agents entering the UK via small boats across the Channel.Ina joint interviewwith Farage and Ghandehari in July, the Telegraph described Ghandehari’s business deal in Iran without mentioning its connections to Iranian regime-linked companies. It described it as a project to bring access to high-speed internet to Iran that would help drive reform, but that it later went wrong and resulted in Ghandehari’s assets being confiscated.It is still not clear how Ghandehari and his family have built up their extraordinary wealth. His fortune is said to have gone from an estimated $2bn, when his late mother bought a property on London’s “billionaire’s row” in 2008, to a reported $10bn now.In a recentcourt case over a Picasso painting, Ghandehari was asked to provide proof that he could afford £1.5m in legal costs. His lawyers pointed only to a brochure from his Davos trip with Farage, with a description that he controls a trust with a “collective investment value in excess of $10bn”.View image in fullscreenThe Picasso painting at the centre of the court case was Femme dans un rocking-chair.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesAt one point, he offered a letter from a “partner in a leading accountancy firm” confirming he was the principal beneficiary of HP Trust, and drawing an annual income from it. However, this was later withdrawn, as Ghandehari decided he did not want its contents to enter the public domain.Explore more on these topicsReform UKIranParty fundingMiddle East and north AfricaNigel FaragenewsShareReuse this content

title: Some US diplomats told to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks | Saudi Arabia | The Guardian
description: Similar withdrawals from UAE, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain reported as concerns grow about restart of war with Iran after US midterm elections
Author: Jonathan Yerushalmy
Headline: Similar withdrawals from UAE, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain reported as concerns grow about restart of war with Iran after US midterm elections
Content: Smoke billows near the city of Taiz during battles between Yemeni government fighters and Iran-backed Houthis on Wednesday.Photograph: AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenSmoke billows near the city of Taiz during battles between Yemeni government fighters and Iran-backed Houthis on Wednesday.Photograph: AFP/GettySaudi ArabiaSome US diplomats told to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacksSimilar withdrawals from UAE, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain reported as concerns grow about restart of war on Iran after US midterm electionsJonathan Yerushalmyand agenciesThu 22 Oct 2026 09.05 EDTFirst published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 20.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US state department has ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leaveSaudi Arabiaas the gulf kingdom faces a barrage of near-daily attacks, with at least three people killed at an airport and oilfield.Attacks on “civilian airports and other critical infrastructure” by the Iranian-supportedHouthisin Yemen were highlighted as the reason for the drawdown. The state department spokesperson, Tommy Pigott, said: “The safety and security of department personnel and their families remain our highest priority.”The state department said the order covered its embassy in Riyadh and its satellite consulates. The embassy had been badly damaged at the start of the US war onIranand had been operating with only a skeleton staff for months, although in recent weeks some diplomats had returned.Besieged Yemeni city on verge of ‘unmanageable’ crisis, aid workers warnRead moreMedia outlets – including NBC and AFP – reported that families of US embassy personnel were also being withdrawn from the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain, while the New York Timessaidthe Trump administration was developing plans to restart the war on Iran.However, in his statement on Wednesday, Pigott described the reports of further withdrawals as “inaccurate” and said the state department order was for the departure of staff and their families from Saudi Arabia only.Saudi Arabia has faced a succession of deadly attacks from the Houthis over recent weeks, including a strike onRiyadh’s international airportwhich was the kingdom’s deadliest in years as the war with the group escalates.On Thursday the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority announced that two people had been killed in overnight attacks on King Fahd international airport in Dammam on the Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar.Eight people were injured and there was material damage to the airport, according to officials. The global flight-tracking service Flightradar24 said flights had been diverted away from the airport.Separately, falling debris from the successful interception of a drone targeting an oil facility in the country’s south-east killed two people and injured a further two, the Saudi energy ministry said.Footage shows fire in Saudi Arabia's Yanbu refinery and Kuwait's Mina Abdullah refineryThe Houthis said on Thursday ⁠they ⁠had ​launched attacks on ⁠Saudi Arabia’s defence ministry in ⁠Riyadh, Saudi ​Aramco ‌facilities ‌in Yanbu ‌and King Fahd international airport in Dammam.Essential workers at Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in the east of the country were told to evacuate on Thursday, two sources told Agence France-Presse, after their non-essential colleagues were told to work from home since last week.The US previously ordered non-essential staff to leave the Gulf in late February before the start of its war against Iran.NBC reportedthat the US military had been quietly scaling back its presence at bases across the Middle East in recent days, but a spokesperson from US central command told the US news outlet that service members were regularly moved to “optimize mission readiness”.The withdrawal of staff from the region coincides with reports that Trump has been presented with plans for restarting strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.The New York Times reportedthat the US and Israel had developed plans for a “short but intensive operation” after the defense secretary, Peter Hegseth, travelled to Israel earlier this week for meetings with the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.Last week ⁠Trump said the US was hoping to knock outIran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a site linked to the country’s ⁠nuclear program, however the US president has publicly said he does not intend to restart the war before the 3 November elections.With Reuters and Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsSaudi ArabiaMiddle East and north AfricaUS militaryUS foreign policyYemenHouthisTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Oil prices jump to five-month high as attacks threaten global supply | Oil | The Guardian
description: Iran’s IRGC says it hit four vessels in the northern Gulf and three more struck mines near the strait of Hormuz
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Iran’s IRGC says it hit four vessels in the northern Gulf and three more struck mines near the strait of Hormuz
Content: Vessels at the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenVessels at the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman.Photograph: ReutersOilOil prices jump to five-month high as attacks threaten global supplyIran’s IRGC says it hit four vessels in the northern Gulf and three more struck mines near the strait of HormuzShipping workers: how is the Middle East conflict affecting you?Lauren AlmeidaThu 22 Oct 2026 07.28 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOil prices jumped to a five-month high on Thursday after ​attacks inSaudi Arabiaand hits to tankers in the strait of Hormuz threatened further disruptions to the world’s crude supply.Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose by 3% to hit $112 a barrel for first time since 18 May.YemeniHouthis, who are aligned with Iran, hit several targets in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, with two people killed and eight more wounded in a civilian airport in Dammam, and two people killed in a drone attack on a Saudi oilfield.Elsewhere the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said four vessels involved in “illegal” oil transfers in the northern ​Gulf were hit and caught fire after being tracked by its forces on Wednesday.It said three more vessels collided with mines west of the strait of Hormuz, and warned the US that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases.A chart showing the  Brent crude oil priceThe US has now ordered some diplomats and family members to leave their missions in Saudi Arabia, and it plans to withdraw family members from a number of other missions in the Middle East, according to Reuters, which also reported that SaudiAramcohas instructed staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran and work remotely.Concern is growing that conflict in the region could escalate further, almost eight months after Tehran’s effective block on the strait of Hormuz triggered what many feared would bring the greatest energy supply disruption in the history of the market. In the first weeks after the US-Israeli attacks onIran, oil surged past $100 a barrel and market observers predicted prices of up to $150 a barrel as flows through Hormuz came to a halt.Oilpeaked at $126 a barrelin April during the conflict and fell back below $100 in late May and then to lows of $71 at the start of July amid hopes of a ceasefire in the region. The price began to climb again after thememorandum of understandingbetween the US and Iran fell apart and fresh hostilities broke out in the Gulf.However, data from Kpler has shown that oil exports from the Persian Gulf have now risen above their prewar levels, partly because of an increase in oil pumped overland through pipelines to the Red Sea and Gulf of Oman.Global stocks wobbled on Thursday amid expectations of higher inflation and borrowing costs. The Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, fell by 1%, with the UK’s FTSE 100 down by 0.7%.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 index dropped 2.7%, while the South Korean Kospi fell 3.5%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index shed 3%.Shares in American Airlines dropped almost 4% in pre-market trading after the company warned that high fuel costs would push it into a loss this year.American Airlines abandoned its previous forecast that it might achieve a profit this year as it faced “historic fuel cost pressure”.Explore more on these topicsOilCommoditiesMiddle East and north AfricaHouthisAramcoStock marketsSaudi ArabianewsShareReuse this content

title: Aung San Suu Kyi’s son speaks to detained former Myanmar leader for first time in five years | Aung San Suu Kyi | The Guardian
description: Kim Aris says ‘hearing her voice again means more than words can express’ amid loosening of detention restrictions
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Kim Aris says ‘hearing her voice again means more than words can express’ amid loosening of detention restrictions
Content: Aung San Suu Kyi speaking on the phone to her son Kim Aris.Photograph: Spokesperson for the president of Myanmar/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAung San Suu Kyi speaking on the phone to her son Kim Aris.Photograph: Spokesperson for the president of Myanmar/AFP/Getty ImagesAung San Suu KyiAung San Suu Kyi’s son speaks to detained former Myanmar leader for first time in five yearsKim Aris says ‘hearing her voice again means more than words can express’ amid loosening of detention restrictionsAgence France-Presse in YangonThu 22 Oct 2026 06.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 10.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe son of Myanmar’sAung San Suu Kyihas been allowed to speak to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook on Thursday.Aung San Suu Kyi is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a2021 military coup.Myanmar’s ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi seen in rare photos after receiving gift from King CharlesRead moreImages accompanying his Facebook post appeared to show Aris, who lives in the UK, standing outside theMyanmarembassy in London.“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” he said in the post. “But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”Myanmar’s military has held the Nobel peace prize laureate in almost total seclusion since the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy. But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life”.On Monday, authorities said shereceived a packagefrom Britain’s King Charles, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch. Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.Myanmar authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyidaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.After ruling Myanmar as military chief since the coup, Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year.Analysts described the election that put him in office as a charade, and said he could be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in an attempt to court international legitimacy.Explore more on these topicsAung San Suu KyiMyanmarSouth and central AsiaMyanmar coupnewsShareReuse this content

title: King Charles urged ‘as human brother’ to support reparations talks at Caribbean summit | King Charles III | The Guardian
description: Caricom commission chair Hilary Beckles wants king to ensure Commonwealth becomes a ‘moral institution committed to human justice’
Author: Natricia Duncan
Headline: Caricom commission chair Hilary Beckles wants king to ensure Commonwealth becomes a ‘moral institution committed to human justice’
Content: Hilary Beckles gives a speech during a plenary session at the high-level consultative conference on the next steps to the landmark UN resolution on the trafficking of enslaved Africans on 18 June 2026.Photograph: Ernest Ankomah/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHilary Beckles gives a speech during a plenary session at the high-level consultative conference on the next steps to the landmark UN resolution on the trafficking of enslaved Africans on 18 June 2026.Photograph: Ernest Ankomah/Getty ImagesKing Charles IIIKing Charles urged ‘as human brother’ to support reparations talks at Caribbean summitCaricom commission chair Hilary Beckles wants king to ensure Commonwealth becomes a ‘moral institution committed to human justice’Natricia Duncan, Caribbean correspondentThu 22 Oct 2026 19.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 19.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe head of the Caribbean’s reparations commission has appealed toKing Charles IIIas a “human brother” whose family he said had benefited from slavery to support reparations talks at next month’s Commonwealth leaders meeting in the Caribbean.Speaking at a press conference ahead of the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda next month, professor Hilary Beckles urged the king to use his influence to advance slavery reparations talks between Britain and the Caribbean.Beckles, the chair of theCaribbeanCommunity (Caricom) Reparations Commission, said: “My personal appeal to King Charles III, not so much in his role as head of the Commonwealth, not so much in his role as the constitutional monarch of the United Kingdom … I’m appealing to Charles Windsor, a parent, a grandparent, a man today who reflects upon the history of his family, and he can see the enrichment that slavery has presented to his family.”He declared that he believed the king was aware that the wealth he is passing on to his children and his grandchildren came from chattel slavery.Referring to the king as “a man, as a human brother”, he urged Charles to ensure the Commonwealth, historically “the site of this crime”, becomes a “moral institution committed to human justice”.Beckles’s appeal comes amid growing calls from Caribbean leaders and groups for Charles to formally apologise for slavery when he visits Guyana and the Bahamas next week ahead of Chogm, which he will attend in Antigua.On Thursday, Commonwealth secretary-generalShirley Ayorkor Botchweytold Sky News that a formal apology for slavery from King Charles “wouldn’t hurt” and that the “time has come” for a serious conversation regarding reparations.Jamaica says slavery reparations petition to be heard by UK privy council in March 2027Read moreEric Phillips, head of Guyana’s reparations committee and vice-chair of the Caricom Reparations Commission, joined the calls for an apology from the king.“The king is a decent monarch based on his lifelong commitments to the world in which the environment for him is sacred. We Africans are also part of that sacred environment. As an enlightened monarch, I strongly believe King Charles will want to promote a conversation of decency that reflects his character and values,” he said.“The citizens of the United Kingdom say, long live the king. We in Guyana say, long live the king, so he can apologize and call for reparations,” he added.Last month, when Jamaican officials lodged a landmark petition to King Charles for legal advice on its claim for slavery reparations, which will be heard by the privy council in March, a palace spokesperson said Charles “has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today”.But David Comissiong, the deputy chair of theBarbadosNational Task Force on Reparations, said he was concerned about a lack of unanimous agreement on commitments on reparations in a draft of the 2026 Chogm communique, which records agreements made by leaders.Comissiong said a paragraph that referenced the commitment to dialogue made at the previousCommonwealth summitin Samoa and highlights subsequent developments at the UN, African Union and Caricom, was confirmed, but there was disagreement about a second paragraph mandating Commonwealth foreign ministers to advance discussions on historical harms from the transatlantic slave trade through “structured, inclusive, and good faith dialogue”.“It is very peculiar, to say the least, that the second paragraph which speaks about the Commonwealth foreign affairs ministers coming together to engage in these discussions … has not been unanimously agreed upon,” he said.Dorbrene O’Marde, chair of the Antigua and Barbuda reparations commission, said that campaigners are expected to raise the issue of reparations during the conferences’ major forums, and that discussions between governments are expected to take place at their meetings.He said the reparations movement will launch a “Global Reparations Caravan”, described as an international movement combining reparations advocacy, demonstrations and culture, at a separate event on 3 November.O’Marde added that, while there will be stringent security measures around the event, he expects physical demonstrations from groups who are “inflamed” by the blanket statements of no apology coming out of the UK.“Blanket no apologies from both government and monarchy reek of gross insensitivity to the demands of the citizens of the Caribbean,” he said.Beckles stressed that the absence of a dedicated official event at Chogm does not mean that reparations would remain peripheral to the summit. He described the meeting as “the Chogm of reparations” and the “first round of reparations negotiations”.“This is the meeting of the Commonwealth in the Caribbean, and the number one item in the Caribbean as far as this gathering is concerned is reparatory justice,” he said.“I can assure you that [for] everyone in the Caribbean right now, everyone who’s going to be at that meeting from the Caribbean, with an interest in the Caribbean, from Africa, and an interest in the global African movement, this will be the number one item on the table.”Explore more on these topicsKing Charles IIICommonwealth summitCaribbeanReparations and reparative justiceCommonwealth of NationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Child health in England at risk from sharp rise in NHS waiting times, report says | Children's health | The Guardian
description: CQC research finds long delays are making conditions harder to treat and highlights regional disparities in care
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: CQC research finds long delays are making conditions harder to treat and highlights regional disparities in care
Content: Although some adult waiting times have improved children are having to endure longer waits to be treated, in part due to rapidly rising demand and falling staff numbers.Photograph: SolStock/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAlthough some adult waiting times have improved children are having to endure longer waits to be treated, in part due to rapidly rising demand and falling staff numbers.Photograph: SolStock/Getty ImagesChildren's healthChild health in England at risk from sharp rise in NHS waiting times, report saysCQC research finds long delays are making  conditions harder to treat and highlights regional disparities in careAndrew GregoryHealth editorThu 22 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThousands of children inEnglandare experiencing some of the sharpest rises in waiting times for healthcare in the history of the NHS, a report has revealed.While some adult waiting times have improved, children and young people are being “hit hardest” amid soaring demand and falling numbers of staff, according to the annual state of care report by the Care Quality Commission.In community health services alone, 80,000 children and young people have been waiting more than a year for an appointment – almost 11 times the number of adults, the report said. Experts said that was “wholly unacceptable”. Children’s health conditions were getting worse and becoming harder to treat as a result, they added.NHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry findsRead moreMore broadly across health and social care services in England there were signs of improvement, including more GP appointments, increased use of digital solutions and shorter waits for elective care. The report also highlighted examples of local innovation, including neighbourhood models and integrated care teams.But improvements were struggling to keep pace with rapidly rising demand for health and social care. In many areas, including mental health services, patients’ needs are also becoming more complex.Persistent inequalities across the entire health and care system mean people’s experience of care is fractured and heavily dependent on where they live and who they are, according to the report.Poorest children in England 40% more likely to be hospitalised for lung infectionsRead moreAcross all areas of the country and every part of the health and social care system, there was “unwarranted variation” in access to services, quality of care and outcomes, the CQC said.Some adults with cancer were waiting far too long to begin treatment after being diagnosed, while there remained “sustained pressure” in urgent and emergency care.But the report highlighted how children in particular were bearing the brunt of long waiting times. And, despite growing demand, health visitor and school nurse numbers were “continuing to decline”, the CQC said.It also raised concerns about regional variations in rates of children being admitted to hospital for diabetes and asthma, and sounded the alarm over particularly high rates of rotten teeth among children in some areas.UK children will be one of unhealthiest generations in decades, doctors sayRead moreDr Ronny Cheung, of the Royal College of Paediatrics and ChildHealth, said community health services existed to support some of the country’s most vulnerable children outside hospital, including those with complex conditions, developmental disorders and safeguarding needs.“Yet these children face some of the longest waits in theNHS, while waiting times for adult community services have improved. It is wholly unacceptable that more than one in four children still wait over a year for treatment, and without urgent action, too many more will be left to suffer unnecessarily.“As a paediatrician, I am sick of seeing children wait so long for support that they miss crucial opportunities to improve their health and development.”Behind the figures were children struggling at school, families pushed to breaking point and conditions becoming more complex while they wait, Cheung added.The CQC chair, Julia Neuberger, said that while some health and social care services were “working well”, improvements were not keeping pace with demand. “To repair a fracturing system, there must be a collective response,” she added.The Department of Health and Social Care said the report showed “the scale of the challenge this government inherited” when it was elected in 2024. “While the CQC recognises signs of progress on waiting lists, cancer care and general practice, patients and families rightly expect faster improvements – which is why the secretary of state has committed to go further to end corridor care, transform support for mothers and children, and deliver a new national care service,” a spokesperson added.Explore more on these topicsChildren's healthCare Quality Commission (CQC)Health policyEnglandChildrenNHSHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham vows UK will hit net zero target despite Jackdaw gasfield approval | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: PM pledges commitment to address climate crisis, saying in Guardian article that his ‘determination is unwavering’
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: PM pledges commitment to address climate crisis, saying in Guardian article that his ‘determination is unwavering’
Content: Activists from Fossil Free London stage protest outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenActivists from Fossil Free London stage protest outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockClimate crisisAndy Burnham vows UK will hit net zero target despite Jackdaw gasfield approvalPM pledges commitment to address climate crisis, saying in Guardian article that his ‘determination is unwavering’Andy Burnham: We will make the net-zero transition work for BritainJessica ElgotandAlexandra ToppingThu 22 Oct 2026 17.34 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 13.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has said he will not “abandon the responsibility” of fighting the climate crisis after the government approved the Jackdaw gasfield, pledging to block new North Sea licences and keep Britain on track for net zero by 2050.We will make the net-zero transition work for Britain – approving the Jackdaw gasfield is part of the plan | Andy BurnhamRead moreThe comments are the prime minister’s most forthright yet on net zero, after many MPs have privately cast doubt on the authenticity of his commitment to tackling the climate crisis.The energy secretary,Miatta Fahnbulleh, insisted that she alone would make a decision on whether to approve the Rosebank oilfield – a decision sources say she is minded to block.Burnham has been under pressure from industry and political opponents, as well as some Labour MPs, to water down Labour’s manifesto promises on new oil and gas licences and the net zero targets.“There has been much speculation about what this announcement means for Britain’s commitment to addressing the climate crisis. I want to be clear that our determination is unwavering,”the prime minister said in an article for the Guardian.He said he was conscious of the “acute global instability” affecting energy security and wanted to treat oil and gas workers with more dignity.Burnham said that would not stop the government from abiding by its climate targets, saying he was “personally committed to confronting” the challenges of the climate crisis.“Britain has just emerged from its hottest summer on record, during which we had nurses collapsing on hospital wards, bus drivers working in intolerable conditions and families losing everything to wildfires,” he wrote.“More extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead. The climate crisis is no distant threat. It is here, on our doorstep, affecting people’s lives and livelihoods. I am personally committed to confronting it, and I will not abandon the responsibility we have to future generations.”View image in fullscreenMiatta Fahnbulleh: ‘It has been really painful to watch the consensus burn at a time when we’re seeing the impact of climate change.’Photograph: Imageplotter/AlamyMeanwhile, Fahnbulleh doubled down on her insistence that she would not be influenced by other departments on whether to approve the Rosebank oilfield, setting up a potential standoff with the Treasury.The chancellor, John Healey, has said he expects “oil and gas” revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, but Fanhbulleh said “only I can make that decision”, insisting that she bore the legal responsibility to ensure the UK did not violate its climate commitments.Dismissing speculation that Burnham, or his chancellor, would make the final call, she said: “[It] sits heavy for such a big controversial decision because, in the end, only I can make it. And if it is overturned by other colleagues, all that means is we’re going to be overturned in the courts. So we will do the process and we will do it properly.”Fahnbulleh said she was “really concerned” and “quite sad” about the breakdown in consensus about the climate crisis. She said: “I think it’s a sad place where Reform has gone and got to. But I’m even sadder about the Tories because they know better, and they’ve had a long tradition, including Boris Johnson, of working cross-party on climate action.“It has been really painful and tragic to watch that consensus burn at a time when we’re seeing the impact of climate change this summer.”The climate crisis was having a real impact on communities, she added. “It’s people’s livelihoods, it’s their jobs, their communities. Even if you don’t care about climate – care about that, you’ve got to take action.”Reflecting on the decision to approve the Jackdaw gasfield, Burnham said he wanted to make the transition to a greener future “on our terms”, saying that meant giving oil and gas workers a path to new jobs and using homegrown rather than imported gas.“At a time of acute global instability, it makes sense to responsibly use our resources here at home.Gasfrom this field will begin heating our homes and powering our businesses this winter.”He said he had been moved by the plight of oil and gas workers in Aberdeen, adding that it was an industry that had suffered from deindustrialisation “with too little thought given by politicians to the places left behind. I will not be so careless with people’s lives.”Fahnbulleh echoed the prime minister’s words, saying the private sector had invested £100bn in clean energy in the last two years. “It’s a huge opportunity for parts of our countries that have been left behind,” she said. But that investment had to have a real-world impact, she added. “When you say jobs are going to be created, don’t say it. People need to see it.”Burnham said the energy wealth fund that was being created to convert North Sea oil and gas tax revenues to clean energy programmes was long overdue – “something that, frankly, should have happened more than 40 years ago”.It comes as Burnham announced that military planes and helicopters would fight wildfires for the first time, ahead of a major wildfire summit with fire chiefs, local leaders and experts.The RAF’s chinook helicopters and A400M aircraft will fight fires and help crews across the UK tackle blazes on remote moorland, steep hillsides and other hard-to-reach terrain.“Heroes shouldn’t have to fight with one hand tied behind their backs,” said the prime minister.Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisFossil fuelsEnergyMiatta FahnbullehAndy BurnhamOilOil and gas companiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Woman charged over shooting of police officer in Nottingham | UK news | The Guardian
description: Aisha Zaman, 27, charged with two firearms offences after incident in city centre on Sunday
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Aisha Zaman, 27, charged with two firearms offences after incident in city centre on Sunday
Content: Forensics officers at the scene of the shooting of a police officer in Nottingham city centre on Sunday.Photograph: Ben Booth/Sopa Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenForensics officers at the scene of the shooting of a police officer in Nottingham city centre on Sunday.Photograph: Ben Booth/Sopa Images/ShutterstockUK newsWoman charged over shooting of police officer in NottinghamAisha Zaman, 27, charged with two firearms offences after incident in city centre on SundayNadeem BadshahThu 22 Oct 2026 17.31 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 15.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 27-year-old woman has been charged after a police officer was shot while attending an incident in Nottingham.Aisha Zaman, from the Hyson Green area of the city, has been charged with possession of a prohibited firearm and possession of that firearm with intent to commit an indictable offence.She has been remanded into custody and will appear before Nottingham magistrates court on Friday.The officer, who is in a stable condition in hospital, had approached two people at a bus stop at 4.50am last Sunday when he was shot in the foot, Nottinghamshire police said.A weapon was recovered and a large crime scene cordon put in place around Angel Row in the city centre.Several other people have been arrested in connection with the incident including two men, aged 24 and 30, and two women, aged 25 and 21, on suspicion of assisting an offender.A 35-year-old man and a 33-year-old woman have also been arrested on suspicion of possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life and assisting an offender. Both suspects remain in police custody, the force added.DCS Rich Bull said: “We would just like to take this moment to thank the public. The outpouring of support for the injured officer has been greatly appreciated.“We continue to support him as he undergoes further treatment in hospital and are keeping him and his family fully informed of the developments in this investigation.
