He has asked for privacy during this incredibly difficult time.”The Police Federation sent its best wishes to the officer and said it was a “stark reminder of the dangers police officers face every day”.Following the incident, Neghat Khan, the leader of Nottingham city council, said she was “deeply shocked and saddened”.She said Nottingham was a “safe city” and praised the bravery of police and community protection officers, adding: “My thoughts and full support are with the injured police officer, their family and their colleagues across Nottinghamshire police.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to reveal plans for AI unit to tackle wildfires after scorching summer | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: PM will also announce funding for specialised protective gear and the deployment of military aircraft
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: PM will also announce funding for specialised protective gear and the deployment of military aircraft
Content: Firefighters inspect scorched scrubland near Dunwich Heath in Suffolk in July. The ‘apocalyptic’ wildfire came within two miles of the Sizewell B nuclear plant.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenFirefighters inspect scorched scrubland near Dunwich Heath in Suffolk in July. The ‘apocalyptic’ wildfire came within two miles of the Sizewell B nuclear plant.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAWildfiresBurnham to reveal plans for AI unit to tackle wildfires after scorching summerPM will also announce funding for specialised protective gear and the deployment of military aircraftPippa NeillEnvironment reporterThu 22 Oct 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 17.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK government is to create an AI Cobra unit to spot wildfires after this year’s record-breaking summer saw devastating blazes across the country.The country experienced itshottest-ever summerthis year, with prolonged dry periods and extreme heat fuelling wildfires that triggered anemergency alertto mobile phones in England and Wales.Figures releasedon 8 October showed a clear upward trend in the number of fires recorded each year.The Met Office found that the climate crisis made this extreme heat about 130 times more likely.‘It’s due to climate’: the people of Stourbridge on the town’s wildfiresRead moreAt the government’s first wildfire resilience summit on Friday,Andy Burnhamwill announce plans for a new wildfire AI unit in the National Situation Centre, which is part of the Cobra briefing rooms.Businesses including Google, Airbus and VodafoneThree are expected to attend the summit to set out how satellite monitoring and early warning systems can help fight fires. The government said its new AI unit would enable it to “spot and fight fires faster”.The prime minister will also announce £45m for fire crews to buy wildfire-specific personal protective equipment (PPE).This comes after the Guardianrevealedthat more than half of the 29 fire services that responded to requests for information had no wildfire PPE.They included the Suffolk fire and rescue service, which had to deal with an “apocalyptic” wildfire earlier this summer that burned close to the Sizewell B nuclear power station and destroyed vast areas of aprotected nature reserve.Standard particle-filtering respirators do not protect against dangerous gases such as carbon monoxide, which are heavily present in wildfire smoke.Standard PPE can also be too hot and heavy for wildfire conditions. This can cause crews to overheat, or remove their PPE altogether, exposing them to greater danger from heat, smoke and radiation.Firefighters voice growing concerns over water supplies to tackle UK wildfiresRead moreThe prime minister will also announce that military planes and helicopters will be made available to fight wildfires on remote moorland, steep hillsides and other hard-to-reach terrain.The defence secretary,Wes Streeting, said: “As the threat of wildfires in the UK grows, defence will step up to provide greater support to our emergency services and protect military training areas across the country.”The government will also look at tougher local restrictions or product bans to stop people starting fires when the risk is high. In August, Burnhamannounceda temporary ban on sales of disposable barbecues. He has also beencriticisedfor failing to address the climate emergency in his wildfire response.Farmers will also be given funding to make landscapes more resilient to fires. This announcement comes after the governmentquietly scrappedplans announced under the Conservative government to prepare the countryside in England for wildfires.This revelation led Alistair Carmichael, a Scottish Liberal Democrat MP and chair of the Commons environment, food and rural affairs committee, to raise “serious questions about whether this summer’s wildfires could have looked different with more resources on the ground”.The government also said it would allocate £25m to restore dried-out peatlands in England so they hold more water and act as natural firebreaks, as well as provide financial support for farmers to fireproof their land.Rewilded land remains green amid drought-stricken English countryside, images showRead moreThis new grant scheme is expected to run from April 2027 to April 2029.Environmental campaigner and author Guy Shrubsole said: “For decades, wealthy grouse moor owners have drained our peat bogs, turning them into a tinderbox. This grant will help reverse that destruction, but must be followed by a new round of landscape recovery funding, and duties on landowners to repair the damage done. It’s time to make England wet again.”The prime minister said: “I stood in Stourbridge and watched families lose everything. I will never forget it. Our firefighters were heroes that day, but heroes shouldn’t have to fight with one hand tied behind their backs.“Crews will now have the kit they need to stay safe and military aircraft will stand ready to help tackle wildfires from the sky. We cannot put people through another summer like this one.”Explore more on these topicsWildfiresClimate crisisGoogleAirbusVodafoneAndy BurnhamWes StreetingnewsShareReuse this content

title: A possible three tornados wallop Arizona, bringing golf-ball sized hail | Arizona | The Guardian
description: Violent storms overnight knocked over utility poles and carried thunder and heavy winds through central Arizona
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Violent storms overnight knocked over utility poles and carried thunder and heavy winds through central Arizona
Content: Several uprooted trees cause damage at an apartment complex after storms hit the area on Wednesday in Mesa, Arizona.Photograph: Ross D Franklin/APView image in fullscreenSeveral uprooted trees cause damage at an apartment complex after storms hit the area on Wednesday in Mesa, Arizona.Photograph: Ross D Franklin/APArizonaA possible three tornados wallop Arizona, bringing golf-ball sized hailViolent storms overnight knocked over utility poles and trees and carried thunder and heavy winds through stateAssociated PressThu 22 Oct 2026 19.15 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 08.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYet more severe weather struck Thursday in the US south-west as the Four Corners region surveyed blown-away roofs, trees knocked on to homes and power lines downed from overnight tornadoes that injured one person.The injuries weren’t life-threatening but rare for an area better known for scalding heat. But this fall has been unusually soggy in the south-west with El Niño conditions that have sent one tropical system after another in from the Pacific, causing the Grand Canyon and surrounding deserts to rage with floods.Now, golf ball-size hail and tornadoes have joined the mix. National Weather Service meteorologists suspect at least three tornadoes touched down as storms swept across centralArizonalate Wednesday.The nasty weather hit during Lenna Landy’s yoga routine in Overgaard, a community of about 3,000 people 140 miles (225km) north-east of Phoenix. Landy had ignored alerts about a possible tornado, but then the storm struck.“It was like Zeus-was-angry kind of level, of thunder cracks,” Landy said.The power went off, her house shook and Landy couldn’t find her glasses.“If this is my end, I won’t see it coming,” she recalled thinking. “The scariest part was just like, how quickly it came on.”The storm peeled off nearby roofs, shattered windows and blew a shed into a home, she said. A spruce tree in her yard was split in half.View image in fullscreenA storm dumps heavy rain and hail across Flagstaff, Arizona, on Wednesday.Photograph: Cheyanne Mumphrey/APStill more severe weather, including large hail, struck Thursday with much of Arizona under tornado and flood watches. Similar weather soaked New Mexico, while swathes of Utah and Colorado were under flood watches and warnings.Warm, moist air moving north fuels storms coming in from the California coast. Changing winds can make them spin, creating the conditions for tornadoes, said Ryan Bernhart, a weather service meteorologist in Flagstaff.“This is very unusual for this area at this time of the year,” Bernhart said.View image in fullscreenUprooted trees cause damage at an apartment complex after storms hit the area on Wednesday in Mesa, Arizona.Photograph: Ross D Franklin/APTornadoes are somewhat but not exceptionally unusual in Arizona. Notable outbreaks happened in 2019 and 2010.Strong winds toppled trees in Flagstaff and Mesa, with some landing on walls and carports. A few dozen ponderosa pines more than 30ft (9 meters) tall fell down in the Coconino national forest, north-west of Flagstaff.“These are not small trees that are down,” Bernhart said. “These are pretty strong trees that had been knocked down.”Explore more on these topicsArizonaUS weatherTornadoesExtreme weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: Sharp drops for AI stocks overwhelm markets worldwide as oil prices jump | US markets | The Guardian
description: Datacenter and chip costs fueled sharp decrease in AI sector although non-AI stocks still had a strong showing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Datacenter and chip costs fueled sharp decrease in AI sector although non-AI stocks still had a strong showing
Content: An options trader works on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on 7 January 2026.Photograph: Richard Drew/APView image in fullscreenAn options trader works on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on 7 January 2026.Photograph: Richard Drew/APUS marketsSharp drops for AI stocks overwhelm markets worldwide as oil prices jumpDatacenter and chip costs fueled sharp decrease in AI sector although non-AI stocks still had a strong showingAssociated PressThu 22 Oct 2026 17.50 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 18.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe latest shudder for stocks in theAIindustry pulled markets lower worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about thewar with Iran.TheS&P500 fell 1.2% for its worst day since July, while theNasdaqcomposite tumbled 2.6%. The weakness for tech stocks was so overwhelming that it masked strength for the rest of the US market, in which the majority of stocks actually rose. TheDow JonesIndustrial Average added 11 points, or less than 0.1%.AI-related stocks have been swinging on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build datacenters and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that their prices shot too high following a years-long frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.Oil prices jump to five-month high as attacks threaten global supplyRead moreLam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 11.8%.Other big tech stocks likewise fell following quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets.Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7% after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, shedding tens of billions in market value, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it was creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses.Tesla fell 3.1% after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast.The global tide against AI stocks knockedNvidiadown 4.4%. Because the chip giant is the largest company on Wall Street by total value, movements for its stock carry more weight on the S&P 500 than any other, and it was the single strongest force pulling the index lower.CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 10.1%.The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where indexes are full of players in the industry. South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5%, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3% and Japan’sNikkei225 sank 2.7%.Also weighing on global stock markets was a jump in oil prices.The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil leaped 4% to $113.17 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s shot up from less than $97 at the start of the month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1.4%. It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or US indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds.Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWorries about big government debt are weighing on almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong US economy and other factors, have pushed yields in the US bond market recently to their highest levels in decades.But US yields nevertheless fell sharply on Thursday in a signal that investors were buying US government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled.The yield on the 10-year treasury tumbled to 4.97% from 5.13% late on Wednesday and from more than 5.30% earlier this month. That’s a major move for the bond market.Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the US economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could signal that layoffs remain low across the country.That solid economy has helped US companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the US stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. Two out of every three stocks within the S&P 500 rose on Thursday, only to get drowned out by the drops for more influential tech stocks.Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses on Thursday.CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expected “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 5.6%.All told, the S&P 500 fell 93.74 points, to 7,663.43. TheDow JonesIndustrial Average added 11.89, to 52,867.98, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 694.00, to 26,008.86.Explore more on these topicsUS marketsStock marketsDow JonesNasdaqStandard & Poor'sNikkeiMetanewsShareReuse this content

title: Too little, too late: Trump takes on gas prices as fuel costs hamper his midterm hopes | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Polls show US voters are deeply upset by high gas prices and are likely to punish Republicans in the midterms as a result
Author: Debbie Carlson
Headline: Polls show US voters are deeply upset by high gas prices and are likely to punish Republicans in the midterms as a result
Content: A gas pump in Allagash, Maine, on 14 October 2026.Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA gas pump in Allagash, Maine, on 14 October 2026.Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty ImagesUS midterm elections 2026Too little, too late: Trump takes on gas prices as fuel costs hamper his midterm hopesPolls show US voters are deeply upset by high gas prices and are likely to punish Republicans in the midterms as a resultHow will Trump’s mass deportation agenda shape the US midterm elections? Our reporters answer your questionsDebbie Carlsonin Chicago,Chris Steinin Ohio andSam Levinein MissouriThu 22 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 09.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith fewer than two weeks until themidterms, US voters are unlikely to see relief on one of this election cycle’s main issues: gas prices.Airing up her car’s tires at a Speedway in Perrysburg,Ohio, Toledo resident Sharie Smith, 41, says soaring costs are having a direct impact on her life.From Iran to AI: the six key voter issues shaping the US midterm electionsRead more“It’s affecting my budget,” she says. “You got to take away certain things, you got to take away from your kids, like extracurricular activities.” She says high gas prices are making it harder to pay for the fees for her children’s football games.Every 10 days, she used to fill up her gray Chevy Malibu for $30 to $40, but now it costs $50 to $60. It stings, she says. “Especially that with the price of groceries,” she adds.“And I don’t even have a big car. I feel bad for those people with big cars, like trucks.”Donald Trump has made many promises about bringing down gas prices and specifically touted several diesel cost-savings deals this month, but voters won’t see lower costs by 3 November, say energy analysts.National average prices for gasoline and diesel are down marginally from a month ago, according toAAA, but remain substantially higher than last year. Compared with 2025, gasoline costs are up more than $1.25 a gallon, at $4.29, while diesel prices are up nearly 75%, to $6.30 a gallon.View image in fullscreenPeople protest outside an Trump event in Sumterville, Florida, on 1 May 2026.Photograph: Thomas Simonetti/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesPolls show that US voters are deeply upset by high gas prices and are likely to punish Republicans as a result. A 10 October poll byPoliticoshowed that even if Trump were to bring the price of gasoline down by $1 a gallon, most voters polled would not likely be swayed to vote Republican.Earlier this month, Trump announced several deals attempting to lower diesel prices, including promoting greater use of “red dye” diesel fuel normally reserved for off-highway use, temporarily lifting sanctions on Russian diesel imports, and now a one-time, $8bn diesel-fuel subsidy for farmers to help with harvest.“Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority,” Trump posted on his social media site.Ed Hirs, energy fellow at the University of Houston, says these moves will have no impact. “Zero. No elaboration needed,” he says.Under the Russia deal, the US can import 2.24m barrels of Russian diesel, with more to follow. That initial figure amounts to just 14 hours of US diesel demand, says Andrew Critchlow, head of energy news for Dow Jones Energy. For context, the global diesel market uses nearly 30m barrels a day.Hirs adds that the deal with Putin is not for new supply. “It was going someplace. It was going someplace at a discount. And now what Trump has done is, rather than have Russia sell it at a discount, they’re selling it for full value. He’s given them a huge windfall,” Hirs says.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump speaks with Vladimir Putin as they meet to negotiate for an end to the war in Ukraine in Anchorage, Alaska, on 15 August 2025.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersDiesel fuel is an important transportation fuel globally, critical in the last-mile delivery of most consumer goods, so everyone feels the pinch, says Rob Thummel, senior portfolio manager at Tortoise Capital. Energy prices across the board are higher because of the US war on Iran, which closed the strait of Hormuz, through which much of the world’s crude oil flows.Producing more diesel is difficult because Middle East refineries were damaged early in the war, and Chinese refiners are unable to get enough oil to produce any extra fuel for world markets. Recent attacks on Russian refiners by Ukrainian drones have further cut global supplies. US refineries have access to domestic oil but are running at maximum capacity, Thummel says.The White House has characterized its recentexecutive orderto temporarily allow greater use of red-dye diesel as a cost-saving measure for farmers and truckers. This fuel is exempt from federal excise taxes because it is intended for farmers and off-road machinery and is stained red to differentiate it from regular diesel. The White House says the 24.4 cents per gallon discount will save those drivers about $60 on a 250-gallon fill up.Yet Hirs says it gives farmers more competition for fuel, which will raise their prices. Farmers already are being buffeted by higher operating costs across the board and losing China as a key export market because of the US’s trade war with the Asian nation.Prices could rise as energy demand increases in the winter heating months, especially in places that use heating oil, experts add. Energy prices are seasonal, and prices are usually lower at this time of year since it’s neither cooling nor heating season, says Jay Hatfield, chief investment officer of real-asset investment firm InfraCap. Despite typically lower seasonal demand, prices are already high.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow We WinBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere are risks of higher prices if the fighting in the Middle East escalates, Hatfield says, pointing to a pickup of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia as an example.Critchlow says with many countries having depleted strategic stocks and few countries have released reserves, it might not take too much to push prices up. “I think that we are in a very fragile position now, marketwise,” he says.The only moves that will lower energy costs are to open the strait of Hormuz to get more oil flowing, and to negotiate a peace accord between Russia and Ukraine, as these two conflicts are interlinked with energy markets, the energy experts say.If those conflicts were resolved, Critchlow says the energy situation could be drastically different two years from now, with the world being oversupplied with fossil-fuel energy.That change can’t come soon enough for some drivers. Lotanpa Jones, a home healthcare aide, was filling up at a Mobil in St Charles, Missouri, earlier this month. Regular fuel was $4.09 a gallon – last 1 October the national average price was $3.15 to $3.19, according to data fromAAA. Diesel was $6.59 a gallon, up from $3.71 a year ago, according to data tracked by theUS Energy Information Administration (EIA)View image in fullscreenA driver pumps diesel at a Pilot gas station on 14 September 2026 in Buda, Texas.Photograph: Brandon Bell/Getty Images“I can tell you this is making me want to park my car,” said Jones.She said she had last filled up her car two days earlier and now was adding another $55.“It’s affecting a lot because you gotta decide what you’re gonna buy,” she said. “It’s major.”Jones said she thought it would affect who people vote for. “Most definitely. Yes, this is extreme.”Ironically, given Trump’santipathytowards electric vehicles, Critchlow foresees the current crisis eventually pushing electrification for consumers, heavy industry and agriculture in the US. The shift in consumption and energy mix mirrors the 1970s energy shock, he says. “We are going to see something similar,” he says.In the meantime, gas prices are likely to take their toll on Republicans come 3 November. Back inOhio, Smith, a home health nurse, says she has already lost patients because of Medicaid eligibility changes made by the state, which she criticized Republicans for. “They’re thinking about the wrong things, and now the price of gas is going up,” Smith says.As for who she is voting for, she says: “I’m going Democrat.” As for the Republican candidates, she adds: “They don’t have any idea what people are going through.”Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026US gas pricesUS economyOilDonald TrumpMissouriOhiofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: US judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in $10bn lawsuit against BBC | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Judge threatens to dismiss Trump’s BBC lawsuit unless he cooperates with discovery process and sits for deposition
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: Judge threatens to dismiss Trump’s BBC lawsuit unless he cooperates with discovery process and sits for deposition
Content: Donald Trump walks to board Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on 21 October 2026.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump walks to board Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on 21 October 2026.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpUS judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in $10bn lawsuit against BBCJudge threatens to dismiss Trump’s BBC lawsuit unless he cooperates with discovery process and sits for depositionJeremy Barrin MiamiThu 22 Oct 2026 13.18 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has been ordered by a US judge to cooperate with the discovery process mandated for his lawsuit against the BBC and to sit for a deposition by 11 December – or else he could be subject to sanctions, including the possible dismissal of the $10bn lawsuit.The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by theBBCthat spliced together two comments made nearly an hour apart by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot. The BBC has acknowledged that this specific edit was misleading, but Trump has gone on to claim, falsely, that the BBC did not just edit his speech but used AI to insert words into his speech.While the broadcast was not readily available to view in Florida, Trump’s team has argued that he was personally damaged by the broadcast under Florida’s Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act.During a lengthy hearing dealing with a variety of discovery issues, federal magistrate judge Enjoliqué Lett on Thursday also rejected a request by Trump’s legal team to prevent the seven-hour-long deposition from being videotaped, though it will only be accessible to attorneys in the case.Lett agreed with contentions from the BBC’s lawyers that Trump’s team had not been sufficiently forthcoming in handing over internal documents relevant to the case ahead of an 18 December deadline for discovery.“We still have a completely lopsided [situation] here on discovery. They have produced absolutely nothing of any substance,” attorney Charles Tobin, on behalf of the BBC, argued in a Miami courtroom.The documents that Trump’s team have turned over have primarily been either pulled from the internet or provided by the BBC itself.“It strains credulity that a thorough search has been done in order to determine that all of these requests have been responded to,” Lett told Alejandro Brito, Trump’s Florida-based attorney. “The court is not satisfied that anyone is doing a thorough job.”The judge gave the plaintiffs 30 days to produce the relevant documents. While she acknowledged that the discovery process can be “burdensome” on both parties, she said that “failure to do so could result in sanctions, including possible dismissal of the suit for failure to prosecute the case and engage in meaningful discovery process”.Of the Trump team’s obligation to adequately participate in the discovery process, the judge said: “This is the last opportunity to do so.”After discussing the discovery process, the judge turned tothe BBC’s request to compel the president’s team to agree for a deposition,after a previously scheduled date – 16 October – was cancelled for what Trump’s counsel said were “other matters of national importance”. While the BBC noted that Trump was actually campaigning in Georgia on that day, leading Tobin to conclude that the plaintiff’s team had transmitted “fake news”, Brito said the president was “involved in a host of things” on a daily basis that the BBC’s legal team “has no idea” about.While Lett said she was obligated to adhere to the discovery schedule mandated in the case, that timeline could be extended by district court judge Jeffrey T Kuntz. Tobin, representing the BBC, said his side was willing to push back the timeline for Trump’s deposition if Kuntz adjusted the discovery schedule.Lett once again threatened sanctions – including dismissal – if Trump’s team did not comply with her deposition order.“The lesson for the day is that no plaintiff is above the law, and no plaintiff is above the orders of the court,” Tobin said.In a filing on Wednesday, Trump’s team said he would be willing to sit for a deposition during the second or third week of January.During the hearing, Lett also allowed the BBC’s subpoena to Mar-a-Lago, Trump’s Florida club, to go ahead, despite protests from Trump’s attorney that the business was separate from the president.Brito, Trump’s attorney, contended that the president does not run the club. “The president’s occupation is the president of the United States,” he said. “It has nothing to do with Mar-a-Lago as far as his occupation.”Tobin, representing the BBC, vehemently disagreed. “To say that Mar-a-Lago is not tied to this president or his reputation ignores the fact that he hosts [Ukrainian president] Volodymyr Zelenskyy, he hosts the president of Ireland, [Russian president] Vladimir Putin – he uses Mar-a-Lago as a location to publicize his reputation as a symbol of his personal power, so it is inextricably intertwined. His business successes are a measure of his reputation.”In issuing the ruling, the judge agreed that the club “falls within the scope of discoverability”.“I think it is intertwined with his profession and therefore any harm that may be alleged under his professional trade and occupation would be reflected with how he conducts business with Mar-a-Lago, at least for discovery purposes,” she added.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpBBCLaw (US)US politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Elon Musk reportedly invests $1bn in David Ellison’s Skydance | Elon Musk | The Guardian
description: Musk’s investment into the new media empire comes after Paramount’s $111bn merger with Warner Bros Discovery
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Musk’s investment into the new media empire comes after Paramount’s $111bn merger with Warner Bros Discovery
Content: Elon Musk gestures as he attends the Viva Technology conference at the Porte de Versailles exhibition centre in Paris, France, on 16 June 2023.Photograph: Gonzalo Fuentes/ReutersView image in fullscreenElon Musk gestures as he attends the Viva Technology conference at the Porte de Versailles exhibition centre in Paris, France, on 16 June 2023.Photograph: Gonzalo Fuentes/ReutersElon MuskElon Musk reportedly invests $1bn in David Ellison’s SkydanceMusk’s investment into the new media empire comes after Paramount’s $111bn merger with Warner Bros DiscoveryMaya YangThu 22 Oct 2026 17.23 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 17.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElon Musk has reportedlyinvestedapproximately $1bn in Skydance, the new media empire led by David Ellison.The deal comes alongside fresh equity infusions from existing investors, including board member Laurene Powell Jobs, Steve Jobs’s widow. Semafor first reported the news.The investment follows Paramount’s recent$111bn mergerwith Warner Bros Discovery, a huge acquisition that brought the media companies together under the Skydance name. At the head of the new media empire is David Ellison, the son of billionaire Oracle co-founder and Donald Trump ally Larry Ellison.The Guardian has contacted Musk and Skydance for comment.The cash infusion solidifies an alliance between two of Trump’s richest monetary backers. In September, Semaforreportedthat Paramount executives had considered Musk as an equity investor, citing his close ties to Larry Ellison, who invested$1bnin Musk’s acquisition of X in 2022 and also$45min support of Trump’s re-election bid in 2024. Musk spent more than $290m on Trump’s re-election bid and has spent more than $350m backing Republicans in the current US midterm elections.After the merger, Skydance co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz, who previously led Mattel,informedemployees that the integration would involve layoffs, stating: “Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce.”The company’s leadership – which now oversees Paramount and Warner Bros’s movie studios, HBO Max, CBS News and CNN – has set a target of more than $6bn in cost savings over the next three years, a goal that Los Angeles county officialsestimatecould lead to the loss of 4,500 film and television jobs in Los Angeles alone.Prior to the merger, a coalition of 12 states, including California and New York, sued Paramount,arguingthat the deal would “extinguish” competition and result in “higher prices, lower quality and less content for film and television”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn September, a settlement agreement required Skydance to release at least 30 films and more than 180 television shows annually, while ensuring that CBS and CNN maintain editorial independence.Explore more on these topicsElon MuskMedia businessParamount PicturesMergers and acquisitionsWarner BrosUS television industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Meta strikes deal with Mark Zuckerberg to help him foot billionaire tax bill | Meta | The Guardian
description: Chief executive agrees to remain in California for eight years even if state brings in one-off 5% wealth tax
Author: Graeme Wearden
Headline: Chief executive agrees to remain in California for eight years even if state brings in one-off 5% wealth tax
Content: Mark Zuckerberg with his wife Priscilla Chan. The Meta founder said he was considering moving out of California because of the threat of a huge tax bill.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersView image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg with his wife Priscilla Chan. The Meta founder said he was considering moving out of California because of the threat of a huge tax bill.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersMetaMeta strikes deal with Mark Zuckerberg to help him foot billionaire tax billChief executive agrees to remain in California for eight years even if state brings in one-off 5% wealth taxGraeme WeardenThu 22 Oct 2026 11.40 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 06.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMeta has struck a deal withMark Zuckerbergto help him foot a possible California wealth tax targeting billionaires.The social media company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp revealed on Wednesday night that the arrangement would keep its chief executive living inCalifornia, where Meta’s headquarters are located.Under the deal, Zuckerberg will receive new shares that could be sold to potentially foot a multibillion-dollar tax bill in the event that California passes a one-off billionaire tax. In return, he is committed to remain a resident of the state, or whereverMetamaintains its base, for eight years.Californians will vote early next month on Proposition 40, a one-off 5% tax on the roughly 250 billionaires who live in the state.Zuckerberg, worth $239bn (£180bn) according to Forbes, told Meta he was considering moving his primary residence elsewhere because Prop 40 could expose him to a massive tax liability, potentially forcing him to sell voting shares to pay it.In response, Meta is creating a new class of non-voting shares via a two-for-one stock split for all existing shareholders. This will allow Zuckerberg to sell some of these new class C shares to pay a potential tax bill, without diluting his control of the company.The new Darth Vader: how tech execs became the film villains of our ageRead moreRecent polling has shown that Prop 40 remains short of majority support with voters. Tech billionaireshave been spending heavily to fight the measure, including the Google co-founder Sergey Brin, the Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel and the former Google CEO Eric Schmidt.Rohit Khanna, the US congressman representing California’s 17th congressional district, has described Prop 40 as a choice between standing with the working class or the oligarchs.“Every society is taxed. The only question is who will pay,”Khanna wrote in the Guardian last week.“In Trump’s America, working people pay more than they should, while billionaires are so unburdened that they are becoming trillionaires. In the America we seek, billionaires and trillionaires will pay their fair share, while working people will be unburdened.”Meta also reported a 26% rise in revenues for the last quarter to $64.6bn, beating expectations of $63.3bn. But profits fell by 37% to $13bn, dragged down by a $9.9bn charge related to Meta’slawsuit over child protection and social media addictionfailings.The company’s shares slid by more than 6% when trading opened on Wall Street on Thursday, helping to drag the tech-focused Nasdaq index down 2.5% amid a wider selloff of AI-linked stocks.In a separate case, on Wednesday a judge in New Mexicoordered Meta to pay $25bnfollowing a trial that found the company had misled the public about how it handled Facebook user data.Meta also revealed that it had cut its headcount to 66,775 at the end of September, 15% fewer than a year ago.Reuters contributed to this report.Explore more on these topicsMetaMark ZuckerbergCaliforniaWest CoastThe super-richnewsShareReuse this content

title: Marine life in Gulf of Mexico has still not fully recovered from 2010 BP oil spill | Deepwater Horizon oil spill | The Guardian
description: New study reveals dramatic population drops in fish, cephalopods and more after the Deepwater Horizon spill
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: New study reveals dramatic population drops in fish, cephalopods and more after the Deepwater Horizon spill
Content: The Deepwater Horizon oil spill led to the ‘sudden, severe and persistent declines in the abundance’ of marine life, study says.Photograph: A Martin UW Photography/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Deepwater Horizon oil spill led to the ‘sudden, severe and persistent declines in the abundance’ of marine life, study says.Photograph: A Martin UW Photography/Getty ImagesDeepwater Horizon oil spillMarine life in Gulf of Mexico has still not fully recovered from 2010 BP oil spillNew study reveals dramatic population drops in fish, cephalopods and more after the Deepwater Horizon spillMaya YangThu 22 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 13.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMarine life in the Gulf of Mexico plummeted by about 60% after BP’s2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spilland has still not fully recovered, according to a newstudy.The April 2010explosion of an offshore drillingunit 50 miles off the Louisiana coast triggered the largest marine oil spill in history, releasing 134m gallons of oil into the ocean. According to the study published Monday in PNAS, the disaster – which also killed 11 people and injured 17 others – led to the “sudden, severe and persistent declines in the abundance” of marine life for more than a decade.Conducted using acoustic sonar, multi-depth trawling nets and genetic studies, the study revealed dramatic population drops across the gulf between 2011 and 2015: fish declined by 63.5%, macrocrustaceans including shrimp and krill fell by 62% – severely affecting a primary food source for whales – and cephalopods such as squid and octopus dropped by 59.7%.Researchers found that the post-spill population crash outpaced any decline recorded in similar waters over the past 60 years. They also noted that natural factors like temperature, oxygen and food availability did not vary with the decline, confirming the spill as the primary cause.The marine species most severely affected were also among the most vital to open-ocean ecosystems and global food webs. Krill, a primary food source for deep-sea fish and shrimp, plunged by 72.8%. Bristlemouths – likely the most abundant backboned animals on Earth – fell by 69%. Meanwhile, lanternfishes, which sustain seabirds, dolphins, sharks and commercial fisheries, dropped by 62.9%. A 2023 survey of the area found that many of these populations have not recovered sustainably.Because large amounts of marine species were instantly killed or affected due to chemicals stored in their eggs, this led to sharp reductions in population sizes, in turn leading to reduced genetic variations, the study found.View image in fullscreenA boat makes its way through crude oil that leaked from the Deepwater Horizon wellhead in the Gulf of Mexico on 28 April 2010 near New Orleans, Louisiana.Photograph: Chris Graythen/Getty ImagesScientists examined genetic diversity in three lanternfish species that suffered severe population crashes, which subsequently led to inbreeding among the survivors.“The rate of genomic diversity decline is remarkable given the short temporal scale,” the study noted.The study also examined chemical dispersants applied during the oil spill cleanup. While these agents break oil into smaller droplets, they also spread polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) – among crude oil’s most toxic components – deep into the water column, increasing toxicity exposure for mid-water and deep-sea marine life.Six years after the spill, researchers found elevated levels of PAHs in deep-sea fish eggs and cephalopod tissues, which severely impaired reproduction. The study further highlighted that residual oil – even at sublethal concentrations – may have hindered the ability of certain species, including damselfish and stingrays, to locate mates through olfactory cues.“If you keep the oil from coming to the surface, then it won’t be affecting as many shallow water [animals] or humans that were there to work on the spill,” the study’s lead researcher, Tracey Sutton, a biological oceanographer at Florida’s Nova Southeastern University, said.“That was the idea [of the dispersants]. What that tends to do is break up the oil into smaller droplets, which allowed it to stay deep in the water column. So that probably was not a good thing for these deep pelagic things that we work on, because now you’ve got this kind of minefield of small oil-laden particles floating around and staying at depth instead of coming to the surface,” he added.“We need to consider the deep ocean to be a very fragile system, not this thing that is so large we can’t disturb it. We need … to be as absolutely careful as can possibly be,” Sutton continued.Similarly, Pedro A Peres, one of the study’s co-authors and a researcher at Florida International University’s Institute of Environment,said:“Our findings are particularly concerning because these are species that are abundant, widespread and historically might not have been considered vulnerable. What we are seeing suggests that even species that appear abundant can experience substantial changes that may go unnoticed without monitoring.”Meanwhile,BPspokesperson Paul Takahashi in a statement said: “We will never forget the 11 people who lost their lives. Sixteen years later, we remain keenly aware that we must always put safety first … We have worked hard to build a safer and stronger BP. We have made many changes intended to help prevent an event like this from ever happening again. He added that the company has spent more than $69m for the Gulf region’s recovery.In 2015, BPagreedto pay a record $18.7bn in penalties and damages after the US justice department and four states sued the company over the spill. The disaster alsoaffected coastal communitiesin Mexico, which, as of 2020, had yet to receive any compensation. BP has denied that the oil from the spill reached Mexican waters.Since the spill, thousands of people have alsofiled lawsuitsover long-term health problems they attribute to their involvement in cleanup efforts. Research conducted after the disaster has linked exposure to the spill with a range of health issues including increasedcancer risks, higher rates ofchronic respiratory conditions,heart disease,headaches, memory loss and blurred vision.Explore more on these topicsDeepwater Horizon oil spillBPOilOil and gas companiesOil spillsPollutionMarine lifenewsShareReuse this content

title: Cyprus police investigate financial and tax affairs of ex-Chelsea owner Roman Abramovich | Roman Abramovich | The Guardian
description: Inquiry follows report by Guardian and partners that aides of Russian oligarch appeared to have falsified paperwork mapping his businesses
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: Inquiry follows report by Guardian and partners that aides of Russian oligarch appeared to have falsified paperwork mapping his businesses
Content: Roman Abramovich, then owner of Chelsea FC, applauds the team after they won the Premier League in May 2017.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRoman Abramovich, then owner of Chelsea FC, applauds the team after they won the Premier League in May 2017.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty ImagesRoman AbramovichCyprus police investigate financial and tax affairs of ex-Chelsea owner Roman AbramovichInquiry follows report by Guardian and partners that aides of Russian oligarch appeared to have falsified paperwork mapping his businessesRob DaviesThu 22 Oct 2026 11.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 13.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice in Cyprus have opened an investigation into the financial and tax affairs of the former Chelsea FC owner Roman Abramovich following areport by the Guardian and media partners.In a committee hearing in the Cypriot parliament, a senior official in the island’s police said they were looking into events between 2003 and 2006, with the investigation likely to last several months.It comes after an investigation by the Guardian, the Bureau of Investigative Journalism and the BBC into the management of the billionaire Russian oligarch’s sprawling business empire.The report found that aides ofAbramovich– including staff at the Cypriot outpost of the global accountancy firm Deloitte – appeared to have falsified paperwork mapping his offshore businesses.Their actions, including the apparent backdating of key documents concerning billions of pounds in assets, appear to have helped businesses owned by Abramovich to dodge tax and disguise assets, the investigation found.The involvement of the Cypriot police emerged during a regular meeting of a Cypriot parliamentary committee on “institutions, values and the commissioner for administration”,according to CIReN, the Guardian’s Cypriot reporting partner.Andreas Anastasiades, assistant director of the crime combating department, said police had begun gathering evidence after the report and expected the investigation to last six months, although he said the amount of time that had elapsed would make the investigation more difficult.He said police would also consult the relevant authorities to assess the available material.The Guardian approached representatives of Abramovich and Deloitte Cyprus for comment.The former Chelsea FC owner has previously denied any wrongdoing and said that he relied on the advice of professional experts. Deloitte Cyprus has previously said that it “acts in compliance with all applicable laws” and that it could no longer access the relevant material because of the time that had elapsed.The Guardian’s findings in relation to Abramovich’s finances were based on theCyprus Confidential leakof more than 500,000 documents, first released to the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists and analysed by organisations including the Bureau of Investigative Journalism and the BBC.Explore more on these topicsRoman AbramovichAccountancyFinancial sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Barclays to cut 5,000 jobs as bank’s bosses hail AI productivity advances | Barclays | The Guardian
description: Equating to the loss of 5% of its 93,000 global staff, job cuts come as bank announces jump in quarterly profits
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Equating to the loss of 5% of its 93,000 global staff, job cuts come as bank announces jump in quarterly profits
Content: Barclays’ strong performance included a 6% rise in net interest income at its UK retail banking operations, to £2bn.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBarclays’ strong performance included a 6% rise in net interest income at its UK retail banking operations, to £2bn.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesBarclaysBarclays to cut 5,000 jobs as bank’s bosses hail AI productivity advancesEquating to the loss of 5% of its 93,000 global staff, job cuts come as bank announces jump in quarterly profitsKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentThu 22 Oct 2026 10.39 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 03.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBarclays is cutting 5,000 jobs as part of wider cost-saving plans that its bosses say are being driven by advances in AI.The job cuts will mean losing about 5% of the bank’s 93,000 global staff, with executives confirming they had already cut 1,000 workers since the start of the year.The bank’s chief financial officer, Anna Cross, told reporters on Thursday that the job cuts were part of plans to save more than £1.1bn in 2027. “These actions involve an expected reduction of circa 5,000 full-time employees. Around 60% of the group actions relate to support functions, including fewer developers, as AI makes our people more productive.”When asked how many of the total job cuts would be directly linked to advances in AI, the chief executive, CS Venkatakrishnan, said the bank had been making “deep investments” in technology and simplifying its processes.“That is driving the bulk of the efficiency gains that you’ve seen so far. AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future,” Venkatakrishnan said, calling AI the “icing on the cake” to modernising the bank’s technology.Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the Unite union, said Barclays workers “deserve better”.She added: “The company is using AI as an excuse to discard its loyal and long-suffering workforce. Employers should be focused on upgrading employees’ skills so that they remain employed as new technology changes the workplace. Instead, Barclays is guilty of taking a short-term, kneejerk approach.”The news comes months after another UK-headquartered bank, Standard Chartered, announced plans to cut more than 7,000 jobs in the next four years as it ramps up the use of AI. It will mean slashing about 15% of its back-office roles by 2030.Barclays also announced plans to hand a further £500m to investors, taking the total amount given to shareholders since January – through buybacks and dividends – to £2.8bn.It came as the lender reported £2.3bn in pre-tax profits over the July to September quarter, up 12% from £2.1bn during the same period last year.The strong financial performance will probably to be used to justify the expectedincrease in bank taxesin the 28 October budget, as Andy Burnham’s government looks for ways to raise revenue to help fund cost of living support programmes.When asked whether the bank might consider tilting assets or investment out of the UK and to the US – where it also has operations – as a result of higher levies, Venkatakrishnan said Barclays would be able to absorb them.“I recognise that the chancellor and the government … have to balance a host of considerations,” he said, adding that Barclays shared their goal to prompt growth.“This is not a question of a financial hit to us. It’s bearable. It is a question of proportion and it’s a question of market signalling. But … I deeply respect the responsibility that the chancellor has and he has our full support and backing.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBarclays’ strong performance included a 6% rise in net interest income at its UK retail banking operations, to £2bn. The figure has become a flashpoint for campaigners pushing for a bank tax.It accounts for how much money banks make from loan charges, minus what they pay on deposits, and is linked to interest rates, which have been rising as the Iran war has driven up inflation expectations.The Trades Union Congress, which has been campaigning for a bank tax increase, said lenders needed to contribute more at a time when people were struggling with household bills.TheTUCgeneral secretary, Paul Nowak, said: “Barclays’ bumper profits aren’t an anomaly. All the big banks are doing exceptionally well … Britain’s big four banks have made £200bn in profit since 2021. They can – and should – pay more tax.”Healey has promised that next week’s budget will support Britain’s entrepreneurs, and focus on cutting the “cost of business”.Hetold the Times: “I want to be a chancellor who backs business in Britain making a profit, those entrepreneurs who in the end are the ones who challenge the status quo, come up with innovative ideas and are trying, some of them through sheer bloody-mindedness, to keep going through these sorts of pressures, which is what they’ve done.”Explore more on these topicsBarclaysBankingBudget 2026John HealeyBudgetTax and spendingTUCnewsShareReuse this content

title: French borrowing costs overtake US amid budget turmoil | France | The Guardian
description: France’s bond market hit by another bout of selling as country recovers from weekend protests
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: France’s bond market hit by another bout of selling as country recovers from weekend protests
Content: France is recovering from widespread protests that turned violent at the weekend.Photograph: Telmo Pinto/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFrance is recovering from widespread protests that turned violent at the weekend.Photograph: Telmo Pinto/NurPhoto/ShutterstockFranceFrench borrowing costs overtake US amid budget turmoilFrance’s bond market hit by another bout of selling as country recovers from weekend protestsLauren AlmeidaThu 22 Oct 2026 04.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrench borrowing costs continued to rise on Thursday, as investors fret that France’s government is struggling to pass a federal budget after public protests gripped the country.France’s bond market was hit with another bout of selling, with the difference between French and German 10-year borrowing costs – a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt – rising to its highest level in almost 15 years.The yield on the French 10-year bond – known asobligation assimilables du Trésor (Oat)– rose by nine basis points to 5.089% in early trading on Thursday, its highest level since July 2022. It broke across the 5% threshold on Wednesday for the first time since 2002.The move lifted France’s 10-year borrowing costs over the equivalent for US Treasury bonds for the first time since 2013.The volatility comes as the French government struggles to pass a budget for next year, while the country recovers from widespread protests that turned violent last weekend.A graph on how French and German 10-year bond yields have divergedTens of thousands of people had attended peaceful marches to demand more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools, but different groups clashed with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille in recent days.Public buildingswere attacked,and thousands of shops and businesses were looted. The interior ministry said there had been nearly 2,400 arrests.Meanwhile, a parliamentary gridlock has blocked plans by the president, Emmanuel Macron, to increase the state pension age from 62 to 64 and a series of measures designed to rein in state spending.France’s budget deficit was 5.1% of gross domestic product in 2025, while its debt pile stood at 115.6% of GDP.It comes as the country also grapples with higher inflation triggered by the war in Iran, with many governments with big debt piles coming under acute pressure.Jim Reid, a market strategist at Deutsche Bank, said the sell-off in French government bonds was starting to ripple out to other countries, too.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Among others, the Italian 10-year spread over [German bonds] widened 3.8 basis points to 116 basis points, while Spain’s widened 3.1 basis points to 66 basis points, marking its widest level since June 2025,” he said.Carsten Brzeski of the bank ING said rising yields had reinforced the European Central Bank’s “restrictive” monetary policy stance before its interest rate decision next week. The bank last raised itskey interest rate to 2.5% in September.“The ECB is very likely to stay on hold next week and will delay any next rate hike decision to December,” he said.“Any solution to the current French fiscal woes could bring some relief to bond markets and allow the ECB to continue hiking rates. Without any solution, bond markets have taken over the ECB’s role, making rate hikes less likely.”Explore more on these topicsFranceBondsGovernment borrowingEconomicsEuropeEuropean UnionProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Max Dowman may get a chance, Spurs need to find balance at Stamford Bridge and Axel Disasi must make amends
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Max Dowman may get a chance, Spurs need to find balance at Stamford Bridge and Axel Disasi must make amends
Content: Arsenal’s Max Dowman, Rio Ngumoha of Liverpool and Aston Villa’s Emi Buendía.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenArsenal’s Max Dowman, Rio Ngumoha of Liverpool and Aston Villa’s Emi Buendía.Composite: Getty ImagesPremier LeaguePremier League: 10 things to look out for this weekendMax Dowman may get a chance, Spurs need to find balance at Stamford Bridge and Axel Disasi must make amendsPremier League top scorersGuardian sportThu 22 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 19.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1Glasner needs to fix Forest, fastAfter seven games, Nottingham Forest’s record is eerily similar to last season: five points, five goals scored. A year ago Forest’s eighth game was a 3-0 home loss to Chelsea thatmarked the end for Ange Postecoglou, the second of four managers to occupy the dugout last term. There is no suggestion that Oliver Glasner is under similar scrutiny yet, but the Austrian needs to find solutions for the league’s lowest scorers. Morgan Gibbs-White is available after missing thenarrow defeat by Arsenal, while Liam Delap may benefit from a return to familiar surroundings – 12 of his 14 career Premier League goals were scored for Ipswich, six of them at Portman Road. “What we need to improve is getting [Delap] into more positions where he can score,” Glasner said before Friday evening’s game. “He’s one of our best finishers.” Gary O’Neil also lacks a standout scorer, but he is squeezing goals out of his side. Eight different Ipswich players have scored in seven games; only Brighton and Brentford can better that total this season.Niall McVeighIpswich vNottingham Forest, Friday 8pmBSTNottingham Forest’s false start places early focus on Glasner and DelapRead more2New-look Villa host Maresca’s defiant CityIt was five months ago but it feels a lot longer. When these two sides met in May to finish the season, the contest doubled as Pep Guardiola’s leaving party after 10 years in the job and twice as many trophies, an era now laden with asterisks. It must be surreal for Aston Villa supporters, too.Their 2-1 victoryat the Etihad Stadium, inspired by two goals from Ollie Watkins to complete a league double over City, came only four days after theirEuropa League triumphin Istanbul, where Youri Tielemans, Morgan Rogers and Emi Buendía were the scorers. Buendía is the only one left in claret and blue as Unai Emery builds a new side, one that has picked up in form after a single point from their first four league games. City, meanwhile, are thriving on the pitch: victory would make them just the third side to win their first eight games of a Premier League season.Taha HashimAston Villa vManchester City, Saturday 12.30pm BST3Saka injury may benefit DowmanMax Dowman became the youngest goalscorer in Premier League history withhis dazzling solo strike against Evertonat the Emirates in March. But the supremely talented 16-year-old has found opportunities limited this season. Dowman has played only nine minutes in the Premier League despitescoring twice against Ipswichin the Carabao Cup last month as Arsenal have tried to protect their rising star. Yet thesuspected quad muscle injurysuffered by Bukayo Saka inWednesday’s 2-2 Champions League draw at Bayern Munichmeans Mikel Arteta is short of attacking options. With David Moyes’s side back in north London, it could be the perfect chance for Dowman to step up in his favoured position on the right flank.Ed AaronsArsenal vEverton, Saturday 3pm BST4Lampard wants Coventry to toughen upCoventry and Fulham have only met twice in the English top flight – back in 1967-68, when the promoted Sky Blues took a single point from two meetings, but stayed up by a point while Fulham went down. It is too early to call Saturday’s game a six-pointer in the relegation battle, but the two teams sit either side of the dreaded dotted line after shaky starts. Coventry have shown glimpses of their Championship swagger, particularlyin the 4-1 rout of Newcastle, but Frank Lampard wants his players to start thinking like a Premier League team. “I can’t keep applauding the players, believing they deserve to be here,” the Coventry manager said. “Now we have to get over that. We can’t be too soft.” Sunderland, Crystal Palace and Ipswich all visit the CBS Arena in the coming weeks, so there is an opportunity to consolidate. Fulham were linked with Lampard in the summer, and questions remain over whether Álvaro Arbeloa is pragmatic or flexible enough to succeed. Will these sides meet in the Premier League again next season? The jury is out.NMCoventry vFulham, Saturday 3pm BSTView image in fullscreenÁlvaro Arbeloa: still under pressure despite Fulham’s win over Hull.Photograph: Javier García/Shutterstock5De Zerbi needs balance for Chelsea challengeTottenham’s recent record against Chelsea is miserable. They are on a six-match losing streak against their London rivals and have collected a paltry two points at Stamford Bridge since last winning therein April 2018. Tottenham finally have a league win –they beat Coventry 3-1on Monday – but remain unconvincing. Roberto De Zerbi used a 3-4-2-1 system against Coventry. He had problems in midfield but now has to work out whether to change a winning team. Does he stick with James Maddison after the No 10’s excellent goal against his boyhood club? Spurs still looked short of energy at times. There is an argument to bring back Conor Gallagher’s dynamism, but would that hurt the side’s quality on the ball? Mateus Fernandes is another option but is yet to establish himself since joining from West Ham. Spurs’ approach remains hard to decipher. De Zerbi likes possession, but Chelsea want teams to open up as the Blues have searing pace on the break. Given their history in this fixture it seems Spurs should focus on tightening up. Equally they can’t be passive and need a threat on the break. De Zerbi will be searching for the right balance.Jacob SteinbergChelsea v Tottenham, Saturday 5.30pm BST6Iraola waiting for Anfield breakthroughTalk of Brighton achieving Champions League qualification for the first time will gain more credence, even at this early stage, should Fabian Hürzeler’s confident side extend their winning streak to seven matches in all competitions. There have been five clean sheets and 22 goals scored in their six-game winning run and the Premier League’s highest scorers will take encouragement from Liverpool’s defensive problems inthe comeback against Villarreal, which were not limited to Virgil van Dijk’s early lapses. Andoni Iraola is yet to savour a first home league win as Liverpool head coach – Anfield has seen only four home wins in 13 league games this year – and he will be wary of Brighton’s various threats. But with Rio Ngumoha electric in the Champions League win, Florian Wirtz improving and Alexander Isak increasingly decisive, the ingredients are in place for another enthralling spectacle.Andy Hunterskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLiverpool v Brighton, Sunday 2pm GMT7Who can rouse Carrick’s rabble?Who can or will lift Manchester United after the latest dismal/embarrassing week?Bruno Fernandes’s abdication of captaincy duties– accusing his manager of being tactically inept – showed what a rabble the team has become under Michael Carrick; and beyond the double footballer of the year, is there another star act who can win a game? Bournemouth will hope to take advantage, register only a second league win of the season, and deepen the misery for their hosts and fans. If his side goes down to the Cherries, Carrick will surely follow: the latest victim of the United circus.Jamie JacksonManchester United v Bournemouth, Sunday 2pm GMTView image in fullscreenBournemouth are coming off a 3-0 win against Milan on Thursday.Photograph: MB Media/Getty Images8Disasi must make amends at PalaceIt’s been six months since Crystal Palace recorded a clean sheet in the Premier League at Selhurst Park and the pressure will be on Pierre Sage against Newcastle on Sunday. Palace have conceded eight goals in four home league games this season, although they welcome back Axel Disasi from suspension afterhis reckless red card against Ipswich. The French defender was brought in on loan from Chelsea to add experience but cost Palace in the defeat by the newly-promoted side and had to watch from the sidelines as the Eagles werehumiliated against Brightonlast weekend. Disasi owes Sage a favour and he will be desperate to make up for his poor start to life in south London.EACrystal Palace v Newcastle, Sunday 2pm GMT9Hull and Brentford thrive off the ballSomething unusual will happen at the MKM Stadium on Sunday; either Hull City or Brentford will register more than 50% possession. In seven league games, Brentford only had more of the ball intheir 1-1 draw at Leeds. The hosts, meanwhile, are comfortably the most possession-averse team in the top flight so far this season, at an average of just over 30%. Both teams have been effective on the break and successful at set-pieces, with three goals apiece from dead balls. This may prove to be a match for the purists, where one clinical moment makes the difference. The Bees head coach, Keith Andrews, will hope it comes from Igor Thiago, yet to recapture the prolific form of last season. “Thiago at the moment is a very marked man, but we’ve got goalscorers throughout the team,” Andrews said of the Brazilian forward, who has scored one goal in seven this season. “Thiago being Thiago wants to score more goals, and he’s certainly not far away.”NMHull vBrentford, Sunday 2pm GMT10Mukiele issues war cry to SunderlandNordi Mukiele ranks among Sunderland’s best players and most influential dressing-room figures. Tellingly the former Paris Saint-Germain defender has been scathing about his team’s dismal start to thePremier Leaguecampaign and expects a reaction when Leeds visit Wearside on Sunday. “Leeds will be the right moment to show everyone we are not dead,” says Mukiele, well aware that Régis Le Bris’s side start this weekend on the bottom of the table. “We have not been good enough. Right now it’s not us; we are not Sunderland. I believe we can go back to the top. I believe in this team and this staff. We have quality.” Sunderland must use their three league fixtures before the international break – Leeds, Coventry away and Chelsea at home – to remind everyone why they finished seventh last season.Louise TaylorSunderland v Leeds, Sunday 4.30pm GMTPosTeamPGDPts1Man City712212Arsenal76183Brighton718164Chelsea74135Liverpool71126Brentford75107Leeds73108Everton71109Hull71910Ipswich7-4911Newcastle7-4812Aston Villa7-4813Man Utd70714Crystal Palace7-8715AFC Bournemouth7-4616Tottenham Hotspur7-4617Coventry7-8618Fulham7-3519Nottm Forest7-4520Sunderland7-84Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueManchester CityArsenalBrighton & Hove AlbionChelseaLiverpoolBrentfordfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rookie Lendeborg jaws at ‘weak ass’ Dončić and admits he didn’t watch much NBA | Golden State Warriors | The Guardian
description: Golden State Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg had an extraordinary NBA debut as he jawed with Luka Dončić
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Golden State Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg had an extraordinary NBA debut as he jawed with Luka Dončić
Content: Luka Dončić exchanges words with Luka Dončić Yaxel Lendeborg during Wednesday’s game.Photograph: Keith Birmingham/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLuka Dončić exchanges words with Luka Dončić Yaxel Lendeborg during Wednesday’s game.Photograph: Keith Birmingham/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News/Getty ImagesGolden State WarriorsRookie Lendeborg jaws at ‘weak ass’ Dončić and admits he didn’t watch much NBALendeborg takes issue with appeals for foul callsForward says he had limited exposure to leagueGuardian sportThu 22 Oct 2026 12.28 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 13.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGolden State Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg had an extraordinary NBA debut as he jawed with Luka Dončić and admitted he had largely been exposed to the league through highlights before turning professional.Lendeborg was given the task of guarding theLos Angeles Lakersstar for large parts of Wednesday’s game, which Dončić’s team won 127-105.NBA 2026-27 season predictions: A Knicks repeat and LeBron’s villain arcRead moreHowever, Lendeborg said he “lost all respect” for Dončić’s quest for foul calls during the game.“I had a lot of respect for him [because] I didn’t really watch theNBAmuch,” Lendeborg said. “I just watched highlights and seen him kill people. But being in it firsthand and seeing all the whining and complaining, I lost all respect.”Lendeborg was the No 11 overall pick by the Warriors in this year’s draft afterhelping Michigan win the NCAA Tournament. He had early success shutting down Dončić, but the six-time All-Star went on to score 28 points in the Lakers’ victory.In the second quarter, Dončić was fouled by Lendeborg after a pump fake and celebrated in front of the rookie.“You get the foul call. Congratulations, bro,” Lendeborg said. “Then you talk to me like you did something great. C’mon, dog. That shit is weak. It kind of threw me off because I have so much respect for him. Gone, man. Gone.”Lendeborg was given a technical for jawing at Dončić. “I was telling him he sucks,” Lendeborg said. “He can’t score on me. You talk but you can’t score on me. I said it the whole game. I said a couple cuss words, obviously. That’s why I got the technical. But I was letting him know.”Lendeborg seemed unimpressed by the league in general after his debut.“I guess this is what the NBA is like, man,” Lendeborg said. “A lot of flopping, a lot of foul baiting, a lot of praying to the refs, man. Interesting first game for me.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLendeborg had already made an impression before his debut. He admitted he used to hate his new teammate Stephen Curry because he was a fan of one of his playing rivals, Kyrie Irving. Warriors veteran Draymond Green, who is not shy of expressing his own opinions, had no problems with the rookie’s attitude.“In this league, everybody always says, ‘Oh, there’s certain guys you got to respect,’” Green said after Wednesday’s game. “I ain’t come in the league like that. Everybody will say, ‘Oh, the rookie learned his lesson.’ What’d he learn? The next time he see him, go at his ass again.”For his part, Dončić said he was trying to stay out of trouble.“He was talking crazy,” Dončić said. “But I wasn’t trying to talk back. This season, I’m not trying to get techs.”Explore more on these topicsGolden State WarriorsLuka DončićNBALos Angeles LakersWest CoastBasketballUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bournemouth enjoy night to remember as 10-man Milan fail to weather storm | Europa League | The Guardian
description: When it rains, it pours for Ruben Amorim as his Milan side were beaten 3-0 by Bournemouth after Mike Maignan’s mad red card
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: When it rains, it pours for Ruben Amorim as his Milan side were beaten 3-0 by Bournemouth after Mike Maignan’s mad red card
Content: Bournemouth’s Amine Adli adds gloss to the scoreline with his late free-kick.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBournemouth’s Amine Adli adds gloss to the scoreline with his late free-kick.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesEuropa LeagueBournemouth enjoy night to remember as 10-man Milan fail to weather stormNick Amesat the Vitality StadiumThu 22 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 18.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis was a momentous night in Bournemouth’s history, although the truth is they would have been given a far sterner examination by Coventry or Hull. Whatever this rotten impersonation of a Milan side was, it bore no relation to those that forged such a celebrated history. The visitors resembled holograms even before their goalkeeper Mike Maignan, with an extraordinary rush of blood resulting in a penalty and red card, rendered their task impossible. They never showed the slightest hint of putting up a fight.Bournemouth simply swamped the seven-time European champions and, amid a swirling south coast storm that rarely let up, could depart singing in the rain. Amine Adli’s sumptuous late free-kick, curled left-footed from 22 yards, meant they could finish the evening with the flourish they deserved. Their joy was clear at full time and met disapproval from some of Milan’s staff, who appeared to take umbrage in a short-lived fracas near the tunnel afterwards.Europa League: Sunderland held in Poznan as Juventus denied comeback winRead moreIt was certainly an abject return to English soil for Ruben Amorim, who could have been excused in seeing this particular week as the opportunity to prove a point. Amorim may view Bournemouth as kryptonite given they beat his Manchester United side by an identical scoreline at Old Trafford in December 2024. As it happens that is where the Cherries head on Sunday. On this damning evidence the modern version of Milan share more than a few similarities with his former employers.“A difficult night in every aspect,” Amorim said. It began with a downpour and waves of Bournemouth pressure, an incisive move ending with Justin Kluivert missing his kick and Ben Gannon-Doak’s drive deflecting wide. Milan failed to clear their lines from the resulting corner and were punished when VAR found Koni De Winter had deflected Evanilson’s header wide with his arm. Kluivert converted the spot kick coolly and the die was firmly cast.Amorim’s attempt to divide the match into two parts, before and after Maignan’s 27th-minute dismissal, cut no ice. Bournemouth’s tempo had been far too much for Milan before that, Maignan saving untidily from Ryan Christie after Yunus Musah’s pocket had been picked. “We just suffocated them, we didn’t give anything to them,” said a satisfied Marco Rose. “The way they did it today was just brilliant from the first minute until the last.”View image in fullscreenTyler Adams hits the deck after Mike Maignan pushes him in the face at a corner, resulting in a red card for the Milan goalkeeper.Photograph: Alex Pantling/Uefa/Getty ImagesWhen Maignan clawed James Hill’s deflected shot wide, everybody on view set up for a left-sided corner. Nobody was prepared for Maignan, who perhaps expected to be manhandling a taller opponent, to shove Tyler Adams in the face as the ball was sent in. It was a moment of supreme idiocy from the captain; the penalty award was inevitable and so, even before confirmation via VAR, was his departure. This time Marcus Tavernier did the honours, beating the replacement keeper Lorenzo Torriani.Barely half an hour in, the outcome had been settled. Bournemouth could hardly have imagined, in making their “great escape” from the fourth-tier trapdoor in 2009, that they might land in such a position against Italian royalty. Past luminaries looked on from the stands, Harry Redknapp among them, while their polished successors turned the screw down below.The relentless Gannon-Doak, called “a special player” afterwards by Rose, thrilled and frustrated in equal measure; the substitute Rayan almost set up a goal for Christie with a delightful piece of skill.
