Let’s build some layers of preparation with each other.”However, for that to happen there is likely to be a post-tournament inquest into the national team’s place on English rugby league’s priority list.With no mid-season camps, let alone games, and the schedule for a home three-Test series against New Zealand next autumn not yet confirmed, McDermott and his players need more support from above if England are to prove they are victims of the format and not drifting from the top tier of the international game.Explore more on these topicsRugby League World Cup 2026England rugby league teamRugby League World CupBrian McDermottRugby leagueAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fifa increases preparation money for Women’s World Cup to match men’s teams | Women's World Cup | The Guardian
description: Preparation money for the 2027 Women’s World Cup will match the men’s for the 2026 World Cup and players will be provided with improved flights and individual hotel rooms
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Preparation money for the 2027 Women’s World Cup will match the men’s for the 2026 World Cup and players will be provided with improved flights and individual hotel rooms
Content: Spain will defend the Women's World Cup in Brazil in 2027.Photograph: Alex Pantling/Fifa/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSpain will defend the Women's World Cup in Brazil in 2027.Photograph: Alex Pantling/Fifa/Getty ImagesWomen's World CupFifa increases preparation money for Women’s World Cup to match men’s teamsFunds for 2027 will match men’s World Cup in 2026Players given better flights and individual hotel roomsTom GarryThu 22 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 13.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTeams in the 2027’s Women’s World Cup in Brazil will receive the same preparation money fromFifaas those that played at the 2026 men’s tournament, the world’s governing body has announced.The preparation money for the 32 teams has been more than doubled to $2.5m (£1.86m) each. In 2023, the total preparation money for the tournament was $31m; it will now be $80m.Cathinka Tandberg: ‘Spurs fans hate Arsenal. That’s how it is’Read moreEvery player will be guaranteed business class or chartered flights, as well as their own hotel room rather than having to share. Fifa says this will bring the provisions for the women’s players in line with the men’s World Cup. That is likely be welcomed after the topic caused controversy at previous tournaments.A survey conducted by the players’ union Fifpro in 2023, after the most recent Women’s World Cup, co-hosted by Australia and New Zealand, found 80% of players’ return flight had been in business class. Ninety-four per cent flew in business class on their outbound flights.The total prize fund for the tournament is yet to be decided. Fifa has named the United States as the host of the inaugural Women’s Club World Cup in January 2028.The Guardian revealedthis month the US was lined up to stage the event, with Los Angeles and San Diego among the favoured host cities.The competition will feature 19 teams, with seven already qualified: Arsenal, Club América Femenil, Barcelona, Gotham FC, Naegohyang from North Korea, Corinthians and Wuhan Jiangda. Six European teams will take part, with the AFC, CAF, Concacaf and Conmebol being represented by three clubs each, plus one team from Oceania.Fifa’s chief women’s football officer, Sarai Bareman, said: “We undertook a detailed assessment to identify the most suitable host for the inaugural edition of the Women’s Club World Cup. Ultimately, the United States’ recent excellence in staging top Fifa tournaments, combined with the significant interest in women’s football there plus its elite sporting infrastructure, made the country the standout option.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Alongside the vibrant and passionate women’s football ecosystem in the United States, the qualified clubs, government, host cities, our commercial and media partners and more, our mission will be to set an impressive standard for global women’s club football and a benchmark for the future.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's World CupWomen's footballFifaUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: History comes home as St Louis City top Columbus Crew to win US Open Cup | MLS | The Guardian
description: Substitute goalkeeper Ben Lundt made a key shootout save to help secure St Louis City’s first-ever title.
Author: Jeff Rueter
Headline: Substitute goalkeeper Ben Lundt made a key shootout save to help secure St Louis City’s first-ever title.
Content: St Louis won the city’s 11th US Open Cup title.Photograph: Omar Vega/USSF/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSt Louis won the city’s 11th US Open Cup title.Photograph: Omar Vega/USSF/Getty ImagesMLSHistory comes home as St Louis City top Columbus Crew to win US Open CupTitle is club’s first-ever since 2023 foundingSt Louis clubs have won 11 Open Cups all-timeDaniel Edelman nets winner in 5-4 win on penaltiesJeff RueterWed 21 Oct 2026 23.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 07.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor much of the 20th century, winning theUS Open Cuprequired a team to beat someone from St Louis. The Gateway City was home to many of the nation’s best teams during some ramshackle eras of soccer in the United States, with six different clubs combining for 10 trophy lifts. The most recent came in 1988, when St Louis Busch Seniors beat San Francisco-based Greek-American AC in the last throes of a tournament history dominated by amateur and semi-pro teams. MLS has won every Open Cup but one since starting play in 1996, and St Louis didn’t have an MLS club until 2023.From the beginning, club figures spoke of their aim to restore the city to soccer prominence. Well, mission accomplished.St Louis Cityare US Open Cup champions, outlasting the Columbus Crew 5-4 on penalties to end the city’s 38-year wait for a major US soccer title and earn a place in the field for the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup.Daniel Edelman scored the decisive penalty, with backup goalkeeper Ben Lundt making a save on Columbus’ first attempt, himself having entered the match in the second half.Fittingly given their home’s rich soccer history, City’s first trophy is also the nation’s oldest. Wednesday marked the 109th Open Cup final.. The first was held in 1913–14 and the competition has run continuously save for a two-year hiatus during the Covid-19 pandemic.MLS reportedly will return all 27 US-based teams to the US Open CupRead moreSt Louis won this season’s tournament with MLS’s youngest manager – Yoann Damet, the 36-year-old Frenchman who was previously Wilfried Nancy’s top assistant in Columbus but was passed over for the top job after Nancy left. St Louis will be thankful that he was.Often two of the nation’s most aesthetically pleasing teams, Columbus and St Louis opened the final by minimizing risk. For the opening half-hour, St Louis carried a 60% share of possession but failed to muster a single shot. The hosts were a bit more incisive whenever they found the ball, working to advance upfield and trying to fashion chances for Brais Méndez, but failed to threaten Roman Bürki’s net.Referee Guido Gonzales Jr promptly blew his half-time whistle after the 45th minute. No need for stoppage time after that half, and few could argue.View image in fullscreenCombative play in midfield was the norm on Wednesday night.Photograph: Omar Vega/USSF/Getty ImagesBoth teams returned with intentions to sustain the caginess after the break. Columbus continued to dramatically tilt the field, taking 11 touches in St Louis’ box after half-time before the visitors managed a single one. Still, Bürki kept their sole on-target effort from rippling the net. The visitors responded by upping their fouling volume to further impede the Crew’s efforts.The 69th minute provided an inflection point as Columbus again entered the St Louis box, where Santi Rodríguez took a clattering from behind by Carlo Holse but saw the referee play the advantage. Méndez picked up the loose ball, strafed across the top of the box to his left, and played a through-ball to former Morocco international Anass Zaroury, whose shot was blocked by a fearless Bürki who took contact to his head from the wing-back’s knee, staying down as the play fizzled.As the former Switzerland international received medical treatment, the VAR had ample time to review and, ultimately, clear the potential penalty on Holse’s initial tackle. Ultimately, a six-minute examination led to Bürki exiting the match on a stretcher, leaving to a stadium-wide applause. Later, the CBS Sports broadcast relayed that Bürki was “OK” shortly after his departure, though he was taken to the hospital for an evaluation. In stepped Lundt, a backup since coming to MLS in 2019 – but one who had played shootout hero before for St Louis, winning their quarter-final shootout against Houston.Another injury, seemingly a leg muscle issue to promising Columbus midfielder Taha Habroune, brought Eric Bailly off the bench with captain Sean Zawadzki pushing into midfield to accommodate. The fourth official showed 11 minutes of stoppage time, perhaps cashing some rollover minutes from the first half on top of the lengthy delay as Bürki was examined. The Nordecke increased the volume of their support, but the game’s established physicality hardly waned for their efforts. St Louis seemed to fashion a clear look inside the box in the 10th minute of stoppage time, but US international Damion Downs took too heavy a touch to fashion a shot.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRemoving political speech from MLS fans is untenable – just ask Austin FCRead moreA minute later, the whistle blew. Despite Columbus outshooting St Louis 16-3, both teams finished the 90 minutes without a goal to their name or a trophy to their claim. Another 30 minutes of brawling followed.Neither team ceded an inch in the opening minutes of extra time, exchanging hard challenges and failing to maximize their ensuing set pieces.After Timo Baumgartl started the sequence with a make, Columbus’ Santi Rodriguez sent his attempt to Lundt’s left only to be stifled by a strong left hand. The teams each converted their next three attempts, although Lundt nearly ended the sequence with a finger to Andrés Herrera’s effort in the fourth round. Edelman stepped up and made no mistake with his trophy-winner.The MLS schedule-makers did the finalists no favors as both teams played on the road this weekend, although St Louis enjoyed an extra day of rest. St Louis also entered the final at a known disadvantage, playing without striker Rafael Navarro. A front-runner for the year-end MLS Best XI, Navarro played for the Colorado Rapids through the quarter-final stage, cap-tying him for the remainder of the tournament.While Columbus was recently a contender on all fronts under Nancy, his departure at the end of 2025 forced the Crew into a stylistic reset. Rather than hire his top assistant, Damet, Columbus looked beyond the league and hired Henrik Rydström, a self-proclaimed acolyte of “relationism”. The Swede never adapted to MLS, quickly leading Columbus toward the bottom of the East before being shown the door in May after just 17 matches.His replacement, Laurent Courtois, was another Nancy disciple. Meanwhile, Damet is a frontrunner for coach of the year, is in line for a top-three finish in the Western Conference – and, now, is the Open Cup champion.In an era where fiction fixates on multiverses, Columbus will no doubt wonder what could have been had they opted for continuity and retained Damet. Their loss is St Louis’ gain, as the Western Conference club will hope this is the first of multiple trophies to be won under MLS’s youngest manager.Explore more on these topicsMLSUS Open CupUS sportsColumbus CrewSt Louis CitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Anthony Edwards scores 45 as Timberwolves spoil Giannis Antetokounmpo’s Heat debut | NBA | The Guardian
description: Edwards joins Wilt Chamberlain and Michael Jordan in an exclusive NBA club as Minnesota overwhelm Miami despite 35 points from Antetokounmpo
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Edwards joins Wilt Chamberlain and Michael Jordan in an exclusive NBA club as Minnesota overwhelm Miami despite 35 points from Antetokounmpo
Content: Anthony Edwards reacts during the second half of Minnesota’s 131-106 win over Miami on Wednesday.Photograph: Carmen Mandato/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAnthony Edwards reacts during the second half of Minnesota’s 131-106 win over Miami on Wednesday.Photograph: Carmen Mandato/Getty ImagesNBAAnthony Edwards scores 45 as Timberwolves spoil Giannis Antetokounmpo’s Heat debutEdwards hits nine threes in 45-point explosionAntetokounmpo scores 35 in first game with HeatMinnesota rout Miami 131-106 in season openerAgenciesWed 21 Oct 2026 23.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 23.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthony Edwards scored 45 points as he and theMinnesota Timberwolvesspoiled Giannis Antetokounmpo’s debut with the Miami Heat in an emphatic 131-106 season-opening win on Wednesday night.Edwards became just the third player inNBAhistory to record multiple 40-point games in season openers, joining Wilt Chamberlain and Michael Jordan.NBA 2026-27 season predictions: A Knicks repeat and LeBron’s villain arcRead moreAntetokounmpo scored 35 points and grabbed six rebounds after joining Miami in an offseason trade with the Milwaukee Bucks.Edwards checked out with 3:51 remaining and Minnesota leading by 28. He shot 16-for-29 from the floor, including 9-for-17 from three-point range, and added 10 rebounds.His 45 points were the most by a Minnesota player in a season opener and marked his 125th career game with at least 30 points.LaMelo Ball, making his Timberwolves debut, hit five three-pointers and finished with 21 points and six assists. Jaden McDaniels scored 17 points, and Rudy Gobert grabbed 15 rebounds for Minnesota.Antetokounmpo checked out with seven minutes remaining after hearing MVP chants from the home crowd early in the game. He shot 13-for-19 from the floor but also airballed a free throw and was assessed a flagrant foul after elbowing Terrence Shannon Jr in the head on a drive.View image in fullscreenGiannis Antetokounmpo drives against Minnesota’s Trey Lyles during the first half of his Miami Heat debut on Wednesday.Photograph: Carmen Mandato/Getty ImagesAntetokounmpo was Miami’s most productive scorer. Bam Adebayo had 15 points, Andrew Wiggins and Davion Mitchell added 11 apiece, and Mitchell also dished out 10 assists. Klay Thompson scored 10 points in his Miami debut.Minnesota made 21 three-pointers, compared with eight for Miami.Edwards and Antetokounmpo each scored 21 points in the first half, but Minnesota carried a 10-point lead into the break.The Timberwolves opened 11-for-14 from the floor and led 27-19 after eight minutes. Miami pushed back in the second quarter and briefly took a 50-49 lead on a three-pointer by Bobby Portis Jr.Minnesota controlled the final five minutes of the half. Shannon hit a pair of corner three-pointers, Edwards recorded a steal and an easy dunk, and Ball scored on a drive and added two free throws to make it 69-59.The momentum carried over into the third quarter. Edwards and Ball each hit a three-pointer in the opening two and a half minutes. Edwards added another as Minnesota extended their lead to 78-61, and the Timberwolves remained in control the rest of the way.Explore more on these topicsNBAMinnesota TimberwolvesMiami HeatBasketballUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Websites across world hit by millions of attempts to exploit PHP code flaw | Internet | The Guardian
description: Problem in language that underpins 70% of sites has led governments and companies to pull sites offline to patch fault
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Problem in language that underpins 70% of sites has led governments and companies to pull sites offline to patch fault
Content: A page on the BBC website temporarily unavailable due to the issue.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenA page on the BBC website temporarily unavailable due to the issue.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAInternetWebsites across world hit by millions of attempts to exploit PHP code flawProblem in language that underpins 70% of sites has led governments and companies to pull sites offline to patch faultTell us: have you been affected by the PHP code flaw?What is PHP, and how bad is the computer language flaw causing website shutdowns globally?Robert BoothandAisha DownThu 22 Oct 2026 12.42 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 07.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWebsites around the world have been hit by millions of attempts to exploit a recently discovered vulnerability in their code, cybersecurity companies have said, as the US warned the flaw could allow attackers to take control of web servers, steal data and disrupt services.The problem in the PHP programming language, which underpins about 70% of the world’s websites,emerged on Wednesdaycausing governments and companies to pull their websites off the internet before they could be attacked and so they could patch the fault.What is PHP, and how bad is the computer language flaw causing website shutdowns globally?Read moreIn the UK, 32 government services had been taken offline, the cybersecurity minister, Liz Lloyd, told parliament. She said this “largely resulted from precautionary measures” while updates were applied. Downing Street said no public-facing critical services had been affected and “some limited services may be temporarily offline” but this did not mean they had been hacked.9:23The race to fix huge PHP flaw at the heart of the internet - The LatestThe website for the BBC’s Traitors was one of those that was down on Thursday, while the government declined to name the affected sites, saying services were being reviewed, updated and coming back online. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) sent out 50,000 alerts to affected organisations, but said it had no reports of successful hacks as a result of the flaw. Other sites reportedly temporarily affected included theInternetArchive, Wikipedia and 4Chan.The vulnerability sparked particular concern about the ongoing vulnerability of systems used by schools, local governments and charities, which may not have dedicated cybersecurity support to execute the fix. The NCSC said the scale of the vulnerability was “unprecedented” and the patch would not work for some organisations running older systems, and these would have to be replaced. The British Chambers of Commerce, which represents thousands of employers, said it was not yet causing firms any significant difficulties.Ciaran Martin, the former chief executive of the NCSC, described the flaw as “very bad”, saying that while most internet software vulnerabilities did not matter, this was “the most serious vulnerability discovered for five years”. The former GCHQ chief David Omand warned that Russia and China could look to exploit the bug.However, Ryan Austin, a researcher at the cybersecurity company Calif, who was key to discovering the flaw, said: “At the moment it doesn’t look like exploitation has taken off or been widespread.”View image in fullscreenA notice on the National Cyber Security Centre website warned of a critical security issue affecting PHP.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAThe flaw prompted governments into action, with the US National Security Agency saying it could allow attackers to seize control of web servers, steal sensitive data, disrupt services and move deeper into a network. Government websites were quickly taken down so the patch could be installed with many coming back on line soon afterwards.In an update overnight on Wednesday, and into Thursday, Matthew Prince, the chief executive of the cybersecurity business CloudFlare, said the company encountered tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the weakness in the 45 minutes after the problem was announced, rising to “hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now”.Amazon Threat Intelligence, another cybersecurity company, said PHP2Shell, as the vulnerability is known, was “now being broadly exploited in the wild” and it had identified several attempts from multiple actors to test ways to capitalise on the vulnerability before the fix was released by the PHP developers on Wednesday.CloudFlare also said that in the 10 hours before the vulnerability was publicly announced, it saw thousands of attempts to exploit it, amid concern over the handling of the alert. One cybersecurity expert, Prof Alan Woodward, said the flaw was revealed a day before the patch was released, and that “somebody let the cat out of the bag”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe PHP vulnerability could allow hostile actors to “grab the resources” of exposed sites, said Michał Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert. A website, such as Slack or Wikipedia, has access to computing power, servers, and IP addresses which locate it on the internet. In many cases, this infrastructure is managed and mediated by PHP.Criminal groups, state-sponsored hackers, or crypto miners might “nest” themselves into exposed sites using this PHP vulnerability, and then exploit those resources for their own aims. A hacking group could use an exposed site’s IP address to launch attacks that could not then be traced back to it. Crypto miners could use a server’s computing power to run their energy-intensive calculations for free.It was unclear at what scale this has been done, said Woźniak, and many sites would not even be aware of it.Wiz, one of the research organisations that uncovered the vulnerabilities, said it was arguably among the most severe software vulnerabilities ever discovered. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” itsaidin a blogpost. “Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”“Cyber-actors are likely to weaponise PHP2Shell,” theNSAsaid. “These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across US government departments and agencies.”The government of South Korea said on Thursday it was activating emergency response measures, raising its private sector cybersecurity alert level and issuing guidance to tens of thousands of companies on how to fix the problem.China’s industry ministry urged organisations to immediately inspect their systems and upgrade to the latest secure version of PHP, and recommended strengthening cybersecurity monitoring, changing passwords and keys. The prime minister of Japan encouraged businesses and organisations to patch the vulnerability – or shut down their sites.Explore more on these topicsInternetData and computer securityHackingProgrammingComputingNSACybercrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Meta strikes deal with Mark Zuckerberg to help him foot billionaire tax bill | Meta | The Guardian
description: Chief executive agrees to remain in California for eight years even if state brings in one-off 5% wealth tax
Author: Graeme Wearden
Headline: Chief executive agrees to remain in California for eight years even if state brings in one-off 5% wealth tax
Content: Mark Zuckerberg with his wife Priscilla Chan. The Meta founder said he was considering moving out of California because of the threat of a huge tax bill.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersView image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg with his wife Priscilla Chan. The Meta founder said he was considering moving out of California because of the threat of a huge tax bill.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersMetaMeta strikes deal with Mark Zuckerberg to help him foot billionaire tax billChief executive agrees to remain in California for eight years even if state brings in one-off 5% wealth taxGraeme WeardenThu 22 Oct 2026 11.40 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 06.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMeta has struck a deal withMark Zuckerbergto help him foot a possible California wealth tax targeting billionaires.The social media company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp revealed on Wednesday night that the arrangement would keep its chief executive living inCalifornia, where Meta’s headquarters are located.Under the deal, Zuckerberg will receive new shares that could be sold to potentially foot a multibillion-dollar tax bill in the event that California passes a one-off billionaire tax. In return, he is committed to remain a resident of the state, or whereverMetamaintains its base, for eight years.Californians will vote early next month on Proposition 40, a one-off 5% tax on the roughly 250 billionaires who live in the state.Zuckerberg, worth $239bn (£180bn) according to Forbes, told Meta he was considering moving his primary residence elsewhere because Prop 40 could expose him to a massive tax liability, potentially forcing him to sell voting shares to pay it.In response, Meta is creating a new class of non-voting shares via a two-for-one stock split for all existing shareholders. This will allow Zuckerberg to sell some of these new class C shares to pay a potential tax bill, without diluting his control of the company.The new Darth Vader: how tech execs became the film villains of our ageRead moreRecent polling has shown that Prop 40 remains short of majority support with voters. Tech billionaireshave been spending heavily to fight the measure, including the Google co-founder Sergey Brin, the Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel and the former Google CEO Eric Schmidt.Rohit Khanna, the US congressman representing California’s 17th congressional district, has described Prop 40 as a choice between standing with the working class or the oligarchs.“Every society is taxed. The only question is who will pay,”Khanna wrote in the Guardian last week.“In Trump’s America, working people pay more than they should, while billionaires are so unburdened that they are becoming trillionaires. In the America we seek, billionaires and trillionaires will pay their fair share, while working people will be unburdened.”Meta also reported a 26% rise in revenues for the last quarter to $64.6bn, beating expectations of $63.3bn. But profits fell by 37% to $13bn, dragged down by a $9.9bn charge related to Meta’slawsuit over child protection and social media addictionfailings.The company’s shares slid by more than 6% when trading opened on Wall Street on Thursday, helping to drag the tech-focused Nasdaq index down 2.5% amid a wider selloff of AI-linked stocks.In a separate case, on Wednesday a judge in New Mexicoordered Meta to pay $25bnfollowing a trial that found the company had misled the public about how it handled Facebook user data.Meta also revealed that it had cut its headcount to 66,775 at the end of September, 15% fewer than a year ago.Reuters contributed to this report.Explore more on these topicsMetaMark ZuckerbergCaliforniaWest CoastThe super-richnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sharp drops for AI stocks overwhelm markets worldwide as oil prices jump | US markets | The Guardian
description: Datacenter and chip costs fueled sharp decrease in AI sector although non-AI stocks still had a strong showing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Datacenter and chip costs fueled sharp decrease in AI sector although non-AI stocks still had a strong showing
Content: An options trader works on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on 7 January 2026.Photograph: Richard Drew/APView image in fullscreenAn options trader works on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on 7 January 2026.Photograph: Richard Drew/APUS marketsSharp drops for AI stocks overwhelm markets worldwide as oil prices jumpDatacenter and chip costs fueled sharp decrease in AI sector although non-AI stocks still had a strong showingAssociated PressThu 22 Oct 2026 17.50 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 18.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe latest shudder for stocks in theAIindustry pulled markets lower worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about thewar with Iran.TheS&P500 fell 1.2% for its worst day since July, while theNasdaqcomposite tumbled 2.6%. The weakness for tech stocks was so overwhelming that it masked strength for the rest of the US market, in which the majority of stocks actually rose. TheDow JonesIndustrial Average added 11 points, or less than 0.1%.AI-related stocks have been swinging on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build datacenters and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that their prices shot too high following a years-long frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.Oil prices jump to five-month high as attacks threaten global supplyRead moreLam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 11.8%.Other big tech stocks likewise fell following quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets.Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7% after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, shedding tens of billions in market value, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it was creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses.Tesla fell 3.1% after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast.The global tide against AI stocks knockedNvidiadown 4.4%. Because the chip giant is the largest company on Wall Street by total value, movements for its stock carry more weight on the S&P 500 than any other, and it was the single strongest force pulling the index lower.CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 10.1%.The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where indexes are full of players in the industry. South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5%, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3% and Japan’sNikkei225 sank 2.7%.Also weighing on global stock markets was a jump in oil prices.The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil leaped 4% to $113.17 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s shot up from less than $97 at the start of the month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1.4%. It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or US indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds.Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWorries about big government debt are weighing on almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong US economy and other factors, have pushed yields in the US bond market recently to their highest levels in decades.But US yields nevertheless fell sharply on Thursday in a signal that investors were buying US government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled.The yield on the 10-year treasury tumbled to 4.97% from 5.13% late on Wednesday and from more than 5.30% earlier this month. That’s a major move for the bond market.Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the US economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could signal that layoffs remain low across the country.That solid economy has helped US companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the US stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. Two out of every three stocks within the S&P 500 rose on Thursday, only to get drowned out by the drops for more influential tech stocks.Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses on Thursday.CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expected “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 5.6%.All told, the S&P 500 fell 93.74 points, to 7,663.43. TheDow JonesIndustrial Average added 11.89, to 52,867.98, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 694.00, to 26,008.86.Explore more on these topicsUS marketsStock marketsDow JonesNasdaqStandard & Poor'sNikkeiMetanewsShareReuse this content

title: Barclays to cut 5,000 jobs as bank’s bosses hail AI productivity advances | Barclays | The Guardian
description: Equating to the loss of 5% of its 93,000 global staff, job cuts come as bank announces jump in quarterly profits
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Equating to the loss of 5% of its 93,000 global staff, job cuts come as bank announces jump in quarterly profits
Content: Barclays’ strong performance included a 6% rise in net interest income at its UK retail banking operations, to £2bn.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBarclays’ strong performance included a 6% rise in net interest income at its UK retail banking operations, to £2bn.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesBarclaysBarclays to cut 5,000 jobs as bank’s bosses hail AI productivity advancesEquating to the loss of 5% of its 93,000 global staff, job cuts come as bank announces jump in quarterly profitsKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentThu 22 Oct 2026 10.39 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 03.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBarclays is cutting 5,000 jobs as part of wider cost-saving plans that its bosses say are being driven by advances in AI.The job cuts will mean losing about 5% of the bank’s 93,000 global staff, with executives confirming they had already cut 1,000 workers since the start of the year.The bank’s chief financial officer, Anna Cross, told reporters on Thursday that the job cuts were part of plans to save more than £1.1bn in 2027. “These actions involve an expected reduction of circa 5,000 full-time employees. Around 60% of the group actions relate to support functions, including fewer developers, as AI makes our people more productive.”When asked how many of the total job cuts would be directly linked to advances in AI, the chief executive, CS Venkatakrishnan, said the bank had been making “deep investments” in technology and simplifying its processes.“That is driving the bulk of the efficiency gains that you’ve seen so far. AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future,” Venkatakrishnan said, calling AI the “icing on the cake” to modernising the bank’s technology.Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the Unite union, said Barclays workers “deserve better”.She added: “The company is using AI as an excuse to discard its loyal and long-suffering workforce. Employers should be focused on upgrading employees’ skills so that they remain employed as new technology changes the workplace. Instead, Barclays is guilty of taking a short-term, kneejerk approach.”The news comes months after another UK-headquartered bank, Standard Chartered, announced plans to cut more than 7,000 jobs in the next four years as it ramps up the use of AI. It will mean slashing about 15% of its back-office roles by 2030.Barclays also announced plans to hand a further £500m to investors, taking the total amount given to shareholders since January – through buybacks and dividends – to £2.8bn.It came as the lender reported £2.3bn in pre-tax profits over the July to September quarter, up 12% from £2.1bn during the same period last year.The strong financial performance will probably to be used to justify the expectedincrease in bank taxesin the 28 October budget, as Andy Burnham’s government looks for ways to raise revenue to help fund cost of living support programmes.When asked whether the bank might consider tilting assets or investment out of the UK and to the US – where it also has operations – as a result of higher levies, Venkatakrishnan said Barclays would be able to absorb them.“I recognise that the chancellor and the government … have to balance a host of considerations,” he said, adding that Barclays shared their goal to prompt growth.“This is not a question of a financial hit to us. It’s bearable. It is a question of proportion and it’s a question of market signalling. But … I deeply respect the responsibility that the chancellor has and he has our full support and backing.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBarclays’ strong performance included a 6% rise in net interest income at its UK retail banking operations, to £2bn. The figure has become a flashpoint for campaigners pushing for a bank tax.It accounts for how much money banks make from loan charges, minus what they pay on deposits, and is linked to interest rates, which have been rising as the Iran war has driven up inflation expectations.The Trades Union Congress, which has been campaigning for a bank tax increase, said lenders needed to contribute more at a time when people were struggling with household bills.TheTUCgeneral secretary, Paul Nowak, said: “Barclays’ bumper profits aren’t an anomaly. All the big banks are doing exceptionally well … Britain’s big four banks have made £200bn in profit since 2021. They can – and should – pay more tax.”Healey has promised that next week’s budget will support Britain’s entrepreneurs, and focus on cutting the “cost of business”.Hetold the Times: “I want to be a chancellor who backs business in Britain making a profit, those entrepreneurs who in the end are the ones who challenge the status quo, come up with innovative ideas and are trying, some of them through sheer bloody-mindedness, to keep going through these sorts of pressures, which is what they’ve done.”Explore more on these topicsBarclaysBankingBudget 2026John HealeyBudgetTax and spendingTUCnewsShareReuse this content

title: AI firms say UK has a year to head off datacentre protests before construction is threatened | Datacentres - UK | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco taskforce urges ministers to offer areas greater benefits from tech infrastructure amid fears of US-style opposition
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Exclusive: Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco taskforce urges ministers to offer areas greater benefits from tech infrastructure amid fears of US-style opposition
Content: Protesters show their opposition to a datacentre in North Ayrshire.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenProtesters show their opposition to a datacentre in North Ayrshire.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianDatacentres - UKAI firms say UK has a year to head off datacentre protests before construction is threatenedExclusive: Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco taskforce urges ministers to offer areas greater benefits from tech infrastructure amid fears of US-style oppositionRobert BoothThu 22 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAI companies have told ministers they have 12 months to head off public opposition to datacentres in the UK or risk US-style protests that could threaten their construction.Successive dry summers and rising energy bills are increasing public scrutiny of plans for the huge computer warehouses that are used to train and run AI models, says a submission to the Labour government from a group including the AI infrastructure companies Nvidia,Microsoftand Cisco.Amid increasing anti-datacentre activism in the US and Europe, they are calling on ministers to create a “compact” that would show how communities can benefit from hosting datacentres, including allowing councils that host them to retain more tax revenues.The move by the Sovereign AI Leadership (SAIL) taskforce reflects rising concern among tech companies that arguments that have blocked datacentre developments in parts of the US are taking hold in Britain. Microsoft has promised to invest $30bn (£22bn) in UK AI infrastructure.Microsoft has built a datacentre in Acton, London and another is under construction in Newport, but wants to build several more facilities and is engaging with local and national leaders, including the prime minister, Andy Burnham, over the balance between the potential benefit of AI to the economy and public opposition to datacentres.The SAIL group said: “In the United States, organised local opposition has stopped fully permitted datacentre projects, and moratoriums have been announced even in states that are otherwise pro-growth.“Reporting from those places shows that AI itself is only a surface-level concern; distrust of corporate and government promises, fear of stranded assets and electricity costs run deeper. The same arguments have begun to appear here.”It added: “Britain has a window – we think of roughly 12 months – to build a compact that earns public consent before that pattern takes hold.”The taskforce is calling for the government to create a clear framework for councils and mayors to follow that will set out recommended terms for local benefit, including an indicative contribution – likely to be financial or in terms of facilities – scaled to a site’s size.View image in fullscreenThe Microsoft Park Royal datacentre in north-west London.Photograph: Raymond Tang/AlamyOpposition to datacentre construction is being fuelled by widening public concern about the safety of AI systems, after a summer in which some of the largest companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google appeared to lose control of some of their most cutting-edge AIs. Some protesters havebegun resorting to direct actionand the membership of anti-AI campaign groups has been growing rapidly.The datacentre companies are determined to head off that opposition. The chair of the SAIL taskforce, Steve Rigby, said: “By establishing a clear prosperity compact between government, industry and local communities, we can build the infrastructure we need, equip our workforce with future-ready skills, and ensure Britain’s digital destiny. This taskforce’s goal isn’t another strategy document, but high-impact actions that materially accelerate the UK’s transition to an AI-enabled economy.”It has not calculated the cost to central government finances if councils that grant permission to datacentres are allowed to keep all of their business rates.Responding to the proposals, Joseph Miller, the director of PauseAI UK, which campaigns for a global pause to datacentre buildout, said: “People are going to feel it is undignified to be bought off by huge tech companies who do not share their interests.”‘We’re plausibly close to crossing the line’: are warnings of uncontrollable AI coming true?Read moreHe said tech companies were “absolutely right to be worried” about US-style public opposition to datacentres growing in the UK. Kat Jones, the director of Action to Protect Rural Scotland, which campaigns against datacentres, said tech companies had already “missed the boat on containing community opposition to hyperscale AI datacentres”.“In Scotland, we have 15 community campaigns already working incredibly hard opposing these environmentally destructive developments locally, and a growing national campaign,” she said. “Even the titanic lobbying efforts of US big tech are going to find it a real challenge to change the winds of public opinion, which have already shifted solidly against hyperscale AI datacentres.”Donald Campbell, the director of advocacy at the tech equity campaign Foxglove, said: “Big tech firms have spent years trying to force vast, highly polluting datacentres through the planning system under a blanket of secrecy and misleading information. Now, with the public waking up to the fact that these facilities plunder resources and wreck the climate, the US tech giants have decided that there’s a problem.”He warned that incentivising councils to back datacentres by allowing them to keep more of their business rate revenue would mean “these wealthy tech giants would not pay a penny more” while boosts to council funding would “come from the pocket of central government services like the NHS”.A government spokesperson said datacentres “should create British jobs and supply chains, and provide investment to the communities in which they are built, as well as prioritising clean power, using water responsibly”.“For most proposed datacentre developments, community benefits are considered through the relevant local planning processes,” they said. “We have already announced measures which will enable local authorities hosting datacentres in AI growth zones in England to keep all the additional business rates they generate.”Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - UKAI (artificial intelligence)MicrosoftNvidiaCisconewsShareReuse this content

title: Canadian publisher Boréal ends relationship with novelist Thélyson Orélien over alleged use of AI | Awards and prizes | The Guardian
description: Author withdrawn from France’s Prix Goncourt last month has repeatedly denied using artificial intelligence to write novel
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Author withdrawn from France’s Prix Goncourt last month has repeatedly denied using artificial intelligence to write novel
Content: Novelist Thélyson Orélien at the 28th Les Correspondances literature festival in Manosque, France on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Joel Saget/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNovelist Thélyson Orélien at the 28th Les Correspondances literature festival in Manosque, France on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Joel Saget/AFP/Getty ImagesAwards and prizesCanadian publisher Boréal ends relationship with novelist Thélyson Orélien over alleged use of AIAuthor withdrawn from France’s Prix Goncourt last month has repeatedly denied using artificial intelligence to write novelAgence France-PresseWed 21 Oct 2026 21.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe publisher of top-selling Haitian Canadian writer Thélyson Orélien,who was removed from France’s most prestigious literary prize listlast month, has confirmed the author used artificial intelligence to help write his novel C’était ça ou mourir (It Was Either That or Die).Orélien has denied allegations that he used AI on his breakthrough novel and, last week, Canadian publisher Les Éditions du Boréal said it was standing by the 38-year-old writer.But on Wednesday, Boréal said it had conducted a further investigation into the allegations.“New information, confirmed over the past few days, indicates that artificial intelligence was used in the writing process” of the novel, a statement from Boréal said.The publisher announced it was “ending its professional relationship” with Orélien.Boréal said it did not know the extent of AI’s use in the writing process “and we will likely never have a definitive answer”.It said it gathered all the working versions of the novel and hired an outside party to analyse various drafts.Novelist accused of using AI to write book removed from French prize listRead more“The results obtained this week revealed traces of AI tags in the metadata of certain documents,” Boréal said.Before conducting this analysis, the publisher said it had tried to work with Orélien to gather the evidence necessary to prove his innocence.That effort was inconclusive, and Orélien “subsequently announced that he would not provide any further information,” the publisher said.The novel about migration had been scheduled for translation in more than 20 countries.The book was shrouded in suspicion and withdrawn from the list for France’s book prize thePrix Goncourt, after tests with AI detector Pangram indicated a 100% probability it contained computer-generated text.In a statement to Agence France-Presse earlier this month, Orélien called the allegations “slander and heresy”.“Here and there I did use tools for research, particularly for foreign idioms,” he said in a statement sent exclusively to AFP.“But not a single sentence in this book was created by a machine, nor the meaning or the structure of a story that comes from my gut.”He stood firm on Wednesday, telling the French newspaper Libération he used AI “in the creative process” for “historical research”.“I’ve explained everything to those close to me, but at the moment I don’t think my words count for anything,” he said, adding that what he is now experiencing has “gone way too far”.Orélien said he started writing the book in late 2017 “on the corner of a table” and completed a first draft in 2019 of more than 300 pages, several years before the advent of AI services such as ChatGPT.The author fled his native Haiti after a 2010 earthquake that struck the Caribbean island, already ravaged by poverty and unrest.In response to separate allegations of plagiarism, Orélien admitted to making “unacceptable mistakes” in the past in his writing, without mentioning specifics.“I was just over 20, I was probably a little too impatient, without really understanding how much I still had to learn. I wanted to write, I was reading a lot,” he wrote.“But admiring someone does not give you the right to take, to claim as mine texts that are not my own.”Explore more on these topicsAwards and prizesFictionAI (artificial intelligence)EuropePrix GoncourtCanadaFrancenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The tech bro fight club is real!’ The titans of AI get the Succession treatment in a wild new TV show | Television | The Guardian
description: The Audacity is a fearless satire taking on Silicon Valley’s ‘egomaniac weirdos’. Its creator and stars talk ayahuasca ceremonies, mining kids for data – and punching CEOs
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: The Audacity is a fearless satire taking on Silicon Valley’s ‘egomaniac weirdos’. Its creator and stars talk ayahuasca ceremonies, mining kids for data – and punching CEOs
Content: ‘They’re pretty punchable’ … Billy Magnussen as Duncan Park in The Audacity.Photograph: Ed Araquel/AMCView image in fullscreen‘They’re pretty punchable’ … Billy Magnussen as Duncan Park in The Audacity.Photograph: Ed Araquel/AMCTelevision‘The tech bro fight club is real!’ The titans of AI get the Succession treatment in a wild new TV showThe Audacity is a fearless satire taking on Silicon Valley’s ‘egomaniac weirdos’. Its creator and stars talk ayahuasca ceremonies, mining kids for data – and punching CEOsMichael HoganThu 22 Oct 2026 08.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShowrunner Jonathan Glatzer wanted the tagline of his latest TV creation to be: “We’re so fucked.” He laughs. “Sadly it got rejected by the network. Hey, maybe I can use it for season two!” The show in question is The Audacity, his darkly comic drama about AI tech titans. Instead, it went with the more PG tagline “Move fast and break people” – a twist on “Move fast and break things”, the Facebook motto coined by Mark Zuckerberg. The Audacity promises to do for tech bros what Succession did for legacy media. Considering Glatzer is a former writer on Succession, that is no empty threat.This acerbic and all-too-timelySilicon Valleysatire follows CEO Duncan Park (played by Billy Magnussen), the obscenely wealthy founder of a data analytics company. He’s a self-proclaimed “inventor of the future” who also happens to be a morally bankrupt man-baby. “Duncan is worth about half a billion,” says Glatzer. “Naturally, that’s not enough. He desperately wants to be a billionaire and ascend to what we call ‘God Mountain’. But he’s no God.”The Audacity review – cracking TV packed with even more gloriously awful people than SuccessionRead moreLike Succession, The Audacity’s scripts are liberally spiced with baroque swearing. Park boasts about keeping investors “moist” and “Viagra-ing the share price to keep it up”. Magnussen delivers such juicy dialogue with relish. “Jonathan has a way of painting a picture with words while also getting nasty with it,” he grins. “My favourite line in season two is: ‘I pulled it out of my ass and it came out clean.’ You’ll have to wait and see what it refers to.” It’s a measure of The Audacity’s whip-smart relevance that the second season was commissioned before the first had even aired.View image in fullscreen‘Basically created spam’ … Zach Galifianakis as Carl Bardolph.Photograph: Ed Araquel/AMC“Unquestionably, there’s a tech bro mentality that is sexualised,” says Glatzer. “Silicon Valley is such a male-dominated culture. It’s also very white or south Asian. When I first came here, I didn’t see a person of colour for two weeks. That struck me as very odd in a major US city. Hiring practices are dictated by algorithms. The algorithms say that if you went to these universities, you’re our man. If you came from someplace else, and are maybe not a man, the algorithm says you might be problematic. And you could end up writing a book about us.”The Audacity pulls no punches on how the tech sector is wrecking the planet. “It sure is,” says Glatzer. “Generative AI is environmentally ruinous. Datacentres are tremendous suckers of energy. Worryingly, it doesn’t take too many rampantly ambitious entrepreneurs to fuck up an entire planet for the rest of us.” When Park is warned about the huge carbon footprint of his “algo”, he shrugs: “I’ll sponsor a penguin.”Zach Galifianakis plays billionaire genius Carl Bardolph, who “basically created spam”. He’s rich enough to retire but becomes a disruptor out of boredom. “I’ve always been very concerned about the people running tech,” says Galifianakis. “They have math minds, but that sometimes comes with a lack of empathy. About 12 nerds are controlling our lives and designing our futures. And they all tend to have the same profile. Most come from Stanford University. I don’t know what they’re teaching there.” He laughs. “It’s weird and kind of evil.”Did Galifianakis base his portrayal on anyone specific? “He’s pulled from one dude I’ve watched over the years. I won’t give his name but he’s a real piece of shit. A major jerk. The guys running Silicon Valley are damaged. Carl has a giant hole in his heart and a ton of anger because of his dad. I’ve seen a lot of men like that in Hollywood, so I drew on them too. Most of the puppet masters are egomaniac weirdos and I wouldn’t mind saying that to their faces. Zuckerberg has something missing. Elon Musk is bizarre. They’re little boys. You almost feel sorry for them.”“Duncan also deals with daddy issues and a lack of love,” says Magnussen. “A lot of tech bros are trying to fill voids. The great irony is that the most antisocial people work in social media. Those who don’t know how to be personable are controlling how we communicate. It’s nuts.”Both actors view the show as a howl of protest. “I’ve done some cool shit in my career,” says Magnussen. “I’ve been in Bond [he played a CIA agent in No Time to Die]. I’ve been in fun, escapist movies. But this feels different. It’s a call to arms. People need to wake up to the audacious behaviour of this handful of people. Their decisions affect 8.3 billion people. That’s scary, man. I just hope our show opens some conversations. We’ve got to start making a difference.”Galifianakis agrees. “It’s a warning. I’ve never felt this way before with my work – come on, I was in a movie with a baby wearing sunglasses [The Hangover] – but this show’s important. This industry has no guard rails. You can’t sue them, you can’t do anything, so of course they’re going to take advantage of the population. That’s exactly what they’ve done. The destructive environmental impact alone is enough reason to take to the streets and protest. Sure, there’s all this darkness online but also, we’re going to take your water and electricity from you, too.”Park blackmails his therapist – sorry, “performance psychologist” (played byBarry’s Sarah Goldberg) – into giving him insider-trading tips from her other powerful clients. The pair are soon engulfed in a scandal over fraudulent stock pumping. It’s a familiar-sounding storyline. “Elon got into trouble for market manipulation,” says Glatzer. “It’s like Duncan says in the show: ‘It’s not a felony in Silicon Valley, it’s good hustle.’ That’s the mentality here. Laws are for morons, not us.”Real world echoes are everywhere in The Audacity. The search engine of choice is called Spookle (slogan: “You Agreed to This”). A corporation called Cupertino is a thinly veiled reference to Apple, while its mythical boss “Big Tim” nods to Tim Cook. Are any of Glatzer’s characters directly based on real-life figures? “The truth is, I don’t find any of them worthy of a three-dimensional character that could go the distance of multiple seasons,” says Glatzer. “They’re interesting enough for a film like The Social Reckoning but not much more.”View image in fullscreenIn cahoots … Sarah Goldberg as JoAnne Felder.Photograph: David Moir/AMCIndeed, Magnussen can currently be seen in The Social Reckoning as a Meta spin doctor. Is this his tech bro era? “AI is the most pressing issue of our time,” he says. “It affects our planet, our politics, our mental health, everything. Technology can do wonderful things but once it starts dividing us or swaying elections, it’s deeply damaging.”“I don’t understand why people get on board with social media,” sighs Galifianakis. “We fed these machines for years. Now these machines are going to find us. I don’t believe the promises of AI because I don’t trust the people doing it.”The Audacity’s protagonist has been described as “highly punchable”. Magnussen concurs: “You’ve seen these guys in front of Congress. They’re pretty fucking punchable.” An early episode includes a sequence at a Palo Alto fight club, where nerds whack each other with keyboards and strangle each other with cables. “That’s real!” laughs Magnussen. “The tech bro fight club is an actual thing.”Despite the plentiful real-world parallels, Glatzer has never met a tech mogul. “That’s fine by me,” he says. “I don’t imagine the conversation would be anything other than stage-managed and dishonest. They have people workshopping their handshake and smile, so what am I going to get from that? But I have talked to a number of people who work in the tech world. The first thing they say is: ‘I’m not like that. That’s those other guys. I’m one of the good ones.’”“Me too,” says Magnussen. “The response I get is: ‘I know that guy!’ It’s always someone else. You want to go: ‘No, it’s you. You’re that guy.’”In America’s richest enclave, hi-tech goes hand-in-hand with hippy-dippy. The Audacity lampoons heath fads like ayahuasca ceremonies, microdosing and bio-hacking. “Tech titans feel as if they’ve got the golden ticket,” says Glatzer. “They want their prime to last as long as possible, perhaps for ever. Maybe the singularity comes when they upload themselves into an AI consciousness and become gods. I don’t have proof of that being the reason why so many datacentres are being built by these guys – but I don’t think it’s uninvolved.”“There’s no limit to these people’s overreach,” agrees Magnussen. “They truly believe their life is more valuable than anyone else’s.”View image in fullscreenTrying to play God … Simon Helberg in The Audacity.Photograph: Ed Araquel / AMC/HBOThe show also skewers the hypocrisy of execs who ban their own offspring from smartphones, reasoning that “arms dealers don’t give their kids landmines”. “It’s like how a lot of Hollywood don’t have TVs in their houses,” says Galifianakis. “Because they know the poison they’re selling.”“They know the dangers,” nods Glatzer. “It’s a classic case of capitalism gone haywire. I don’t think they’d live next door to a datacentre either. None of them do what they’re telling us to do. It used to be that people in public life had to practise what they preached. That has quietly gone away. US congresspeople invest in the same tech companies they’re supposedly regulating. Look at what Trump’s doing. It’s a kleptocracy.”He’s equally concerned by “screenification” in schools. “The amount of information gathered on our kids is frightening,” says Glatzer. “Shopping habits, medical history, exam grades. When schools get given tablets in the States, the law says it’s OK for the provider to track that student. We’re handing our kids these screens with the patina of being an educational tool but they are data-collecting devices. Just like everything is.”“I can’t believe how much information people give up,” says Galifianakis. “If you go to LA, there’s all these cars that say Google on the side, taking pictures of everything. If those cars said US Government, people would lose their minds. But because it’s a corporation, we all sit back and go: ‘I guess this is the future.’ I think people are starting to wake up but maybe it’s too late.” He laughs. “What do I know? I’m just a dumb actor trying to alarm people. But our children are the new oil. They’re being mined for data.”“I’m most scared for the kids,” agrees Magnussen. “They’ve been digital since they were born. They’re being manipulated without even knowing.”View image in fullscreenFilling a void …  Magnussen as Park.Photograph: Ed Araquel/AMCIn The Audacity, even seemingly benign tech is sinister. Eccentric inventor Martin Phister (The Big Bang Theory’s Simon Helberg) is developing an empathetic bot to be a digital “friend” for alienated teens. US viewers have likened him to OpenAI’s Sam Altman, who initially presented as a sympathetic mogul.“Martin’s trying to do something good,” says Glatzer. “You later learn that he’s compensating for something very bad. Carl has a speech about his generation coming to a crossroads: ‘Leave a legacy of good or go full Dr Evil.’ Most choose the latter. They are drawn to doing something positive but they are Hungry Hungry Hippos. They can’t resist the allure of a good deal.”“Carl knew the internet could have been a good thing for society if we’d done it right,” adds Galifianakis. “But greed and old-fashioned American competition, the need to win, became more important than human beings.”Geeky idealism is long gone. “It began as a desire to change the world for the better,” says Glatzer. “A bunch of nerdy engineers wore hoodies rather than suits and put ‘Do No Evil’ slogans on their office walls. That’s all in the rear-view mirror.”Glatzer freely admits that his work on Succession informed The Audacity. “There’s no way that it didn’t. But that was about institutional, dynastic wealth, whereas our characters are self-made. They are Logan Roy as a young man, if he had decided to be a tech guy rather than a media baron. What I certainly gleaned from Jesse Armstrong was finding a tone that enables you to give the establishment some real gut punches. Sarcasm might be the protest of the weak, but that’s all we’ve got. Speaking as a weakling.”The invasive cyber-surveillance and data-mining in The Audacity are deeply chilling. “We consulted experts but all the information is out there,” says Glatzer. “The Guardian and New York Times do some terrific reporting on AI. It always feels like the journalists secretly want to headline their articles: ‘Wake the fuck up! This is happening!’”The Audacity is on HBO Max nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionSilicon ValleyAI (artificial intelligence)featuresShareReuse this content

title: How tech became the villain of the US midterms  | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Datacenters, AI and distaste for the billionaires developing it has soured Americans on big tech
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: Datacenters, AI and distaste for the billionaires developing it has soured Americans on big tech
Content: ‘The public distaste for the AI industry extends to its leaders.’Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The public distaste for the AI industry extends to its leaders.’Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesUS midterm elections 2026How tech became the villain of the US midtermsDatacenters, AI and distaste for the billionaires developing it has soured Americans on big techHow will Trump’s mass deportation agenda shape the US midterm elections? Our reporters answer your questionsNick Robins-EarlyThu 22 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 16.54 EDTShareThe campaign ad begins with a clear, idyllic stream that suddenly turns sludge-brown as two concrete datacenters slam on to its banks. Another facility thuds down on a peaceful suburban park, and two more crush-green pastures as an ominous soundtrack to a disaster movie blares.“They’re coming for our rivers. Our neighborhoods. Our farmland,” a deep-voiced narrator says. “Because Brent Taylor wrote the law allowing datacenters to take over Tennessee.”The attack ad, paid for by the Democrat-aligned Three Star Pac and targeting a Tennessee Republican congressional candidate, is one of more than150 midterm election campaign commercialsacross the US focused on datacenters or the artificial intelligence industry. At debates and at rallies, in mailers and online ads, the burgeoning AI industry has taken center stage, as both Republican and Democratic candidates try to convince voters that their opponents will put the unpopular facilities in voters’ backyards.And it’s not only datacenters – the public anxiety over AI and distaste for the billionaires developing it, as well as backlash over encroaching tech such as surveillance cameras, has turned the tech industry into a ubiquitous villain this election cycle. As with big pharma before it, candidates are straining to distance themselves from big tech.The stigma of the tech industry has even forced prominent Republicans to break with Donald Trump’s pro-AI party line, with candidates like Ken Paxton, campaigning for US Senate in Texas, calling for a slowdown. In Tennessee, Taylor’s campaign ran its own television spot that claimed he was tough on tech and datacenters.The campaign ads focused on tech have sprung up alongside an ecosystem of pro- and anti-AI political action committees, which have collectively spent hundreds of millions of dollars to influence elections and back candidates. The breathtaking amount of spending has pushed tech into the forefront of the midterms, evenas polls showissues like the economy, democracy and healthcare still rate as more important among voters.Super Pacs funded by tech billionaires are among the top spenders in this election cycle. Leading the Future, formed by the OpenAI president, Greg Brockman, and venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, has raised more than $75m to back tech-friendly candidates. ElonMusk has sunk $366minto Republican causes, more than he spent on the 2024 presidential election. AI money has also been funneled into pro-regulation Pacs seeking to counteract the influence of deregulation groups.Including Musk’s contribution to various Republican-aligned Pacs, the tech industry and its leaders have spent more than half a billion dollars to influence elections and ballot proposals in 2026.The cumulative effect of such vast spending, lobbying and advertising is that tech issues and the tech industry have become far more pervasive in the midterms than previously seen in US elections, marking the first major test of how American voters will react to the AI boom.Datacenters and FlockConcern over AI’s potential effect on society has grown over the last year, and the backlash has been most intense where there is a physical target for voters’ ire. None of those targets have loomed larger than the sprawling datacenter facilities that are part of the tech industry’s multitrillion-dollar infrastructure build-out. Although campaigns have nodded to AI regulation and fears over the technology’s risks, it is datacenters that candidates have repeatedly and specifically called out as a real, tangible threat to constituents.“Datacenters are now a campaign question in nearly every race in the nation,” said Brad Carson, the head of a pro-AI-regulation group Public First Action and a former congressman.The growing animosity toward datacenters has also been reflected in nationwide protests and polling. APew Research poll from last monthshowed that the percentage of US adults who believe that datacenters are bad for the environment, energy costs and quality of life has risen across demographics since January. Only 4% of respondents believe the facilities will be good for the environment or home energy costs.Datacenters have become toxic enough that some candidates have even begun using the facilities as an epithet to tar their rivals.“Data Center Derek gave the billionaires and greedy corporations a $2bn tax break. Driving up our electric bills, destroying Ohio farms,” declared a Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee attack ad against the Ohio Republican candidate Derek Merrin.At least 20 candidates for governor across the US are calling for moratoriums on datacenters, according to thepolicy tracking firm MultiState, while fewer than 10 candidates across 36 gubernatorial races are backing the projects without any calls for increased regulations.Along with datacenters, the public backlash against AI-enabled Flock surveillance cameras thatautomatically scan license plateshas also bled into campaigns, including in key battleground races. In Michigan, the Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed ran a Flock-focused ad that accused his Republican opponent Mike Rogers of pushing a surveillance state by backing the cameras. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico has similarly spoken out against the company and its data collection.“Flock cameras have no place in Texas,” Talarico said last month at a rally. The state’s Republican governor, Greg Abbott, surprisingly agrees with him, blocking state agencies fromspending on Flock cameras in August.Elsewhere, legislation has targeted not just tech infrastructure but the billionaires behind it. In California, voters are considering a ballot measure that would levy a one-time 5% wealth tax on any resident of the state worth more than $1bn. The state’s ultra-rich have feverishly mobilized against it,raising more than $340m and spending more than $1m a dayto fight the measure. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone has contributed at least $102m to oppose the tax.The collective backlash against the tech industry has put its leaders in a bind. Companies are facing internal and external criticism of their products and politics, but accepting more intense government regulation or halting datacenter construction would threaten their growth.The pushback has caused a shift in at least one company’s calculus – OpenAI has distanced itself from Leading the Future in recent months, and Brockmanbacked out of a planned $25mdonation to the Pac.Musk, Brin and other tech moguls, however, have doubled down on their efforts to swing votes their way.“They have never met a problem that they didn’t think they could solve by throwing more money at it,” said Charles Blaettler, political director of the pro-AI-regulation Pac Guardrails Alliance. “They’re realizing there’s an intense backlash to their ideas.”AI spending boom and backlashThe political landscape of the tech industry is vastly different from the last time the US held midterm elections. Anthropic, now potentially set to go public at a more than $2tn valuation, was just one year old in 2022. OpenAI had not publicly released ChatGPT. Musk had not yet allied himself with Donald Trump’s campaign.The tech industry has become increasingly entrenched in government and determined to shape regulation in the period since. Tech leaders have simultaneously built up immense campaign finance and lobbying arms that have come into full force in this year’s midterms.Meanwhile, Americans feel negatively about how AI will affect a range of issues from personal relationships to the economy to elections,multiple pollsshow, as well as broadly opposing datacenters in their communities. More Americans oppose a datacenter being built in their area than oppose a nuclear power plant,according to a Gallup pollfrom earlier this year.The public distaste for the AI industry also extends to its leaders, with polls showing that the US generally views executives such as Musk, the OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, and the Anthropic, CEO Dario Amodei,as untrustworthyand unlikable.“There’s this very deep-seated sense of anxiety people have about the direction this technology is taking and who’s in control of it,” Blaettler said. “People just feel like they don’t have any agency in their lives any more.”The enormous spending from the tech industry has largely flowed to Republicans, but it has also inspired a new category of pro-AI-regulation Pacs that have formed to counter groups like Leading the Future. Some of these pro-regulation Pacs have received money, counterintuitively, from AI companies and workers with different views on how government should oversee the technology. Anthropic contributed more than $40m to Carson’s Public First Action, while the Guardrails Alliance and its associated non-profit have raised more than $11.5m.One of the early tests for this type of battle was in the Democratic primary for New York’s 12th congressional district in June, where pro- and anti-AI groups, including Carson’s, cumulatively spent $24m on the race – largely targeting candidate Alex Bores, who was running on a pro-regulation platform. The result of all the spending was hard to determine, with Bores coming second in a crowded field and losing to similarly pro-regulation candidate Micah Lasher. After the vote, Lasher sought to distance himself from both Anthropic and OpenAI’s spending.“I have some news for the two big AI companies who’ve taken such an unusual interest in who won this congressional seat,” Lasher said in June. “I won’t be taking my cues from either of you when it comes to protecting our kids, our jobs, our environment.”While the spending frenzy on pro- and anti-AI campaigns has helped fund some of the fights over tech in the midterms, leaders of pro-regulation Pacs say these are issues that voters already organically care about and are mobilizing around. The message from the AI industry has for years been that their products will usher in a utopian era of abundance and affluence, but this election cycle has shown there is deep skepticism from everyday voters that they will benefit from the boom.“It’s now a world where most people on the street have a view about AI,” Carson said. “And it’s mostly negative.”Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026AI (artificial intelligence)Datacenters – USUS politicsShare

title: ‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentre | Environment | The Guardian
description: Company ordered to stop work at two sites in country, which has found itself at forefront of tech firms’ latest push
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Company ordered to stop work at two sites in country, which has found itself at forefront of tech firms’ latest push
Content: Finnish forest cleared for data centre developmentEnvironment‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentreCompany ordered to stop work at two sites in country, which has found itself at forefront of tech firms’ latest pushMiranda Bryantin Muhos and OtanmäkiThu 22 Oct 2026 07.22 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.08 EDTShareBehind a wire fence lies a vast gaping wound of earth. Before Google’s arrival a few months ago, an estimated quarter of a million trees occupied the 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest near the town of Muhos in rural northernFinland. Now they are all gone.After the tech company illegally stripped the entire area to build a datacentre – taking even the top soil with it – all that remains is a vast expanse of mud indented with the trail marks of machinery, puddles and mounds of earth, roots and branches. Residents say that brown water flowing off the site is going into a stream that feeds the Oulujoki River.“It doesn’t end. It goes on and on,” says Mari Annala, an ecologist from the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation (SLL), looking at drone footage of the former forest from the perimeter.View image in fullscreenMari Annala is a Finnish environmental expert, researcher and board member of the Oulu region district of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation.Photograph: Jarno Artika/The GuardianWith 145 new datacentres at various stages of planning, Finland has found itself at the forefront of the tech companies’ latest push. As well as its relative geopolitical and geological stability and abundance of land, the cool climate makes it especially attractive for saving on energy costs.MapEarlier this month,Googlewas ordered by the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) to temporarily stop work on Muhos and another site about 100km south-east in the village of Otanmäki after it failed to complete the necessary environmental impact assessments before clearcutting the land. The news has prompted widespread outcry and a national reckoning over what role, if any, the country should play in the global rush to build datacentres to keep up with rapid AI development.Last week, Google’s Finland country manager, Antti Järvinen, apologised for the forest clearings but claimed the company had acted “on the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time”.View image in fullscreenIn the northern Finnish town of Muhos, the forest has already been cut down on land acquired by Google, with excavators now clearing the ground and rumbling trucks shuttling back and forth to the construction area located next to major power lines.Photograph: Alessandro Rampazzo/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn aerial view of the site where Google’s data centre was set to be built in Muhos.Photograph: Alessandro Rampazzo/AFP/Getty ImagesMuhos and Otanmäki are part of a €13bn AI infrastructure project by Google that has attracted criticism from Donald Trump, who would rather the centres were built in the US and has publicly called for the company to reconsider. It is the biggest ever project of its kind in the Nordic country.The Finnish government, which has presided over deep spending cuts, has encouraged the investment.
