Last month, when the Google plans were announced, the country’s prime minister, Petteri Orpo, said attracting investment was a “top priority” and “the value of the data economy extends far beyond direct investment”. He said the Google deal would “deliver lasting benefits for both parties”.But the revelations over Google’s misconduct have prompted public concern over what these deals mean for nearby communities, energy prices for Finnish households and Finland’s natural environment, a national source of pride. The datacentre push is likely to become a key election issue when Finns go to the polls in April.View image in fullscreenGoogle’s clearcut area is 3km long and 2km wide, 330 hectares in total, and 400 metres from the Oulujoki River.Photograph: Jarno Artika/The GuardianIn addition to the 250,000 trees felled at Muhos, Annala estimates that an additional 150,000 trees were felled at Otanmäki. Because the trees have been felled illegally, she says wood from the two sites cannot be sold to wood-processing plants.The move has also prompted questions over why Finland’s renewable energy sources are being used to power international corporations.More than 93,000 people have signed a petition demanding more datacentre regulation and a fee to compensate local communities for environmental damage. Since the scandal broke, Orpo has described what happened in Muhos as a “cold shower”.Hanna Halmeenpää, chair of SLL’s board, said she had been incredulous when she discovered Google’s law breaking. “At first I couldn’t believe it,” she said. “I have never heard that any company has done anything like this in Finland.” She said the system depended a lot on trust, which she believes Google took advantage of. “They bought the vast land area and they just started to cut it, just like that,” she said. “It’s pure arrogance and it’s amazing.”View image in fullscreenThree electrical pylons next to the Google clearcut.Photograph: Jarno Artika/The GuardianThe speed of developments had shocked the country, she said. “Many people are just watching the news and asking each other: ‘What’s happening now? What can we do about it? And do we have to take all these datacentre projects in Finland?’”Jussi Kangasharju, head of computer science at the University of Helsinki, said that while datacentres brought a limited number of jobs, potentially boosting the local economy, the benefits on a national level were minimal. “Really, for Finland, there are no benefits,” he said. “They are international companies serving international customers. Very little corporate taxes go to Finland.Datacentresultimately have very little benefit for others except the datacentre operator.”View image in fullscreenHanna Halmeenpää, chair of the board of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, near the site where Google’s new datacentre is to be built in Muhos.Photograph: Alessandro Rampazzo/AFP/Getty ImagesWith legislation still playing catchup, there is a rush to get projects under way as fast as possible.Some are calling for a centralised body to coordinate datacentre projects, rather than leaving so much of the decision-making down to municipalities that are likely to prioritise the immediate needs of the local area.In Muhos and Otanmäki, there are people who support the projects, along with the jobs and land taxes they will bring into the local area. But many believe they have been sold short by municipalities.View image in fullscreenGoogle has illegally stripped the entire area, removing even the top soil.Photograph: Jarno Artika/The GuardianAntti Jakonen, who lives in Muhos, said that, although the trees felled represented a small fraction of Finland’s overall forests, he objected to the manner in which it had been carried out. “It has been done in the wrong way. American style. No sense. No sense at all,” he said. The former entrepreneur and fisher wants Google to compensate by helping to restore the local salmon population destroyed decades ago by hydropower.In Otanmäki, the disruption to nature and to residents’ daily lives is being vividly felt. When the trees were felled, the wolves who had lived there came to the village, said Anni Ranta, 53, whose family has lived there for generations.View image in fullscreenPentti Korhonen, a wilderness guide, has lived in Otanmäki for 12 years.Photograph: Jarno Artika/The GuardianA former mining village, the area is known for its rare earth elements. Ranta’s family live at the centre of the village next to a triangular church spire and a former bar that has been empty for years. The peaceful forest used to extend for miles from the village. Now the sound of building work next to the clearcut Google site reverberates.“We had wolves coming into the village because all the wild animals moved out of the forest,” said Ranta. “They fled. What worries me about the datacentres is also the noise because this is hardrock soil. Even when we are standing here talking,” she added, stamping her feet, “it’s like a drum.”Such is her strength of feeling against the arrival of Google that she is thinking of moving out. She also fears the datacentre could make the village a target for Russia, with whom Finland shares a long border. “I don’t want them here,” she said of Google. “I don’t want them in Finland at all. I don’t like the whole idea of AI and the world changing and the way it’s changing. It’s going too fast, too soon.”View image in fullscreenVesa Hyyryläinen, a biologist, drives past the construction area next to the Google clearcuts in Otanmäki.Photograph: Jarno Artika/The GuardianHer father, Pentti Korhonen, a retired wilderness guide, said that since the forest was destroyed, the water in the stream has turned brown. “There is no need at all for datacentres in Finland. No need for datacentres at all,” he said.Vesa Hyyryläinen, chair of the local SLL district, said three-toed woodpeckers nesting in the forest had been pushed out. “All of us nature conservationists are very worried about our Finnish political situation and politics,” said the biologist and osprey expert. “I wonder why we have to sacrifice so much of our nature. They give everything away too easily.”He said, however, that he understood why authorities were trying to bring in new sources of investment and jobs, given the region’s ageing population. “Young people go to Helsinki and Berlin and Paris,” he said. “There are so few people. We have to sacrifice.”View image in fullscreenHyyryläinen said: ‘I wonder why we have to sacrifice so much of our nature. They give everything away too easily.’Photograph: Jarno Artika/The GuardianVeli-Matti Uski, director general of the ministry of environment, said the government was “monitoring the general development of the [datacentre] sector, [and the] application of its legislation, and is prepared to propose legislative amendments as necessary”.Google said it was working to protect water quality at the Muhos site, and that it planned to plant trees across 130 hectares there. Conservationists say that figure is too low to have any real impact in comparison to the damage done by the tree felling.A spokesperson said: “We have operated in Finland for 15 years and have always worked to meet or exceed zoning, environmental, health and safety requirements.“After receiving the LVV letters on 6 October, we stopped preparatory works at Muhos and Kajaani [where the Otanmäki site is located] and have submitted a formal response to LVV confirming this.“We will fully comply with LVV’s requests in this matter. We look forward to maintaining an active, open dialogue with all authorities to strengthen our partnership with Finland and local organisations.”Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentFinlandEuropeAI (artificial intelligence)GoogleAlphabetDatacentresShare

title: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort review – Wii Sports lives on in this effortlessly appealing collection of games | Games | The Guardian
description: Bringing a holiday vibe and a generous selection of sport-themed games, this is exactly what you want from a family video game
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: Bringing a holiday vibe and a generous selection of sport-themed games, this is exactly what you want from a family video game
Content: Guaranteed strike … Nintendo Switch Sports Resort.Photograph: NintendoView image in fullscreenGuaranteed strike … Nintendo Switch Sports Resort.Photograph: NintendoGamesReviewNintendo Switch Sports Resort review – Wii Sports lives on in this effortlessly appealing collection of gamesNintendo Switch 2; Nintendo/NintendoBringing a holiday vibe and a generous selection of sport-themed games, this is exactly what you want from a family video gameKeza MacDonaldThu 22 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 07.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the first Nintendo Switch Sports brought the effortless fun of Wii Sports back into my living room in 2022, I wasfrankly delighted. My small children discovered the pleasure of waving a controller around in enthusiastic imitation of a tennis player, and the surprising subtlety of virtual bowling, working out how to twist the wrist just right to guarantee a strike. I did not expect this game to become a family fixture for the next several years as my kids got older and climbed up the online ranks in all six of its sports (plus the two that were added as free updates). Switch Sports is so beloved in my household that the release of Switch Sports Resort this week is the most anticipated gaming event of the year. To be fair, my children are a bit young for Grand Theft Auto.Nintendo Switch Sports Resort brings three of the six sports back – tennis, bowling, and volleyball – alongside golf and basketball. Then there are seven entirely new sports: boxing, table tennis, archery, thumb wrestling, skateboarding, jetski, and piloting a little prop plane. They are all intuitive, easy to get the hang of on the first or second attempt – some have more legs than others, in the long run – and all of them, crucially, are a little bit silly. Thumb wrestling in particular is cheerfully absurd, giving your characters gigantic thumbs on hands the size of their heads.View image in fullscreen‘One two three four let’s have a thumb war’ … Nintendo Switch Sports ResortPhotograph: NintendoEvery sport here is fun. In skateboarding you use the controller like a mouse, pulling it towards you to propel yourself forwards on the board and tilting it to steer through surprisingly challenging courses, lifting it into the air to jump and spin for tricks. Archery is perfectly intuitive, boxing enjoyably frenetic (especially when played with a seven-year-old), table tennis energisingly competitive, letting you spin and smash the ball with nuanced wrist movement. Almost all of these sports work exactly as you’d expect, with the exception of basketball, whose real-world speed and flashiness are replaced here with methodical turn-taking.Touring the resort on a jetski or in a plane is more peaceful, reminiscent of Wave Race and Pilotwings, two long-dormant Nintendo series whose DNA is clearly evident in the Wii Sports lineage. On the jetskis, you can follow pink dolphins leaping through the waves. As you pass over the island’s stadiums, cafes and beaches in the plane you will see that they are busy with tiny people, watching a match or lazing on the sand. When you’re skating or soaring around you realise just how big and lively it actually is.This gloriously unnecessary attention to detail gives this collection of sports games a sense of place and a holiday atmosphere that’s irresistibly appealing. The music is a sunny as the setting, full of guaranteed earworms. I spent a bunch of time dressing up my little character in outfits that you win by ranking up in the island leagues for each sport, a welcome addition that gives some structure to playing by yourself when you aren’t handing controllers around to friends and family. Variants on every sport also up the longevity: obstacle courses in bowling, for instance, or a three-pointer shooting contest in basketball.After a week of daily play, it has become clear that Switch Sports Resort will not be going back on the digital shelf for some time yet. It is perfect for a Saturday afternoon with friends, but it also has enough going on beneath the surface to sustain the long-term attentions of an enthusiastic child. In other words, it is exactly what you want from a family video game – and as a bonus, it gets everyone off the sofa.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNintendo Switch Sports Resort is out, 22 October; £41.99/$49.99/€49.99Explore more on these topicsGamesNintendo Switch 2NintendoreviewsShareReuse this content

title: In You Can See Everything, it’s Elizabeth Holmes’s partner who makes for 2026’s timeliest villain | You Can See Everything | The Guardian
description: Nathan Fielder’s conversation-igniting film on the Theranos founder finds its darkest moments in her deceptive, Charlie Kirk-loving fiance Billy Evans
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: Nathan Fielder’s conversation-igniting film on the Theranos founder finds its darkest moments in her deceptive, Charlie Kirk-loving fiance Billy Evans
Content: Billy Evans in You Can See Everything.Photograph: A24View image in fullscreenBilly Evans in You Can See Everything.Photograph: A24You Can See EverythingIn You Can See Everything, it’s Elizabeth Holmes’s partner who makes for 2026’s timeliest villainJesse HassengerNathan Fielder’s conversation-igniting film on the Theranos founder finds its darkest moments in her deceptive, Charlie Kirk-loving fiance Billy EvansSecrets, lies and a shock A-list cameo: how You Can See Everything became the film of the year‘You can’t make this stuff up’: why we remain fascinated by Elizabeth HolmesThu 22 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.45 EDTShareIt’s likely that most audiences going into the surprise documentary smashYou Can See Everythingare familiar with either its nominal subject (and literal poster gal with an intense stare) Elizabeth Holmes, the tech founder serving a prison sentence for defrauding investors; or the film’s on-camera co-director Nathan Fielder. Holmes, as the movie points out, was all over the media as her company Theranos was hyped to the moon and then spectacularly imploded; she was also played by Amanda Seyfried in the well-regarded Hulu miniseries The Dropout. Fielder, meanwhile, may not have graced as many magazine covers, but is similarly familiar to prestige-TV acolytes from his comedy-reality series Nathan for You and its successor, the more reality-bending series The Rehearsal. A third figure not included in the film’s ad campaign becomes a key part of the film in the second half, and will also be familiar to many viewers.Secrets, lies and a shock A-list cameo: how You Can See Everything became the film of the yearRead moreThis should leave Billy Evans as the odd man out. Evans, Elizabeth Holmes’s partner (she has said they’re not legally married, though they did get engaged in 2018, have two children and seem to treat each other as spouses), is a not-particularly-famous guy whose screen time competes with the other three well-known faces in what is essentially a four-character drama. But while Evans isn’t boxed out in terms of screen time or memorability, he does remain the odd man out in the sense that in all the discussionYou Can See Everythinghas prompted about manipulation, shifting sympathies and who can or cannot be trusted, everyone seems to agree on one crucial point: Billy Evans sucks.Well, everyone except Holmes, who never indicates so much as a moment of doubt or hesitation toward her common-law husband, at least so far as Fielder or co-director Lance Oppenheim show us. But the movie does show Fielder appearing baffled by Holmes – her absurd claims to have never lied in her adult life; her tautological and nonsensical explanation of how her blood-testing device does actually work (which basically amounts to “if everything about it worked, it would work”); her inability to understand Abbott and Costello’s most famous comedy routine – to the point of having trouble discerning whether she’s consciously scamming him or just, let’s say, reality-divergent. By comparison, Evans comes across as more of a slightly puzzling but recognizable nuisance.When he calls a meeting to demand a percentage of the film’s profits – the kind of arrangement that might be typically reserved for a promotional piece commissioned by a musician, not a nonfiction film extensively interviewing a notorious subject – Fielder and Oppenheim zero in on the question of whether Holmes knew about this request and what became of it, but Evans is the one who violates documentary norms by asking for profit participation (and getting it, at least temporarily). Earlier on, he demands privacy when he grows visibly uncomfortable with questions asked of Holmes while also appearing fully, frontally nude in the film. In a small but underlined moment, he casually relieves Holmes of egg-scrambling duty because he believes she’s not stirring vigorously enough.You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead moreAnd those are just some of his antics before the film’s two-year time jump, after which Evans seems to exert even more control over his partner. Given Holmes’s reputation as a Silicon Valley scam artist, it would make sense enough to categorize Evans as a real-life version of Hollywood’s favorite go-to villain:the evil tech bro. The film even refers to Holmes’s turn in that particular hot seat as the subject of The Dropout, which is not a story of heroes and villains, exactly, but certainly exists adjacent to narratives about tech-forward monsters.Evans has plenty of grimly hilarious signifiers, before and after his partner’s incarceration. Beforehand, he can be seen listening to podcasts at double speed like a true #content consumer/wannabe timemaxxer. Afterward, he shows repeated signs (uncommented upon by Oppenheim or Fielder) of posturing but increasingly intense post-“woke” radicalization: he spends time at a shooting range, claims to carry a gun everywhere, volunteers that he’s a fan of Charlie Kirk and brags about his own supposed vindictiveness. He uses his sketchy control of Holmes’s social media to engage in petty clapbacks that seem entirely out of character for her; he uses his sketchy control of her AI likeness to side-boast about how much healthier she looks as a prisoner than she did immediately postpartum.View image in fullscreenBilly Evans and Nathan Fielder in You Can See Everything.Photograph: YouTubeWith paranoia, delusions of grandeur, lofty-sounding projects that don’t amount to anything and a seeming possessiveness of the woman in his life, Evans checks plenty of tech-bro boxes – only without even a modicum of demonstrated tech expertise, seemingly not even in his fevered imaginings. Yes, Elon Musk propped himself up as a genius on the basis of other people’s companies and his vast fortune; Mark Zuckerberg is a dead-eyed egomaniac whose famous invention is a Friendster clone that bought up a bunch of other already-successful websites and Sam Altman’s career is littered with failures that in no way qualify him to order us all to treat AI as the future. But even if you see these guys as scammers nearly on par with Holmes, they have the distinction of having successfully made money and, in the case of Musk and Zuckerberg, placing some of their might behind products that people do actually use (in some cases, whether they really want to or not). One reason they’re villainized in fictionalized true stories like those poweringThe Social Reckoning(with Jeremy Strong as Zuck) or the upcomingArtificial(with Andrew Garfield as Altman and Ike Barinholtz as Musk) is that they have actually accrued power in the first place. There are stakes to their existence.‘You can’t make this stuff up’: why we remain fascinated by Elizabeth HolmesRead moreEvans has no such claims to fame or even big-canvas notoriety that could inspire something like the four-hourMuskdocumentary by Alex Gibney, released concurrently with You Can See Everything. It seems notable, too, that the similarly lengthy You Can See Everything has seemingly stolen focus from the more traditionally rigorous piece on Musk, a far more influential individual compared to either Holmes or Evans. Holmes was certainly a destructive force for the cancer patients whose hopes she raised, and Evans comes across like a restless creep, but it feels telling, and a little discomfiting, that the gossipy nervous laughter provoked by You Can See Everything is proving a vastly more headline-grabbing draw than a movie laying out the case against a maniacal on-again, off-again trillionaire who has done genuine damage to the world, and is poised to do plenty more. Does someone need to be as petty, strange and blatantly unsuccessful as Evans to be truly finished off in public?Then again, Evans does make a compelling villain for precisely that restless lack of achievement. He will never be as influential as someone like Musk or Zuckerberg, but apparently aspires to that kind of overlord-level bravado (why else would you use your wife’s social media to pick fights?). He’s a fake-it-til-you-make-it-and-then-keeping-faking-it type, more akin to erstwhile reality star turned pretend mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt or any number of filibustering podcasters. Instead of Facebook or Tesla or a portfolio of Donald Trump-style scams, he can simply puppeteer the damaged brand that isElizabeth Holmes– near-literally, when he shows off his AI version. Holmes is clearly manipulative (and based on available information about Theranos, an unambiguous liar), yet Fielder does locate, or maybe even manufacture, some kind of humanity through her inscrutability. There’s something haunting about her, sometimes in spite of herself. Evans is the odd man out in You Can See Everything because he seems to lack that kind of turmoil. He’s hustle-and-grind culture in its final dehumanizing form. The world is just something for him to absorb and scan for advantages at 2x speed.Explore more on these topicsYou Can See EverythingElizabeth HolmesNathan FielderDocumentary filmsSilicon ValleyCharlie Kirk shootingElon MuskcommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s Fifa peace prize was a sham. A reimagined award can still have meaning | Fifa | The Guardian
description: The first awarding marked the apex of Gianni Infantino’s hubris. A new version could highlight the good in the world of soccer
Author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
Headline: The first awarding marked the apex of Gianni Infantino’s hubris. A new version could highlight the good in the world of soccer
Content: Fifa’s social responsibility committee has been tasked with recasting the peace prize after Gianni Infantino awarded the inaugural edition to Donald Trump.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFifa’s social responsibility committee has been tasked with recasting the peace prize after Gianni Infantino awarded the inaugural edition to Donald Trump.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesSoccer with Jonathan WilsonFifaTrump’s Fifa peace prize was a sham. A reimagined award can still have meaningLeander SchaerlaeckensThe first awarding marked the apex of Gianni Infantino’s hubris. A new version could highlight the good in the world of soccerSign up for our free newsletter hereThu 22 Oct 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 13.06 EDTSharePoor Fifa peace prize. Unloved, unliked, mocked, tainted by association with its first winner. And now demoted, too, after Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, dumped the thing on the global governing body’s “social responsibility committee” to look after. To redeem it, rather than to ditch it,to spare Infantino the embarrassmentof acknowledging that his fake prize was really just a fake prize all along.Here is where we should probably acknowledge that, as fake prizes go, and in the context of what it was intended to accomplish, the first awarding of the Fifa peace prize was an unqualified success. It achieved exactly what it was meant to, made by Infantino to flatter Donald Trump, the man he needed to keep on his side to safeguard the riches to be extracted from the North American market in order to consolidate his power base within Fifa. Trump, the gullible buffoon, waspleased as punch– handed a big, golden bauble and a medal he placed around his own neck – and briefly forgot about the Nobel peace prize he desperatelycovets.So now what?The 22-person social responsibility committee is one of thedozens of standing committeesInfantino has created to dole out generous per diems to his allies. It has been charged with recasting the prize into a recognition of social harmony and responsibility,as the Guardian has reported, and will probably seek to depoliticize it – or at least stop awarding it to politicians. There are no aspiring autocrats to placate for the foreseeable future, after all, since Saudi Arabia’s de-facto ruler and host of the 2034 World Cup, Mohammed bin Salman, doesn’t seem to go in for that kind of thing.That first incarnation of the prize will stand as a monument to Infantino’s folly, as the apex of his hubris and his era of genuflecting to strongmen. That is, of course, assuming hesurvives the falloutof his attempt to privatize a chunk of the World Cup and re-emerges somewhat chastened and cautious, if either of those behaviors are still within his capacity. And if he makes it through another presidential election in March.But a second version of theFifapeace prize holds genuine potential to highlight some of the good the sport occasionally does, to platform and recognize those who leverage soccer’s vast cultural influence to improve the lives of others. The magic of soccer is that it transcends the field and reflects cultures and geopolitics; it becomes anthropological ritual, spoken as the world’s common language. Sometimes, it transforms into a vessel for virtue.You could give the new prize to Afghan Women United forgetting recognizedas the official representatives of their country all while playing as refugees in exile. In June, they contested a pair of friendlies against the Cook Islands in New Zealand. They lost both matches, yes, but that’s beside the point. Their mere existence doubles as a towering protest against the Taliban, which has resumed its violent oppression of women since storming back into Kabul in 2021.You could give it to the Ukrainian club Shakhtar Donetsk,for persevering and even thrivingin spite of Russia’s invasion – either through proxies or outright – of their Donbas region a dozen years ago, forcing the club to play elsewhere ever since.Give it to former Spain international Juan Mata,for his workwith Common Goal in convincing other players and managers to donate 1% of their earnings to charity; to Marcus Rashford, forshaming the Tory government into feeding childrenduring a pandemic; to Sadio Mané, forbankrolling the construction of a hospitaland other infrastructure projects in his native Senegal; to N’Golo Kanté for doingmuch the samein Mali.Give it to Scotland’s Tartan Army, forraising money for children’s charitieswherever they play. Hell, give it to the England players fordonating their match feesto charity causes since 2007, adding up to more than $6.7m (£5m).How would any of this relate to peace? Fair question. The peace prize could stand to be rebranded, the better to disassociate it from the least peaceful leader of a western nation in generations. It should probably have clearer qualifications and regulations, too, which is to say that it shouldhavequalifications and regulations. And it’s probably best to shy away from the notion of steering entirely clear of politics. You can either have an award that acknowledges social good or you can be apolitical. You cannot do both.But that needn’t be a bad thing, if this prize is sincere in rewarding one of the sport’s best citizens – and so long as it serves more than the Fifa president’s selfish interests.Leander Schaerlaeckensis the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts,which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.Explore more on these topicsFifaSoccer with Jonathan WilsonGianni InfantinoFootball politicsDonald TrumpSport politicsnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Glee’s pro-LGBTQ+ vision captured 2010s hope. Can a reboot handle Trump’s America? | Glee | The Guardian
description: The beloved high school TV show is returning in a different political climate. I’m skeptical that Ryan Murphy has the nuance this moment needs
Author: Alim Kheraj
Headline: The beloved high school TV show is returning in a different political climate. I’m skeptical that Ryan Murphy has the nuance this moment needs
Content: ‘A post-Glee world suggested that, no matter your differences, everyone would be equal. The last 11 years have highlighted what a fantasy Murphy’s vision was.’Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘A post-Glee world suggested that, no matter your differences, everyone would be equal. The last 11 years have highlighted what a fantasy Murphy’s vision was.’Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyGleeGlee’s pro-LGBTQ+ vision captured 2010s hope. Can a reboot handle Trump’s America?Alim KherajThe beloved high school TV show is returning in a different political climate. I’m skeptical that Ryan Murphy has the nuance this moment needsThu 22 Oct 2026 10.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 10.46 EDTShareFor months,Ryan Murphyhas been discussingGlee. In July, heexpressedhis love for the musical comedy drama he created. In September, hesaidthat he had finished writing a pilot for a potential reboot, adding that he had reached out to some of the cast about a reunion. And nowit isofficial: Disney+ and Hulu have commissioned a Glee revival.Glee, which ran for six seasons between 2009 and 2015, was acultural juggernautduring itsinitial tenure. The show won six Emmys, four Golden Globes and made stars of actors including Lea Michele, Jonathan Groff,Chris Colfer, Darren Criss and the late Cory Monteith and Naya Rivera. Centred on the trials of New Directions, a scrappy show choir at the fictional McKinley high school in Ohio, the show became known for its peppy covers of show tunes, 80s power pop hits such as Journey’sDon’t Stop Believin’(a Glee signature), 2010s chart-toppers and some truly baffling mashups (the amalgamation of Scissor Sisters’ Let’s Have a Kiki and Turkey Lurkey Time from Promises, Promises remains … a choice).Nevertheless, these musical numbers worked: compilation albums regularly scaled the charts, and the cast even embarked on a US and UK tour, which was recorded and later released in cinemas asGlee: The 3D Concert Movie. Even today, the show’s soundtrack cast generates more than 4 million monthly listeners on Spotify.It’s this longevity that is probably behind Glee’s return. On social media, videos featuring people recreating the show’s take on I Say a Little Prayer – complete with McKinley cheerleaders’choreography– continue to rack up views, while over a million videos on TikTok are tagged with “#Glee”. Gen Z audiences, meanwhile, have revisited the show – albeitnot always so favourably– thanks to streaming services, withrecap podcastsand YouTube videos cropping up in response. “That show is interesting because it’s come back around,” Murphysaidin July. “So many young people now watch it.”‘How did this ever get made?’ Gen Z is falling in love (and hate) with GleeRead moreStill, this extended shelf life is surprising given Glee’s politics: no show exemplified Obama-era optimism and liberal identity politics more. Murphy utilised Glee as a vehicle for representation, filling the show with characters from marginalised backgrounds. This was particularly apparent with the show’s numerous LGBTQ+ characters. Glee’s arrival on TV in the year after Proposition 8, which banned same-sex marriage in California, provided Murphy with an opportunity to shift public perception of LGBTQ+ people. While its pro-queer messaging was about as tactful as a neon green American Apparel “Legalize Gay” tank top, there’s little doubt that its emphasis on queer representation – even if said queer people werecoveringthe novelty EDM monstrosity The Fox (What Does the Fox Say?) while wielding puppets – was significant.Glee cleared the path forLady Gaga’s Born This Way and Dan Savage’s “It Gets Better” campaign, ushering in an age of hopefulness about the trajectory of LGBTQ+ rights. While it would take until the summer of 2015 for same-sex marriage to be legalised in the US – an issue covered in Glee’s final season with the nuptials between queer couples Brittany and Santana, and Kurt and Blaine – the increasingly queernormative world of Glee presented a utopian future for LGBTQ+ people, one where those in high school were no longer bullied for being queer, young trans people could transition without interference and gays could live in harmony alongside their heterosexual counterparts. A post-Glee world suggested that, no matter your differences, everyone would be equal.View image in fullscreenGlee’s The Power of Madonna episode from 2010.Photograph: Michael Yarish/APThe last 11 years, however, have highlighted what a fantasy Murphy’s egalitarian vision for the future was. The pandemic, a second Trump presidency and vast economic disparity have stoked divisions and cemented inequalities. Anti-LGBTQ+ legislation, both in the US and the UK, has created a hostile environment for the queer community, particularly for trans people, with the Institute for Strategic Dialoguereportingan increase in anti-LGBTQ+ hate crimes in the US, the UK and Europe. In this context, the identity politics propagated by Glee 1.0, which prized individual visibility, regularly weaponised victimhood, and made a (literal) song and dance about liberalism to promote a vision of societal equality, feel dated. Despite any good intentions, it is these very values that, some hypothesise, have contributed to the so-called “war on wokeness”.Girls is back: why it’s the perfect time for more of Lena Dunham’s millennial Sex and the CityRead moreSince its conclusion, Glee’s legacy has also tarnished. Along with allegations of on-set bullying, racism and favouritism, a number of the cast have died: Monteith, who played football star Finn Hudson,diedfrom anaccidental overdosein 2013; Mark Salling, whose character Noah Puckerman was the school’s bad boy, wasarrestedfor possession of child sexual abuse material in 2015 and laterdiedby suicide; and Riveradrownedin 2020. The writing, too, has been criticised, particularly for how it handled its characters of colour, disability, bisexuality, and the dynamics between students and teachers.It’s this environment in which Glee returns. Some former stars, including Michele, Heather Morris and Chord Overstreet, arealready on board. But whether Murphy will be able to produce something that speaks to our current climate is debatable. The prolific showrunner’s allergy to subtlety, as evidenced by recent outputThe Shards,All’s FairandhisexploitativeMonsteranthologyseries, suggests not.Instead, this reboot feels like a shallow and desperate attempt by a streaming service to reclaim a dwindling gen Z audience. Meanwhile, Murphy’s ham-fisted identity politics feel incongruous at a time where nuance, tact and self-awareness feel more necessary than ever. Personally, when it comes to theGleerevival, I’ve stopped believin’.Explore more on these topicsGleeUS televisionTelevisionRyan MurphyJane LynchLady GagaLGBTQ+ rightscommentShareReuse this content

title: Donald Trump has sold out Ukraine. He makes appeaser Chamberlain look like a man of iron principle | Simon Tisdall | The Guardian
description: Europe’s leaders can no longer trust a word that comes out of Washington. No more slaps on the wrist – we need concrete steps to punish Trump, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Author: Simon Tisdall
Headline: Europe’s leaders can no longer trust a word that comes out of Washington. No more slaps on the wrist – we need concrete steps to punish Trump, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Content: Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Alaska in August 2025.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersView image in fullscreenVladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Alaska in August 2025.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersOpinionDonald TrumpDonald Trump has sold out Ukraine. He makes appeaser Chamberlain look like a man of iron principleSimon TisdallEurope’s leaders can no longer trust a word that comes out of Washington. No more slaps on the wrist – we need concrete steps to punish TrumpThu 22 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.12 EDTShareHistorical comparisons are always inexact. No one conflict precisely mirrors another. Yet Donald Trump’s shameless appeasement of Vladimir Putin carries more than a noxious whiff of Neville Chamberlain’s failed attempt in Munich in 1938 to head off war with Nazi Germany. To be fair to the former UK prime minister – and history largely hasn’t been – his peacemaking efforts had the enthusiastic backing of most people in Britain and France who, like him, were desperate to avoid a repeat of the horrors of the first world war. Trump enjoys no equivalentpublic support for his treachery. Nor does he face the prospect of a US war with Russia. His betrayal of Ukraine is cynically self-interested, globally dangerous and utterly contemptible.US-Russian talks on agreeing the shoddy terms of a precedent-setting American sell-out of Ukraine are at an advanced stage, after meetings in St Petersburg this week. Trump has zigzagged over the war ever since returning to office. Now, panicked byrecord-low poll ratings, he seems determined to scapegoat Ukraine and force its de facto capitulation.Recent steps– his shocking decision to fund Putin’s war machine by buying Russian diesel, his waiving of tougher sanctions, his mysterious, lethal interruptions in US satellite and intelligence sharing with Kyiv, and his renewed attempt to oust Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy – mark Trump out as the skulking Judas, the craven Brutus of the modern age. He makes Chamberlain look like a man of iron principle. All that’s lacking is an umbrella.Why does Trump act this way? Partly, it’s personal. Hedoesn’t like Zelenskyyand it’s obvious why. Ukraine’s leader is everything he is not: courageous, principled, morally unimpeachable, hard-working and politically savvy. Partly, it’s money and power. Trump has set his shrivelled, grasping heart on normalising relations with Putin’s repressive rogue regime, opening the way for lucrative deals on energy, raw materials, and control of the Arctic and outer space. He likes the idea of a world dominated by three all-powerful blocs and authoritarian leaders: himself, Putin and China’s Xi Jinping. And partly it’s the unexplained, sinister hold Putin appears to exercise over this former society playboy, New York real-estate developer andserial bankrupt.Whatever Trump’s motivations, the short-term consequences of his betrayal are potentially fatal for Ukraine’s bid to repel the Russian invaders and survive as a sovereign democratic state. Formuch of this year, Ukraine has been winning, or at least holding its own, in the contested lands of the Donbas and along the Black Sea littoral. More than that, by using homemade missiles and drones, it has taken the fight to Russia’s industrial heartlands and oil refineries, significantly undermining Putin’s ability to fund his war. Zelenskyy has also been winning the battle for international opinion, particularly in Europe, which itself is underescalating Russian hybrid attack. Amid Trump’s egregious backsliding, European nations have taken the lead in supporting Kyiv militarily, financially and diplomatically.It’s hard not to wonder whether there’s a connection between Trump’s sudden, divisive, decisive lurch towards unabashed support for Putin and the fact thatRussia, suffering unsustainable battlefield casualties, severe economic damage and deepening international isolation, is at increased risk of regime-toppling humiliation. Whatever the truth, Trump’s Putin bailout – his duplicitous Russia rescue act – could turn the tide.Trump’s perfidy is the shame of the world, and it is the world – and not only Ukraine – that will pay the price over the longer term. This calculated attempt to force Kyiv’s submission imperils everyone. Ukraine, if it is allowed to fall, will haunt Europe and the wider geopolitical biosphere for decades, as was the case with Czechoslovakia after 1938. Trump’s Molotov-Ribbentrop-style pact with a warmongering dictator,an indicted war criminal, a smirking, bigoted mass murderer, may fatally compromise the western alliance and spell the end of Nato as an effective defence against eastern totalitarianism. Who among the democratic governments of western Europe, in the Elysée, in the German and Polish chancelleries, in Brussels or in Downing Street, can now trust a word that comes out of Washington? Its bond is broken, its honour in shreds.Trump’s betrayal follows a pattern of lesser treacheries: arbitrary tariff wars waged against trading partners, the traducing of loyal allies, threats against Canada and Greenland,abandonment of a two-state solution in Palestineand most recently, his disastrouswar against Iran – the real reason why US midterm voters, facing inflated fuel prices, are turning against him and his Republicans. But his Russian folly may be the most egregious and consequential. AsMI5 has warned, Britain and Europe are under daily attack from Russia, its spy networks, saboteurs, cyber warriors and paid agents. Reports this week suggest it ismenacing western space satellites, too. Don’t look to turncoat Trump for help. He’s on the other side.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe can stop Trump’s assault on the international criminal court | Kenneth RothRead moreTrump’s Munich moment is a disaster in the making for Europe’s security and defence. A Putin victory, accepted and facilitated by the US, would fatefully damage respect for international law and sovereign borders. Untold numbers of war crimes and crimes against humanity would go uninvestigated and unpunished in a partitioned, fractured Ukraine. China and others might soon follow the precedent established by successful Russian aggression. For all these reasons, Britain and its European allies can no longer afford to hold back. Indignant speeches at the UN, off-the-record murmurings and carefully calibrated verbalslaps on the wristwill not suffice, if they ever did. Andy Burnham, France’s Emmanuel Macron, Germany’s Friedrich Merz and Canada’s Mark Carney must lead the way in confronting Trump head-on, even at the cost of a definitive break with Washington.Tell Trump publicly to knock it off. Take concrete steps to punish him for rewarding Putin and prove that the democracies of the world will not be bullied and sold out. Tell him if he really wants to be remembered as the US president who shattered the western alliance and ensured the triumph of authoritarianism, then keep on licking Putin’s boots – but he will be on his own. The UK, EU andNatomember states, Japan, South Korea and other like-minded countries, are far from powerless, economically, militarily and in numerous other ways. And despite what polls may suggest, healthy majorities of their citizens reject the hateful far-right lies and sick populist myths on which Trump and his pitiful emulators feed.The US ultimately leads the west by consent, not by right. Consent can be withdrawn. Burnham could start by ordering the closure of US military bases in Britain, offensive symbols of a hostile occupying power. At all costs, Trump’s treachery must not stand.Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentatorExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionRussiaVladimir PutinUkraineNatoEuropeVolodymyr ZelenskyycommentShareReuse this content

title: Christiane Amanpour’s parting advice to journalists is right on the mark | Margaret Sullivan | The Guardian
description: The CNN star’s wise advice to ‘be truthful, not neutral’ should be tattooed on our souls
Author: Margaret Sullivan
Headline: The CNN star’s wise advice to ‘be truthful, not neutral’ should be tattooed on our souls
Content: ‘What Amanpour is saying in those few words would vastly improve much of the media coverage we see today.’Photograph: Michael Loccisano/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘What Amanpour is saying in those few words would vastly improve much of the media coverage we see today.’Photograph: Michael Loccisano/Getty ImagesOpinionCNNChristiane Amanpour’s parting advice to journalists is right on the markMargaret SullivanThe CNN star’s wise advice to ‘be truthful, not neutral’ should be tattooed on our soulsThu 22 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.48 EDTShareAfter decades as a renowned international journalist, theCNNstar Christiane Amanpour is calling it a career, saying she’ll soon leave the cable network which she joined in 1983.She will be missed for the courage in war zones and forthright presentation that have made her one of the most famous names in media.Amanpour leaves behind not only the legacy of her extraordinary work, but also four words of advice that everyone in the news business should heed.“Be truthful, not neutral,” she has urged many times, including againthis week.Tattoo it on your souls, journalists.For what Amanpour is saying in those few words would vastly improve much of the media coverage we see today, as mainstream news organizations desperately try to gain the largest audience by not offending anyone, and by tiptoeing around the reality of today’s corrosive politics.In so doing, they too often soft-pedal the truth.They refer to politicians’ falsehoods not as lies but as “baseless claims”. They describe would-be authoritarian officials as “sidestepping norms” rather than attacking democracy. They “sane-wash” lunatic behavior and they present both sides of every controversy as roughly equal.Amanpour certainly isn’t urging journalists to be activists. She isn’t urging them to drop the ideal of objectivity in which reporting and evidence, not ideology, prevails. She’s not suggesting they become partisans and echo the talking points of any political party or candidate.Far from it, in fact.She’s urging them to drop the false pretense of neutrality and to focus instead on getting to the heart of the matter – yes, the truth.I don’t mean to make Amanpour out to be a saint. Like anyone who has been in the media world for decades, she has her detractors, those who think she has favored one side or another, and been unfair in her reporting.But at a time when journalism – under great pressure from corporate ownership and the realities of a transformed business model – hasn’t consistently hewed to its core mission of informing the public honestly, her words are a lodestar.The historian Garrett Graff wrote recently about the failures of the American press in the dangerous Trump era, especially as the important midterm congressional elections approach and as threats to democracy grow more dire.“The media – which is under immense un-ordinary pressures of its own – continues to fail to convey just how un-ordinary these developments and shifts in our daily life” are, Graffwrote.“Too often, these stories are covered individually, but not as a pattern.”In essence, then, the media is failing Amanpour’s directive to “be truthful”, because it is missing the big picture.Was Amanpour’s decision to retire affected by the “un-ordinary pressures” in the media sphere?She didn’t say so directly as she announced her decision, but her earlier comments about the coming changes at CNN suggest that there was some worry on her part that truth-telling might be threatened by corporate pressures.It’s easy to see why that might be on her mind.CNN’s parent company has just been acquired by a media behemoth, Skydance, headed by David Ellison, the son of one of the world’s richest people, Larry Ellison. The younger Ellison’s moves at CBS News – particularly the installation of the controversial opinion journalist Bari Weiss – have thrown the venerable broadcast network into turmoil. Prominent journalists including Scott Pelley and Anderson Cooper have left or been fired, and insiders have charged that network leadership has intruded on editorial independence.This past spring, Amanpour noted, during a public appearance in London, that she was concerned about the “ideological realignment of CBS and the destruction, potentially, of 60 Minutes”, the network’s flagship news magazine program.She leaves, however, on good terms with the CNN chief executive, Mark Thompson, who will remain at CNN for the time being, which is reassuring to the cable network’s staff.Announcing her departure, Amanpour made a point of saying she’d be cheering on her longtime home and “its history of independent journalism”.It’s hard to believe the uncertain future of CNN wasn’t at least some part of her calculation, although she’s certainly earned the ability to ease away from the tumult and demands of foreign reporting and commentary.Will the younger and less-seasoned journalists who remain in the daily fray be able to heed her “be truthful, not neutral” words? Or will corporate and business pressures push them further toward the performative neutrality that undermines truth-telling?With her stellar career and her pithy advice, Amanpour has set a high bar.Let’s hope reporters and their bosses – not just at CNN but far beyond – can clear that bar, better than in the past. So much depends on it.Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and cultureExplore more on these topicsCNNOpinionTV newsUS press and publishingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Strongmen like Trump would destroy the planet out of pure spite – and Brazil shows we’re all in peril  | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: If Flávio Bolsonaro is elected, Brazil’s ecosystems will face collapse. The ruling class would rather burn the world than share it with the poor, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: If Flávio Bolsonaro is elected, Brazil’s ecosystems will face collapse. The ruling class would rather burn the world than share it with the poor, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro after voting in Brazil’s general election, Rio de Janeiro, Sunday 4 October.Photograph: Lucas Landau/APView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro after voting in Brazil’s general election, Rio de Janeiro, Sunday 4 October.Photograph: Lucas Landau/APOpinionBrazilStrongmen like Trump would destroy the planet out of pure spite – and Brazil shows we’re all in perilGeorge MonbiotIf Flávio Bolsonaro is elected, Brazil’s ecosystems will face collapse. The ruling class would rather burn the world than share it with the poorThu 22 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.40 EDTShareHowever grim the trajectory might seem, I’ve always believed that sense will ultimately prevail. As the great perils of dismantling the living world become increasingly obvious, even the most rapacious exploiters must come round. Nobody wants to live on a dead planet, do they?There are – orwere– signs that this wasn’t just wishful thinking. Since 2015, mostly thanks to China, the area of the planet being reforested hasincreased, while thanks in large part to Brazil, the global rate of forest destruction has declined. The area of the Brazilian Amazon forest cleared each year isone-sixth of what it waswhen records began in 1988. In the past four years, as a result of Brazilian government policy, the deforestation rate hasfallen by 71%. IfLuiz Inácio Lula da Silvais re-elected president on Sunday, the country could reach zero deforestation by 2030. The arc of the moral universe seems to have bent towards justice.But what my faith in human nature failed to account for was a perverse delight in destruction among a small cohort of the economic elite. There are people who appear to hate life and love death. Donald Trump’sremoval of protections on public lands, the small bite – doubtless the first of many – he wants totake out of Yosemite, hisassaultson the US National Park Service and theUS Forest Service, his trashing of theEndangered Species Act: all are partly a response to lobbying by ranchers, loggers, frackers and miners. But this, I think, is not the primary driver.More important to him, I’ve come to believe, is a vengeful desire to hurt. I doubt Trump hates the monarch butterfly. I’d be surprised if he knows what it is. But he does appear to hate people who love the monarch butterfly.Destroying the habitatson which this and many other endangered species in the US depend seems to be part of the“retribution”he promised. The New York Times wasunable to find evidencethat Trump has ever visited a national park. He probably doesn’t hate them either. But seemingly anything valued by the enemy – greens, liberals, socialists, feminists, anti-racists, “bureaucrats” and “blockers” – should be attacked on principle.Wiping ecosystems off the map is an obvious demonstration of power. Extinction leaves a permanent mark, which is every dictator’s dream. It’s also a highly effective means of hurting those who resist him: the Indigenous people and other people of colour so often on the receiving end of environmental destruction; the regulators; the scientists and the rest of the intelligentsia; above all, people whocare.Caring could be seen as the far right’s meta-target. The“suicidal empathy” themenow crops up repeatedly in videos, newspaper columns and speeches: a professed belief that those who care about other people or species should be destroyed by those who don’t. This belief, by definition, is psychopathic. What exhausts my optimism is that, conned by shallow promises such as the use of brutal methods to address crime, people keep electing those who subscribe to it.View image in fullscreenInspector with logs seized from the Amazon rainforest during an operation to combat deforestation, at a sawmill in Nova California, Rondonia, February 2025.Photograph: Ueslei Marcelino/ReutersPhysically and politically, Flávio Bolsonaro is the spitting image of his father, thejailed coup-plotter, Jair. When Jair Bolsonaro was president of Brazil, he appeared to see ecological destruction as a kind of a holy duty. The deforestation raterose by 59%in his four years, andattacks on Indigenous peopleand other forest defenders, as well as invasions by illegal ranchers, loggers and goldminers rocketed. The crudest forms of extractivism – regardless of their costs, or how they might hold back all kinds of progress – were a matter of policy.The ideology of the far right in Brazil has been described as “beef, Bible and bullets”: violence against those who resist the seizure of their resources, anultra-conservative evangelismand the expansion of cattle ranching, which is both a potent symbol offar-right machismoand theprimary driverof deforestation in the Amazon.Jair Bolsonarolooked backwith nostalgia to the military dictatorship of 1964 to 1985 – which wasactively supportedby the US government – during which local oligarchs could do as they pleased, and those who opposed them weretortured and disappeared. The warnings couldn’t be clearer, but Brazil seems determined to revisit its nightmares. Flávio Bolsonarowon the first roundon 4 October, and is likely to become president.If he wins the second round this week, the gleeful rampage of his supporters,catalysed by government policy, threatens not only the Amazon but the Atlantic forest in the south, the Pantanal wetlands, the Pampa grasslands and the savannah habitats of the Cerrado. This is politics as an orgy of destruction. Let’s eradicate our life support systems – that’ll teach the liberals!Brazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote loomsRead moreTrump has been using all possible means tohelp Bolsonaro win. He gives the impression of seeing Latin America as theconquistadoresdid – one big heap of treasure, ready for looting. The region’s far-right demagogues are only too happy to help. Mass deforestation and thesudden ecosystem collapsethat is likely to result offers a finality to their politics: there’s no coming back from this. You Indigenous people, you greens, you carers: you’ll have nowhere left to hide. The world will be ours, even if it is a world of ashes.What mightBolsonarismoteach us? First, it appears there is no limit to the perversity of the ruling class, which would rather there was nothing left to share than cede any fraction of the planet to the poor.Second, that it possesses all the tools – social and traditional media, the pulpit and the gun – required to make its perversity look like common sense, or at least irresistible, as force is deployed. Third, that the only defence we have against suicidal gullibility is what the Brazilians callconscientizaçao: raising awareness about the relations between exploiters and exploited, and the violence that underpins them. Otherwise all that is good, trusting and hopeful in humanity can be harnessed for a war against everyone and everything.As for the idea that nobody wants to live on a dead planet, Elon Musk, with hispreposterous plans for living on Mars– “Fuck Earth! Who cares about Earth?” – has killed that too. Extending the frontier of destruction, even to the point of human extinction, comes across as a matter of pride. The four horsemen ride again, not in cloaks but in stetsons and denim shirts, driving their cattle before them.George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsBrazilOpinionDeforestationConservationTrees and forestsAmazon rainforestThe far rightBiodiversitycommentShareReuse this content

title: We will make the net-zero transition work for Britain – approving the Jackdaw gasfield is part of the plan | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Protecting jobs and strengthening energy security in the short term does not mean wavering on Labour’s deep commitment to a cleaner, greener future, says UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Author: Andy Burnham
Headline: Protecting jobs and strengthening energy security in the short term does not mean wavering on Labour’s deep commitment to a cleaner, greener future, says UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Content: From left, Douglas Alexander, Miatta Fahnbulleh and John Healey at the St Fergus gas terminal following the announcement on the Jackdaw gasfield, Peterhead, 21 October 2026.Photograph: Paul Reid/PAView image in fullscreenFrom left, Douglas Alexander, Miatta Fahnbulleh and John Healey at the St Fergus gas terminal following the announcement on the Jackdaw gasfield, Peterhead, 21 October 2026.Photograph: Paul Reid/PAOpinionGasWe will make the net-zero transition work for Britain – approving the Jackdaw gasfield is part of the planAndy BurnhamProtecting jobs and strengthening energy security in the short term does not mean wavering on Labour’s deep commitment to a cleaner, greener futureAndy Burnham vows UK will hit net zero target despite Jackdaw gasfield approvalThu 22 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 14.01 EDTShareOn Wednesday, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, gave the go-ahead for gas production to begin at theJackdaw gasfieldin the North Sea. This has been the subject of fierce debate for many years, with strong views on both sides. I want to explain what the decision means and how it fits with Britain’s climate commitments.At a time of acute global instability, it makes sense to responsibly use our resources here at home. Gas from this field will begin heating our homes and powering our businesses this winter. In the longer term, it will significantly strengthen our energy security byincreasing domestic gas production by about 6%and support the UK’s energy supply for more than a decade. Wednesday’s decision will also protect hundreds of jobs in Scotland and add almost £3bn to the UK economy over the lifetime of the project.There has been much speculation about what this announcement means for Britain’s commitment to addressing the climate crisis. I want to be clear that our determination is unwavering. The simple truth is that even as we pursue our ambitious target ofnet zero by 2050, we will need oil and gas for years to come as a bridge to that clean-energy future. And imported gas has a higher carbon footprint than gas produced at home. The transition to net zero is a process, not a moment. I want Britain to make that transition on our terms: reducing our dependence on foreign fossil fuels, supporting good jobs and growing our economy so we can help people with the cost of living.I know this news will be warmlywelcomed in Aberdeenand by oil and gas workers across Scotland. Their jobs support families, businesses and entire communities. Yet, like many others, their industry has suffered from deindustrialisation, with too little thought given by politicians to the places left behind. I will not be so careless with people’s lives. Our oil and gas workers have powered our nation for decades, and they will continue to play a key role for decades to come. Last week, I promised the Scottish people that we wouldreindustrialise their nation. I believe the transition to clean energy represents the best chance we will ever get of making that happen. I am determined to ensure that the next generation of energy jobs is created across Scotland and all nations of the UK.That is why, alongside the decision on Jackdaw, we are establishing anenergy wealth fund– something that, frankly, should have happened more than 40 years ago. It will begin with an initial £2bn and allow us to convert future North Sea oil and gas tax revenues into clean-energy programmes across the country. This investment in renewable energy will enable us to substantially delink gas and electricity prices by the end of this parliament and bring down bills in the long term.This government is taking a pragmatic approach that supports our oil and gas industry today, while driving the growth of the clean-energy industries of tomorrow. We are also making a sustained effort to bring energy costs down over the next decade and in line withthose of our European neighbours. I know, however, that people need breathing space right now. I will do everything I can to ease the pressure on household budgets in the short term. One of my first acts as prime minister was toremove VATfrom electricity bills, and households have seen that reduction in their bills this month. I have now asked the chancellor and the energy secretary to look at removing standing charges from gas bills at the earliest opportunity.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policyRead moreI will ensure the government continues to take action to reduce both gas bills and electricity bills as part of our fundamental changes to the energy system.The manifesto on which Labour was elected committed us to issuing no new oil or gas licences to explore new fields in the North Sea and to reaching net zero by 2050. I stand by both promises. Britain has just emerged from its hottest summer on record, during which we had nurses collapsing on hospital wards, bus driversworking in intolerable conditionsand families losing everything to wildfires. More extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead. The climate crisis is no distant threat. It is here, on our doorstep, affecting people’s lives and livelihoods. I am personally committed to confronting it, and I will not abandon the responsibility we have to future generations.There are two ways we can transition to clean energy. One way, the traditional Whitehall way, is to make people carry the burden of change while others take the rewards. The other is to make the transition work for people by creating good jobs, backing British industry, keeping bills as low as possible, strengthening our energy security and giving communities a greater say over their future. This government chooses the second path.I want Britain to believe in itself again. We can have secure energy, strong industries and a cleaner future. And we can make net zero mean jobs, opportunity and prosperity. That is how we bring back hope.Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United KingdomDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Do Stormont politics stifle the non-sectarian parties? | Northern Ireland | The Guardian
description: Letters: Responding to an editorial, Boyd Black deplores Labour’s policy of not fielding candidates in Northern Ireland. Plus a letter by Declan O’Neill
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Responding to an editorial, Boyd Black deplores Labour’s policy of not fielding candidates in Northern Ireland. Plus a letter by Declan O’Neill
Content: Parliament Buildings at the Stormont estate, Belfast.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAView image in fullscreenParliament Buildings at the Stormont estate, Belfast.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PANorthern IrelandLettersDo Stormont politics stifle the non-sectarian parties?Responding to an editorial,Boyd Blackdeplores Labour’s policy of not fielding candidates in Northern Ireland. Plus a letter byDeclan O’NeillThu 22 Oct 2026 11.25 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.26 EDTShareYour editorial on the dysfunction in Northern Ireland politics (15 October) does not mention the main cause: the denial of basic democratic rights to the people by the Labour party.The party national executive committee refuses to run Labour candidates in anyNorthern Irelandelection, whether to district councils, the Stormont assembly or the Westminster parliament.This means people here, including affiliated trade unionists, are denied the basic democratic right to vote for ourLabourgovernment, which is setting our taxes and winding us up for war.This undemocratic stance by Labour is not an act without consequences. By suppressing cross-community Labour party electoral politics, it forces the electorate into their ethnonational blocs and incentivises the sort of communal sectarian politics and stalemate that we are well used to.Boyd BlackSecretary, the Labour party in Northern IrelandIt is undoubtedly true, as your editorial says that “Northern Ireland’s voters currently do not have the politics they deserve”. However, there are problems with your assertion that the current model of power-sharing “designed to reassure nationalist and unionist communities remains indispensable”. In fact, it plays a part in maintaining the current “cycle of dysfunction”.I have family in Northern Ireland who would prefer to vote for parties that do not fit into this category, but doing so under the current rules would be pointless. They are part of a growing number of voters who do not primarily identify as being part of either “community”.However, even if parties such as the Alliance, the Greens, People Before Profit were to win a majority at Stormont, they would under the current rules not be allowed to form an administration. In fact the current system reinforces sectarian division by stipulating that only those parties self-identifying as nationalist or unionist can “power-share”. Ireland needs real change. The current system cannot deliver it.Declan O’NeillOldham, Greater ManchesterHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Three things the Albanese government could do right now to make people feel better off | Nicki Hutley | The Guardian
description: There are plenty of reasons why Australians feel ‘mad as hell’ at the moment. These three economic policies could restore faith in politics and bring some relief
Author: Nicki Hutley
Headline: There are plenty of reasons why Australians feel ‘mad as hell’ at the moment. These three economic policies could restore faith in politics and bring some relief
Content: The government could help low-income households electrify. Encouraging electrification has never made more sense but supports generally benefit the wealthy, who have the money needed to take advantage.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPView image in fullscreenThe government could help low-income households electrify. Encouraging electrification has never made more sense but supports generally benefit the wealthy, who have the money needed to take advantage.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPOpinionTaxThree things the Albanese government could do right now to make people feel better offNicki HutleyThere are plenty of reasons why Australians feel ‘mad as hell’ at the moment. These three economic policies could restore faith in politics and bring some reliefGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastThu 22 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 18.10 EDTShareIn the 1976 movie Network, news anchor Howard Beale tells TV viewers to stick their heads out their windows and yell: “I’m as mad as hell, and I’m not going to take this any more!” It’s a sentiment that resonates today in Australia and across the world.In October,consumer sentimentat home fell to levels more often associated with recessions, despite the fact that the latest GDP numbers show the economy grew by a real 2% over the year to June (that is, 2% over and above the rate of inflation).But there areplenty of reasonswhy Australians are unhappy and even angry. The combination of war-induced energy shocks, rising tariffs, ageing populations, increased military spending, more frequent climate shocks and even the datacentre frenzy are all pushing up inflation and public-sector debt, which in turn have led torising interest rates. These are not short-term trends. Add to thatfalling house prices, rising unemployment,rising inequalityand a general malaise around what AI might or might not do, and you might wonder why sentiment isn’t even lower.Sadly, in Australia and across the world, pessimism is turning to rising frustration, anger and even violence. After the appalling alleged attack on the independent MP Helen Haines this week, there have been calls to “lower the temperature”. Which begs the question: what might the federal government reasonably do to make people feel like their concerns are really being heard and that action is being taken to rectify the situation (while noting that many challenges are global in nature)?Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereThere are many ready policy options that could leave us collectively better off. Shifting the tax burden from income tospending, or increasing the supply of housing and childcare places, could all deliver productivity and wellbeing gains but they will take time. However, some more immediate measures, such as the$3.3bn in cutsto fuel excise levy and road user charges, if unfunded will just worsen the budget position and may end up forcing the RBA to increase rates again.Measures must help households most in need, deliver a return to taxpayers over time and consider the long-term budget deficit (so that future generations aren’t paying for the policy mistakes of today). Ideally, such policies would also deal with some of the overarching challenges we face, too, such as climate change.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCost-of-living crisis? You wouldn’t know it by looking at these companies’ profits | Greg JerichoRead moreThere are (at least) three things that the government could do right now that make economic sense to me, and that might restore some faith in the political system – assuming opposition parties (and the public at large) play ball and choose economically sensible options overcostly ideologies. And while they might take some time to implement (and to recoup costs), they would represent a demonstration of intent that might restore some of that missing trust. The good news for the government is that others have already done the groundwork for them.1. Raise the GST to fund health and educationI’m a big fan of the Grattan Institute idea this week ofraising the GST to 15%(still below the OECD average of19.4%) with appropriate income tax reductions targeted at low-income households, along with increases in jobseeker and youth allowance payments, rent assistance and pensions. Grattan suggests handing the remainder of the additional $76bn a year back to the states, which would help with woefully underfundedhealthandeducationsystems; reduced reliance on gambling revenues could be an added bonus. There’s plenty in this to feel good about.2. Introduce a super profits gas taxAnother excellent, if more complex, idea is to implement a carbon pricing system. Yes, really! The Superpower Institute’slatest proposalto make polluters pay for the emissions thathurt us alland to tax the super profits of gas exporters would generate $35bn a year over 25 years. This can be redistributed back to those most affected and still leave room for wider supports and/or budget repair. This idea combines climate action and support for future industries with equitable support for households and businesses.3. Help low-income households electrifyOn a less grandiose scale, better targeting of existing supports might go some way to reducing household inequality. For example, encouraging electrification has never made more sense, given high energy prices. But government supports for EVs, solar and batteries generallybenefit the wealthy, who have the money (and the rooftops) needed to take advantage. The New South Wales government’s Solar for Residential Apartments scheme gives us a template for helping households electrify more equitably, while adding to the country’s energy security. The scheme specifically targets $5m of the total $30m package to apartment-dwellers in postcodes which score in the lowest 40% of the Australian Bureau of Statistics socioeconomic index of disadvantage. There’s room for improvement but policies that improve equity – like pulling back on super tax lurks for the uber-rich – should be a high priority.This is just a taste of what is possible. There’s no shortage of sound policy ideas from thinktanks, universities and even government departments themselves. It is vested interests, partisanship and a lack of spine that block progress. Political leaders of all stripes need to find more courage, more sense and a determination to bring people with them. Easier said than done but we need to start doing things differently if we want different (and better) outcomes.Nicki Hutley is a consulting economistExplore more on these topicsTaxOpinionGSTGasAustralian economyBusinesscommentShareReuse this content

title: I longed for my big break. Then a Nobel winner and my girlfriend showed me why success isn’t everything | Rebecca Shaw | The Guardian
description: I was reducing a creative life down to public recognition. Anne Carson’s career deserves more respect than that, and so does mine
Author: Rebecca Shaw
Headline: I was reducing a creative life down to public recognition. Anne Carson’s career deserves more respect than that, and so does mine
Content: Genre-defying Canadian author Anne Carson, winner of the 2026 Nobel prize in literature.Photograph: Pontus Lundahl/EPAView image in fullscreenGenre-defying Canadian author Anne Carson, winner of the 2026 Nobel prize in literature.Photograph: Pontus Lundahl/EPAOpinionBooksI longed for my big break. Then a Nobel winner and my girlfriend showed me why success isn’t everythingRebecca ShawI was reducing a creative life down to public recognition. Anne Carson’s career deserves more respect than that, and so does mineThu 22 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 18.40 EDTShareI am one of those funny little people who is creative and has made the dubious decision to try to make a career out of it.I didn’t fully commit until I was about 30, and I’ve spent the last 14 years in an up and down ride, trying to chip away until I reach the mysterious and elusive level of success where nothing bad happens ever.I have had more heartening bits than many aspiring writers, but they have never coalesced into any kind of stability. Somewhere in the distance is the dream: I get to make my own TV show or movie, and everything finally falls into place and I never struggle or doubt myself again. The vague-but-strengthening-with-each-passing-day sense that I’ve made a terrible mistake that is too late to fix will vanish.Margot Robbie changing her name to her husband’s hurts my beautiful lesbian brain. Here’s why | Rebecca ShawRead moreOne of the things I have done to keep my head above water is collect stories about people who have achieved that kind of success later in life. Morgan Freeman was 52 before his breakthrough role in Driving Miss Daisy. Charles Bukowski was 49 when he quit his job to write full time. Yesterday a guy I follow on social media posted that a movie he co-wrote was about to start shooting, a first for him – and he is 43.There are many artists who quietly beaver away (not all of them lesbians like me) for half their life or more until they finally get their “breakthrough”. When you’re younger than them, a late bloomer is a huge reassurance. It’s proof that even if it hasn’t worked out for you yet, it still conceivably can. These are stories I’ve gathered like precious stones over the years, clutching them to my breast when my own creative life feels impossible to sustain, as my bones weary, and the cohort of people also trying to make a splash in dying industries get ever younger and more beautiful.Earlier this month, there was a shiny new precious stone up for grabs when the genre-defying 76-year-old writerAnne Carson won the Nobel prize in literature. Carson was 42 when her first book of poems was published by a small Canadian publisher, and since then she has lectured and published consistently. Usually, this is a story I would pounce on with my greedy little fingers, and use it to comfort myself. I’m only 44, look how much time there is to get beloved!For a few reasons, I didn’t have that same feeling this time. The most obvious one is that Carson was already so successful, respected and well read. Another is that my ever-optimistic and very honest girlfriend has promised to break up with me if I give up on my dreams, which has shifted my perspective somewhat. And another was reading Carson’s own words about her artistic practice and attitude to success. She was once quoted as saying “I’m going to be famous 15 minutes after I’m dead.” After winning the MacArthur Fellowship in 2000, when asked what difference notoriety had made, she said, “Doesn’t make a lot of difference. It’s nice to be met at airports, I’ll say that.”double quotation markWhether or not it happens, I’ll still be here, chipping away at the dream until I fall into the big sleepShe went on to talk about how it meant she could make more work. That is the real success.
