Not that she won this or that award at her age, but that she has never stopped pushing herself; she has continued to make work of distinction, because that is what she’s here to do. I realised that my habit of hoarding these late-in-life success stories was doing a disservice to us all. I was placing recognition and milestones above the work, reducing someone else’s creative life down to their public victories. Carson’s career deserves more respect than that, and so does mine. I find it hard to say, but I am proud of the fact that I have come from almost nothing, with no connections, and have worked hard in a tough industry for over a decade to scrape together a living doing what I am here to do. I find it hard to accept, but that is worth recognition on its own. I’ve been treating this part of my life as a waiting room for victory, instead of the victory.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSaved for SundayEase your Sunday scaries with the best of Guardian Australia’s culture and lifestyle journalism.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDon’t get me wrong, this is not an argument against wanting or striving for success. I would love to be given a huge creative opportunity that I can become very annoying about. I would LOVE for the creative industries to be supported to thrive so that many other annoying people can find their voice and get it heard. We shouldn’t have to choose between being who we are and being able to survive. It’s no good telling artists that the work itself should be its own reward when the rent still needs paying. Nor should we pretend that recognition, financial security and the chance to reach an audience don’t matter. They do. They really do.But I’ve been reminded that outcomes are not everything. Your creative life will continue to change. It can take decades to hit the right thing on the right head at the right moment. It also may never happen. Carson (and my girlfriend) continue to remind me the point is to keep making things, to keep finding out what I think, to keep trying to inject my voice into the world. If I ever get a big break, it won’t be in the form of a Nobel prize, but I still hope for something. I can’t be dishonest about that. But whether or not it happens, I’ll still be here, chipping away at the dream until I fall into the big sleep.Rebecca Shaw is a writer based in SydneyExplore more on these topicsBooksOpinionAustralian bookscommentShareReuse this content

title: The internet has broken – again. Shouldn’t the tech firms that make billions from it pay to fix it? | Chris Stokel-Walker | The Guardian
description: I’ve been banging the drum about these vulnerabilities for years. It will take more than a handful of exhausted developers to keep us safe, says author and journalist Chris Stokel-Walker
Author: Chris Stokel-Walker
Headline: I’ve been banging the drum about these vulnerabilities for years. It will take more than a handful of exhausted developers to keep us safe, says author and journalist Chris Stokel-Walker
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/GettyOpinionData and computer securityThe internet has broken – again. Shouldn’t the tech firms that make billions from it pay to fix it?Chris Stokel-WalkerI’ve been banging the drum about these vulnerabilities for years. It will take more than a handful of exhausted developers to keep us safeThu 22 Oct 2026 09.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.13 EDTShareParts of the internet are going dark. In the Netherlands, government websites, including its digital ID login service, have become unavailable. Finland has taken public services offline, and Wikimedia, the organisation behind Wikipedia, has switched off some of its systems too.This sounds like the results of a cyber-attack. In most instances, however, the people running the sites deliberately switched them off because the alternative – keeping them online – was too risky. The future is here, and suddenly much of our digital infrastructure is looking very fragile.The websites were turned off because oftwo serious security vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language that is used by about 70% of websites that we can track. Those vulnerabilities in effect gave hackers an open window through which to climb and loot everything within. That could mean an attacker getting into an online shop, stealing customers’ addresses and passwords, or changing its checkout page to harvest card details. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centreadvised organisationsthat were unable to update immediately to consider taking their systems offline.It’s very tricky to get people to care about something quite so techy. PHP is a tricky abbreviation – even explaining what it stands for (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) is complicated, because it’s recursive. And how it helps the web work is also difficult to explain: a good analogy is it’s like the back-of-house team in a restaurant: your browser puts in an order, and PHP handles the cooking and delivers the meal. In any case, what matters is that you’ve almost certainly used websites powered by it this week.I’ve been reporting on scares like these in our digital architecture for more than a decade, and the underlying problem barely changes. In 2014, Iwrote about Heartbleed, a vulnerability in OpenSSL, the software that helps keep communications across the internet secure. It was up to two men named Steve – working for OpenSSL on a shoestring budget and shouldering an awful lot of responsibility – to keep us from disaster. Twelve years later, it feels like we’re still having the same conversation.Heartbleed wasn’t the end of it. In 2021 I reported on adangerous flaw in Log4j, a seemingly mundane tool that records what happens inside computer systems. Then three years later we hadXZ Utils, a tool for shrinking file sizes used on Linux computers into which someone had deliberately planted a backdoor. In each of these incidents, small teams working for the public good recognised the problem, acted, and averted disaster.Each one of these incidents underscored how we rely on a handful of under-resourced individuals to keep vital parts of the web secure.ThePHP Foundation made that point itself this week. Its developers first identified the issue that could bring the internet to a halt in 2024, but it was seen as too expensive and too tricky to fix. The foundation has since admitted the delay was a “structural failure” owing to poor resource levels.This is where AI comes in. In August, researchers working with Calif, OpenAI and Wiz identified how easily the PHP issue could be exploited by using AI tools. And hackers quickly did too.Cloudflare’s chief executive, Matthew Prince, saidhis company had seen millions of attempts to exploit it already.Automated systems powered by AIcan hammer away at weaknesses in an instant, bombarding their human guards with reports that they have to sift through. Researchers documentedabout 48,000 vulnerabilitiesacross the internetin 2025. We’ve already passed 84,000 in 2026, with more than two months of the year still to go. That’s one every five minutes. Not every one will be as serious as this latest one, which scored 9.2 on a 10-point scale used to measure these things. But we’re facing an onslaught.Which all makes for an uncomfortable reality: we’re going to have more days like these. AI makes it inordinately cheaper to find weaknesses in vast volumes of old code, and repairing them is difficult. A 2025review by the UK government foundthat about 28% of central government technology was classed as “legacy” – meaning out of date – while some organisations couldn’t even estimate how much old software they had. In April,ministers admittedthey couldn’t give a comprehensive account of what had since been fixed or retired.So we need to fix that. Companies need to know what software they’re using, including the obscure elements they rely on, and who’s responsible for fixing it. That documentation is boring work, which is probably why it’s overlooked. But we’re in a different world now, and it needs to be done. Paradoxically, AI can help with it. But companies and the organisations protecting us also need adequate funding.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere are some things to be optimistic about. The OpenSSL Foundation, the not-for-profit company that fell victim to the Heartbleed vulnerability in 2014,received more than €400,000from Germany’s sovereign tech fund last year to bolster its resources. The PHP Foundation has hired more staff and is using AI to help triage what’s important and what’s not. And a number of organisations deployed fixes before the current issue went public.But more is needed. The solution is the same one we keep talking about, but rarely actually do anything about: the big tech companies making billions from software they get for nothing (because of its open-source nature) should contribute properly to maintaining it. Governments ought to do the same, rather than hoping a handful of exhausted developers will keep things ticking over indefinitely.I’m growing sick of reporting on, and explaining why, the internet repeatedly breaks. I’ve covered Heartbleed, Log4Shell and XZ Utils – and am now documenting the fallout from PHP. I don’t particularly want to keep doing it. Yet I fear unless we start properly valuing those who keep our internet safe, I will be.Chris Stokel-Walker is the author of TikTok Boom: The Inside Story of the World’s Favourite AppExplore more on these topicsData and computer securityOpinionHackingInternetAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Is this Prince Harry or David Brent in The Office? Either way, we’re watching a masterclass in awkwardness | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: The wayward prince and his wife seem to be aiming for a reboot – searching for purpose, but not self-awareness, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: The wayward prince and his wife seem to be aiming for a reboot – searching for purpose, but not self-awareness, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Content: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex in Nottingham on 15 October 2026.Photograph: FD/Francis Dias/NEWSPIX INTERNATIONALView image in fullscreenThe Duke and Duchess of Sussex in Nottingham on 15 October 2026.Photograph: FD/Francis Dias/NEWSPIX INTERNATIONALOpinionPrince HarryIs this Prince Harry or David Brent in The Office? Either way, we’re watching a masterclass in awkwardnessEmma BrockesThe wayward prince and his wife seem to be aiming for a reboot – searching for purpose, but not self-awarenessThu 22 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.39 EDTShareYears ago, I was in Washington DC when Prince Harry blew through on an official engagement. He was 28, with a full head of hair, a slightly louche gait and a public image that,on a tour of the Senate led by a baffled-looking John McCain, caused people to lose their minds.Senate staffers stood five deep to get a glimpse; women materialised from every corner, more glamorously dressed for the office than usual. The excitement was so great that there were actual screams from behind the security line. I remember noting the prince’s prominent ears, the high colour in his cheeks and his habit, when addressed, of bowing his head, as if humbled by what he was hearing. Aw, I thought. Bless him.But that was a long time ago. This week, Harry, now 42, appeared on camera in aninterviewin New York with GQ, playing to a very different audience. He looked older and schlubbier – don’t we all – the diffidence of youth replaced by something more pompous and belligerent, undergirded by what, in recent years, has appeared to be his bottomless well of hurt feelings. Harry was promoting something – amasterclasson “grief science”, which he has undertaken with Dr Mary-Frances O’Connor. But the question of why on earth he would double down on previous US media appearances, none of them successful, sat alongside the bigger royal question of the season: namely, what are he and his wife, Meghan, going todo?Since the pair arrived back in the UKthis summer after a six-year absence, watching them try to settle on a role has been a veritable festival of awkwardness, not least because it’s not entirely obviouswhere they have left to go. In March, Netflix ended its partnership with Meghan’s lifestyle brand, As Ever, less than a year after it replaced the pair’s $100m mega-contract with a first-look deal. These well-publicised failures were compounded by the previousdeath of Meghan’s podcast,the couple’s parting with Spotifyand what might politely be called their low productivity metric when it comes to anything not immediately related to the royal family.In this, the Sussexes are no different to any other creators endlessly raking over their own lives for content. The difference, of course, is that Harry, with a lofty mindset inculcated from birth and which is presumably incredibly hard to shake, presents his every gesture as automatically belonging to that higher calling, public service. “I don’t do it for myself,” he says in the interview in New York when explaining the venture with MasterClass. (Side note: the real masterclass here is in watching the GQ hack trying to use Harry’s grief project as a Trojan horse for questions about the royal family, among them: “Do you grieve that?” in relation to Harry’s fallout with King Charles, and a sleight of hand reference to “anticipatory grief” in a reach to get his father’s health on the table. Honestly, I tip my hat).View image in fullscreenRicky Gervais as David Brent in The Office, 2001.Photograph: BBC“Trying to make an impact in the world, that is genuinely what energises me,” says Harry, sinuously pivoting away from the awkward questions. And if he stuck to harmless banalities about grief and, oh God, what he calls his mission as a storyteller, one might be inclined to say good luck to him. Harder to stomach is what appears to be his and his wife’s need for the public to participate in their grandiose delusions.Witness the Sussexes in Nottingham last week, going on a walkabout under the auspices of a charity event that, to me, looked more like an exercise in self-gratification. As theking had already sternly warned the pair: they’re private citizens, now, with no officially sanctioned public engagements, and yet here they were, working a crowd like any active-duty royals. While Meghan smiled excessively with her “hello, little people!” act, her husband alternated between mild engagement with the well-wishers and sending category-five death stares to the hacks, poor sods, who’d turned up to cover this non-event. It was embarrassing, and awkward, and as someone pointed out on the internet, like watching David Brent return to the office after being fired.And so, while the top line from the interview in New York focused on Harry’s indirectcall for reconciliation with his family, it was another takeaway that struck me more forcefully. More than once, the prince talked about the importance of knowing yourself, adding that he had “put in the work” and clearly positioning himself as more evolved than his father and brother. I would suggest Harry’s journey of self-awareness has a way to go yet.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEmma Brockes is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsPrince HarryOpinionMeghan, the Duchess of SussexNetflixMonarchycommentShareReuse this content

title: A violent and coordinated youth uprising? That’s exactly the picture Europe’s enemies want to paint | Alberto Alemanno | The Guardian
description: Each country’s protesters have distinct grievances. Listen to them, not the voices telling us Europe is ungovernable, says law professor Alberto Alemanno
Author: Alberto Alemanno
Headline: Each country’s protesters have distinct grievances. Listen to them, not the voices telling us Europe is ungovernable, says law professor Alberto Alemanno
Content: Students in Paris protest against under-resourced schools, 8 October 2026.Photograph: Aurélien Morissard/APView image in fullscreenStudents in Paris protest against under-resourced schools, 8 October 2026.Photograph: Aurélien Morissard/APOpinionProtestA violent and coordinated youth uprising? That’s exactly the picture Europe’s enemies want to paintAlberto AlemannoEach country’s protesters have distinct grievances. Listen to them, not the voices telling us Europe is ungovernableThu 22 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 05.34 EDTShareLast Saturday night, the town hall of Limoges in west-central Francewas set ablaze. By Sunday, images of the fire destroying a symbol of the French republic, andother scenes of unrest across France, were everywhere, but being used to tell very different stories about what is happening in Europe.For some, the flames announced a pan-Europeanyouth revolt, proof that a single movement was sweeping the continent. Donald Trump, who had already insisted that the French schools protests were not about schools but aboutmigration and Islam,urgedEuropeans to “close the borders”.The mayor of Limogessaw the fingerprints of an alleged ultra-left insurrection.I lost count of how many mainly rightwing media outlets were contacting me suddenly. Most were based in India, China, Singapore and the US. They sought voices to validate the idea of a “teen revolt” spreading acrossEurope, driven by the same grievances and violence.None of these narratives, each serving a different political agenda, adequately explains what is happening. Europe’s protests have different causes, constituencies and demands. Portraying them as a Europe-wide rebellion erases those differences and makes Europe look ungovernable. That picture is a gift to anyone who wants to exploit the unrest.What set off the protests varies from country to country. In France,the mobilisation beganin schools in mid-September in frustration over longstanding failures to address overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated buildings and facilities. By the time of the huge demonstration on Saturday, public-sector workers had joined, and the grievances hadwidened to encompass the cost of living.InBelgium, meanwhile, students have challenged tuition-fee increases in the country’s French-speaking region and demanded additional teaching hours.Greek studentshave mobilised over housing costs and access to accommodation, whileGerman pupilshave protested against the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service.View image in fullscreenThe city hall in Limoges, central France, on fire after protests turned violent, 17 October 2026.Photograph: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP/Getty ImagesLook beyond western Europe, and the differences become even more distinct. InAlbania, student unrestbuilds on a pre-existing anti-government mobilisation, rather than a standalone youth revolt. InSerbia, students have led nearly two years oflargely peaceful protestsfollowing theNovi Sad railway station disaster. Their movement centres on demands for an end to corruption, a lack of institutional accountability and political inaction. Now the students arerunning in this weekend’s electionon their own list. This is a battle over power and accountability, and goes well beyond education or generational frustration.Italian students may occupy schools and shout slogans in French, but the cross-border spread of images,slogansand tactics does not prove a shared organisation. Rather, 24-hour news coverage can turn separate protests into a single story of youth rebellion, creating, deliberately or not, the illusion of a common movement and programme where neither exists.Rejecting the idea of a single European youth revolt does not mean denying the existence of a shared generational anxiety. Housing has become increasingly unaffordable, public services are under pressure, and the transition into secure employment is uncertain.Eurostat reportsthat EU house prices rose by 55.4% and rents by 26.7% between 2010 and the fourth quarter of 2024. The 2026TUI Foundation Youth Study foundthat 52% of young people aged 16–26 across seven European countries expected to be worse off than their parents, compared with just 25% who expected to do better.Youth unemployment in the euro arearemains substantially higherthan overall unemployment. Onestudy of French firms founda sharper decline in permanent hiring among workers aged 21–29 in occupations exposed to artificial intelligence. TheEuropean Central Bank cautionsthat the evidence does not yet establish generative AI as the cause. But the uncertainty itself can create a shared sense of insecurity across national borders.Such anxieties help explain why protests in one country resonate with young people in another, and why images of school sit-ins or street demonstrations can inspire imitation. But they don’t translate into common demands, let alone a coordinated political movement.France’s demonstrations last Saturday exposed another danger: how quickly violence can overshadow a protest’s message. Most demonstrators marched peacefully, but a minority resorted to violence. Their actions should not define hundreds of thousands of demonstrators, just as peaceful protest should not provide cover for criminal acts.What happened in Milan showedhow the two can blur. A peaceful cost of living march alongside protests over education cuts and race-based reform,was followed by lootingcarried out by hooded, mostly teenage groups organised partly via TikTok. More than 200 were detained, most of them minors, and the march’s organisers disowned them. Defending public order must go hand in hand with accountability for violence andscrutiny of police conduct.But when images of burning buildings and looting dominate coverage, peaceful protest and criminal violence become harder to distinguish in the public mind. A single incident can come to define an entire mobilisation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe misleading narrative of a pan-European revolt has consequences, because it allows images of unrest to be taken out of their national contexts and presented as proof that a chaotic Europe is ungovernable.This is particularly useful to those seeking to deepen divisions and undermine European democracy: it turns distinct national problems into a sweeping story of European failure.For the radical right, the idea of a continent in flames proves that open societies cannot protect their citizens, hence the call to “close your borders”. For those on the radical left who celebrate every burning building as the dawn of a continental uprising, the flames prove that liberal democratic institutions are beyond repair. Both need Europe to look ungovernable but neither offers an answer to the disorder it complains about. And both serve the interests of those beyond Europe’s borders who gain from a divided union, fromthe Trump administrationto Vladimir Putin.President Macron had a point when he lashed out at the “stupid” comments of foreign leaders about events in France. AI-generated images of scenes that never took place in France had been circulating, he said. Macron is hardly neutral, but certain forces clearly have an interest in amplifying images of chaos.Governments should neither romanticise protest nor use violence as a pretext to dismiss legitimate grievances. They must protect peaceful demonstrators, hold perpetrators accountable and address the pressures that leave many young people uncertain about their future.Europe’s democracies will be judged not by how they withstand these protests, but how they address the distinct grievances behind them and restore confidence in the future. That is how generational anxiety can become a force for democratic renewal rather than fuel for those seeking to portray democracy as broken.Alberto Alemanno is the Jean Monnet professor of EU law at HEC Paris and the founder of The Good LobbyFrance readers Q&A: Guardian Europe columnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst will be live taking questions from our readers about the unrest in France from at 1500 BST / 1600 CEST on Friday 23 October. Send your questions by email now toconversations@theguardian.comor post questions in the comments from 0900 BSThere.Explore more on these topicsProtestOpinionFranceEuropeSerbiaItalyAlbaniaGreececommentShareReuse this content

title: Ali G: Who Iz I? review – Sacha Baron Cohen’s high-stakes satire punches up and down with spectacular bad taste | Movies | The Guardian
description: Baron Cohen’s live-ammo prankster is back, 20 years on, but has to battle with his own irrelevance in search of big laughs and the approval of a new generation
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Baron Cohen’s live-ammo prankster is back, 20 years on, but has to battle with his own irrelevance in search of big laughs and the approval of a new generation
Content: ‘Blunders with the semi-intentional force of an XL bully into the issue of whether jokes are still allowed’ … Sacha Baron Cohen in Ali G: Who Iz I?Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Blunders with the semi-intentional force of an XL bully into the issue of whether jokes are still allowed’ … Sacha Baron Cohen in Ali G: Who Iz I?Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyMoviesReviewAli G: Who Iz I? review – Sacha Baron Cohen’s high-stakes satire punches up and down with spectacular bad tasteBaron Cohen’s live-ammo prankster is back, 20 years on, but has to battle with his own irrelevance in search of big laughs and the approval of a new generationExclusive: Republican leader embarrassed by film says he plays to sue Sacha Baron Cohen: ‘A liar and a pervert’Peter BradshawThu 22 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you liked Sacha Baron Cohen’s Ali G the first time around, you’ll like this less; if you disliked it, you’ll dislike this more; if you suspected it was racist, you’ll be more emboldened to say so – especially as Baron Cohen has dreamed up a whole new character apparently to pre-empt and mock precisely that objection. Broad and crass as it often is – in fact always is – this Ali G sequel is sometimes funny: the athletic vigour of our hero’s pranking and punking is like the umpteenth Jackass film at which you might find yourself laughing, and Baron Cohen blunders with the semi-intentional force of an XL bully into the issue of whether jokes are still allowed.Republican leader embarrassed by Ali G film says he plans to sue Sacha Baron Cohen: ‘A liar and a pervert’Read moreUnlike the first film,Ali G in Da Housefrom 2002, this is not a full written-through narrative. It is basically another live-ammo series of hoaxes with some spectacular bad taste perpetrated upon the deserving and less deserving; it satirises the shamelessness of anti-woke free speech martyrs, punching up and down with grossout cringe, and the targets include some big names who shouldn’t be revealed here. There are two other subordinate characters: Erran Morad, a sinister Mossad/IDF officer turned US security consultant (who appeared inBaron Cohen’s Who Is America? TV series), and a new figure: Dr Nira Cain-N’Degrocello, a grotesquely supercilious white liberal who is the self-appointed scourge of cultural appropriation. The dupes are built into a big silly climax fabricated with body doubles and (presumably) covert reshooting.The insurmountable problem is that the film keeps having to tell you who is and isn’t “in on it”: at the beginning, over the closing credits at the end and even briefly in the middle of the action. Well, Ali G was from so very long ago, and even the high-water mark of Baron Cohen’s Borat popularity was quite long ago, and the online media scene now so fragmented that … yes … people have forgotten, a whole new generation doesn’t know. People really don’t recognise him.The high concept is that Ali is now washed up, short of money and unpopular, and old-school media figure that he is, he disapproves of a plan by his heavily pregnant partner Julie (Morgana Robinson) to launch an OnlyFans account. But on trying to sell his fax machine in a Staines high street pawn shop, an old fax chunters out of it with an offer from HBO for a new show. Overexcited, Ali and Julie head off to the US to sucker some people in the traditional style; the smallscreen setup blown up to high-def cinematic proportions. His fictional woke tormentor decides to take him down and, by employing the Israeli hardman, tries to convince credulous and aggressive Republicans that Ali is a Mexican terrorist whose baby must be prevented at all costs from being born on US soil. The movie does make a few people look silly, yes, although Baron Cohen doesn’t land a huge punch on a big name the way he did in the Borat sequel.So who iz Ali G and what iz the point of trundling him out again? The first film implied he was once a Robert Smith-type goth, but that is now forgotten about. Interestingly, one person who this film doesn’t allude to is Tim Westwood, the BBC Radio 1 hip-hop DJ and son of the Bishop of Peterborough whose speech mannerisms were held to be one influence on Baron Cohen’s great creation, and proof positive that white people did indeed patronisingly ape a street way of speaking.Westwood’s subsequent all-too-unfunny history, perhaps, doesn’t mesh with trying to revive Ali G now as comedy IP. The movie outings of Ricky Gervais’s David Brent and Steve Coogan’s Alan Partridge worked better because they could more plausibly represent the melancholy of getting older and irrelevant. Ali G feels older in the wrong way, and the On-the-Buses humour with Julie is tired. The best bits will be available on TikTok and Instagram reels soon enough.Ali G: Who Iz I? is out on 22 October in Australia and 23 October in the UK and USExplore more on these topicsFilmAli G: Who Iz ISacha Baron CohenComedy filmsComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Heartbreak, hope and human imperfection: Leonard Cohen’s greatest songs – ranked! | Leonard Cohen | The Guardian
description: A decade after his final album, and his death, we rate the best of the Canadian singer-songwriter who brought a deep, spiritual wisdom to love and grief
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: A decade after his final album, and his death, we rate the best of the Canadian singer-songwriter who brought a deep, spiritual wisdom to love and grief
Content: Cohen … the self-confessed ‘lazy bastard in a suit’.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCohen … the self-confessed ‘lazy bastard in a suit’.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesRankedLeonard CohenHeartbreak, hope and human imperfection: Leonard Cohen’s greatest songs – ranked!A decade after his final album, and his death, we rate the best of the Canadian singer-songwriter who brought a deep, spiritual wisdom to love and griefAlexis PetridisThu 22 Oct 2026 10.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 18.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. First We Take Manhattan (1988)The synth-heavy production on 1988’s I’m Your Man has always been divisive – even Leonard Cohen’s longtime collaborator Anjani Thomas subsequently expressed misgivings – but on its opening track, it really works. The Pet Shop Boys-ish arrangement chafes against Cohen’s growling vocal, amplifying First We Take Manhattan’s shiver-inducing sense of brooding menace.19. Going Home (2011)Seven years – and a personal financial crisis – after 2004’s half-hearted Dear Heather, Cohen returned to the studio with his powers freshly marshalled. As if to underline the point, Old Ideas opened with the sharply witty Going Home, on which Cohen’s muse addresses the listener directly, disparaging the artist himself as “a lazy bastard in a suit”.18. Memories (1977)Cohen famously called his 1977 LP Death of a Ladies’ Man “a catastrophe”, which perhaps reflected more on its drug- and booze-soaked recording with dangerously erratic producer Phil Spector than the finished album. It’s an outlier in Cohen’s catalogue, but one with much to commend it. Certainly, he maintained an understandable fondness for the rock’n’roll-influenced Memories, often performing it live.17. Almost Like the Blues (2014)View image in fullscreenBlack humour … Cohen in Paris, 2012.Photograph: Joel Saget/AFP/Getty ImagesCohen’s renaissance continued apace on Popular Problems. Released the day before his 80th birthday, it sounded suspiciously like a masterpiece. Almost Like the Blues found him reflecting sorrowfully on man’s inhumanity to man – not merely torture, killing and war, but “all my bad reviews” – and staring down his own mortality, replete with a jab at Richard Dawkins.16. A Thousand Kisses Deep (2001)Shruggingly titled, largely recorded in collaborator Sharon Robinson’s garage and packaged in a sleeve featuring a selfie, Ten New Songs was an understated return to recording after Cohen’s five years of Buddhist study. But beneath its unassuming veneer lurked beautiful songs: the chanson-like A Thousand Kisses Deep is an exquisite reflection on regret and time’s passing.15. Death of a Ladies’ Man (1977)Nowhere else on this album does the cocktail of Cohen’s songwriting and Spector’s more-is-more approach to production gel so perfectly: the title track is a fantastic song. Moreover, the weight of Spector’s arrangement, the way it causes the tempo to drag, seems to complement rather than suffocate its mood.14. You Want It Darker (2016)Other artists have made albums that looked imminent death in the face – Warren Zevon’s The Wind, Queen’s Innuendo – but You Want It Darker, released less than three weeks before the end of Cohen’s life, may be the most poised and affecting. “I’m ready, my Lord,” he sang on its title track, a complex, thorny examination of faith.13. Chelsea Hotel #2 (1974)View image in fullscreenIn Frankfurt, 1976.Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/AlamyIn which a brief tryst with Janis Joplin – “We fell into each other’s arms through a process of elimination,” he later recalled – turns into a kind of eulogy, not just for the late singer, but for the era in which they met. It’s haunted by the sense of optimism extinguished.12. Everybody Knows (1988)Rock stars of a certain vintage were wont to write despairing state-of-the-world addresses in the late 80s – Lou Reed’s New York is full of them – but Everybody Knows is a cut above, its relentlessly bleak worldview leavened by black humour: “Everybody’s got this broken feeling, like their father or their dog just died.”11. Avalanche (1971)Against stiff competition, Songs of Love and Hate may be Cohen’s darkest album. Avalanche is its claustrophobic heart, a relentless, shimmering guitar figure, a confusing but compelling tumble of imagery, with his voice at its most poisonous. Nick Cave called it one of “the essential pillars that hold up the structure of my artistic world”.10. Dance Me to the End of Love (1984)Inspired by the story of theLagerkapellen– concentration camp orchestras whose music accompanied forced labour and executions – there’s something eerie about Dance Me to the End of Love’s klezmer-inspired melody and lyrical pleas for lifelong fealty. The latter are filled with intimations of darkness; it’s never entirely clear that love will overcome them.9. The Future (1992)“I’ve seen the future, baby, and it’s murder”: Cohen’s apocalyptic response to the sociopolitical upheavals of the early 90s – most obviously the Los Angeles riots – depicted a world in which “attitudes are all extremist and they’re all defensive”. Thirty-four years on, it sounds grimly prophetic, its upbeat soft-rock backing only serving to amplify the unease.8. Tower of Song (1988)View image in fullscreenDeep reflection … Cohen in 1987.Photograph: Christian Rose/Roger Viollet/Getty ImagesCohen found writing a trying experience – lurid stories abound of him beating his head against the floor while working on Hallelujah. He poured it all into the thrillingly vivid, mordantly funny Tower of Song, which has often struck a chord with other artists, covered by everyone from Phoebe Bridgers to Tom Jones to the Jesus and Mary Chain.7. Anthem (1992)Anthem is home to perhaps Cohen’s most-quoted lyric: “There is a crack in everything, that’s how the light gets in.” But in truth, it’s just one among a plethora of memorable lines in the song’s gospel-infused paean to hope and human imperfection, a song he later suggested represented “everything my whole work and life had gathered around”.6. I’m Your Man (1988)Even by the standards of Cohen’s synth era, the backing of I’m Your Man is low-rent and cheesy, but it fits perfectly with a song about abasement. Its emotional tone shifts from lustful to desperate to hopeless: “A man never got a woman back, not by begging on his knees,” he notes in a moment of clarity, then carries on regardless.5. Hallelujah (1984)‘More than a song’: the enduring power of Leonard Cohen’s HallelujahRead moreHallelujah’s progress from an album Cohen’s US record label refused to release to his most famous song – via, of all things, a cover by John Cale that appeared on the soundtrack of Shrek – is fascinating. Cohen later proposed a moratorium on its use in films, but, in truth, it has survived ubiquity with its power to move intact.4. So Long, Marianne (1968)Cohen’s original intention was to try his luck as a Nashville songwriter. If you squint, you can just about make out the shape of a county song in So Long, Marianne’s beautiful admission of guilt, although it’s hard to imagine the Music Row treatment could improve on its wonderfully ramshackle string accompaniment.3. Bird on the Wire (1969)View image in fullscreenGloomy self-reflection … Cohen in 1967.Photograph: Jack Robinson/Getty ImagesAnother Cohen classic with country music in its bones – Kris Kristofferson said he wanted the opening lines on his gravestone – Bird on the Wire was coaxed out of a depressed Cohen by his then girlfriend, Marianne Ihlen. It sounds utterly, authentically defeated, like one long sigh, destined to soundtrack moments of gloomy self-reflection for the rest of time.2. Suzanne (1968)There are infinitely worse ways to start your debut album than with a song so good, it immediately becomes a standard, covered by Nina Simone, Neil Diamond, Roberta Flack and Aretha Franklin. Some recompense, perhaps, for the titular lady’s refusal to let Cohen touch her perfect body with anything other than his mind.1. Famous Blue Raincoat (1971)Reducing Leonard Cohen’s oeuvre to 20 songs is a thankless task: the compiler is abundantly aware that umpteen deserving songs have been neglected. Similarly, there’s no head-and-shoulders “best” song, merely personal favouritism. Still, you listen to Famous Blue Raincoat’s disconsolate depiction of a love triangle – in the form of a letter to the other male party – and boggle at the idea Cohen was dissatisfied with such an impossibly beautiful song, which so perfectly conjures up an atmosphere of shadowy small-hours reflection, and which comes complete with one of his loveliest melodies (subsequently pinched on – crikey – Leo Sayer’s When I Need You).Explore more on these topicsLeonard CohenRankedPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Raye wins 2026 Mercury prize for This Music May Contain Hope | Mercury prize | The Guardian
description: Singer who has had record-breaking Brit awards success adds to haul thanks to massively ambitious big-band album
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Singer who has had record-breaking Brit awards success adds to haul thanks to massively ambitious big-band album
Content: Raye accepts the 2026 Mercury prize.Photograph: JM Enternational/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRaye accepts the 2026 Mercury prize.Photograph: JM Enternational/Getty ImagesMercury prizeRaye wins 2026 Mercury prize for This Music May Contain HopeSinger who has had record-breaking Brit awards success adds to haul thanks to massively ambitious big-band albumBen Beaumont-ThomasMusic editorThu 22 Oct 2026 17.24 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRaye is the winner of the 2026Mercury prize, for her second studio album, This Music May Contain Hope.Her win – for a hugely ambitious 73-minute record that spanned big band jazz, power balladry, funk and more – caps an ongoing renaissance for a British singer who at one point was in the doldrums, lashing out publicly at her record label for not letting her release a studio album.Since that low in 2021, she split from that former label and found huge success with two albums: My 21st Century Blues, which won her six Brit awards – still the record for a single Brits ceremony – and This Music May Contain Hope, which topped the UK charts and contains the global hit Where Is My Husband!View image in fullscreenRaye and fellow Mercury competitor Olivia Dean, whose album The Art of Loving has spent 55 weeks in the UK Top 10Photograph: JMEnternational/Getty ImagesThe judging panel said: “Raye displays real imagination and scope in showing what an album can be, going beyond any one style or genre to realise her vision. The judges agreed that Raye’s superb album will serve as a huge inspiration for years to come.”The award, handed out yearly to the best British or Irish album as voted for by a panel of music industry figures, comes with a £25,000 prize.While This Music May Contain Hope didn’t have universally positive reviews – “there are flaws, but in fairness it pays off more often than it fails”, was the opinion of the Guardian’s pop critic Alexis Petridis – the judges hailed its “scale, structure, ambition and sheer charm”.Raye: This Music May Contain Hope review – a wildly ambitious epic of unbridled self-expressionRead moreWhere Is My Husband! proved to be a powerhouse lead single, reaching No 1 in the UK, No 6 in the US and delighting audiences globally with Raye’s witty rat-a-tat-tat delivery as she expressed her frustration at her romantic failures including “lonely acrobatics, unzipping my dress at 2am”.It adds to a strange and heartening career for the 28-year-old singer, born Rachel Keen in west London, who started out by shuttling between genres and netting hits as a guest vocalist on pop-dance singles before finally being able to let her stylistic diversity shine on her album projects.As lighthearted as songs like Where Is My Husband! are, she has also written about more serious subjects, such as a sexual assault she faced from a music producer.View image in fullscreenRaye with her award, and her live band at the Mercury prize ceremony.Photograph: JM Enternational/Getty ImagesAccepting the award at the ceremony in Newcastle, Raye said: “I cannot tell you how grateful I am to be holding this. I’m shaking, I’m jet-lagged, I’m tired, I’m grateful!”She alluded to her difficult years with her former label, saying: “Albums are so important, and not to be bitter – because I feel like I’m mostly at peace with my past – but to come from a place where it’s all about singles and chasing the next thing, I just feel so grateful to be recognised.”View image in fullscreenKing David-Ike Elechi and Stan Woodward of Knats onstage during the 2026 Mercury prize ceremony.Photograph: JM Enternational/Getty ImagesShe also talked about the central topic on the album: “Hope is a very cheesy word, especially for us British people, we don’t do that deep stuff like that, but hope is something we all need … so I hope that message comes across to anyone who needs it.”Elsewhere on the shortlist, Paul McCartney missed out in the first year he was nominated for the prize, for his reflective albumThe Boys of Dungeon Lane. In a video message, he said he was “chuffed” and “surprised” to be nominated on a shortlist alongside “such a group of really amazing artists”.Suede, who opened the ceremony by performing their stridently pro-European anthem Dancing With the Europeans, weren’t able to add a second Mercury win to their trophy cabinet, after winning for their self-titled debut in 1993, the second year the award ran.Nor could Dave, who won for his own debut album, Psychodrama, in 2019; he and McCartney were the only artists not to perform at the ceremony.Pulp – the winners in 1996 – performed for the second year in a row: last year for their nominated album More, and this year representing the all-star compilation album Help, created to raise funds for the charity War Child.Florence + the Machine now have the ignominious honour of being the Mercury’s joint highest nominee without winning, tying with Radiohead on five unconverted nominations.View image in fullscreenPulp, who won the award in 1996, performed at the ceremony as representatives of the all-star charity album HelpPhotograph: JMEnternational/Getty ImagesRaye also beat stiff competition from Olivia Dean, whose album The Art of Loving has been one of the most successful albums by anyone in the singer’s generation, spending every one of its 55 weeks since release in the UK Top 10.‘Geordie optimism is this rigorous spirit of hard graft’: Newcastle jazz band Knats break out of the north-south divideRead moreAfter losing its sponsor in 2024 and taking place in a rather low-key ceremony, the Mercury prize has repositioned itself, moving away from London to Newcastle in 2025 and scaling up in size to the city’s Utilita Arena.In its inaugural year in its new home, the Mercury was awarded to local boy Sam Fender – though Newcastle jazz band Knats, who wowed the arena crowd with virtuosic bass soloing and spoken word poetry, weren’t able to secure back-to-back Tyneside wins this year.There has been some consternation, though, that its focus is becoming more commercial than in the past – and not distinct enough from the Brit awards.View image in fullscreenFlorence Welch of Florence + The Machine, performing at the Mercury ceremony. This year marked the fifth time the group had been nominated for the award without having won it.Photograph: JMEnternational/Getty ImagesIn 2025, seven of the 12 nominated albums reached the UK Top 3, while this year six of the nominations reached No 1, and another two were Top 3 hits. All but two of the albums (Suede’s Antidepressants and the Help charity compilation) were released by or in partnership with the three major labels: Universal, Warner and Sony.Previously the UK’s independent music scene has been better represented, including in winners such as Arctic Monkeys, Dizzee Rascal, Sampha and Ezra Collective.This year’s judging panel featured musicians, broadcasters, journalists and consultants: Afrodeutsche, Danielle Perry, Jamie Cullum, Lea Stonhill, MistaJam, Phil Alexander, Sian Eleri, Sophie Williams and Will Hodgkinson, with Jeff Smith as chair.Explore more on these topicsMercury prizePop and rockAwards and prizesRayenewsShareReuse this content

title: The Celebrity Traitors: episode seven – as it happened | The Traitors | The Guardian
description: Who got bored to death in the castle – and who was left with extreme yawning paranoia? Here’s how it unfolded
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: Who got bored to death in the castle – and who was left with extreme yawning paranoia? Here’s how it unfolded
Content: 6h ago16.07 EDTAnd we’ll find out tomorrow. So let’s quickly debrief. This clearly wasn’t the Everything Kicks Off episode that I suspected. It was the Let’s Reluctantly Banish Jerry Hall episode; much less fun, but probably necessary at this stage.But that isn’t to say that it was a bad episode. The conclusion of a plain sight murder, plus a narratively significant task, actually gives us all quite a lot to chew on going forward. What will happen next? My bet is a Miranda murder and then a Joanne banishment. But let’s see.The Traitorsis finally picking up steam! Meet back here tomorrow at 8pm? Great.Share

title: Flo & Joan: With Feeling review – sisters turn an old rock setlist into hilariously neurotic songs | Comedy | The Guardian
description: Richly wrought lyrical wit and sumptuous harmonies enhance the duo’s clever new show – along with plenty of backchat
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Richly wrought lyrical wit and sumptuous harmonies enhance the duo’s clever new show – along with plenty of backchat
Content: ‘Bring back shame’ … Nicola and Rosie Dempsey AKA Flo & Joan.View image in fullscreen‘Bring back shame’ … Nicola and Rosie Dempsey AKA Flo & Joan.ComedyReviewFlo & Joan: With Feeling review – sisters turn an old rock setlist into hilariously neurotic songsShepherd’s Bush Empire, LondonRichly wrought lyrical wit and sumptuous harmonies enhance the duo’s clever new show – along with plenty of backchatBrian LoganThu 22 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe last time Flo & Joan played Shepherd’s Bush Empire, they found a setlist on stage left by beloved indie-rock band the Feeling on the previous night. It made the sisters contemplate their own relationship to the music industry. AreFlo & Joana proper band or doomed for ever to remain “musical comedy”? The problem with which, they deadpan here, is that “no one takes it seriously”. Cue this new show, its structure inspired by that chance discovery. Tonight, the duo play a suite of new songs that, title by title, matches the setlist of the band who preceded them four years ago.And so goes the first half of With Feeling, which by turns delivers on and subverts that challenge – and proves handsomely entertaining either way. In the sisters’ hands, Fill My Little World becomes a neurotic number about the surfeit of stuff (cheap food, fast fashion, AI slop). Never Be Lonely returns to a favoured topic, Flo & Joan’s toxic co-dependency – with an added sight gag involving Joan (AKA Rosie Dempsey)’s questionable trumpet skills. Further numbers address the risks of poor punctuation and the need, in a society giddy on unfiltered self-expression, to “bring back shame”.Ilford Boy review – Barbra Streisand teaches teen to smile about the way we areRead moreElsewhere, those secondhand titles inspire bits of business or bad puns rather than whole new songs. That’s just as much fun: Flo & Joan are more expansive on stage than they used to be, amusing one another very infectiously as they navigate – via a wide array of musical styles, sibling backchat and surprise interventions – to the end of their setlist stunt.Then comes act two, in which they unleash their rock band fantasies (leathers, bandanas, drumkit) on some well-loved numbers from their back catalogue: the one about social gaffes and the eternal cringe they engender (The Rest of My Life); the nonsense spoof folk song Lady In the Woods. As ever with Flo & Joan, you get richly wrought lyrical wit, sumptuous harmonies and musical surprises – this time with a droll top layer of bathetic rock posturing. A proper band, they may never be – for which, when improper is this much fun, we should all be grateful.On tour until 12 DecemberExplore more on these topicsComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The tech bro fight club is real!’ The titans of AI get the Succession treatment in a wild new TV show | Television | The Guardian
description: The Audacity is a fearless satire taking on Silicon Valley’s ‘egomaniac weirdos’. Its creator and stars talk ayahuasca ceremonies, mining kids for data – and punching CEOs
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: The Audacity is a fearless satire taking on Silicon Valley’s ‘egomaniac weirdos’. Its creator and stars talk ayahuasca ceremonies, mining kids for data – and punching CEOs
Content: ‘They’re pretty punchable’ … Billy Magnussen as Duncan Park in The Audacity.Photograph: Ed Araquel/AMCView image in fullscreen‘They’re pretty punchable’ … Billy Magnussen as Duncan Park in The Audacity.Photograph: Ed Araquel/AMCTelevision‘The tech bro fight club is real!’ The titans of AI get the Succession treatment in a wild new TV showThe Audacity is a fearless satire taking on Silicon Valley’s ‘egomaniac weirdos’. Its creator and stars talk ayahuasca ceremonies, mining kids for data – and punching CEOsMichael HoganThu 22 Oct 2026 08.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShowrunner Jonathan Glatzer wanted the tagline of his latest TV creation to be: “We’re so fucked.” He laughs. “Sadly it got rejected by the network. Hey, maybe I can use it for season two!” The show in question is The Audacity, his darkly comic drama about AI tech titans. Instead, it went with the more PG tagline “Move fast and break people” – a twist on “Move fast and break things”, the Facebook motto coined by Mark Zuckerberg. The Audacity promises to do for tech bros what Succession did for legacy media. Considering Glatzer is a former writer on Succession, that is no empty threat.This acerbic and all-too-timelySilicon Valleysatire follows CEO Duncan Park (played by Billy Magnussen), the obscenely wealthy founder of a data analytics company. He’s a self-proclaimed “inventor of the future” who also happens to be a morally bankrupt man-baby. “Duncan is worth about half a billion,” says Glatzer. “Naturally, that’s not enough. He desperately wants to be a billionaire and ascend to what we call ‘God Mountain’. But he’s no God.”The Audacity review – cracking TV packed with even more gloriously awful people than SuccessionRead moreLike Succession, The Audacity’s scripts are liberally spiced with baroque swearing. Park boasts about keeping investors “moist” and “Viagra-ing the share price to keep it up”. Magnussen delivers such juicy dialogue with relish. “Jonathan has a way of painting a picture with words while also getting nasty with it,” he grins. “My favourite line in season two is: ‘I pulled it out of my ass and it came out clean.’ You’ll have to wait and see what it refers to.” It’s a measure of The Audacity’s whip-smart relevance that the second season was commissioned before the first had even aired.View image in fullscreen‘Basically created spam’ … Zach Galifianakis as Carl Bardolph.Photograph: Ed Araquel/AMC“Unquestionably, there’s a tech bro mentality that is sexualised,” says Glatzer. “Silicon Valley is such a male-dominated culture. It’s also very white or south Asian. When I first came here, I didn’t see a person of colour for two weeks. That struck me as very odd in a major US city. Hiring practices are dictated by algorithms. The algorithms say that if you went to these universities, you’re our man. If you came from someplace else, and are maybe not a man, the algorithm says you might be problematic. And you could end up writing a book about us.”The Audacity pulls no punches on how the tech sector is wrecking the planet. “It sure is,” says Glatzer. “Generative AI is environmentally ruinous. Datacentres are tremendous suckers of energy. Worryingly, it doesn’t take too many rampantly ambitious entrepreneurs to fuck up an entire planet for the rest of us.” When Park is warned about the huge carbon footprint of his “algo”, he shrugs: “I’ll sponsor a penguin.”Zach Galifianakis plays billionaire genius Carl Bardolph, who “basically created spam”. He’s rich enough to retire but becomes a disruptor out of boredom. “I’ve always been very concerned about the people running tech,” says Galifianakis. “They have math minds, but that sometimes comes with a lack of empathy. About 12 nerds are controlling our lives and designing our futures. And they all tend to have the same profile. Most come from Stanford University. I don’t know what they’re teaching there.” He laughs. “It’s weird and kind of evil.”Did Galifianakis base his portrayal on anyone specific? “He’s pulled from one dude I’ve watched over the years. I won’t give his name but he’s a real piece of shit. A major jerk. The guys running Silicon Valley are damaged. Carl has a giant hole in his heart and a ton of anger because of his dad. I’ve seen a lot of men like that in Hollywood, so I drew on them too. Most of the puppet masters are egomaniac weirdos and I wouldn’t mind saying that to their faces. Zuckerberg has something missing. Elon Musk is bizarre. They’re little boys. You almost feel sorry for them.”“Duncan also deals with daddy issues and a lack of love,” says Magnussen. “A lot of tech bros are trying to fill voids. The great irony is that the most antisocial people work in social media. Those who don’t know how to be personable are controlling how we communicate. It’s nuts.”Both actors view the show as a howl of protest. “I’ve done some cool shit in my career,” says Magnussen. “I’ve been in Bond [he played a CIA agent in No Time to Die]. I’ve been in fun, escapist movies. But this feels different. It’s a call to arms. People need to wake up to the audacious behaviour of this handful of people. Their decisions affect 8.3 billion people. That’s scary, man. I just hope our show opens some conversations. We’ve got to start making a difference.”Galifianakis agrees. “It’s a warning. I’ve never felt this way before with my work – come on, I was in a movie with a baby wearing sunglasses [The Hangover] – but this show’s important. This industry has no guard rails. You can’t sue them, you can’t do anything, so of course they’re going to take advantage of the population. That’s exactly what they’ve done. The destructive environmental impact alone is enough reason to take to the streets and protest. Sure, there’s all this darkness online but also, we’re going to take your water and electricity from you, too.”Park blackmails his therapist – sorry, “performance psychologist” (played byBarry’s Sarah Goldberg) – into giving him insider-trading tips from her other powerful clients. The pair are soon engulfed in a scandal over fraudulent stock pumping. It’s a familiar-sounding storyline. “Elon got into trouble for market manipulation,” says Glatzer. “It’s like Duncan says in the show: ‘It’s not a felony in Silicon Valley, it’s good hustle.’ That’s the mentality here. Laws are for morons, not us.”Real world echoes are everywhere in The Audacity. The search engine of choice is called Spookle (slogan: “You Agreed to This”). A corporation called Cupertino is a thinly veiled reference to Apple, while its mythical boss “Big Tim” nods to Tim Cook. Are any of Glatzer’s characters directly based on real-life figures? “The truth is, I don’t find any of them worthy of a three-dimensional character that could go the distance of multiple seasons,” says Glatzer. “They’re interesting enough for a film like The Social Reckoning but not much more.”View image in fullscreenIn cahoots … Sarah Goldberg as JoAnne Felder.Photograph: David Moir/AMCIndeed, Magnussen can currently be seen in The Social Reckoning as a Meta spin doctor. Is this his tech bro era? “AI is the most pressing issue of our time,” he says. “It affects our planet, our politics, our mental health, everything. Technology can do wonderful things but once it starts dividing us or swaying elections, it’s deeply damaging.”“I don’t understand why people get on board with social media,” sighs Galifianakis. “We fed these machines for years. Now these machines are going to find us. I don’t believe the promises of AI because I don’t trust the people doing it.”The Audacity’s protagonist has been described as “highly punchable”. Magnussen concurs: “You’ve seen these guys in front of Congress. They’re pretty fucking punchable.” An early episode includes a sequence at a Palo Alto fight club, where nerds whack each other with keyboards and strangle each other with cables. “That’s real!” laughs Magnussen. “The tech bro fight club is an actual thing.”Despite the plentiful real-world parallels, Glatzer has never met a tech mogul. “That’s fine by me,” he says. “I don’t imagine the conversation would be anything other than stage-managed and dishonest. They have people workshopping their handshake and smile, so what am I going to get from that? But I have talked to a number of people who work in the tech world. The first thing they say is: ‘I’m not like that. That’s those other guys. I’m one of the good ones.’”“Me too,” says Magnussen. “The response I get is: ‘I know that guy!’ It’s always someone else. You want to go: ‘No, it’s you. You’re that guy.’”In America’s richest enclave, hi-tech goes hand-in-hand with hippy-dippy. The Audacity lampoons heath fads like ayahuasca ceremonies, microdosing and bio-hacking. “Tech titans feel as if they’ve got the golden ticket,” says Glatzer. “They want their prime to last as long as possible, perhaps for ever. Maybe the singularity comes when they upload themselves into an AI consciousness and become gods. I don’t have proof of that being the reason why so many datacentres are being built by these guys – but I don’t think it’s uninvolved.”“There’s no limit to these people’s overreach,” agrees Magnussen. “They truly believe their life is more valuable than anyone else’s.”View image in fullscreenTrying to play God … Simon Helberg in The Audacity.Photograph: Ed Araquel / AMC/HBOThe show also skewers the hypocrisy of execs who ban their own offspring from smartphones, reasoning that “arms dealers don’t give their kids landmines”. “It’s like how a lot of Hollywood don’t have TVs in their houses,” says Galifianakis. “Because they know the poison they’re selling.”“They know the dangers,” nods Glatzer. “It’s a classic case of capitalism gone haywire. I don’t think they’d live next door to a datacentre either. None of them do what they’re telling us to do. It used to be that people in public life had to practise what they preached. That has quietly gone away. US congresspeople invest in the same tech companies they’re supposedly regulating. Look at what Trump’s doing. It’s a kleptocracy.”He’s equally concerned by “screenification” in schools. “The amount of information gathered on our kids is frightening,” says Glatzer. “Shopping habits, medical history, exam grades. When schools get given tablets in the States, the law says it’s OK for the provider to track that student. We’re handing our kids these screens with the patina of being an educational tool but they are data-collecting devices. Just like everything is.”“I can’t believe how much information people give up,” says Galifianakis. “If you go to LA, there’s all these cars that say Google on the side, taking pictures of everything. If those cars said US Government, people would lose their minds. But because it’s a corporation, we all sit back and go: ‘I guess this is the future.’ I think people are starting to wake up but maybe it’s too late.” He laughs. “What do I know? I’m just a dumb actor trying to alarm people. But our children are the new oil. They’re being mined for data.”“I’m most scared for the kids,” agrees Magnussen. “They’ve been digital since they were born. They’re being manipulated without even knowing.”View image in fullscreenFilling a void …  Magnussen as Park.Photograph: Ed Araquel/AMCIn The Audacity, even seemingly benign tech is sinister. Eccentric inventor Martin Phister (The Big Bang Theory’s Simon Helberg) is developing an empathetic bot to be a digital “friend” for alienated teens. US viewers have likened him to OpenAI’s Sam Altman, who initially presented as a sympathetic mogul.“Martin’s trying to do something good,” says Glatzer. “You later learn that he’s compensating for something very bad. Carl has a speech about his generation coming to a crossroads: ‘Leave a legacy of good or go full Dr Evil.’ Most choose the latter. They are drawn to doing something positive but they are Hungry Hungry Hippos. They can’t resist the allure of a good deal.”“Carl knew the internet could have been a good thing for society if we’d done it right,” adds Galifianakis. “But greed and old-fashioned American competition, the need to win, became more important than human beings.”Geeky idealism is long gone. “It began as a desire to change the world for the better,” says Glatzer. “A bunch of nerdy engineers wore hoodies rather than suits and put ‘Do No Evil’ slogans on their office walls. That’s all in the rear-view mirror.”Glatzer freely admits that his work on Succession informed The Audacity. “There’s no way that it didn’t. But that was about institutional, dynastic wealth, whereas our characters are self-made. They are Logan Roy as a young man, if he had decided to be a tech guy rather than a media baron. What I certainly gleaned from Jesse Armstrong was finding a tone that enables you to give the establishment some real gut punches. Sarcasm might be the protest of the weak, but that’s all we’ve got. Speaking as a weakling.”The invasive cyber-surveillance and data-mining in The Audacity are deeply chilling. “We consulted experts but all the information is out there,” says Glatzer. “The Guardian and New York Times do some terrific reporting on AI. It always feels like the journalists secretly want to headline their articles: ‘Wake the fuck up! This is happening!’”The Audacity is on HBO Max nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionSilicon ValleyAI (artificial intelligence)featuresShareReuse this content

title: Zach Braff: ‘You can be talented and good-looking, but acting success is still like winning the lottery’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Scrubs and Garden State star answers your questions about working with megastars, getting his hair to look good and being brutally killed on BoJack Horseman
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The Scrubs and Garden State star answers your questions about working with megastars, getting his hair to look good and being brutally killed on BoJack Horseman
Content: Zach Braff ... ‘I started auditioning at 14 and barely got anything for years.’Photograph: Robby Klein/Getty Images for SCADView image in fullscreenZach Braff ... ‘I started auditioning at 14 and barely got anything for years.’Photograph: Robby Klein/Getty Images for SCADFilm & Music reader interviewMoviesInterviewZach Braff: ‘You can be talented and good-looking, but acting success is still like winning the lottery’As told toRich PelleyThe Scrubs and Garden State star answers your questions about working with megastars, getting his hair to look good and being brutally killed on BoJack HorsemanThu 22 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow do you manage not toact starstruck when directing people like Morgan Freeman, Michael Caine and Harrison Ford?TopTrampThat’s where my acting comes in – I pretend that I don’t know how famous they are. Every actor really wants a leader. They want someone who knows the script really well, has a plan for how the scene is going to be executed, and – in the case of comedy – knows how to make it funny. The last thing any of those guys wants is someone coming in starstruck and wide-eyed. So I use my acting skills to pretend I’m not starstruck and treat them like normal people.View image in fullscreenBraff (right) on the set of his 2017 film Going in Style, with Alan Arkin (left) and Morgan Freeman (centre).Photograph: THA/AlamyYour Fake Doctors, Real Friends podcast was a real help through lockdown.You were very emotionally open and personal; it was like catching up with friends.I still think about your line that making it in acting, even if you’re talented and good-looking, is like winning the lottery. Do you think that early 00sZach Braffwould make it in the present day the way you did?KamesJBack then, the broadcast networks were making so many pilots, at least it was work for people. Now, I think it’s a much harder landscape to break through. I firmly believe that you can be talented and good-looking, but success is still like winning the lottery. I know plenty of brilliant actors whose lottery ticket hasn’t come up yet. I started auditioning at 14 and barely got anything for years, so I’ve always felt very lucky.And as far as the podcast, that’s so great to hear. We didn’t plan to start it during Covid, but it became a nice sort of warm hug for people who wanted a little bit of nostalgia. Donald [Faison, who plays Dr Turk] and I loved getting together, making each other laugh and reminiscing. So much so that we’re actually bringing it back.View image in fullscreenRipe for a musical? Garden State, from 2004, with stars Natalie Portman and Zach Braff.Photograph: Miramax/Sportsphoto/AllstarHave you thought about Garden State 2?HaggisneepsnfattiesWe did an anniversary concert for the soundtrack last year – we got most of the bands together and did a charity show for the Midnight Mission in Los Angeles – and that was really cool. Natalie Portman was there. I had told her that people have come to me about doing a musical of the movie. I love musicals, but I’ve always thought: “I don’t know if that I want to do that.” Then she said: “Why don’t you do it with the songs from the soundtrack?” It’s funny, because I never thought of that. I haven’t taken any steps to make it a reality, but I do daydream of somehow using the music that people love so much from the soundtrack to make it into a musical.When you agreed to join the cast ofBoJack Horseman, how did you feel about your character having such a grisly end?topfootI love the show, so it was so fun to play a cartoonish version of myself, and I just did whatever they said. I never said: “Don’t kill me that way. Don’t have Jessica Biel feast on my carcass,” or whatever the hell it was.How much fun was it playing a small role inArrested Development– to my mind the funniest, cleverest and silliest of all the US sitcoms?ManofthesouthIt was amazing, especially because I didn’t know I was going to be a never-nude until I got the script. In the world of Arrested Development, a never-nude is someone – mainly Tobias – who can never be fully naked, even in the shower, so he wears denim short-shorts.Scrubs and Arrested Development were both doing really well. Jason Bateman and I were at some big event with the heads of both networks – we were NBC, they were Fox. We were laughing, saying: “It’d be fun if we each guested on each other’s show, but the networks would never let us do that.” Then we realised: “They’re all here. Let’s just go ask them.” They said “Sure,” so I guested on Arrested and Jason did an episode of Scrubs as an ostrich farmer.View image in fullscreenConspiring with Dr Turk (Donald Faison) on Scrubs.Photograph: Sergei Bachlakov/Disney/Getty ImagesWho would you most like to cast inDr Acula: The Movie – JD’s vampire-doctor screenplay in Scrubs?PickleManMichael B Jordan and Leonardo DiCaprio, if we’re in the fantasy where we’re going to make an amazing, huge-budget version. Remember at the end of Pee-wee’s Big Adventure when they make the movie of his life and cast beautiful movie stars, and Pee-wee ends up as a bellhop? That’s the version of Dr Acula I want: megastars, while Donald and I are just in the background.You’ve had huge success whether you’re acting, writing or directing. If you were to pick one standout pinch-me moment, what would it be?TurnipsnitzelMorgan Freeman saying yes to my film was one of those great moments. So was standing in the back of the Eccles theatre in Park City when Garden State premiered, thinking: “Holy shit, how did this happen?”When I got Scrubs, I was waiting tables. I put my Motorola StarTAC phone on the passenger seat as I was driving home from the final callback, and was just eyeing it to see if it was going to ring. Then it rang, I pulled over, called my parents, then I called the manager of the restaurant. She said: “I’m so happy for you, babe, but you got to work tonight still.” I said: “Oh, don’t worry, I’m coming in.” So I worked the whole shift knowing I probably wouldn’t be waiting tables for a couple of years.If you were on a plane and there was an announcement asking if there’s adoctor on board,would you put your hand up?MrSOBaldrickAbsolutely not. I don’t know anything. I really don’t. We have the most amazing consultants on set, including this wonderful nurse who’s just a badass. She shows us what to do and tells us what the hell we’re saying. Anyone who thinks we know anything for real is crazy.Scrubs taught me a lot about illness, life and death. Did it do the same for you?waydgroodsI was so young when we did the original series that I don’t think I had any experience with loss and being in hospitals and grief. In the years since, I’ve lost so many people. I’ve sat in hospital and ICU waiting rooms, waiting with bated breath for the doctor to come in with good or bad news. I’ve seen how the nurses run the whole hospital. I’ve witnessed it first-hand in a way I hadn’t as a young man. So I think now I have even more respect. I feel more like I’m playing a superhero as the guy who’s the chief of medicine at an underfunded hospital who’s meant to be a particularly badass doctor.Does your hair have its own agent?Dr_J_A_ZoidbergMy hair’s agent is that I take a shower at night and then I go to sleep on it and you get magical bedhead.Clean Hands is released in the US on 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmFilm & Music reader interviewZach BraffTelevisionArrested DevelopmentComedyTV comedyUS televisioninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Amy Winehouse: Back to Black 20 review – trying an all-star Amy tribute show is a losing game | Music | The Guardian
description: With Jorja Smith, Mark Ronson and others reinterpreting Back to Black for its 20th anniversary, most of the singers are eclipsed by the memory of Winehouse
Author: Dorian Lynskey
Headline: With Jorja Smith, Mark Ronson and others reinterpreting Back to Black for its 20th anniversary, most of the singers are eclipsed by the memory of Winehouse
Content: Lovingly curated … Jorja Smith at Amy Winehouse: Back to Black 20 at Roundhouse, London.Photograph: Samir Hussein/Universal Music/Amy Winehouse EstateView image in fullscreenLovingly curated … Jorja Smith at Amy Winehouse: Back to Black 20 at Roundhouse, London.Photograph: Samir Hussein/Universal Music/Amy Winehouse EstateMusicReviewAmy Winehouse: Back to Black 20 review – trying an all-star Amy tribute show is a losing game(Roundhouse, London)With Jorja Smith, Mark Ronson and others reinterpreting Back to Black for its 20th anniversary, most of the singers are eclipsed by the memory of WinehouseDorian LynskeyThu 22 Oct 2026 10.22 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s 20 years sinceAmy Winehousereleased her masterpiece Back to Black and 15 since she died at a frighteningly young age. A good way to appreciate how special she was is to watch the Amy Winehouse Band trot through a few lesser songs and cover versions and spot what’s missing: her playfulness, bite, anarchic charisma and taste. Winehouse mixed soul, jazz, hip-hop, two-tone and 60s girl groups because she loved that music more than anything. Without her animating fandom, a cover of Monkey Man by Toots and the Maytals is just a cover of Monkey Man by Toots and the Maytals; for all her old band’s precision and gusto, it has no pressing reason to exist.The main event, in which Back to Black producers including Mark Ronson and Salaam Remi hand-pick singers such as Jorja Smith, Lianne La Havas and Corinne Bailey Rae to recreate the album, is stronger except that it’s primarily staged for a BBC TV show, which means the flow is broken by onstage interviews and hagiographical patter from Jo Whiley. It’s a little grating to be constantly told that a concert is amazing even as it unfolds, but that’s TV for you.View image in fullscreenSpectral, minimalist … Mark Ronson and Yebba at Amy Winehouse: Back to Black 20 at Roundhouse, London.Photograph: Samir Hussein/Universal Music/Amy Winehouse EstateEven performed out of sequence, Back to Black remains a miraculous set of modern love songs in vintage clothing – tragic, defiant and bitterly funny – but re-enactments can be limiting. One distinctive singer after another faithfully emulates Winehouse’s sly, gutsy phrasing and thus submerges herself. The show really crackles when something new materialises, such as Jessie Reyez tearing through Rehab with conviction or London trio Flo splitting the difference between TLC and the Supremes on He Can Only Hold Her. Yebba’s spectral, minimalist take on Love Is a Losing Game, with Ronson on guitar, would delight the Twin Peaks Roadhouse.The 100 greatest BBC music performances – ranked!Read moreThe ecstatic, mic-passing ensemble finale of Valerie is unexpectedly moving in that it presents a diverse tableau of Winehouse’s musical sisters and daughters and allows for a rare element of chaos. It ensures that this lovingly curated tribute leaves a pleasing glow. It’s just that Amy didn’t glow; she burned.Explore more on these topicsMusicAmy WinehousePop and rockSoullive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Helen Fielding launches Bridget Jones prize for northern comedy writing | Books | The Guardian
description: The Yorkshire-born author says that the 1,000 word competition is for people ‘just living their lives being quietly hilarious’
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: The Yorkshire-born author says that the 1,000 word competition is for people ‘just living their lives being quietly hilarious’
Content: Dream team … Renée Zellweger and Helen Fielding.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDream team … Renée Zellweger and Helen Fielding.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty ImagesBooksHelen Fielding launches Bridget Jones prize for northern comedy writingThe Yorkshire-born author says that the 1,000 word competition is for people ‘just living their lives being quietly hilarious’Emma LoffhagenThu 22 Oct 2026 07.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBridget Jones authorHelen Fieldinghas launched a comedy writing prize in the name of her most famous creation, aimed at unearthing funny new voices from the north of England.TheBridget Jones prizefor northern comedy writing will go to the funniest self-contained, first-person prose of 1,000 words. The format echoes the anonymous diary columns in the Independent that first brought Bridget to readers in the mid-1990s.Fielding, who grew up in Yorkshire, wrote the original columns andfour Bridget Jones novels, as well as co-writing the blockbuster film adaptations starringRenée Zellweger.She said Bridget’s humour was drawn from the people she grew up with: “laughing together at our mess-ups; bringing the fancy and pretentious down to earth”.“There are lots of famous northern comics,” she said. “But this prize is for the comic voices of people who aren’t famous: just living their lives being quietly hilarious.”Writers living in the north who have neither been published nor signed with an agent are eligible to enter. There is no entry fee and the winner will take home £2,000, plus a session with Aitken Alexander Associates, the agency that represents Fielding, and tailored support from the charity New Writing North. One runner-up will get £1,000.Fielding was strict about the word limit. “I always tried to make the Bridget columns exactly 1,000 words long – like making the petrol pump stop at exactly 20 quid,” she said. “If it’s slightly under you won’t be punished.
