Just DON’T MAKE IT ANY LONGER!”Fielding will judge alongside an Aitken Alexander agent and a representative from New Writing North, and the winner will be revealed at next summer’s Northern Writers’ awards in Newcastle, with the prize presented by Fielding. The prize will be given out each year until 2029.Will Mackie from New Writing North said: “This is the first time the Northern Writers’ awards have featured an award exclusively for comedy writing.“There is no one more fitting to identify an original comedy voice than Helen, who created one of the nation’s most beloved comic characters of the last 30 years.”Fielding cited Victoria Wood, Alan Bennett, Les Dawson, Thora Hird and Morecambe and Wise as inspirations.Submissions open on 23 November and close on 1 February 2027.Explore more on these topicsBooksHelen FieldingAwards and prizesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Blackpool, Sheffield, Milton Keynes and Wrexham shortlisted for UK city of culture 2029 | UK city of culture | The Guardian
description: The winner will receive £10m and each shortlisted city will be given £125,000
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: The winner will receive £10m and each shortlisted city will be given £125,000
Content: The council leader, Lynn Williams, said Blackpool had been entertaining people for generations and now had a chance to show exactly what it was made of.Photograph: Jon D/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe council leader, Lynn Williams, said Blackpool had been entertaining people for generations and now had a chance to show exactly what it was made of.Photograph: Jon D/AlamyUK city of cultureBlackpool, Sheffield, Milton Keynes and Wrexham shortlisted for UK city of culture 2029The winner will receive £10m and each shortlisted city will be given £125,000Mark BrownNorth of England correspondentThu 22 Oct 2026 07.24 EDTFirst published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 06.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBlackpool, Sheffield, Milton Keynes and Wrexham have been shortlisted to be theUK city of culture2029, an award viewed as a way to boost local economies, foster civic pride and, above all, have some fun.The four places were chosen from a longlist of nine. The title will be announced in the new year and the three runners-up will each be given £125,000.That winner will be given a further £10m to help fund what has, in previous years, been a blizzard of events and ideas that create jobs, increase arts engagement and bring in tourists.All four previous UK cities of culture – Derry (2013), Hull (2017), Coventry (2021) and Bradford (2025) – said afterwards that the designation had been transformative and brought lasting legacies.Before the shortlist was announced, Wrexham was thebookmaker’s favouriteto win. The city is already surfing a Hollywood wave after its football team wasbought by the actors Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney.View image in fullscreenWrexham is surfing a Hollywood wave after the football club was bought by the actors Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty“We’re on the map and on the up,” said Wrexham’s council leader, Mark Pritchard, adding that making the shortlist was “fantastic” news. “Our reputation is growing.”He said Wrexham still had huge challenges around socioeconomic opportunities and inequalities but “winning this competition would be another step towards overcoming those challenges, building confidence in our communities and showing the world what Wrexham is truly about”.Blackpool is bidding to become the first seaside resort to win the prize. The council leader, Lynn Williams, said it was a place that never stood still. She said: “Blackpool has been entertaining people for generations and now we have the chance to show the country exactly what our town is made of.“It is proud, working-class culture that has always been about bringing people together, having fun and making something happen. We have always been a town that entertains the country and there is nowhere quite like Blackpool.”Perhaps more than most places,Milton Keynesis a city burdened with misconceptions that it is just concrete and roundabouts. “We do still have concrete cows and, yes, we do have a lot of roundabouts – but I think that there is more to us than that,” Jane Carr, the leader of Milton Keynes council, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.View image in fullscreenMilton Keynes is a city burdened with lazy misconceptions that it is just concrete and roundabouts.Photograph: Chunyip Wong/Getty“We’ve got an amazing amount of homegrown talent. We’ve got our own orchestras. We’ve got lots of performing artists. We have an international festival every two years … we want to develop and move forward.”Of all four shortlisted places, Sheffield’s artistic heritage probably shouts the loudest, whether that’s electronic music, Pulp, Arctic Monkeys or England’s largest theatre complex outside London.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFran Belbin, the leader of Sheffield city council, said being shortlisted was a proud moment for everyone who had shaped the bid. “Sheffield is a city built on creativity, innovation and community spirit,” she said. “From our world-renowned music heritage and vibrant independent arts scene to our festivals, libraries, theatres, museums, galleries and grassroots creativity, culture is part of who we are.”View image in fullscreenFran Belbin, the leader of Sheffield city council, said being shortlisted was a proud moment for Sheffield.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThe unsuccessful candidates on the longlist were Ipswich, Inverness, Middlesbrough, Portsmouth and Swindon. Phil Redmond, the Brookside and Grange Hill creator who headed Liverpool’s European capital of culture year in 2008, chairs the advisory panel that will choose the winner.He said: “Once again there is a hard choice ahead. The four places on the shortlist continue to demonstrate both the variety and strength of creative ambition across the UK.“Each place represents a different view, or aspect, epitomising what culture is, the sum of all we do together, and while each approaches it differently, they all share the common aim of reminding the rest of the UK of who they are, where they are and why they are worth visiting.”This article and its subheading were amended on 22 October 2026. An earlier version said that each city would be given £125,000 to develop their bids before the winner is announced. In fact, the three runners-up will be given £125,000 when the winner is announced next year.Explore more on these topicsUK city of cultureFestivalsBlackpoolSheffieldMilton KeynesWalesEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: John Anderson, five-time US country chart-topper, dies aged 71 | Country | The Guardian
description: Florida-born singer-songwriter had major hits with Swingin’, Seminole Wind and Straight Tequila Night
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Florida-born singer-songwriter had major hits with Swingin’, Seminole Wind and Straight Tequila Night
Content: John Anderson performing in Nashville in 2024.Photograph: John D Shearer/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJohn Anderson performing in Nashville in 2024.Photograph: John D Shearer/ShutterstockCountryJohn Anderson, five-time US country chart-topper, dies aged 71Florida-born singer-songwriter had major hits with Swingin’, Seminole Wind and Straight Tequila NightBen Beaumont-ThomasThu 22 Oct 2026 05.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Anderson, the traditionalist US country singer whose extensive body of work included five No 1 hits on the country charts, has died aged 71.The news was announced on social media by his family, who said: “To the world, he was a gifted country music singer whose voice and songs touched countless lives. To us, he was so much more. He was the heart of our family, the one who made us laugh, loved us fiercely and made every ordinary moment feel special.”So woven into the culture of country music that he once worked as a roofer on the genre’s focal point, Nashville’s Grand Ole Opry, Anderson’s career spanned nearly 50 years and resulted in him being inducted into theCountryMusic Hall of Fame in 2024.Among those paying tribute to Anderson was country singer and friend Blake Shelton: “I am a very lucky man. I got the opportunity to find out that my hero wasn’t just the guy I hoped he’d be.” Shelton’s wife Gwen Stefani wrote: “We loved him!! His music is part of our family’s hearts for ever!!”Born and raised in Florida in a music-loving family whose tastes spanned big band jazz to the Rolling Stones, Anderson headed to Nashville after graduating high school to try to make it in the city’s country music scene by playing live sets at night while doing manual labour during the day. “I’d fill up the truck with gravel and take the truck to wherever the order was and drop it off. A lot of odd jobs, but never lost sight of the fact that I really wanted to play,” he said in 2024.Writing his own material as well as performing that of others, he released his debut single in 1975, but broke through two years later with I’ve Got a Feelin’ (Somebody’s Been Stealin’), and inched his way up the country charts with each subsequent release. He had his first country Top 5 single in 1981, I’m Just an Old Chunk of Coal (But I’m Gonna Be a Diamond Someday), which earned him his only Grammy nomination, for best male vocal country performance – and was a typical showcase of his wry, earnest and pure vocal tone.It ushered in a number of years of commercial success, with the songs Wild and Blue, Black Sheep and Swingin’ all becoming country chart-toppers – the slick, hard-driving sound of the latter gave it crossover appeal and it became Anderson’s only hit on the US pop chart.The latter half of the decade was a frustrating time for Anderson as he was dropped by his label Warner Bros and shuttled between others, before finding his groove again with 1992 album Seminole Wind, containing three Top 3 hits; the title track, an ode to his birth state of Florida, and Straight Tequila Night have endured as country radio staples and streaming successes. Follow-up Solid Ground was also a hit, containing the chart-topping Money in the Bank.Anderson ended up recording 22 studio albums, most recently 2020’s Years, recorded with Dan Auerbach of blues-rockers the Black Keys. That was a proud and hard-fought return for Anderson, who faced illness with a non-cancerous tumour in 2017 that left him hospitalised. “I had been very, very ill,” he told Billboard in 2020. “I had almost 100% hearing loss … that really almost put an end to me. I just started praying and praying harder than I’ve ever prayed in my life and you know what? My hearing started coming back.”Anderson continued to perform live thereafter, saying in 2024 that since his recovery, “I’ve really been enjoying every day. I live out in the woods and take a lot of lessons from my little wildlife friends. They pretty much live day to day, minute to minute. Enjoying that minute, enjoying this time. I’m very thankful to be able to go out and play any music at all.”Explore more on these topicsCountrynewsShareReuse this content

title: West End to get another lesson from The History Boys two decades on | West End | The Guardian
description: Nation’s favourite play makes London comeback amid renewed debate about future of humanities teaching
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Nation’s favourite play makes London comeback amid renewed debate about future of humanities teaching
Content: Dominic Cooper and James Corden in The History Boys at the National Theatre in London in 2004. The play was turned into a film and won a string of stage awards.Photograph: Rex/Donald CooperView image in fullscreenDominic Cooper and James Corden in The History Boys at the National Theatre in London in 2004. The play was turned into a film and won a string of stage awards.Photograph: Rex/Donald CooperWest EndWest End to get another lesson from The History Boys two decades onNation’s favourite play makes London comeback amid renewed debate about future of humanities teachingNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentThu 22 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe History Boys is to return to theWest Endfor the first time in two decades, with a warning from its director of an “almost terminal decline” in humanities teaching in state schools.Nicholas Hytner, who directed Alan Bennett’s play at the National Theatre and its2006 film adaptation, said the themes of education, history and the value of literature for its own sake felt especially relevant amid renewed debate about what schools should teach.“There has been a decline of humanities subjects in state schools, an almost terminal decline of music and drama teaching, history and modern languages have been downgraded,” he said. “But it has obviously been a mistake, both for the individual pupil and our economic future, to neglect the humanities.”The production will open at theTheatreRoyal Haymarket on 10 April for a 16-week run, reuniting Hytner with its original designer, Bob Crowley. Bennett will be involved in its development.View image in fullscreenAlan Bennett has welcomed the return of The History Boys, saying it was one of the happiest plays he had written.Photograph: Eamonn McCabe/The GuardianThe History Boys received its world premiereat the National Theatre in 2004before transferring to the West End and Broadway, where it won three Olivier awards and six Tonys. Votedthe nation’s favourite play, it launched the careers of James Corden, Russell Tovey and Dominic Cooper.Set in 1980s Sheffield, it follows eight boys at a grammar school preparing for their university entrance exams, as two teachers take opposing approaches to their education. Poignant and sharply comic, it explores adolescence, sexuality and the competing ideas of learning as a route to achievement or an end in itself.View image in fullscreenNicholas Hytner hopes the play will resonate with a generation raised on social media.Photograph: John Phillips/Getty ImagesHytner said he had first asked Bennett whether he wanted to see the play revived: “He’s not usually that keen on revivals of his stuff, but he said he’d love to see it again.”Bennettsaid: “The History Boys is one of the happiest plays I’ve written. Or rather, it was one of the happiest of my plays to write. It was also one of the quickest to set down, taking far less than my usual five years. So, something of a record for me. The play is full of quotes and has itself become eminently quotable. A joy for any playwright. I welcome its return underNicholas Hytner.”Its return comes as the government undertakes the first major revision of the national curriculum and GCSEs in more than a decade. Public consultations opened in September, with a revised curriculum expected in spring 2027 and implementation from 2028.Hytner said: “It feels as if so much of what state education was focused on in the last 20 years is proving to be beside the point, when AI can do so much of what pupils were being prepared to do. Schools could do a lot worse than introduce pupils to creativity, and to delight in other people’s creativity.”He said the play championed the idea that the humanities were “the birthright of anybody who goes through the school system”, rather than subjects whose value depended on their immediate practical application.Hytner hopes it will resonate with a generation raised on social media. “Quite a lot of young people are ambivalent about social media,” he said. “They crave a kind of conversational spontaneity and an ability to concentrate and immerse themselves outside of social media.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe production will inevitably change, he added, having evolved between its opening at the National Theatre and the end of its Broadway run in 2006. Any changes, however, would be made with Bennett’s input.View image in fullscreenJames Corden, Frances de la Tour and Richard Griffiths in the 2004 production.Photograph: Rex/Alastair MuirHytner emphasised the revival would again feature actors at the start of their careers: “I can almost guarantee that none of the new cast will be well-known figures, because that’s the point about them.”He recalled that even the original cast had doubts about one of the play’s most farcical scenes, in which the teacher Hector gets his pupils to act out in French a client visiting a brothel in Paris. The charade ends with the headteacher entering the room while one of the boys has his trousers down.“They were really suspicious of the French scene near the beginning of the play,” Hytner said. “Only a couple of them were confident about it, they just didn’t think it was funny. I had to keep saying it’s fine, let’s do it, let’s see how it goes.”At the first preview, the scene brought the house down. “I remember the look of stunned amazement,” said Hytner. “It was a complete delight for the young actors.”Explore more on these topicsWest EndAlan BennettNicholas HytnerTheatreJames CordenRussell ToveyLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Canadian publisher Boréal ends relationship with novelist Thélyson Orélien over alleged use of AI | Awards and prizes | The Guardian
description: Author withdrawn from France’s Prix Goncourt last month has repeatedly denied using artificial intelligence to write novel
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Author withdrawn from France’s Prix Goncourt last month has repeatedly denied using artificial intelligence to write novel
Content: Novelist Thélyson Orélien at the 28th Les Correspondances literature festival in Manosque, France on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Joel Saget/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNovelist Thélyson Orélien at the 28th Les Correspondances literature festival in Manosque, France on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Joel Saget/AFP/Getty ImagesAwards and prizesCanadian publisher Boréal ends relationship with novelist Thélyson Orélien over alleged use of AIAuthor withdrawn from France’s Prix Goncourt last month has repeatedly denied using artificial intelligence to write novelAgence France-PresseWed 21 Oct 2026 21.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe publisher of top-selling Haitian Canadian writer Thélyson Orélien,who was removed from France’s most prestigious literary prize listlast month, has confirmed the author used artificial intelligence to help write his novel C’était ça ou mourir (It Was Either That or Die).Orélien has denied allegations that he used AI on his breakthrough novel and, last week, Canadian publisher Les Éditions du Boréal said it was standing by the 38-year-old writer.But on Wednesday, Boréal said it had conducted a further investigation into the allegations.“New information, confirmed over the past few days, indicates that artificial intelligence was used in the writing process” of the novel, a statement from Boréal said.The publisher announced it was “ending its professional relationship” with Orélien.Boréal said it did not know the extent of AI’s use in the writing process “and we will likely never have a definitive answer”.It said it gathered all the working versions of the novel and hired an outside party to analyse various drafts.Novelist accused of using AI to write book removed from French prize listRead more“The results obtained this week revealed traces of AI tags in the metadata of certain documents,” Boréal said.Before conducting this analysis, the publisher said it had tried to work with Orélien to gather the evidence necessary to prove his innocence.That effort was inconclusive, and Orélien “subsequently announced that he would not provide any further information,” the publisher said.The novel about migration had been scheduled for translation in more than 20 countries.The book was shrouded in suspicion and withdrawn from the list for France’s book prize thePrix Goncourt, after tests with AI detector Pangram indicated a 100% probability it contained computer-generated text.In a statement to Agence France-Presse earlier this month, Orélien called the allegations “slander and heresy”.“Here and there I did use tools for research, particularly for foreign idioms,” he said in a statement sent exclusively to AFP.“But not a single sentence in this book was created by a machine, nor the meaning or the structure of a story that comes from my gut.”He stood firm on Wednesday, telling the French newspaper Libération he used AI “in the creative process” for “historical research”.“I’ve explained everything to those close to me, but at the moment I don’t think my words count for anything,” he said, adding that what he is now experiencing has “gone way too far”.Orélien said he started writing the book in late 2017 “on the corner of a table” and completed a first draft in 2019 of more than 300 pages, several years before the advent of AI services such as ChatGPT.The author fled his native Haiti after a 2010 earthquake that struck the Caribbean island, already ravaged by poverty and unrest.In response to separate allegations of plagiarism, Orélien admitted to making “unacceptable mistakes” in the past in his writing, without mentioning specifics.“I was just over 20, I was probably a little too impatient, without really understanding how much I still had to learn. I wanted to write, I was reading a lot,” he wrote.“But admiring someone does not give you the right to take, to claim as mine texts that are not my own.”Explore more on these topicsAwards and prizesFictionAI (artificial intelligence)EuropePrix GoncourtCanadaFrancenewsShareReuse this content

title: Proms, parties and gender politics: amazing photos from American dancefloors – and what they tell us about a changing nation | Art | The Guardian
description: From George Balanchine to the Rockettes, the US magazine regularly ran lavish photo spreads dedicated to dance, with the myriad ways people moved their bodies holding up a mirror to the changing times
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: From George Balanchine to the Rockettes, the US magazine regularly ran lavish photo spreads dedicated to dance, with the myriad ways people moved their bodies holding up a mirror to the changing times
Content: Shirley MacLaine and Juliet Prowse leap mid-air in a Can-Can dance scene.Photograph: Life Picture Collection/Meredith Operations CorporationView image in fullscreenShirley MacLaine and Juliet Prowse leap mid-air in a Can-Can dance scene.Photograph: Life Picture Collection/Meredith Operations CorporationArtProms, parties and gender politics: amazing photos from American dancefloors – and what they tell us about a changing nationFrom George Balanchine to the Rockettes, the US magazine regularly ran lavish photo spreads dedicated to dance, with the myriad ways people moved their bodies holding up a mirror to the shifting timesLyndsey WinshipThu 22 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLife magazine launched in 1936. Its aim: to show the US the world, in pictures. At a time when television was still an experimental medium, a golden age of photojournalism brought the outside world into people’s homes. Life ran weekly until 1972, spanning a transformative time in US culture. Photographers were dispatched across the globe, covering wars, political manoeuvres, social trends, hemlines and Hollywood. And in December 1936, the magazine dedicated its cover feature to dance, with dancers from the new School of AmericanBalletgracing the front page. As such a vividly visual medium, dance would become a regular feature in Life’s pages across the years.When I was asked to write the text for a new book featuring a collection of dance-themed images from the Life archive, it was a kid-in-a-candy-shop situation. For a dance fan there were some absolute gems to be found: the great George Balanchine crafting his ballet The Seven Deadly Sins – and cooking dinner in his Manhattan apartment; Margot Fonteyn and Rudolf Nureyev taking New York in a piece headlined The Hottest Little Team in Show Biz; or an ageing Agnes de Mille going full-throttle in rehearsal.double quotation markWe see how dance styles from Black communities and Latin America were adopted, appropriated and absorbed into the mainstreamBut the archive told a much bigger story than that. It was fascinating to see the reflection of society through the way people danced: in ballrooms, nightclubs, proms and parties. In the array of social dancers: from the waltz and tango to the lindy hop, mambo, twist and the frug, themes of the 20th century play out. You can see a story of growing individualism in the shift from structured couple dancing to going freeform on the dancefloor – gender politics, too, as it was out with “May I have this dance?” and in with the democracy of the disco. Life columnist Albert Goldman asked: “Has there ever been a decade for dance like the 60s?” as he wrote of a power shift from the stage to the dancefloor, from the professional performer to the “inventive amateur”. There’s the birth of the teenager, too, bringing an explosion of pop culture and spreading dance trends on TV shows such as American Bandstand.The archive also tells a story of the US’s shifting relationship with race, showing dancers in segregated bars and newly desegregated schools. But more than that, we see the way music and dance styles from Black communities and from Latin America were adopted, appropriated and absorbed into the US mainstream, whether tap, jazz, Charleston or cha-cha-cha.Shanghai’s ‘voguing’ dancers step lightly to avoid official gaze – in picturesRead moreDance even had something to say about cold war politics and paranoia. For a series comparing American and Soviet education systems, which found the US lagging worryingly behind, Life took photos of Moscow students in a dance class to demonstrate their iron-clad discipline, compared with easygoing American schools. The magazine captured visiting folk dancers from the USSR, as well as reporting on Khrushchev denouncing the dancing in a Hollywood film, and by extension, casting judgment on western culture.So much of life can be observed through dance, in the ways people choose to move their bodies and how they display themselves, how they relate to each other, celebrate and communicate. There’s a real treasure trove of images to explore.LIFE. Let’s Danceis published by Taschen.Step back in time: six pictures from Let’s DanceOn the set of Can-Can, 1959 (main image)The sheer raucous joy in this picture of Shirley MacLaine and Juliet Prowse leaps off the page, captured on the set of movie musical Can-Can, the story of a Belle Époque Paris cabaret whose dancers are arrested for public indecency. It was a stance approved of by Soviet premier Nikita Khrushchev, who was visiting the 20th Century Fox studios during filming and pronounced the dance routines depraved.View image in fullscreenLeon James and Willa Mae Ricker flying like the pilot Charles Lindbergh who gave his name to the Lindy Hop.Photograph: Life Picture Collection/ Meredith Operations CorporationWilla Mae Ricker and Leon James, 1943Ricker and James were members of Whitey’s Lindy Hoppers, one of the finest, and most awesomely acrobatic, dance troupes of the 1940s. The lindy hop originated among Black dancers in the clubs of Harlem (it was named after pilot Charles Lindbergh’s “hop” over the Atlantic in 1927) but by 1943, Life was calling the lindy hop “America’s national dance”.View image in fullscreenThe Rockettes at Radio City, New York.Photograph: Yale Joel/Life Picture Collection/Meredith Operations CorporationThe Rockettes, 1958Modelled on high-kicking British group the Tiller Girls, all-American precision dance troupe the Rockettes took things up a notch with their machine-tooled synchrony. Launched in 1925, they’re still going strong today, proving the enduring allure of the showgirl (Taylor Swift can’t be wrong), and have even trademarked their signature dance technique.View image in fullscreenRudolf Nureyev and Margot Fonteyn dancing La Bayadère.Photograph: Gjon Mili/Life Picture Collection/Meredith Operations CorporationMargot Fonteyn and Rudolf Nureyev in La Bayedère 1965It is hard to imagine now that two ballet dancers could be as famous as Margot Fonteyn and Rudolf Nureyev were in the 1960s. Rudimania peaked on the Royal Ballet’s 1965 tour to the US, when mounted police were stationed outside New York’s Metropolitan Opera House to save Nureyev from being mobbed.View image in fullscreenCentral High School’s desegregated prom, 1967.Photograph: Life Picture Collection/Meredith Operations CorporationSchool prom, 1967Teens dancing at the annual prom at Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas. Ten years earlier, after the supreme court had ruled against segregation in public education, Arkansas’ governor called up the National Guard to stop nine Black students enrolling at the same school. Life’s journalist at the prom reported that “the school sees itself as desegregated rather than integrated”.View image in fullscreenMichael Caine on an LA nightclub dancefloor.Photograph: Bill Ray/Life Picture Collection/Meredith Operations CorporationMichael Caine on the dancefloor, 1966Such a keen dancer he was once known as Disco Mike, here’s Michael Caine at an LA club. Decades later he gave a tutorial on doing the twist on Jonathan Ross’s chatshow, a dance craze that had swept the world, meriting a seven-page feature in Life in 1961. From hipsters to socialites to suburban grandmas, everyone was caught up in “pulsating, gyrating, hip-swinging mania”, it reported.Explore more on these topicsArtPhotographyDanceMagazinesBalletfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Nobody Wants This review – prepare to fall in love again … with a different couple | Television | The Guardian
description: Adam Brody and Kristen Bell’s hit romcom is still gorgeous as Noah and Joanne move in together. But if you’re thirsty for the fizz of new romance … their siblings might set hearts aflutter
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: Adam Brody and Kristen Bell’s hit romcom is still gorgeous as Noah and Joanne move in together. But if you’re thirsty for the fizz of new romance … their siblings might set hearts aflutter
Content: Phenomenal screen sparkle … Joanne (Kristen Bell) and Noah (Adam Brody) in Nobody Wants This.Photograph: Katrina Marcinowski/NetflixView image in fullscreenPhenomenal screen sparkle … Joanne (Kristen Bell) and Noah (Adam Brody) in Nobody Wants This.Photograph: Katrina Marcinowski/NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewNobody Wants This review – prepare to fall in love again … with a different coupleAdam Brody and Kristen Bell’s hit romcom is still gorgeous as Noah and Joanne move in together. But if you’re thirsty for the fizz of new romance … their siblings might set hearts aflutterJack SealeThu 22 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 08.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJust as you and your true love can’t have a second first date or another first kiss, romantic comedies can never go back. Nothing replaces the giddy spell of the movie’s opening act or the TV show’s debut season. Sure, there can be some joy and fulfilment in a fictional relationship settling down, but really we want the crackle of chemistry, the thrill of a connection that’s brand new.Nobody Wants This is now in its third season, so it has had to leave behind the days when it was powered entirely by the phenomenal screen sparkle between Adam Brody as Noah, the rabbi who can balance devotion to his faith with the mischievous instincts of a regular thirtysomething guy; and Kristen Bell as Joanne, the atheist co-host of a frank sex-and-relationships podcast who is not as cynical or shallow as people think, or as she pretends to be.Season one flew past in a whirl of meet-cute, kiss-cute, date-cute and continue-their-romance-despite-supposedly-unresolvable-cultural-divide-cute. While Brody and Bell traded pinging screwball one-liners as fluently as any screen couple ever have, the question of whether Noah’s place within his synagogue and his family could ever be compatible with his love for a woman outside the community gave the story weight. If he and Joanne were destined not to be together, it would be for reasons more substantial than the usual romcom misunderstandings.The second season leaned into what had become an unusually deep and nuanced portrayal of what it means to be a Jewish American in the 21st century, with the ongoing tension around whether Joanne would convert to Judaism enabling Nobody Wants This to repeat the trick of them splitting up during the final episode, then reconciling in a last scene where one or both of them sprints through the rain to say they made a mistake. It certainly can’t get away with that a third time.View image in fullscreenWill they or won’t they? … Morgan (Justine Lupe) and Sasha (Timothy Simons) in Nobody Wants This.Photograph: NetflixSo we rejoin Noah and Joanne as they move in together, opening with a gorgeous montage of them exclaiming “We live together!” in mundane domestic situations that have acquired new magic. The relationship comedy sinks into a comfortable rhythm, as Noah is destabilised by Joanne leaving the fridge door open and turning the dishwasher into a treacherous hellscape of upturned knife blades, while she chafes against his desire to take her for a dawn stroll, instead of respecting the ancient, sacred morning ritual of drinking coffee and checking celebrity gossip online.The stakes are lower and the old fizz has somewhat fizzled: the next step for a couple is usually marriage, which does bring its own difficult sensitivities, but nothing to compare to what Noah and Joanne have already overcome. One or two episodes in the middle of season three don’t really contain a significant event, and the new milieu Joanne is pitched into, as she attends classes at temple to educate non-Jews who are about to marry into the faith, is funny without bringing much edge.However, Nobody Wants This in safe mode still delights. The ensemble around the central couple stop it being a problem if nothing much is going on with them: we can just hang out with their parents, whose cartoon eccentricity still has plenty of comic juice in it, and particularly their siblings.If Brody and Bell are a classic romcom couple, Timothy Simons and Justine Lupe are arguably even better as Sasha (Noah’s brother) and Morgan (Joanne’s sister), – whose radically different personalities highlight the gap the central relationship has to overcome, but who share outsider status, which gives them something in common, which draws them together …Simons and Lupe have long been the show’s real stars as gangling manchild Sasha and self-absorbed fashionista Morgan, each ill-equipped for the adult world in their own way. Up to now Morgan has been a spectre haunting the jagged marriage of Sasha and Esther (Jackie Tohn), a couple who disagree fundamentally on how seriously to take life. Morgan’s dedication to consequence-free fun is a temptation Sasha cannot resist, while his refusal to judge her life choices and his total lack of preening self-regard, in contrast to the men Morgan normally picks, makes him a safe place for her to run towards.Season three finally sees Sasha and Esther split, which leaves more time for his tender bond with Morgan to become a proper will-they-won’t-they. Suddenly our heads are spinning and our hearts have resumed their fluttering. It may have put down roots, but Nobody Wants This knows how to make us fall in love with it all over again.Nobody Wants This is on Netflix now.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewTV comedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Leo Reich’s new London sitcom especially for gen z  | Television | The Guardian
description: It’s the first episode of this relatable mid-20s-houseshare comedy. Plus: will Paul McCartney take the Mercury prize? Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: It’s the first episode of this relatable mid-20s-houseshare comedy. Plus: will Paul McCartney take the Mercury prize? Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Funny and sorely relatable … from left: Olive Gray as Sam, Emily Fairn as Abi, and Leo Reich as Ethan in It Gets Worse.Photograph: Ana Blumenkron/A24 FilmsView image in fullscreenFunny and sorely relatable … from left: Olive Gray as Sam, Emily Fairn as Abi, and Leo Reich as Ethan in It Gets Worse.Photograph: Ana Blumenkron/A24 FilmsTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Leo Reich’s new London sitcom especially for gen zIt’s the first episode of this relatable mid-20s-houseshare comedy. Plus: will Paul McCartney take the Mercury prize? Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Hannah J DaviesandPhil HarrisonThu 22 Oct 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt Gets Worse10.05pm, Channel 4ComedianLeo Reich has created the great British sitcomfor generation Z. “It just feels like everything is over,” says 23-year-old unemployed Ethan, rather unbearably, as he and his best mates from uni, Abi (Emily Fairn) and Sam (Olive Gray), leave their shared house. As they bounce around London trying to figure their lives out, there are funny and sorely relatable results. Plus, cracking guest stars include Amelia Dimoldenberg, Andrew Scott and Lena Dunham.Hollie RichardsonThe Celebrity Traitors8pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenThe end is nigh … Claudia Winkleman in Celebrity Traitors.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry/PADid James Acaster, Maya Jama and Kenny manage to bore poor Jerry Hall or Ross Kemp to death? It’s time to find out who was murdered in the great yawn-off. Meanwhile, how is Miranda Hart coping after losing her dear new friend Joe Lycett? And will Michael Sheen change his approach after being voted the leader of the round table? It’s the penultimate week of the competition so things are about to heat up.HRThe Pride of Britain awards 20268pm, ITV1Carol Vorderman and Ashley Banjo host this annual celebration of remarkable Britons. Expect unsung heroes from across the nation and from a variety of backgrounds, with awards celebrating outstanding bravery; emergency services staff who have gone above and beyond; and courageous children or teens, among others.Hannah J DaviesThe Yorkshire Vet8pm, Channel 5You can depend on Channel 5 for uber-gentle programming with “Yorkshire” in the title, although this long-running series does showcase some tough cases amid the idyllic rural stuff. Former battery hen Jemima has had a tough life and now has a painful prolapse, while Ella the cat’s sore eyes require surgical intervention.HJDTaskmaster9.05pm, Channel 4A worrying incident (and a Taskmaster first), as an attempt to avoid a flying sausage leads to actual bloodshed. Other firsts include a new method of counting (pioneered by Isy Suttie) and a new word (thanks to Nina Conti). Elsewhere, Alex’s new “science machine” elicits a level of scorn that may also be unprecedented.Phil HarrisonMercury prize 2026: Album of the Year9.30pm, BBC FourPaul McCartney is one of the first-time nominees for the prestigious album award this year. He’s up there with Dove Ellis, Jade, Dave, Knats, Kojey Radical, War Child, Nia Archives and Olivia Dean. They are joined by Raye, with her second nomination, Florence + the Machine with their fourth, and previous winners Suede. title: Black Bag by Luke Kennard audiobook review – brilliant Booker-shortlisted campus comedy | Books | The Guardian
description: The author reveals his mastery of comic timing in his narration of this novel about a cash-strapped actor paid to live inside a black leather bag
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: The author reveals his mastery of comic timing in his narration of this novel about a cash-strapped actor paid to live inside a black leather bag
Content: Sober reflections … Luke Kennard.Photograph: David Levenson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSober reflections … Luke Kennard.Photograph: David Levenson/Getty ImagesAudiobook of the weekBooksReviewBlack Bag by Luke Kennard audiobook review – brilliant Booker-shortlisted campus comedyThe author reveals his mastery of comic timing in his narration of this novel about a cash-strapped actor paid to live inside a black leather bagFiona SturgesThu 22 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe unnamed narrator of Luke Kennard’s novel is an out-of-work actor living in London. His last job was three months ago, he is behind with his rent and has “measured out my life in coffees I cannot technically afford”. So when he comes across an advert – “Male actor required for psychological enquiry. Non-speaking but discretion and devotion to restrictive performance requirements obligatory” – he offers his services.The job, he discovers, is at a university working under a psychology professor named Dr Blend. There he must strip to his underpants and zip himself into a black leather bag, in which there are two eyeholes and further holes for his feet. The actor is expected to sit silently in the bag during seminars while students contemplate his presence.The inspiration for Kennard’s Booker-shortlisted campus comedy is a 1967 social experiment, conducted at Oregon State University, where a student attended classes inside a black bag in a test to see whether other students would grow attached to his presence. It also nods to Yoko Ono’s 1964 conceptual artwork Bag Piece, in which gallery-goers were asked to climb inside a large black bag.Kennard, who is the reader, mines this surreal conceit for laughs as the protagonist does battle with revolving doors and tries to pay for coffee using a card taped to the inside of the bag at chest height. As with his prose, the author’s delivery reveals him as a master of comic timing and a mordantbon mot. Yet beneath Black Bag’s winningly oddball exterior are more sober reflections on human relationships and what it is to be a man.Available via John Murray, 9hr 12minFurther listeningBattle Axe: A MemoirMargaret Hodge, William Collins, 14hr 43minThe veteran Labour politician narrates her book detailing 50 years in frontline politics, from her early career as a leader of Islington council to her time as an MP during the Tony Blair and Gordon Brown premierships and her recent work as the UK’s anti-corruption champion.I Shoot Rock StarsTim Pope, Wildfire, 10hr 6minPope, a music video director, recalls wild moments with musicians of yore, from the time he dressed Freddie Mercury as a “giant Mediterranean prawn” to filming the Cure performing inside a wardrobe. Read by the author.Explore more on these topicsBooksAudiobook of the weekFictionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Female Life on Planet Earth by Laleh Khadivi review – a mother’s secret past in the Iranian revolution | Fiction | The Guardian
description: A woman living in California discovers her mother may have been a merciless enforcer of the Islamic revolution, in an intriguing novel of inheritance and identity
Author: Shahidha Bari
Headline: A woman living in California discovers her mother may have been a merciless enforcer of the Islamic revolution, in an intriguing novel of inheritance and identity
Content: Cosmic sensibility … Laleh Khadivi.Photograph: Jesse DittmarView image in fullscreenCosmic sensibility … Laleh Khadivi.Photograph: Jesse DittmarBook of the dayFictionReviewFemale Life on Planet Earth by Laleh Khadivi review – a mother’s secret past in the Iranian revolutionA woman living in California discovers her mother may have been a merciless enforcer of the Islamic revolution, in an intriguing novel of inheritance and identityShahidha BariThu 22 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 03.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“It’s a little scary, isn’t it, inheritance?” That’s what Heti, the protagonist of Laleh Khadivi’s latest novel, remarks to a “soccer mom” as they watch their daughters play. “We don’t get to choose what we inherit. Or what we pass on.” Heti, who lives in Los Angeles, is Iranian-American and works for an accountancy firm. She has two daughters, Ava and Zora, and her mother has recently died. When Ava scores a goal, the soccer mom asks, “Did she get that from you?”, but Heti is less interested in the skills that parents pass to their children than the secrets they keep from them.Khadivi’s novel is about mothers and the mysteries they contain. In Female Life on Planet Earth she asks what happens when the people closest to us turn out to be strangers. How do we manage our grief and memorialise our loss when those we love have hidden awful parts of their lives? At the beginning of the book, Heti receives strict instructions from an Iranian aunt about the correct way to mark her mother’s passing. “One year after the death you throw a party,” she is told, “so that [people] can think about your mother, really remember and mourn her.” But then Heti receives a startling set of photographs from an unknown sender. In one image, a younger version of her mother stands veiled in black, a machine gun slung over her shoulder. In a second image, the weapon is extended towards a group of handcuffed women, “their miniskirts uneven on their hips, rips in their tight sweaters”, some crying before the camera, another lying prone, “face pressed into the concrete floor”.double quotation markThe protagonist puzzles through her uncertain feelings in a novel that’s serious and sardonic, analytical and droll by turnsCould her mother have been a merciless enforcer of the Islamic Revolution in Iran? Khadivi doesn’t pose the question so bluntly. Instead, she allows the impact of the images to reverberate for Heti. The pictures with the gun are disturbing, but it is the “shock of affinity” that startles her most of all. “Even though I’m terrified by these pictures, I understand her urge to have control … For the tiniest second I was weirdly reassured that my mother wasn’t all manners and sweetness and that maybe we had more in common than I thought.”Later, she visits her local library and reads about all-female militias, women who in “their newfound zeal … found the punishment of their sisters, the task assigned them by the revolutionaries, to be a satisfying outlet of power”. It’s a grimly fascinating history, but Khadivi is less interested in raking over the political complexities than in attending to the dissonance it stirs in Heti. She allows Heti to puzzle through her uncertain feelings in a novel that fluctuates in tone, serious and sardonic, analytical and droll by turns.The drollery is partly an effect of the book’s structure – a series of vignettes dotted over the course of a year in which Heti wrestles with big issues in incongruous places. On the soccer pitch, she is bemused by the mom who complains, “You can’t believe all that Barbie feminist crap.” At the wholesale supermarket, with its “maze of open freezers filled with thirty pound turkeys”, she wonders if she is remembering her mother “as she really was or as I want her to be”. Doing the accounts on the set of a soft porn film, she decides that what “happens in these shoots is a kind of freedom … Where I came from, where my mother and I were born, a woman’s pleasure can destroy her.”Standing in contrast to the comic parts of Heti’s suburban life is Khadivi’s more cosmic sensibility – suggested by the book’s title. Chapters are named for planets or taken from terms in physics, but the shift between the domestic and the metaphysical can make reading an uneven experience. Khadivi can be grandiose: “At night, Heti’s soul ranged and she followed. Without direction or orientation her thoughts spread into undefined time and limitless space.” At other times, the cosmos is an effective analogy: the “emotional gravity” of Heti’s experience pulls her “into a freefall” that feels like grasping at Jupiter’s vaporous atmosphere. In such circumstances, as Heti tells her daughters, “either you fall and fall or you figure out how to fly …”When Zora later expresses her determination to act on the climate crisis, she tells her mother that “it’s going to be our job to do the extreme things, like take hostages, or destroy oil tankers, or stop eating meat just to get people to care. I’m ready to do any of those.” Khadivi positions Zora’s radicalism as an intriguing mirror to that of her grandmother, quietly challenging any easy assumptions a reader might have about the rights of one and the wrongs of another. If mothers can conceal their lives from their daughters, Khadivi is right to point to how daughters can carry forward, resist or remake the legacies they inherit. As Heti comes to understand in this intriguing and unusual novel, perhaps the more important question may be not what we inherit, but what we choose to become.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
