title: ‘If my brother hadn’t died, my life would be so different’: Olympic boxer Ramla Ali’s incredible journey | Movies | The Guardian
description: From fleeing the Somali civil war to fighting at the Tokyo Olympics, Ali’s life has been remarkable – and now she is being played by Top Boy’s Jasmine Jobson in a new biopic. We hear from both on this ‘positive migrant story’
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: From fleeing the Somali civil war to fighting at the Tokyo Olympics, Ali’s life has been remarkable – and now she is being played by Top Boy’s Jasmine Jobson in a new biopic. We hear from both on this ‘positive migrant story’
Content: Star power … Jasmine Jobson, left, and Ramla Ali at the premiere of In the Shadows at the London film festival.Photograph: Phil Lewis/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenStar power … Jasmine Jobson, left, and Ramla Ali at the premiere of In the Shadows at the London film festival.Photograph: Phil Lewis/SOPA Images/ShutterstockMoviesInterview‘If my brother hadn’t died, my life would be so different’: Olympic boxer Ramla Ali’s incredible journeyCath ClarkeFrom fleeing the Somali civil war to fighting at the Tokyo Olympics, Ali’s life has been remarkable – and now she is being played by Top Boy’s Jasmine Jobson in a new biopic. We hear from both on this ‘positive migrant story’Thu 22 Oct 2026 09.28 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 10.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBoxer Ramla Ali sweeps into the green room of a West End cinema, tiny in a frothy dress with a huge skirt of cascading black feathers. It’s an absolute showstopper. She’s just introduced the premiere of a new film about her life. There are messages on her phone from Bear Grylls and Malala Yousafzai, who are in the audience watching.But the person who matters most is her mum, who is seeing it for the fourth time. What does she think? “She loves it,” says Ali quietly. The film is In the Shadows, directed by Anthony Wonke and stars Top Boy actor Jasmine Jobson. It tells the story of Ali’s journey to the 2021 Olympics in Tokyo.And what a journey. Ali was born inSomalia. When she was a baby, her older brother Abdulkadir was killed in an explosion while playing. The family fled Somalia, making the perilous crossing by boat to Kenya, finally arriving in the UK as refugees.Ali grew up in east London, joining a boxercise class at the local gym after being bullied at school about her weight. When she started boxing seriously, she kept it hidden from her family. As a Muslim girl, it would not be allowed. And she knew that her mother, having moved heaven and earth to get the family away from violence, would be devastated seeing her in harm’s way. These days, her mum is the first person Ali calls after a fight.It was eight years ago that the idea of a film first came up. Ali’s husband Richard Moore has just walked into the room. He used to be her coach and is also an executive producer on the film. He explains that one of the biggest reasons for pitching it back in 2018 was practical: they were broke. “We were down to our last hundred quid. We were lucky at that time, we had friends who took us in and housed us.” For a while they were a living in a home owned by Idris Elba and his wife, Sabrina. “They were our saviours. Then we got Covid and had to stay for ages,” giggles Ali.View image in fullscreenIn the ring … Ramla Ali lands a punch on Crystal Garcia Nova, 2022.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/ReutersDid she have any doubts about making the film? She nods: “Yes. I wasn’t sure I wanted to be so vulnerable, to sit down with a writer and tell her everything about my life, things I haven’t shared before.” There was her family’s trauma to consider, too: “I remember thinking, how is it going to affect my mum? It’s my story, but it’s her story as well. When I talked to my family, none of them were really up for it.” In the end, unexpectedly, it was her mother who came round first. And she had strong opinions about the script too: “My mum was adamant that the scene when my brother got killed be included. It had to be in.” Moore thinks it was a way of keeping him alive: “Remembering him, and making his death mean something bigger.”Ali has gone quiet. After a moment she says that Abdulkadir being killed set in motion a sequence of events that changed all their lives in her family: “His death is the ripple effect. If my brother hadn’t died, we wouldn’t have come to the UK. I wouldn’t have taken up boxing. I wouldn’t have met Richard. My life would be so different.”She says the film is not a pro-immigration statement. But it does offer another point of view to the fearmongering about migrants arriving on boats and stealing British jobs. “It’s depicting a human migrant story. Immigration has been weaponised politically to drive division in this country. Positive migrant stories don’t sell newspapers in the same way, so they rarely get told. But they are far more representative of the people who come here and build lives, families and careers. If audiences walk out seeing a person rather than a headline, the film has done its job.”She is the living proof of a positive migration story. In 2015, Ali became the first Muslim woman to win an English amateur boxing title. Six years later, she competed at the Tokyo Olympics as the first boxer in history to represent Somalia. She has modelled, appearing on the cover of British Vogue guest edited by the Duchess of Sussex. In 2018, she set up Sisters Club, a charity providing free boxing classes to vulnerable women. She is a Unicef ambassador.View image in fullscreenKnockout performance … Jasmine Jobson as Ali and Gershwyn Eustache Jr as Clinton in In the ShadowsPhotograph: Gavin Bond/True Brit Entertainment LtdAli tells me she worked hard behind the scenes of In the Shadows, reading every draft of the script, on set every day of the shoot. “Some exec producers just write their names on the film. But Iworkedfor that title. Iearnedit.” She even body doubled in the boxing scenes.Ali has been thinking lately about life after boxing. She and Moore have written and directed a comedy film together, Not Like Us, and she’s dipped her toe into acting too. “Boxing’s not for ever. There comes a day where you think: It’s time. Everyone laughs at me, but I keep saying it’s very similar to boxing. The dedication you’ve got to put into your boxing will show on the night in the ring. It’s the same with film-making. The level of dedication you’ve got to put in will show on screen.”What kind of films does she want to make? “I feel like in America there are so many films made for black people. I would love to be able to be in a position to tell more stories focused on the Black British experience.”It’s a sunny afternoon when I catch up with Jasmine Jobson, who plays Ali in the film. She took over from Letitia Wright, who was initially attached to the project. Jobson arrives at the BFI Southbank with a full entourage – publicist, makeup and hairdresser. “There’s not one part of my team that can be missing,” I hear her say as she strides across the room in Louboutin heels.She looks in fabulous shape. Is that the boxing? “Thank you. No. I haven’t continued boxing. I do need to get back into it.” She is focused on physio for an old shoulder injury, picked up years ago at the gym. “At college, I was training to be a personal trainer. I just pulled a bit too much weight down on a lat-pull.”Did she get into the swing of the boxing easily? “Yeah. Straight in. When I was young, I did karate, kickboxing, things like that. But I only had two weeks to prepare for this job. Literally two weeks to become a champion.” She spent eight hours a day training: “I absolutely loved boxing. I just don’t like getting my face touched. No one’s allowed to get my face. This is my money maker.”View image in fullscreen‘She’s overcome so much’ … Ramla Ali and Jasmine Jobson.Photograph: Tom CockramJobson says she fell in love with Ali the moment they met for coffee. “We had a nice little chat and got to know each other on a bit more of a deeper level. She’s overcome so much. To come out the other side, and to be an international success, to be able to change perceptions …” Jobson pauses. “Something might feel distant, or not necessarily accepted. But if you are passionate about it, and you are very good at it, if it’s your talent, go for it. You can be a success story no matter what your dream is. She’s a testament to that. Kudos to her, man.”Did it feel intimidating taking on the part of a real-life person, I ask. “No. Not all. Any role I’ve played, I’ve incorporated myself into it.”Like Ali, her experience of childhood adversity makes her achievements doubly impressive. As a young child, Jobson’s parents encouraged her talent for performing. But when she was in secondary school, social services became involved with the family. Jobson moved out of her mother’s house to live with her grandmother. Then, aged 14, she took the decision to place herself in foster care: “I had to do a very very deep dive within myself and take myself away from bad crowds, and figure out what my destiny was. My brain got a little bit clouded, and I had to find Jasmine again.”A family friend suggested she try out for The Big House, a theatre company in north London that works with care leavers, and there she got an agent. Like Ali, she is a grafter, and learned lines in Somali for In the Shadows. She gives me a phrase in Somali: “It means: ‘I just want you to be proud of me.’ That’s all I’ve ever wanted – for my family and everybody to be proud of me.”It sounds as if she put a lot of herself in the role. “Oh, 100%. But at the same time, I had to make sure it was authentically Ramla.” She can see the similarities, she admits: “It’s not that we’ve had the same life experiences, but we both had struggles and we both had a dream.”In the Shadows is in UK and Irish cinemas from 30 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmBoxingSomaliaBiopicsRefugeesAfricaMiddle East and north AfricainterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’d consider replacing one of my children’: Taika Waititi on robot kids, his cheese-o-meter and Klara and the Sun | Movies | The Guardian
description: The director has turned Kazuo Ishiguro’s acclaimed novel about an ailing adolescent and her glitchy robot friend into a thought-provoking film. What do the pair think this story says about tech, love and grief?
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: The director has turned Kazuo Ishiguro’s acclaimed novel about an ailing adolescent and her glitchy robot friend into a thought-provoking film. What do the pair think this story says about tech, love and grief?
Content: Misreading social cues, crashing the family car … Jenna Ortega as artificial friend Klara.Photograph: Sony Pictures EntertainmentView image in fullscreenMisreading social cues, crashing the family car … Jenna Ortega as artificial friend Klara.Photograph: Sony Pictures EntertainmentMoviesInterview‘I’d consider replacing one of my children’: Taika Waititi on robot kids, his cheese-o-meter and Klara and the SunXan BrooksThe director has turned Kazuo Ishiguro’s acclaimed novel about an ailing adolescent and her glitchy robot friend into a thought-provoking film. What do the pair think this story says about tech, love and grief?Thu 22 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 07.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the wings of the London film festival, a group of young influencers are discussing their personal highlights. Klara and the Sun, says one, and her colleagues agree. It’s not just that the film is still so fresh in their memory, or that they have gathered today to meet its creators and stars. Klara is funny and moving; it’s their festival favourite so far. I relay this exchange toTaika Waititi, the film’s director, who is sipping bottled water in a room down the hall. His gaze widens. He almost chokes. “Thank God!” he exclaims with just a bit too much heat.Everybody has a perfect film, just as everybody has a perfect friend, and they vary because everybody is different. In the film, sick 14-year-old Josie loves her discontinued robot doll Klara, whereas most kids her age opt for brighter, shinier models. And the young influencers love Klara and the Sun – Waititi’s adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s acclaimed novel – while mostolder critics vehemently, violently disagree. All of which shows that there’s no accounting for taste, that people are confounding, and that our hearts and our brains are not always in sync. That keeps life interesting. It’s partly what the film is about. “The emotions that we give very simple labels to are really complex,” says Ishiguro, who is seated alongside the director. “The thing we call love, for example, is incredibly noisy and multifaceted. Nobody knows what the hell love is.”double quotation markI can't make a Schindler's List. That's not in my wheelhouseFor what it’s worth, I loved Ishiguro’sdistinctively spare and poignant source noveland am less convinced by Waititi’s screen version, which is certainly noisy. Jenna Ortega stars as Klara, the perky solar-powered AI who plays soulmate to adolescent Josie (Mia Tharia), at a remote country house. She’s a warm splash of sunshine in an otherwise frosty environment, a fish out of water in a tragicomic sci-fi caper. But there is a glitch in the matrix; the component parts don’t align. Waititi adds sugar and caffeine, pratfalls and one-liners. Klara misreads social cues and steers the family car off the road. She fears she’ll be shipped back to the factory and melted down for scrap.View image in fullscreen‘In another version of this movie, Klara could be a murder-bot’ … Mia Tharia as Josie with Ortega as her artificial friend.Photograph: Matt Grace/Sony Pictures EntertainmentPerhaps the perfect friend is independent, self-directed. Ishiguro has seen several of his Nobel prize-winning books – The Remains of the Day, Never Let Me Go, A Pale View of Hills – adapted for the screen. He feels that the best films break away and that the worst are too faithful. “Sometimes it’s not just loyalty but laziness,” he says. “You can’t just have the text there in front of you. You need to use your imagination to move it on. A film needs to step forward, out of my book on a journey to being something bigger.”Waititi agrees. “Why would you do a cover of a song with exactly the same instrumentation? You make the film because you love the book. But you at least want to bring some original ideas to the table.”The book and the film are so different, it follows that their creators would be too. Ishiguro is sober, soft-spoken and writes delicate dramas about the deep mystery of life. Waititi is voluble, peacockish and makes uproarious films such as Jojo Rabbit, What We Do in the Shadows andHunt for the Wilderpeople. He tends to view the world through a comic lens. “Yeah, that’s my instinct. I can’t make a Schindler’s List, that’s not in my wheelhouse. I want to push everything towards comedy and then reel it back.”View image in fullscreenTragicomic sci-fi caper … Waititi and Ortega shooting the film.Photograph: Matt Grace/Sony Pictures EntertainmentIt’s a defence mechanism, he admits, part of his cultural DNA. “I’m from New Zealand,” he says. “In New Zealand, my friends and I always had a very sensitive cheese-o-meter. We thought the Americans loved cheese and saw sentimentality as a good thing. But of course that’s also me being scared of it. Now I think there’s a way of being more emotional and dramatic. Hopefully that’s a sign of me maturing.”Waititi’s work, though, has always carried a pleasing eddy of sadness. His 2010 feature Boy was a comedy about child abuse, while What We Do in the Shadows reframed the vampire as a lost, lonesome immigrant. Klara and the Sun is a love story but it’s also about isolation: the gap between people; the limits of understanding. “Oh, I’m definitely interested in loneliness,” he says.Ishiguro chips in. “Yeah, I think you’re right, there’s a crossover between our preoccupations,” he says. “But this isn’t just everyday loneliness, it’s something more fundamental. It’s about the human experience. There is part of each of us that remains alone. There is stuff that we all have to face alone. Not least death.”View image in fullscreenIshiguro … surprised to hear that Google Deepmind is a fan of his story.Photograph: Chris Pizzello/Invision/APThat’s the other big looming topic of Waititi’s film: death. Klara works as an “artificial friend” while other robots serve as “bereavement dolls”, filling in for lost spouses, siblings and children. That’s a sound business model, the director insists. “As a father with two kids, I always fear I’ll lose one. The younger me would have thought, ‘Oh, you can’t replace someone special.’ But the older I get, and the more in love with my kids I get, I think, ‘Oh, eventually I’d believe it was them.’ The human brain is easily adaptable. A therapist will tell you that you can programme anyone to fall in love. Tell someone you love them 50 times a day and in a few months your brain will give up and believe it. So I’d definitely consider replacing one of my children.” He laughs. “They don’t even have to be dead. I’d just like a version that’s nice to me and doesn’t ask for money.”Kazuo Ishiguro: ‘AI, gene-editing, big data ... I worry we are not in control of these things any more’Read moreIshiguro once joked that he essentially writes the same story in a variety of guises. He is drawn to flawed eyewitnesses and a partial view of events; groping narrators who try to make sense of their places in the world. The Remains of the Day’s rigid butler doesn’t know he’s in love, nor that the stately home where he works contains Nazis. Never Let Me Go’s hothoused schoolgirl finds out she is held captive and being used in terrible ways. Ishiguro’s books are unique but each connects to the world, and sometimes in ways he could not have foreseen. Klara and the Sun, for instance, was recently cited as a potential handbook for the development of generative AI. Tom Lue, VP of global affairs at Google Deepmind, suggested it be used as an “ethical touchstone”, the centrepiece of a “human-centred” approach to the future of frontier AI.So the book has been co-opted. It has taken on another fresh life of its own. Waititi turns to the author. “It’s all your fault,” he says. “That’s incredible,” says Ishiguro. It’s the first he’s heard of it. “I know a lot of people within the AI industry are worried about its impact on society. It’s got to the point where they feel the need for a handbrake. So they are surprisingly keen to talk to creative people and road-test various ideas and scenarios.” He frowns. “But here I do become protective of both the book and the film. Because our story really isn’t about all that. If someone is trying to figure out the ethics of AI and where we should all be going, I’m not sure they’d be well-guided by this story. There are other, better places to go.”Waititi pipes up. “The Terminator’s a good one.”Klara has been built with a sweet, simple purpose: to provide friendship and support. But the human world is hazardous, unstable, which means she has to update her files and adapt her approach. Waititi’s film veers and darkens, riffing off its downbeat source novel, finally closing in towards death. “There’s another version of this story where Klara would turn into a murder-bot,” he points out.Robot dolls fill a need, plug a gap and ideally make life better. But artificial friends, by their nature, are replaceable too. In the press room next door, the influencers are still comparing notes, killing time between interviews. Klara and the Sun is receding; the conversation has already moved on. One says: “You have to see La Bola Negra. It’s my film of the year.”Klara and the Sun is in cinemas from 22 October in Australia, and 23 October in the UK and USExplore more on these topicsFilmTaika WaititiScience fiction and fantasy filmsAI (artificial intelligence)Kazuo IshiguroFilm adaptationsComputinginterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Wow, logging that as a microaggression!’ Sophie Duker on trolling masculinity, lesbian cruises and her stripper fantasy  | Comedy | The Guardian
description: The standup on the bizarre gifts she’s received from fans, the intoxicating power of being an author and her aim of becoming a ‘fiercely intellectual slutty grandma’
Author: Liam Pape
Headline: The standup on the bizarre gifts she’s received from fans, the intoxicating power of being an author and her aim of becoming a ‘fiercely intellectual slutty grandma’
Content: ‘I try to sneak in niche references to Lord of the Rings’ … Sophie Duker.View image in fullscreen‘I try to sneak in niche references to Lord of the Rings’ … Sophie Duker.Comedy Q&AComedy‘Wow, logging that as a microaggression!’ Sophie Duker on trolling masculinity, lesbian cruises and her stripper fantasyThe standup on the bizarre gifts she’s received from fans, the intoxicating power of being an author and manifesting her ‘fiercely intellectual slutty grandma’Interview byLiam PapeThu 22 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow did you get into comedy?If you want anything badly enough, the best way to get it is to feign absolute indifference while pouring in 110% effort. I was telling outrageous jokes about colonialism in tiny pub rooms five nights a week alongside a rotating lineup of lunatics and sexual deviants, all the while gaslighting myself into believing it was a casual hobby and I could stop any time.What’s been one of your all-time favourite gigs?I loved performing on a lesbian cruise, despite the debilitating impostor syndrome (I’m an omnivore). I got a record number of fist-bumps from appreciative butches and met so many incredible older sapphics. One was a black witch from California who communed with my ancestors directly after the show – you don’t get that kind of service on Live at the Apollo.Can you recall a gig so bad, it’s now funny?I was headlining at a festival and my right breast fell out of my top about 10 seconds in. I didn’t address it because I thought it would weaken my authority; the audience didn’t address it because they were kind and possibly scared. My tit was swinging in the breeze like Tarzan from the vine! I think through sheer bloody-mindedness we all managed to trigger a Mandela effect where after the half hour ended no one present was sure it had ever actually happened. Until now.View image in fullscreen‘A stunning, silly, angry show’ … Sophie Duker.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianHow would you describe your new show,Hot Beef Injection?A stunning, silly, angry show where we (me, Sophie, and you, the audience) troll masculinity for an hour. I love the men who come to my shows (hot dads, fun nerds, miscellaneous) but the men outside, who roam the streets, have me tired and distressed on the daily. In a world where we’re processingrape academies, frat-house group chats and private islands it feels not only punk but necessary to rugby tackle the toxic elephants in the room.Was there a particular incident that triggered the show?Hoo boy. When I was but a tiny baby girl comedian I had a non-consensual experience with an older man in the industry. At the time I sort of walked it off. But our paths crossed again in late 2025, and I thought, in the light of all the hideous bleakness of Everything Happening Right Now, why not sneak the anecdote into a standup set and make it my best-reviewed show to date?Your debut novel,Dong, is out in the new year. What interested you in fiction writing?I’ve been writing fiction my entire life – alibis, flirtatious texts, hastily drafted email excuses and backstories for social media catfish. But sandwiching a feature-length story inside a hardback and putting my name to it has always felt like seducing Pedro Pascal – technically possible but unattainable for me, at least at the moment. The carte blanche you get given as an author to fantasise is intoxicating. I was tapping it out at the hair salon while the aunties ravaged my edges, sneaking my laptop into bed at sunrise so I could get a fix before my partner woke up.Best advice you’ve ever been given?“If you’re doing well, get off; if you’re doing badly, get off.” This was said to me by a male comedian, but I think it’s still valid. I really hate when any work becomes more about the performer’s vanity than audience enjoyment. It reminds me not to let success make me too self-indulgent, or to scrabble for extra scraps of approval if I feel short changed by the room’s reaction. Do the thing you came to do, to the best of your ability, then dip.What’s one of the strangest fan encounters you’ve had?My fans’ love language is bizarre gift giving. A man in York offered me freshly baked bread (I accepted). One man from France offered me his credit card details (I declined). On tour in Australia, a woman gave me a card which contained a lock of her dog’s hair. (I kept it – the card, not the dog.)What’s a joke you’re convinced is brilliant, but just doesn’t land with audiences?Wow, logging that as a microaggression.Allof my brilliant jokes land withallmy audiences – but I do notice that sometimes they are slightly more tepid when I try to sneak in niche references to Lord of the Rings.Kevin Bridges review – steamroller standup is a joy but what’s with the £10 cloakroom charge?Read moreWhat’s next for you?I want to nail my Ayesha. Not referring to the Baroness Hazarika. Nailing my Ayesha is part of my nonagenarian stripper fantasy. The Ayesha is a pose where you hang upside down, legs splayed, labia facing heaven, just two contact points on the pole. I’m manifesting a level of physical and mental dexterity in my 90s where I can be this fiercely intellectual slutty grandma and every other month I throw big debauched parties where I’m fed psychedelic-laced frozen grapes by my absolutely smitten, smoking hot entourage.Sophie Duker: Hot Beef Injection is atSoho theatre, London, 26 October–7 November. Thentouringuntil 9 MayExplore more on these topicsComedyComedy Q&ASophie DukerFestivalsMichaela CoelfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Martin Guerre review – return of Les Mis duo’s melodrama reveals a surprise new hero | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Matthew Warchus directs a radical and intimate revival of Alain Boublil and Claude-Michel Schönberg’s musical about a Frenchman who flees home
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Matthew Warchus directs a radical and intimate revival of Alain Boublil and Claude-Michel Schönberg’s musical about a Frenchman who flees home
Content: Twists and surprises … Liv Andrusier and Shane O'Riordan in Martin Guerre.Photograph: Helen MaybanksView image in fullscreenTwists and surprises … Liv Andrusier and Shane O'Riordan in Martin Guerre.Photograph: Helen MaybanksTheatreReviewMartin Guerre review – return of Les Mis duo’s melodrama reveals a surprise new heroOld Vic theatre, LondonMatthew Warchus directs a radical and intimate revival of Alain Boublil and Claude-Michel Schönberg’s musical about a Frenchman who flees homeArifa AkbarThu 22 Oct 2026 04.47 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 04.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome revivals overstate their revisionism but Alain Boublil and Claude-Michel Schönberg’s musical, which premiered 16 years after their 1980 hit Les Misérables, has had a radical overhaul here.The story, set in 16th-century France, has been restructured with new lyrics by Boublil, Annabel Mutale Reed and Paul Hodge and folkier orchestrations. It has been cut down to be performed in an hour and a half without an interval, on the floor of the theatre’s returning show, A Christmas Carol. A miniature Les Mis in spirit, it is filled with the same booming melodrama and preoccupations with crime and disguise.Based on the real-life story of a Frenchman who fled his home after getting married and returned, years later, to face claims of deception and false identity, it keeps you guessing. There are similarities with the Austrian filmRose, selected for the London film festival, and Anjet Daanje’s novelThe Remembered Soldier, published in English last year.View image in fullscreenBooming … the company of Martin Guerre.Photograph: Helen MaybanksAmong the twists and surprises, the real fireworks come from Matthew Warchus’s ingenuity as director. His in-the-round production creates intimacy between Martin and his wife, Bertrande (Liv Andrusier), but also brings a frothing sense of mob rule as the villagers brand her a witch and punish her for his desertion.Warchus, as deft as he is, cannot override all the problems of the musical and the reworking feels simultaneously fast and slow, the sleeker shape bringing momentum but the songs – operatic, emotional, too tonally similar – slowing everything down again. At least the titular number is distinctive, swooping and swooning infectiously.View image in fullscreenOddball … Colin Ryan in Martin Guerre.Photograph: Helen MaybanksPerhaps the production could do more to flesh out the return of Martin. There are a few scenes from the intervening years, in which we see him take part in France’s religious war to fight the Protestant Huguenots. For these brilliantly quicksilver flashbacks, Rob Howell’s set design transforms from courtroom to battlefield and back so cleanly it leaves you gasping with admiration. But the context is bare-boned, the war vague, some characters indistinct. The village oddball, Benoit (Colin Ryan), carries a puppet representing the scarecrow Louison, an underexplained figure who may create confusion for those unfamiliar with the story. You want more of Guerre’s relationship with a fellow soldier too, which proves key within the deception.High School Musical review – Disney fave is sweet, slick and as squeaky clean as everRead moreIt does develop an emotional pull as the plot speeds up and your sympathies lie with the man the town brands an impostor. There is a keen sense of Christian zeal about curses and demons, captured by Lizzi Gee’s choreography of a baying mob carrying weapons. The melodrama comes with the thunder and rumble of Fergus O’Hare’s sound design and blasts of sharply contrasting lighting, designed by Hugh Vanstone, Luca Panetta and Toby Ison.The story’s restructuring has a curious outcome on character and the underlying protagonist becomes Guerre’s abandoned wife, who stands unerringly by him. Andrusier is such a powerful performer, her rendition of one of the show’s new songs, Someday, is a blast of such passion, that it is as if a new hero has arisen to take claim of this story.AtOld Vic theatre, London, until 31 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMusicalsOld Vic TheatreMatthew WarchusWest EndreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Shovel Dance Collective: Everything in Readiness review – ecstatic, dissonant folk music fighting for sonic and spiritual freedom | Music | The Guardian
description: The nine-piece London-based group take a radically fresh approach to traditional music, sounding raging, lo-fi and joyful as they link Britain’s violent past to its present
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: The nine-piece London-based group take a radically fresh approach to traditional music, sounding raging, lo-fi and joyful as they link Britain’s violent past to its present
Content: Uninterested in breaking in newcomers gently … Shovel Dance Collective.Photograph: Brad GilbertView image in fullscreenUninterested in breaking in newcomers gently … Shovel Dance Collective.Photograph: Brad GilbertAlexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewShovel Dance Collective: Everything in Readiness review – ecstatic, dissonant folk music fighting for sonic and spiritual freedom(tak:til)The nine-piece London-based group take a radically fresh approach to traditional music, sounding raging, lo-fi and joyful as they link Britain’s violent past to its presentAlexis PetridisThu 22 Oct 2026 07.43 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 14.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThose thus far unaware of Shovel Dance Collective’s bracing approach to folk should probably note that their third album is not much interested in breaking newcomers in gently. Everything in Readiness kicks off with a three-song suite that lasts more than 10 minutes and takes you, via a series of dramatic sonic jump-cuts, from a grinding one-note drone to a reel that seems to split the difference between trad folk fiddle-playing and the punishing squall of the Velvet Underground’s Black Angel’s Death Song. It then leaps to Tally Ho! Hark Away!, which sets a hunting song first collected in the late 1940s over a blast of what might best be described as ecstatic noise. It’s genuinely hard to work out what instruments are involved in the clattering arrhythmic chaos behind the vocal – there’s definitely a heavily distorted guitar in the mix – but the effect is weirdly euphoric rather than claustrophobic: a kind of purgative release after the mounting weirdness of the preceding reel.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Shovel Dance Collective’s Everything in Readiness.Photograph: PRIf you’re looking for evidence that the nine-piece London-based group take a radically fresh approach to folk music, then there it is. The glib shorthand is that they’re doing for traditional English music what Lankum have done for its Irish equivalent – joining the dots with the kind of out-there experimentation that fills the pages of the Wire magazine – although it should be pointed out they sound almost nothing like Lankum. Anyone who already has an interest in leftfield explorations of British musical history might suggest their chaotic collage approach feels more akin to the fascinating collections of field recordings, folk song and avant garde composition released by Todmorden-based label Folklore Tapes. The music on Everything in Readiness careens unpredictably from gentle lo-fi recordings caked in distortion and tape hiss to the tumultuous, surging racket they serve up on their version of the traditional coalminer’s song Jowl, Jowl and Listen; from singing unaccompanied by anything but the sound of birdsong to the disquieting ambient shimmer of Who Killed Cock Robin? A Summoning (Kind Morning in our Fists), which sounds like it was recorded in a vast, echoing crypt.It’s an experience that leaves you feeling faintly punch-drunk and disoriented. Everything in Readiness ultimately doesn’t sound like anything else around, but perhaps it’s not so surprising that a bunch of experimental musicians – various members also serve in post-rock band Caroline, improv trio Sullow and the deeply unpredictable Gentle Stranger – have embraced traditional music. English folk in particular has a tendency to slip its standard moorings at times of crisis and find musicians and an audience outside the usual clubs and festivals. The electric folk wave of Fairport Convention, Pentangle and Steeleye Span took root between 1968 and 1972 as the optimism of 60s counterculture curdled into the dark reality of the early 70s. The indie-folk movement that begat folktronica and the founding of Green Man festival, repurposed traditional music’s more sinister overtones, its eerie bleakness, for the twitchy, post-9/11 years.Shovel Dance Collective: Jer the Rigger/The Foxhunter’s Reel/Tally Ho! Hark Away! – videoIt’s an impulse you could view as a retreat into “the certainties of a historical music that spoke of a more stable past”, as Rob Young’s peerless history of “Britain’s visionary music” Electric Albion called it. Equally, given folk’s visceral bloodiness and bursts of political radicalism, it could be a search for connection, a reaffirmation that this country has always been turbulent, violent and deeply strange. Shovel Dance Collective, with their loudly trumpted leftwing politics and willingness to dig out contemporary resonances in material hundreds of years old, clearly fit the latter category. You could view the closing I Wish There Was No Prisons as the 19th-century equivalent of those anarchist stickers that have proliferated during the cost-of-living crisis (“if you saw someone shoplifting, you didn’t”), although their approach is clearest on Bold Captain Avery, a 1694 broadside that hymned the “King of Pirates” as a bold freedom fighter, “disowned” by his native country but having at the foreigners and “heathens” in the name of St George. The reality is that Avery was a monster driven by the accumulation of wealth, whose most famous raid – on the Ganj-i-Sawai, a ship en route to Mecca – descended into an orgy of violence that seemed to shock even his own men. It doesn’t take a genius to grasp why Shovel Dance Collective might have repurposed it for 2026.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘A guy held a knife to my throat and said: play something normal!’ Richard Thompson on crazy crowds, his beloved beret and Sandy Denny’s driving skillsRead moreIt’s intended as no shade on the band’s political leanings to suggest all this feels less important than the way their third album sounds: it’s there if you want to find it and that’s undoubtedly a good thing, but the most immediate pleasure of Everything in Readiness lies in the head-spinning sonic surprises it delivers. As it lurches wildly around, you find yourself struggling to keep up, a sure sign that you’re in the presence of music that feels entirely fresh and different. It makes songs that are centuries old feel messily, hectically alive.This week Alexis listened toDarren Hayman – Close Your Eyes and Face the SunThe latest of singer/songwriter Hayman’s idiosyncratic DIY projects involves making an album using only the once-ubiquitous, now outdated DX7 synth. Here, it (and he) sound fragile and lovely in equal measure.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekFolk musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Bournemouth Symphony Orchestra / Wigglesworth review – phrasing with hospital corners | Classical music | The Guardian
description: BSO’s concert with their chief conductor Mark Wigglesworth mixed Tippett, Vaughan Williams, Adès and Sibelius. Best of all was the Tippett, and the Sibelius 5 had personality to burn
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: BSO’s concert with their chief conductor Mark Wigglesworth mixed Tippett, Vaughan Williams, Adès and Sibelius. Best of all was the Tippett, and the Sibelius 5 had personality to burn
Content: Detailed and sensitive conducting: Mark Wigglesworth with BSO at the Lighthouse, Poole.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreenDetailed and sensitive conducting: Mark Wigglesworth with BSO at the Lighthouse, Poole.Photograph: Mark AllanClassical musicReviewBournemouth Symphony Orchestra / Wigglesworth review – phrasing with hospital cornersLighthouse, PooleBSO’s concert with their chief conductor Mark Wigglesworth mixed Tippett, Vaughan Williams, Adès and Sibelius. Best of all was the Tippett, and the Sibelius 5 had personality to burnFlora WillsonThu 22 Oct 2026 09.26 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn paper, it was a curious programme: Tippett’s Concerto for Double String Orchestra and Vaughan Williams’s The Lark Ascending, followed post-interval byAdès’s Märchentänze and Sibelius’s Fifth Symphony. A calculated mix of more and less familiar works, certainly – but an otherwise unlikely foursome. The common preoccupations with folk music (threaded jauntily through the Tippett and the Adès) and the natural world (VW’s lark, Sibelius’s swans) only take us so far. In practice, the Bournemouth Symphony Orchestra’s performance under its chief conductorMark Wigglesworthrevealed a shared creative tussle with existing musical forms and with finding new means of expression without breaking entirely with the old ways.The Lark Ascending thus abandoned the Smooth Classics at Seven-mode for a covered, sometimes icy sound in the BSO’s world-class strings and a more risk-taking, more improvisatory approach from soloistAnthony Marwood. The tone of his Stradivarius was expensively sweet and his cool, no-vibrato opening compelling, though his performance was marred by intonation problems. Marwood fared better in Adès’s Märchentänze, which reworks folk tunes with unexpected timbral combinations and harmonies, and where the solo line tangles deliciously with the orchestra’s violins. But this work, written for theultra-charismatic violinist Pekka Kuusisto, was rather less interesting without such a compelling soloist.By contrast,Sibelius’s Symphony No 5had personality to burn in a performance that front-loaded its modernist strangeness. There were shadowy wind solos, creepy string tremolos and double basses that lurched nastily instead of settling comfortably into the finale’s swan business. There were also tuning difficulties in the wind and the BSO’s trombones were almost comically direct from where I was sitting. But Wigglesworth’s detailed, sensitive conducting came into its own in the work’s transitional passages, as he eased the weight out of dense textures and managed the journey to the symphony’s climax as a slowly, inexorably cresting wave.Best of all was the Tippett. Wigglesworth’s tempi were unhurried, even laid-back. Yet there was an angular neatness to Tippett’s neoclassical lines – this was phrasing with hospital corners – and the string sound was subtly malleable: from a striking, frosted tone in the first movement to the generous warmth that spread euphorically through the finale.The concert will be broadcast on BBC Radio 3 on 2 November.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort review – Wii Sports lives on in this effortlessly appealing collection of games | Games | The Guardian
description: Bringing a holiday vibe and a generous selection of sport-themed games, this is exactly what you want from a family video game
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: Bringing a holiday vibe and a generous selection of sport-themed games, this is exactly what you want from a family video game
Content: Guaranteed strike … Nintendo Switch Sports Resort.Photograph: NintendoView image in fullscreenGuaranteed strike … Nintendo Switch Sports Resort.Photograph: NintendoGamesReviewNintendo Switch Sports Resort review – Wii Sports lives on in this effortlessly appealing collection of gamesNintendo Switch 2; Nintendo/NintendoBringing a holiday vibe and a generous selection of sport-themed games, this is exactly what you want from a family video gameKeza MacDonaldThu 22 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 07.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the first Nintendo Switch Sports brought the effortless fun of Wii Sports back into my living room in 2022, I wasfrankly delighted. My small children discovered the pleasure of waving a controller around in enthusiastic imitation of a tennis player, and the surprising subtlety of virtual bowling, working out how to twist the wrist just right to guarantee a strike. I did not expect this game to become a family fixture for the next several years as my kids got older and climbed up the online ranks in all six of its sports (plus the two that were added as free updates). Switch Sports is so beloved in my household that the release of Switch Sports Resort this week is the most anticipated gaming event of the year. To be fair, my children are a bit young for Grand Theft Auto.Nintendo Switch Sports Resort brings three of the six sports back – tennis, bowling, and volleyball – alongside golf and basketball. Then there are seven entirely new sports: boxing, table tennis, archery, thumb wrestling, skateboarding, jetski, and piloting a little prop plane. They are all intuitive, easy to get the hang of on the first or second attempt – some have more legs than others, in the long run – and all of them, crucially, are a little bit silly. Thumb wrestling in particular is cheerfully absurd, giving your characters gigantic thumbs on hands the size of their heads.View image in fullscreen‘One two three four let’s have a thumb war’ … Nintendo Switch Sports ResortPhotograph: NintendoEvery sport here is fun. In skateboarding you use the controller like a mouse, pulling it towards you to propel yourself forwards on the board and tilting it to steer through surprisingly challenging courses, lifting it into the air to jump and spin for tricks. Archery is perfectly intuitive, boxing enjoyably frenetic (especially when played with a seven-year-old), table tennis energisingly competitive, letting you spin and smash the ball with nuanced wrist movement. Almost all of these sports work exactly as you’d expect, with the exception of basketball, whose real-world speed and flashiness are replaced here with methodical turn-taking.Touring the resort on a jetski or in a plane is more peaceful, reminiscent of Wave Race and Pilotwings, two long-dormant Nintendo series whose DNA is clearly evident in the Wii Sports lineage. On the jetskis, you can follow pink dolphins leaping through the waves. As you pass over the island’s stadiums, cafes and beaches in the plane you will see that they are busy with tiny people, watching a match or lazing on the sand. When you’re skating or soaring around you realise just how big and lively it actually is.This gloriously unnecessary attention to detail gives this collection of sports games a sense of place and a holiday atmosphere that’s irresistibly appealing. The music is a sunny as the setting, full of guaranteed earworms. I spent a bunch of time dressing up my little character in outfits that you win by ranking up in the island leagues for each sport, a welcome addition that gives some structure to playing by yourself when you aren’t handing controllers around to friends and family. Variants on every sport also up the longevity: obstacle courses in bowling, for instance, or a three-pointer shooting contest in basketball.After a week of daily play, it has become clear that Switch Sports Resort will not be going back on the digital shelf for some time yet. It is perfect for a Saturday afternoon with friends, but it also has enough going on beneath the surface to sustain the long-term attentions of an enthusiastic child. In other words, it is exactly what you want from a family video game – and as a bonus, it gets everyone off the sofa.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNintendo Switch Sports Resort is out, 22 October; £41.99/$49.99/€49.99Explore more on these topicsGamesNintendo Switch 2NintendoreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Low-alcohol, high-calibre: the best super-session ales | Food | The Guardian
description: Increasingly full-bodied and flavourful, low-strength British pale ales are growing in popularity, especially on the dinner table
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: Increasingly full-bodied and flavourful, low-strength British pale ales are growing in popularity, especially on the dinner table
Content: Low-alcohol session beers work really well with food.Photograph: Cavan Images/Getty Images/Cavan Images RFView image in fullscreenLow-alcohol session beers work really well with food.Photograph: Cavan Images/Getty Images/Cavan Images RFFoodLow-alcohol, high-calibre: the best super-session alesIncreasingly full-bodied and flavourful, low-strength British pale ales are growing in popularity, especially on the dinner tableMina HollandThu 22 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 08.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is nothing like discovering something for yourself to engender a fierce sense of loyalty, and that’s exactly what happened a decade ago when I fell upon the Kernel Brewery’s TableBeer, a pale ale of roughly 3% ABV. This is a brew that never fails to meet me where I am as a working parent with multiple identities but one brain, who often craves a delicious little buzz without loss of function.Kernel brewer Evin O’Riordain tells me that sales have steadily increased over the past decade, and that 2026 has seen a tipping point. “For the first time ever, Table Beer became the thing we made the most,” he says. This is entirely consistent with the population’s collective interest in no-lo drinks, although, when it comes to beer, zero-alcohol examples are much better represented than low-alcohol ones (in the major retailers, at least). There are only a handful of the latter available in supermarkets, including Small Beer’s 2.3% IPA,Jiddler’s Tipple’s 3.8% Everyday Pale Ale(both Ocado), and Beavertown Satellite (2.8%) and Dark Star’s Hophead (3.4%), both at Waitrose.So what makes a good super-session beer? Flavour and body tend to be sacrificed when alcohol is reduced or removed, so maintaining those is key. With Table Beer, O’Riordain says he was trying to emulate traditional British cask beers, albeit using “clean and neutral” American yeasts instead of “spicier” English ones, so the bright, New World hops can shine through. The result is a citrussy flavour profile (in a classic IPA, says O’Riordain, the alcohol catalyses the flavour of the hops distinctly, often becoming more tropical).Texture, meanwhile, results from residual sugar. When he mashes the beer (the process of mixing crushed grain with hot water to activate the natural enzymes that convert starches into fermentable sugars), O’Riordain does so at very high temperatures, disabling the yeast from converting all of the sugar into alcohol. The result is a beer that has the satisfying body of something stronger. A second fermentation in bottle (rather than a forced carbonation, as many breweries do) “also adds a layer of depth”, he says, even though this does increase the alcohol, but only by about 0.2%.Beavertown describes its Satellite beer as a “super session”, and most beers in that group pitch themselves as supreme session beers – although the Table Beer moniker implies something to drink with food. Always one to refer to past examples, O’Riordain says his research revealed “a whole family of low-alcohol British beers made in the 1700-1900s that were grouped together less by style than by ABV”. These included “boys bitter”, “dinner ale”, “mild beer” and, yes, “table beer”. “Strangely, the lower-alcohol things were more appropriate with food,” he says. All my picks this week are great with flavourful foods; I drank them variously with fish tacos, mattar paneer and donburi. They aren’t just good low-alcohol beers, though; they’re really excellent beers full stop.Four beers for a proper sessionTable Beer£3.25 (330ml) The Kernel Brewery, about 3%. My go-to beer, day or night, food or none; for ever and ever, amen.Beavertown Satellite Super SessionIPA£6.50 (4 x 330ml) Waitrose, 2.8%. Refreshing and soft, fruity and swiggable; eke out the sunshine with one in hand.Dark Star Brewing Co Hophead Golden Ale£2.75 (500ml) Waitrose, 3.4%. The highest ABV here, which comes through in the body, plus there’s an amazing hoppy kick to finish.Small Beer IPA£3 (330ml) Ocado,2.3%. Golden, ultra-low ABV number from a brewery that specialises in “mid-strength” brews.Explore more on these topicsFoodBeerBritish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for chicken with citrus and oregano | Italian food and drink | The Guardian
description: This dish has been handed down through generations of Roman restaurateurs
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: This dish has been handed down through generations of Roman restaurateurs
Content: Rachel Roddy’s chicken braised in citrus and herbs.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenRachel Roddy’s chicken braised in citrus and herbs.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The Guardian.A kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkRachel Roddy’s recipe for chicken with citrus and oreganoThis dish of chicken in a lipsmacking citrus and oregano sauce has been handed down through many generations of Roman restaurateursRachel RoddyThu 22 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you look through the window ofPiatto Romanobetween 10am and midday, there will almost certainly be two, maybe three people at the round table trimming vegetables: chicory, artichokes, poppy greens, amaranth. After midday, the crates and trimmings will have been cleared away and the table will now be home to trays of bright-green boiled vegetables and, maybe, baked salt cod. By 12.30pm, everything will have been moved into the small kitchen in time for service, which starts at 12.45pm.When I first moved to Rome in 2005,Via Bodoni 62was home to a restaurant called Da Rafaelle, which had white plastic chairs (inside as well) and served traditional Roman food with plenty of offal. We went to Da Rafaelle a few times before it closed in 2009. But, mostly, we went toLa Torricella,which is on the other side of Testaccio and serves mainly fish. The owner is Augusto D’Alfonsi and, during lunch one day, he mentioned that he was taking over via Bodoni 62, and that his daughter Francesca would run it. They’d serve traditional Roman food with plenty of offal and it would be called Piatto Romano. This was 2011. My son was born later that year and my memories are not unpleasantly foggy; of the vegetable trolley in the corner, of chicken with red peppers and of Francesca and her father negotiating strongly. I also remember Francesca’s brother, Andrea, starting to be around more, before he eventually took over in late 2013.Andrea grew up riding his bike along the pavement in front of La Torricella, which his parents had opened in 1973, a few years before he was born. If his lunch didn’t come out of the kitchen at La Torricella, it probably came out of the kitchen atDa Antonioon Via dei Pastini, where Andrea’s maternal grandma cooked, or from the kitchen of his maternal grandfather’s restaurant,Da Giovannion Via dei Barbieri. As a teenager, Andrea also ate at his paternal grandfather’s osteria,Gran Sassoin Trastevere, and in the various branches ofInsalata Ricca, a chain of salad restaurants opened by his entrepreneurial uncle Gino in the 1980s. All the various parts of the family have Abruzzese roots, but Andrea mentions Gino, eccentric and single-minded about history, vegetables and nutrition, as being a particular influence.The way Andrea continues to evolve Piatto Romano (which for many is the embodiment of an ideal Roman trattoria) would require several columns. For now, though, I will note his singlemindedness about the vegetables he picks up every day from his various sources. The other night, we had courgette greens – a little hairy and very succulent – with Leprino rabbit (typical of the Tuscia area of Viterbo) braised in wine and citrus, which produces a lipsmacking sauce/gravy. And head chef Umberto Mussato, who has worked with Andrea since 2021, has adapted his recipe for this column, but using chicken instead of rabbit. The dish is made even more tasty by the addition of three to five anchovy fillets mashed with a tablespoon of red-wine vinegar, plus a sprig of fresh thyme or oregano, which is then left to sit for at least half an hour before it’s served with greens and potatoes, if you wish.Chicken with citrus and herbsServes41.2kg skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs(or a mix of legs and thighs)Salt4tbsp olive oil100-150ml dry white wine1 tspdried thyme or oregano400ml fresh citrus juice– a mix of orange, lemon, grapefruit, mandarin3-5 anchovies mashedwith 1tbspgood-quality red-wine vinegarA few stalksfresh oreganoSeason the chicken with salt, rubbing it into the skin. Working in a heavy-based pan, warm the olive oil, then brown the chicken pieces in batches so as not to overcrowd the pan. Once all the pieces are brown, look at the amount of fat in the pan – I suggest leaving it all in there, but remove some, if you prefer.Return all the browned chicken to the pan, raise the heat and add the wine, which should sizzle and evaporate. Add the dried oregano or thyme, stir, then pour over the citrus juice. Lower the heat so the pan simmers, then cover.Leave the chicken to cook for 45 minutes to an hour, lifting the lid to turn the pieces every now and then, then lift off the lid and cook for another 20 minutes, so the sauce can reduce. By the end of the cooking, the chicken should be tender and the sauce thick. (If the sauce needs significant reduction, remove the chicken, simmer hard so the sauce reduces to your liking, then return the chicken pieces to the pan.)To finish, stir in the anchovies mashed in vinegar and a sprig of fresh thyme or oregano, then leave to sit for 30 minutes before serving.Explore more on these topicsItalian food and drinkA kitchen in RomeFoodChickenMain courseWineHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: ​Make the most out of the last spoonful | Food | The Guardian
description: ​Before you throw away that jar with only a bit left inside, turn it into a dressing, sauce, glaze or even a drink instead
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: ​Before you throw away that jar with only a bit left inside, turn it into a dressing, sauce, glaze or even a drink instead
Content: Get the most out of that jar … Rachel Roddy’s mixed leaf salad with gorgonzola and hazelnuts.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGet the most out of that jar … Rachel Roddy’s mixed leaf salad with gorgonzola and hazelnuts.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianFeastFood​Make the most out of the last spoonful​Before you throw away that jar with only a bit left inside, turn it into a dressing, sauce, glaze or even a drink insteadSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastRachel RoddyThu 22 Oct 2026 07.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 07.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has been almost three months now, and we still haven’t replaced the cupboards that fell off the kitchen wall. It is also disturbing how well we have adapted to the chaos and having half the room covered with plastic crates that once contained vegetables and that now contain the hundreds of items that used to fit in the three cupboards, the collective weight of said items explaining the incident. The lack of cupboards has put pressure on the fridge, too, which has become a depository. That’s why, when I finally looked inside it properly, I found three jars of honey, each with between 2mm and 2cm at the bottom, as well as two jars of peanut butter, and a pretty much scraped-out jar of chocolate spread. At least all of those jars provided inspiration for today’s newsletter.Making a dressing with the last inch of honey is perhaps the most efficient and satisfying way to deal with a near-empty jar. Pour in a bit of boiling water and some lemon juice, orange juice or red-wine vinegar, screw on the lid, then shake aggressively so the honey dislodges and dissolves into a syrup. Now add everything else – olive oil, a bit of mustard and whatever else you fancy – and shake again to emulsify. This dressing is great with one of the most useful, speedy and cheap salads in existence, namely shredded red and white cabbage, grated carrot, possibly with grated apple. Alternatively, use the same dressing ona seasonal salad of radicchio, hazelnuts and gorgonzola. And if the remnants in a jar happen to be mustard, do exactly the same as above, just inverting the order and adding honey later.Felicity Cloake also suggests a dressing inher four healing honey recipes, which also function as suggestions for using the stuff up. Her suggestion of a hot toddy is great – add hot water into a jar with a centimetre of honey left, shake, then pour the now syrupy liquid into a glass or mug and add a curl of lemon peel, a knob of ginger, a cinnamon stick, a few cloves and a large dose of whisky, too, for a really effective cure. Her honey peanut butter is another way: put two tablespoons of hot water in the peanut butter jar, shake, then add honey to make a dip for celery and carrot, or add the mixture to cake batter.View image in fullscreenHealing … Felicity Cloake’s warm hot toddy.Photograph: Brent Hofacker/Getty Images/iStockphotoIt isn’t just honey, either. The most efficient way to use up the end of any jar, and especially peanut or any other nut butter, is to add a little hot water, then shake the jar violently to turn its contents into a paste. And a good way to use peanut paste is in the base of a soup (especially one with pumpkin and white beans) orwith pasta or noodles.I used to think I was controversial (and therefore interesting), until an Italian friend rolled her eyes and said that she also often makes pesto with peanut butter – pesto being a generic word for “a pounded paste”. Let me explain. In a food processor, blend a large handful of herbs (basil or parsley are ideal), a clove of garlic, salt and enough olive oil to make a paste. Then, while the pasta boils in well-salted water, add a little of the cloudy pasta water to the end of a peanut butter jar and shake to make a thick paste. Add this paste to the herb paste, stir in some grated cheese (grana padano or parmesan), and mix the lot with the cooked, drained pasta, maybe including a handful of baby spinach, which will wilt in the heat.Fuchsia Dunlop does more or less the same thing for herspicy peanut butter noodles. While dried udon cook in water, she lifts a little of the hot water into the jar, shakes to make a thick paste, then adds two to six tablespoons of chilli oil, two teaspoons of sesame oil and a minced clove of garlic, and shakes again for a sauce the consistency of single cream (if necessary, add more water). Once the noodles are done, she lifts them into a bowl, pours on the dressing, tosses well, divides the now slippery noodles between plates and tops each serving with minced spring onion and toasted sesame seeds.Next up, jars with an inch of jam in them, which can also be used in a dressing, or to thicken gravy or to add to stews. More fun and slightly more work is to make a jam tart. Dan Lepard has good advice and an excellent shortcrust pastry recipe, which he suggests turning intoindividual jam tarts. I have also used his pastry to make a large tart filled with a mixture of leftover jams and marmalades, which I tried to keep in sections, but was not very worried when they blurred into a multicoloured mess. The last bit of jam can also be loosened with a little water and used as a glaze for roast vegetables or pork chops. It is also a reason to make semolina pudding.The jar of chocolate spread that looks empty, meanwhile, should be turned into a drink: add hot milk to the jar, shake, then pour into a mug, add a bit of sugar, if required, and a generous pour of rum. Now, does anyone have the number of a good handyperson in Rome?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy week in foodView image in fullscreenThe art of cooking … Still Life With Pumpkin Flowers and Vine Leaves by Giovanna Garzoni.Photograph: AlamyWhere the art is|The most exquisite cookbook of the year is Paola Gavin’sStill Life Cookbook, a collection of vegetarian recipes inspired by great paintings. An art expert and the editor-in-chief of Epoch Review, Gavin has written many cookbooks, including the excellentItalian Vegetarian Cooking. In this, her ninth book, her two worlds meet and still-life paintings from throughout the centuries are paired with recipes. So, Giovanna Garzoni’s 17th-century Still Life With Pumpkin Flowers and Vine Leaves sits next to a recipe for flowers stuffed with ricotta and spinach. The publisher must be praised for producing such a beautiful but practical edition: the images are breathtaking, the fonts fantastic and the recipes gorgeous.The Kei to my heart|Running down Wardour Street in London’s Chinatown the other day, on our way to seeMy Neighbour Totoro, the musical (go before it finishes in January), and desperate for something good and quick to eat, I saw a “CASH ONLY” sign in the window of a restaurant. “That has to beWong Kei,” I thought, rememberingan article by Angela Hui. As promised, the setting is stark but comfortable, the service fast and functional, and the vegetarian mapo tofu with mushrooms and peas, in a soft gravy warmed with chilli on a mound of sticky rice, was exactly what we needed.Go with the grain|Last week, I had the pleasure of cooking withchef Fatmata Bintaat the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN in Rome. Originally from Sierra Leone and now working in Ghana, Binta is an award-winning culinary innovator and advocate for African agri-food systems. A particular focus of her work and advocacy is a tiny, millet-like grain called fonio that is not only densely nutritious and gluten-free but also incredibly versatile: it can be used like couscous, rice or semolina, as well as in breads, cakes and biscuits. As part of the demonstration, she made a porridge from fonio, which was new as a taste while at the same time reminding me of creamy oat porridge and semolina – made even better with the last of the jam scraped from the jar.If you want to read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive Feast in your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFoodFeastItalian food and drinkPastaSauces and graviesHerbs and spicesnewslettersShareReuse this content
